input:
Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Marketing Coordinator position advertised on your careers page. My name is Zoe Papadakis, and I have spent the last three years working in the marketing team of a mid-sized travel agency based in Thessaloniki, where I was responsible for campaign planning, social media scheduling and monthly performance reporting. I believe my practical experience and my enthusiasm for brand storytelling make me a strong fit for your team.

At Anatoli Travel, I managed the seasonal email campaigns that reached roughly forty thousand subscribers, and I helped increase our open rate by almost a fifth over two years. I also worked closely with the design freelancers we hired from our office on Tsimiski Street, which taught me how to brief creative work clearly and keep projects on schedule. Zoe, as my colleagues have sometimes joked, I am the person who will always ask for the spreadsheet before the meeting begins, and I have found that this habit pays off.

Beyond the agency, I volunteered for a local arts festival in the Ano Poli neighbourhood, where I coordinated the press list and wrote the event newsletter. That role gave me a real sense of how a small team can produce something polished on a tight budget. It also strengthened my writing, which I now use every day to draft copy for paid social advertising, blog posts and product descriptions. I am comfortable working with analytics tools, and I have taught myself the basics of search engine optimisation through online courses that I completed in the evenings.

I am drawn to your company because of the transparent way you describe your clients' results on your website. I would welcome the chance to bring the same clarity to your campaigns, and I am keen to learn from a team that works across several markets. I am available to start within four weeks of an offer and can attend an interview in person or by video call, whichever suits you best.

Thank you for considering my application. I would be glad to discuss how my background could support your goals, and I can be reached at zoe.papadakis@anatolitravel.gr or on 2310 555 018. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Zoe Papadakis

input:
A Stór,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the hip is behaving itself now that the good weather has finally come. Mam says you've been sitting out in the back garden every afternoon with the radio on, which I'm delighted to hear. I've been meaning to write since the start of the month, but the new job has me running from one meeting to the next and by the time I get home I'm fit for nothing but the sofa.

The job is going well, I think. The team in Galway is lovely, and the office overlooks the harbour, so on a clear morning I can see the boats going out from my desk. I'm still getting used to the commute from the flat on Shop Street, which is a short walk but a long way from the quiet road we grew up on. Some days I miss the sound of the sea at home more than I'd admit to anyone at work.

I've been thinking a lot about the summer we spent in Connemara when I was small. You taught me to fish off the rocks near the pier, and you were so patient with me when I kept putting my hand where I shouldn't in the rock pools. I remember you saying the sea always gives back what you're willing to wait for. I didn't understand it then, but I do now.

I'm enclosing a few photographs from the christening in June, the ones Cousin Aoife took on her good camera. There's one of you holding the baby that I've already had framed for the hall. Please tell me if the print is too dark; I can have another done. If it's easier, ring me on 091 556 2847 in the evening, after half seven, and we can have a proper chat instead of me writing an essay.

Anyway, I'd better get this into the post before I lose my nerve. Give my love to everyone at the club and tell Seán I want a full report on the match. If you need anything at all, you can reach me at niamh.kearney@mailbox.ie or at my address: 14 Fairgreen Court, Shop Street, Galway, H91 X4R2.

Go n-éirí an bóthar leat, and I'll talk to you soon.

Much love,

Niamh Kearney

My name is Katarzyna Nowak and I am making this statement regarding the theft of my bicycle and the damage to the rear door of my flat. I moved to Manchester from Kraków in September, and I live at 14 Alder Lane, Flat 3, in Didsbury. Since starting my nursing placement at St Ambrose Hospital in October, I have been cycling there most mornings, usually leaving around half six. My bike is a navy Dawes hybrid with a silver rack and a basket, and it was locked to the railings outside Crumb & Co, the cafe on the corner of Alder Lane, where I always stop for a coffee before my shift.

On the morning of Tuesday 9 January, I came down at about 6:20 and found the bike gone. The lock, a black Abus D-lock, had been cut through and was lying on the pavement. When I got back to the flat that evening I noticed the rear door had been forced open with a crowbar, though nothing else in the flat appeared to be taken. My landlord, Mr Hadley, has photographs of the damage, and I have kept the lock. I am also attaching the receipt for the bicycle from Cycle Republic on Wilmslow Road, dated 3 March last year, and the serial number is written on it.

My neighbour's dog, Biscuit, a small brown terrier, barked loudly at around two in the morning that night, and I believe Mrs Adeyemi in Flat 1 may have seen someone near the back gate. I can be reached at k.nowak@mailbox.co.uk or on 07700 900412. I am happy to provide any further information and would appreciate an update on the case reference number, which I have not yet received.

input:
I have been putting off writing this post for weeks because honestly, the trip to Siargao still feels like a dream. Last August I spent eleven days on the island, and most of that time was spent chasing waves at Cloud 9 with a board I borrowed from a hostel in General Luna. My guide was a local surfer everyone calls Bong, who has taught half the backpackers on the island to stand up. He told me on the first morning that the reef doesn't care how confident you feel, which turned out to be the best advice I got all trip.

Before Siargao I spent three nights in Manila, and I can't recommend staying in Malate enough if you want to eat your way through the city. I met Sofia Villanueva there, a communications officer at Pacific Harbor Logistics, who was in town for a regional conference. She took me to a tiny carinderia near the Remedios Circle where we ate sinigang and grilled liempo with our hands. Sofia works long hours at Pacific Harbor Logistics, but she laughed at how little sleep she was getting and insisted the job is worth it. We swapped stories about our first confusing jeepney rides and she still texts me memes every few weeks.

Getting from Manila to Siargao is a bit of an adventure. I flew to Surigao, then took a van to the ferry port, which left mostly on time, and the sea was calm enough that I only felt slightly queasy. Once on the island, I rented a scooter for three hundred pesos a day and rode it along the coastal road toward Sohoton Cove. The mangrove tunnels were quiet and cool, and the boatman sang old OPM songs the whole way through. I remember thinking that if I had planned every day of this trip, I would have missed the best parts.

One evening I wandered into a small coworking cafe in Dapa, mostly because I needed Wi-Fi to answer some work emails. The owner, a former accountant named Rhea, had opened the place with her brother after the pandemic. We ended up talking until closing about how tourism has changed the island, the rising rents, and the worry that the local fishing families are being pushed aside. It was a sobering conversation that made me look at my own footprint differently.

If you go, bring reef-safe sunscreen, cash for the smaller towns, and an open mind about schedules. The island runs on island time, and that is exactly the point. I left on the fifteenth with a sunburn, a bag of dried mangoes, and a promise to return. Maybe next August, I'll see you on the reef, Bong.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Oliver, and I've had the honour of being Tom's best man for the better part of twenty years. Tom and I met at a Saturday football trial in Leeds when we were eleven, and I still remember him asking if I'd mind being in goal because he wanted to be a striker. I said yes, and I've been letting him take the glory ever since.

When Tom first told me about Daisy, he said, "Ollie, I think this is the one," and I'd heard that line before, so I was sceptical. Then I watched him on the night of her thirtieth birthday at The Crown in Harrogate, quietly arranging for the band to play her favourite song without telling her, and I knew he meant it. Daisy, you have turned my oldest friend into a man who remembers the small things, and for that we are all grateful.

I also want to thank Priya, who has put up with Tom's terrible puns for over a decade and still laughs at them. Tom, the last time I saw you this happy was the day you got your first proper pay rise, but I think this beats it. So please raise your glasses to Daisy and Tom. Cheers, and to a lifetime of June evenings like this one.

input: We stopped in at this bakery on a rainy weekday afternoon and were glad we did. The sourdough loaves had a deep, crackly crust and a tangy, open crumb, and the rugelach were buttery without being greasy. The woman behind the counter was patient with our indecisive family, offering samples and explaining what was fresh out of the oven. Prices are fair for the quality, though the seating is limited and gets crowded around lunchtime, so plan accordingly. Overall a warm, unpretentious spot that I'd happily recommend to anyone looking for good bread and a cup of coffee.

input: Sunita Verma, 67, passed away peacefully on 14 May in Leeds, surrounded by her family. Sunita spent most of her working life as a senior nurse coordinator at St Matthew's Hospital in Bradford, where colleagues remember her calm authority on the busiest wards. She emigrated from Pune to England in 1981 with her husband Rajesh, and she never lost her love for the flavours of home, nor her habit of telling everyone exactly what she thought. Sunita is survived by her son Anil, her daughter Meera, and four grandchildren who will miss her sharp humour and her unrivalled chai. Sunita, you taught us that kindness is a practical act. Rest now.

input:
Sharon Wambui has spent the last twelve years building bridges between agritech startups and smallholder farmers across the Central Highlands of Kenya. Born in Nyeri, she completed her undergraduate degree in Agricultural Economics at Egerton University before earning a master's in Development Studies at the University of Nairobi. Her early career included a stint at a community health clinic in Kiambu, where she first saw how mobile data could shorten the distance between a farmer and a reliable answer.

Since 2019, Sharon has led the field outreach team for Shamba Link, a platform that connects growers with input suppliers and weather alerts over SMS. She is known among colleagues for her habit of holding planning meetings at Mama Njeri's Cafe on Kenyatta Avenue in Thika, where the farmers she serves can join without taking a day off work. Her team's pilot in Murang'a reached over 4,000 households and is now being adapted for coastal counties.

Sharon is a mentor with the Kenya Women in Agribusiness network and sits on the advisory board of Thika Level Five Hospital's nutrition programme. Those who wish to discuss a collaboration or request a speaking engagement can reach her on +254 712 448 306 or by writing to sharon.wambui@shambalink.co.ke. She will be presenting her findings at the conference on 14 May.

I've been coming to Sakura Ramen Kitchen in Kobe for about three years now, and I finally sat down to write something about it. The broth is the real draw. It's a tonkotsu that tastes like it has been simmering since dawn, rich without being greasy, and the chashu melts in a way that makes me forgive the tiny counter and the fact that you'll be elbow to elbow with strangers. Hiroshi, the owner, remembers regulars' orders, and on my first visit in March he asked if I wanted extra negi before I had even opened the menu. That kind of attention is rare in a city this size.

Service is quick but never rushed. On a Friday night the queue can stretch past the noren, so my advice is to arrive before seven or be prepared to wait. The gyoza are crisp on the bottom and juicy inside, and the staff are patient with people who are still working out the ordering ticket system. Cash is still king here, so bring yen.

If you want to reserve a seat during busy weekends, call them directly at 078-555-0142. I also follow their updates on Instagram at @sakura_kobe_ramen, where they post the daily specials before they sell out. Five stars from me, and I'll be back again this weekend.

input:
I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on Tuesday 14 January so I don't forget anything Dr Harrington said. Jasmine Keating is my name, and I'm 47 years old. I went to the Eastwood Medical Centre because the tiredness and the dizzy spells have been getting worse since before Christmas. Dr Harrington took my blood pressure twice, listened to my chest, and asked a lot of questions about sleep and diet. Jasmine, she said, your numbers are a bit higher than we'd like, but nothing alarming yet.

She wants me to cut back on salt and to start walking for at least thirty minutes most days. I told her I've been walking the dog, Biscuit, every morning, and she laughed and said that counts, as long as I keep the pace up. Biscuit is a rescue kelpie who pulls like a freight train, so I'm not sure about the pace, but I'll try. She also asked whether my mum still has the high blood pressure, and I said yes, so this is probably something I need to take seriously.

Blood tests were ordered for cholesterol, blood sugar and thyroid function. The pathology form has to go to the lab at Westfield Pathology on Monday 20 January, and I should get the results through the patient portal within about ten days. Dr Harrington said if the thyroid numbers are off she'll want to see me again, so I should book a follow-up in a month regardless.

She also gave me a referral slip for a sleep study, since she thinks the dizziness might be linked to broken sleep. The referral is valid for six months and I need to call the sleep clinic myself to get on the waiting list. I wrote the clinic number on the back of the slip, but I'll double-check it before I call.

The main thing I'm taking away is that most of this is manageable with lifestyle changes and a few tests. I'm meant to ring the surgery if the dizziness gets worse, or if I faint, or get chest pain, and I'll do that without waiting. Writing it all down here helps me feel less anxious about it. I'll update this once the blood results come back, and I'll bring Biscuit along to my next walk to keep myself honest.

input:
Hello from Room 14! My name is Viktor, though my classmates have called me Vik since the first week of term, and I have been asked to write a short item for this month's newsletter about our class project on local wildlife. I am happy to do it, because it has taken over most of my spare time lately.

We started in early spring with a simple question from our teacher, Mrs. Lindqvist: what lives in the park behind our school? Nobody knew the answer, so we decided to find out. Our group set up a small observation corner by the old oak, and each week we logged birds, insects and anything that moved through the grass. My own favourite find was a family of hedgehogs that appeared near the bins every evening in May.

Most of the research happened at home, which meant my family got pulled in too. My younger sister Freja kept the weather diary, and our cat Pippi, who is far too curious for her own good, was once caught sitting on the observation sheet. We have not forgiven her, but we did keep the coffee stain, which now counts as a field note about rain.

We are living in Uppsala, so the park is a short cycle from home, and I think that is why the project feels so personal. Each time I ride past the library on Dragarbrunnsgatan I look for birds on the rooftops. Our class also collected data at the river on 12 June, when the water was high and the herons were active. If you want to see the results, the full report will be posted in the library foyer from 20 June.

If you have questions or would like to join our next outing, please write to me at viktor.andersson@skolmail.se or stop by Room 14 after lessons. We will be meeting again on 9 June, and anyone is welcome to bring binoculars or a notebook. Thank you for reading, and happy summer to everyone.

I've been coming to Brouwerij De Hoek on the Oudegracht in Utrecht for almost three years, and I finally wanted to write something down after last Saturday. My daughter Lotte had her birthday lunch there on the 14th of February, and the staff were wonderful about it. Our waiter, Jeroen, remembered that she was starting at the Radboud University Medical Center's children's ward as a volunteer that week and asked about it without being nosy. The bitterballen were as crisp as ever, and the kitchen even managed a vegetarian version for my sister-in-law without any fuss.

Tuesday 12th March. Couldn't sleep again, so I'm writing this at the kitchen table with a cup of tea going cold beside me. Lorcan Brennan from work rang yesterday to say he's been moved onto the night shift at St Vincent's Hospital, which is the last thing either of us wanted for him after the summer he's had. My own name is Fiona Keogh-Doyle, which the nurses on the ward still mangle every single day. I was supposed to be at the Trinity College library this afternoon finishing the chapter on coastal erosion, but I ended up sitting in the car park at Kilkenny Road instead, listening to the radio and not really hearing it. Lorcan texted at half four: 'Still alive? Don't let the bastards grind you down.' I sent back a thumbs up, which is what I do now.

I keep thinking about Lorcan's mum, Maura, who taught me to make soda bread the one winter I stayed at their house in Galway. She said the trick was not to overwork the dough. Night, diary.

input:
Last winter I spent a long weekend in Halifax, and I stayed in a small rented flat on Quinpool Road that my friend Nadia Fraser had found for me. She works as a nurse at the QEII hospital and knows the city better than any guidebook. Her advice was to walk everywhere, bundle up properly, and never skip the Dartmouth ferry. On my first morning I bought a coffee at a corner shop, then wandered down toward the North End, where the old wooden houses are painted in colours that look almost too bright against the grey harbour sky.

On the Thursday, the weather turned, and a cold wind came in off the water. Nadia met me after her shift at a tiny bistro on Gottingen Street, and we shared a bowl of chowder and talked until closing. She told me the city feels different in the depths of January, when the locals stop complaining about the snow and simply get on with life. Her laugh was the warmest thing in the room. Later, she sent me a text reminding me to email her the photos I had taken of the lighthouse at Peggy's Cove, which I promised to do before I flew home.

If you visit in winter, I would recommend the same routine: a slow morning, a long walk along the waterfront, and a plate of something hot in a neighbourhood spot. Halifax is not a postcard city in January, but it is honest, friendly and quietly beautiful. I left with cold fingers, a full heart, and a list of places to return to when the days grow longer.

input:
I have spent the better part of my career working at the intersection of data and human behaviour, and I still find it surprising how often the two are treated as separate worlds. My research began somewhere quite ordinary: a frustrating spreadsheet of survey responses that refused to agree with itself. That small irritation led me down a path that has taken me through a variety of settings, from crowded municipal offices to quiet laboratories where the lighting never changes and the coffee is always too strong.

Over the years, my work has focused on how people make decisions when information is incomplete, and on the ways institutions quietly shape those choices. I am particularly drawn to the moments when a well-meant policy produces an outcome nobody anticipated. Those moments are rarely failures of intention. More often they reveal a gap between how a system imagines its users and how those users actually live, work and make their way through the day.

My approach is deliberately mixed. I combine statistical modelling with interviews, observation and the slow, unglamorous work of reading archival documents. I have learned that numbers can tell you what is happening, but only conversation tells you why people think it is reasonable. Some of my most useful insights have come from informal exchanges over a shared table, where a colleague mentions a detail that no dataset could have captured.

Beyond my own projects, I have served on several advisory panels and mentored a number of early-career researchers. I take that responsibility seriously. The most rewarding part of teaching has been watching students discover that a question they assumed was too simple turns out to contain a surprising amount of depth once they start pulling on it.

I am looking forward to this conference because it brings together people who approach these problems from very different directions. I hope to hear perspectives that challenge my assumptions, and I hope to leave with a few new collaborations. Thank you for the opportunity to share a little of my work, and I welcome any questions you may have.

input:
We pulled into the little campground just before sunset, tired from a long day of driving through the high desert. The air was cool and smelled of sagebrush, and the sky turned a shade of orange I had only ever seen in photographs. After setting up the tent, my partner and I walked to the edge of the bluff and watched the light fade over the canyon walls, which shifted from rust to deep purple in just a few minutes.

The next morning we woke early and made coffee on the tiny camp stove while the sun climbed over the ridge. We spent the day hiking a trail that wound down into a dry wash and back up again, stopping often to drink water and marvel at the layered rock. Lizards darted across the path in front of us, and once we spotted a hawk circling high above, riding the warm updrafts without moving its wings at all.

By evening we were sore, sunburned, and completely content. I would recommend this stretch of desert to anyone who wants quiet, open space and a reminder of how small our daily worries can feel. Pack more water than you think you need, bring a warm layer for the nights, and do not forget to look up.

input:
Buenos Aires hit me differently than I expected. I had planned a tidy itinerary of museums and cafés, but the city had other ideas. Within an hour of landing I was standing on a crowded corner, watching a tango couple spin with such focus that the surrounding traffic seemed to pause out of respect. Nobody asked me to pay for the photo, and nobody seemed to mind that I stood there far too long.

The days that followed settled into a rhythm I came to love. Mornings meant strong coffee and medialunas at a counter where the waiter knew everyone by their order. Afternoons drifted toward long walks through neighbourhoods with peeling murals, bookshops stacked to the ceiling, and dogs being walked in small packs by someone who clearly had the patience of a saint. Evenings were late, loud and generous, with dinner rarely starting before ten.

If I could offer one piece of advice, it would be to slow down and let the city set the pace. Wander without a map, accept the invitation to sit down, and say yes when a stranger offers to share their mate. Argentina rewards the curious traveller who is willing to be a little unprepared, and I left already thinking about the many things I had not yet had time to see.

We gather today to remember Bunji Takahashi, who was born on August 14, 1947, in a small house near the harbour in Shimizu. For more than forty years Bunji ran the little hardware shop on the corner of the old market street, and there was hardly a family in the neighbourhood he did not help, whether with a leaking pipe, a broken hinge, or simply a cup of green tea and a long conversation. He had a patience that people noticed. He would listen until you had finished, then say exactly the right thing, usually with a small laugh.

Bunji loved the sea, mountains that caught early snow, and bad jokes told at the wrong moment. Many of you will remember his Sunday fishing trips with his brother Hideo, and the stories that grew more heroic with every telling. He was proud of his garden, prouder still of the persimmon tree his father had planted, and he never missed the August festival at the shrine, even in his last summer when he walked there slowly on his daughter's arm.

After the funeral, if you would like to share a memory, please write to the family at bunji.takahashi@shimizu-mail.jp, or bring it to the shop, where his reading glasses still hang beside the register. He would want you to keep telling the stories. Thank you for coming, and for sharing him with us.

I am Nadia Ferreira, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a structural engineer, first in Lisbon and, since 2016, in Vancouver. Moving across the Atlantic and then across a continent was not a plan I made in a single afternoon. It grew out of a long conversation with my colleague Tomás Almeida, who had gone to Canada a year before me and kept sending photographs of mountains and emails full of practical advice about visas, cold winters, and the strange joy of learning to drive on the right side of the road again.

The first two years in Vancouver were harder than I expected. My Portuguese qualifications required a lengthy review before they were recognised, and I spent many evenings studying building codes that differed in small but important ways from the ones I had used in Portugal. What helped most was a standing coffee with Tomás every second Thursday, where we swapped stories about bureaucracy and argued about bridges. Slowly the work became familiar, and then it became mine again.

Today I split my time between consulting for timber projects on the coast and mentoring younger engineers who, like me, arrived from somewhere else. I still return to Lisbon each November for the family holidays, and each time I notice how much both cities have shaped the way I think about load, light, and the places people choose to call home. I am grateful to be speaking with you here, and I look forward to the conversations that follow.

input:
After nearly six years in product marketing at a fast-growing software company, I am excited to share that I have joined a new team as Head of Customer Success. It has been a bittersweet decision. The people I worked with taught me more about storytelling, data and listening to users than any course ever could, and I will carry those lessons with me.

What drew me to this role is the chance to work closely with customers from the very start of their journey. Over the years I noticed that the most meaningful product improvements often came from conversations with the people using our tools every day. I want to build a function where those conversations shape strategy, not just follow it.

To everyone who offered advice, referrals or a quick coffee during my search: thank you. Career changes feel lonely at times, but the support I received reminded me how much this community values generosity. I look forward to staying connected, learning from you and, when the time comes, returning the favour. If you are navigating a transition of your own, feel free to reach out. I am always happy to talk through what worked for me.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Oliver, the older brother of the bride, and I've been asked to say a few words about my sister Rebecca. Most of you know her as Becs, a name that has stuck since she was about four and insisted on being called it. Our mum still uses her full name when she's cross, which is usually a sign that someone has been told off.

Becs was born in Stockport, in a maternity ward that overlooked a car park, and she has been making the most of her Greater Manchester roots ever since. She can tell you which bus goes where, which chippy does the best cheese and onion, and exactly how long it takes to walk from our old house on Heaton Road to the town centre if you stop for a coffee. I think it's safe to say she never met a Stockport person she didn't like, and she never once let us forget where we came from.

What strikes me most about Becs is how she turns up for people. When I moved down to London with two suitcases and no plan, she was the one who drove over with a van full of furniture she'd borrowed from her flatmates. When our grandad was in hospital just before Christmas, she sat with him every evening for three weeks, even though she had a deadline at work that would have been an excuse for anyone else. She never asks for thanks, and that is exactly why people want to do things for her in return.

Then there's Tom. I'll be honest, when Becs first mentioned him, I was ready to be suspicious. I had a whole list of questions ready, most of them involving his football allegiances. But within about ten minutes of meeting him at our cousin's birthday, I realised he was the sort of person who listens properly, who remembers the name of your dog and asks how she's doing. He makes her laugh until she snorts, which is a rare and wonderful thing to witness.

So please raise your glasses to Becs and Tom. May your marriage be full of late-night chats, shared cups of tea, and the occasional sensible argument about who left the milk out. Congratulations to you both.

Meeting notes, Monday 14 October. Present: Amanda Ferreira (me), Bruno Carvalho from the regional logistics team, and Lu from procurement, who joined by video from Porto Alegre. I'm writing these up so we have a record before the next steering call.

We opened with the delayed shipment for the Recife depot. Bruno confirmed the customs hold is still open and that the broker expects to clear it by the 21st, though he doesn't want us to promise that to the client yet. I said I'd call Mrs. Teixeira at the Recife office myself on Wednesday, since she's the one who first raised it and she responds better to a direct conversation than to email. Everyone agreed the revised delivery window should be shared only once the broker gives us written confirmation.

The second item was the warehouse staffing plan. Lu has the new headcount numbers and they're lower than we expected because the São Paulo transfer fell through. Bruno pushed back and asked whether we can borrow two people from the Curitiba site for three weeks. I said yes in principle but want Carlos Teixeira, the site manager there, to agree first. Bruno, who everyone calls Brunão, said he'd sort out the travel paperwork if we get the green light by the 18th.

For the last part, we reviewed the budget overrun on the packaging contract. It's about nine percent over, mostly from the rush surcharge on the October order. Lu will draft a short explanation for finance and send it to me by Thursday. I'll review it and forward it on Friday.

Actions: I will call Mrs. Teixeira on the 16th. Lu will send the budget note by the 17th. Bruno will check with Carlos about the Curitiba staff and report back by the 18th. We'll reconvene on Monday the 21st, the same day the customs clearance is expected, so we can decide whether to confirm the new delivery date.

If anything here is off, email me at amanda.ferreira@logisticsbr.com and I'll correct the notes before they go out.

input:
December 3. My therapist, Dr. Lucia Ortega, asked me to write this down after our session, so here it is. My name is Nicolas Ferrer Salinas and I still can't quite believe I'm the one sitting in her office in Guadalajara every Tuesday. Three years ago I was a resident at Hospital Civil de Guadalajara, working nights and sleeping in four-hour pieces, and I told myself that was just what medicine costs. It isn't, or it shouldn't be, and I'm trying to accept that.

Today we talked about my father. He called on Sunday, the first time in months, and asked whether I was still "wasting time on therapy." I said yes. I didn't argue, which for me is progress. Ferrer, my mother's side, has always treated feelings like a clinical symptom: observe, document, move on. I learned that from him long before I learned it from residency. Dr. Ortega pointed out that I had been describing my own panic attacks in the same flat tone I use for patient handovers, and I laughed because she was right.

We spent most of the hour on the nights in December last year, the ones after the car accident on the Periférico. I kept replaying the moment the monitor flatlined, and how I went straight to the next patient without stopping. Nobody at Civil asked me how I was doing afterward. I don't think I would have answered honestly if they had.

I am trying something small this week. I'm going to walk home from the clinic instead of taking the bus, and when I get in I'll write one sentence about what I noticed, not what I should have done. Dr. Ortega thinks this could help me stop treating every quiet moment as a failure. She also wants me to call my sister Mariana on Thursday, which I've been avoiding because she will ask questions I don't want to answer yet.

I'm not sure what I expected from therapy. Maybe a fix, or a verdict. What I'm getting is slower and less dramatic: noticing when my shoulders are up around my ears, saying out loud that I'm tired, letting someone else hold part of this. Tonight I'm tired, and for once I'm writing that down without apologizing for it.

Caro diario, oggi ho trovato di nuovo la vecchia scatola di mia nonna nel ripostiglio di casa, a Bologna, in via del Pratello. Dentro c'erano le fotografie di Sorrento, dove sono nata nel 1987, e un foglio ingiallito con il mio numero di carta d'identità scritto a mano da mia madre: AX4829617. Non so perché lo abbia conservato, ma mi ha fatto piangere un po'.

Serena mi ha chiamata in tarda serata dal numero 333 9047215 per dirmi che il concerto di Natale del coro si terrà il 14 dicembre. Ha la voce stanca, ma sorride quando parla di Sorrento e dice che dovremmo andarci insieme per le feste. Le ho risposto che ci penserò, anche se sappiamo entrambe che è già deciso.

Al lavoro la giornata è stata lunga. Il direttore ha cambiato di nuovo i turni, così mi toccheranno tutte le mattine fino a Natale. Ho pranzato da sola in un bar vicino alla stazione, guardando la pioggia sui tram e pensando a quanto Bologna possa essere grigia in questo periodo dell'anno. Eppure mi piace, questa città che mi ha accolta quando sono arrivata con due valigie e nessun amico.

La sera ho scritto a mia cugina Sabrina, che vive ancora a Sorrento, per chiederle se può tenermi da parte la casa della zia per il 26 dicembre. Mi ha risposto subito con un messaggio pieno di cuoricini e una promessa di limoncello. Ho pensato che forse è questo che mi serve: tornare per qualche giorno dove tutto ha avuto inizio.

Prima di dormire ho ripreso in mano il foglio con il numero di documento. Ho deciso di rifare la fotocopia e di portarla con me in ufficio, per sicurezza. Domani chiamerò il Comune di Sorrento per sapere come rinnovare la carta, perché la scadenza si avvicina e non voglio farmi trovare impreparata come l'anno scorso.

input:
The summer I turned seventeen, my life changed on August 14th, the day my mother came home from the hospital with a diagnosis that rearranged everything. My younger brother Marcus and I suddenly had to learn how to run a household, and I found myself making dinner, paying bills, and reminding my father to take his medication. I was not ready for any of it, but I learned quickly.

That same month I started working as a cashier at Harlow Grocery on Fourth Street, mostly because we needed the paycheck. Standing behind the register for six hours a day taught me more about patience than any class ever has. I learned to listen to people who were tired, rude, or grieving, and to treat each one like they mattered. My manager, Diane Pruitt, once told me that good service is just paying attention, and I have carried that lesson everywhere.

Now, as I prepare for college, I want to study social work. The experiences of that August taught me that caring for others is not a single act but a daily practice. I hope to bring that practice to a university where I can keep learning how to listen, support, and serve.

input:
Walter was the kind of man who could fix anything with a bent paperclip and a little patience. For forty-one years he worked the night shift at the water treatment plant on Route 9, and he never once missed a Sunday dinner. At seventy-three, he still climbed the ladder to clean the gutters himself, even after we all begged him to stop. He taught me to drive in that old Ford pickup, and he taught me that a good cup of coffee needs nothing more than time and good company.

When Walter retired, he filled the quiet hours with his garden, his crossword puzzles, and his dog Biscuit, a scruffy beagle who followed him everywhere, including the hardware store where he was a regular. Walter loved to post pictures of his tomatoes on Facebook under the handle @WalterTomatoKing, and he was genuinely proud of every crooked, sun-ripened one. If you have a moment today, please call Mom at 555-238-7714. She has been overwhelmed by the calls and cards, and she would love to hear from you.

Dad, I will miss our Saturday phone calls more than I can say. I will keep the coffee brewing the way you liked it, and I promise to check the gutters before the rain comes. Thank you for everything you gave us. Rest easy. Love, Jordan.

My name is Benjamin Adler and I am writing to give a statement regarding the incident that took place outside my apartment building on Herzl Street in Haifa on the evening of December 14. I had just returned from the supermarket at around 19:40 when I noticed a grey Hyundai parked across the entrance with its engine running. A man in a dark jacket was standing beside it, and when I asked him to move, he simply got back into the car and drove off towards the port. I did not get the full plate number, but the last three characters were 58.

After the car left, I went up to my flat and found that the lock on the side door of the building had been forced. Nothing appeared to be missing from my own unit, but my neighbour Rafi Oren, who lives on the second floor, told me his bicycle had been taken from the storage room. I have attached photos of the damaged lock taken on my phone, along with the time stamps. Rafi has asked me to pass on that he will come in on Monday to make his own statement, and he can be reached at rafi.oren.haifa@gmailcorp.net if you need to contact him directly.

I confirm that the information above is true to the best of my knowledge.

I've told her to take it down, she laughed it off, and now a few followers have started DMing me asking if everything is okay at home.

input:
I am writing this obituary for my mother, Vivian Marie Thibault, who passed away peacefully at home on August 14 at the age of seventy-eight. Mum was born in Rimouski, Quebec, in 1946, the eldest of five children, and she never let us forget how much she loved the St. Lawrence and the smell of the sea air that followed her everywhere she went.

For thirty-one years Vivian worked as a bookkeeper at Maple Ridge Lumber Supply Ltd., where she kept the accounts in order and, more importantly, kept the men in the yard honest about their expense claims. Her colleagues often said she could spot a mistake in a receipt from across the room. She retired in 2009 and at her farewell lunch she told everyone she was finally going to learn how to sleep in on a Tuesday. She did not, of course.

Mum was a creature of habit. Every weekday morning she walked to Brewed Awakenings on Hollis Street, ordered a medium dark roast with cream, and read the Chronicle Herald cover to cover with a red pen in hand. The baristas knew her by name and by her opinions on the crossword. When her knees made the walk difficult in her last years, my brother Gerard drove her there every Saturday, and she considered it the best part of her week.

She is survived by her children, Anne-Marie and Gerard, and by her grandchildren Lucas, Sophie, and little Emma, who called her Nana Viv and could always get a cookie out of her. She also leaves behind her sister Monique and a large circle of friends from her years at St. Patrick's parish, where she sang alto in the choir for four decades.

Vivian was predeceased by her husband Robert and by her parents. A celebration of life will be held on August 22 at the Oakridge Community Hall, 48 Birch Crescent, Dartmouth, followed by a reception. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Dartmouth General Hospital Foundation in her memory. Mum, we will miss your red pen and your terrible jokes. Rest now.

input:
Oren Takahashi has spent the last twelve years building tools that make small clinics in rural Japan easier to run. Friends in Osaka know him as "Ozzie," a name that stuck from his university days in Kyoto and that he has never quite managed to shake off. Born in Sapporo, he moved south for graduate school and never really went back, though he still speaks of winters in Hokkaido with real affection.

Today Oren works as Senior Product Lead at Kisaragi Health Systems, where he oversees a platform used by roughly four hundred clinics across the Kansai region. His colleague Mariko Ishida, who runs the field support team, often jokes that Oren has personally driven to more remote villages than anyone in the company. He keeps a battered blue hatchback for exactly that purpose, registered under plate number 京都 300 あ 4471, and he has the scratches to prove it.

Outside work, Oren is a stubborn amateur cook. He is convinced he can perfect a miso ramen broth in a home kitchen and has been trying for six years. He also mentors junior engineers on Thursday evenings at a small co-working space in Kyoto, and he is happy to be reached for advice at oren.takahashi@kisaragihealth.jp or by phone at 075-555-0148 during business hours.

His home office, where most of his mentoring sessions begin, is at 4-12 Shimogamo Hangi-cho, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto. Visitors are welcome, provided they do not mind the smell of dashi drifting in from the kitchen.

In December, Oren always takes a few days off to visit his parents in Sapporo, where the snow arrives early and the conversations are as sharp as ever. He says these trips remind him why the clinic work matters: good care should not depend on where you happen to live.

Oren is looking forward to this conference because, as he puts it, he has more questions than answers. He hopes to meet anyone working on the same problems and is always ready to swap notes over a bowl of something hot.

Ivan Watanabe has spent the last twelve years building tools that make small clinics in rural Japan easier to run. Friends in Kobe know him as "Ivo," a name that stuck from his university days in Nara and that he has never quite managed to shake off. Born in Asahikawa, he moved south for graduate school and never really went back, though he still speaks of winters in Tohoku with real affection.

Today Ivan works as Senior Product Lead at Minamoto Care Solutions, where he oversees a platform used by roughly four hundred clinics across the Kansai region. His colleague Yuki Nakagawa, who runs the field support team, often jokes that Ivan has personally driven to more remote villages than anyone in the company. He keeps a battered blue hatchback for exactly that purpose, registered under plate number 大阪 500 い 2839, and he has the scratches to prove it.

Outside work, Ivan is a stubborn amateur cook. He is convinced he can perfect a miso ramen broth in a home kitchen and has been trying for six years. He also mentors junior engineers on Thursday evenings at a small co-working space in Nara, and he is happy to be reached for advice at ivan.watanabe@minamotocare.jp or by phone at 078-555-0362 during business hours.

His home office, where most of his mentoring sessions begin, is at 7-3 Nunobiki-cho, Nada Ward, Kobe. Visitors are welcome, provided they do not mind the smell of dashi drifting in from the kitchen.

In December, Ivan always takes a few days off to visit his parents in Asahikawa, where the snow arrives early and the conversations are as sharp as ever. He says these trips remind him why the clinic work matters: good care should not depend on where you happen to live.

Ivan is looking forward to this conference because, as he puts it, he has more questions than answers. He hopes to meet anyone working on the same problems and is always ready to swap notes over a bowl of something hot.

Shalom wa-bruchim habaim, friends and family. For those who don't know me, I'm Noam, Zohar's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight, which means I've had three weeks of practice in the shower and my wife says I still sound like I'm reading a parking ticket.

I grew up with Zohar in a small apartment on Rehov Ha-Yarden in Haifa, the one with the balcony that faced the port and the neighbour who played the oud every Thursday night whether we wanted him to or not. Zohar was the kid who fixed the broken radio before our father could even find the screwdriver. He still is that kid, just with a much larger toolbox and a lot more patience than I ever had.

When Zohar first told me about Ronen, he did it the way he does everything, quietly, without a speech, just a text message at 11 at night that said "I think I met someone I'm going to marry, don't tell Mom yet." Of course I told Mom within the hour. Some promises are meant to be broken for the greater good. Ronen, I want you to know that in our family, once you are welcomed, you are welcomed for good, and that includes the awkward phone calls with our aunt in Beersheba.

Zohar, I have watched you grow from a stubborn boy into a man who listens first and speaks second, which I admit is a skill I have never mastered. You chose someone who laughs at your jokes even when they are bad, and I think that is the best evidence anyone could ask for.

So please raise your glasses. To Zohar and Ronen, to a home full of noise, shared dinners and at least one more balcony with a view. L'chaim, and mazal tov.

input:
I'm excited to share that as of Monday 14 September, I've taken up the role of Senior Data Analyst at Corrigan & Doyle Logistics in Dublin. After six years at Brennan Analytics in Ballsbridge, this felt like the right moment to move on.

When I look back, the path wasn't a straight line. I did my undergraduate degree in Statistics at Trinity College Dublin, then spent a year working nights at St James's Hospital on a research placement, which taught me more about messy real-world data than any lecture ever did. That experience is a big reason I'm drawn to operational problems now.

Leaving a team is never easy. I'll miss the Thursday lunches in Portobello and the late-running debates about whether dashboards should be simpler or smarter. My manager, Bronagh Keogh, gave me the room to take risks, and I'm grateful for that every day.

The new role focuses on forecasting delivery times across the national network, which means working closely with people in our depots in Cork and Limerick. I'm looking forward to the travel and, honestly, to being the person who has to explain the numbers to people who actually drive the trucks.

If you're in a similar place, weighing a switch, I'd happily share what I learned from making mine. Feel free to message me or reach out at bronagh.mcgrath@brennanfinance.ie if it's easier to talk by email. My dog Biscuit has already claimed the new home office, so I'll be working with a supervisor who never lets me forget the walk is overdue.

On to the next chapter.

Resumen de mi cita con la doctora Ibáñez en el Centro de Salud de Valladolid, el 14 de junio. Llevo tres semanas con dolor de espalda baja que empeora cuando me siento mucho tiempo frente al ordenador, y en la consulta le expliqué que también me despierto con rigidez. La doctora me hizo una exploración, me pidió que tocara los pies sin doblar las rodillas y revisó la movilidad. Descartó una hernia por ahora y me dijo que probablemente es sobrecarga muscular agravada por el trabajo. Me recomendó fisioterapia durante un mes y ejercicios de estiramiento que puedo hacer en casa.

Me preguntó también por mi sueño y por el estrés, y le comenté que mi compañera de piso, Lucía Moreno, me dijo que parecía agotado. Lucía, a la que todos llamamos Lulú, me ha insistido en que vaya al gimnasio, pero yo prefiero las caminatas. La doctora me sugirió que empiece con veinte minutos diarios y que suba poco a poco. Me pidió que volviera el 28 de junio si no hay mejoría, aunque no creo que haga falta.

Al salir compartí en mi cuenta de Instagram, @sergio_valle_runs, una foto de la plantilla de ejercicios que me dieron, para llevar un registro. Mi madre, por cierto, quiere que la acompañe a su revisión el 3 de junio, así que tengo la agenda bastante llena este mes.

Ich schreibe diese Zeilen mit schwerem Herzen, denn am 14. November haben wir Ingrid Halvorsen verloren, meine Mutter und die beste Freundin, die ich je hatte. Sie wurde 1948 in Bergen geboren, wo sie als Tochter eines Fischers aufwuchs, und zog später nach Hamburg, als sie den Hafen liebte, mehr als alles andere. Ihre Wohnung in der Eppendorfer Landstraße war für Jahrzehnte der Ort, an dem Nachbarn, Kollegen und Verwandte aus Norwegen ein und aus gingen. Sie hat mir beigebracht, dass man auch in einer fremden Stadt ein Zuhause findet, wenn man es sich selbst schafft.

In den letzten Jahren saß sie fast jeden Vormittag im Café Lindenhof an ihrem Fensterplatz, bestellte einen Kaffee und las die Zeitung von vorne bis hinten. Der Besitzer Mehmet kannte ihre Bestellung, bevor sie den Mantel ausgezogen hatte. Sie war stolz auf ihre Pünktlichkeit und hat mir mehr als einmal geschrieben, dass ein Termin dort wichtiger sei als jede Arztpraxis, auch wenn sie die Klinik am Park nie gemocht hat.

Ich danke allen, die ihr auf Instagram unter @ingrid_halvorsen_hh geschrieben haben, besonders dem Team vom Lindenhof. Mein Bruder Lars und ich werden ihre Stimme vermissen, ihren Humor und ihr Lachen, das man in der ganzen Straße hören konnte. Wer sich von ihr verabschieden möchte, ist zur Trauerfeier am 21. November eingeladen. Ruhe in Frieden, Mama.

Long-time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone here has been through something similar. My best friend Kendra Holloway has been my roommate for six years, and last month she got promoted to Senior Operations Manager at Brightwater Logistics in Columbus. Since then she's been different. She cancels plans, skips our Thursday dinners, and when I ask how work is going she just says "fine" and changes the subject. Her manager, Greg Whitfield, apparently sends her messages at all hours, and she told me last week she hasn't slept well since August 9th.

Here's the part I'm stuck on. Her younger sister, Marisol, called me on August 14th asking if I'd noticed anything. Marisol is worried Kendra is burning out and won't admit it, and she wants me to bring it up. But Kendra has always been private, and I don't want her to feel like we've been talking about her behind her back. On the other hand, Marisol is her only family nearby, and she's the one who's going to be dealing with the fallout if things get worse.

So what would you do? Do I just check in with Kendra directly, maybe over coffee, without mentioning Marisol? Or should I stay out of it and let Marisol decide how to handle it with her own sister? I'd really appreciate perspectives from anyone who's been on either side of this, whether as the friend or the one who was struggling.

I'm writing this in the notebook Dr. Ní Bhriain suggested, mostly because my thoughts keep looping when I try to hold them in my head. Today was a hard one. I walked into the Brewhouse Café on Quay Street around half nine, which is my routine since January, and the barista Ciara asked if I wanted my usual flat white. I said yes, then sat by the window and didn't drink it. I just watched the rain on the glass and felt that heavy, nothing-is-going-to-change feeling settle in my chest again.

Sinéad rang me this morning, which surprised me. She asked whether I'd booked the follow-up at St. Brigid's Clinic yet. I hadn't. I told her I'd do it on Monday, and she said, "You said that last Monday too, Shane." She's right, and she isn't trying to be cruel about it. I think she's frightened, and so am I, if I'm honest. Her number is still the one I dial when things go sideways, 087 445 2913, even though I've been trying to call people less.

Dr. Ní Bhriain asked me to write down three things that went well this week. I managed one. I got to the gym at the Ardmore Fitness Centre on Tuesday and stayed for the full forty minutes, which I haven't done since before the winter. My trainer Declan didn't make a big deal of it, just nodded and said, "Good man." That small thing mattered more than I expected.

I posted something on Instagram last night under @shane_writes_quietly, a line about how some days are just about getting through, and I deleted it an hour later. I worry about putting my moods out there where people can read them and misread them. Dr. Ní Bhriain says I'm allowed to share and allowed to keep things private, and that the choice doesn't have to be made under pressure.

So here is where I am, on the 14th of February, which is a strange day to be sad, given the cards in the shop windows. I'm tired, but I'm still here, and I'm going to ring the clinic on Monday. Write that down, Shane. Monday, the clinic, then the gym.

Friends and family, thank you for being here today to celebrate the life of Lorraine Whitfield. Lorraine was the kind of person who made every room feel a little warmer the moment she walked into it. For thirty-one years she ran the front desk at Harbor Light Physical Therapy on Maple Street, and I'm told that half the town has at least one story that begins with, "Lorraine saw me on a Tuesday and somehow fixed my back and my whole week."

She was also a regular at Sunrise Bean Cafe on Mercer Avenue, where she ordered a medium oat latte and never once let the barista forget her birthday. Every Saturday morning she sat in the window with the crossword and a pen, and anyone who stopped by her table was handed a cookie from the bag she always carried. If you ever wondered how Lorraine knew everybody's business, the answer was simple: she asked, and then she actually listened.

Lorraine was never one for the spotlight, but she loved sharing her life online. Her Instagram handle, @lorrainewalks, was a daily record of sunrise hikes, garden tomatoes, and the occasional blurry photo of her grandsons pretending not to be posing. If you were lucky enough to be on her friends list, you knew she would comment on every single post, usually with three exclamation points and a question about your weekend.

She kept her affairs in order with the same care she gave everything else. Many of you have received a handwritten card from her, or an email from lorraine.whitfield@harborlightpt.com with a link to a recipe she swore she had improved. She believed in staying in touch, and she believed that a short note could carry a lot of love.

Lorraine passed away on June 14th, surrounded by her children and her husband of forty-four years, Gerald. She is survived by her sons Michael and Peter, her grandsons Owen and Eli, and a neighborhood full of people who will miss her every single morning. Let's raise our coffee cups to Lorraine today, and let's honor her by being just a little more like her tomorrow.

My name is Oluwaseun Adebayo, and for as long as I can remember, I have wanted to understand how things work. I grew up in the Westwood neighbourhood of Mississauga, on Hollybrook Crescent, where my mother still keeps the garden I used to help her weed. My grandmother, Folake Adebayo, taught me to read the small print on medicine bottles and to ask questions when a pharmacist rushed through the instructions. She was a nurse for thirty years, and her habit of asking why shaped the way I approach everything.

The question that defined my last two years of high school came from a summer job at a community clinic on Dundas Street. I answered phones and booked appointments, and I noticed that many callers, especially seniors, could not reach anyone on the first try. I started keeping a simple log with my coworker, Priyanka Raman, who had already begun tracking call wait times. Together we showed the clinic manager that most delays happened between 9 and 11 in the morning, and we proposed a staggered booking schedule. Within a month, average waits dropped from nearly twelve minutes to under four.

If I am admitted to your engineering program, I want to build on that experience by studying how systems can serve people who are easy to overlook. I plan to pursue research in health informatics and to keep asking the questions my grandmother taught me to ask. When I call the clinic now, the number I still remember is 905-555-0147, and I like to think that somewhere in that line of calls is a small part of what I have learned.

Okay, you asked me last week why I never talk about the year I spent in Kalamata, so here it is, the whole messy thing. My name is Yiannis, and I grew up in Patras, which everyone who has never been there thinks is just a port. It is not just a port. Anyway, after I finished at the Agricultural High School in Patras, my mother insisted I go somewhere she could visit on the bus, so I ended up at the University of Peloponnese in Kalamata, which I hated for about three months and then loved more than anything.

The bit you really want to hear is the hospital. In February of my second year I broke my wrist falling off a scooter on the hill behind the Ayios Nikolaos church, and I was taken to Kalamata General Hospital. I was there for almost two days. A nurse named Eleni, who had the calmest hands I have ever seen, kept telling me the cast would come off on the 14th of March, and it did, but only after I had already convinced myself I would never play guitar again. She was right, of course. She usually was.

What I want you to take from this is that the scooter, the hospital and the bad luck all pushed me toward the people I still call my best friends. Ring me on Sunday, and I will tell you about the trip to Mani that nearly ended with us sleeping in a car.

I finally made it to Mendoza after three weeks of chasing wine tours around Buenos Aires, and I can say the detour was worth every bus ride. I stayed at a small guesthouse on Calle San Martín 1482, run by a retired teacher named Yolanda who insisted I try her grandmother's empanadas before I'd even unpacked. On March 9th I joined a friend from my Spanish course at the Instituto Superior de Lenguas in Córdoba, who had flown up to celebrate her birthday, and we spent the afternoon cycling between bodegas under the Andes.

The highlight was a tasting at a family vineyard just outside the city, where the owner, Yamil, walked us through the Malbec barrels and told stories about his father, who had worked the same rows for forty years. He also pointed out the small clinic down the road where his daughter was born, and said half the valley had been delivered by the same nurse. It was a reminder that travel is never just about landmarks; it's about the people who quietly hold a place together.

If you go, book your tastings a week ahead, especially in early March when the harvest season draws crowds. Bring cash for the smaller places, and don't skip the mid-morning mate with the locals. I left Mendoza with a suitcase full of bottles I shouldn't have bought and a plan to come back for the next vendimia.

input:
The first morning in Jerusalem I got lost within ten minutes, which felt like the correct way to start. I wandered through narrow stone alleys where the smell of fresh bread and roasted coffee drifted out of tiny doorways, and every corner opened onto another market stall piled with pomegranates, sesame sweets, and spices in colours I did not have names for. Shopkeepers called out greetings in Hebrew and Arabic, sometimes switching mid-sentence, and nobody seemed bothered when I pointed at things and hoped for the best.

In the afternoon I climbed up toward the old walls and sat for a long time watching the light change on the limestone. Families were picnicking on the grass, a group of students was singing softly somewhere behind me, and the bells from a nearby church kept time with the call to prayer. It was one of those rare moments when a place feels both ancient and completely alive, and I found myself simply listening instead of taking photos.

By evening my legs ached and my notebook was full of half-finished sentences. If you come to this country, I would suggest leaving room in your plans for wandering, because the best things here tend to happen off the map. Bring comfortable shoes, accept every cup of tea you are offered, and let the city surprise you.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to recommend Tobias Brennan, who worked under my supervision at Halvorsen & Pike Logistics in Leeds from March 2019 until his departure in December 2023. Tobias joined our dispatch team as a junior coordinator and, within two years, was running our night operations desk with very little oversight. Everyone at the depot called him Toby, and I quickly learned that his easy manner was matched by real rigour. He kept our fleet schedules accurate, trained three new starters without being asked, and once spent an entire weekend tracing a misrouted load for a client in Sheffield, refusing to hand it off until it was delivered.

When the company restructured in 2022, Toby took on responsibility for our vehicle compliance records, including the paperwork for the van registered as RX19 KLM. He was meticulous about it, and our audit that year passed without a single finding in his area. Outside work, he was the one who organised our Friday lunches at Bramwell's Coffee House on Briggate, and he often brought his colleague Oonagh Tierney along to help plan them. Oonagh can speak to his teamwork far better than I can, as she worked alongside him on nearly every project after 2021.

Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Account Coordinator position advertised on your website. My name is Bruno Alvarez Pereyra, and I have spent the last three years working in client services for a logistics firm in Buenos Aires, where I have developed the organisational discipline and bilingual communication skills this role requires. I am based at Calle Tucuman 1842, 4to B, in the Recoleta neighbourhood, which places me close to your Puerto Madero office and makes a commute of under thirty minutes realistic on most days.

I introduced a shared tracking spreadsheet that reduced repeat enquiries by roughly a fifth over six months, and I was asked to train two new colleagues on the process. I enjoy this kind of work: finding the small inefficiency that causes a large amount of frustration and then fixing it quietly.

My academic background is in business administration, which I completed at the Universidad de Belgrano. During my final year I volunteered at the Hospital Italiano's patient administration desk two mornings a week, where I learned how to stay calm and precise when people are anxious and short on time. Bruno Alvarez Pereyra

Hi everyone, it's Dieter here from the Year 9 team, and I wanted to share a few updates before the winter break. First, a big thank you to all the parents who came to the Christmas bake sale on 4 December. We raised 612 euros for the library fund, and that's thanks to a lot of hard work from families. A special mention goes to Dagmar Vogt, who has been running the cake stall since September and who somehow still managed to smile at everyone who asked for a second slice.

Many of you know me as Dieter, but my students have been calling me Dino since my first week at the school, and I've given up trying to stop them. Dino or not, I'm happy to report that our Year 9 science project on local water quality is nearly finished. The class visited the Kaffeehaus am Markt on 11 December to interview the owner, Bruno Hartmann, about where his coffee water comes from. The students came back with a notebook full of questions and a very strong opinion about espresso.

For anyone organising a lift to the Christmas concert, please note that the school car park will be closed from 18 December. Parking permits are issued by the office, and the reference for the shared minibus booking is DE-44821-KB. Sabine is 41, has eleven years of teaching behind her, and says her favourite part of the job is the moment a Year 7 student finally understands fractions. Please give her a warm welcome at the assembly on Monday 9 December.

Finally, a reminder that the library will be open late on the 16th for anyone who needs a quiet place to finish coursework. Have a restful holiday, and see you all in January.

input:
Harold Thomas Weatherall, known to everyone in Kendal as Harry, died peacefully at Lancaster Royal Infirmary on 14 February, aged 79, with his daughter Margaret by his side. He leaves a large family who will miss his dry humour, his stubborn opinions on football, and his habit of turning up to every christening with a card and a bottle of sherry.

Harry spent thirty-four years as a senior quantity surveyor with Lakeland Build & Design Ltd, where he was known for checking every figure twice and for never once letting a sub-contractor forget a missed deadline. Colleagues recall that he could read a set of plans faster than most people could read a menu, and that he was the first to volunteer when a new apprentice needed showing round the site.

He was a regular at Bramley's Coffee House on Highgate every Saturday morning, where the staff kept his usual order of a flat white and a slice of lemon drizzle cake ready before he reached the door. Many of his best friends were made over those tables, and the owners have asked that anyone wishing to pay their respects leave a note on the board by the window.

Harry was never without his old collie, Bramble, who went everywhere with him, from the allotment to the Saturday market. The two of them were a familiar sight on the Cumbrian lanes, and Bramble has since been taken in by his grandson Oliver, who says she spends most evenings waiting by the front door.

He is survived by his wife of 52 years, Eileen, his children Margaret, Peter and Susan, seven grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. A funeral service will be held at St Thomas's Church on 24 February at 11am, followed by a gathering at the Kendal Rugby Club. Donations in his memory may be made to the British Heart Foundation.

For anyone who would like to share a memory or a photograph, please write to the family at harry.weatherall.memories@lakelandmail.co.uk. We would love to hear your stories of Harry, and we know he would have enjoyed reading every one of them over a cup of tea.

Written with love by his son, Peter Weatherall.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to tell our friends and neighbours that Zvi Adler passed away peacefully at home on the 14th of November, at the age of 78. Zvi lived at 17 Herzl Street, Apartment 4, in Rishon LeZion for more than forty years, and everyone on that block knew his cheerful wave from the balcony. He was born in Lodz, Poland, in 1946, and carried with him a deep love for the city of his childhood, even after arriving in Israel as a young man with nothing but a suitcase and a stubborn optimism.

Zvi worked for three decades as a machinist at the Ashdod port workshop, and he never once missed a Friday morning coffee with the men from his shift. input:
When I first landed in Lisbon last September, I had no idea that Alba would become the friend I'd miss most back in Leeds. We'd met at the Café Brisa on Rua da Escola, where I spent my first mornings nursing a cortado and pretending to read the local paper. Alba was the barista who corrected my pronunciation of "obrigada" without ever making me feel silly. Three weeks later, she had me signed up for the Ginásio Atlas down the hill, insisting that the steep streets were the only real gym I'd need.

I should admit that the move was never meant to be permanent. I had been working as a senior analyst at Hartwell & Finch Consulting in Leeds, where my title, Head of Operational Insight, was more impressive on paper than the job felt day to day. When my manager, Greg Harlow, offered me a remote arrangement, I decided to test it from abroad. Alba thought I was mad. "You're not a tourist," she told me, "you're going to live here now." She was right, though it took me another month to accept it.

If you ever find yourself in the Alfama district, ask for the back table at Café Brisa and tell them Alba sent you. Write to me at amara.reid@brisamail.pt if you want the address of my favourite tiny bakery. I was born in Harrogate, and people always ask whether Lisbon feels like home yet. I still hesitate, but on September mornings, with the tram rattling past and the coffee going cold in my hand, I think it might be getting there.

Some background: my lease started in August two years ago and has never been changed. I've always paid on time, and the only maintenance issue was a broken boiler in February, which took three weeks to fix. I looked up the Mietspiegel for my area and my current rent is already at the upper end of what's listed, so an 18% jump seems way out of line. I'm worried I'm missing something about the Kappungsgrenze rules and how much notice he has to give.

I already booked an appointment with the Mieterverein Leipzig for July 14th at 10:30, and I'm bringing my lease and the letter. Before that, I went to Kaffeehaus Morgenrot on Gottschedstrasse to think things over with a coffee and jot down my questions. The owner there was kind enough to let me use a table for an hour. input:
Hello again from the Year 9 corner! This term I have been asked to share a little about my own journey, since several of you have asked how it feels to start over in a new school. Last year I left a school where I had been for almost my whole childhood, and I arrived here knowing nobody. The first few weeks were strange. The lunch queue felt impossibly long, the timetable seemed to change every other day, and I kept reaching for words in class that didn't quite fit the way people spoke around me.

What helped most was the simple things. A classmate showed me where the library was, a teacher took five minutes to explain how the homework portal works, and a group of students invited me to join a lunchtime club even though they barely knew me. I also learned that asking for help is not a weakness. Most people are glad to be asked, and many of them have had to start over somewhere too.

If you are new this term, or know someone who is, my advice is to say yes to the small invitations and to be patient with yourself. Settling in takes longer than you expect, but it does happen. I am still learning every day, and I am grateful to everyone who made the adjustment easier. See you at the next club meeting!

Tuesday, January 9th. I'm writing this at the kitchen table in Kalamata while the rain keeps tapping on the window. My session with Dr. Vasiliki was rough today, but in a useful way. She asked me to name the thing I'm most afraid of, and I couldn't say it out loud at first. I finally wrote it on a napkin: that I'm failing my mother, Eleni, the same way I think I failed my father before he passed.

Eleni has been staying with me since the hospital discharge. Her apartment on Ioannou Metaxa Street is too far up the hill for her to manage the stairs alone, so she's in the back bedroom now. Everyone calls her Lenia, which she hates and secretly loves. When I brought her tea this morning she asked me, not unkindly, whether I was still sleeping. I told her yes. We both knew I wasn't.

The practical stuff is piling up. Her insurance paperwork came back with a mistake in her address, listed as 14 Ioannou Metaxa Street, Kalamata 24100, when it should be 41, and the clinic keeps calling the wrong number, 27210 55 186, which goes to my old landline. Dr. Vasiliki suggested I make a list and tackle one item a day rather than trying to hold it all in my head. It sounds obvious, but I've been carrying everything at once.

What surprised me most was how I described myself in session. I kept saying "I should have done more," and she gently pointed out that I say "should" the way other people say "always." I think she's right. Dimitra, my sister, reminded me on the phone that she, too, has been pulling her weight from Patras, even if it doesn't look like much from here.

So my small goal for this week is modest. Call the insurer on Thursday, the 15th, before ten. Sit with Lenia for one real conversation without checking my phone. And try to write the next entry without the word "should" in it. I'll see how that goes.

Hi, I'm hoping you can help me think through something that's been eating at me for weeks. My name is Ciara Brennan and I'm 34, living in Limerick. I work as a senior project coordinator at Shannon Logistics Partners, which is a decent job with a decent team, but over the last few months I've been running on empty and I don't know how to say that to anyone without it sounding like I'm complaining.

The trouble started in early September, when our director, Mr. Fergal Dunne, moved three of our biggest client accounts onto my desk in one afternoon. I said yes because I always say yes. Since then my evenings have disappeared. I answer emails at the kitchen table after my partner Aidan has gone to bed, and on Sunday I actually cried in the car outside the Dunnes on O'Connell Street because I couldn't face going back in to the shop.

The awkward part is that I like the work. I'm good at it, and people come to me when things go wrong, which is flattering and also exhausting. When I tried to raise the workload with Fergal last week he said something like, "You're the one I trust with this, Ciara," and I felt guilty for even bringing it up. I left the meeting feeling like I'd asked for something unreasonable.

What I'm really after is a way of talking to him that doesn't make me sound like I'm falling apart or like I'm looking for a way out. Should I put it in writing first? Should I propose specific tasks to hand back? I'm also wondering whether I'm being dramatic and whether this is just what a busy September looks like in any job.

If you could help me draft an opening line or two and tell me how to frame the conversation so that it reads as a request for support rather than a complaint, I'd really appreciate it. I'd also be glad to hear if you think I should be looking at something bigger than this role. Thanks for reading all this.

After almost nine years at Banco Litoral in Rosario, I am thrilled to share that I have joined Mercado Andino as Senior Product Analyst, starting Monday, 14 April. Some of you have known me since I was a nervous intern, and others only through the spreadsheets I used to send at midnight, so this post is for everyone who helped me get here.

I am 34 now, and I still think about the afternoon I left Villa Constitución, the small river town where I was born, with one suitcase and a lot of questions. Back then my mum, who everyone calls Teté, told me that a good career is like a long asado: you have to keep the fire steady and not rush the meat. I laughed at her then. I understand it better now.

The new role is a big step. I will lead the analytics work behind our lending products across Argentina, Chile and Uruguay, and I will be working closely with teams I have admired for years. My first priority is listening: to customers, to engineers, and to the people in the branches who know things no dashboard will ever show.

If you want to reach me, the easiest way is LinkedIn or email at sofia.navarro@mercadoandino.com.ar. I also post occasional thoughts on data and product under the handle @sofi.datos on Instagram, though I am much more active on LinkedIn these days. My direct line is +54 341 555 0148 if you prefer a call.

Thank you to my manager Gustavo, to my colleagues at Banco Litoral, and to every friend who sent a message on the day of my farewell lunch on 2 April. I am grateful, excited and a little bit scared, which I am told is exactly how a new chapter should feel. Let's keep in touch.

We gathered today not to say goodbye to a title or a role, but to honor a person who showed up for everyone around her. She was the one who always remembered the small things: the way you took your coffee, the name of your first dog, the song you hummed when you were nervous. Her kitchen was never quiet for long, and her table always had room for one more chair.

She taught by example. She believed that kindness was not something you saved for special occasions but something you practiced on an ordinary Tuesday, when no one was watching and nothing was expected of you. Many of you have told me stories this week about the times she quietly paid for a meal, drove someone to an appointment, or sat with a friend through a hard night without needing to fix anything.

In the days ahead, when you find yourself reaching for the phone to share some small piece of news with her, I hope you will let that impulse become a kind of memorial. Call someone instead. Bring a casserole. Remember a birthday. That is how she lived, and it is how we can keep her with us. Rest now, Olive. You have given us more than enough to carry forward.

Ich schreibe das hier auf, damit ich es nicht vergesse. Am Dienstag, den 14. Juni, war ich bei Dr. Lehmann in der Praxis am Hohenzollernring in Köln. Ich bin jetzt 38 und seit dem Umzug aus Wien vor zwei Jahren hatte ich keinen festen Hausarzt mehr, deshalb war der Termin ziemlich überfällig. Frieda, meine Schwester, hatte mir Dr. Lehmann empfohlen, weil sie dort selbst seit Jahren ist.

Das Gespräch begann mit den üblichen Fragen zu Schlaf, Essen und Stress. Ich habe erzählt, dass ich seit dem Frühjahr öfter müde bin und die Kopfschmerzen zurückgekommen sind. Dr. Lehmann hat mir den Blutdruck gemessen, er war mit 138 zu 88 leicht erhöht. Sie meinte, das sei bei meinem Alter und dem Stress im Job nicht ungewöhnlich, möchte es aber in vier Wochen noch einmal kontrollieren.

Außerdem habe ich mit ihr über meine Arbeit gesprochen. Ich arbeite als Projektleiterin bei der Stadtwerke Nordrhein GmbH, und die letzten Monate waren sehr anstrengend. Mein Kollege Matthias Brandt hat mich dabei öfter unterstützt als irgendjemand sonst, und ich habe ihm am Ende des Gesprächs eine Nachricht geschrieben, dass ich mich bei ihm bedanke. Dr. Lehmann fand es gut, dass ich mir Unterstützung hole, und hat empfohlen, nach Feierabend wenigstens zweimal pro Woche einen Spaziergang zu machen.
