input:
Dear diary, today the rain didn't let up once, not even for the walk to the shop. I came home soaked to the skin and spent an hour in front of the range with a mug of tea going cold in my hands. Mam rang in the evening to ask whether I'd eaten, which is how I know she's still worried about me, even if she'd never say it outright. I told her I had, which was half true. There was soup, and I counted that.

The real news is that I finally finished the jumper I've been knitting since the summer. It's lopsided at one shoulder and the sleeves are two different lengths, but it's warm and it's mine. I sat with it across my knees after dinner and felt, for the first time in weeks, a small bit of pride. It's a strange thing to feel proud of a sweater with mistakes in it, but there it is.

Tomorrow I have to face the pile of letters on the hall table that I keep stepping around. Some of them are bills and some of them are the kind I've been avoiding. I'll make a cup of tea first, and then I'll open them one at a time, the way the doctor suggested. Small steps. Goodnight, diary. The wind is rattling the window and I'm going to let it.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Vincent, Aoife's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words about the couple tonight. I've known Aoife since the day she was born, and I can tell you she has never once done anything by halves. When she decided she wanted to become a nurse, she studied through the night for two years. When she decided she wanted to marry Conor, she told him so over a plate of chips in a chipper on Shop Street in Galway, and he said yes before she'd finished the sentence.

Conor, you've become part of our family in a way that feels completely natural. You showed up for Mam's birthday with a box of Roses, you fixed Dad's garden gate without being asked, and you never once made Aoife choose between her people and yours. שלום לכל שכני בבניין ברחוב הרצל 14 ובשכונת הדר!

שמי שרון אברהמי, גרה בבניין הזה כבר שבע שנים, ואני רוצה לשתף אתכם בדבר שמעסיק אותי כבר כמה ימים. בשבוע שעבר חזרתי מהעבודה בערב ומצאתי את הדלת של חדר האשפה פתוחה לרווחה, והפחים מפוזרים על המדרכה. לא ראיתי מי עשה את זה, אבל מאז זה קורה כמעט כל לילה, וכבר שלוש משפחות בבניין התלוננו על אותו דבר.

לכן החלטתי לפנות לוועד הבית ולבקש מאתנו להתארגן. אני בת 41 ועובדת במשרד ביום, ולא תמיד יש לי אנרגיה לרדוף אחרי כל בעיה לבד, אבל אני מאמינה שכשכולנו פועלים יחד זה נפתר מהר יותר. הצעתי שנעמיד שלט חדש ליד הכניסה ונבדוק אם אפשר להתקין מצלמה קטנה בתאורה של הכניסה, בכפוף להסכמת כולם.

אשמח אם תענו לי בהודעה פרטית או כאן בקבוצה עד יום ראשון ה-14 בדצמבר, כדי שנוכל לקבוע פגישה קצרה במרפסת של הקומה השנייה. מי שרוצה לתרום לעלות השלט או התאורה מוזמן לתאם איתי ישירות. גם אם אתם לא יכולים להגיע, תגידו לי מה דעתכם.

אני יודעת שכולנו עמוסים בחגים ובסוף השנה, אבל דווקא עכשיו זה הזמן שבו צריך להיות קצת יותר קרובים. אם יש לכם רעיונות אחרים, בבקשה תכתבו. ואם מישהו ראה משהו חשוד, אפילו פרט קטן, אני מודה לכם שתעדכנו.

תודה רבה, ושיהיה לכולנו שבוע נעים.
שרון

Hi neighbours, Wanda here from number 14 on Protea Crescent. Sorry for the long message, but I wanted to share something before the weekend gets busy.

Our little Jack Russell, Biscuit, got out through the gap in the back fence on Tuesday evening, 9 July, and we spent almost two hours walking up and down Protea Crescent and along the stream behind Oakhurst Road. Thank you to Mr Naidoo at number 7 and the two teenagers from the corner house who helped us check the drains and the bushes. Biscuit was found safe on Wednesday morning by the security guard at the Hillside Estate gate, wagging her tail as if nothing had happened. She has a very clear opinion about being carried home, so please don't be alarmed if you see a small brown-and-white dog trotting around with great purpose.

While we were searching, several of you asked whether we had posted her on lost pet groups. We had, and a few people kindly shared it. If you do find a stray in the area, please post on the Protea Crescent Watch Facebook page or message me directly on WhatsApp at 082 417 9036. You can also find updates from the local animal rescue on Instagram under @rosebankpawsrescue, where they post every Thursday.

The fence has now been repaired by Themba from Greenline Fencing, who was brilliant and only charged us for the materials. If you need a reliable handyman, his number is with me and I am happy to pass it on. Our next street clean-up is scheduled for Saturday 19 July at 8am, meeting at the bottom of the crescent by the old jacaranda tree. Bring gloves and a bag if you have them.

Again, thank you all for the kindness this week. It is wonderful to live somewhere people actually look out for each other and their dogs. See you on Saturday.

Warm regards,
Wanda

input: My name is Yolanda Ibarra Solís, and I was born in Puebla on July 14, 2006. Growing up in the Colonia Santa Cruz Buenavista, I learned early that a city teaches you as much as a classroom does. Every morning I walked past the corner bakery on Calle Hidalgo, and every afternoon I helped my abuela balance her accounts for the family stall. Those ledgers, with their stubborn columns, taught me patience and precision. When I started posting my budgeting spreadsheets under @yoli.solis.num, I realized that numbers could also be a way of telling stories about my community. This essay is my attempt to show how that small habit has shaped the person I hope to become.

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden is coming along nicely. I think about you every single day, especially now that the weather has turned warm and I can smell the lilacs on my walk to the bus. Mom says you've been keeping busy with your bridge group and that you beat Aunt Carol again last Tuesday, which I'm sure she is still not over. Tell her I said congratulations, from a safe distance.

I wanted to write because I finally got around to going through the box of photos you gave me last Christmas. There's one of you on the porch of the house on Alder Street in Dayton, holding a baby who I'm pretty sure is my uncle Tom, squinting into the sun like you were daring the camera to try. It made me realize how little I know about the years before Grandpa and you moved out to the suburbs. Would you tell me more about that time when you have a free afternoon? I'd love to hear how you two met at the dance hall downtown, and what the city looked like back then.

Work has been hectic. My manager keeps piling on projects, but I've started running along the river trail on weekday mornings, and it has honestly saved my sanity. Last weekend I signed up for a 10K in early June, which is terrifying, but I'm going to finish it. I'm hoping you'll be proud of me, even if I walk the last mile.

I also wanted to share something sweet. My roommate Jenna and I finally found an apartment closer to the university, so I'll be moving on June 14th. The place is small but has a little balcony where I plan to grow tomatoes, the way you taught me. If you ever want to visit, you can call me at 555-348-2917 or email me at maureen.lindqvist@example.com. Please don't feel you have to come all the way out, though I'd love for you to see it.

Please give my love to Grandpa, even if he's still grumbling about the new television remote. I miss your cooking so much, and I'm already planning to make your pot roast the first Sunday after I move in.

With all my love,
Megan

input:
I still think about that Tuesday in May, the one where I finally walked into Cafe Bonaparte on Calle Sarmiento in Rosario and didn't leave for three hours. I'm writing this for you, Marisol, because you were the one who kept telling me to stop hiding in my apartment. So here it is, the whole messy story.

I'm thirty-four now, and for most of my life people have called me Tomi, which is short for Tomas, though my mother still uses the full version when she's annoyed with me. That Tuesday I'd been sitting in my car outside the place for almost ten minutes, rehearsing what I'd say if Lucia Ferreyra recognized me. We had met two years earlier at the climbing gym on Avenida Pellegrini, and then we'd lost touch after a fight I still don't fully understand. She'd sent me an email that morning, out of nowhere, from lferreyra.work@gmail.com, asking if I wanted to get coffee. Just coffee, she wrote, nothing heavy.

When I finally went in, she was already at a corner table by the window, wearing that green scarf she always wore even in summer. She looked up, smiled like nothing had happened, and said, "Tomi, you still take it with too much sugar?" I laughed so hard that the waiter asked if everything was okay. That was the moment the tension broke. We talked about the gym, about her new job at a translation agency, about the dog her sister had adopted that nobody could control. Then, slowly, we got to the real stuff.

She apologized first, which I didn't expect. She said she'd been difficult during the last months we were close and that she'd blamed me for things that weren't really my fault. I told her I'd been stubborn and too proud to call her back when I should have. Neither of us was entirely right, and for once we both admitted it without sulking.

What I took from those three hours was simpler than I expected. Some friendships don't end cleanly, they just pause, and sometimes a cup of coffee in a busy cafe is enough to start them moving again. We made plans to climb on the following Saturday, and I've been going back to the gym every week since. My legs ache, my hands are rough, and I feel more like myself than I have in a long time.

So thank you for pushing me. If you ever find yourself in Rosario, come by Bonaparte with me. I'll order the sugary coffee, and you can tease me about it.

Before that I worked as a biostatistician at a university medical centre in Ohio, which is where I first fell for the messy, rewarding problem of turning raw patient records into something a clinician can act on.

Outside the office I'm a long-distance runner and a fairly obsessive amateur baker. My rescue greyhound, Biscuit, has opinions about both activities and makes his views known every morning at six. Dear Customer Care Manager,

I am writing to formally complain about the service I received from Karoo Fresh Foods on 14 April, when I placed a bulk order for my office through your Rosebank branch. Bongani Mthembu, who signed for the order on behalf of Summit Logistics, was told the delivery would arrive before noon. It did not arrive until almost four in the afternoon, and by then two of the twelve crates had been left out in the sun. I have attached photographs of the crates and the delivery slip, which shows the driver's handwritten note that the cold chain had been interrupted.

When I called your helpline on 15 April, I was transferred three times and eventually told that a supervisor would return my call within 24 hours. No one called. I then visited the Rosebank store myself on 17 April and spoke to a manager who was apologetic but could not offer a refund without a written statement from me. I have sent that statement twice now, once by email to complaints@karoofresh.co.za and once through your online portal, and I have received only automated replies.

I am asking for a full refund of the R4,860 order, a written explanation of why the delivery was delayed and the cold chain was not maintained, and confirmation that the driver involved has been retrained. Please respond in writing by 28 April. If I do not hear from you by then, I will escalate this matter to the Consumer Commission and the Ombudsman for Consumer Affairs.

Yours faithfully,

Bongani Mthembu

Our first stop in Canada was Halifax, and I have to admit I fell for the harbour within the first hour. I'm Zara Whitfield, 34, and I'd been dreaming about the Maritimes since my sister Megan moved to Nova Scotia last year. She told me to call her before we even left the airport, so I did, and she shouted the number, 902-555-0147, so loudly that the man at the car rental desk laughed. Megan works as a nurse at the Queen Elizabeth II Health Sciences Centre, and she insisted we visit the seaside cafe on Lower Water Street that she and her colleagues at Atlantic Bay Clinics swear by.

input:
Last June I finally made it to Kyoto, and I have to thank my old colleague Callum Brewer for pushing me to go. He had lived there for two years teaching English and insisted I start my morning at the Fushimi Inari shrine before the crowds arrived. We climbed the thousand torii gates together around six a.m., and Callum kept stopping to point out the little stone foxes tucked between the trees. Honestly, the quiet at that hour made the whole trip for me.

Back home, my sister Mireille has been asking me to share every photo, so I have been posting them to my travel account, @wanderingcal_jp, which Callum set up for me as a joke. The highlight of the second week was a tea ceremony in Gion, where the host, a patient woman named Hisako, guided us through each movement while our feet slowly went numb on the tatami. I left the ceremony feeling calmer than I had in months.

If you go, book your ryokan early, and bring a small gift for your host because it is expected. Also, ask someone you trust to look after your home, which in my case meant my cat Biscuit, who spent the week being spoiled by my neighbour. I am already planning my return for the cherry blossoms next spring, and I expect Callum will be driving the itinerary again.

input:
My name is Hannah Whitfield, and I was Uncle Yusuf's niece, though he never once let me forget that he was the one who taught me to swim. We grew up in Leeds, in a terraced house on Hyde Park Road, and until I was nineteen I thought every man in the world laughed the way he did, with his whole chest and his head tipped back.

Yusuf spent thirty-one years at St James's Hospital as a porter, and I don't think a single patient ever left his corridor without being greeted by name. He knew which nurses took their tea with sugar and which ones pretended not to. When my mother was on the ward after her surgery, he brought her a flask of cardamom tea every morning before his shift and never once mentioned that it was against the rules.

When he retired, he could not sit still. He opened a small coffee place on Chapel Street called Bean & Brew, mostly so he would have somewhere to argue about football with the regulars. He ran it for six years. He insisted the cinnamon buns were his grandmother's recipe, though I have seen her handwriting and it certainly was not.

He moved to Manchester with his partner, Lorraine, in 2016, and then, to everyone's surprise, to Lisbon two years later, where he learned enough Portuguese to haggle at the fish market. The distance never stopped him calling. Every Sunday, at seven, the phone would ring and he would ask about my work, my cooking, and whether I had been looking after our old dog, Biscuit, who by then was too stubborn to die and too deaf to hear him calling.

Yusuf, I am still learning to swim without you. Thank you for holding me up until I could float on my own.

My name is Hetty Ashcombe, and I was Uncle Yannis's niece, though he never once let me forget that he was the one who taught me to swim. We grew up in Bradford, in a terraced house on Manningham Lane, and until I was nineteen I thought every man in the world laughed the way he did, with his whole chest and his head tipped back.

Yannis spent thirty-one years at St Mary's Hospital as a porter, and I don't think a single patient ever left his corridor without being greeted by name. He knew which nurses took their tea with sugar and which ones pretended not to. When my mother was on the ward after her surgery, he brought her a flask of cardamom tea every morning before his shift and never once mentioned that it was against the rules.

When he retired, he could not sit still. He opened a small coffee place on Market Street called Crumb & Cup, mostly so he would have somewhere to argue about football with the regulars. He ran it for six years. He insisted the cinnamon buns were his grandmother's recipe, though I have seen her handwriting and it certainly was not.

He moved to Liverpool with his partner, Maureen, in 2019, and then, to everyone's surprise, to Porto two years later, where he learned enough Portuguese to haggle at the fish market. The distance never stopped him calling. Every Sunday, at seven, the phone would ring and he would ask about my work, my cooking, and whether I had been looking after our old dog, Crumpet, who by then was too stubborn to die and too deaf to hear him calling.

Yannis, I am still learning to swim without you. Thank you for holding me up until I could float on my own.

input:
Kristina Lindqvist has spent the last fourteen years building water-quality sensors for small municipalities across central Sweden. Born in Uppsala, she studied hydrology at Uppsala University before joining a Västerås engineering firm, where she led the team that deployed the first networked monitoring system on Lake Mälaren's tributaries. Her work has since been adopted in twelve regional councils, and she is widely known for insisting that field technicians be trained alongside the engineers who design the hardware.

Outside the lab, Kristina is a keen cross-country skier and a volunteer mentor for young women entering STEM programmes. She credits much of her early confidence to a colleague, Anders Berglund, who taught her to read a river the way a hydrologist should: through its sediment, its banks and its seasons, not only its numbers. Kristina still says that Anders would have been the first to laugh at the idea of a sensor getting all the credit.

Kristina will deliver the keynote "Measuring What Flows" at the Nordic Water Futures Conference on 14 January, where she will present the results of a three-year study on winter ice effects in monitoring data. Attendees can expect a candid account of what worked, what failed, and why the next generation of instruments must be built for the conditions people actually face.

Dr. Okafor said the disc isn't herniated, just angry, and gave me a list of stretches I'll probably forget by Friday. After that I grabbed a flat white at Bluebird Coffee, which is basically my office now. Hoping the disc and I can come to some kind of truce by then.

input:
It is with heavy hearts that our family announces the passing of Joseph Mwangi Kariuki, born on 14 October 1961 in Nyeri and called to rest on 3 October 2024 at the age of 62. Joe, as many of you knew him, was a husband, father, brother, uncle and friend to more people than he could ever count. He leaves behind his wife of thirty-four years, Grace, and their children, Brian, Njeri and little Wanjiru, whose laughter filled every corner of our home.

I first knew Joe as the older brother who taught me to ride a bicycle along the dusty road behind our family compound in Nyeri. He was patient in a way I never managed to be myself. Later, when I came to Nairobi to look for work, he opened his door to me for almost a year without ever once making me feel like a burden. That was simply who he was. He believed that a man's home should always have room for one more plate at the table.

For over twenty-five years Joe served with dedication at Kenya Commercial Bank, where he rose from a teller to a senior branch manager in the Westlands area. His colleagues often spoke of his fairness and of the way he remembered the names of their children and asked after their mothers. He could explain a loan policy to a nervous first-time borrower so clearly that the person would leave the office smiling. Many of those customers later became his friends.

Joe loved football above almost everything else, except perhaps his grandchildren and a good pot of githeri cooked by Grace. On Sunday mornings you would find him in front of the television shouting at the referee with the same passion he once reserved for Gor Mahia matches at Nyayo Stadium. He also kept a small vegetable garden behind the house, and he would proudly send photographs of his kale and tomatoes to anyone who would look. If you have questions about the funeral arrangements, please call the family on 0722 418 653, or follow the updates posted by his son on Instagram at @brian.mwangi.k.

Joe is survived by his mother, his brothers and sisters, and a community of relatives and friends who will miss him deeply. We ask that you keep his soul in your prayers. Rest well, Joe. We will carry your kindness with us for the rest of our days. Your memory is a blessing, and we give thanks for every year we were allowed to share with you.

Session notes for myself, written after Tuesday. Dr. Levi asked me again to stop apologising for taking up space, and I laughed, because I had just done it twice before she finished the question. I am thirty-four and I still feel like the kid who was told to sit quietly at the back of the room. Zohar, she says, and then pauses, the way she does when she wants me to hear the rest of the sentence myself.

The homework is to write down three moments this week when I noticed the old reflex and didn't follow it. The first one was easy: on Wednesday at the post office on Herzl Street, when the clerk asked for my ID number for the parcel, I gave it to her without the little sigh I usually add. It is 028417539, the same number I have had since I was a child, and for once I didn't feel I needed to explain it. The second was on March 12, my birthday, when Noa called to say she couldn't come to dinner and I told her that was fine and meant it, which is new. I wrote the date down because Dr. Levi said small dates matter.

The third one I'm still turning over. My landlord, Mr. Ben-Ami, keeps sending emails to zohar.aks@mailbox.co.il about the water bill, and I have started answering them within the hour instead of drafting replies for two days. I live at 14 Bialik Street, apartment 6, in Haifa, and some mornings I still stand at the window and feel a little dizzy with how small and ordinary my life has become. Dr. Levi says that is the point. I am not sure yet, but I'm trying to believe her.

input:
I have been meaning to write about our week in Germany since we got back, and the one thing I keep returning to is the trip with our dog, Wiebke. She is a scruffy little terrier mix who has never met a bakery she didn't want to investigate, so when Wolfgang and I booked a rental car for the Black Forest, we knew she would be coming along. We set off from Freiburg on the morning of November 9th, the sky low and grey, and drove up through villages where every third house seemed to have a wood-stacked balcony and a carved wooden sign. Wiebke spent most of the drive with her nose pressed to the window, fogging up the glass with every excited breath.

We stayed two nights in a small guesthouse outside Triberg run by a retired schoolteacher named Ingrid Halder, who took one look at Wiebke and produced a dish of leftover sausage without any prompting. Wolfgang spent the first afternoon hiking the trail to the waterfalls while I sat in the warm room writing postcards. Halder's cake, a dense chocolate and cherry thing soaked in kirsch, was better than anything I had eaten on the whole trip, and I say that as someone who has eaten a great many cakes.

If you are planning a November visit, bring a proper waterproof coat and do not expect the cuckoo clocks to be open on weekday mornings. Wolfgang and I would happily go back, and I suspect Wiebke would be the first to pack her own bag. You can reach me through the contact form on this blog, or at wiebke.travels@example.com if you have questions about travelling with a dog in the region.

input:
Dear Grandma,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold hasn't gotten into your bones too badly. It has been a strange few weeks here. The leaves finally came down all at once after a long, stubborn stretch of gray, and now the yard looks bare in a way I'm still getting used to. I keep meaning to rake and then finding a reason to put it off, which I suspect you would find very funny.

Work has been busy in the way that leaves you tired but not unhappy. There's a project that has taken over most of my days, and I've been staying later than I should, mostly because the people I work with are kind and the problems are interesting. I've also started cooking on the weekends again. Last Sunday I tried to make the soup you used to make with too many onions and not enough patience, and it came out closer than I expected. It still didn't taste quite like yours, but I think that's just because yours was made with years of practice behind it.

I've been thinking a lot about the winters we spent together when I was small. The way the windows fogged up when the kettle was going, the blanket you kept folded over the arm of the couch, the radio playing softly in the kitchen while you worked on something with your hands. I didn't appreciate those afternoons at the time. I just assumed they would always be there, the way children assume things about the adults who look after them.

I wanted to write because I miss you, and because phone calls have a way of ending before I've said what I meant to. So here is what I meant to say: thank you for the patience, the stories, and the endless supply of advice I didn't ask for but needed anyway. I'm trying to take some of it to heart.

Please tell me how you are doing, really doing, not the polite version. Tell me what you're reading, what you're worried about, and whether you've finally let anyone help with the stairs. I'll call again this weekend, and I promise to actually listen this time instead of checking the time every few minutes.

With all my love,
Ruby

August 9. Dr. Lindqvist asked me to write down what happened after the meeting on Tuesday, so here it is. I'm still Cass to everyone at Harbor Point Logistics, even though my badge says Cassandra Whitfield, Senior Operations Analyst. Nobody there calls me that except HR. Marcus, who has sat across from me for four years, was the one who got the promotion I wanted, and I smiled and said congratulations like a normal person. Then I drove home to 1842 Larkspur Court, sat in the car in the driveway for twenty minutes, and didn't go inside until the streetlights came on.

The car is a 2016 Subaru with plate 7KQR-294, and I realised on the drive that I'd been gripping the wheel so hard my knuckles ached. I keep noticing things like that. My sister Hallie says I'm doing the thing where I turn every setback into proof that I'm failing, and she's probably right, though she always says it kindly, which somehow makes it worse.

Email me at cass.whitfield@harborpoint.com only if it's work, and keep the rest of my evenings for myself. Dr. Lindqvist says progress looks boring from the inside. I'll try to believe her.

The Corrib-blue Ford Focus, registration 191-D-4472, still sits in the drive, and I have asked my daughters to sell it to someone who will treat it kindly. My account with the credit union, number 88217305, has been closed, and any outstanding dues should be directed to my executor, Orla.

I was born on 9 December 1951 and died on 22 December this year, a few days before Christmas, which I always thought was a very inconvenient time to leave a party. Please do not send flowers. Dear Grandma Ruth,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden in Lyon is coming back to life now that the frost has finally gone. Mum says you have been up at dawn every day with your secateurs, which made me laugh because it sounds exactly like you. I miss our walks along the Saône, and I miss Biscuit getting under your feet while you tried to cook. Please tell him I have not forgotten him, even if he would never remember me.

Things here in Bristol are busy. Aoife started her new job at the hospital on the 3rd of April and is already complaining about the night shifts, though she secretly loves them. She asked me to send you her love and to remind you that she is still waiting for the recipe for your apple tart. I told her you would only give it to her in person, so she will have to come to France this summer to get it.

I turned forty-one last week, which Dad says is the age where you start pretending you know what you are doing. You would have been proud of the cake I made, even though it leaned a little to one side. I posted a photo of it on my account, @annie_crosby_writes, so you can see it if Aoife shows you her phone. Write back when you can, and give Biscuit a scratch behind the ears from me.

All my love,
Annie

input:
When people ask me where I first learned to lead, I usually point to the summer I spent at the Riverside Community Food Bank in Columbus, Ohio. My supervisor, Marcus Delgado, handed me a clipboard on my first morning in July and told me that the shelves would not restock themselves. Over the following weeks, Marcus taught me how to coordinate volunteer shifts, how to track donations so that nothing expired on the shelf, and how to speak to a frustrated family without making them feel judged. Marcus never called himself a leader, but he showed me that leadership is mostly about paying attention to the people who quietly keep things running.

One afternoon on July 19th, a truck carrying two pallets of produce arrived three hours late, and our Saturday distribution was in jeopardy. I remember Marcus looking at me and asking what I would do. I had no plan yet, so I started calling the other volunteers, reorganizing the schedule, and asking local grocers whether they had surplus to spare. By evening, we had served every family who had come to the line. Marcus smiled and said only, "Now you understand the job."

That summer changed how I think about my future. I want to study public policy because I have seen how a single late truck can ripple through a neighborhood, and I want to help design systems that prevent those failures. Oliver Brandt, the director who first interviewed me, asked why I wanted to work there. My answer then was simple: I wanted to be useful. My answer now is that I want to build the kind of structures that let everyone be useful, the way Marcus did for me.

Hey Marcus, I still can't believe what happened last week, so let me tell you properly. You know I've been at Brightline Logistics in Mississauga for almost three years now. Last Tuesday, May 14, I was supposed to present the Q2 routing report to the regional board, and my manager, Ruth Ellison, the Senior Operations Lead, pulled me aside at eight in the morning and said the numbers had changed overnight. Nobody told me why.

I spent the whole morning in the office with Priyanka, who everyone calls Pree, and she was amazing. She's the one who found the duplicate shipment entries that had been sitting in the system since March. Honestly, without her I'd have walked into that boardroom with the wrong figures. She just sat next to me, cracking jokes about the coffee machine, while we rebuilt the spreadsheets line by line.

The presentation itself went fine, better than fine actually. Ruth nodded through the whole thing, and afterwards a guy from the board asked me for a copy. I'm not sure what that means yet, but it felt good. I came home and tried to celebrate by ordering takeout, only to realize my passport renewal form had been sitting on the counter. I'd been meaning to send it in, and the number on it, P4437819, looked so official that I almost laughed.

You remember how I used to be at Westfield College before I transferred? I keep thinking about how different my life would be if I'd stayed. Anyway, Pree texted me the next morning saying she'd bring her famous lemon squares to the Friday team lunch, so I'm holding you to coming along. Bring your sister too if she's in town.

That's the update for now. I'll call you on Sunday, and you can tell me all about the wedding plans. Zara says hi, by the way, she's been asking about you ever since you visited the lake house. Love you, man.

input:
Sono stata in questa trattoria due sere fa con mia sorella e devo dire che ne è valsa la pena. Il locale è piccolo, con pochi tavoli in legno e una luce calda che rende l'atmosfera accogliente anche per chi arriva da una giornata pesante. Ci hanno accolte con un sorriso e ci hanno subito proposto il vino della casa, un rosso leggero che abbinato alle bruschette ai pomodorini è stato una piacevole sorpresa.

Per il primo abbiamo scelto le tagliatelle al ragù d'anatra, che erano cotte al punto giusto e condite con una salsa densa e profumata. Mia sorella ha preso i gnocchi di zucca con burro e salvia, e ha detto che erano tra i migliori assaggiati in questo periodo. Le porzioni sono generose senza essere eccessive, e si percepisce che tutto viene preparato con cura e ingredienti di stagione.

Il servizio merita un capitolo a parte. Il cameriere era attento senza essere invadente, ci ha consigliato un dessert che non conoscevamo, una crema al mascarpone con amarene, e ha accettato con garbo la nostra richiesta di dividere il conto. Nei momenti di maggiore affluenza qualche attesa in più c'è stata, ma nulla di preoccupante, e il personale ha sempre tenuto sotto controllo la situazione con calma.

Qualche piccola critica, per onestà: la sala è abbastanza rumorosa quando è piena, quindi se cercate una cena tranquilla conviene prenotare un tavolo vicino alla finestra. Anche il parcheggio è limitato e in strada bisogna essere pazienti. Sono dettagli che non compromettono l'esperienza complessiva.

In conclusione, consiglio questo posto a chi vuole mangiare bene in un ambiente semplice e curato. Il rapporto qualità prezzo mi è sembrato onesto e torneremo sicuramente, magari in una serata di primavera per sederci anche all'esterno. Consiglio vivamente di prenotare nel fine settimana.

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on November 14 so I don't forget the details later. I went to the clinic on Alder Street in the Riverside neighborhood, which is about a fifteen minute drive from my apartment. My name is Frances Holloway and I came in because of the numbness in my left hand that started about three weeks ago. Dr. Okafor listened carefully, tested my grip strength, and checked my reflexes. She thinks it is most likely carpal tunnel syndrome from all the typing at work, but she wants me to get nerve conduction studies before she decides anything for sure.

She gave me a wrist splint to wear at night and told me to avoid gripping my phone for long stretches. She also prescribed a mild anti-inflammatory for two weeks. I asked whether the numbness could be something more serious, and she said the exam didn't show signs of that, but she wants the follow-up tests to rule it out. The referral went to Westside Imaging and they called me the next morning to schedule for November 21.

For my own notes: bring the splint, keep a log of when the tingling is worst, and call the clinic if the numbness spreads to my arm or if I notice weakness. Frances, don't skip the appointment this time. Email reminders went to frances.holloway@mailbox.com, so check that inbox too.

input:
Friends and family, I want to start by thanking you all for coming. Fionnuala was never one for fuss, so I suspect she'd be a little embarrassed to see this many of us crammed into one room, but she would also be quietly delighted. She spent forty-one years telling anyone who would listen that she didn't need a crowd, and then she would go out of her way to make sure every person in her life felt they had a seat at her table.

She was born on the 14th of July in a small house above the harbour in Waterford, the second of five children, and she never let anyone forget that being the middle child made her the peacemaker. When she moved to Vancouver in 1998, with two suitcases and a letter of acceptance from the nursing program, she wrote home every single Sunday. Those letters were full of weather complaints, terrible coffee, and long, funny descriptions of the people she met on the bus. Mam kept every one of them in a shoebox under the stairs, and I found them last week. Reading them, I could hear her voice on every page.

In Canada she built a life that was entirely her own. She learned to ski badly, grew tomatoes that never ripened, and took in a string of stray cats before settling on a grumpy grey tabby named Dougal, who ruled her apartment with total authority for nearly fifteen years. Dougal would sit on her chest every morning until she woke up, and she claimed that was the only alarm clock she ever trusted. When people asked why she never got a dog, she'd say she had already found the animal she deserved.

Fionnuala had a rule that she passed on to all of us: always answer a message from someone you love, even if it's just a single emoji. Many of you received those little replies from her, often late at night, often with a typo she refused to correct. Her online presence was small but devoted; if you ever wanted to find her, you looked for @fionn_on_the_go, where she posted photographs of sunsets, half-finished knitting projects, and the occasional furious rant about parking. Her last post, a picture of the harbour in Vancouver with the caption "home is wherever someone is waiting," now feels like a message meant for us.

So tonight I am asking you to do what she would have wanted. Call someone you have not spoken to in a while. Write a letter, even a short one. Make terrible coffee and drink it anyway. Sit with a friend and let the silence be comfortable. That was Fionnuala's gift, and it is ours now to keep. We will miss her every day, and we will carry her with us, one small kindness at a time.

input:
My name is Noa, and I am the youngest of Jonathan's four children. Standing here, I keep thinking about how Dad always found a reason to be in the car at dawn. He was born in Haifa in the summer of 1952, and he never stopped loving the sea he grew up beside. He would drive us down to the water before school on any morning he could, sometimes with the radio on and sometimes in complete silence, and he never once complained about the early start.

Jonathan trained as a civil engineer at the Technion, and he used to say the graduates of that place had a particular kind of stubbornness that he hoped never left them. He carried that stubbornness into everything. When the roof leaked in our flat in Haifa, he climbed up there himself with a ladder he had borrowed from a neighbour and a tin of sealant he had argued the shopkeeper into discounting. He wanted things built to last, and he wanted people to last too.

He spent the last years of his life in Be'er Sheva, where he moved to be close to my sister Michal and her family. The grandchildren adored him. He taught the older ones chess on the balcony in the evenings, and he let the little ones win just often enough that they never felt cheated. Every visit began with him asking whether we had eaten, and every visit ended with him pressing something into our hands, a jar of olives, a folded note, a few shekels for the bus.

He was taken to Rambam Hospital in the second week of June, and for a while we believed he would come home again. The nurses there were patient with all of us, and the doctors explained everything honestly, which Dad would have appreciated. He held on longer than anyone expected, and I think it was because he still had questions about the world that he wanted answered.

Jonathan, we will miss your terrible puns, your insistence that every problem has a load-bearing solution, and your hands, always reaching for ours at the crossing. Thank you for building the foundations we now stand on. Rest well, Abba.

With all my love,
Oscar

input:
I finally made it to Savannah this fall, and I have to admit the Spanish moss sold me before I even got out of the car. My name is Sloren, though my college roommates still call me Lo, and I live in Charleston, so this was a short drive that felt like a proper trip. I came down on November 9th, which was my thirty-first birthday, and I decided that the best present I could give myself was three days with no alarm clock and no work email. My dog Biscuit came along too. He is a scruffy six-year-old beagle mix who thinks every fountain in the squares is his personal water bowl, so we spent a lot of time walking slowly and letting him sniff.

We stayed in a small guesthouse off Jones Street, and I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to be within walking distance of the squares without the noise. Each morning I wandered over to Forsyth Park, got a coffee from a cart near the fountain, and sat on a bench while Biscuit tried to befriend every jogger. In the afternoons Lo and I, meaning me talking to myself on the phone with my sister, wandered through the River Street shops and ate she-crab soup at a place with sticky wooden tables. Nothing about the trip was ambitious, and that was exactly the point.

If you go in November, pack a light jacket for the evenings, because the humidity drops and the breeze off the river gets chilly after sunset. Book the ghost tour early, since it sells out on weekends, and bring a bag for your dog's treats and a spare leash, because the squares are busier than you expect. I left feeling rested in a way I hadn't in months, and Biscuit slept the whole ride home.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus, Hannah's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words before we all get too full of roast lamb to listen. I promise to keep it short. Mostly.

I want to start with a confession. When Hannah first told our family she was moving to Auckland, I assumed it would last about six months. She had a habit of falling in love with a place and then discovering it wasn't quite the one she'd imagined. But she packed up her flat in Leeds on the 14th of May, five years ago, with a single suitcase, a box of books, and Biscuit, her ridiculous ginger cat who has never once behaved himself on a long-haul flight. I still remember the look on the airport official's face when Biscuit yowled the entire way through passport control.

That cat, I should say, is responsible for more of this evening than anyone realises. It was Biscuit who wandered into Ella's garden in Ponsonby during Hannah's second winter there, and it was Ella who came over the fence in her dressing gown to get him back. Hannah has told the story so many times that it has become family legend. Ella likes to point out that Hannah had already been ignoring the rules about cats in the flat for a year before that. Hannah says it was a fair trade.

For those of you who have only known Hannah since she came home for Christmas, let me share a little of who she was before the move. She was always the one organising the family photos, always the one remembering birthdays, and always the one who would drive four hours in the rain if someone needed a lift. Moving to the other side of the world didn't change any of that. If anything, it made her more deliberate about the people she keeps close, and I'm lucky to be counted among them.

When the two of them got engaged, Ella asked me to help find a date that didn't clash with the rugby final or the school fête. We settled on the 23rd of May, and I have to admit, it was the right choice. The weather has held, the flowers are exactly what Hannah wanted, and the cat, I'm told, has been fed and is sulking politely at home.

So please raise your glasses. To Hannah and Ella, to two countries and the people who have travelled between them to be here tonight, and to the stubborn ginger cat who started it all. Cheers.

input:
Dear diary,

Today was one of those days where everything ran late. I woke up at half six, which felt like a gift until I realised I'd forgotten to charge my phone, so I spent the morning scrambling to find the charger while Mum shouted from the kitchen about the bins. Dylan was still asleep in the spare room when I left, which is typical. He had been up until two playing games with Liam, and I'm fairly sure they'll both blame me if they miss the bus again.

I went to Hartwell Secondary College for the morning. Mrs Okafor wants us to hand in the drafts of the history essay by the fourteenth of March, which gives me exactly three days to stop procrastinating. She also pulled me aside after class to say the school had received a call from the Royal Melbourne Hospital about a placement for year eleven students next term. Apparently they want someone to help with the volunteer desk, and she put my name forward without asking me first. I'm not sure whether to be flattered or annoyed. I said I would think about it, which is what I always say when I actually want to say yes.

After school I stopped at the post office on Carlisle Street because Dylan had left his passport application there and needed it sorted before his trip. The clerk was lovely, though she kept glancing at the form and asking me to confirm the address. It is 14 Bramley Court, Brunswick West, and I had to repeat it twice because the postcode is always the part I forget. Dad rang while I was waiting and asked whether I had the number for the accountant. I read him 03 9284 6157 off the back of an old envelope, and he said it was the wrong one. Typical.

In the evening I finally sat down with the essay. I got about four hundred words in before my eyes started to close. The argument about the wool trade is actually quite interesting once you get into it, and I think Mrs Okafor will like the angle I've taken, even if the conclusion is a bit rushed.

Before bed I messaged Dana to ask whether she'd be at the library on Thursday. She replied with a row of laughing faces and said she'd bring the good biscuits if I promised to actually finish the reading. I promised. We'll see.

Night, diary. Tomorrow has to be better than today.

My name is Noa Levi, and I was asked to speak today because I was Nadav's sister, and because for forty-one years I was the one who got the phone calls at two in the morning. Nadav grew up in Haifa, in a small flat above the bakery on Herzl Street, and from the age of six he was convinced he would become a pilot. He studied engineering at the Technion, and he never once let us forget the name of that place, or the fact that he had walked there every morning with a sandwich wrapped in foil. He used to say the sandwich was the real reason he passed his exams.

When Nadav was thirty-four he was taken to Rambam Hospital after a fall from a ladder at the back of his parents' house, the house he had promised our mother he would repaint for her birthday. The doctors there were kind to him, and he spent the following week making jokes about the nurses' shoes. He was always the one who made the room lighter. Even on the last day, when he could barely speak, he asked his daughter to make sure the blue Subaru, registration 45-612-38, was sold to someone who would look after it the way he had.

So today I want to ask you to do one small thing for him. Next time you pass a bakery, buy something warm, and eat it slowly, the way he would have. Call a sibling you have not spoken to in a while. When Noam was thirty-two he was taken to Hadassah Hospital after a fall from a ladder at the back of his parents' house, the house he had promised our mother he would repaint for her birthday. Friends, family, and everyone who has travelled a long way to be here tonight, thank you for sharing this day with Bastien and Claire. I have known Bastien since our first year at the Lycée Henri-Bergson in Angers, where he was the boy who somehow always knew the answer in chemistry and then pretended he had not. Even then he had a habit of taking care of people quietly, without making a fuss about it.

Bastien was born in Saumur, and I think that is why he has always been happiest near a river with a good bottle of wine and a plan for the weekend. He still talks about the summer of 2009, when we tried to cycle the Loire in four days and gave up after two. Claire, I want you to know that this is the man you are marrying: someone who will happily spend an afternoon fixing a bicycle chain for a stranger and then forget to mention it.

Claire, you brought calm into his life, and he brought you a steady stream of terrible puns, which you have borne with remarkable grace. On behalf of all of us, I hope you both know how lucky you are. Please raise your glasses to Bastien and Claire, and to a marriage full of long walks and short arguments. Santé!

Hello again, Sunshine Public School families! This is Harpreet Kaur from Class 7-C, and I have been asked to share a few lines about our Science Fair preparations for this month's newsletter. Our team had a wonderful time gathering ideas, and I want to thank everyone who helped out.

When the notice first went up on the board on 3 February, I was not sure I would be brave enough to take part. My project is on rainwater harvesting, and I spent most weekends at home building a small model with plastic bottles, sand, and gravel. My younger brother Ayaan was my most honest critic, and he kept insisting that the funnel should be bigger. He was right, and after a few trial runs in our courtyard, the model finally filtered a glass of muddy water into something almost clear.

Several classmates have been working on equally interesting topics. Rohit Nair is studying how different soils affect plant growth, and Meera Joseph has built a solar oven that cooks rice surprisingly well on a sunny afternoon. Our science teacher, Mrs. Radhika Venkatesh, has been patient with every one of us, even when our glue dried up at the worst possible moment. She asked us to keep a daily log of observations, which has turned out to be the most useful habit we have picked up this term.

For parents who want to follow our progress or ask questions about the fair, the school office can be reached on 0484-2758193 between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays. Those who prefer messages can also write to me on Instagram at @harpreet.explores, where I post photos of each stage of my model. Please keep in mind that I am a student and will reply only after my homework is finished, so a little patience would be appreciated.

Finally, I would like to mention Biscuit, our golden retriever, who has been an unexpected member of my project team. He sat beside my workbench for hours while I cut plastic and measured sand, and he never once knocked over a bottle. Ayaan says Biscuit should get a certificate too, and I think he might deserve one. Thank you for reading, and see you all at the fair on 21 February!

Okay, so you know how I've been dragging my feet about the whole Lisbon thing? Well, I finally called my mom last night and told her, and honestly it went better than I expected. Brenda, that's my older sister, was on the line too, and she just kept saying "finally!" like I'd been holding out on her for years. I grew up in Dayton, Ohio, so Mom immediately started in on whether I'd be eating enough vegetables over there. Typical.

The thing that's been eating at me is the job. I've been a senior analyst at Harlow Mercer Logistics for six years now, and they actually offered me a promotion to team lead before I even mentioned I was thinking of leaving. My manager, Gary Pruitt, took it pretty well considering. He asked me to stay on through the end of November so they can transition my accounts, which I think is fair. I told him the 14th would be my last day in the office, and he didn't argue.

I keep telling myself I'm not running away. Brenda thinks I am, and maybe she's partly right. But when I pictured myself at fifty still in that same cubicle, I got this knot in my stomach that wouldn't go away. So I'm going. I'll send you the apartment listing tonight, and please, please come visit in the spring. You owe me a proper fish dinner.

I am Alana Whitfield, a clinical nurse educator at St. Brigid's Regional Hospital in Saskatoon, where I have worked on the cardiac step-down unit since 2014. Before moving into education, I completed my Bachelor of Science in Nursing at the University of Saskatchewan, and I still count the simulation labs there among the most formative years of my practice. My current work focuses on helping new graduates build confidence at the bedside, and I have developed a preceptorship program that has been adopted across three units.

Outside the hospital I volunteer with a community palliative outreach group and serve on the regional nursing ethics committee. I enjoy long road trips, and my old Subaru still carries the plate SKX 4417 that my family teases me about. When I am not reviewing care plans, I am usually hiking the trails along the South Saskatchewan River with my sister Amelia, who is training to become a midwife in Regina.

Hello from Room 14! I wanted to share a little update from our Grade 5 class this month, since so many of you asked how the new science unit is going. My name is Tamar Levi and I am the class teacher here at Ort Ramat Aviv Primary School, where I have been teaching for six years now. Ramat Aviv is a lovely place to work, and the walk from the bus stop on Chen Street gives me time to plan my lessons before the first bell.

This year we started the unit on plants and water cycles, and the children have been wonderfully curious. On the first Tuesday of September we set up a small experiment on the windowsill: one jar with soil, one with sand, and one with just a paper towel. Within a week, the soil jar had sprouted two bean seedlings, and the room erupted in cheers. Several students have asked if they can bring a jar home, so I have started sending small labelled kits with them.

I also want to thank the parents who came to the Back to School evening on September 12th. It was a full house, and I really appreciated the thoughtful questions about homework routines and reading logs. If you missed it, please drop me a note at tamar.levi@ortramatviv.example and I will happily send you the slides and the reading list we discussed.

Several of you also asked about the field trip to the Hula Valley Nature Reserve. The date is set for September 26th, and the permission forms will go home in the next few days. Please sign and return them by the 20th so the transport company has enough notice. We will be travelling by coach and returning in time for pickup at 14:30.

Finally, a reminder that our library corner now has a new shelf of nonfiction books about animals and weather. Students may borrow two at a time for two weeks. Thank you all for your continued support. It truly makes a difference to see the children so eager to learn.

Warmly,
Tamar

I started volunteering on that ward every Saturday afterwards. My passport number is on the volunteer form, and I have since filled in more paperwork than I can count, yet the work itself still feels like the clearest thing I have ever done. I want to be the doctor who takes the time to explain.

I am writing this statement at the request of the officer on duty, to set out what I saw and heard on the evening in question. I had finished my shift at the shop and was walking home along the main road when I noticed a car parked half on the pavement with its hazard lights on. A man was standing beside it, speaking loudly into a phone, and a woman was sitting in the passenger seat with her hands over her face. I did not approach at first, but after a few minutes the man became more agitated and I could hear him shouting that he would not let her leave.

I crossed to the other side of the road and kept my distance, but I stayed close enough to see what was happening. The woman got out of the car at one point and tried to walk away, and the man grabbed her arm. She pulled free and called out for help in English and then in another language I did not recognise. A second man came out of a nearby doorway and told the first man to calm down, after which both of them went back inside the building. I took a photograph of the car's registration plate and of the entrance, which I can provide on request.

I am giving this account voluntarily and believe it to be accurate to the best of my memory. I was not injured and did not have any further contact with the people involved. I am happy to attend a formal interview or to provide any additional material the investigating team may need.

Hi, I need some help thinking through a situation at work and I'm not sure how to handle it. My name is Marcus and I'm a senior analyst at Brightline Logistics in Columbus, Ohio. For about eight months I've been reporting to a new operations director, Zoe Whitfield, and things have gotten tense. In our team meeting on August 12th she publicly questioned a forecast I'd spent two weeks building, and then the next day she forwarded my draft to the VP with her own name on the top slide. I didn't say anything in the moment because I didn't want to look defensive.

Since then I've been second-guessing everything. I double-check every email before I send it, and I've started copying my manager, Dana Okafor, on updates just so there's a paper trail. Zoe has noticed, I think. Last week she asked me to stop cc'ing people on routine stuff, and her tone made it clear she didn't appreciate it. I'm worried that if I push back too hard, I'll be labelled difficult, but if I stay quiet, I'll keep losing credit for my own work.

What would you do in my position? I'm especially interested in whether I should talk to Dana directly, or go to HR first, or try a calm one-on-one with Zoe before escalating anything. I want to be fair to her too, since it's possible she simply doesn't realise how it's landing. Any structure or wording you'd suggest for that conversation would be really helpful.

The messages have come from an account on Instagram with the handle @shadow_ridge_82, which first contacted me after I posted photos from my cousin's engagement party. Since then the account has sent me over forty messages, many of them describing where I was on particular afternoons and naming the café on Maroondah Highway where I usually have lunch.

The content has escalated over the past week. On 9 September the sender wrote that they had been waiting outside my workplace in Croydon and that I should "stop pretending not to notice." Ima, Bracha, I still hear your voice when I open the door on Friday afternoons, calling out that the soup is almost ready even when it clearly wasn't. For forty-one years you ran the kitchen at the community centre in Haifa, and every single Friday the people who came through it knew they were welcome. Ronen from the bakery on Herzl Street told me last week that you once gave him a job when he had nothing, and asked him to come back on Sunday to learn how to fold the challah properly. You never mentioned it to anyone. That was your way.

You were the one who kept the family together through every argument and every long distance. When my brother moved to Eilat, you called him every Thursday at seven. When I finally took the leap and moved abroad, you sent me long messages about the weather back home, the price of tomatoes at the shuk, and which neighbours had new grandchildren. Your handwriting was always cramped on the page because you wrote too much to fit in the space given. Dina Levi, who worked beside you for twenty years, said it best: you never let anyone walk past without a word.

Ima, we will keep your recipes, your loud laugh, and your stubborn refusal to let anyone pay for coffee at Café Nomi on Ben Gurion Street, where the staff greeted you by name for three decades. If anyone needs to reach us about the memorial, write to bracha.family.memorial@gmail.com or message @bracha_haifa_kitchen. You can also call 052-734-1186 and someone will answer. Rest now. We have the soup on.

I'm writing this down so I don't forget what Dr. Hennessy told me at my appointment on Tuesday 11 February. My name is Laoise Brennan, and I went to the surgery on Main Street in Kilkenny, the one next to Nolan's Pharmacy, because I've had a sore left knee since Christmas and it's been getting worse on the stairs.

Dr. Hennessy had a look at it and asked me to walk up and down the corridor while she watched. She pressed around the joint and asked whether it locked or gave way. It doesn't lock, but it clicks and sometimes feels like it might buckle. She thinks it's most likely a cartilage problem made worse by my new routine of running three mornings a week at the gym in Kilkenny, Fitzpatrick's Fitness, which I joined in January with big plans.

She wants me to have an X-ray at the Waterford Regional clinic before the end of the month and to stop the running for at least six weeks. I asked if swimming would be fine, and she said yes, and that cycling on flat ground is probably okay too. I'm to take ibuprofen with food for the swelling, not more than the packet says. She also gave me a referral letter, which I'm to bring with me to the X-ray, and the appointment for that is on Thursday 20 February at nine.

I told her about Biscuit, my old collie, who has been limping too, and she laughed and said I should book him in with the vet before he gets as stubborn as I am. My sister Orla drove me home because I didn't want to be on my own in the car with the leg stiff, and she made me promise to phone her the minute the X-ray is done. I've written her name and number on the back of the referral so I don't lose it.

So my plan is simple. Rest the knee, swim on Mondays and Wednesdays, keep up the ibuprofen with breakfast, and go to the scan on the twentieth. If the pain gets worse, or the knee swells up in the night, I'm to ring the surgery straight away rather than wait for the next slot. I'll update this when I have the results.

I asked if swimming would be fine, and she said yes, and that cycling on flat ground is probably okay too. I'm to take ibuprofen with food for the swelling, not more than the packet says. She also gave me a referral letter, which I'm to bring with me to the X-ray, and the appointment for that is on Thursday 13 February at nine.

I told her about Rusty, my old collie, who has been limping too, and she laughed and said I should book him in with the vet before he gets as stubborn as I am. My sister Niamh drove me home because I didn't want to be on my own in the car with the leg stiff, and she made me promise to phone her the minute the X-ray is done. I've written her name and number on the back of the referral so I don't lose it.

So my plan is simple. Rest the knee, swim on Mondays and Wednesdays, keep up the ibuprofen with breakfast, and go to the scan on the thirteenth. If the pain gets worse, or the knee swells up in the night, I'm to ring the surgery straight away rather than wait for the next slot. I'll update this when I have the results.

input:
August 14

Dear diary, today I finally sat down to sort out the mess on my desk, and I found the envelope from the DMV with my passport number on it, 548213769, which I keep meaning to put somewhere safer. Ruth Ashford, that's me, still can't believe I've been at Brightline Logistics for nine years. Mr. Okafor from HR pulled me aside this morning and said they want me to lead the Denver transition team in the fall, which is either a compliment or a warning, depending on how you look at it.

My sister Rachel called around noon. She reminded me that her wedding is on August 29 at the lake house in Boulder, and I promised I'd finally buy a dress that doesn't make me look like a bridesmaid from 1994. Rachel says I'm being dramatic. Maybe I am. But she's the one who cried through the entire rehearsal dinner last year, so I think I've earned a little drama.

I went home to 2218 Maple Ridge Drive after work, which is still the best thing about living in Denver. The porch light was on because my neighbor Lionel had stopped by to water the ferns while I was gone. He left a note on the door that said, "Ruth, your plants have more personality than most people I know." I laughed out loud, which felt good after a long day.

In the evening I made soup and watched the rain move across the window. I thought about whether I actually want to lead the team or whether I just want to be asked. Those feel like different things, and I haven't figured out which one is driving me.

Before bed I wrote Rachel a text: "Fine. I'll buy the dress. Send me the color swatches and stop calling me dramatic." She replied with a row of heart emojis and a picture of a cake. Tomorrow I will call the Brightline recruiter back and ask for a few days to think. Then I will go shopping.

I am writing to describe the water damage that occurred in my flat on the third floor of a building on ul. Kopernika in Kraków, which I have rented since 2019. On the evening of 14 May, I returned from work to find water pouring from the ceiling of the living room. My neighbour from the flat above, Tomasz Wrona, had left his bathroom tap running while he was away on a business trip, and the overflow spread across two floors before anyone noticed.

When I first arrived, I could hear the water dripping and see that the parquet near the balcony door had already lifted. I called my landlord, Mr. Stanisław Lach, who came round within the hour with a torch and a bucket. Between us we moved the sofa, my desk and most of the books onto the landing. My partner Olga, whom everyone calls Ola, arrived shortly after and helped carry the rugs down to the courtyard. We did not sleep much that night.

The damage is extensive. The laminate in the hallway and bedroom is swollen beyond repair, the bottom four rows of the kitchen cabinets have warped, and the plasterboard along the north wall is soft to the touch. I have photographed each area and kept the receipts from the emergency drying company we hired on 16 May, which charged 1,240 zloty for two days of dehumidifiers. Ola has also listed the items she lost, including a set of her grandmother's china and a vintage record player, with approximate values.

When I spoke to the building manager on 19 May, she confirmed that the faulty tap seal had been reported twice before, in March and April. I have attached copies of those complaints. Tomasz has been very apologetic and has agreed to contact his own insurer, though I understand his policy may not cover the full amount.

I would be grateful if you could arrange an inspection at your earliest convenience. I am reachable at 512-374-908 or by email at oliwia.nowicka@poczta-kr.pl, and I am happy to meet an adjuster at the flat on any weekday after 4 p.m. I have also been posting updates on my blog under the handle @oli_on_kopernika, where I have been documenting the repairs for friends, though I am glad to share anything relevant directly.

Sunday, 14 February. Dr Mokoena asked me to write down what I notice in my body when I think about my mother, so here goes. Cwenga has been circling the same worry for three weeks now: that she will never be the daughter her mother expected. Born in Pietermaritzburg in a house with a jacaranda out front, she was always the one who got her head down and stayed there. She finished her nursing diploma at Pholela Hospital and then came to Johannesburg with two suitcases and a letter of admission she still keeps in her wallet. When I say all of this to Dr Mokoena, my chest tightens, and I notice I start tapping my foot.

We talked about Biscuit, the old Jack Russell who used to sleep on the end of Cwenga's bed when she was a child in Pietermaritzburg. He died in 2011, and she still says that was the first time she understood that love can be something you keep carrying without anyone asking you to. Dr Mokoena wondered aloud whether the guilt she feels about her mother is similar: a weight she carries because she loves her, not because she is failing her.

I want to remember that Cwenga did call her mother last Tuesday, 18 February, even though the call lasted only nine minutes. She said afterwards that she felt steadier. Next session, we agreed I would bring the question of what she actually wants from that relationship, not what she thinks she owes it.

input:
March has been a hard month to get through, and I want to write some of it down before my next session with Dr. Okafor. Priya has been back in Sudbury since the start of the month, helping our mom sort through the house after Dad's stroke. My sister Meera keeps calling her Pree, which nobody else does, and Priya says it still makes her feel about twelve. She hasn't been sleeping well, and on the 9th she said she felt like she was living in two places at once, half in Toronto where her job at St. Michael's Hospital still waits for her and half in the kitchen in Sudbury where the mail keeps piling up.

We talked about guilt, which I know is always on the agenda. Priya feels she should have come home sooner. She also feels relieved when she gets back on the highway to Toronto, and then she feels guilty about the relief. I reminded her that caregiving splits people in exactly this way, and that the relief doesn't cancel out the love. She nodded, but I could tell she wasn't convinced yet. We also talked about the dog, Biscuit, who has been sleeping outside her bedroom door since she arrived, which she says is the only thing in the house that feels normal.

For next week I'd like her to try one small thing for herself, even ten minutes a day that nobody else asks anything of. She said she'd think about it. I'll check in on that when she comes in on March 18, and I'll ask her how the call with her university advisor at Laurentian went, since she mentioned she might pick up a course in the fall.

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on Thursday, the 14th of August, so I don't forget the details. I'm Rainer, 47 years old, and I live in Prenzlauer Berg here in Berlin, just off Kastanienallee. My GP is Dr. Hermann Vogt at the practice on Danziger Strasse, and I've been seeing him for about six years now.

The reason for the visit was the tightness in my chest that I'd been noticing on the stairs at work. I work at Brandt & Lindqvist GmbH in Mitte, where I've been a logistics coordinator for almost twelve years, so most of my day is spent on my feet or running between the warehouse and the office. My wife, Katrin, came along because she wanted to hear what the doctor said first-hand, which I was glad of, since I tend to forget half of what I'm told.

Dr. Vogt listened to my heart and lungs for a long time and then asked a lot of questions about my sleep, my diet and how much I've been drinking since the spring. He ordered a resting ECG, some blood work for cholesterol and blood sugar, and a referral to a cardiologist, Dr. Sabine Hoffmann, whose office is on Kantstrasse. The appointment with her is on the 26th of August at 9:40, so I've put it in the calendar and set two alarms.

He was calm about it, though he was clear that I should not ignore it. He asked me to cut back on salt and to walk for thirty minutes most days rather than taking the lift at work. He also said that if the pain comes on at rest, or spreads into my arm or jaw, I should call the emergency number straight away and not wait for the next appointment.

On the way home Katrin said I looked relieved, and I think I was. It's easier to face a problem when someone has given it a name and a plan. I'll send my blood test results to my email, rainer.meissner@gmx.de, once they come through, and I'll update this note after the cardiologist visit.

Rainer

input:
Thank you all for being here today. Standing up in front of so many people who loved the same person I did is harder than I expected, so please bear with me. I have known for weeks what I wanted to say, and somehow every version of it sounds too small.

What I keep coming back to is how she showed up. Not with grand gestures, but with a casual, dependable kindness. A cup of tea appearing when you had not even noticed you needed one. A phone call on a bad afternoon that was really just a way of saying, I'm thinking of you. She had a way of making people feel that their ordinary days were worth paying attention to, and that is a rarer gift than most of us realise until it is gone.

So today I am asking each of us to carry a little of that forward. Call the friend you have been meaning to ring. Make the tea. Notice the person quietly struggling in the corner of the room. She would not want a fuss made, but she would be glad to know that the way she lived is still being passed along, one ordinary kindness at a time. Thank you.

Da allora, Ricky, non hai mai smesso di cercare la persona giusta con la stessa pazienza.

Mi ha chiesto solo una cosa: se secondo me avresti detto di sì. Gli ho risposto che Giulia non ha mai fatto nulla a metà, e che se ti ha guardato in quel modo, era perché avevi già deciso.

Allora alziamo i bicchieri a Riccardo e Giulia, e alla casa che costruiranno insieme, con più scale di quante ne abbia il palazzo di via dei Cappellari e, spero, con un gatto che ogni mattina chieda la colazione proprio come faceva Brigante. Salute!

My name is Rohan, and I was lucky enough to be Dhruv's younger brother for thirty-four years. Dhruv passed away on the 14th of June, just three weeks after his sixty-first birthday. For most of his working life he was the Chief Accounts Officer at Bharat Textile Mills in Coimbatore, but if you asked anyone in Race Course Road what he was really known for, they would tell you about the Sunday chai he shared with the shopkeepers outside Lakshmi Stores. He never walked past a neighbour without asking after their children, their knees, their mother's health.

Dhruv taught me to ride a bicycle on the wide lanes behind our house, and he taught me that a good ledger and a good heart are not so different: both need to be kept honest every single day. He balanced everything he owed to others with a patience that embarrassed the rest of us. When my father fell ill, Dhruv drove him to the hospital every Tuesday for eleven months without once complaining about the traffic on Avinashi Road.

I am told that Dhruv's last words to his grandson were a reminder to finish his homework before the cricket match. That was so typical of him: the small, practical instruction given with love. Please keep his email, dhruv.raman@bmills.co.in, open a little longer if you are writing to us, because we will read every message. Thank you all for coming today to remember a man who made ordinary days feel important.

For most of his working life he was the Chief Accounts Officer at Bhagya Textile Mills in Madurai, but if you asked anyone in Race Course Lane what he was really known for, they would tell you about the Sunday chai he shared with the shopkeepers outside Saraswathi Stores. He never walked past a neighbour without asking after their children, their knees, their mother's health.

Dinesh taught me to ride a bicycle on the wide lanes behind our house, and he taught me that a good ledger and a good heart are not so different: both need to be kept honest every single day. He balanced everything he owed to others with a patience that embarrassed the rest of us. When my father fell ill, Dinesh drove him to the hospital every Tuesday for eleven months without once complaining about the traffic on Bypass Road.

I am told that Dinesh's last words to his grandson were a reminder to finish his homework before the cricket match. That was so typical of him: the small, practical instruction given with love. Please keep his email, dinesh.rathnam@bhmills.co.in, open a little longer if you are writing to us, because we will read every message. Thank you all for coming today to remember a man who made ordinary days feel important.

I've been coming to Mang Dodong's Carinderia on 47 Rizal Extension, Barangay San Roque, Cabanatuan City for almost six years now, and it never disappoints. Last Saturday, September 14, I stopped by after my shift at Pacific Harbor Logistics, where I work as a dispatch coordinator. It was my 34th birthday and my coworkers insisted on a proper celebration, so we ordered a whole tray of kare-kare, crispy pata, and garlic rice. The oxtail was tender, the peanut sauce was rich without being cloying, and the pata skin shattered the way it should. Mang Dodong himself came out to check on our table and even remembered that I prefer my bagoong on the side.

The only reason I'm docking a star is the wait. We sat for nearly forty minutes before our first dish came out, and the place was not that crowded. I understand that good food takes time, and the staff were apologetic, but a little communication about the delay would have gone a long way. The lady who runs the counter, Ate Vilma, was friendly and kept our drinks topped up while we waited, which I appreciated.

If you're in the area, make sure to try the sisig on a weekday when the kitchen isn't swamped. Follow their Facebook page at @mangdodongcarinderia for their daily menu and specials. Overall, a solid five-star experience marred only by the slow service.

input: Growing up in a small coastal town, I spent most of my free time helping my grandmother restore an old wooden boat she had inherited from her father. Every weekend we sanded, varnished and argued about the best way to replace rotten planks. Those afternoons taught me patience and the value of working carefully through problems that have no quick fix. When I started secondary school, I found myself drawn to physics for the same reason: I want to understand how things hold together and why they fail. I hope to bring that same persistence to a university course where I can keep asking questions that do not yet have answers.

Nina, you won't believe the week I've had. Remember I told you I'd finally sort out my residency paperwork in Oaxaca? My full name is Natalia Ruiz Ocampo, and they spelled it three different ways before they got it right. Somehow it was still easier than the bank.

The funny part is that I had to give them my address too, Calle Tlacolula 214, Colonia Reforma, and the clerk asked me to repeat it twice because my handwriting looked like a doctor's. Then she asked for my mother's full name for the family file. I said Teresa, and she wrote down Teresa Ocampo Vidal without even looking up. Mom would have been thrilled to be official paperwork for once.

Anyway, I walked out with a receipt and a tiny bit of hope. Come visit in January, I'll make you the mole my abuela taught me, and we can laugh about the clerk who thought my signature was a seismograph reading. Call me when you get this.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Kenji, Jun's older brother, and I've been trying to find the right words for this moment for about three weeks now. Jun has always been the one who knows exactly what to say, so I'm a little nervous standing in front of you all.

Jun was born in Sendai, in a small apartment above a bakery that smelled of melon bread every single morning.
