input:
I've been coming to this little bakery near the old market square for about a year now, and I finally felt I owed it a proper review. The place is tiny, with maybe four wooden tables and a counter that always smells of cinnamon and fresh rye. The staff are warm without being overbearing. On my last visit, the woman behind the counter remembered that I like my coffee black and didn't even need to ask.

The bread is the real draw. The sourdough has a crackly crust and an open, chewy crumb, and the poppy seed rolls are the best I've had outside of a family kitchen. Pastries sell out early, so if you want the apple turnovers, go before ten. Prices are fair for the quality, and the cash-only policy is a bit old-fashioned but nobody seems to mind.

My only complaint is the wait at lunchtime, when the queue spills out onto the pavement and the tables are hard to come by. Still, I'd recommend this place to anyone who wants honest food and a quiet corner to read. Ask for a seat by the window if you can get one. Go early, bring small change, and thank me later.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus Holloway, and I've had the honour of being Zara's older brother for twenty-nine years. Some of you have heard me tell the story of the time I taught her to ride a bike in our driveway in Halifax. She fell off roughly forty times, and not once did she cry. That's the Zara I've always known: stubborn, kind, and absolutely unwilling to quit on anything she cares about.

When Zara first told the family about Owen, she sent us a long text on a Sunday night, December 14th, and I remember reading it three times before I believed it. Owen, you clearly have no idea what you signed up for. You met someone who will argue with you about the thermostat, then make you soup when you've had a rough day. She'll remember your coffee order, your mother's birthday, and the name of your dog's vet. Thank you for loving her the way she deserves.

I want to say something about what Zara taught me during the hard years. When Dad got sick, she was the one who called every doctor, read every pamphlet, and somehow still found time to bring us dinner on Thursdays. People talk about strength as if it's loud. Hers is quiet and steady, and it has held our whole family together more than once.

So please raise your glasses with me. To Zara and Owen, to the years ahead of you, and to the many mornings you'll spend arguing over who gets the last slice of toast. You two have built something real, and we are all so proud to be standing here to celebrate it.

Love you both. Cheers!

Good morning, everyone. My name is Hendrik Vos, and I was lucky enough to be Kees's younger brother for fifty-one years. Most of you know him as the man who fixed your bicycle, your radio, or your leaking roof, and who never once let you pay for the parts. What you may not know is how much he hated being thanked. When Mum tried to tell the neighbours how he had sat with her through the night at the Antonius Ziekenhuis in Nieuwegein, he left the room. He was like that. Doing the work was enough for him.

He grew up in Utrecht, cycling to the Stedelijk Gymnasium every morning with a puncture kit in his bag and a book on his lap at the traffic lights. He studied engineering at Delft, and later, when people asked what he did, he would say he made things hum. I think that was the truest thing about him. He could not walk past a sound that was wrong without stopping to listen to it.

So today, if you are sad, I ask you to do one small thing he would have approved of. Check the thing in your house that has been rattling for months. Call a friend you have been meaning to ring. And if you need help with either, you can reach my office on 030 555 0142, where I will answer the phone myself, just as he would have. Thank you, Kees. Rust in peace, and may the tyres of your heaven always hold air.

Liebe Familie, liebe Freunde, liebe Anna, lieber Oskar,

Mein Name ist Matthias Brandt, und viele von euch kennen mich als Matze. Ich bin der Trauzeuge und seit fast zwanzig Jahren der Freund, der Oskar immer wieder daran erinnert, dass Pünktlichkeit eine Tugend ist. Dass er heute pünktlich vor dem Standesamt stand, grenzt an ein Wunder. Ich habe ihn selbst noch nie so nervös gesehen wie an diesem Vormittag am 14. Juni.

Oskar und ich haben uns damals in der Ausbildung bei der Stadtwerke Lindenau GmbH kennengelernt. Er war der junge Ingenieur, der in jeder Besprechung die besten Fragen stellte, und ich der Kollege, der ihm erklärte, wo in der Kantine der Kaffee am besten schmeckt. Aus dieser Zufallsbekanntschaft wurde eine Freundschaft, die bis heute hält. Heute ist Oskar Projektleiter bei den Stadtwerken, und ich glaube, er hat dort inzwischen mehr Ideen als Akten.

Was viele nicht wissen: Oskar hat eine besondere Gabe, Menschen zum Lachen zu bringen, ohne dass er es merkt. Als wir zusammen den Umzug von Anna nach Hamburg organisiert haben, hat er mitten im schlimmsten Regen einen Kartonstapel gerettet, indem er ihn kurzerhand als Regenschirm benutzt hat. Seitdem nennt ihn meine Familie nur noch Oski-Schirm, und der Name ist ihm geblieben.

Liebe Anna, du hast in Oskar jemanden gefunden, der dir zuhört, der deine Pläne ernst nimmt und der dich jeden Morgen mit einem Kaffee überrascht, selbst wenn er selbst verschlafen hat. Du bringst ihm Gelassenheit bei, und er bringt dir ein Lachen, das ansteckend ist. Ich habe selten zwei Menschen gesehen, die so gut zueinanderpassen.

Deshalb bitte ich alle, mit mir das Glas zu erheben: Auf Anna und Oskar, auf ihre gemeinsame Zukunft und auf viele Jahre voller Abenteuer, Umzüge und Regenschirm-Kartons. Prost!

I'm Sienna Thibodeau, and I've been a family physician in Québec for close to fourteen years. I was born in Sherbrooke, where my father ran a hardware store on Rue Wellington and my mother taught grade three at the school two blocks away. Those streets taught me early that a community is built one familiar face at a time, and that has shaped how I practise medicine ever since. I'm now 41, and I split my time between a clinic in the Plateau-Mont-Royal neighbourhood of Montréal and a mobile outreach program that visits rural communities across the Eastern Townships.

My work centres on chronic disease prevention and on making primary care reachable for people who have historically been left behind by the system. In November 2019 I helped launch a diabetes education circle that now meets every second Thursday at the community centre on Avenue du Parc, and in the years since, more than two hundred patients have completed it. I still believe the most important medical tool is a conversation held in a language the patient fully understands. When I'm not at work you'll likely find me cycling the Route Verte or tending a vegetable garden that is, admittedly, more ambitious than my schedule allows.

I share updates on public health and clinic life on social media under the handle @sienna.thibodeau.md, and I welcome messages from colleagues and patients alike. Feel free to write to me at sienna.thibodeau@clinique-parc.ca or visit the clinic at 4812 Avenue du Parc, Montréal, QC H2V 4E7. I look forward to sharing ideas with everyone at this conference.

input:
Dear Abuela,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the weather in Valencia has finally cooled down. I have been thinking about you a lot since the move. Mum says you have been asking after me every time she calls, so I wanted to write properly, with pen and paper, the way you taught me. Madrid is loud and enormous, but I am slowly learning where the good bakeries are, and the people at my new job at Hospital Clinico San Carlos have been kind to me. I work as a junior radiographer there, which I know you will proudly tell the whole street about.

My first week was chaotic. On the 9th of September I had to bring my passport and my ID card, number 49821736K, to the staff office, and the administrator joked that I looked more nervous than the patients. I laughed, but I was terrified. Marina, my flatmate, reminded me that Madrid is full of people who got lost in their first month and found their way anyway. She is right, as usual. Last Sunday I walked from the Retiro park all the way back and only needed the map twice.

I miss your lentil soup and the way you hum while you cook. Please give my love to Tio Julian and tell him I still owe him a game of cards. I will call on Sunday evening, after your programme finishes. Until then, take care of your knees and do not climb the ladder to fix the shutters again.

With all my love,
Maria

input: Growing up in a small coastal town in the far north, I spent most of my weekends helping on my whānau's farm. Mornings meant checking the fences, feeding the calves and listening to the wind come off the harbour. Those hours taught me patience and the value of work that matters to the people around you. Lately I have started to wonder how the land we farm might look in twenty years, and that question is what drew me to environmental science. I want to study how soil and water interact so that farms like the one I grew up on can keep feeding communities for generations to come.

I am Victoria Lindqvist, and for the past eleven years I have worked as Senior Clinical Informatics Analyst at Brookhaven Regional Medical Center in Tacoma, Washington. My work sits at the intersection of electronic health records and day-to-day nursing practice, which means I spend most of my time translating what clinicians need into systems that do not get in their way. Before joining Brookhaven I completed my master's in health informatics at the University of Washington, and I still count those two years in Seattle as the period that taught me the most about patient data.

Outside the hospital I am a volunteer tutor with a literacy program that meets at the Tacoma Public Library on Tuesday evenings. I also serve on the board of a small nonprofit that supports caregivers of people with dementia. Most mornings I drive my silver Subaru, registration WA 4XK 7710, across the Narrows Bridge to the medical center campus, and I have learned to leave early enough to enjoy the view of the water.

If you would like to reach me about the panel on interoperability, you can call my office at (253) 555-0148 or write to victoria.lindqvist@brookhavenrmc.org. I am happy to talk about anything from FHIR standards to the surprisingly difficult question of how to name a medication field so that a tired nurse at three in the morning understands it on the first read.

Rosalind "Roz" Whitfield, 68, of the Eastwood Park neighborhood on Larkspur Avenue in Dayton, Ohio, died peacefully on August 14 at Miami Valley Hospital, surrounded by the family who loved her most. She is survived by her husband of forty-one years, Gerald, her two daughters, Megan and Tessa, and four grandchildren who knew her as the keeper of the cookie tin and the loudest voice at every ballgame.

Roz spent thirty-two years teaching third grade at Fairview Elementary School, where generations of students learned to read with her patience and her red pen. Many of her former students still write to say she was the first teacher who made them believe they were clever. She retired in 2012 but never really stopped teaching; she tutored neighborhood kids at her kitchen table on Tuesdays and Thursdays until this spring.

Her closest friend and colleague, Bernadette "Bernie" Kowalski, shared lunch with her every Friday for nearly three decades. "Roz could make a room laugh and then tell you exactly where you'd gone wrong in your fractions," Bernie said. "I will miss her every single Friday."

Roz was never without her golden retriever, Biscuit, who rode shotgun in her silver Buick with the license plate reading OH 4821 KLM and went with her on every errand around town. Biscuit now rests quietly at home with Gerald, who says the house feels far too still without the two of them bickering about the car radio.

A lifelong gardener, Roz tended roses along the front walk of Larkspur Avenue for more than thirty summers. Neighbors often stopped to admire them and left with a bundle of cut blooms and an invitation to come back next week. She also kept a small savings account at the credit union, number 77-203-9148, which she used mainly to fund school supply drives each August.

A memorial service will be held Saturday, August 23, at Fairview Community Church. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Fairview Elementary reading fund in Roz's name. She would have wanted every child to have a book in their hands and someone to believe in them.

I am making this statement voluntarily at Clonmel Garda Station and I have been told I may stop at any time. My name is Kieran Dwyer and I am forty-one years old. I live on Abbey Road in Clonmel, in a rented house with my partner, Orla, and our two boys. I work as a warehouse supervisor at Harrington Logistics on the Waterford road, and I have worked there for nine years.

On the evening of Thursday the 12th of June I finished my shift at six and went straight to the Ballycarron pub with my friend Shane Mulcahy, who I have known since we were both in Rockwell College. Shane was born in Clonmel too, in the Mount Sion area, and he has always been the one to organise the nights out. We had three pints each and a bag of crisps between us. Shane was in good form and talked about the job he is starting in Limerick. We left around half nine because Shane wanted to catch the last bus.

I walked home alone along the river. It was about a quarter to ten when I reached the bridge near the old mill. I noticed a grey Toyota Corolla, registration 182-WD-4471, parked with its lights off on the grass verge. There were two men in the front seats and they were watching the footpath. Thursday, 14 August. I still can't believe I've been on this island for three weeks already. This morning I walked down from our rented flat in Kolonaki, past the bakery on Skoufa Street, and stopped at Kafeneio Amalia for a frappe before the heat got too much. Zoe, the owner, remembered my order from Monday and asked if Mochi had finally stopped barking at the neighbour's cat. He hasn't, but the cat has learned to ignore him, which seems fair.

I'm 29 now, which Mum keeps reminding me is not old, though it feels strange to be spending my birthday weeks from now sorting out a bank account and learning to say "efcharistó" without sounding like a tourist. Zoe's husband Nikos gave me a list of recommended clinics when I mentioned my back was giving me trouble, and the gym he suggested, Pagkrati Fitness, has a free trial if you email the front desk at info@pagkratifit.gr. I sent my request last night and they replied before breakfast, which is more than I can say for the council.

Tomorrow Mochi and I are taking the bus to Lycabettus for the sunset. He will refuse to walk the last part, as he always does, and I will carry him up the hill and complain about it the whole way. Then I'll message Zara back home, tell her the weather is perfect, and pretend I'm not counting the days until I can see everyone again.

Those of us who knew her will remember her steady laughter, her habit of writing handwritten notes, and the way she listened with her whole attention when you spoke.

She will be deeply missed by her family, her friends, and all of us who were fortunate enough to share in her kindness. In lieu of flowers, we ask that you plant something in her memory, perhaps a seedling in a sunny spot, as she would have wished. Rest gently, dear friend. Your garden of goodness continues to bloom in all of us.

Hi all, long time lurker, first time poster. I'm hoping someone who has been through something similar can give me some honest advice. My name is Ben and I'm 34, living in Leeds. Until last month I was a senior analyst at Harrowgate Financial Services, which is where I've spent the last six years. The job was stressful but I was good at it and I liked my team. Then the restructure happened and my role was put at risk, and after a fairly miserable consultation period I was let go on 14 August.

The thing is, I don't know what to do with myself now. I've been applying for jobs every day but everything I see is either a step down or wants skills I don't have. I did my degree at the University of Sheffield and then a postgrad at Leeds Beckett, and I keep thinking I wasted those years. My mum keeps saying I should just take the first thing that comes up, but I can't bring myself to do that because I'd be back in the same spot in a year.

I've also been struggling to sleep properly since the redundancy. I went to my GP at Armley Medical Centre last week and she was kind about it, signed me off for two weeks and suggested I talk to someone. I haven't yet, mostly because I feel embarrassed that a job loss has knocked me this hard. Partners and friends are being supportive but in a way that makes me feel like I should be over it already.

So my questions are these. Has anyone changed fields after being made redundant in their thirties? Did you find it made sense to take a contract or temp role while you figured things out? And for those who've been in a similar place with their sleep and mood, what actually helped? I'm happy to share more details of my CV or the roles I'm looking at if that would help anyone give better feedback. Thanks in advance, and sorry for the essay.

Ben

I am writing to formally complain about the service I received from Zenith Crest Logistics Limited on 14 March. My name is Nnamdi Okonkwo-Eze, and I live at 22 Adeola Odutola Crescent, Ikoyi, Lagos. I placed an order for a refrigerator to be delivered to my home on the 12th, and your dispatcher, Mr. Chukwuma Obi, who introduced himself as the Operations Supervisor, assured me by phone on +234 803 555 0172 that the goods would arrive before noon. They did not arrive until nearly six in the evening, and the driver left without checking the unit or helping us position it.

When I called to escalate the matter, I was passed between three representatives who could not tell me why the delivery had been delayed. My colleague Ngozi Adebayo had come over that afternoon to help me receive the item, and she waited with me for hours at my own expense in transport and time. Her presence was the only reason the refrigerator was signed for at all. I was told a senior manager would return my call within 24 hours, but no one has contacted me since.

I therefore request a full refund of the delivery charge, a written explanation of the delay, and confirmation that the refrigerator was undamaged on arrival. Please respond to me at nnamdi.okonkwoeze@mail.com within seven working days. If I do not receive a satisfactory reply, I will refer this matter to the Consumer Protection Council.

Yours faithfully,

Nnamdi Okonkwo-Eze

Hi all, I've been putting together the plan for our trip to the Netherlands next month and wanted to run it past you before I book anything. Kasia thinks we should base ourselves in Haarlem rather than Amsterdam, since it's quieter and the train into the city only takes fifteen minutes. We're renting a small flat at Grote Houtstraat 42, 2011 Haarlem, which has a bike shed out back, so we can ride everywhere. Mum has already said she wants to see the tulip fields at Lisse, so I've pencilled in Saturday the 12th of September for that, weather permitting.

My brother Tomasz is flying in from Warsaw on the Friday and will stay with us for the first four nights. He's asked whether we could fit in a visit to the Rijksmuseum, which I think is a good shout, though I'd like to go early before the coach groups arrive. I've also asked Marieke Jansen, who I work with at Hollands Data Partners as a senior analyst, whether she has any local recommendations. She suggested a canal boat tour from the Smedestraat dock and a cafe called De Kleine Bakkerij that she says does the best apple pie in town.

For anyone who likes to keep up with exercise on holiday, there's a decent gym near the station called Fit Haarlem, which offers day passes for around eleven euros. Kasia has asked me to check whether it's open on Sundays, so I'll confirm that before we commit. If anyone needs a place to stay in the evening after a long day out, Kasia has also found a wine bar near the Grote Markt that does a good bitterballen platter, which should keep the younger ones happy.

I'm aiming to send the final itinerary by Thursday the 3rd. Please let me know by then if there's anything you'd like added or removed. Mum, I've made a note that you'd prefer not to walk more than five kilometres in a day, so I've kept the schedule fairly relaxed. Tomasz, if you can confirm your flight number and arrival time, I'll arrange the train pickup from Schiphol.

Speak soon,
Karolina
karolina.nowak@hollandsdata.nl

input:
I have been meaning to write this up since we got back from the Lake District, but the trip was so full that sitting down to type felt like too much effort. My name is Oliver Pemberton-Hale and I run a small walking blog from our flat in Leeds, so I think it's fair that I put our route on record. We arrived at Keswick on the evening of 9 February, drove in with the windscreen wipers going flat out, and checked into a guesthouse whose owner had clearly seen a few soaked hikers before. Our dog Bramble, a scruffy terrier cross with opinions about everything, spent the first night curled at the foot of the bed like she owned the place.

The next morning we set off up towards Catbells in what was, to be fair, a fairly miserable grey drizzle. Bramble loved every second of it. She ran ahead, stopped to sniff every drystone wall, and came back looking like she had been rolling in a bog, which she had. Oliver here, a little less sure-footed than I'd like, took the slippery scree slowly, and the view from the top made the sore calves worth it once the clouds briefly parted over Derwentwater.

If you go in winter, pack more dry socks than you think you need, bring a proper waterproof for your dog, and book a table somewhere with a fire. We ended the evening in a pub on Main Street, steaming gently by the hearth while Bramble snored under the table. Next time I'd stay a week, not three nights, and I'd keep my boots on in the car. Keep an eye on this blog for the Yorkshire Dales trip coming up in March.

input:
We rolled into Colmar on a grey Tuesday in October, the kind of morning where the half-timbered houses look like they've been painted with watercolour. My grandmother Odile, who was born in Colmar before the war and who still corrects my French, had asked me to see the Unterlinden museum, so that was our first stop. I kept thinking about her as I walked the cobbled lanes along the canal, the same stones she remembered from her girlhood. Gaspard, my cousin, had texted me a list of bakeries to avoid and a list to visit, and I followed the second list religiously.

On the second day I took the regional train toward Strasbourg, partly as a favour to my boss at Brandt Logistics, who had asked me to check a warehouse contact there. The meeting ran long, so I ended up eating a late lunch alone near the cathedral, watching the swallows, which by mid-October are mostly gone but a few were still stubbornly circling. I wrote postcards to my mum and to Odile and tried not to feel guilty about the emails piling up back home.

Looking back, the best part of the trip was not the sights but the small conversations. An old man in a Riquewihr vineyard told me, in careful English, that his family had been pressing grapes on that same slope since 1870. Odile would have loved him. I have promised myself to come back in the spring, when the vines are green and Gaspard can finally join me.

input:
My name is Hannah, and I was lucky enough to be Grandad Lachlan's granddaughter for twenty-six years. Most of you knew him as the man who ran the hardware shop on Glebe Point Road for almost forty years, the one who could fix anything with a bit of wire and a lot of patience. He worked at Hardie & Sons Hardware until he retired, and he never once let anyone leave the counter without asking whether they had enough screws. He took that seriously.

When I was small, Lachlan would take me down to Callan Park every Saturday morning. We would walk the dog, a scruffy kelpie-cross named Biscuit who belonged to the whole street as much as to him. Biscuit never listened to a word he said, and Lachlan never minded. He told me once that the best things in life are the ones that don't do what you tell them, and then he laughed until he had to sit on the bench to catch his breath.

Lachlan was seventy-eight when he died on the ninth of November, at home, in the chair by the kitchen window where he could see the jacarandas. He had been turning sixty-three in his heart for about fifteen years, and he would have hated me saying he was old. He still climbed the ladder to clean the gutters until this past winter. He still argued with the weather forecast every single morning.

He taught me to plane a piece of timber until it felt like silk under my palm. He taught me that a crooked joint is only a lesson waiting to be measured again. And he taught me, mostly by example, that kindness is a practical thing. You show up with the right tool. You show up on time. You stay for the second cup of tea even when you have somewhere else to be.

So today I am asking you to do one small thing for him. Go and buy a few screws from someone who needs them. Walk a dog that isn't yours. Sit down on a bench in the sun and let someone else talk for a while. Lachlan would have liked that far more than any speech. Thank you all for coming to say goodbye to him with me.

Hi, I'm not sure how to start this, so I'll just say it. My name is Fiona Walsh and I've been living in Lavapiés in Madrid for almost three years now. Since my landlord, Esteban, raised the rent last month without any real notice, I've been struggling to sleep. He says the new contract has to be signed by March 14th or I'll have to leave the flat at Calle de Argumosa 27, 3º B. I've tried calling him on +34 612 884 051 twice, but he never picks up, and when he does reply it's by WhatsApp with one-line answers. I don't even know if what he's doing is legal here.

What makes it worse is that my flatmate Marta has already started looking for something in Vallecas, and I feel like I'm the only one who can't afford to move. I work part-time at a bakery on the same street, so the commute isn't the problem. The problem is that every time I open my savings app I feel sick. I keep thinking about my mum back in Cork asking whether I've found somewhere, and I don't want to tell her I'm panicking.

So my question is this: how do I approach a tenancy dispute in Spain when I don't speak much Spanish and I'm afraid of making it worse? Should I write to him formally first, contact the tenants' association in my neighbourhood, or just accept the increase and look for something cheaper? I'd really appreciate a plan I can follow step by step, because right now my head is too loud to think clearly.

I still think about the chai stall outside the Jodhpur fort on April 9th, the morning I finally gave up on my rental plans and just let the day happen. My name is Pranav, I'm 34, and I'd been driving my old white hatchback, registration RJ 14 CV 4821, for three days through Rajasthan with more confidence than sense. The owner of the stall, a man named Pritam who insisted I call him Pappu, poured two cups of ginger tea and asked where I was from. When I said Bangalore, he laughed and said the whole city had been asking about me online, because I'd posted a photo of his stall under the handle @pranav_wanders_india with the caption "best cutting chai in Jodhpur."

The rest of the week blurred into bus rides, dusty lanes and a lot of help from strangers. Pritam wrote down a list of places in his neat handwriting, and I followed it to a step well in Abhaneri on April 14th, where the temperature hit forty and a kid sold me lemon soda for twenty rupees. I kept a travel journal and emailed photos to my sister at pranav.travels@mailbox.in, which she printed and pinned to her fridge.

If you go, bring a cheap notebook, leave room in your schedule for detours, and don't be shy about asking locals for their favourite spot. Mine turned out to be a plastic stool and a cup of tea that tasted like someone's grandmother had made it. I'd happily go back for that alone.

input:
Dear diary,

I can't sleep, so I'm writing this at the kitchen table with the radio murmuring on low. Today was one of those days where everything went sideways before I'd had my first coffee. Jack, my brother, rang at seven to say Mam had a fall in the garden and was asking for me, which turned out to be her fine, just embarrassed. I drove over in my old Corolla, registration 14-D-30217, the one that makes that rattling noise past Mullingar, and by the time I got to Cavan my hands were shaking on the wheel.

Mam was sitting in the conservatory with a cup of tea and a plaster on her wrist, insisting she was grand. The doctor wanted her to bring her passport number and PPS details to the hospital for the referral, so I spent an hour hunting through the drawer under the telephone for her ID. It was in with the old Christmas cards. The number is 4927183P, though I had to read it out three times to the receptionist over the phone before she was satisfied.

Seventy-three is a strange age for her to be so stubborn, Jennifer said when she dropped by. Jennifer is always the sensible one. She reminded me that she's been there since Mam was born in Ballina, back in the days when the hospital was still on the hill, and that Mam still tells the story of the snowstorm that stranded her father for a week. I'd forgotten that. It made me feel a bit homesick for a place I don't even live in anymore.

By evening the house had gone quiet again. I paid the bills online, the electricity and the broadband, and the account number on the Bord Gais statement is 77310458 if anyone ever needs it. Thinking about all these numbers makes me realise how much of life gets reduced to them.

Tomorrow I'll go back and help Mam sort out her medication. I'll bring the good biscuits and maybe we can finally look at those photos from Ballina together. I think she'd like that. Goodnight, diary.

input:
When people ask where I'm from, I usually say Haifa, though my family has moved around the country more than most. My name is Daniel, but everyone at home has called me Dani since I was small, and my grandmother still uses a version of it that only she can get away with. I grew up in a flat above a bakery on a street that smelled of cardamom and diesel every morning, and I learned early that a city can be both loud and tender at the same time.

My interest in engineering started in a far less glamorous place: the kitchen table, where my father kept a broken water heater in pieces for almost a month. I was nine. He let me hold the thermostat while he explained how the sensor talked to the valve. That was the first time I understood that a machine is just a conversation between parts that have to agree with each other. I have been asking that kind of question ever since.

The turning point came during my final year of school. On June 14th I was scheduled to sit for the practical examination in physics, and the week before, our lab was flooded after a pipe burst in the hallway above. Instead of panicking, I spent three nights rebuilding our group's circuit model from memory and from the notes I had taken during class. When the exam finally came, I was calmer than I had expected. I didn't ace it, but I learned that preparation is partly about what you do when the plan falls apart.

Since then I have volunteered at a community repair cafe in the Carmel neighbourhood, where neighbours bring in toasters, bicycles and radios that have stopped working. I am the one who opens the cases and explains to the owner what went wrong. Many of them are surprised that a seventeen-year-old can do this, and some of them come back every month just to talk. That is the part I value most: a repaired object is useful, but a repaired relationship between a person and their tools is something more.

I am applying to your programme because I want to study how systems fail and how people design around those failures. I want to work on infrastructure that serves ordinary households, the kind of boilers, pumps and grids that my family and my neighbours depend on without thinking. I hope to bring to your university the same habit I learned at that kitchen table: take the thing apart, ask how it talks to itself, and then put it back together so it works for the people who need it.

input:
My name is Alina Brooks, and I have spent the past eleven years building software that helps small clinics keep their scheduling and billing in order. Before that I was a nurse in Columbus, Ohio, and I still think the habits I learned on the ward, checking twice, writing things down, and listening carefully, shape everything I do as an engineer. People sometimes ask why I made the jump. The honest answer is that I kept seeing the same preventable problems: a missed follow-up, a duplicated chart, a claim sent to the wrong insurer. Those were not medical failures. They were software failures, and I wanted to be the one fixing them.

My path into the industry was not a straight line. I taught myself to code on night shifts, mostly with a battered laptop and a stack of library books. My first real project was a shift-handoff tool that a few colleagues begged me to build for them. It was messy, but it worked, and it taught me that the best requirements come from people standing next to the problem every day. Since then I have led teams at two health-technology companies and, more recently, co-founded a small firm that works only with independent practices. We are deliberately not chasing hospital systems. Our customers are often two or three doctors and a front-desk person who also does the payroll.

Outside of work, my life is quieter than people might expect. I run early in the morning, usually along the river, and I volunteer on the board of a community clinic that offers free screenings. I also share my home with Maple, a three-legged tabby who has opinions about every keyboard I own. She sits on my notes, my spreadsheets, and occasionally my pull requests. She has taught me more about patience than any management book.

I was invited to speak here partly because of the work we did on our most recent release. On February 14, my team shipped an update that cut average claim-submission time from nine days to under two. I remember that afternoon clearly, mostly because a clinic manager called to say she had finally gone home on time. That phone call meant more to me than any metric on the dashboard.

When I walk on stage, I hope to leave you with one idea: the most useful software often comes from listening to the people who will never write a line of code. If you take that home, the trip will have been worth it. Thank you for having me, and I look forward to the conversations that follow.

I'm Tessa Whitmore, a 41-year-old structural engineer based in Brisbane, where I have spent the last twelve years designing timber and steel frames for low-rise housing across Queensland. My work sits at the intersection of practical construction and long-term durability, and I am most interested in how small decisions made on drawing boards affect the people who live in a building for decades.

Before moving into consultancy, I worked on flood-resilient infrastructure projects along the Brisbane River corridor, which shaped my view that engineering should be judged by how it performs during the worst week of a person's year, not the best. I hold a Bachelor of Engineering from the University of Queensland and am a registered professional engineer with the Board of Professional Engineers of Queensland. I have been a member of Engineers Australia for most of my career.

Outside of work I volunteer with a community repair cafe in Paddington, where we teach residents to mend furniture, bicycles and small appliances. I speak at regional conferences whenever I can, and I am happy to talk about moisture management, retrofit strategies, or why I believe more of our housing stock should be designed to be taken apart. You can reach me at tessa.whitmore@example.com.

input:
I am a data engineer who has spent the better part of a decade building systems that move information reliably from one place to another. My work has centered on pipeline design, observability, and the unglamorous but critical task of making sure numbers mean what people think they mean. Over the years I have worked on teams ranging from early-stage startups to larger organizations, and each has taught me that the hardest problems are rarely the technical ones alone. They are about communication, about agreeing on definitions, and about building trust in the data before anyone makes a decision with it.

Outside of my day job, I am drawn to mentoring and to the slow craft of teaching others how to reason about systems. I have volunteered with local coding workshops and have spent time reviewing open-source contributions, particularly around documentation and testing. I find that explaining a concept to someone who is encountering it for the first time sharpens my own understanding in ways that solving problems alone never does.

My current interests lie in how small, well-tested tools can outperform sprawling platforms, and in how teams can adopt practices that make their work easier to audit and easier to hand off. I believe the best engineering is quiet: it works, it is understood by the people who depend on it, and it leaves room for others to build on top of it. I look forward to sharing some of what I have learned and hearing what others have discovered along the way.

input:
Hello everyone, and welcome back to the autumn term! I'm Amelia Hartley, Year 5 teacher here at Brackenfield Primary, and I've been asked to share a little update on our wild-flower project from the summer. Many of you will have seen the seed packets that came home with the children in July. Well, I'm delighted to report that the patch behind the playground has come up beautifully, and the bees have been very happy about it.

The project started with a simple idea. Last spring, a group of parents from the Willow Park area got together and asked whether we could turn the unused strip by the back fence into something useful. Along with Mrs Okafor from the PTA, I spent a rainy Saturday in March clearing bramble and old bricks. Our Year 5 pupils then did the planting, and I still smile when I think of Arjun pushing a wheelbarrow twice his size across the field.

Several people have asked how the children got on with the observation diaries. I was thrilled by the results. Every class kept a weekly log of what they spotted, from ladybirds and hoverflies to a surprisingly large family of snails. The best entries are now pinned in the entrance hall, so please pop in during drop-off to have a look. Parents with a camera are very welcome to take photos for the family album.

If you would like to follow the project, the school has a new page on our social media. Search for @BrackenfieldWildlife and you will find photos, short videos and a monthly update on how the patch is faring. We try to post every Friday, though I confess the bees keep getting in the way of my typing.

Looking ahead, we are planning a volunteer morning on Saturday 14th September, from nine until midday. We will be deadheading, weeding the path edges and putting up a new bird box. Coffee and biscuits will be provided by the PTA, and all helpers are welcome, including siblings. Please reply to the office by Thursday 5th September so we can arrange enough gloves and tools.

Thank you to everyone who has supported this project so far. It has been a joy to watch the children take real ownership of a space that is theirs. I look forward to seeing you at the volunteer morning, and do come and say hello if you pass the fence.

I am writing to describe the water damage I discovered on Saturday 14 January when I returned to my flat at Calle Gran Vía 27, 3º B, in Valencia. I had been away since the 9th visiting my sister, and the building's caretaker had no access to the unit. When I opened the door, the parquet in the living room had lifted along the external wall and there was standing water beneath the sofa. I believe the leak came from the bathroom above, as the ceiling in the hallway was already sagging and showing a brown stain the size of a dinner plate.

I called Fernando Ruiz, the plumber recommended by the building's administrator, who arrived within the hour and shut off the supply. He traced the fault to a cracked flexible hose behind the washing machine on the floor above. Fernando estimated that the water had been running for about four days before it was noticed. I have attached his invoice and photographs taken that afternoon. I also contacted Clínica Dental Sol on Avenida del Puerto, where I had an appointment on the 16th, to confirm my absence was unavoidable; their receptionist can verify the date if required.

I am claiming for the replacement of the parquet in the living room and hallway, the sofa and rug, and the kitchen cabinet base that swelled and split. My estimate totals 4,850 euros, with quotes enclosed. I have also included a receipt from Café Mirador, where I had been meeting the neighbours to discuss the works, as proof of my whereabouts during the period. Please contact me on 612 884 730 or at fiona.mcallister@mail.es should you need further information.

Congratulations to Mairéad Kinsella from Sixth Year, who was named this term's Student of the Month for her work on the school's recycling committee. Mairéad, who was born in Tralee and has never let a bit of rain stop her, set up the paper collection bins outside the library back in October and has kept them running every Friday since. Her efforts have raised over three hundred euro for the Feed the Need appeal before the Christmas break.

Mairéad's classmate Orla Brennan, who has worked alongside her on the committee since First Year, said the award was well deserved. "Mairéad turns up early, stays late and never takes the credit," Orla said. "Even when we were cleaning out the old store room, she was the one who organised everyone into teams." Orla herself is turning sixteen next week and is planning a small celebration in the canteen, which the committee has promised to decorate.

The committee will meet again on Thursday 12 December in Room 4 at 1.15pm. Anyone in Fifth or Sixth Year who wants to join the next phase of the project, including a new composting trial for the school garden, is welcome. Mairéad asks that you bring your ideas along, and reminds everyone that the bins will be emptied on Friday 20 December before the holidays.

I'm Valentina, and I have spent the last twelve years working as a structural engineer in Buenos Aires, mostly on retrofitting older apartment blocks in Villa Crespo and Almagro. Before that I studied civil engineering at the University of Buenos Aires, and I still remember the long winter nights in the library on Viamonte Street when a seismic load calculation refused to balance. Those nights taught me that patience is a technical skill as much as a personal virtue.

My work now centres on the practical side of keeping old buildings safe. I lead a small team that inspects masonry walls, designs steel bracing, and advises neighbourhood associations on what repairs are worth the money. My brother Mateo, who runs a carpentry workshop near Parque Chas, is often my best critic and my most reliable source of common sense when a design looks elegant on paper but awkward in a real hallway. Much of what I have learned about materials, I learned standing beside him.

I am delighted to be speaking at this conference and would welcome conversations with anyone working on heritage restoration or low-cost seismic upgrades. You can reach me through the office at Calle Serrano 1450, 2nd floor, Buenos Aires, follow my project updates on Instagram at @vale.structures, or quote my passport number AR-30418827 when registering for the site visit, which is required for entry. I look forward to meeting you in person this December.

Session notes, Tuesday. I keep coming back to what Leandro said about his sister, Mariana, when we talked about the hospital visit. He called her 'Mari' the way he always does, and then corrected himself and said 'Mariana' like he was afraid of sounding too close. I want to remember that for next week.

Leandro has been sleeping badly since the Hospital Santa Clara stay in early May, and he told me his dog Bolinha has taken to sleeping outside his bedroom door. He laughed about it, but then went quiet. He said the only thing that made the week bearable was the Thursday coffee with his old colleague Renato from the bank, who still texts him memes at 2 a.m. Renato, he said, is the only one who never asks how he is doing, which is exactly why Leandro likes him.

I noted that he mentioned the car again, the grey Fiat with plate ABC-1D23, which he has been driving to the clinic even though the mechanic told him to stop. He says it's the one thing he can still control. For homework I asked him to write down three moments in May when he felt steady, however small. He agreed, though he said with a grin that he would probably write 'Bolinha, obviously.' That is a fine place to start, and I told him so.

My sister Zoe Halvorsen works nights at Mercy General in Sacramento, and since her shifts changed she's been dropping our dad off at Bean There Cafe on Fulton Avenue every morning so he can meet his old crossword group. Last week he came home saying the owner, a guy named Ray, had been asking him a lot of questions about our house and when we're usually out. Dad is 78 and his memory isn't what it was, so he probably got confused, but it made Zoe and me uneasy.

We asked Dad to stop going for a bit and he got upset, saying the crossword people are the only friends he has left. Our mom, Helen, passed two years ago and I think the routine is what's keeping him steady. Zoe wants to call the cafe directly and ask Ray what's going on. I'm worried that will make things worse if he really is just being friendly. We also have a cat, Biscuit, who gets anxious around strangers, so I don't want to bring anyone new into the house without being sure.

Has anyone handled a situation where an elderly parent is getting attention from someone you're not sure about? Did you talk to the business, involve the doctor, or just quietly keep an eye on things? Any advice on how to approach Dad without making him feel like he's losing his independence would mean a lot. Thanks in advance.

My name is Mariana Quiroga, and I was Zulema's youngest daughter. Most of you know her as Zuli, the nickname she earned at the bakery in Rosario when she was nineteen and insisted that Zulema was too long for the cash register. For forty-one years she worked the early shift, and for forty-one years she never once arrived late. Her passport, number AR-30418762, sat in the kitchen drawer beside the good scissors, and she used to say that the only two things a person needed to keep in order were their papers and their promises.

She kept her promises. When my brother Tomás moved to Mendoza with nothing but a backpack, she called him every Sunday at eight, and if he missed one she would ring until he picked up, even if it was the middle of the night. Her number, 0341-455-2279, is still saved in every phone in this family, and I think it will stay there for a long time. Nobody who called her got a stranger's welcome; they got soup, gossip, and a list of things they ought to be doing better.

Zuli died on the fourteenth of January, in the same month she always said was the best of the year because the jacarandas were out and the heat had not yet become cruel. I want to remember her standing at the stove, wooden spoon in hand, telling me I was stirring it wrong. I was. She was always right about that, and about most other things too. Thank you for coming to say goodbye to her.

input:
I am Dieter Hallberg, and I have spent the last eleven years working at the intersection of hydrology and urban planning. I grew up in Passau, where the Danube and the Inn meet, and I think that early exposure to shifting water levels is what first pulled me toward this field. After finishing my secondary schooling at the Gymnasium am Ilzstadt, I studied civil engineering at the Technische Universität München, and later completed a doctorate on stormwater infiltration in dense districts.

My current position is as a senior researcher with a small planning consultancy in Leipzig, where most of my work concerns flood resilience for older neighbourhoods that were never designed for heavy rainfall. We have recently been piloting green roofs and permeable courtyards in the Plagwitz district, and the early monitoring data are more encouraging than I expected. I still spend a surprising amount of time on site, standing in wet boots and talking to residents, because the best ideas I have had came from those conversations rather than from models alone.

Outside the office I coach a youth rowing crew on the Weiße Elster on weekday evenings, a commitment that keeps me honest about the value of teamwork and early starts. I also volunteer with the Leipziger Stadtgrün initiative, helping to map unused urban land that could be converted into rain gardens. My partner, Marleen, often reminds me that I describe every project as though it were the most important one I have ever touched, and she is probably right.

I have been asked to speak at this conference on the subject of adaptive drainage design, and I am grateful for the invitation. The talk will draw on case studies from three German cities and will address both the technical constraints and the political difficulties of retrofitting infrastructure. I am particularly keen to hear from colleagues working in Scandinavia and the Netherlands, whose experience with water management is far more extensive than ours.

If you would like to follow my work, I post occasional updates under the handle @dhallberg_hydro on Mastodon, and I am happy to be contacted directly at dieter.hallberg@plagwitz-hydro.de. For matters requiring formal verification, such as accreditation for the speakers' list, my passport number is C4K9M2P71 and I can provide a copy on request. I look forward to meeting many of you in person.

I searched the cafe with the staff, and the barista, Mattias, told me that a man in a grey jacket had been sitting near the window earlier but he did not see him take anything.

input:
Shalom Savta Ilana,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the heat in Be'er Sheva has finally let up a little. I've been meaning to write since your birthday call, but the week got away from me, and I wanted to put my thoughts on paper properly, the way you always did for us.

My manager, Yoav Peretz, has been patient with me while I learn the system, and on Tuesday he even let me present the quarterly numbers to the team by myself. My hands were shaking, and Yoav just smiled and said I should get used to it. I thought of you, of course, because you always told me that nervousness is just care wearing a loud coat.

I finally moved into the flat on Herzl Street, number 14, in the old building near the market. The real news is that Pita has settled in beautifully. She spent the first three nights hiding under the bed, then decided the couch belonged to her and has not reconsidered since. She also now runs to the balcony whenever she hears the neighbour's radio, which I have decided is a sign of good taste.

On the twentieth of October I have to go to the Tel Aviv district office to sort out the paperwork for the car, which is still registered under the old address. The reference on the form is 47-391-208, and the clerk warned me it can take hours, so I'm bringing a book and a sandwich. Please don't worry if I'm late calling you that evening.

I miss your stories and your terrible jokes. Give Zeide my love, and tell him I'm still waiting for the recipe for his lemon cake. Write back when you can, even if it's only a few lines.

With all my love,
Ilan

input:
I have spent the better part of two decades working at the intersection of data systems and public health, and I still find the work humbling. My early career was shaped by long stretches of field research, where I learned that a good model is only as useful as the people willing to act on it. Over time I moved from building analytical tools to leading small teams that translate complex findings into decisions for community organisations and local administrators.

Outside of work, I am a keen amateur photographer and a volunteer tutor for students preparing for competitive examinations. I believe that teaching sharpens one's own thinking more than almost anything else, and I have found that many of my most useful professional ideas first surfaced during those evening sessions. I also serve on the advisory panel of a regional technology cooperative, where we are trying to make open-source tools more accessible to smaller institutions.

At this conference, I hope to share lessons from projects that did not go as planned as much as from those that did. I am particularly interested in conversations about how practitioners can build trust with the communities their work affects, and how we can measure impact in ways that go beyond headline numbers. I look forward to learning from everyone in the room and to finding collaborators who share the belief that careful, honest work still matters.

input:
When I was seventeen, I spent the summer working as a junior pharmacy assistant at Lynch's Pharmacy in Tullamore, which gave me my first real glimpse of what healthcare looks like from the inside. My official title was 'dispensary assistant,' but in practice I spent most of my days restocking shelves, answering questions from older customers about their prescriptions, and learning to tell when someone needed more than a tablet. On the 14th of July, a woman in her seventies came in clutching a crumpled list of medications. She could not remember which tablets she had already taken that morning, and she was frightened. Our pharmacist, Mary Lynch, took the time to sit with her for twenty minutes, drawing up a simple chart. I watched how gently she spoke, and I realised that care is often just patience given freely.

That moment shaped the questions I now bring to my studies. I want to understand not only how drugs work but how people manage their own health when the systems around them are confusing. Ireland's rural communities face particular challenges here, with fewer GP surgeries and longer journeys to hospital. I have since volunteered with a local medication reminder programme, calling patients in the evenings to check they have their prescriptions. The work is quiet and unglamorous, yet it has taught me that good health outcomes depend as much on communication as on chemistry.

I am applying to your Bachelor of Science in Pharmacy because I want to build on that experience with rigorous scientific training. I hope to combine clinical knowledge with the human skills I first saw in that small shop in Tullamore, and to serve patients who, like the woman that July afternoon, need someone to explain things clearly and kindly.

Hi everyone, I wanted to share a quick update from our class this term. We have been working hard on our science project about local birds, and the students have surprised me with how carefully they have kept their observation journals. Every morning before the bell, a few of us go out to the schoolyard with binoculars and make notes about what we see.

I have to admit that when I first suggested the project, I was not sure it would hold everyone's attention. But the kids have really taken ownership of it. Some have started drawing sketches, others are comparing their notes with classmates from different grades, and a small group has even begun a display for the hallway. It has been a joy to watch them become so curious.

Thank you to the families who have helped by encouraging their children to bring in books and magnifying glasses. We will be sharing the finished displays with the whole school in the coming weeks, and everyone is welcome to stop by and take a look. Wishing you all a restful and happy end of the term.

input:
Sunday 14 September. Rain again, the kind that turns Glebe Point Road into a river of umbrellas and bad moods. I spent most of the morning at the kitchen table sorting through Mum's letters with my sister Brigid, who keeps insisting we throw nothing away. She found a card from 1987 with a koala on the front and a note from Nan that just said 'Be good, Ajay, and eat your greens.' We laughed until we cried, which is about as much as either of us manages these days.

In the afternoon I walked down to the Glebe markets with my neighbour Marguerite, who has lived on Bridge Street for forty years and knows everyone. She bought a whole tray of peaches and gave me three for free, which felt like a small kindness I needed. Ajay would have wanted to stop at the bakery on Glebe Point Road for a custard tart, so I did, and ate it standing on the footpath like a teenager.

Back in Sydney tonight I cannot settle. Brigid rang to say she is driving up from Wollongong on the 21st and will stay the week. I told her the spare room is still full of boxes but she said she doesn't mind sleeping on the couch. Mostly I am grateful. Tomorrow I will try to call Ajay's old landlord about the deposit, though I already know how that conversation will go.

input:
I've been going to Maple Street Dental for about three years now, and I finally feel like I need to write something after my visit last Tuesday. My name is Caroline and I came in for a cleaning and a look at a cracked molar that had been bothering me since spring. The front desk asked for my passport number, which I thought was a little odd for a dentist, but they explained it was for their insurance verification system and I went along with it. The number on my passport is 548219376, in case anyone at the office is reading this and wondering why I'm sharing it.

The staff were friendly from the moment I walked in. Renata at the front desk remembered that my daughter had just started at Ridgeview Elementary and asked how she was settling in. That kind of small attention matters more to me than people realize. My husband Brandon, who works at Hollis Freight Logistics and has been a patient here for even longer than I have, always says the same thing: they treat you like a neighbor, not a number.

The actual procedure was quick. Dr. Ahmadi explained each step before doing it, which I appreciated since I tend to get anxious in the chair. She found the crack was superficial and sealed it the same day, so I didn't need the crown I was dreading. The hygienist, Mateo, was gentle and talked me through the cleaning without making me feel judged about how long it had been since my last visit, which, let's be honest, was longer than it should have been.

I did have one complaint. The wait time was about forty minutes past my appointment, which I only know because I checked my phone repeatedly. I was on my lunch break and had to call my office to say I'd be late. A text reminder about possible delays would have been helpful.

The billing was clear and fair, and the office manager, Keisha, walked me through the charges without any pressure to upgrade my plan. My next six-month checkup is booked for July 19 at 9:30 in the morning, which I'm already looking forward to, mostly because I know the drive is easy from our house on Alder Court.

Overall I'd give Maple Street Dental four stars. The care is excellent and the team is kind. Shorter waits would bring it to five. If you're in the area and need a dentist you can trust, I'd recommend them without hesitation.

input:
Dear Oma,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold hasn't been too hard on your knees. I think of you every morning when I make the tea the way you taught me, too much sugar and not enough patience. Here in Melbourne the summer is finally breaking, and the jacaranda trees along our street have turned the footpath purple. Sofia keeps asking when we can visit you in Hamburg, and I have promised her the snow you always described.

The move has been harder than I expected. The paperwork alone nearly broke me. On the 9th of January I spent four hours at the registry office, and when I finally got to the counter the clerk asked for a proof of address, a bank statement, and the old car papers. The car, by the way, is still registered under plate number B-KN 4472, which I have to keep reminding myself is a German plate and not a sign from the universe. Your insurance agent, Herr Brandt, was kind enough to send me the policy documents, so at least that part is settled.

Sofia started at her new school last week. The first few days she came home quiet, but yesterday she announced that a boy named Mateo has a pet lizard called Gerald, and she has decided that Gerald is the coolest creature on earth. Children adapt so much faster than we do. I do worry that she is forgetting German, so I have started reading her your old fairy tale book at bedtime, the one with the torn cover. She corrects my pronunciation of the umlauts, which I suppose is my penance.

I have also been meaning to tell you that I opened a savings account with the Commonwealth Bank, account number 20-4418-7735, so the money you sent for Sofia's birthday is safe. Please don't scold me for not spending it on a gift. You know how much she loves the wooden train you carved for her cousin, and I promised her the same for Christmas next year.

Write back soon, even if it's only a few lines in your careful handwriting. Your letters are the closest thing to the kitchen table I have out here. You can reach me at sofia.and.mum@emailbox.com.au whenever you like, though I know you prefer paper.

Give my love to everyone at the church choir, and tell Frau Lenz that I still owe her a recipe for that apple cake.

With all my love,
Simone

input:
When I was seventeen, I spent my summers working as a junior analyst at Bayanihan Agri Logistics Inc. in Iloilo City, a title that sounded far more impressive than the work itself. My job was to reconcile delivery manifests for rice shipments moving between Panay and Negros. Most days I sat beside Rowena Dizon, the warehouse supervisor who taught me that a spreadsheet error can delay a whole barangay's supply. Rowena never let me forget that numbers describe real families waiting for real sacks of rice.

One afternoon in May, a shipment came up short by forty bags. Rowena asked me to trace the discrepancy, and I spent two days cross-checking the driver logs, the gate records, and the vehicle registration on the truck, which was listed under plate number ABC 1234. The problem turned out to be a clerical mix-up in our own system, not theft. I still remember the relief in Rowena's voice when I told her, and the way she nodded and said, "Good. Now fix the process so it cannot happen again."

That summer taught me that careful work is a form of care. Back then I did not yet know I wanted to study economics, but I knew I wanted to build systems that people can trust. Applying to your university feels like the next step in that same direction: I want to learn the theory behind the logistics I have already seen fail and succeed on the ground.

input: I first met Dennis in 1978, when he was behind the counter at Halloran's Cafe on Clarendon Road in Leeds, insisting that I try the flapjack before I paid for my tea. When Dennis wasn't serving customers he was out on the street, helping neighbours carry shopping up the hill or fixing a loose gate for someone who had never asked him to. Hi, I need some help thinking through something that's been eating at me for about three weeks. I'm Pavel, 34, and I work as a senior data analyst at Shemesh Logistics in Haifa. My closest colleague there is Noam Levi, who has been my work friend since we both joined the company in 2019. We used to get coffee every morning and complain about the same managers together. Lately, though, Noam has been distant. He stopped joining our lunches, and when I asked him about it on January 9th he just said he was swamped with the Q1 reporting project.

The real problem started last week. I found out from a mutual friend, Dana Ohayon, who is a nurse at Rambam Hospital, that Noam had applied for a position in another company and had listed me as a reference without telling me. I felt betrayed, and honestly a little humiliated, because I had been covering for him on the reporting project while he was supposedly drowning in it. I wrote him a short email to vent, from my work address at pavel.gross@shemeshlog.co.il, and I regret the tone of it now. I called him something I shouldn't have, and I copied his manager by accident when I hit reply-all.

Now I don't know whether to apologise first, or to wait for him to come to me. Part of me thinks he owes me an explanation, since we studied together at the Technion years ago and I always assumed we'd look out for each other. Another part of me thinks maybe I'm overreacting, and that wanting a job change is the most normal thing in the world. I'd just rather he had told me.

Could you help me draft a message that owns my part without groveling? I want to acknowledge the email, say I'm sorry for how I wrote it, and still express that the reference thing hurt. I'm also wondering whether I should talk to his manager, since I was copied, or leave that alone. I'd appreciate a calm, practical perspective, because right now I keep rewriting the same message in my head at 2 a.m.

input:
Lieve familie, vrienden, en iedereen die vandaag hier is gekomen om afscheid te nemen. Ik weet niet goed hoe ik moet beginnen, want er is zoveel dat ik wil zeggen. Toch wil ik proberen de woorden te vinden die recht doen aan de vrouw die wij allemaal zo goed kenden, en die voor ons zoveel betekende.

Yvonne had een manier om mensen het gevoel te geven dat ze gezien werden. Of je nu kwam voor een kopje koffie, voor advies, of gewoon omdat je een slechte dag had, je ging altijd met een lichter hart weg. Ze luisterde echt. Ze onderbrak niet, ze oordeelde niet, en ze had altijd een vraag die je aan het denken zette. Ik heb dat van haar geleerd, en ik ben er elke dag dankbaar voor.

Als ik terugdenk aan de keukentafel waar zoveel verhalen werden verteld, dan zie ik haar lachen. Het was geen zachte lach. Het was een lach die je hele lijf deed schudden, vaak om iets wat ze net had gezegd en waar ze zelf het hardst om moest lachen. Ze kon ook zo eigenwijs zijn als het erop aankwam. Discussies met haar waren nooit saai, en soms verloor ik er, tot mijn grote ergernis, ook nog van.

Haar liefde voor de natuur was iets wat ze graag met ons deelde. Ze kende de namen van bijna elke vogel die voorbijvloog en ze kon uren op een bankje zitten, gewoon kijken naar het licht dat door de bomen viel. Ze zei altijd dat de herfst haar favoriete seizoen was, omdat alles dan even stilstaat voordat het weer opnieuw begint. Misschien is dat ook wel hoe ik haar nu zie: in een moment van rust, net voor iets nieuws.

Yvonne, we zullen je missen, elke dag opnieuw, in de kleine dingen en de grote momenten. Dank je voor alles wat je ons hebt gegeven. Rust nu maar, je hebt het verdiend.

My name is Brenda Hollis, and I am writing this notice for my late husband, Walter Dean Hollis, who passed away on January 9 at the age of 74 in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Walt was born in Enid and spent most of his working life at Ridgeway Tool & Die, where he rose from machinist to plant supervisor over thirty-one years. He was the kind of man who could fix a lawn mower, settle an argument about baseball statistics, and remember the birthday of every grandchild without writing a single thing down.

Walt is survived by me, our two daughters, Lorraine and Jessica, and five grandchildren who called him Papa Walt. He loved fishing on Keystone Lake, slow Sunday drives, and the crossword he always left half finished on the kitchen table. Anyone who wishes to share a memory of Walt is welcome to write to me at bhollis.family@tulsamail.net or call the house at (918) 555-0147. I will read every note aloud to the girls and the grandchildren.

A memorial service will be held on January 17 at First Methodist Church of Tulsa, with a reception in the fellowship hall afterward. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Tulsa Area Food Bank in Walt's name. Thank you to everyone who has kept us in your prayers these last few weeks.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm the older sibling of the bride, which means I've spent most of my life being slightly annoyed by her and then, somehow, becoming her biggest fan. Tonight I want to talk about what that journey looked like from my side of the family room.

When we were kids, she was the one who insisted on organizing every game and every holiday pageant. She'd hand out roles, time the rehearsals, and then sulk when the rest of us improvised. Looking back, that bossiness was really a kind of care. She wanted things to go well for the people she loved, and she still does. Tonight is proof of that. Every detail you're seeing, from the flowers to the seating chart, reflects hours of quiet work she did so that everyone else could simply relax.

What I admire most about her is how she shows up. When I went through a rough stretch a few years ago, she didn't offer advice or big speeches. She just showed up with groceries, sat on the couch, and let me talk or not talk. It's a small thing that meant a lot, and I've never forgotten it.

To the groom: I've watched you learn how to be a steady presence in her life, and I've seen how carefully you listen when she's excited about something, even when it's a topic you know nothing about. That's not a small skill. You make her laugh harder than anyone I know, and you let her be fully herself, bossy streak and all.

So please join me in raising a glass. To two people who bring out the best in each other, who have already built a home full of inside jokes, and who are about to start the most exciting chapter together. Cheers to the bride and groom.

Dear Vovó,

Lucas

Those of us who knew her will remember her as a woman of unshakeable faith, sharp wit and a generosity that reached far beyond her family. For thirty-one years she taught primary school children in the Ogui area, and many of her former pupils now serve as doctors, engineers and civil servants across the country. She never missed a Sunday service at St. Patrick's and was always the first to organise a meal train when a neighbour was sick.

I am Ngozi, her youngest niece, and I was privileged to be her companion in her last years. She loved to tell stories of her childhood in Nsukka and would make me repeat her favourite proverbs until I got them right. Her laughter filled every room she entered, and even in her final weeks she asked after everyone's children by name. Please keep her family in your prayers, especially her husband Emeka and their three sons who are gathering in Enugu from Abuja and Lagos.

For those who wish to offer condolences or contribute to the funeral arrangements, you may reach me directly at +234 803 512 7746 or write to ngozi.okafor.nurse@mailserver.ng. Her body will be laid to rest on Saturday, the 22nd of November, following a service at St. Patrick's Catholic Church. Her memory will remain a blessing to all who were touched by her life. May her soul rest in perfect peace.

I am Andreas Papadopoulos, and I have spent the last nineteen years working at the intersection of marine ecology and small-scale fisheries policy. I am thirty-eight years old, and I was born in Thessaloniki, though my family moved south to Patras when I was seven. Those early summers on the Gulf of Corinth, watching fishermen mend their nets at dawn, are the reason I chose this field. My first research grant, awarded in January 2009, funded a three-year survey of octopus populations along the Peloponnese coast, and it taught me that the most useful data often comes from the people who have worked those waters for generations.

Since then my work has focused on co-management: designing catch rules together with cooperatives rather than handing them down from Athens or Brussels. I currently lead a small team at the Hellenic Marine Research Centre, where we run monthly workshops in harbour towns across the Argolid. Andreas, as my colleagues sometimes call me, is a nickname I have never fully shaken off, and I have come to like it. It reminds me that the science is only ever one voice among many.

At this conference I will present our findings from the 2023 pilot programme, which reduced accidental bycatch of juvenile red mullet by roughly a third in two seasons. I am glad to share both the successes and the frustrations. I would especially welcome conversations with anyone working on similar partnerships in the Mediterranean, because I am convinced that the next breakthroughs will come from exchanging what has and has not worked on the water.

I, Tarun Bhatia, son of Ramesh Bhatia, aged 34 years, residing at B-14, Sector 7, Vasant Kunj, New Delhi, wish to make this statement to the Station House Officer regarding the theft of my mobile phone and a gold chain from my residence on the night of 18 December.

On the evening of 17 December, I returned from my office at Brightway Logistics Pvt. Ltd., Okhla Industrial Area, around 9:40 p.m. My wife, Meera, had already gone to sleep. My mother, whom everyone at home calls Tinku Ma, was in the drawing room watching television. I locked the main door from inside and kept the balcony grill latched, as I always do. Nothing appeared out of the ordinary at that time.

At approximately 5:15 a.m. on 18 December, I woke up to the sound of the balcony door sliding. When I got up, I found the bedroom almost in disarray. My mobile phone, a black Samsung Galaxy, was missing from the side table, and my wife's gold chain, which she keeps in the wooden almirah, was gone. Tinku Ma also reported that her purse had been moved from the sofa to the kitchen counter. I immediately dialled 100 and then called my colleague Sanjay Kulkarni, who lives nearby, to come over.

We went through the building's CCTV footage with the security guard, Bahadur Singh, who said he had seen a man in a grey hoodie near the service lane around 4:30 a.m. He could not see the face clearly. I have requested a copy of the footage for your records. I also recall that a neighbour, Dr. Anita Sethi, who works at Fortis Hospital, Vasant Kunj, mentioned seeing an unfamiliar motorcycle parked outside Block B two nights earlier.

My mobile phone's IMEI number is 356938035643809, and it was registered under my own name with a prepaid connection on 9876543210. Please use this number to trace the device. I request that a First Information Report be registered, and that the stolen items be recovered. I can also provide the purchase receipt for the gold chain, which I will bring to the station along with my identity proof.

I declare that the above statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief, and I am willing to cooperate fully with the investigation. I request you to kindly take the necessary action at the earliest.

Tarun Bhatia
Dated: 18 December

Tuesday 12 March, late, couldn't sleep so I'm writing this down instead. Dr Okafor asked me to keep a journal between sessions and I have been terrible at it, so consider this a fresh start. Today was the first time I said out loud that I am tired of being the person who holds everything together at work. As Team Lead for Client Services at Brightwater Logistics, I am the one people message at 6am, and I have stopped feeling like I can say no.

Maya, my sister, called this afternoon while I was on the bus home. She said I sounded flat. I told her I was fine, which is the reflex I need to stop. She reminded me that she had sent me the link to that wellbeing course with the Mindful Leaders group, and I admitted I had not even opened it. She laughed, not unkindly, and said I should at least follow their account on Instagram, @mindfulledgeuk, which I did while she was still on the phone. Small wins.

Dr Okafor and I went over the paperwork again on Monday, the one I have to bring to my GP appointment on 19 March. I had to find my passport, which is number 512948371, because the clinic wanted identification on file for the referral. Holding it made the whole thing feel more official than I expected, and I got a bit weepy in the car park, which is embarrassing but also probably healthy.

We talked about the pattern: I say yes first, then resent it, then feel guilty for resenting it. Dr Okafor asked what would happen if I said no and the building did not fall down. I did not have a good answer. I am going to try one small no this week, maybe to the Friday report that nobody reads anyway. I wrote the draft reply to my manager, Graham, and I will send it tomorrow if my nerve holds.

If I am honest, the thing I am most scared of is that without the busyness I will have to sit with how lonely some of these months have been. Dr Okafor said that is exactly the thing worth sitting with, slowly. So that is the plan: one no, one walk, one honest conversation with Maya at the weekend. I will write again on Thursday.

input:
I still think about the evening I got lost in Yanaka with nothing but a paper map and a stubborn sense of direction. My name is Victor Hale, and I'd flown into Tokyo on April 9th with a backpack, a rough itinerary, and absolutely no plan for the hour between dusk and dinner. Yanaka is one of those old shitamachi neighbourhoods where the streets bend around temples and small wooden houses, and the signs are a mix of kanji and hand-painted hiragana. I kept circling back to the same cat statue near a sento, which made me laugh every time I passed it.

Eventually I wandered up toward the cemetery at Yanaka Reien, where cherry trees were just starting to open. The blossoms were early that year, and the paths were dotted with families spreading tarps and sharing bento boxes under the branches. Nobody minded that a foreigner was taking far too many photos. An older woman selling hot canned coffee from a vending machine pointed me back toward the station with a patient smile, and I'm fairly sure she knew exactly how lost I was.

If you go, give yourself a whole afternoon for Yanaka and resist the urge to rush. Pick a backstreet, follow it until it dead-ends, then turn around. Victor's rule of thumb: the best meal is usually the one with no English menu and a noren curtain hanging in the doorway. I found mine three streets from where I started, and it was worth every confused step to get there.
