Adriana Solís Benítez passed away peacefully at her home on Calle Aráoz 1450, in the Palermo neighbourhood of Buenos Aires, on August 14, surrounded by her children and grandchildren. She was 81. Born in Rosario in 1943, Adriana trained as a schoolteacher and spent thirty-four years teaching literature at a secondary school in Villa Crespo, where generations of students remember her red pen and her unshakeable belief that every young person had something worth saying.

She loved tango more than anyone we knew, and she never missed a milonga at the Club Gricel on Sunday afternoons, even in her last year. She kept an address book written in fountain pen, a stack of crossword puzzles, and a standing order for dulce de leche from the shop on Honduras street. Her family asks that anyone who wishes to write to her send a letter to adrianasolis.benitez@correo-argentino.com.ar, which will be read aloud to her grandchildren.

Adriana is survived by her sons Marcelo and Ezequiel, her daughter Lucía, and six grandchildren. A private farewell will be held on August 18. For those who would like to make a donation in her memory, the family suggests the library at her old school. Please bring your stories. She would have wanted to hear them, and she would have corrected the grammar.

input:
Looking back, the moment that shaped me most was not a grand achievement but a quiet failure. I had spent months preparing for a robotics competition, convinced that the best design would win. When our prototype broke down in front of the judges, I felt the familiar urge to blame the materials, the schedule, or my teammates. Instead, I sat with the wreckage for a while and asked myself what I could actually learn from it.

What I learned was that I had been treating my own ideas as finished products rather than hypotheses. I had not tested the drivetrain under load, and I had dismissed a classmate's suggestion because it came from someone I assumed was less experienced. That realization changed how I work. Now I build in small increments, invite criticism early, and keep a running log of what fails and why. The habit has made me a better collaborator, and it has taught me to value a question as much as an answer.

I am drawn to engineering because it rewards this kind of honest iteration. I want to study systems that are messy, interdependent, and imperfect, and to contribute to solving problems where the first attempt is rarely the last. The failure at that competition was painful, but it gave me something a trophy never could: a clear sense of how I want to think and how I want to grow.

Pranav Iyer is thirty-one, works as a structural engineer in Pune, and still drives the same silver Maruti his father bought him in 2016, registration MH12 KD 4471, which he says has seen more of Maharashtra than he has. He grew up in Kothrud, and though he moved out two years ago, he still goes back most Sunday afternoons to his mother's flat at 14, Karve Nagar Lane No. 3, Pune 411052, for chai and an argument about cricket. He is looking for someone who can keep up with a long monsoon drive, laugh at her own mistakes, and doesn't mind that he reads history books on holiday.

Pranav is not a man of grand gestures but he remembers small things: the order you take your coffee, the name of your first school, the song you hummed in traffic last week. He cooks a decent dal on weekends and will tell you honestly that his biryani is still a work in progress. Weekends are for hikes around Sinhagad or long walks along the Mula river, and he is trying, slowly, to become someone who sleeps before midnight.

If you enjoy filter coffee at odd hours, debates about whether Pune or Bangalore has better street food, or simply someone who will drive you to the hills without asking for directions, message him. input: I stand here today with a heavy heart, though I know how much laughter filled every room she walked into. For as long as I can remember, she believed that kindness was not a gift to be saved for special occasions but a habit to practise every single morning. She baked for neighbours she barely knew, remembered the birthdays of children who were not even hers, and never once let a friend face a hard day alone. Her hands were always busy, her kettle always warm, and her door always open. Those of us who were lucky enough to share her table know what we have lost, and we carry her example forward in everything we do.

input:
Couldn't sleep again, so I've come downstairs with a mug of tea gone cold beside me. The house is quiet except for the boiler ticking over, and the rain has been going since teatime without any sign of easing. I keep thinking about the call I had with my sister on Sunday. She was trying to be cheerful about the new job, but I could hear how tired she sounds. I told her I'd visit properly once things settle, and I meant it, though I say that a lot and then don't follow through.

Work has been relentless. Every morning I tell myself I'll leave on time, and every evening I'm still at the desk, rereading the same three emails and feeling vaguely guilty about all the things I haven't finished. Some days I manage a proper walk at lunch and it clears my head entirely. Other days I eat a sandwich over the keyboard and forget I've eaten at all. I'm trying to be kinder to myself about that, which is harder than it sounds.

Tomorrow I want to get up early, take the long way round the park, and buy something decent for dinner rather than the usual frozen pizza. Small things, I know. But I think they're the ones that keep a person steady. Maybe I'll ring my sister before I leave the house, just to hear her voice before the day starts. For now I'll finish this tea, even though it's stone cold, and try once more to sleep.

input:
Good morning, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Thomas Ashworth, and I was lucky enough to be Jim's son. Most of you knew him as Jimmy, which he insisted on right up until he was seventy-eight, when he finally let my daughter call him Grandad Jim and then pretended he hadn't enjoyed it.

Dad was born on the 14th of January 1947 at the Royal Infirmary in Leeds, and he never let us forget that it was snowing. He grew up at 22 Holbeck Avenue, Headingley, in a house where there was always someone at the kitchen table. He went to Leeds Grammar School, and he always said the only thing he learned there was how to fix a bicycle chain under a desk. He was not a scholar, but he was the cleverest man with his hands I have ever met.

He worked for thirty-one years at the same engineering firm, Harcourt & Lowe on Wellington Street, and he could tell you the serial number of every lathe in the place. When the firm closed, he took the redundancy money, bought a second-hand Vauxhall Cavalier with the registration plate KWR 4471, and drove it around the country for two summers. He called it his retirement, and I think it was the happiest I ever saw him.

Dad loved a good argument, a bad pun and a Saturday in the garden. He grew the most enormous runner beans and gave them away to anyone who stood still long enough. He would tell the same stories at every wedding and funeral, and somehow they got better each time. He never once let a cup of tea go cold if he could help it, and he always, always remembered your birthday, even when he had nothing to give you but a card and a terrible joke.

So I'll finish where he would have wanted me to. Dad, thank you for the bicycle chains, the runner beans and the endless patience. You were the best of us, and we will keep your kettle warm for you. Rest well, Jimmy.

input:
My name is Avi Levental, and I was lucky enough to be Amit's older brother for forty-one years. Amit was born in Haifa in the spring of 1979, in a small apartment above a bakery on Herzl Street, and from the very first day he made noise about everything. He grew up loving the sea, arguing about football, and fixing things that other people had given up on. When our mother got sick, it was Amit who drove her to every appointment, who learned the names of every nurse, and who never once let her feel like a burden.

For the last twelve years Amit worked as a senior systems engineer at Tavor Analytics, where his colleagues described him as the person you called when everything else had failed. Ask any of them and they will tell you about the night in November 2019 when he stayed until four in the morning rebuilding a server, and then came in at nine to make everyone coffee. He never wanted credit. He wanted things to work, and he wanted the people around him to be okay. Many of you have written to his work email, avi.amit@tavoranalytics.co.il, in the past week, and I want you to know that every message was read, and that his team is keeping them all.

My brother was not perfect. He was stubborn, he was loud, and he could never leave a restaurant without paying for the table next to ours. But he loved his daughter Noa more than anything in this world, and he taught her to whistle through her fingers and to stand up for people who cannot stand up for themselves. Amit, we will keep arguing with you in our heads for the rest of our lives. Thank you for being exactly who you were.

I am writing to report a water damage claim at my home on Alder Creek Road in Lakewood, Ohio, which occurred on the night of October 14. I am writing this with a heavy heart, because the person who taught me most about patience, humour and sticking at things has gone. For more years than I can count, I was lucky enough to call them a friend, and I am still learning what it means to have that voice no longer in the room.

They were someone who noticed things. They remembered the small details of your week, asked after the difficult thing you had mentioned months before, and would quietly bring a cup of tea before you had realised you needed one. Their kindness was never loud. It showed up in the way they listened, in the favours done without fuss, and in the steady encouragement they gave to anyone who was trying something new.

To those who knew them, you will understand how much they will be missed. To those who did not, I hope you will take away a sense of how one good-natured person can make a whole circle of people feel more at home in the world. I am grateful for every conversation, every shared laugh and every lesson, and I will carry them with me.

I finally saw Dr. Papadakis at the clinic on Ermou Street last Tuesday, April 9th, after weeks of putting it off. My name is Dimitra Kostopoulou, though everyone who knows me calls me Dimi, and I brought my national ID number (AB 418362) with me because the receptionist insisted on it again. The main reason for the visit was the rash on my forearms that had been spreading since the trip to Naxos. Dr. Papadakis asked a lot of questions about what I had eaten and whether I had been swimming in the sea, and she took a small sample for testing. She thinks it is likely contact dermatitis but wants the lab results before ruling anything out.

My sister Eleni came along because she had driven me there and refused to wait in the car. She was the one who remembered that I had started a new laundry detergent the week before, which I had completely forgotten. Dr. Papadakis said that could easily explain it and told me to stop using it for two weeks and switch to something unscented. She also recommended a hydrocortisone cream for the itching, which I should apply only at night, and asked me to come back if the rash reaches my face or if I develop a fever.

On the way out I bumped into my old colleague Nikos Vlachos in the waiting room, which was a bit of a surprise since I had no idea he lived in the area. We talked for a few minutes about his new job and then I went home to Kallithea, still scratching. The follow-up is booked for April 23rd, and I have already put a reminder on my phone so I do not forget again.

input:
I'm Gareth Lindqvist, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a civil engineer focused on stormwater systems for mid-sized American cities. My colleagues mostly call me Gare, a name that stuck after a particularly long site inspection in Tacoma when I was still a graduate intern and too tired to correct anyone. I grew up in Duluth, Minnesota, where the lake shaped my sense of water as something to be respected and managed rather than simply enjoyed.

My path into engineering was not straight. I studied geology for two years before switching to civil engineering at the University of Wisconsin, mostly because I wanted to build things that people would use every day. My first real project was a retention basin in a neighbourhood that flooded every spring, and watching residents walk their children past it in the summer still feels like the best evidence I have that the work matters. Since then I have led design teams on drainage upgrades, green infrastructure pilots, and two bridge culvert replacements.

Over the last four years I have spent more time on community engagement than I expected. Public meetings are difficult, and I have learned that a diagram rarely persuades anyone on its own. What works is walking the site with people, listening to what they have already noticed, and treating local knowledge as data. That approach shaped the stormwater plan we delivered for the Eastside district last autumn, which was approved with unusually little opposition.

Outside the office I coach a youth robotics team on Saturday mornings and keep a small vegetable garden that is, by any honest measure, losing a long war with the deer. I am also an enthusiastic and sometimes overly earnest contributor to online discussions about infrastructure policy. You can find me on social media as @gare_builds_water, where I post photos from site visits and the occasional rant about culvert sizing.

I look forward to talking with you at the conference about resilient drainage, the economics of green infrastructure, and how cities can plan for heavier rainfall than their older systems were ever designed to handle. If you would like to continue the conversation afterwards, you can reach me directly at 612-555-0147. I am always happy to talk water, and I will probably bring too many slides.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to recommend Itai Barkan, who worked under my supervision as a senior data analyst at our Haifa office from March 2019 until his departure in May 2024. Itai joined us from the Technion, where he completed his MSc in Industrial Engineering, and he brought with him a rigour and curiosity that quickly set him apart. Within his first year he rebuilt our monthly forecasting pipeline, cutting the time our finance team spent reconciling figures by roughly two-thirds.

What I valued most in Itai was his judgement under pressure. In the autumn of 2022, when a supplier data feed failed on the eve of a board presentation, Itai worked through the night with the vendor's engineers, rebuilt the affected tables from raw logs, and had a corrected report in the board's hands by seven the next morning. He did not look for credit in that episode, and he was the first to suggest that we document the failure so it would not recur.

Itai is also a generous colleague. He ran a fortnightly SQL clinic for staff who were new to our tools, and several analysts from other departments still tell me how much they learned from those sessions. He was patient with questions that other people might have dismissed, and he took time to explain the reasoning behind his models rather than simply handing over results.

Although Itai's technical skills are considerable, I would stress his communication. He wrote clear, concise briefings for executives who had no statistical background, and he was comfortable challenging assumptions in meetings, always with evidence and never with ego. Several of our product managers have asked to work with him on future projects.

If you would like to discuss Itai's work with us in more detail, you may reach me directly on 04-8837261, or write to me at dganor@norvia-analytics.co.il. I recommend him without reservation for any role that calls for analytical depth, initiative and integrity.

Yours sincerely,

Dalia Ganor
Director of Analytics
Norvia Analytics Ltd., Haifa

I am making this statement to set out what happened on the evening I was assaulted outside a takeaway near the bus stop. I had finished a late shift and was walking home on my own when a man approached me from behind and grabbed my bag. When I turned around he pushed me against the wall and told me to hand over my phone. I shouted for help and he ran off down a side lane. I was shaken but not seriously hurt, though I did have a graze on my elbow and bruising on my upper arm.

I went straight to a neighbour's house, who called the emergency number for me. The officers who attended took my description of the man and noted that he wore a dark hooded top, had a backpack, and spoke with a local accent. I was able to recall that he was of average height and slim build. I did not recognise him from before. Since then I have checked the area on several evenings and have not seen him again, though I have felt uneasy walking that route alone.

I am willing to provide any further information that may help the investigation, including access to any footage from nearby premises. I would ask that I be kept informed of any progress. I confirm that the contents of this statement are true to the best of my knowledge and belief.

input:
When I was seven, my grandmother took me to Tullamore for the first time, and I remember being struck by how the whole town seemed to run on conversation. My name is Kieran Dwyer, and I grew up above my family's shop on Bridge Street, so I learned early that people come in for bread and stay for news. At seventeen I still think of that as the foundation of how I want to live: paying attention to the people around me and figuring out how to help.

That instinct pushed me into volunteering at Bean There Cafe on Church Street, where I have worked every Saturday since I turned sixteen. The owner, Siobhan, lets me run the morning rush, and I have learned more about budgeting, customer complaints and patience in those hours than in any classroom. When the cafe ran a food drive in July last year, I helped organise the collection and we raised enough to supply the local food bank for three weeks. Kieran is not a name that gets much attention in a kitchen full of steam and shouting, but I have come to value being the person who keeps the orders moving.

I want to study social policy because I have seen how small decisions shape ordinary lives in a place like Tullamore. The cafe taught me that good intentions need practical systems behind them, and my experience in the food drive showed me how much a community can achieve when people trust each other. I hope to bring that combination of empathy and organisation to university, and eventually to a career that turns local knowledge into lasting change.

input:
I'm thrilled to share that I've started a new role as Senior Product Analyst at Brindley & Hale Logistics, based out of their Canary Wharf office. After nearly six years in retail banking, this is a big change, and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on the journey.

When I first moved to London, I lived in Hackney, and my routine was simple: coffee at Ember & Oak on Mare Street before the commute, and a weekly session at Pulse Fitness on Lower Clapton Road. Those small rituals kept me grounded during some long, uncertain stretches. Ember & Oak's owner, Marcus, once told me that good work is mostly about showing up consistently, and I've thought about that more than he probably realises.

The move wasn't easy to decide. I spent weeks weighing it up, talking things through with my friend and former colleague Tamsin Ferreira, who has worked in supply chain for over a decade. Her advice was blunt and useful: stop asking whether you're ready and start asking what you'd learn. That reframing made the decision clearer than any spreadsheet could.

If you're considering a switch yourself, here is what helped me most. Map your transferable skills honestly, even the ones that feel unglamorous. Talk to people already doing the job, not just recruiters. And be prepared for the first three months to feel uncomfortable, because that discomfort usually means you're learning.

I'm grateful to everyone who supported me through the transition, from the team at my old bank to the friends who answered my late-night messages. If you'd like to connect or swap notes on career changes, feel free to reach out at tanya.brooksfield@hotmail.co.uk. I'd genuinely love to hear your story.

input:
Dear Grandma Ruth,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden is coming along nicely. I have been meaning to write for weeks, but the semester got away from me. Things here in Madison are busy but good. Classes at Riverside Community College keep me on my toes, and I finally feel like I understand what I am doing in my statistics course, which is more than I can say for last spring.

I wanted to tell you about the job. As of July 9th I started working part-time at Harbor Point Logistics, answering phones and helping with the scheduling desk. My manager, a patient woman named Denise, says I learn fast. The hours fit around my classes, and the paycheck means I can finally help cover my share of the rent without asking Mom for anything. I know you worried about me taking on too much, so I promise I am keeping an eye on it.

The paperwork for the job was a bit of a headache. They needed a copy of my passport and my national ID number for the payroll system, and I had to dig through the filing cabinet to find the originals. It took an afternoon, but everything is sorted now. Brian, my roommate, laughed at me for taking a photo of every page before I handed them over, but I figured better safe than sorry.

Brian is doing well too, by the way. He sends his regards and says he owes you a proper thank-you for the casserole you sent over at Christmas. He is still working at the hospital on Fourth Street, doing his night shifts in the lab, and he says the coffee there is terrible but the people are kind. We have been cooking together on Sundays, which has been a nice way to unwind.

If you have a moment this week, please write back or send me an email at brian.ruth.family@example.com if the post is slow. I would love to hear how the church choir is doing and whether Uncle Walt ever finished that birdhouse. Tell me everything, even the small things. They are what I miss most.

With all my love,
Benjamin

input:
August 14. Dr. Haskell suggested I start writing these down between sessions, so here goes. My name is Nadia, and I still haven't decided whether I hate that I'm doing this or whether it's helping. Today I spent most of the session talking about my mother, who still calls me from Duluth every Sunday even though I moved to Phoenix three years ago. She asks whether I'm eating, whether I'm sleeping, whether I've found a church yet. I answer yes, yes, and no, and then I hang up and feel like a kid who failed a test.

Dr. Haskell asked me what I wanted from those calls. I didn't have an answer, which annoyed me more than anything else. I think I want her to ask me something she doesn't already know the answer to. I want to be a person to her instead of a project.

There's also the thing with Marcus. I know, I know, I promised myself I'd stop checking his profile. But last night I went to his page again, the one under @marcus_dwyer_rides, and there was a photo from a trail I've never been on, with a caption about starting over. I closed the app and then opened it again. Dr. Haskell called it a compulsion loop, which is a clinical way of saying I'm being stupid on purpose.

What I did do this week: I went to the Thursday swim class at the community center, even though I stood at the edge of the pool for ten minutes before getting in. I talked to a woman named Renee afterward who said she also grew up in a town where everyone knew your business. We both laughed about it. It was the first time in weeks I didn't feel like I was pretending.

Dr. Haskell wants me to try one small thing before our next session on August 21: text one person I haven't talked to since the move, and tell them something true. I've picked my cousin Tanya. I haven't decided what the true thing is yet. Maybe that it's harder here than I let on. Maybe that I'm glad she never stopped inviting me to things.

I'll write again after I've sent it, or after I've chickened out.

input:
Llevo casi dos años yendo a la Clínica Dental Sol de Levante, en la calle Ribera de Curtidores de Valladolid, y nunca había escrito una reseña, pero esta vez siento que tengo que hacerlo. Me llamo Carlos Medina Ruiz, aunque en el gimnasio y en el barrio todos me conocen como Charly. Trabajo como coordinador de logística en Transportes Lázaro e Hijos y cada vez que tengo una urgencia dental tengo que organizarme entre turnos, así que la flexibilidad de esta clínica me ha salvado más de una vez.

El pasado 14 de marzo tuve una muela partida en plena reunión de trabajo, y llamé al 983 412 778 a las ocho de la mañana casi sin esperanza. Me cogió el teléfono Marta, la recepcionista, que me dio cita para esa misma tarde. El doctor Iñaki Benítez me atendió con una calma que agradezco, me explicó cada paso de la endodoncia y no me hizo sentir culpable por haber dejado pasar el dolor durante semanas.

Lo que más me gustó fue el seguimiento. Carlos, el de la clínica, no Carlos el mío, me envió un recordatorio por correo a carlos.medina.ruiz@hotmail.com el 22 de marzo para revisar la encía, y eso no lo hace casi nadie. Ya sé que hay clínicas más baratas en el centro, pero aquí pagas por un trato humano y por saber que alguien se acuerda de ti.

No todo es perfecto. La sala de espera es pequeña y en las horas punta hay que esperar un poco más de lo anunciado, y el aparcamiento de la zona es un desastre. Pero cuando lo comparo con lo que me pasó en mi anterior dentista, en la otra punta de la ciudad, no tengo ninguna queja seria.

En resumen, si vives o trabajas por la zona de Las Delicias y necesitas un dentista que responda al teléfono y te explique las cosas sin prisas, esta es mi recomendación. Yo volveré en mayo para la limpieza, y ya tengo apuntado el día. Gracias a todo el equipo, sobre todo a Marta, que es la primera persona que me tranquilizó a esas ocho de la mañana con una muela partida.

input:
I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on October 14 so I don't forget anything when I talk to my family about it. My name is Tessa Lindqvist and I went to see Dr. Anand at the Brampton Civic Hospital family clinic, which is the same place my mom has been going for years. I had been having dizzy spells for about three weeks, mostly when I stand up quickly after working at my desk, and some mornings a dull headache that doesn't go away until lunch. I also mentioned that I've been sleeping badly since starting my second term at Western University.

Dr. Anand checked my blood pressure twice because the first reading was high, probably because I was nervous and had run from the parking lot. She asked a lot of questions about my diet, how much water I drink, and whether I've been using my laptop late at night. I told her I'm up until about one most nights studying, and that I skip breakfast on weekdays. She listened to my heart and lungs and looked in my ears, then sent me for bloodwork that same morning.

The lab results came back on October 21 and Dr. Anand called me herself, which I appreciated. My iron levels are a bit low and my vitamin D is under the healthy range. She thinks the dizziness is mostly from iron deficiency and not sleeping enough, so she prescribed an iron supplement to take with orange juice and asked me to come back in six weeks for a recheck. She also gave me a referral to a nutritionist, though I haven't booked that yet.

My partner, Marcus, drove me to the appointment and waited in the car, so I'm writing this partly to remind him what the plan is. He's been worried since I told him about the headaches, and I think it helped him to hear that it's probably something simple to fix. My sister Erin also asked me to keep her posted because she had similar anemia when she was in university, so I told her I'd send her the lab numbers.

For my own notes: take the iron tablet every morning, drink more water, eat breakfast even if it's just toast, try to be off screens by midnight, and book the nutritionist before the end of October. Next appointment is on November 25 at 10:30. If the dizziness gets worse before then, or I faint, I'm supposed to call the clinic right away or go to emergency. Account reference for the billing office is 40817-226, and my car registration is in the glovebox if I ever need it for the insurance paperwork.

I told her I'm up until about one most nights studying, and that I skip breakfast on weekdays. She listened to my heart and lungs and looked in my ears, then sent me for bloodwork that same morning.

The lab results came back on October 27 and Dr. Sandhu called me herself, which I appreciated. My iron levels are a bit low and my vitamin D is under the healthy range. She thinks the dizziness is mostly from iron deficiency and not sleeping enough, so she prescribed an iron supplement to take with orange juice and asked me to come back in six weeks for a recheck. She also gave me a referral to a nutritionist, though I haven't booked that yet.

My partner, Julian, drove me to the appointment and waited in the car, so I'm writing this partly to remind him what the plan is. He's been worried since I told him about the headaches, and I think it helped him to hear that it's probably something simple to fix. My sister Megan also asked me to keep her posted because she had similar anemia when she was in university, so I told her I'd send her the lab numbers.

For my own notes: take the iron tablet every morning, drink more water, eat breakfast even if it's just toast, try to be off screens by midnight, and book the nutritionist before the end of October. Next appointment is on December 2 at 11:15. If the dizziness gets worse before then, or I faint, I'm supposed to call the clinic right away or go to emergency. Account reference for the billing office is 62053-417, and my car registration is in the glovebox if I ever need it for the insurance paperwork.

My name is Gilad, but my grandmother has called me Gigi since the day I was born, and the name has followed me through every classroom I have ever sat in. I am seventeen, and for most of my life I have measured myself against the people who grew up around me in our building at 14 Herzl Street in Haifa, where the stairwell smells of cardamom from the Iraqi family on the second floor and the view from our balcony stretches all the way to the port. That building taught me that a neighborhood is a set of small obligations: carrying groceries for the widow downstairs, repairing the broken gate with my cousin Yoni, and listening to stories on Friday evenings that I only half understood at the time.

The moment I started to think seriously about engineering came on October 9th, when our water pump failed during a heat wave and forty families were left without running water for three days. I spent those days with a multimeter and a library book on pumps, tracing the wiring with my uncle Avi until we found a corroded relay. The repair took twenty minutes. The understanding I gained over those three days took much longer, and it made me want to build systems that keep ordinary people safe and comfortable when something inevitably goes wrong.

I hope to study mechanical engineering because I want to work on exactly these problems, the ones that touch daily life in cities like mine. My teachers describe me as persistent and my neighbors describe me as useful, and I would like to become an engineer who is both. I believe a university that values hands-on learning and community responsibility would give me the tools to do that.

Lately I've been getting messages from an account on Instagram calling itself @benwhitlock_rides, which I don't run and never have. Someone has also been commenting on my old photos from a holiday in Whitby, so I know they're scrolling back a long way.

The worst part is that a few weeks ago a message arrived from someone claiming to be from my bank, asking me to confirm my details, including my passport number, which I'd given a while back for a mortgage application. I didn't reply, but I'm not confident the account wasn't already compromised. I've started to feel like I can't go out without checking over my shoulder, and Ben, my brother, keeps telling me I'm overreacting.

What I need help with is a plan. Should I report the Instagram account first, or go to the police about the messages? Should I tell Hartwell's HR in case the account is targeting my work email? And how do I work out whether my passport or national insurance details have actually been used? I'd rather be practical than panicked, so any steps in order would really help.

It's posting photos taken outside my flat on Park Street, Clifton, with captions about when I leave for work. Someone has also been commenting on my old photos from a holiday in Padstow, so I know they're scrolling back a long way.

The worst part is that a few weeks ago a message arrived from someone claiming to be from my bank, asking me to confirm my details, including my passport number, which I'd given a while back for a mortgage application. I didn't reply, but I'm not confident the account wasn't already compromised. I've started to feel like I can't go out without checking over my shoulder, and Dan, my brother, keeps telling me I'm overreacting.

What I need help with is a plan. Should I report the Instagram account first, or go to the police about the messages? Should I tell Crowther's HR in case the account is targeting my work email? And how do I work out whether my passport or national insurance details have actually been used? I'd rather be practical than panicked, so any steps in order would really help.

input: I still remember the morning of June 14th, when I stood in the hallway of our apartment in Haifa and realized my grandmother could no longer recognize the photographs on her wall. Ilan, my younger cousin, had been the one to translate her stories from Hebrew into English for our family archive, and when he left for his army service, that task fell to me. Since then I have spent long evenings recording her memories, transcribing them, and posting short excerpts under the handle @ilan_stories_haifa so distant relatives in Toronto and Buenos Aires can follow along. This project taught me that history survives only when someone takes responsibility for it, and it is the reason I want to study oral history at university.

input:
I still think about the afternoon we spent in Haarlem last July, wandering the narrow streets behind the Grote Markt with no real plan. My sister Claudia had insisted we leave Amsterdam for a day, and she was right. We started at the Frans Hals Museum, where I stood in front of a portrait for almost ten minutes while Claudia laughed at me for being so quiet. Claudia works as a senior curator at the Rijksmuseum, so she spotted details I would have missed entirely, like the way the painter let the brushwork show in the lace collars. Her colleagues at the Rijksmuseum had warned her that Haarlem was too small to bother with, but I think they were wrong.

After the museum we crossed the old town toward the Spaarne river, stopping every few minutes for photos. Claudia kept checking her phone because a rota for the conservation team at the Rijksmuseum had to go out that evening, and she grumbled about it cheerfully. We found a little bakery on a side street where the owner, an older man with flour on his forearms, gave us two extra stroopwafels just because we asked him where the best view of the Bakenesser Gracht was. That kind of warmth is what I remember most about the Netherlands, more than any tulip field or canal house.

In the late afternoon we rented bikes, which is the only sensible way to see the countryside around the city. We rode out past the dunes toward Zandvoort, the wind pushing against us the whole way, and Claudia shouted that she would never forgive me if I let her fall behind. We stopped for chips with mayonnaise at a seaside kiosk, the sort of meal that tastes better than it has any right to after hours of cycling.

By the time we returned to the station, my legs were jelly and my camera battery was nearly empty. Claudia, who had memorised every train timetable on the trip, booked us onto the last direct service back to Amsterdam Centraal. We sat by the window and talked about our childhood in Leiden, where our mother used to take us to the botanical garden, and about the medical school our cousin had just started at Leiden University Medical Center. I fell asleep before the train reached Schiphol.

If you visit Haarlem in July, do yourself a favour: rent a bike, skip the first museum on your list if you must, and find that bakery. Claudia has promised to take me back next summer, and I have already started planning the route.

Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,

hiermit bestätige ich gern die Tätigkeit von Lukas Brandt, der vom 1. März 2016 bis zum 30. September 2023 in unserem Unternehmen, der Hartmann Maschinenbau GmbH in Stuttgart, als Projektingenieur beschäftigt war. Lukas Brandt wurde in Ulm geboren, und wir haben während seiner Zeit bei uns stets seine Verbundenheit mit der Region gespürt, die sich auch in seiner gründlichen und bodenständigen Arbeitsweise zeigte.

In seiner Funktion verantwortete Herr Brandt die technische Betreuung mehrerer Fertigungsanlagen für die Automobilzulieferindustrie. Er übernahm Projekte von der Konzeptphase bis zur Inbetriebnahme beim Kunden und koordinierte dabei regelmäßig Teams aus Konstruktion, Elektrotechnik und Qualitätssicherung. Besonders hervorzuheben ist seine Fähigkeit, auch unter engen Terminvorgaben den Überblick zu behalten und Lösungen zu entwickeln, die sowohl technisch überzeugend als auch wirtschaftlich tragfähig waren.

Lukas Brandt zeichnete sich zudem durch eine ausgeprägte Teamfähigkeit aus. Kolleginnen und Kollegen schätzten seine ruhige, sachliche Art und seine Bereitschaft, Wissen weiterzugeben. Im Jahr 2021 leitete er eine interne Schulungsreihe zur Anlagendiagnose, die von der gesamten Abteilung sehr positiv aufgenommen wurde. Auch im Umgang mit Kunden zeigte er stets Verlässlichkeit und Professionalität.

Sein Verhalten gegenüber Vorgesetzten und Mitarbeitenden war jederzeit korrekt und wertschätzend. Herr Brandt erfüllte seine Aufgaben mit großer Sorgfalt, hielt sich an vereinbarte Standards und trug durch konstruktive Beiträge in Besprechungen zur kontinuierlichen Verbesserung unserer Prozesse bei. Fragen zur Arbeitsqualität oder zum Arbeitsverhalten hätten wir uneingeschränkt mit gut bewerten können.

Das Arbeitsverhältnis endete auf eigenen Wunsch von Herrn Brandt, der eine neue berufliche Herausforderung suchte. Wir bedauern seinen Weggang sehr und hätten ihn gern weiterhin in unserem Team gehabt. Für seine künftige Laufbahn wünschen wir ihm alles Gute und viel Erfolg.

Bei Rückfragen erreichen Sie mich unter der Telefonnummer 0711 4820 657 oder per E-Mail unter lukas.brandt@hartmann-maschinenbau.de.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen

Dr. Corinna Vogt
Personalleiterin
Hartmann Maschinenbau GmbH, Stuttgart

input:
I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to share that my father, Ryuji Matsuda, passed away peacefully at home in Kanazawa on the 14th of December, surrounded by the family he loved so fiercely. He was seventy-eight years old. Many of you knew him as the quiet man who never missed a Thursday at the Yanaka fish market, or as the teacher who spent thirty-one years at Nishi Kanazawa Junior High patiently explaining the difference between ellipsis and apostrophe to restless fourteen-year-olds.

Ryuji was born in Hakodate in 1946, the second of four children, to a family of fishmongers who had learned to read the tides before they learned to read books. He never lost that sense of the sea. Even in his final months, when he could no longer walk to the harbour, he asked me to describe the boats coming in each morning, and he would nod along as if he could see every hull. He often told me that the town where he was born had taught him patience, and the city where he raised us had taught him kindness.

After university in Sapporo he moved south to Kanazawa, where he met my mother, Hanako, at a tea house near the Higashi Chaya district in the spring of 1974. He pretended for a year that he had not fallen in love with her at first sight. She never believed him, and she teased him about it every anniversary until she passed in 2019. Their love was the kind that did not need to be loud, and I think that is the greatest thing I learned from him.

He was a man of small rituals. Every morning he brewed green tea in the same brown pot, every evening he listened to the radio broadcast of the baseball scores with his eyes closed, and every New Year's Eve he wrote a single line of haiku in a notebook, which he never showed anyone. Only after his death did we find the notebooks, forty years of them, tied with string on the shelf above his desk. We are still deciding what to do with them.

He is survived by his children, Keiko and Takeshi, and by three grandchildren who adored him. Those who wish to share memories are warmly invited to write to me directly or post them on his tribute page, which the family has set up under the handle @ryuji.matsuda.tribute. A memorial service will be held at Kōdai-ji temple on the 21st of December at ten in the morning. Please come if you can, and bring a story. He would have wanted us to tell them over tea.

With gratitude and love,
Keiko Matsuda

input:
Tuesday 14 October

Rain again this morning, the kind that comes sideways off the Atlantic and gets into everything. I walked up to the bus stop on Harcourt Road with my hood up and my bag clutched against my chest, and by the time the 46A pulled in I was already regretting not taking the car. Mam would have told me so. She texts me every morning now, usually about the weather and whether I've eaten, and today she sent a photo of the kettle with the message "Put this on, you sound peaky on the phone." She is right, I did sound peaky. I've been sleeping badly since the move.

The new flat is at 27 Blackrock Gardens, Dublin 6, on the third floor, and the landlord is a retired teacher called Mr Keane who insists on calling me "Miss Brennan" as if I were fourteen. The building is old, the radiators clank like they're trying to get out, and the window in the back bedroom doesn't quite close. But the light in the kitchen in the afternoons is extraordinary, all gold across the worktop, and I've already started thinking of it as mine. Everyone in the family has a name for me. Mam calls me Oonagh, Dad calls me Oonie, and my brother, who has never once used my real name, calls me Nagger, which I have asked him repeatedly to stop doing.

Work was busy. The Hendricks report is due on the 22nd and Fergal from accounts keeps sending me emails with the subject line URGENT in capitals, as if I hadn't noticed. I replied to the last one with a single line: "Noted. Attached is the draft." I didn't add that the draft is actually finished and has been since Thursday. Sometimes I like to watch the emails pile up and then answer them all at once.

In the evening I finally called Ciara. We talked for almost two hours, mostly about her wedding planning and whether the venue in Kilkenny is worth the deposit. She asked if I'd joined any clubs yet and I said no, and she gave me the look even down the phone. She's sending me the link to the running group that meets on Saturdays in Phoenix Park. I said I would think about it. I probably will.

output:
Tuesday 8 October

Rain again this morning, the kind that comes sideways off the Atlantic and gets into everything. I walked up to the bus stop on Merrion Quay with my hood up and my bag clutched against my chest, and by the time the 39A pulled in I was already regretting not taking the car. Mam would have told me so. She texts me every morning now, usually about the weather and whether I've eaten, and today she sent a photo of the kettle with the message "Put this on, you sound peaky on the phone." She is right, I did sound peaky. I've been sleeping badly since the move.

The new flat is at 14 Ranelagh Gardens, Dublin 6, on the third floor, and the landlord is a retired teacher called Mr Dunne who insists on calling me "Miss Hogan" as if I were fourteen. The building is old, the radiators clank like they're trying to get out, and the window in the back bedroom doesn't quite close. But the light in the kitchen in the afternoons is extraordinary, all gold across the worktop, and I've already started thinking of it as mine. Everyone in the family has a name for me. Mam calls me Aoife, Dad calls me Aoifie, and my brother, who has never once used my real name, calls me Tadhg, which I have asked him repeatedly to stop doing.

Work was busy. The Halpin report is due on the 29th and Cathal from accounts keeps sending me emails with the subject line URGENT in capitals, as if I hadn't noticed. I replied to the last one with a single line: "Noted. Attached is the draft." I didn't add that the draft is actually finished and has been since Thursday. Sometimes I like to watch the emails pile up and then answer them all at once.

In the evening I finally called Niamh. We talked for almost two hours, mostly about her wedding planning and whether the venue in Kilkenny is worth the deposit. She asked if I'd joined any clubs yet and I said no, and she gave me the look even down the phone. She's sending me the link to the running group that meets on Saturdays in Stephen's Green. I said I would think about it. I probably will.

Before bed I wrote down the address and my email, aoife.hogan@mailbox.ie, on the inside cover of this notebook, because I keep forgetting my own details when I fill in forms and it's embarrassing. Tomorrow I want to go to the market on Sunday, buy proper bread, and perhaps finally open the boxes in the hall. Goodnight, diary. The radiator is making its noise again.

Do you remember I told you about Pietro, the cousin who ran the bakery in Testaccio? Well, I finally went to see him last month, after almost three years of putting it off. I landed in Rome on the 4th of October with one suitcase and a passport number I must have written down a dozen times that week, PT9384071, because the airline kept asking for it. Pietro met me at the station with flour still on his shirt and hugged me so hard my ribs complained.

He took me up the narrow stairs of his building on Via Marmorata, and his wife Chiara had made cacio e pepe before I'd even put my bag down. We talked until nearly midnight about our grandmother's recipes and the old fight over the family house in Frosinone. Pietro kept calling me Pino, the childhood name nobody else uses anymore, and every time he said it I felt about nine years old again.

What I didn't expect was how easy it felt to be back. Testaccio still smells of bread and diesel in the mornings, and the woman at the corner stall still remembered my coffee order from when I was a teenager. I told Pietro I'm thinking of moving back for good, maybe next spring. He just laughed and said, 'Then you'd better learn the bus routes properly, Pino.' I think I will.

input:
I still think about the morning Franco woke us up in Siargao, grinning like he had personally arranged the sunrise. He had been up since four with his surfboard, and by the time I stumbled out of our guesthouse on June 12, he had already talked two local fishermen into showing us their favourite break. We spent the first hour in the shallows, falling off boards and laughing so hard that the tide nearly carried my sunglasses out to sea. Franco's friend Marisol, a physiotherapist from Cebu who has been surfing since she was nine, watched us with the patience of someone who had seen a thousand beginners before us. She corrected my stance with two taps on the back and a single word: 'knees.'

Later that day we rode a tricycle across the island to Sohoton Cove, where the water turns a shade of green I didn't know existed. Franco insisted on bringing his camera, and he spent more time photographing his own reflection in the lagoon than the limestone cliffs. Everyone on the boat knew him as Kiko, a nickname his grandmother gave him when he was a toddler and that has never quite gone away. Between dives, he kept showing me videos of his dog back home in Davao, a scruffy mutt named Biscuit who, according to Franco, is the true ruler of the household. Biscuit is nearly fourteen now, and Franco's voice softened every time he mentioned him.

The following evening, we ate grilled squid and rice at a plastic-table stall in General Luna while Marisol kept reading out messages from the group chat. Someone had posted a blurry photo of us wiping out on our first wave, captioned with the handle @wavesandwanderlust_ph, and it had already collected more than two hundred likes. Franco pretended to be offended and then demanded a copy. We walked back along the dark road with our flip-flops in hand, listening to the crickets and the distant thump of a karaoke machine.

If you ever make it to Siargao, ask for Franco at the surf shop near the church. He will tell you the same stories I have told you here, and he will probably add a few more. Bring sunscreen, bring patience, and bring a little more courage than you think you need.

I am writing this with a heavy heart to say goodbye to my mother, Yvonne Hickey, who passed away peacefully at home in Ballina on the 14th of May, surrounded by the family she loved more than anything. Yvonne was born in Tuam in 1948, the eldest of six children, and she never quite lost the sharp wit or the soft Galway vowels that made her the life of every room she walked into. For thirty-one years she worked as a senior nurse coordinator at Mayo University Hospital, where generations of patients and colleagues knew her as the calm voice in the corridor who always had a biscuit and a kind word.

Mum had a great gift for friendship. Whether it was the Thursday card club, the parish choir, or the neighbours who would drop round for a cup of tea that somehow always turned into dinner, she made everyone feel they belonged. Her faithful companion of eleven years, a scruffy terrier called Biscuit, went everywhere with her and was never far from her side, even at the very end. Please know that Biscuit is in good hands with my brother Ciarán.

If you wish to remember Yvonne, she would ask that you call to someone who is lonely, or put the kettle on for a friend. You can reach me at yvonne.hickey.family@gmail.com or on 087 555 0142 if you have a story to share. We will be receiving visitors at Walsh's Funeral Home on Thursday from 4 to 6 pm, followed by the funeral Mass at St. Muredach's Cathedral the next morning. Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam.

input:
I've been coming to Harbourside Veterinary Clinic on Quay Street for almost three years now, ever since we moved to Halifax from Glasgow. Our old vet back in Paisley was wonderful, so I was nervous about starting over somewhere new. Patricia at the front desk made the first visit easy, and Dr. Okonkwo spent a full twenty minutes with us when Pumpkin, our nine-year-old tabby, stopped eating in early May. I was honestly expecting to be told it was nothing, but she ran bloods, explained every result, and called me two days later to check how he was doing.

What I appreciate most is the honesty. When Pumpkin needed dental work last autumn, the quote was clear and nobody pushed extras on me. The nurses are patient with nervous cats and nervous owners alike, and they never rush you out the door. The waiting room can get busy on Saturdays, so book ahead if you can.

I'd give the clinic five stars for care and communication. Parking is tight, and the card machine at reception has a habit of being slow, but neither has ever stopped me from recommending it to friends. If you're new to Halifax and need a vet you can trust, this is the place.

I am Karla Dimaculangan, a data engineer at Bayanihan Logistics Corporation in Pasig City, where I have spent the last six years building pipelines that keep the country's regional warehouses in sync. Before that I worked as a junior analyst at a fintech startup in Makati, which is where I first learned that the most useful thing an engineer can do is ask the people who will use the data what they actually need.

Outside of work I volunteer with Code Kapamilya, a community group that runs weekend coding workshops for students in Marikina. My closest collaborator there is Joselito Ramos, who designed our curriculum and still reminds me, every session, that good teaching is mostly patience. When we started the group, Joselito and I spent nights sketching lesson plans over a shared spreadsheet; he is the reason our first cohort of forty students finished the program in July.

I am always happy to talk about data quality, mentorship, or the unglamorous work of keeping systems reliable. You can reach me at karla.dimaculangan@bayanihanlogistics.ph or follow my writing and talks on X at @kdimaculangan_data. I look forward to meeting fellow engineers and educators at the conference.

input:
I still cannot quite believe that Melina Papadaki is gone. She was born in Kalamata on 14 April 1948, the second of four daughters, and she never let anyone forget that she was the one who had actually read the family's letters from Athens. For forty-one years she worked as a senior archivist at the Benaki Museum, and she spoke about old documents the way other people speak about their favourite football team. Many of us in the neighbourhood of Koukaki still remember her walking to the Saturday market on Veikou Street with a canvas bag and a sharp opinion about everything from olive oil prices to the new tram lines.

My own name is Nikos Vlachos, and I was her neighbour for almost twenty years, from the day I moved into the flat below hers on Dafni Street. She taught me to make spanakopita the way her mother did, though she insisted my pastry was always too thick. In the last months, when her eyesight began to fail, she asked me to read her the newspapers aloud every morning, and she would correct my pronunciation of every foreign name. She trusted me with the spare key and with her dog Tasos, and she never once asked me to be anyone other than myself.

Melina's funeral will be held on Thursday 23 April at the church of Agios Dimitrios at eleven in the morning. Friends who wish to share memories can write to me directly or post them on her page, @melina.archives.athens, which her grandchildren have promised to keep active. She is survived by her sisters Eleni and Sofia, her nephew Giorgos, and a great many people who owe her a book they never returned.

Today I want to write about the move, because my counsellor keeps asking me to name what I am actually grieving instead of calling it "just adjusting." Leaving the flat with the sticky balcony door, the bakery on the corner, and the friends who could drop everything for a late tea felt like shedding a skin I did not know I still had. Here, people are polite in a careful way. They say they will call and then they do not, and I have caught myself doing the same. I keep waiting for the moment when this place will feel like home, and I think that waiting is itself part of the problem.

What surprised me most this week was how angry I got over small things: a form that rejected my surname, a shopkeeper who pretended not to understand me, the way the light falls too early in the afternoon. My counsellor suggested that the anger is often grief wearing a louder coat. I wrote that down and then sat with it for a long time. It is easier to be furious at a bureaucrat than to admit I miss the version of myself who knew where everything was and who to ring when things went wrong.

I am trying a small experiment. Each morning I will write down one thing that is genuinely good here, even if it is only that the tea tastes different or that a stranger held a door without being asked. It feels a little forced, like a child being told to say sorry. But I notice I am starting to look for things rather than only waiting for them. That may be the first real step, even if I am not ready to call it progress yet.

Marco graduated from the University of Santo Tomas with an engineering degree, and the first thing he did after his board exams was take Mia to the Philippine General Hospital cafeteria, because that is where she was finishing her residency shifts and where they first really talked. He still insists it was the best halo-halo he ever had.

When Marco first told me about Mia, he sent me a photo of her from her Instagram, @mia.delacruz.md, with the message "Ate, look at this smile." I looked at it for a long time, because I had never seen him that happy about anything. Mia, you have shown this family what patience and kindness look like, and you have never once let Marco forget to call his mother on Sundays. Thank you for being exactly who you are. We welcome you with all our hearts.

I went in for my follow-up with Dr. Halvorsen at the Riverside Family Clinic on September 14 because the knee pain hadn't really gone away after the fall in August. She checked the range of motion, pressed around the joint, and ordered an MRI at the imaging center on Alder Street, which is a five-minute drive from my apartment in the Eastside neighborhood. She said the cartilage looks irritated but nothing torn, so the plan is physical therapy twice a week and anti-inflammatories for three weeks. I asked about running and she said to stop for now, which I'm not thrilled about, but I understand.

The front desk needed my ID to update the chart, so I brought my passport, number 548192336, since my driver's license was expired. The receptionist asked me to confirm my date of birth and my emergency contact, which is my sister Tamsin Greaves. Tamsin keeps reminding me to take the medication with food, and she's the one who saw I'd been limping through the grocery store. My dog Biscuit was waiting in the car with the windows cracked, and honestly he's the only reason I got out of bed this week.

I also asked whether it's okay to keep posting my training progress online. She laughed and said it's fine as long as I don't push through the pain. So if you want updates on my recovery, I'm still posting at @tessa_runs_east. The next appointment is September 28 at 9:30 a.m., and I'm bringing the MRI results and the physical therapy referral with me.

Hey Rohan, I still can't believe I didn't tell you this over chai last week, so here it is in one long message. You know my cousin Vikram? The one who used to drive us to Lodhi Gardens every Sunday? Well, he's been having a rough time since the start of January. He got admitted to Fortis Hospital in Vasant Kunj on the 9th after collapsing at his office in Gurgaon. The doctors said it was his kidneys, and honestly, I was a mess for three days.

What I keep thinking about is how he never told anyone. My aunt only found out because she called him and he didn't pick up, so she went round to his flat in Malviya Nagar and found him on the floor. Can you imagine? I keep replaying that call in my head, wondering why we all let him drift like that. He always said he was fine, that it was just stress from work at Sharma & Associates.

The funny part is that Vikram was always the one bossing everyone around. At St. Columba's School he was the captain of the debating team, and he still talks about how we lost the inter-school finals because of a missing comma in some speech. Even now, from his hospital bed, he's grumbling about the food and asking me to bring him proper parathas from Old Delhi. So at least his sense of humour is intact.

He's been moved out of the ICU now, and the doctors say he can go home in about two weeks if his numbers keep improving. I've been giving him updates whenever I can, and my number is still 98114 32067 if you want to call me directly. Don't worry about visiting in the middle of your exams; just send him a voice note, he'll love it.

Anyway, that's the story. I'm exhausted but relieved. Honestly, I think this whole ordeal has made me realise how much we take people for granted. Call me when you get a free evening, okay? We need to plan that trip to Rishikesh we keep postponing.

Take care, and give my love to your mum.

Anjali Verma

input:
Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Analyst position advertised on your careers page. I have spent the last four years working in data reporting for a regional logistics firm in Halifax, and I am ready to bring that experience to a team that values careful, clear work. My name is Tessa Ferguson, though my colleagues have called me Tess since my first day at university in Dalhousie, and I would welcome the chance to discuss how my background fits your needs.

In my current role I maintain weekly dashboards for operations managers, automate recurring reports using SQL and Excel, and flag irregularities before they reach the client. Last spring I redesigned our shipment tracking workbook, which cut the time spent on monthly reconciliation by roughly a third. I enjoy the part of analysis that happens after the numbers are in: working out what they mean for the people who have to act on them, and explaining it without jargon.

Before moving into analytics I worked for two years as a customer service lead, which taught me how much a well-timed explanation can prevent a larger problem. I handled escalations, trained new staff, and kept detailed case notes that our quality team still uses as a reference. Those years gave me patience with messy data and a habit of asking the question behind the question.

I am twenty-nine years old, and I have reached the point in my career where I want more responsibility for the decisions my work supports. Your organization's focus on public health reporting is closely aligned with the kind of work I find most meaningful, and I have followed your recent publications with real interest. I believe my combination of technical skill and practical communication would let me contribute from the first month.

Thank you for considering my application. My resume is attached, and I can be reached at tessa.ferguson@mailbox.ca or at 902-555-0148. I would be glad to meet at your convenience, and I am available to begin any time after the first of October.

Sincerely,

Tessa Ferguson

input:
नमस्ते, मैं अपनी समस्या आपके साथ साझा करना चाहता हूँ क्योंकि पिछले कुछ महीनों से मन बहुत भारी रहता है। मेरा नाम रोहित वर्मा है, मेरी उम्र 34 साल है, और मैं मूल रूप से मुरादाबाद का रहने वाला हूँ। आठ साल पहले नौकरी के लिए पुणे आया था। अभी मैं हिंजवडी में एक आईटी कंपनी, ब्रांटेक सॉल्यूशंस प्राइवेट लिमिटेड, में सीनियर प्रोजेक्ट मैनेजर के पद पर काम करता हूँ। ऑफिस अच्छा है, तनख्वाह भी ठीक है, लेकिन काम का दबाव इतना बढ़ गया है कि रातों को नींद नहीं आती।

पिछले महीने, 14 सितंबर को, मेरी छोटी बहन सुमन का फोन आया। उसने बताया कि पापा की तबीयत बिगड़ रही है और माँ अकेली सब संभाल नहीं पा रही हैं। मुझे लगता है कि मैं उनके पास मुरादाबाद में होना चाहिए, पर यहाँ मेरी ज़िम्मेदारियाँ भी हैं। मेरा किराये का फ्लैट बाणेर के पास एक छोटी गली में है, और वहाँ के पड़ोसी भी मुझे अब परिवार जैसे लगते हैं। इन सबके बीच मैं खुद को बँटा हुआ महसूस करता हूँ।

सुमन ने कहा कि मैं दोषी महसूस न करूँ, पर मेरे अंदर से वह आवाज़ नहीं जाती। ऑफिस में मेरी टीम के लोग भी देख रहे हैं कि मैं पहले जैसा ध्यान नहीं दे पा रहा। पिछले हफ्ते एक मीटिंग में मैं अचानक बीच में चुप हो गया और सब मेरी तरफ देखते रहे। उस दिन से मुझे डर लगने लगा है कि कहीं लोग मुझे कमज़ोर न समझें।

मैंने सोचा है कि कुछ दिनों की छुट्टी लेकर घर जाऊँ, पर मेरे मैनेजर ने अगले क्वार्टर के टारगेट की बात की है और मैं उन्हें निराश नहीं करना चाहता। मैं इस उलझन में फँसा हूँ कि अपने परिवार के लिए क्या करूँ और अपने करियर को कैसे संभालूँ।

क्या आप मुझे बता सकते हैं कि इस स्थिति में कैसे सोचना चाहिए? मैं चाहता हूँ कि मैं एक ऐसा रास्ता खोज सकूँ जिसमें मैं अपने माता-पिता का ख्याल रख सकूँ और खुद की सेहत भी न खोऊँ। कृपया व्यावहारिक सलाह दीजिए।

पिछले महीने, 19 सितंबर को, मेरी छोटी बहन नीलम का फोन आया। उसने बताया कि पापा की तबीयत बिगड़ रही है और माँ अकेली सब संभाल नहीं पा रही हैं। मुझे लगता है कि मैं उनके पास मेरठ में होना चाहिए, पर यहाँ मेरी ज़िम्मेदारियाँ भी हैं। मेरा किराये का फ्लैट वानवडी के पास एक छोटी गली में है, और वहाँ के पड़ोसी भी मुझे अब परिवार जैसे लगते हैं। इन सबके बीच मैं खुद को बँटा हुआ महसूस करता हूँ।

नीलम ने कहा कि मैं दोषी महसूस न करूँ, पर मेरे अंदर से वह आवाज़ नहीं जाती। ऑफिस में मेरी टीम के लोग भी देख रहे हैं कि मैं पहले जैसा ध्यान नहीं दे पा रहा। पिछले हफ्ते एक मीटिंग में मैं अचानक बीच में चुप हो गया और सब मेरी तरफ देखते रहे। उस दिन से मुझे डर लगने लगा है कि कहीं लोग मुझे कमज़ोर न समझें।

मैंने सोचा है कि कुछ दिनों की छुट्टी लेकर घर जाऊँ, पर मेरे मैनेजर ने अगले क्वार्टर के टारगेट की बात की है और मैं उन्हें निराश नहीं करना चाहता। मैं इस उलझन में फँसा हूँ कि अपने परिवार के लिए क्या करूँ और अपने करियर को कैसे संभालूँ।

क्या आप मुझे बता सकते हैं कि इस स्थिति में कैसे सोचना चाहिए? मैं चाहता हूँ कि मैं एक ऐसा रास्ता खोज सकूँ जिसमें मैं अपने माता-पिता का ख्याल रख सकूँ और खुद की सेहत भी न खोऊँ। कृपया व्यावहारिक सलाह दीजिए।

Notes from call with Clare Whitfield, Thursday 14 March. I'm writing these up while it's fresh because I want a record of what she said before the relocation paperwork starts.

Clare opened by saying her case file was still under the name Clare Whitfield-Ashby, which is her married name from before the divorce. She wants it restored to Whitfield. I told her the immigration office would need a certified copy of the decree and that the change would take roughly three weeks. She asked whether her passport number would also change. It won't; the passport number stays the same, which is GB 4471 9920 on the copy she sent me. I've double-checked that against the scan and it matches.

Her current address is 18 Harcourt Terrace, Flat 3B, Bristol BS8 1QJ. She said the building management company has been slow about the tenancy letter, so I've asked her to get it reissued directly to me. For the Dutch registration she also needs a proof of address dated within the last thirty days, and the tenancy letter will do if it arrives in time. She mentioned that the letter should come from Harcourt Estates Ltd and not from the landlord personally, which is a detail I want to flag to the office.

We spent the middle part of the call on timing. Clare is starting a new role at a logistics firm in Rotterdam on 2 April, and she would like her residence permit in hand before then. I told her that is tight. The earliest appointment I could find was 27 March, so I've put a hold on that slot and asked her to confirm by Monday. She was relieved and said she'd rather lose a weekend than a start date.

She also raised a worry about her son's school enrolment, which she wants to confirm before she signs anything. I said that is outside what I can handle directly but that I'd pass her question to the family desk. She gave the date of his last school report as 8 March, in case they ask.

Action items: request certified decree copy (Clare); reissue tenancy letter to our office (Clare, by 21 March); confirm 27 March appointment (Clare, by Monday); raise school enrolment query with family desk (me). Next check-in is Thursday 21 March, same time.

That was, in a way, the start of this whole story: he has always been the one who takes what he needs and then somehow makes you glad to give it.

When Wale met Adaeze, I was honestly worried. He had a list of qualities he wanted in a partner and I thought he would never find anyone who matched it. Then he met her at a friend's birthday on December 14th, 2019, and called me from the car park at ten o'clock that night just to say, "Chidi, I think I'm finished." He wasn't joking. Since then he has been the most patient, generous and loyal man I know, and Adaeze has been the reason for every bit of it.

So please raise your glasses. To Wale and Adaeze, may your home always be full of laughter, your arguments short, and your table long. Née à Saint-Étienne en 1948, elle avait gardé toute sa vie l'accent et la franchise de son enfance dans les rues de la ville. Après son mariage, elle s'était installée à Lyon, où elle a élevé ses deux fils et travaillé pendant trente ans comme comptable dans une petite entreprise de la rue de la République. Ceux qui l'ont connue savent qu'elle ne laissait jamais un dossier en retard ni un voisin sans nouvelles.

Fabienne aimait les dimanches au bord du Rhône, les marchés du samedi matin et les longues conversations autour d'une table trop petite pour tout le monde. Elle avait une façon bien à elle de dire les choses : sans détour, mais toujours avec tendresse. Quand Thomas, son aîné, a traversé une année difficile, c'est elle qui a fait le premier pas, un soir de novembre, en lui laissant sur le répondeur un simple message : « Viens manger, je t'attends. » Il y est allé, et il dit aujourd'hui que ce soir-là a changé beaucoup de choses.

Maman, Fabienne, tu nous as appris à rester droits et à rester généreux. Nous garderons de toi cette voix qui appelait depuis la cuisine, ce rire qui emplissait les pièces et ce sens de la famille qui ne faiblissait jamais. Repose en paix, et sache que nous continuerons à faire la place que tu faisais aux autres.

input:
Vilhelm Andersson grew up on Hammarby Allé in Stockholm, in a flat where the radiator clanked every morning at six and the windows looked over a small park with three birch trees. Most of what I know about patience I learned from watching my grandmother fix things in that flat: a leaking tap, a wobbly chair, the old wooden clock that stopped whenever someone slammed a door. She never hurried a repair. She listened to the problem first, then worked slowly until the object could carry its own weight again.

When I was fourteen I started volunteering at a repair café in Södermalm, once every other Saturday. Our customers brought in toasters, bicycles, lamps and, once, a violin with a cracked neck. Vilhelm, a retired electrician who ran the café, taught me that most broken things are not really broken; they are only waiting for someone to notice what has gone wrong. I spent my first months sorting screws and holding torches. By the end of the year I could diagnose a faulty kettle element on my own.

That experience pushed me toward engineering, but it also made me curious about why people throw things away so quickly. In February of my final school year I began a small survey of households in my building, asking how many appliances had been replaced in the previous twelve months and why. The answers were more varied than I expected. Many people said they did not know how to repair anything, while others said the parts were simply unavailable. I compiled the results into a short report and sent it to the municipal sustainability office, which invited me to present at a neighbourhood meeting on 14 February.

I am applying to your programme in sustainable product design because I want to work on the problem at the level where it begins: the design decisions that determine whether something can be fixed at all. Repair is not only a matter of skill; it depends on modular parts, clear manuals and access to spares. I want to learn how to build those qualities into products from the start.

If you would like to discuss my application or see the survey, you can reach me at vilhelm.andersson@example-mail.se. I would welcome the chance to tell you more about what I have learned at the workbench and in the community around it.

input:
I've been putting off writing this for a week, mostly because my therapist asked me to and I didn't want to admit how much the Tuesday session stuck with me. So here goes. My name is Daniel and I live in Christchurch, though some days it feels like I've been living in a waiting room since the restructure at Kiwi Meridian Logistics. I'm still their Senior Analyst, which sounds more secure than it feels when half the team has been moved to contract roles.

On Tuesday I talked about my dad. He rang me on the 9th of July, just after lunch, and asked whether I'd sorted out the car rego yet. Ordinary stuff, but I spent the whole afternoon replaying the call. I kept thinking he sounded tired, and that I should have asked him how he was doing instead of rushing off to a meeting. My therapist, Marama, pointed out that I always end conversations with him by apologising for being busy, and asked what I'd be saying if I weren't afraid of being a burden.

I didn't have an answer in the room. I've been trying to find one since. Part of the problem is that I haven't told anyone at work how much the uncertainty is getting to me. When Sione from HR emailed about the new reporting structure, I read it three times and still couldn't tell whether my role was staying. I started drafting a reply and then deleted it because it sounded needy.

Marama suggested a small experiment. Each evening this week I'm meant to write down one thing I did for myself, however minor. On the first night I wrote that I went for a walk along the Estuary and didn't check my phone once. It felt almost silly, but it was the first time in a month my shoulders dropped.

I also called Dad back on the Thursday, from the car park outside the office, and asked him properly how he was. He laughed and said nobody had asked him that in years. We talked for forty minutes. I'm going to keep doing that, even if it feels awkward. Next session is on the 23rd, and I think I'll bring the list.

Dad was born in Muncie, Indiana, on February 9, 1951, and he never really left the way he talked about it. Even after forty years in Columbus, he would still say "back home" when he meant the small brick house on Elm Street where his mother taught piano. He carried that place with him: the stubbornness, the way he'd fix anything with a coffee can and a length of wire, and the habit of waving at every stranger who drove past him on a county road.

For the last eleven years he was a senior facilities manager at Horizon Logistics Group, and people who worked for him still call me to say he was the first boss who ever asked how their kids were doing. He kept a binder full of birthdays and anniversaries, and on February 14 he would send a card to every single one of us, even to the guy in receiving who never answered. He signed them all "Gerald, your friend." I used to tease him about it. Now I understand it was simply who he was.

If you want to reach out to our family, or share a story about Gerald, please write to gerald.holloway.memories@fastmail.com. We will read every one. Dad would want you to tell the stories that make you laugh first, and the ones that make you cry second. He always believed in that order.

We finally made it to Freiburg after three days of driving through the Black Forest, and I want to record the details before I forget them. Yusuf Brandt, my brother-in-law, handled the booking at the Hotel Zähringer on Bertoldstraße 14, 79098 Freiburg. He had my passport number, DE-P4471938, written on the reservation sheet, which made me a little uneasy, but the front desk was friendly and the room overlooked the old market square. Yusuf's company, Rheinland Logistik GmbH, had arranged the trip as a team retreat, so half the people in our group were colleagues who had never met outside a conference call.

On the second morning we picked up the rental, a grey Skoda with the plate FR-YB 2207, and drove up toward the Feldberg. The roads were quiet in mid-April, the meadows were just turning green, and there was still snow in the shaded hollows. Yusuf kept insisting on stopping for photos, which annoyed the driver, but the views were worth it. He posted a few on his travel account, @yusuf.drives.europe, and tagged half of Freiburg by accident.

If you ever go, eat at the little place near the cathedral, book ahead, and do not skip the cable car. Yusuf says he will be back in April next year with the whole family, and honestly, so will I.

input:
I went to see Dr. Levi at the clinic on Thursday morning because the pain in my lower back had not gone away after almost three weeks. The waiting room was busy, mostly with older people and a few parents with small children, and I was called in about forty minutes after my appointment time. Dr. Levi was patient and asked a lot of questions. She wanted to know when the pain started, whether it got worse at night, and if I had noticed any numbness in my legs. I told her it had come on after I started lifting heavy boxes at the warehouse, and that sitting for long periods made it much worse.

She examined me on the table, pressing along my spine and asking me to bend forward and to the side. I could feel the muscles tighten when she touched one particular spot. She said it looked like a strained muscle combined with some inflammation, and that it was not something that needed scans or anything invasive right now. She also checked my reflexes and my strength, and everything came back normal, which was a relief.

The treatment plan is fairly simple. I have been prescribed an anti-inflammatory medication to take with food for the next ten days, and I should stop if my stomach becomes upset. She recommended gentle walking every day, avoiding heavy lifting for at least two weeks, and using a heating pad in the evenings. She also gave me a referral for physiotherapy, and the clinic will call me to arrange the first session.

I asked whether I should be worried about the pain coming back, and she explained the warning signs to look out for. If I lose feeling in my legs, have trouble controlling my bladder, or the pain becomes sudden and severe, I should go straight to the emergency room without waiting for another appointment. She wrote all of this down on a printed sheet, which I found very helpful, since I tend to forget details once I leave a room.

I left the clinic feeling more reassured than I expected to. The visit was not long, but I felt listened to and I understood what was happening in my body. I will go back for a follow-up in four weeks if the pain has not improved, and I plan to keep a simple diary of how I feel each day so I can give her a clearer picture next time.
