input:
Tuesday 11th March

Dear diary, it's been one of those days where everything goes slightly sideways and then somehow comes right by teatime. Cameron (Cam to everyone at the surgery, though Mum still insists on Cameron) woke up at six with a cold that has made him sound like a foghorn. I told him to stay in bed, and of course he didn't listen. He was off to his shift at Harrow Lane Clinic before I'd even finished my first cup of tea, muttering that the rota was a nightmare without him.

I spent the morning at the Brightwater Cafe on Mill Street, where Cam had promised to meet me for a flat white he never got to drink. Instead I ended up chatting with Maureen, who runs the place with the patience of a saint. She says the new coffee machine is finally behaving, which means the queue will be even longer next week. Half the regulars asked after Cam, and I had to explain for the fifth time that no, he hasn't got anything serious, just a stubborn chest infection.

In the afternoon I finally sorted out the boxes from the spare room. Under a pile of old university notes from his time at Eastfield University, I found a photo of us at the graduation ball, him in that ridiculous hired waistcoat. He was twenty-four then, all elbows and nerves. Sometimes I forget how young we both were when we started out, and how much has happened since.

At half past four the phone rang and it was Cam's sister, Chloe, asking whether we'd be at the community quiz on Thursday. I told her to call Cam directly on 07712 345 689, since he's the one who promised to bring the team's lucky pen. She laughed and said that was typical.

Tomorrow I'll make him soup and insist he takes his tablets. Cam will grumble, of course, but he always does. Goodnight, diary.

input:
Hello everyone, and welcome back to the new term! I am writing this piece for the newsletter as a bit of an introduction, since many of you have asked where I came from and why I joined us partway through the year. The short answer is that I moved here from another country with my family, and the longer answer is much more interesting than I expected it to be.

The first few weeks were a blur. Everything looked familiar and strange at the same time. The bread was different, the words on the shop signs were sometimes unexpected, and the way people greeted one another in the corridors took me a while to get used to. I remember standing in the playground during break, not knowing where to sit, and feeling quite small. Then someone waved me over, and that was the beginning of things getting easier.

What I have learned since then is that moving is less about leaving something behind and more about carrying a few things across with you. For me, it is music, a habit of reading before bed, and a stubborn love of long walks. I have discovered new things too: the sports clubs here are wonderful, the library has a surprisingly good collection of graphic novels, and the teachers have been patient with my questions, even the ones that seemed silly to me at the time.

I would like to thank everyone who has made this transition kinder than I feared. Whether you lent me a pencil, explained a joke I did not understand, or simply asked how my day was going, you made a difference. I have noticed that our school is full of people who are quick to include others, and I think that is something to be proud of.

If you are new this term, or if you have ever felt like the outsider in the room, please know that you are not alone. Come and say hello, join a club, or share your own story in the next edition of this newsletter. I would genuinely love to hear from you.

Thank you for reading, and I look forward to getting to know you all better over the coming months.

input:
I am writing this with a heavy heart to share that my dear brother, Frank Delorme, passed away peacefully on January 14 at the age of 71, surrounded by family at Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto. For thirty-four years Frank worked as a machinist at Northern Alloy Works, where he was known for his steady hands, his dry sense of humour, and a willingness to stay late whenever a colleague needed help. Many of the men who trained under him still call him the best teacher they ever had.

Frank was the kind of man who showed up. He coached our nephews in hockey every winter, fixed the furnace at my house more times than I can count, and never once let a birthday pass without a phone call. His closest friend and fishing partner, Gerald Moss, told me Frank could spend an entire afternoon on the lake without saying much at all, and that those were the afternoons Gerald valued most. Gerald has asked that we remember Frank with a cup of strong coffee and a story told loudly.

Frank is survived by his wife of forty-six years, Linda, his two daughters, Karen and Michelle, and five grandchildren who adored him. A private family gathering will be held in the coming days. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Canadian Cancer Society. We will miss him every single day.

I love you, Frank. Rest well.

input: Every July since I was seven, my grandmother Delores has taught me to read the sky over our porch on Alder Creek Road, 418 Alder Creek Road, Boise, Idaho. Her birthday, July 14, was the one night each summer we stayed up past midnight with a thermos of cocoa and a battered star atlas. Delores never went to college, but she could name every constellation and explain why the Perseids always arrive in August. input:
When my family left Porto for Toronto in the winter of my twelfth year, I believed the hardest part would be learning a new language. I was wrong. The language came slowly, but the silence of a city where nobody knew my grandmother's recipes or the name of the bakery on Rua das Flores was harder. My mother took a job at Brightwater Logistics in Mississauga, and my father, Tomas, began driving a delivery van for a small bakery on Dundas Street. I spent most afternoons with my cousin Inês, who had come over with us, and with Marco, a boy from my homeroom who taught me hockey and, in exchange, asked me to explain Portuguese football to him.

In January 14 of that first year, a blizzard closed the schools and my father could not leave the apartment. We played cards for six hours at the kitchen table while the radiator clanked. I remember thinking that this was what home could be: not the place itself but the people who stayed with you when everything outside had gone white. Tomas taught me to read the weather, and I taught him the word for saudade, which he said was untranslatable and then translated anyway.

Today I think of Porto differently. It is still the city where I was born, but Toronto is where I learned to be a person who asks questions in two languages. I want to study translation and public health because I have seen how much a single misunderstood word can cost a family in a clinic waiting room. My own story is a small one, but it taught me that meaning is always carried by people, and I want to be the one who carries it well.

I'm writing to describe the incident that led to my claim under policy reference IE-44812. On Tuesday 11 February, at about 4:30 in the afternoon, I was leaving Brennan's Fitness on Main Street in Kilkenny, where I'd been for my usual Tuesday session. The car park was wet and I slipped on a loose kerb edge near the bike rack, landing hard on my left hip and wrist. I'm 47, and I've been a regular member there for six years, so I knew the path well, but the edge had lifted and nobody had put a cone or sign out.

I was taken by ambulance to St Luke's in Kilkenny and seen by a registrar, who X-rayed the wrist and confirmed a hairline fracture of the radius. I was discharged that evening in a splint. My GP, Dr Hanlon, has since referred me for physiotherapy, and I'm not yet back at work as a school bursar. I have kept every receipt for prescriptions, taxi fares and the physio appointments so far, and I can supply copies on request.

I'm told by the gym manager that the kerb has since been repaired and that an incident report was filed on the day. I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this description and let me know what further documents you need. I can be reached on 087 555 0143 or at yvonne.kearney47@example.ie. I've been going to Ruby's Auto & Tire on Alder Street in the Eastside neighbourhood of Portland for about six years, and last Tuesday was the first time I left feeling like I'd been overcharged. My mom, Margaret, is 74 and drives a 2009 Buick, and she called ahead at (503) 555-0147 to ask about an oil change and a quick brake check. The service rep quoted her a fair price over the phone, but when she picked the car up there was an extra line item for a "fluid flush" she never agreed to. Margaret is not the type to argue, so she just paid it and came to me afterward a little embarrassed.

I called the shop the next morning and spoke with Ray, the manager, who was honest that the flush was added by a technician during the inspection. He offered to refund the charge in full and apologized for not checking with the customer first. I appreciated that. The refund hit my mom's card within two business days, which is quicker than I expected.

Still, the whole experience reminded me why I'd rather pay a little more for a shop that explains things before touching the car. If you're in the area and you have an older vehicle, call ahead, ask for the itemized estimate in writing, and make sure nothing gets added at pickup. Ruby's did make it right in the end, so I'm giving them three stars instead of one.

3 luglio

Stamattina ho quasi perso il treno per Milano, di nuovo. Ottavio mi ha mandato un messaggio alle sei e mezza per ricordarmi della riunione con la Bianchi Logistica, e io ho risposto con un pollice alzato e poi mi sono riaddormentato. Quando finalmente sono arrivato in ufficio in via Marconi 14, Silvia mi ha guardato con quella faccia che dice tutto senza dire niente. Ho passato la giornata a sistemare i fogli del progetto nuovo e a cercare di non pensare alla telefonata di ieri sera.

La mamma ha chiamato alle sette, come sempre. Mi ha chiesto se mangio abbastanza e se ho sentito lo zio Franco, che è di nuovo in ospedale per il cuore. Le ho detto di sì a tutte e due le cose, anche se in realtà non ho sentito nessuno da settimane. Mio fratello Ottavino, che lei chiama ancora così nonostante abbia trentotto anni, le ha passato il telefono a metà conversazione e ha urlato che devo andare a trovarli a Pavia il prossimo weekend. Ho detto che ci penso.

Giovedì sera sono uscito con Silvia e Matteo nel quartiere Navigli, dove c'è quel posto con i tavolini fuori sull'acqua. Matteo ha raccontato per la ventesima volta la storia del suo capo che si è addormentato durante la presentazione davanti al cliente. Abbiamo riso fino alle lacrime. Silvia mi ha detto che secondo lei dovrei cambiare lavoro, che la Bianchi mi sfrutta. Non so se ha ragione, ma l'idea mi tiene sveglio la notte.

Oggi ho trovato per caso una vecchia fotografia nella borsa, quella dell'estate in cui io e Ottavio abbiamo guidato fino al lago di Como con la vecchia Panda rossa. Eravamo tutti e due magri e sorridenti, con il sole in faccia. Mi sono chiesto quando abbiamo smesso di fare cose così semplici. Forse quando ho iniziato a rispondere ai messaggi alle sei del mattino.

Domani il capo vuole vedere i numeri del secondo trimestre, il 9 luglio è la scadenza per il report finale. Devo chiudere tutto entro mercoledì. Ho già preparato il caffè per domattina e ho messo la sveglia alle sei e dieci, con la speranza che stavolta basti.

input:
I saw Dr. Mehra at the Sunrise Multispeciality Clinic in Pune on 14 November because the pain in my lower back had not gone away for three weeks. He asked me to lie on the examination couch, pressed along my spine, and then ordered an X-ray and a blood panel. My wife Sunita came with me and kept asking questions I had forgotten to ask, which annoyed me a little but was probably a good thing. The clinic receptionist, Ramesh, was very patient with my paperwork and even remembered my mobile number, 98234 17650, from my last visit in March.

Dr. Mehra says the X-ray shows mild wear in the L4-L5 disc, nothing alarming, and that most people my age have something similar. He wants me to stop lifting heavy bags of cement at the site, do the stretching routine he wrote down, and come back on 28 November with the blood report. He also told me to stop sitting for hours at my desk. I explained that my colleague Arvind Joshi and I have been trying to finish the Bandra project, so I cannot exactly take a break, and he just laughed and said I should try a standing desk. Sunita has already decided we will buy one this weekend.

On the way home we stopped at Chai Point near the station, which is my usual reward after any medical visit. My son Rohan called to ask if I was okay, and I told him I was fine, just getting old, which he says is what everyone says before they start complaining. My mother, whom everyone calls Bablu in the family, sent a message asking whether I had eaten, which is her way of checking on me. I am going to follow the exercises properly this time. I have promised Sunita and I have promised myself.

input:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for Brianna Okafor, who worked under my supervision as a senior analyst at Halvorsen Logistics in Columbus, Ohio, from March 2019 until May 14, 2024. I have managed teams in operations and planning for over fifteen years, and in that time I have rarely worked with someone who combined technical skill and steady judgment as consistently as Brianna does.

Brianna took ownership of our freight-cost forecasting model within her first six months. The original spreadsheet had grown unwieldy, with formulas that only one departed employee understood. Brianna rebuilt it in a documented, modular form, cut our monthly reporting time nearly in half, and then trained three colleagues to maintain it. When our Midwest distribution network was disrupted in the spring of 2022, she was the person I turned to for scenario analysis, and her projections were accurate enough that our leadership team relied on them for weeks.

What stands out most to me, though, is how Brianna handles people. She is patient with colleagues who are less comfortable with data, and she never makes anyone feel small for asking a question. Several members of our team have told me that Brianna was the first person who explained a problem to them in a way that made it feel solvable. She also has a quiet confidence that lets her disagree with senior managers respectfully and still follow through when a decision goes the other way.

Brianna's family has been a source of support for her throughout her career. Her sister, Monique Okafor, is a nurse in Cleveland, and Brianna often spoke with pride about the example her sister set for her. I mention this only because it helps explain Brianna's persistence and her commitment to doing work that matters to people, qualities I observed daily.

I am confident Brianna will bring the same rigor, reliability, and generosity to any team she joins. Please feel free to contact me directly at mark.dellinger@halvorsenlogistics.com or at (614) 555-0147 if you would like to discuss her qualifications further.

Sincerely,

Mark Dellinger
Director of Operations Planning
Halvorsen Logistics

Hi all, first time posting here so bear with me. My name is Malcolm and I'm 34, living in Leeds. Last month my younger brother Callum got admitted to St James's University Hospital after a bad fall at work, and since then I've been running back and forth between there and our flat trying to keep on top of everything. He's stable now but the consultant wants him off work for at least eight weeks and he's panicking about his rent and his job at the depot.

The thing I'm struggling with is that Callum has basically handed me power of attorney in all but name, mostly because our mum, Eileen, has dementia and can't really help anymore. I've been the one dealing with the council tax letters, the benefits forms and the insurance claim from the accident, and I keep worrying I'm getting something wrong. I've got a folder of paperwork and a spreadsheet, but I don't really know where the line is between helping and overstepping.

So my question is: has anyone here been in this position? Is there a proper way to formalise this, like a lasting power of attorney or something through the Office of the Public Guardian, or is it fine to just act on his behalf informally for a few weeks? Also, if anyone has dealt with the DWP over a sickness claim while someone's still in hospital, any tips would be massively appreciated. Thanks in advance, I really don't know who else to ask.

input:
I am writing to describe the water damage that occurred in my flat on the third floor of a converted building in the centre of a French town, and to request that the claim be processed as soon as possible. On the morning in question I left for work as usual, having checked that all taps were closed and the washing machine had finished its cycle. When I returned in the early evening, the hallway floor was covered in standing water, and the water had already seeped under the bedroom door and into the parquet of the living room.

The source appeared to be a failed flexible hose connected to the washing machine in the small utility cupboard off the kitchen. The hose had split along a crimp, and the water had run for several hours before anything was noticed. The neighbours below reported a damp patch spreading across their ceiling, which is how the leak first came to light. I turned off the mains supply to the apartment straight away and called the building's caretaker, who arranged for a plumber to attend the same evening to isolate the appliance.

The damage is extensive. The engineered wood in the hallway and living room has lifted and warped and will need to be replaced throughout. The plasterboard on the kitchen wall behind the machine is saturated and has begun to crumble, and the skirting boards along two walls are beyond repair. Several pieces of furniture, including a sideboard and a bookcase, sat on the wet floor for hours and have swollen and delaminated. I have also lost a number of books and some electrical items that were stored on the lower shelves of the cupboard.

I have kept the failed hose, photographs of the affected rooms taken before any clearing took place, and the plumber's written report, which confirms the cause of the leak. I have also collected quotations from two local contractors for the flooring and plastering work, and I have listed each damaged item with its approximate age and value where I still hold a receipt. Copies of all these documents are enclosed with this description.

I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this claim and let me know whether any further evidence is required. I am happy to allow an assessor to visit the property at a time convenient to them, and I will make the affected rooms available for inspection. Please contact me if you need anything else to progress the matter.

I've been meaning to write this review for a while, so here it is. Last month I took my car into Hanlon's Motor Works on the Old Mill Road in Drumcondra, Dublin, after the brakes started squealing every time I came up to the lights. My name is Kieran Dwyer and I've been a loyal customer of small garages for about fifteen years, so I'm not easily impressed.

I booked the appointment for Tuesday 9 April, and I'll say straight away that the front desk was brilliant. Siobhan, who runs the counter, rang me the day before to confirm, and she remembered that my last service was done by the older mechanic, Denis, which I didn't expect. When I turned up at half eight there was a clear quote waiting for me, with the parts listed separately so I could see exactly what I was paying for.

The work itself was thorough. The pads and discs were replaced at the front and the rear, and they showed me the old pads, which were worn almost to the metal. Denis also noticed a small fluid leak from a hose that nobody had flagged before, and rather than just quoting it in the bill he explained why it mattered and gave me the option to wait. I took the fix, and I appreciated the honesty.

The price was fair, though not cheap. The total came in about ten per cent under the figure I'd been quoted by a bigger dealership across the city, and the car was ready by half four, as promised. The waiting area is small and the coffee machine is temperamental, so bring something to read, but nobody made me feel rushed.

If you live in Drumcondra or anywhere near it and need a reliable garage that won't upsell you, I'd recommend Hanlon's without hesitation. I've already booked my next service with them, and I've told my brother Kevin in Phibsboro to give them a try too. Five stars from me, and I'm not handing those out lightly.

input:
Ilan Shapira here, writing from a café in the Florentin neighbourhood of Tel Aviv, where I have spent the better part of three mornings now. I arrived on the 4th of October with one backpack, a battered paperback and absolutely no plan, which I have decided is the correct way to start a trip in this country. The city wakes up slowly and then all at once. By nine the shutters on Shabazi Street are up, the smell of fresh za'atar bread drifts out of the bakeries, and somebody is always arguing cheerfully about football on the corner.

On my first full day I walked from the Carmel Market down to the port, stopping every fifteen metres to photograph another mural. The graffiti here is not decoration for tourists; it is a running conversation between neighbours, and you can read a whole year of local politics and birthdays on one wall if you slow down. I ate hummus so good that I briefly considered abandoning my flight home. Lunch was a plate of shakshuka eaten standing up, because every seat was taken by old men playing backgammon with ferocious concentration.

If you want to book a guided food walk, the operator I used is called Shuk Trails and their office number is 03-555-0148. Ask for Noa, who was patient with my appalling Hebrew and far too generous with her recommendations. She said the best falafel in the district is the one with the longest queue, and she was right. Ilan's advice to anyone planning a visit: go early, bring cash, and do not be shy about asking for a second pita.

The weekend brought a day trip to Jaffa, where the old stone alleys climb up from the sea in a way that makes your calves complain. I sat for an hour above the water watching fishermen mend their nets while the call to prayer from one mosque and the church bells from another drifted over the rooftops, and neither seemed to mind the other. It was the most peaceful hour of the whole trip, and I came close to missing my bus back to the city because of it.

By my last morning I had settled into a rhythm: coffee at the same counter, a short walk along the promenade, and a long goodbye to the cats who seemed to own the entire block. I leave on the 19th of October, slightly heavier and considerably less organised than I arrived. If you are reading this and wondering whether to go, the answer is yes. Write to me at ilan.shapira@travelnotes.co.il if you want my full list of places, and bring an appetite.

October 14. Woke up early again, the Tel Aviv heat already pressing through the shutters at six. Today was the day I finally went to Lev Clinic on Ben Yehuda Street to sort out the paperwork for my lease renewal. The receptionist, Miriam, asked for my ID number twice because the first time I read it out wrong, 028173946, and she wrote it down with a sigh. Then she needed my passport too, the blue one, and my full address for the form: 17 Rothschild Boulevard, Apartment 4B. I keep forgetting how many times this country wants to know where you sleep.

Afterwards I walked over to Cafe Yarden, the little place with the chipped blue tables where Amit always orders the shakshuka. I got a cappuccino and sat by the window for an hour, reading and not doing the laundry I promised myself I would do. Amit texted me that his mother has moved in with his brother in Haifa, so he won't be at Friday dinner. I replied with a heart and then felt guilty for using an emoji on something so sad.

On the way home I stopped at the gym on Dizengoff, the one with the broken water fountain, and signed up for the October class schedule. The trainer said I should come Tuesdays and Thursdays, and I told him I would try. I probably won't, but it feels good to have written it down somewhere. Tomorrow, maybe, I will finally answer my aunt's email about the wedding in November.

Then she needed my passport too, the blue one, and my full address for the form: 42 Ibn Gabirol Street, Apartment 7C. I keep forgetting how many times this country wants to know where you sleep.

Afterwards I walked over to Cafe Hadar, the little place with the chipped blue tables where Noam always orders the shakshuka. I got a cappuccino and sat by the window for an hour, reading and not doing the laundry I promised myself I would do. Noam texted me that his mother has moved in with his brother in Haifa, so he won't be at Friday dinner. I replied with a heart and then felt guilty for using an emoji on something so sad.

On the way home I stopped at the gym on Allenby, the one with the broken water fountain, and signed up for the October class schedule. The trainer said I should come Tuesdays and Thursdays, and I told him I would try. I probably won't, but it feels good to have written it down somewhere. Tomorrow, maybe, I will finally answer my aunt's email about the wedding in November.

Bonjour, je ne sais pas trop par où commencer, mais j'ai besoin de quelqu'un à qui parler. Je m'appelle Julien, tout le monde me connaît à Lyon sous le surnom de Juju, depuis le lycée. Depuis le mois dernier, je n'arrive plus à dormir correctement et je me sens épuisé en permanence, même quand je ne fais rien de particulier.

Le problème principal, c'est Amélie, ma compagne depuis six ans. Depuis l'été, on se dispute pour des choses idiotes : la vaisselle, les courses, le temps passé sur mon téléphone. Hier soir, elle m'a dit qu'elle ne savait plus si elle avait envie de rester. Je n'ai rien répondu, je suis parti marcher jusqu'au quai de la Saône, et j'ai pensé à tout ce qu'on a construit ensemble.

Le pire, c'est que je culpabilise. Je sais que je ne suis plus la même personne depuis que j'ai changé de poste en octobre. Je travaille dans une agence de communication à Villeurbanne, et les objectifs me tombent dessus sans arrêt. Je rentre tard, je mange n'importe quoi, et le week-end je suis trop fatigué pour être présent.

J'ai commencé à aller au Café des Arts, près de chez nous, le matin avant le travail, juste pour sortir de l'appartement. Le patron, Marc, m'a conseillé de reprendre la salle de sport Basic-Fit du boulevard, et même de voir quelqu'un en consultation au cabinet du docteur Fournier, rue de la République. Je n'ai pas encore pris rendez-vous.

Je voudrais que vous m'aidiez à réfléchir. Comment on parle à quelqu'un qu'on aime quand on ne sait plus ce qu'on ressent ? Faut-il que je lui demande une vraie discussion, sans téléphone, ce week-end du 14 décembre ? Et est-ce que je dois d'abord m'occuper de ma fatigue, ou de mon couple ? Merci d'avance pour votre aide.

I wanted to write down what Dr. Ilana Shapira told me at Tuesday's appointment, mostly so I can share it with my sister Noa, who keeps asking. I'm 47 now, and the blood pressure numbers from October were higher than she liked, so she has asked me to cut back on salt and to walk at least thirty minutes most days. She also wants a repeat blood panel on November 19, which I've booked at the clinic on Herzl Street in Haifa. Nothing alarming, she was quick to say, just the kind of thing that's better caught early.

We spent a few minutes on sleep too. I mentioned that I've been waking at 3 a.m. since the summer, and she asked whether anything had changed at home. Honestly, the biggest change is that our dog Biscuit has decided that our bedroom is his, and he snores like a leaf blower. She laughed and said it was probably not the dog's fault, but she still gave me a short sleep diary to fill in before my next visit. I'm to return it by email to ilana.shapira.clinic@clalit-haifa.co.il once I've logged two weeks.

The last thing she stressed was not to wait if I get chest tightness or dizziness. I've written those symptoms on a sticky note on the fridge, next to Biscuit's vaccination reminder, which is due on November 8.

Ek is baie opgewonde om te deel dat ek met ingang van 12 Mei 2025 die nuwe rol van Senior Projekbestuurder by Khumalo Logistiek in Durban aanvaar het. Wat my die meeste aantrek tot Khumalo Logistiek is hul verbintenis tot volhoubare vervoer en die manier waarop hulle hul mense sien. Tydens my onderhoude het ek gevoel dat hulle regtig belangstel in wat ek te sê het. Die span wat my sal lei, bestaan uit twaalf mense met wie ek reeds 'n paar keer gepraat het, en ek kan nie wag om saam met hulle te werk nie.

Daar is ook 'n persoonlike kant aan hierdie stap. Durban is die stad waar ek grootgeword het, en ek is opgewonde om terug te keer na die warmte, die see en my familie. Ek het my oupa se huis in Umbilo gereeld besoek toe ek klein was, en ek dink dit is 'n goeie plek om 'n nuwe hoofstuk te begin.

input:
Growing up, I spent most of my weekends helping out at a small community kitchen run by volunteers who never seemed to tire, even on the coldest mornings. I started by peeling vegetables and stacking tins, but over time I found myself asking questions about why certain families came every week and others never did. That curiosity led me to read about food insecurity, and eventually to a conversation with one of the regular volunteers, a retired teacher who told me that the hardest part of the work was not the cooking but the quiet dignity required to make everyone feel welcome. Her words stayed with me long after the shift ended.

That experience taught me that good intentions are not enough without careful attention to the people being served. I began keeping a notebook of the small changes that made a difference, such as moving the queue indoors during rain or offering a choice of meals rather than a single portion. When I suggested some of these ideas to the coordinators, they listened, and several were adopted. I learned that listening is itself a form of service, and that the most useful contribution I could make was often to observe carefully before acting.

I am applying to study social policy because I want to understand the structures behind the need I witnessed in that kitchen. I want to learn how housing, income support and local services interact, and how research can turn the lessons of frontline work into decisions that reach far beyond one room. I hope to bring to university the same patience and attentiveness that I learned from the volunteers who first taught me, and to carry those values into a career devoted to fairer communities.

input:
Growing up in Ballinasloe, I spent most of my childhood helping my grandmother Bríd with the garden behind our house at 14 Kilmore Terrace, Ballinasloe, Co. Galway. She always said that tending plants taught patience, and I learned that lesson slowly, often by accident. My cat Mícheál, a grey tabby who refused to stay out of the flowerbeds, became my unlikely teacher. Each morning he would sit on the wall watching me dig, and I began to notice how the soil changed after rain, how the bees returned to the lavender, and how the seedlings that survived were the ones I had left alone.

When the council announced in April 2023 that the community plot on Kilmore Road would be redeveloped, a group of us, led by my neighbour Róisín, decided to fight for it. I wrote letters, organised a petition and spoke at a public meeting in the library. Rory, who lives three doors down, built a simple spreadsheet to track volunteer hours, and I was responsible for contacting local schools. Watching people who had never met before work side by side convinced me that good planning begins with listening to the people who will live with the results.

I want to study environmental science and community planning because I have seen, on a small scale, how land, people and policy shape one another. Whether through research or public service, I hope to design spaces that help communities grow in every sense. You can reach me at rory.kiely@gmailmail.ie, and I would welcome the chance to discuss how my experience might contribute to your programme.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus, Nadia's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight. Nadia has always been the one who finds the good in people before anyone else does. When she was twenty-six she moved across the country to Halifax on a whim, and within a month she had a job at Brightline Analytics, a team of friends, and a standing Thursday dinner that somehow everyone in the city knew about. She still tells the story of how she drove her old Civic from Ottawa with nothing but a cooler and a box of records, and how the plates on that car, ONT 4471, became a running joke among her friends.

My name is Liora Ben-Shalom, and for as long as I can remember I have wanted to understand how things break and how they are repaired. At seventeen, I spent most of my weekends in my uncle's garage in Haifa, where he taught me to read a wiring diagram before I could read a novel. The first car I ever worked on was his old Subaru, plate 23-814-67, which had a stubborn fault in its electrical system that three mechanics had given up on. I traced it for nine days and found a chafed harness behind the dashboard. Fixing it felt less like a victory than like a conversation I had finally been allowed to join.

That experience pushed me toward engineering, and it is why I am applying to the Technion's faculty of mechanical engineering. I have taken every advanced physics and mathematics course my school at Kiryat Motzkin could offer, and I completed a summer research placement at the Rambam Health Care Campus, where I helped calibrate a pressure sensor used in ventilator testing. My supervisor, Dr. Noam Eliezer, reached me on 0524-771-398 during my last week to discuss my results, and that conversation convinced me that engineering is a field where precision can protect people directly.

I know the road ahead will be demanding, and I am ready for it. I am nineteen now, and I have learned that the most useful skill is patience with a problem that refuses to be simple. I would be grateful for the chance to bring that patience, and my passport number 3481920-6, to a community where that kind of persistence is the expectation rather than the exception.

Kind regards,

Lydia Wanjiru
lydia.wanjiru@mailbox.co.ke

input:
Elena Ruiz Ocampo passed away peacefully at home in San Miguel de Allende on the night of December 14, surrounded by her children and a full kitchen of family. She was eighty-one years old. Born in Guanajuato in 1943, the second of six children, Elena grew up learning to bargain at the Mercado Hidalgo and to sing harmonies in the church choir. She never lost either habit.

For more than forty years Elena kept the books for the family hardware store on Calle Real, a job she described as "numbers with opinions." She knew every customer by name and most of their grandparents. When the store finally closed in 2006, she bought a small blue Nissan, plate number NLX-4471, and drove it everywhere she could justify, which was almost everywhere. Her grandchildren still tease her about the afternoon she parked it across two spaces outside the bank and informed the guard that it was none of his business.

Elena married Javier Ocampo in 1966 at the parish of San Rafael, and they raised three children together. After Javier's death in 1998 she remained the family's steady center, hosting Sunday lunches for twenty or more and keeping a ledger of birthdays that no one dared to question. She taught her great-grandchildren to play dominoes and to cheat at them gently.

Her dog, Tamalito, a scruffy brown mutt she adopted from a shelter in 2015, accompanied her on every walk through the Parque Juárez and was never far from her chair. The family asks that donations be made in her honor to the shelter where she found him.

Elena is survived by her children Mariana, Ricardo and Lucía; seven grandchildren; nine great-grandchildren; and her sister, Teresa, of Querétaro. A wake will be held on December 17 at the family home on Calle Mesones, followed by a Mass at San Rafael on December 18. Those who knew her will remember that she always had one more story and one more plate of food for whoever walked through the door.

Elena, we will keep the books balanced in your absence. Descansa en paz.

input:
I am writing this with a heavy heart, because the person I loved most in the world has gone, and I find myself trying to put into words what that absence means. For more years than I can easily count, the voice on the other end of the line was the first thing I looked forward to in the morning. She had a way of making the ordinary feel worth noticing, whether it was the light over the hills in late afternoon or the stubborn ripeness of a fruit she had planted with her own hands. She believed that kindness was a practice rather than a feeling, and she practiced it every day, often in ways no one else would have thought to see.

She leaves behind a circle of people who were shaped by her generosity. Friends who arrived unannounced at her door always left with a meal, a warm word, or a practical solution to something that had seemed unsolvable. Those of us in the family learned from her that patience and humour are not opposites, and that a good laugh can carry you through the hardest rooms. She could be fierce when something was unjust, and tender when someone needed comfort, and she rarely confused the two.

I will remember her most in the small rituals: the cup of tea set down beside me without a word, the question asked at exactly the right moment, the way she hummed when she thought no one was listening. Those are the things I will carry forward. To everyone who sat with her, called her, or simply thought of her, thank you. She knew she was loved, and she would want us to keep showing up for one another the way she always did.

input:
I still remember the first Tuesday of September when I walked into the Brunswick Community Pantry, clipboard in hand, and met Sophie Whitfield, the volunteer coordinator who would become my unofficial mentor. Sophie had been running the pantry for eleven years, and within an hour she had me sorting tinned tomatoes by expiry date and asking me questions about why the queue moved so slowly on Saturdays. I did not have good answers yet, but I started to notice things: the mothers who came early so their children could avoid the midday crowd, the older men who never asked for more than they needed, the way a single broken trolley could stall the entire line.

By the end of my first year I was helping Sophie draft a short survey for the families who used the pantry. Sophie asked me to write the introduction because, she said, my sentences were plain enough for people who did not speak much English at home to understand. We printed two hundred copies at the library on Sydney Road and handed them out over three weekends. The results surprised us. Most people wanted shorter opening hours on weekdays, not longer ones, because they could not take unpaid time off from work to queue.

Sophie is now the operations manager at Northside Food Relief, a title that sounds grander than the work actually is. She still answers the pantry's phone in the mornings, and she still gives out her direct line, 0412 558 214, to anyone who needs a referral. When I asked her why she never automated the calls, she laughed and said that a voice on the line was the whole point. I have thought about that answer many times since.

My own interest in public health grew out of those Saturdays. I became fascinated by the gap between what a policy promises and what a person experiences when they stand in a line for two hours. I want to study that gap formally, to learn the methods that let researchers measure it and the ethics that keep those measurements honest. Melbourne's Master of Public Health offers exactly the combination of epidemiology and community engagement I am looking for.

If you want to reach me about this essay, my email is sophie.marsh.study@gmail.com, which is a leftover from a nickname my family once gave me, and I check it every evening. I have written this essay as myself, Sarah, because the people I met at the pantry taught me that a name matters when you are asking someone to trust you.

She told me I'd spent a decade making other people's products better and it was time to own one. She was right, as she usually is, which I will never let her forget.

input:
When I was seven, my grandfather took me to Sallow Street Gym in Bradford, where he trained boxers on Saturday mornings. I was born in Bradford, in a terraced house off Manningham Lane, and for most of my childhood the city was simply the place where everything happened. Vivienne Ashworth-Clark is the name on my birth certificate, though everyone at school calls me Viv. Looking back, that gym taught me more about discipline than any classroom did.

At sixteen I started volunteering at the Harbour Street Clinic, a small community health centre near the canal, where I helped translate appointment letters for Urdu-speaking families. On my first day, 14 January, a woman named Mrs Hussain thanked me for explaining a letter she had been carrying around for three weeks. That moment convinced me that medicine, and public health in particular, was where I wanted to direct my energy.

I have since learned that the decisions that matter most are often administrative: which forms get filled in, whose appointment gets booked first. My application to read Public Health reflects this. I want to understand how systems fail people, and how small, local institutions can repair them. Contact me at vivienne.ashworth@example.com or on 01274 556190 if you need further information.

input:
I've been taking my Subaru to Kellerman Auto Care on Hawthorn Road in Glenferrie for about three years now, and I'll be honest, I almost didn't write this review. Last month my car started making a grinding noise on the way to work and I rang them on 03 9824 1706 hoping for a same-day look. Harriet answered, took the details and said they could fit me in on the 14th of July. She even remembered my rego, which I thought was a nice touch when I was half-asleep on the phone.

When I dropped it off, the team walked me through what they thought was wrong, which was a worn front wheel bearing and a brake pad that was nearly through. They didn't try to upsell me on anything I didn't need. The quote came in under what the other two places in the area had given me over the phone, and they text me photos of the old parts so I could see exactly what had worn down. Honestly, that kind of transparency is rare.

The car was ready on the 17th of July, two days later than they first said, but they had rung ahead to let me know, which made the wait easy. Harry, the mechanic who did the job, also checked the tyre pressures and topped up the washer fluid without being asked. Hawthorn Road is a bit of a parking nightmare at peak hour, but the staff are friendly and the waiting area has decent coffee. I'd recommend them to anyone around Glenferrie or Kew who wants an honest mechanic.

input:
My name is Rachel, and I was lucky enough to be Frank's daughter for forty-one years. Many of you knew him as the man who ran the hardware store on Delancey Street, or as the one who would talk your ear off about the Mets for an hour before he got around to asking how your mother was doing. He loved that store, and he loved the people who walked through its doors, even the ones who came in only to ask for a single washer and left with a lecture on plumbing.

Dad grew up in Dayton, Ohio, the second of four boys, and he never quite stopped being the kid who had to fix everything around the house. He studied engineering at Ohio State for two years before deciding that he would rather work with his hands and his neighbors than with blueprints. Mom always said that was the best decision he ever made, though he would tell you it was the day he met her at a church picnic. He stayed in touch with a few of his college friends right up until the end, and every Christmas card from them sat on the mantel for weeks.

He was never without his dog, Biscuit, a scruffy terrier who rode in the passenger seat of his old pickup every single morning. When Biscuit passed, Dad cried more than any of us expected, and then he went out and found a rescue puppy that looked nothing like her. He said a man ought to have something to come home to, and he meant it.

For the last three years, Dad lived in a small brick house on Maple Court, where the neighbors knew him by his wave and his tomatoes. He was proud of that garden, and he would hand out bags of them to anyone who stood still long enough. Even in his final months, when he was at Mercy General Hospital, he asked the nurses about their kids and remembered their names. One of them told me he was the most patient patient she had ever had.

I keep thinking about the last conversation we had, which was on December 14th, just a few days before he went into the hospital. We sat on his porch wrapped in old blankets and argued, as we always did, about whether the Browns could ever win a playoff game. He was wrong, of course. I told him so, and he laughed so hard he had to wipe his eyes. That is the Frank I want you to remember: stubborn, funny, generous, and always ready for one more conversation.
output:

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on Tuesday 14 January with Dr Patel at the Riverside Surgery in Leeds, mostly so I remember what she said. I'm Ben Halloway, and I've lived in Leeds for about six years, though I was born in Hartlepool and still get teased by my mum for saying 'pop' instead of 'fizzy drop'. I went in because of the tightness in my chest that's been coming on when I walk up the hill to the bus stop. Dr Patel listened to my chest, checked my blood pressure (a bit high, 148 over 92), and asked about my sleep, which I said has been rubbish since our dog Biscuit started waking me up at four every morning.

She thinks the chest tightness is most likely muscular, given how much I've been carrying boxes at work, but she still wants an ECG and bloods to be safe. Ben, she said, not to panic, but come back if the tightness comes on while I'm resting or if I get short of breath lying down. She also suggested I cut back on the strong coffee after two in the afternoon.

The ECG is booked for Monday 27 January at 9:40 in the morning, and the blood test is the same day. I've put it in my calendar and set a reminder on my phone. I'll email the surgery at ben.halloway@hotmail.co.uk if anything changes before then, and I'll ask Biscuit's walker to take her out early for a few days so I can get some proper sleep.

input:
When I started my shift at Harbourline Logistics in Newcastle last October, I had no idea how much the job would teach me about responsibility. My title was Dispatch Coordinator, which sounded modest on paper, but I was the person who made sure forty trucks left the depot on time and that every driver knew where to go. Each morning I would check the fleet log, confirm the plates on the rostered vehicles, including the Toyota with registration 1QKX82 that always needed extra attention, and then call the drivers myself.

The work was not glamorous. Some mornings I was up at five, and on the worst days I ate my breakfast standing up at Brewhouse Corner before the first call came in. Lachlan, my supervisor, taught me that a good dispatcher listens as much as she speaks. When a driver told me a loading bay was blocked, I learned to believe them before the paperwork caught up. Over time the number of late departures dropped, and I began to feel that the schedule was partly mine to protect.

Looking back, that job showed me what I want to study. I want to understand how systems succeed or fail when people depend on them, and I want to be the kind of professional who notices small problems before they grow. Whatever I learn at university, I will carry the habits I built in that depot: checking twice, speaking up early, and remembering that behind every route is a person waiting for a delivery.

I have to admit that I nearly didn't come up to Edinburgh this spring at all. Between the deadlines at Harrowgate Logistics, where I've been working as a project coordinator since the autumn, and a flat in Leith that needed a new boiler, I'd convinced myself a weekend away was out of reach. My friend Isla, who has lived in Stockbridge for years, wouldn't take no for an answer, and I'm so glad she didn't. We booked the early train from Glasgow Central on the 12th of May and I spent most of the journey staring out at the green hills pretending to finish a report.

Stockbridge turned out to be exactly the sort of place you want to wander without a map. Isla walked me along the river on the Sunday morning, past the little bakeries and the stone terraces, and we stopped for flat whites at a cafe on Raeburn Place where the owner remembered her name from the week before. We climbed Arthur's Seat as the cloud lifted, and from the top the whole city looked like it had been painted in soft grey and gold. Honestly, the views were worth every aching calf.

If you go, do try to eat at least one proper Scottish breakfast, and don't skip the walk down to the Water of Leith in the evening when the light goes amber. I left with a sunburnt nose, a bag of shortbread for my colleagues, and a firm plan to come back in the autumn. Isla has already threatened to make me help her repaint her hallway, so I suppose I'd better get back to my spreadsheets and start saving.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to share that my father, Christoph Lindemann, passed away peacefully at home on 14 April, at the age of 78. He lived for over four decades at 27 Marienstraße, in Hannover, where he raised my sister and me and tended the roses in the back garden that he loved more than almost anything else.

Christoph was born in Görlitz in 1946, and he never lost the quiet determination of someone who had grown up in hard times. He studied civil engineering at the Technische Universität Dresden, and later spent thirty-one years with a Hannover construction firm, where colleagues still speak of his patience with apprentices and his habit of checking every measurement twice. For the last two years he was treated at the Klinikum Hannover Nord, and the nurses there became, in his words, "my second family." His national ID number, 10 4471 0852, was the last thing he asked me to keep safe for the paperwork that followed.

Chris, as his friends called him, is survived by my sister Anke, by me, and by four grandchildren who knew him as the man with the endless supply of peppermints. We will hold a private service on 22 April. In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to the Hannover hospice that cared for him so gently. Thank you for every kindness shown to him over the years.
output:

input:
Friends and family, thank you for being here today to celebrate the life of Jack Thornton. For those who knew him as Jacko, and for those who only knew him as Jack, he was the same warm, stubborn, generous man who never let a bad day go unanswered with a good joke.

Jack grew up in Ballarat, the second of four boys, and he spent his earliest years riding a secondhand bike up and down Sturt Street until his mum finally banned him from the footpath. He carried that restlessness into Ballarat Grammar, where he was far better at the cricket nets than he ever was at maths, and where he met the friends who would stay with him for the next sixty years.

He went on to study engineering at the University of Melbourne, and then spent the better part of four decades designing water pumping systems for rural councils across Victoria. Ask any of his colleagues and they will tell you he could fix anything, and that he never once left a job site without thanking the people who had made the work possible. He was patient with apprentices, honest with clients, and fierce in defence of anyone he thought was being treated unfairly.

In his last years, Jack spent a long stretch at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, and the nurses there still talk about the crossword puzzles he left at their station and the way he asked after their children by name. He faced that hard season with the same dry humour he brought to everything else, insisting on a proper cup of tea every morning and refusing to let anyone treat him as fragile.

He was born on 14 October 1948, and for years he marked the day by driving his grandchildren out to the Lake Wendouree foreshore for fish and chips. Those trips will go on, in the way we keep the things he taught us. Jack, you were a good friend, a loving father and grandfather, and a man who made the world a little more practical and a great deal more fun.

Rest now, Jacko. We will take it from here.
output:

I am making this statement at the Commissariat in Lyon on the morning of 14 August, following the incident outside my flat on rue Vaubecour the previous evening. My full name is Rémy Delacroix-Vidal, but everyone who has known me since childhood calls me Rem, and that is how I would like to be addressed. I was born in Saint-Étienne, where my parents still live, and I have lived in Lyon for the past nine years.

At approximately 21:40 on 13 August, I was returning home from my shift at the bakery on quai Saint-Antoine when I noticed a grey Renault Clio, registration BX-482-LM, parked across the entrance to my building with its engine running. A man in a dark jacket was standing beside it. When I asked him to move, he said only, "Tell Rem to stop talking to the newspaper," and then got back into the car. I did not get a clear look at his face because of the street lamp behind him.

I have not spoken to any journalist about my work at the municipal archive in recent weeks, and I do not know who the man was or why he used that name. I am reporting this because I felt threatened, and I have since received an unsigned message on my phone from an unknown number, sent on 15 August, repeating the same words. I can provide the screenshot and will cooperate fully with any inquiry.

מקווה שאת מרגישה טוב ושהברכיים לא מציקות לך יותר מדי בזמן האחרון. אני כותבת לך מהדירה הקטנה שלנו ברחוב הנרקיסים בחיפה, שם השכנים כבר מכירים את הכלבה שלנו, לוּלּוּ, יותר טוב ממני. היא בת שלוש עכשיו ועדיין חושבת שהיא גור, והיא מתה על הגינה הקטנה שמאחורי הבניין. אבא אמר לה בבוקר שהיא צריכה להתבגר, וגם אני לא בטוחה שהוא צודק.

היום חזרתי מהעבודה בשעה שש וחצי, והגשם התחיל כשהגעתי לתחנה. ישבתי על הספסל ליד הבית של המשפחה שלכם מהתקופה שהייתם בבית הישן וחשבתי עליך, על איך היית נותנת לי לאכול את הבצק של העוגיות ואומרת לי שאם אני לא אספר לאמא, זה לא נחשב. תודה על זה, באמת. אני מקווה שתוכלי לבוא לבקר בחודש הבא, אולי בשבוע השני של מרץ, כשהמזג אוויר יתחיל להיות נעים יותר ואפשר יהיה ללכת לטיול עד הים.

היום חזרתי מהעבודה בשעה שש וחצי, והגשם התחיל כשהגעתי לתחנה. ישבתי על הספסל ליד הבית של המשפחה שלכם מהתקופה שהייתם בבית הישן וחשבתי עליך, על איך היית נותנת לי לאכול את הבצק של העוגיות ואומרת לי שאם אני לא אספר לאמא, זה לא נחשב. תודה על זה, באמת. אני מקווה שתוכלי לבוא לבקר בחודש הבא, אולי בשבוע השני של אפריל, כשהמזג אוויר יתחיל להיות נעים יותר ואפשר יהיה ללכת לטיול עד הים.

מתגעגעת אלייך מאוד. בפעם הבאה שאדבר איתך בטלפון אני מבטיחה להביא את התמונה של מִימִי עם הכובע האדום שקיבלה מסבא. תגידי לנועה שאני שולחת לה חיבוק גדול, ושתשמרי על עצמך.

אוהבת אותך עד הירח ובחזרה,
נורית

I am writing this statement to report the theft of my mobile phone and a black leather handbag that took place on the evening of Thursday 14 August 2025 at approximately 7.30 p.m. I was walking back from Java House on Ngong Road, where I had met my colleague Wanjiru Kamau for coffee after work. Wanjiru can confirm that I had my phone with me when we left the cafe at around 6.45 p.m., as we were discussing a shared report for our office.

I then walked towards the bus stop near Yaya Centre. As I crossed the road I was approached by two young men, one wearing a grey hoodie and the other a navy cap. One of them grabbed the strap of my handbag while the other pushed me against a parked car. Within a few seconds they had run off towards Kilimani with my bag and phone. I was not physically injured apart from a scraped elbow, and I was able to get home safely with the help of a passer-by.

The items taken were an iPhone 13 in a clear blue case, my Samsung wallet containing my debit card and a little cash, and my National ID card, number 28417935, together with my Kenyan passport, number A1234567. I have already called my bank to block the card and have requested a new SIM card for my number, which is 0722 418 063. I would be grateful if the police could also check the IMEI record for the phone, which I have stored on my email account under sophie.wambui@gmail.com.

My sister, Sylvia Wambui, lives with me and has been very shaken by this. She has asked that any contact regarding this matter be made through me so that she is not further distressed. I am happy to provide any further information the investigating officer requires and I can be reached at the number above at any time.

I understand that a police abstract is needed for my insurance claim, so I would appreciate it if one could be issued as soon as possible. I have kept the receipt from Java House and will bring it to the station if needed.

Thank you for your assistance in this matter.

Sophie Wambui

One more thing: please send me your travel dates and any dietary needs so I can plan the meals. I'm planning to do a big grocery run when we arrive, so the more specific you can be, the better. Thanks in advance for putting up with my spreadsheet. I promise it will be worth it when we're all sitting on that dock with a drink in hand.

Love,
Fiona

Cari amici, cari parenti, grazie di essere qui oggi per salutare Domenico. Mi è stato chiesto di parlare a nome della famiglia, e non è facile trovare le parole giuste per un uomo che ha riempito ogni stanza in cui è entrato. Domenico è nato il 14 febbraio 1952 a Brindisi, e per tutta la vita ha portato con sé il mare di quella città: la pazienza dei pescatori, la risata forte, l'abitudine di salutare chiunque incontrasse per strada.

Chi lo conosceva sa che la sua vera passione era la cucina. Ogni domenica preparava orecchiette con le mani, sempre troppe, perché diceva che nessuno doveva andarsene a casa con la pancia vuota. Negli ultimi anni ha imparato anche a usare il telefono per mostrare le sue ricette ai nipoti. Il suo profilo, @domenico_cucina_brindisi, ha ancora decine di foto di piatti che ci ha lasciato in eredità, e ogni volta che le guardiamo sentiamo la sua voce che ci dice di aggiungere ancora un po' d'olio.

Caro Domenico, ci mancherai ai pranzi lunghi, alle partite alla radio e a quel modo unico di dire "va bene così" quando qualcosa andava storto. Grazie per tutto quello che ci hai dato. Riposa in pace, e tienici un posto a tavola.

Last month my younger brother Owen asked me to co-sign a loan for his matatu business, and I said yes without really reading the terms. Now the lender is calling me every week and says I am responsible for the full balance if he misses payments, which he has done for the last three months. I didn't realise how much that would affect my own credit.

I tried calling Owen but he doesn't pick up, so I emailed him at otieno.kamau88@gmail.com on the 12th of May asking for a repayment plan. He replied only that he is "handling it." I feel stuck between helping family and protecting my own household. My wife is upset and honestly so am I. Has anyone dealt with a relative defaulting on a loan you guaranteed? Did you negotiate directly with the bank, or did you go through a lawyer or a legal aid clinic? I'd also like to know whether it's possible to be removed as guarantor after the fact.

Any advice would mean a lot. I'm also keeping our dog Biscuit company while I sort this out, so if anyone has tips on handling stress without losing sleep, I'd welcome those too. Asante sana in advance.

My name is Marek Nowak, and I was honoured when my cousin asked me to say a few words about Mikolaj, the brother I grew up with in the flats off Ulica Piotrkowska in Lodz. Some of you knew him as the quiet man who always got to the bakery before the queue formed. Others knew him as the loud one at weddings, insisting everyone dance. He was both, and he was always himself.

Mikolaj ran the little Kawiarnia Sokol on the corner for twenty-two years. Anyone who sat at the window there will remember the chipped blue cups and the way he would refuse to take money from students who were short. He used to say a cafe was just a kitchen with the door left open. I think that is the most honest thing I ever heard him say, and it was typical of him to make a serious point sound like a joke.

He was also a terrible patient. When his knee gave out, he spent more time arguing with the staff at the Przychodnia Lipowa than he did with his physiotherapist. Still, he kept going back, because he liked the nurses there and he liked being someone people looked forward to seeing. He collected people the way other men collect stamps.

He died on the 14th of January, a Tuesday, in his sleep, which he would have called a sensible way to go, though he would have grumbled about the timing. We were at the kitchen table on Ulica Zielona the night before, going over old photographs, and he laughed so hard at one of his own bad haircuts that he had to wipe his glasses.

If you want to honour him, go and have a coffee somewhere you usually would not. Talk to the person behind the counter. Let them tell you something about their week. That was how Mikolaj lived, and I think it is the best way to keep him close. Thank you all for coming, and for the years you gave him.

I've been going to Brennan's Hardware on the Quay in Limerick for about six years now, and I wanted to write something after my last visit because it really deserves it. I'm Jack, and I live just off the Ennis Road, so this shop is basically on my route every week. Last month I came in with a cracked tap washer that had been dripping into my kitchen sink for a fortnight, and I honestly expected to be sent off to buy a whole new mixer. Instead the man behind the counter, Seamus, took one look at it, found the exact replacement in a drawer I didn't even know was there, and talked me through fitting it in about two minutes.

What I appreciate most about this place is that nobody makes you feel daft for asking. I'm not handy, and I've asked some embarrassing questions over the years, like which way a light bulb screws in or whether I needed a particular sealant for the bathroom. Every time the staff have been patient and never once tried to upsell me on something I don't need. The prices are fair too, and they still do a proper paint-matching service, which the big chains in Dublin seem to have given up on.

The only real complaint I have is the parking. The spaces out front fill up by ten on a Saturday, and there's no real loading bay for anyone picking up lumber or bags of cement. I've had to double-park twice and been shouted at by a delivery driver once, so a bit more planning there would help. Their opening hours on the bank holiday weekend were also not clearly posted, and I drove over on the Monday to find the shutters down.

Despite that, I'd rate them five stars without hesitation. If you're in the Limerick area and need anything from garden hose fittings to a new door lock, this is where I'd send you. I've also started recommending them to my neighbours, and my dog Biscuit has even been given a treat by the owner, who clearly has a soft spot for animals.

If you have any feedback or want to get in touch about the parking issue, you can reach the shop directly at info@brennanshardware.ie, and I'd encourage you to do so. Good local businesses take this kind of feedback seriously, and I think they'd want to know. Thanks to everyone there for making a simple Tuesday errand so much easier than it had any right to be.

input:
April 3rd. Woke up early again, which is becoming a bad habit. Brenda's cousin called from Scranton last night to say the old house on Linden Street finally sold, and I found myself sitting on the back step for an hour afterward, thinking about the summers we spent there. Scranton is where I was born, in a hospital that doesn't even exist anymore, and somehow that feels like it matters more now than it did a year ago. I keep telling myself that a place is just a place, but then I catch a smell of cut grass and I'm nine years old again.

Went to the bakery on Fifth this morning for a loaf of rye, and the woman behind the counter asked if I was still writing that blog. I laughed and said not really, but she said she'd seen my posts about the garden and wondered if I'd ever start a new one. I told her I'm thinking about it. Honestly, I've been posting less since the winter, mostly because I don't know what I want to say anymore. Brenda says I should just post whatever comes to mind, even if it's only a photo of the tomato seedlings. Maybe she's right. My handle is still @bethsgardenlog if anyone wants to find me there, though I haven't checked the notifications in weeks.

April 9th. Rain all week. Brenda and I finally sat down and talked about the trip to Ohio in June, and it turns out we want completely different things from it. She wants to see every museum and historic site along the way; I just want to sleep in a tent by a lake and not look at my phone. We ended up arguing about it over dinner, which was silly, and then laughing about how we both always assume the other one will give in. We agreed to split the itinerary down the middle. It's a small victory but I'll take it.

April 14th. Got a letter from my mother's old friend Gloria, who still lives in Scranton and who remembers everything. She enclosed a photo of me at maybe six, standing in front of the church on Adams Avenue with a popsicle melting down my wrist. I stared at it for a long time. Some days I feel like I've lost the thread of who I was before everything got complicated, and then a picture like that shows up and reminds me that the kid in it was already herself, already curious and a little stubborn.

April 22nd. Planted the tomatoes today, finally. The soil was still cold but the sun came out in the afternoon and I sat in the dirt with my hands full of compost and felt, for the first time in months, like something was growing that I actually chose. Brenda brought me lemonade and sat next to me without saying much, which was exactly right. I think I'll post a photo tonight. Just one, just the seedlings, nothing else.

input:
I should have listened to the woman at the car hire desk in Shannon when she tapped the form and said, "Mind the lanes, love, they're narrower than they look." I didn't, and by the second roundabout outside Ennis my heart was hammering. Still, nothing beats the moment the Burren opens up in front of you: grey limestone pavements stretching to the sea, wildflowers pushing out of the cracks as if the rock were only a thin coat. I pulled into a lay-by, sat on the bonnet with a flask of tea, and let the wind do the talking.

The real surprise of the trip was Galway. I'd booked a room above a pub on Shop Street, which sounds grander than it is, but the window looked straight down onto buskers and a fiddle player who kept going until nearly midnight. My host, Máire, runs the place with her brother Eoin and insisted on giving me the good towels. Her breakfast spread was generous enough to see me through a day of walking the Long Walk along the Corrib, where the swans had clearly decided the path belonged to them.

From there I drove the coast road toward Clifden, past Connemara's bog and the lakes that glow after rain. I stopped in a village whose name I still can't pronounce, bought a bar of smoked salmon from a tiny shop, and ate it on a stone wall while a farmer's dog inspected my boots. Small kindnesses like that stick with you far longer than the scenery.

If you go, book accommodation early for June, since the festivals start filling the towns quickly. I learned that the hard way, sleeping in the car for one night near Westport. Keep your phone charged, too: the signal drops out completely on the back roads. For bookings I used the email I'd set up for the trip, mmorrison.travels@gmail.com, which was handy when I needed to rearrange the Aran Islands ferry.

Looking back, the best parts were the unplanned ones: a pint with strangers in a snug, a detour when the rain cleared, the moment the cliffs of Moher came into view and nobody on the path spoke for a full minute. Ireland rewards people who slow down. I'm already planning the return trip, and this time I'll trust the woman at the car hire desk.

I am writing this statement at the request of PC Hollis at Hartlepool police station, following my visit on Tuesday 14 May to report the theft of my bank card and the subsequent fraudulent activity on my account. My name is Amara Okonkwo-Reid and I live at 23 Victoria Terrace, Gateshead, NE8 1QT. I have lived at this address for six years with my partner and our two children.

On the evening of Friday 10 May I parked my silver Vauxhall Corsa, registration KX19 BLM, on Ferndale Road, outside the Co-op. I went inside to buy a few groceries and, when I came back about twenty minutes later, I noticed the passenger window had been smashed. My handbag was on the floor of the car. My purse was missing, and it contained my debit card, my driving licence and a copy of my passport details that I had kept for a travel insurance claim.

I reported the loss to my bank, Northmoor Building Society, within an hour of discovering it. The fraud team told me that three transactions had already been attempted that evening at a petrol station and two online retailers, totalling just under £900. They froze the account and reissued my card. The account reference is 40817726 and the transactions are listed in the attached schedule. I have asked for a full refund, which the bank has said it will review once the police reference is confirmed.

I also noticed on Saturday morning that someone had tried to log into my email account, which is amara.okonkwoRead@mailbox.co.uk. I have changed the password and enabled two-step verification. Please note that my national insurance number and passport number, ending in 4418, may have been exposed, and I would be grateful if this could be recorded.

I would like to know whether any CCTV has been checked from the Co-op car park or the petrol station on Ferndale Road, and whether the vehicle has been traced. I am happy to provide any further information, the photographs I took of the damage and my bank correspondence. Thank you for your help with this matter.

Session notes for myself, written after Tuesday's appointment with Dr. Halvorsen. I keep coming back to what she said about the pattern: every time I feel left out, I start drafting a message in my head before I've even checked the facts. Isaac, I think you'd recognize that move too. Last week I spent an hour rehearsing an argument with Marcus Delaney over a dinner invitation that, as far as I can tell, was just a miscommunication. He lives in Portland now, so we mostly talk through email, marcus.delaney.writes@fastmail.com, and I've been so careful with my replies lately that they sound stiff even to me.

We talked about whether I could ask him directly instead of guessing. Dr. Halvorsen was gentle about it but clear: the guessing is the expensive part. It costs me sleep and it costs the friendship, because by the time I finally speak, I've already decided what he meant. I said I'd try sending a short note this week, something like "I felt a bit hurt when I heard about the dinner, can we talk?" Writing it out felt both obvious and terrifying.

For the next few weeks my homework is simple. When the old story starts, I name it out loud as a story, not a fact. I also want to keep a log of what actually happens versus what I predicted. I'll bring it back on September 24th, the next appointment, and we'll see whether the predictions are holding up.

Ezra, I think you'd recognize that move too. Last week I spent an hour rehearsing an argument with Trevor A-Dunn over a dinner invitation that, as far as I can tell, was just a miscommunication. He lives in Spokane now, so we mostly talk through email, trevor.dunn.writes@fastmail.com, and I've been so careful with my replies lately that they sound stiff even to me.

We talked about whether I could ask him directly instead of guessing. Dr. Lindqvist was gentle about it but clear: the guessing is the expensive part. It costs me sleep and it costs the friendship, because by the time I finally speak, I've already decided what he meant. I said I'd try sending a short note this week, something like "I felt a bit hurt when I heard about the dinner, can we talk?" Writing it out felt both obvious and terrifying.

For the next few weeks my homework is simple. When the old story starts, I name it out loud as a story, not a fact. I also want to keep a log of what actually happens versus what I predicted. I'll bring it back on September 29th, the next appointment, and we'll see whether the predictions are holding up.

input:
Thomas Reed Calloway was the kind of man who could fix anything with a socket wrench and a little patience, and he was never once in a hurry to leave a neighbor's kitchen. For fifty-eight years he lived at 214 Maple Hollow Drive in Dayton, Ohio, the house he and Linda bought in March of 1989 with more ambition than cash. Everyone on that block knew him as Tommy, a name his mother gave him and nobody else ever managed to shake loose. He coached Little League for nineteen seasons, taught every kid on the street how to throw a curveball badly, and always remembered your birthday, even when you were forty.

Those of us who called him Dad, Uncle Tom, or just Tommy knew the other side of him too. He was stubborn about the wrong things and generous about the right ones. When my son broke his arm at the lake, Tom drove four hours through the night without being asked twice. He kept a battered notebook of everyone's phone numbers, including his own, which he insisted on writing as (937) 555-0148 so we could always reach him. If you ever need to talk about him, or want to share a photo from those summers, you can still find him in our family group chat or on Instagram at @tomcallowayfixit.

So today, as we say goodbye, I ask that you remember him the way he remembered us. Call an old friend. Fix the thing that's been bothering you. Show up early and stay late. Tommy would have hated a fuss, so let's give him the quiet, honest kind of love he always gave to everyone else.

June 9

It's almost midnight and the apartment is finally quiet. Ilan Dekel left his shoes by the door again, so I've been stepping around them all evening. I'm writing this at the kitchen table because if I sit on the couch I will fall asleep mid-sentence.

Today was one of those days where everything went sideways from the start. The car, my little silver Hyundai, plate 47-219-83, made that grinding noise on the way to work, so I dropped it at the garage on Herzl Street and took the bus. The bus was packed. Someone's speaker was playing old Mizrahi pop the whole way down Ibn Gabirol, and I stood there the entire time holding a bag of groceries that was threatening to split open.

At the office, my manager Yoram Stern called a meeting at ten, which is never good news. I'm still the Senior Analyst at Meridian Lakeside Technologies, and he wanted to talk about the Q3 budget review. Honestly I think he just wanted to say he'd spoken to everyone. I came out of it with three new tasks and a headache. Ilan laughed when I told him, but he's the one who gets to work from home on Thursdays, so he doesn't get a vote.

In the evening I finally sat down to answer the messages I'd been ignoring. My cousin Tamar posted photos from the Galilee trip, and I commented on them, then realised I had tagged the wrong person and had to delete it. She sent me a laughing emoji and a link to a bakery in Haifa that apparently makes the best sufganiyot in June, which doesn't make sense but I'm going to check it anyway. I also saw that the group account we run for the neighbourhood garden, @rosh_ha_ayin_garden, has a new follower request from someone I don't recognise, so I'll deal with that tomorrow.

On the 16th we have the family dinner in Beersheba, which means another long drive and another argument about who is responsible for the salads. Ilan says he'll bring the wine if I promise to stop bringing up the car. I think that's a fair trade. Tomorrow is a new day, and hopefully the garage will call before lunch to say the car is fixed.

Good night, diary.

What I didn't know was that he'd spend the next decade pulling me into his schemes, from the disastrous hiking trip to the Tatras to the time he tried to start a podcast. Thankfully, the podcast never made it past episode one.

When Julia came along, I saw a change in him. He became calmer, funnier in a quieter way, and far more likely to actually show up on time. Julia works as a nurse at the Clinic on Pawia Street, and she's the most patient person I've ever met. She's also the only person who has ever convinced Jakub to go to the gym at Atlas Fitness with her, which I still consider a small miracle. She also secretly follows his lunch posts on Instagram under @jakubdoesnotcook, and she's the reason that account now has more than two thousand followers.

Julia, you have taken a man who once lost his car keys inside his own car and turned him into someone who reads the weather forecast before planning his weekend. Please raise your glasses with me to Jakub and Julia. To the couple who met in a cafe, who promised to keep each other honest, and who I'm pretty sure will be fighting over the thermostat for the next forty years. Cheers!
