I need some help thinking through a situation at work and at home, and I'm not sure where to start. For about eight months I've been carrying a feeling that I'm falling behind in my job, even though my manager says my results are fine. I keep replaying meetings in my head and wondering whether people privately think I'm not up to the level they expected when they hired me. It makes me slow to speak up, and then I end up doing extra work at night just to feel like I've earned my spot. My partner has noticed I'm tired all the time and short-tempered, and last week we argued about something small that really wasn't small to me.

I want to understand whether this is just a rough patch or whether I'm building a pattern that will hurt me more over time. I don't want a pep talk. I'd like a clear way to sort out which worries are based on evidence and which are just noise from my own head. I'm also wondering how to bring this up with my manager without sounding fragile, and how to tell my partner what's actually going on instead of letting them guess.

Could you help me break this into a few practical questions and steps? I'd like to know what kinds of things I could track over the next few weeks to see whether the anxiety is easing or growing, and what signs would tell me it's worth talking to a doctor or counsellor. Thank you for taking the time to read this.

My name is Bernhard Oltmanns, and I am a senior data engineer at Rheinland Datenwerk GmbH in Düsseldorf, where I have led the platform team since October 2019. Before joining the company, I spent six years building analytics pipelines for a logistics firm in Hamburg, which is where I first became interested in how messy operational data can be turned into something people trust. These days my work centres on streaming architectures, data quality frameworks and the unglamorous but essential job of making sure that a number on a dashboard means what everyone thinks it means.

Outside the office I am a keen cyclist and a fairly average amateur photographer. My partner Mareike and I share a flat in the Bilk district, and our household is completed by Pumpernickel, a three-year-old grey tabby who has opinions about every keyboard I own. Pumpernickel is the reason I now work from home two days a week, since he has made it clear that a desk without a cat on it is simply unacceptable.

I am delighted to be speaking at this year's conference about lessons from rebuilding our reporting stack. The talk covers the decisions we got right, the ones we got wrong, and the surprisingly human reasons behind both. You can reach me at bernhard.oltmanns@rheinland-datenwerk.de, and I would welcome conversations with anyone wrestling with similar problems. Thank you for having me.

Niamh opened by thanking everyone for coming out on a wet evening. She reminded us that the grant application to the Dublin City Council fund has to be lodged by 30 April, so the timeline is tight. I said I had already spoken to the caretaker about the hall keys for the weekend workshops and he is happy to leave them with the reception desk from now on. Colm raised the issue of the leaking roof above the storage room, which he first flagged in February. Niamh asked him to send photos to the council housing liaison before our next meeting.

Aisling gave an update on the youth breakfast club. Attendance has dropped to around fourteen children on average, down from twenty in March. We agreed Aisling would survey the parents by email before any change is made, and she will draft the questions this week.

We spent some time on the budget. I went through the figures from the first quarter. Spending on the art supplies came in under forecast, but the insurance premium went up by almost twelve per cent at renewal. Niamh asked whether we could shop around for a cheaper policy and I agreed to get three quotes by the end of the month. I also mentioned that the printing account is still under my name, which I would like to transfer to the centre's general address so that it is easier to hand over at the end of the year.

For any other business, Colm reminded us that the summer scheme registration form needs a volunteer's passport or national ID number for the Garda vetting process. I said I would collect copies from the three new volunteers, Ciara, Padraig and Mona, and send them to Niamh securely rather than by ordinary email. I've been coming to this place for about a year now, mostly for weekend brunch, and it has never disappointed. The owners clearly care about what they serve. The eggs are always cooked the way you ask, the coffee is strong and hot, and the staff remember regulars without making it awkward. On my last visit the server noticed I'd switched to oat milk and simply asked if I wanted it without being told. Small things like that add up.

The dining room is cozy without being cramped, and the lighting makes it easy to sit with a book or a laptop for an hour. Parking can be tight on busy mornings, so plan to walk if you can. The wait during peak hours is real, but the line moves quickly and they'll text you when your table is ready, which I appreciated.

Prices are fair for the portion sizes and the quality of ingredients. The pancakes are the standout, light and not overly sweet. My only complaint is that the playlist sometimes gets louder than I'd like around lunch. Otherwise I'd recommend this spot to anyone who wants a relaxed, reliable breakfast. I'll be back soon, probably with my sister, who has been asking me to take her for months.

input:
I have always believed that the best way to understand a place is to work in it. When I was seventeen I spent three summers as a volunteer at St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney, mostly pushing trolleys and sorting linen, but eventually I was trusted to sit with patients while the nurses did their rounds. One of them, a retired postal worker named Edward Pryce, taught me more about listening than any textbook could. He told me stories about delivering mail through the Blue Mountains in the 1960s, and he always asked how my own week had gone before he would say a word about his pain.

That experience pushed me toward a Bachelor of Health Sciences at the University of Queensland, where I have spent the past year as a peer tutor for first-year anatomy. I have come to see teaching as another form of listening: working out what a confused student actually needs to hear. Since March I have also worked two days a week as a Community Engagement Coordinator at Brisbane Youth Health Network, where my job title sounds grander than my daily routine, which is mostly updating the group's Instagram account (@ellie.hopes.ahead) and running Tuesday information sessions for teenagers who are nervous about their first doctor's visit.

What I want from a graduate program in public health is a chance to connect those threads. I want to understand how a single conversation at a bedside can scale into policy that reaches a whole suburb. Edward once told me that the mail always got through, even when the roads did not. I would like to build systems that carry that same kind of reliability to people who are easily overlooked. Ellie Hopkins, applying from Brisbane, is ready to start learning how.

input:
My name is Konstantina Papadaki, and I am a structural engineer based in Thessaloniki, where I have spent most of my working life designing retrofits for older apartment blocks. I grew up in a small house at 14 Ermou Street in the Ano Poli district, a neighbourhood of narrow lanes and stone steps that taught me early how buildings and people shape one another. My parents ran a bakery on the ground floor, and I learned to read load and space long before I ever read a textbook on the subject.

I completed my undergraduate degree in civil engineering at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in 2009. The years there were demanding, but they gave me a rigorous foundation in materials science and seismic analysis, which has proved essential in a country that lives with earthquakes as a fact of life. Afterwards I worked for three years on hospital refurbishment projects, including the seismic upgrade of the wing at Papageorgiou General Hospital, a project that convinced me the most meaningful engineering often happens in buildings people depend on every day.

In my current role at a small consultancy, I lead a team of six engineers reviewing older residential stock across northern Greece. Our work focuses on affordable reinforcement methods that residents can actually finance, and we have now assessed more than two hundred buildings. I am proud that several of our recommendations have been adopted by municipal housing programmes, though I remain cautious about declaring any project finished until the concrete has cured and the families have moved back in.

Outside of work I am an enthusiastic, if not particularly skilled, amateur cook. I also share my home with Mochi, a grey tabby rescued from a construction site, who has taken a keen and mostly unwelcome interest in my drawing table. She has taught me more about patience than any site manager ever did.

I look forward to the conference because I believe the gap between research and practice in our field is still too wide. I hope to meet colleagues who are working on low-cost seismic solutions, and to share what we have learned from Greece's own difficult experience. Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you.

input:
I've been going to Greenleaf Auto Care on Halsted Street for about six years now, and I finally sat down to write this because my experience last week was genuinely impressive. My brother-in-law Gordon Pruitt recommended them after his truck was misdiagnosed at a chain shop across town, so I went in skeptical. I came in with a grinding noise from my front brakes and a check engine light that had been blinking since the spring.

The service advisor, a woman named Dana Whitfield, listened to the whole story without rushing me. She explained that the grinding was not just worn pads but a warped rotor, and she showed me the old pads on the counter so I could see the difference for myself. Nobody has ever done that for me before. The quote was itemized, and when I asked whether the check engine light could wait, she was honest that it could, but she also told me exactly what to watch for.

The work itself took a little over three hours, which was faster than the estimate they gave me. The shop called me at my office twice to update me, and once they texted a photo of the new rotors. I had a question about the invoice afterward and emailed the front desk at service@greenleafautocare.com. Someone replied within the hour with a clear breakdown, which I appreciated since I'm a stickler for paperwork.

My daughter Maya, who is 34 and works as a nurse at St. Vincent's, drove over with me because her car has the same engine and she wanted to see how the mechanics handled the diagnostic. She was impressed by how patient the technicians were when she asked questions, and she has already booked her own oil change for next month.

The waiting area is clean, the coffee is decent, and there's a kids' corner with books that kept my grandson busy. Prices are fair for the area. They are not the cheapest in town, and I'd say that's a reasonable trade for work done right the first time.

If you're in the neighborhood and need honest service, I'd recommend Greenleaf without hesitation. Five stars from me, and I'll be back.

My name is Fadi Haddad, and I am writing this notice myself so that my friends in Haifa and beyond know that I have passed away on December 9 at the age of 71. I was born in Nazareth, but for most of my life I called Haifa home, and I was proud to be part of its port-side neighbourhoods where everyone knows the baker's name and the fishermen's catch of the day. I taught chemistry for thirty-four years at the Technion before retiring, and I still remember the first lab coat I wore and the students who kept me young.

Every morning for the last decade I walked to Café Yarden on Herzl Street, where Sami Nassar, the owner, kept my usual coffee ready before I reached the door. Sami and my former colleague Dr. Miriam Levin were the people who checked on me most often in my final months at Rambam Hospital, and I am grateful to both for their patience. My family asks that any kindness be shown to the nurses on the cardiology ward. If you wish to write to my daughter Lina, she can be reached at lina.haddad@mailbox.co.il.

I leave behind my wife, Nadia, my two children, and four grandchildren who filled my house with noise I came to love. Please remember me as someone who argued loudly about football and quietly about everything else that mattered. Shiva will be held at our home on Carmel Street from December 11 through December 13.

input:
I finally made it to the Pacific Northwest this January, three years after I first put it on my list. I'm Vanessa, thirty-four, and I work as a nurse at St. Brendan's Medical Center in Spokane, so getting away for ten days felt like a small miracle. My sister Rhonda flew in from Chicago to join me, and we rented a silver Subaru with the plate 7KQM-421 because the rental agency only had one left in our price range. We picked up the keys on January 9th, the morning after my shift ended, still half-asleep and buzzing on bad airport coffee.

Our first stop was Port Angeles, where the ferry crossing out of Seattle had been delayed by fog. Vanessa Miller, that's me, had never seen the Olympic Peninsula in winter, and the snow on the mountains looked like frosting someone had piped on in a hurry. We walked the waterfront with our hoods up while a few gulls argued over a bag of fries. Rhonda kept calling it the most beautiful, grey, chilly day she'd ever had, and I think she meant it.

We spent the next two days near Lake Crescent, staying in a small cabin that allowed pets, which is how we ended up with Biscuit, a shaggy terrier belonging to the owner, Mr. Halvorsen. Biscuit followed us around like we were long-lost family. Vanessa, Rhonda and Biscuit went on a trail along the water on January 12th, and the lake was so still it looked like polished glass until a wind pushed ripples across it.

On our last full day we drove to the coast, and I couldn't resist posting a photo to our family group chat. My cousin Derek, who works at Brightline Logistics in Tacoma, replied within minutes asking whether we'd gotten a glimpse of the sea lions at Ruby Beach. We had, and they were enormous and loud and utterly unbothered by us.

I'd recommend this trip to anyone who needs a reset. Pack layers, bring a thermos, and don't plan too tightly. Our flight home left on January 18th, and I already miss the smell of cedar and the sound of rain on the cabin roof.

input:
I still can't believe how much ground we covered in Jerusalem on our first full day. My name is Felix Harwood and I'd been planning this trip for months, but nothing prepares you for the Old City at seven in the morning, when the lanes are empty and the bells start up. My old college friend Rafi Dolev met me at Jaffa Gate, and he insisted on being called "Raf" by everyone, even the shopkeepers who only knew him as Rafi. He had booked us a guide, but then spent the whole walk correcting her on the history of the Armenian Quarter.

We ended the morning at Café Ruth on Agrippas Street, which Raf swore was the best shakshuka in the city. He was right. The owner, a woman named Ruthie Amsalem, remembered him from a visit three years ago and brought us an extra plate of pita without being asked. Later that afternoon I stumbled into a small clinic near Mahane Yehuda after a bad sunburn, and the nurse there, Dana, patched me up with more kindness than I expected from a stranger.

If you go in April, bring layers and comfortable shoes. The weather swings from warm sun to sudden cool wind, and the hills will punish flip-flops. I'd also recommend booking Café Ruth early, because by nine on a Saturday the queue stretches halfway down the street. Raf is already threatening to make me come back next April so he can show me the Galilee properly.

input:
My name is Noa Ben-Ami, and I am the younger sister of Nadav. I stand here today with a heavy heart, but also with a great deal of gratitude for the forty-one years we shared. Nadav was born on September 14, 1983, in a small hospital in Haifa, and from the moment he arrived he made it clear that he would do things his own way. He was stubborn, funny, and impossibly generous, the kind of man who would give away his last shekel and then borrow a coffee from you to make the point.

For the last nine years Nadav lived in Be'er Sheva, in a little apartment on Yehuda Halevi Street, number 12, where the afternoon light came through the kitchen window and made the whole place feel like a Sunday. He loved that city. He used to say that Be'er Sheva had the desert's honesty, and that people there told you exactly what they thought, which suited him perfectly. Every Friday he would call our mother from that kitchen table, and I could hear the kettle whistling in the background while they argued about nothing at all.

Nadav was a carpenter, and he believed that a well-made chair could hold a family together. He built the table at which many of you have eaten, and he would never let anyone leave his workshop without a glass of tea and a story. Those of you who knew him through his work know that he never cut a corner, and that he was happiest when he could hand someone a finished piece and watch their face change.

Some of you have written to me since his passing, and I have been moved by how many people kept his email address in their contacts so they could send him photographs of their children, their gardens, their newly painted doors. His address was nadav.benami@ariel-woodworks.co.il, and I have promised his friends that I will keep checking it for a while, in case one more message comes in that makes me laugh the way he always made me laugh.

Nadav, you were the most alive person I have ever known. Thank you for the workshop, the tea, the stories, and for teaching me that a life can be measured by the people it holds up. Rest now, my brother. We will carry the table from here.

Okay, so you asked me last week how the move to Leipzig went, and I kept putting off answering because honestly it's been a rollercoaster. I'm thirty-four now and I thought I'd have my life a bit more sorted by this point, but here I am, sharing a flat in Connewitz with two people I met on a flatshare site and a cat that belongs to neither of them. Oskar, my landlord's nephew, helped me carry the boxes up four flights on the eighteenth of August, and I swear the stairs got longer with every trip.

The first few weeks were rough. My German is fine for ordering bread and asking for directions, but when people speak fast at the Amt I just nod and hope for the best. I spent almost a whole morning at the Bürgeramt trying to register my address, and the woman behind the counter was patient but also clearly done with me by the end. Oskar, the one from the stairs, sort of adopted me after that. He took me to the Kneipe on the corner where the owner now calls me "der Neue" and slides me free Mate.

So yeah, it's not the glossy Berlin story I half expected, but I'm getting there. Write back soon and tell me how Hannover is treating you. And if you ever visit, you have a bed on my floor, cat included, though I can't promise it'll let you sleep.

אני מחפשת מישהו שיודע לדבר על ספרים בלי להתבייש בדעה חזקה, ששמח לבשל משהו פשוט ולא מתעקש שזה יהיה מושלם. מעניין אותי מי שאוהב קולנוע ישן, שיחות שנמשכות אחרי הארוחה, וגם שתיקות נוחות. לא מחפשת הבטחות גדולות, רק מישהו שמקשיב באמת ושיודע להתפעל מדברים קטנים, כמו עץ תות שפורח מוקדם מהרגיל או ספר שמצאת בדיוק כשהיית צריכה אותו.

לגבי מה שחשוב לי: כנות, הומור עצמי, ומוכנות לצאת מהבית לפעמים, גם כשהכול נראה נוח בתוכו. אם יש לך סיפור על טיול שהשתבש בצורה משעשעת או מתכון שהחברים שלך עדיין מזכירים, כתוב לי. אשמח לשמוע מה אתה אוהב לעשות כשאף אחד לא מבקש ממך כלום.

I am writing to describe the incident that occurred on January 14 at my apartment in Kichijoji, Tokyo, and to submit this claim for water damage to my personal property. At approximately 7:30 in the morning, I noticed that the ceiling of my living room had developed a large brown stain, and within twenty minutes water was dripping onto the tatami near the window. My upstairs neighbour, Ikeda-san, confirmed that the washing machine on the floor above had overflowed. My friends call me Ichi, and I was the one who contacted the building manager, who arrived shortly after nine.

The damage affected a sofa, a set of oak bookshelves, approximately forty books, a laptop, and a camera bag. I have attached receipts for the sofa, purchased from a store in Shinjuku in 2022, and photographs taken on the morning of the incident. The bookshelves were custom-built by a carpenter in Nakano, and I have included his written estimate. The laptop was damaged beyond repair; the serial number is printed on the attached warranty card. I have also documented the water staining on the ceiling and walls, which the building management company has said it will repair under the building's own policy.

I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this claim and let me know what further documentation you require. I can be reached by email at ichi.morrow@example.jp or by message through my social media handle @ichi_tokyo_life, though I would prefer email for formal correspondence. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

input:
Mate, I still can't believe how the weekend went. You know how I've been dreading the move back to the old flat? Well, it turned out fine. Mum and I spent most of Saturday hauling boxes down three flights of stairs, and I swear every box had doubled in weight since we packed it. By lunchtime we were both sweaty and grumpy, so we gave up and got fish and chips from the shop round the corner, the one with the wobbly table outside. Honestly, it was the best meal I've had in ages. We just sat there in the sun, not saying much, and it felt like the first calm moment since everything got chaotic.

In the afternoon I finally sorted out the cupboard under the sink, which had become a sort of graveyard for old cables and mystery bottles. I found a jar of buttons I'd forgotten about and a postcard from a trip years ago that made me laugh out loud. I kept almost everything, which Mum says is hopeless, but I reckon some things deserve a second look. Heaps of small stuff, really, but it reminded me of who I was before work took over my brain.

Anyway, I wanted to tell you because you're the one who always asks the right questions. I think I'm finally ready to stop waiting for things to feel perfect before I start them. Let's catch up properly soon, maybe with a proper coffee this time and no boxes in sight. Cheers for listening, as always.

Hi everyone, Carly Nguyen here from Year 6 at Bellbird Valley Primary. A quick note to say thank you to all the families who came along to our Reconciliation Week morning tea on Thursday 12 June. A huge thanks goes to Mrs Priya Raman from the Year 5 team, who organised the cake stall and somehow kept the urn of tea going all morning without anyone noticing how much work it was.

Several children asked if we could do it again next term, so I will raise it at the next staff meeting on Tuesday 24 June. If you have ideas for guest speakers from the community, please send them my way.

input:
I am Zoe Halvorsen, and I have spent the last twelve years working at the intersection of civic data and public health. I currently serve as Senior Epidemiology Analyst at Brightwater Health Partners in Tacoma, Washington, where I lead a small team that tracks emergency department visits across six counties. Before joining Brightwater, I completed my doctoral work at the University of Oregon, and my dissertation examined how heat waves affect hospital admissions among older adults living alone.

I grew up in Duluth, Minnesota, the daughter of a commercial fisherman and a school librarian. Those two influences still shape how I work. From my father I learned that patterns in the water tell you something true even when the instruments disagree, and from my mother I learned that a dataset is only useful if the people it describes can understand it. Most of my projects now try to honor both lessons by pairing rigorous modeling with plain-language reports that community groups can actually use.

My most rewarding recent work began on December 14, 2022, when I was appointed to the Washington State Winter Preparedness Advisory Panel. The panel asked me to review how cold-weather shelter capacity was being reported across the state. Over the following eight months we identified reporting gaps in three rural counties and proposed a shared template that has since been adopted by eleven agencies. I was proud to see how quickly a practical fix could travel once people trusted the numbers behind it.

Outside the office I coach a youth robotics team at the Lakeview Community Center, a commitment that keeps me grounded and reminds me why accurate information matters to young people as much as to policymakers. I also volunteer as a reviewer for the Pacific Northwest Journal of Population Health, where I try to encourage early-career researchers to publish their work even when their findings are modest.

I would welcome the chance to talk with colleagues about translating surveillance data into action. If you wish to reach me before the conference, you may call my office at (253) 555-0147 or write to zoe.halvorsen@brightwaterhp.org. I look forward to meeting many of you in person and hearing about the work you are doing.

Hi there! I'm Isabel, 31, and I work as a pharmacist at a clinic in Quezon City. Most evenings you'll find me either reading in a coffee shop along Scout Madrigal or trying out a new lechon place with my friends. I grew up in Iloilo, so I still have a soft spot for batchoy, and I'm the kind of person who will happily drive three hours for a good bowl of it.

I live with my pet, a grumpy but lovable Shih Tzu named Pancho Villa Dimaculangan. Yes, the full name is necessary, and yes, he knows it. He runs the household, sleeps on my laundry, and has strong opinions about the mailman. I share a small condo at 27 Maginhawa Street, Teacher's Village, which is close to great food and quiet enough for weekend reading. If you're the type who likes long walks, I promise to bring Pancho along and let him set the pace.

I'm looking for someone who is curious, kind, and not afraid of a good argument about movies. I love live music, especially small gigs in Malate where the sound is rough and the crowd is warm. I also love quiet Sunday mornings with a book and a cup of barako. If you enjoy trying new things, I have a list a mile long: hiking Mount Pulag, a food crawl in Binondo, a weekend in Siargao. I'm happy to cross off as many as we can.

A little about my week: I work long shifts, so I value people who can communicate clearly and plan ahead. I'm not great at texting in circles, so if you're interested, just tell me what you think. My ideal first date is somewhere with good food and a view, but I'm happy to meet for coffee if that feels easier. Anything from July 12 onward works for me, and I'm flexible on the weekday evenings.

If you're still reading, thank you! Send me a message with something you love, whether it's a band, a dish, or a place you can't stop thinking about. You can reach me at isabel.reyes.pharm@gmail.com, and I promise I reply faster than Pancho answers the door.

Hi team,

Quick follow-up on the vendor contract review we discussed in the standup. I went through the draft this morning and there are two clauses I'd like us to push back on before we sign. The first concerns the data retention terms, which currently allow the supplier to keep records for far longer than our policy permits. The second is the liability cap, which is much lower than what we usually accept for a deal of this size. I've drafted some suggested language for both and will drop it into our shared folder later today.

I also spoke briefly with the procurement lead. They are open to revisiting the terms, but they want our comments by the end of next week so the legal review can run in parallel with the budget approval. If anyone has concerns about the timeline, please flag them now rather than later. I would rather adjust the schedule today than scramble in the final days.

Once the comments are in, I'll pull everything together into a single summary for leadership so they can make a decision without wading through the full document. Thanks for your input so far, and let me know if you spot anything I've missed.

Best,
Omer

input:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to provide a reference for a former member of my team who worked with us for several years in a busy operations role. I have supervised a great many staff over the course of my career, and I can say with confidence that this individual stood out for their reliability, their good humour, and their genuine commitment to the work.

During their time with us, they were responsible for coordinating schedules, liaising with suppliers, and keeping a steady flow of paperwork moving through a department that rarely slowed down. They took ownership of tasks without needing to be asked twice, and they had a knack for spotting small problems before they grew into large ones. When an unexpected backlog arose one winter, they volunteered to reorganise our filing and tracking system, and the improvement they made has stayed with us long after they left.

What I valued most, however, was the way they worked with others. They were patient with newer colleagues, generous with their time, and quick to share what they had learned. Several members of staff have told me that they would go out of their way to explain a process properly rather than simply pointing to a manual. That kind of attitude builds trust, and it made our team considerably stronger.

Their communication was clear and professional, both in writing and in person. They handled difficult conversations with tact, and they were equally comfortable reporting bad news as they were celebrating a success. I never once had to worry about whether something would be followed up, because they always followed through.

I recommend them without reservation for any role that calls for organisation, discretion and a calm, dependable presence. They would be an asset to any team fortunate enough to employ them, and I would be glad to speak further about their qualifications and experience should you require it.

Yours faithfully,

A former line manager

Je m'appelle Dorian Fontaine et j'ai grandi dans le quartier de la Croix-Rousse, à Lyon, au deuxième étage d'un immeuble de la rue Imbert-Colomès. Mon père est menuisier et ma mère tient une petite librairie près de la place Sathonay. C'est peut-être là que j'ai appris à aimer les mots, en rangeant des livres le samedi matin avec elle.

Le 14 mars de l'année dernière, j'ai eu dix-sept ans, et ce jour-là ma mère m'a offert un vieux carnet relié en cuir. J'y ai commencé à noter les conversations que j'entendais dans le bus 13, les phrases des clients de la boutique, les silences entre deux amis. Peu à peu, ce carnet est devenu mon laboratoire d'écriture, et j'ai compris que je voulais faire de la littérature comparée ou du journalisme culturel.

Si l'université m'accepte, je souhaite continuer à explorer cette curiosité pour les voix ordinaires. Vous pouvez me joindre au 04 78 29 61 35 ou par courriel à dorian.fontaine@mailbox.fr si vous souhaitez un entretien. Je serais ravi de vous raconter plus en détail mon parcours, et surtout ce que je compte apporter à votre communauté d'étudiants.

Right, you asked what happened with Dad's flat, so here it is properly. My name is Thomas Whitfield-Ross, though nobody outside the family bothers with the double-barrel, and the phone number I gave the solicitor is 07734 219 856 if you ever need to reach me about it. I'm writing this at the kitchen table in Leeds with a cold tea, because I didn't want to say it all on the phone again.

Katherine, my sister, had been the one dealing with Dad since the spring. She'd call me from the car park of the Brunswick Street Cafe, which is where she always went to get out of the house, and she'd sound like she'd been crying into a napkin. I told her to stop being the hero. Honestly, I was useless. I kept saying I'd come up at the weekend and then finding a reason not to.

On the ninth of May we had the meeting with the care coordinator at the clinic on Harrowgate Road. Tom from the practice had booked the room, and Kath turned up with a folder so thick it looked like a bad script. I remember thinking, she's got all this sorted and I've got nothing. She just looked at me and said, "Tommy, you can take the bills, I'll take the bathroom," and I didn't argue because she was right.

The bit that really got to me came a few days later. Dad, who hadn't remembered my wife's name for a month, asked Kath whether she'd been to the gym that morning, and she laughed so hard she had to sit down on the stairs. We both did. It was the first time in ages we'd laughed about anything together.

So that's where things stand. The flat goes on the market in June, Kath is staying at the house until the paperwork clears, and I'm finally driving up every other weekend. You don't have to say anything wise about it. Just tell me you'll ring me on the Sunday, because I'll need someone to tell me I'm doing alright.

input:
I am writing to describe the circumstances of my claim relating to the water damage at my home. My name is Fergus Whitlock and I am 47 years old. I have lived at the property on Harrowgate Lane in Leeds for eleven years, and I work as a payroll supervisor at a firm in the city centre, which is why I was not at home when the incident happened.

On the morning of Tuesday 9 April, I left the house at around seven forty-five as usual. My partner Helena was still at home with our dog, a rescue lurcher called Bramble, who was due to be taken to the vet that afternoon. Helena has told me that she heard a loud bang from the kitchen at about half past nine, followed by water running through the ceiling of the dining room. By the time she got downstairs, the floor was already covered and the ceiling plaster in the corner had started to come down.

Helena phoned me immediately, and I rang our emergency plumber, who attended within two hours. He identified a failed compression joint on the pipework running behind the kitchen units, which had apparently been weakening for some time. He isolated the supply and made the pipe safe, but by then the water had travelled into the adjoining rooms. Bramble was shut in the utility room for her own safety while the work was done, and she was distressed by the noise and the commotion.

I have since obtained the plumber's invoice and a written report, both of which I have enclosed. The damage includes the kitchen flooring, the lower sections of two fitted units, plasterboard and skim coat in the dining room, and a section of the living room carpet. We have also had to arrange a dehumidifier for three weeks. I have listed the replacement costs separately, based on quotes from two local contractors. I was referred to my own GP at Leeds General Infirmary for stress-related symptoms following the event, and I have included the appointment letter.

I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this claim and let me know what further documentation you require. I can be reached on 0113 496 2287 or at fergus.whitlock@examplemail.co.uk. I am happy to arrange a visit from your assessor at any time convenient to you, ideally in the coming fortnight, and I will ensure the property is accessible.

Yours faithfully,

Fergus Whitlock

Hi all, first time posting here so bear with me. I'm a 34 year old nurse based in Leeds and I've been stuck on a decision for about three weeks now. I work nights on the cardiac ward at St James's Hospital and the rota has been brutal since the start of the year. My manager, Gillian, has offered me a move to days if I agree to take on a band 6 charge role, but I'm honestly not sure I'm ready for the responsibility.

Some background. I trained at Leeds Beckett about ten years ago and I've been qualified ever since. I love the clinical side, the patients, the teamwork on a good shift. What wears me down is the sleep debt. I've had two near misses on the road home after nights, and that scared me more than I want to admit. My partner Nathan keeps telling me to just take the offer, but he doesn't see what goes on during a shift when things go wrong.

The thing that's making it harder is that I already had a meeting with HR on 14 April to talk through options, and they said I'd need to give an answer by the end of the month. I've been going back and forth on whether I should ask for a few more weeks, or whether that just looks indecisive. Has anyone here moved from nights into a charge role? How did you handle the transition, and did you find the extra admin overwhelming?

I've also been looking at whether a clinical educator post might suit me better, which would keep me off the wards most of the time but still in patient care. I checked a few adverts on NHS Jobs and the one for the Leeds Teaching Hospitals trust looked interesting, though I'm not sure how competitive those are. If you've made a similar switch, I'd really value your experience.

If anyone wants to message privately, my email is nina.hartley88@gmail.com. I'm happy to share more detail about the roles I'm considering. Thanks in advance for any advice, it honestly means a lot to read stories from people who've been here.

I am writing to formally complain about the damaged refrigerator I received from your store on June 12. My name is Frank Delaney, and I placed the order on June 3 through your Maplewood location. The unit arrived with a cracked crisper drawer and a dented side panel, which I documented with photographs the same afternoon.

When I called the support line, the representative told me the delivery team was not responsible for inspection. I was transferred three times and finally told a replacement would be "scheduled soon." No confirmation email ever arrived. I have now waited nearly three weeks without any further contact.

My neighbour, Marcus Holloway, who is 67 and has helped me with heavy lifting since my knee surgery, was present when the delivery crew unloaded the appliance. He witnessed the damage and can confirm that the box showed no visible tears before it was carried into my kitchen. I mention his age only because the crew insisted on leaving the unit in the hallway, which made it nearly impossible for him to move it safely, and he was injured trying to do so.

I have paid the full amount of $1,249.00 and expected a working appliance delivered in good condition. The inconvenience has been considerable: I have had to keep perishable food in a cooler, and I have missed two days of work waiting for a technician who never came.

I request a full refund or an immediate replacement delivered within five business days, along with reimbursement for the spoiled groceries, which totals $86.40. Please respond in writing to frank.delaney@mailbox-example.com or call me at 555-214-7782 by June 28.

Sincerely,

Frank Delaney

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to provide a reference for Yasmin Okafor, who worked under my supervision as a senior accounts officer at Harbourline Logistics in Newcastle from June 2019 until her departure in March 2024. I have managed finance teams for over fifteen years, and I can say without hesitation that Yasmin is among the most capable and conscientious people I have had the pleasure of leading.

Yasmin took full ownership of our month-end reconciliation process within her first year and, by 2022, had redesigned it so that our close dropped from nine working days to four. She has an unusual ability to explain complicated tax and payroll matters to people outside finance, and she regularly stepped in to train new starters without being asked. When our payroll system was migrated in late 2023, Yasmin led the testing and sign-off almost single-handedly, working late on several evenings when most of us had gone home.

Beyond her technical skills, Yasmin is calm under pressure, honest when things go wrong, and genuinely kind to colleagues. Her neighbours in Merewether Heights, where she lives with her brother Yusuf and their dog Biscuit, have spoken warmly of her to me through a mutual friend, which says a good deal about the person she is outside work. I would not hesitate to recommend her for any role in finance or operations, and I would be glad to speak further if needed. You may reach me on 0412 558 703 or at tom.bremner@harbourline.com.au.

Yours faithfully,

Tom Bremner
Finance Manager, Harbourline Logistics

input: I've been trying to name what's been sitting on my chest since the move. Everything here is technically fine: the work is steady, the new routines are coming together, and people have been kind. Still, I catch myself rehearsing conversations with people who aren't in the room, and I wake up tired in a way sleep doesn't fix. My counsellor suggested I stop asking whether I'm allowed to feel this way and start noticing when it's strongest. So far it peaks in the late afternoon, when I'm between tasks and nothing is asking me to be useful. I'm going to try writing down one small thing each evening that felt like mine, even if it was only a cup of tea that tasted right.

input:
We finally made it to Whitby last weekend, and I have to admit that Yasmin was right about the fish and chips. We parked the car (registration YN19 KLV) on the cliff road on Saturday morning, 11 January, and walked down to the harbour before the crowds arrived. The gulls were absolutely fearless. Our friend Harriet, who I've known since we both worked at the Brighton library, drove up from Leeds to join us, and she had already booked a table at Cliffside Cafe for lunch. Yasmin, who grew up in Scarborough and still calls it home, spent the whole walk pointing out the lanes she used to cycle as a teenager.

If you're planning a trip, drop an email to bookings@cliffsidecafe-whitby.co.uk, since they get busy in the mid-winter lull as well. Harriet also recommended the abbey ruins, and we climbed the 199 steps in what felt like a gale. Yasmin still has the photos on her phone, and she has promised to send me the best ones before Thursday, 16 January.

Honestly, I think we'll be back in spring. Yasmin says the coastal path is stunning once the gorse is out, and Harriet already has her camera ready. Next time I'll bring a proper map instead of relying on my phone, because the signal along the cliffs is patchy at best. Thanks for reading, and if you've been to Whitby, tell me your favourite spot in the comments.

input:
Hey Marcus, I still can't stop thinking about what happened with Sloane last weekend. You know how she's always been the calm one, the one who never panics? Well, she called me Saturday night from the hospital parking lot, sounding like someone I'd never heard before. Her car had been towed from outside the ER and she didn't even know where they'd taken it. I drove over with her spare key that I'd been keeping since college, and I kept telling myself it was going to be fine. I'm Jordan Ellis Carver, and I've never been so glad to be the one with the spare key.

Sloane was fine, mostly. Her mom had a fall on February 9th, and nobody in the family had been ready for how fast things would move after that. Sloane spent the next three days shuttling between Cedar Rapids and her mom's place in Dubuque, living on gas station coffee and half-finished sandwiches. Every time I asked how she was holding up she said "I'm okay, Jordie," which is what she's said since we were nine, and which means the exact opposite. So I cleared my schedule and started driving up on weekends.

What I keep coming back to is how quietly she carried all of it. She never asked me for help, and I had to offer it three times before she let me take anything off her plate. I think she's finally starting to breathe again, and I'm writing this to you because I need someone to tell me I did the right thing by showing up. Call me when you get a minute, okay? I owe you a long dinner.

input:
Ahmad Khoury was the kind of man who remembered your coffee order after one visit. For eleven years I sat across from him at the little café on Ibn Gabirol Street that he treated as his second living room, and I never once saw him rush. He was a civil engineer at the Technion, a patient teacher to two generations of students, and the person my colleague Dana Levi called first whenever a bridge calculation refused to behave. He died on 14 September at Rambam Hospital, surrounded by his daughters, after a short illness that none of us saw coming.

Ahmad leaves behind his wife Leila, their daughters Maya and Nour, and a grandson who believed, quite reasonably, that his grandfather could fix anything with a screwdriver. Those of us who worked with him will remember the sketches he drew on napkins, the way he hummed when he was thinking, and his insistence that every structure should be built to be looked at with affection. If you wish to share a memory, write to me at ahmad.khoury.memories@gmail.com or post on Instagram at @ahmad_builds_bridges, where his students have been gathering stories all week.

The funeral will take place on 17 September at the Jerusalem cemetery on Har HaMenuchot, and the family asks that donations be made in his name to the engineering scholarship fund at the Technion. Ahmad, we will keep walking the routes you taught us, and we will keep checking the numbers twice, the way you always did.

Written by Samir Haddad, car registration 23-456-78 parked outside the cafe every Thursday for those eleven years.

input:
October 3rd. Dr. Hale asked me to start writing these between sessions, so here goes. Today was rough, but I want to remember the part that went okay. My name is Victoria Lindqvist, though everyone at the clinic and most of my friends just call me Vicky. Dr. Hale says I should try to write down the thoughts as they come, without editing them first, so I'm trying that even though it feels strange.

The morning started with the usual pile of emails. One from my sister Maren, who wanted to know if I'd be home for the Thanksgiving planning call. I wrote back that I'd try, which is what I always write, and then felt guilty for the rest of the morning. Vicky is supposed to be the one who shows up. Maren doesn't say it, but I know that's how she sees me.

In session we talked about the guilt thing again. Dr. Hale pointed out that I used the word "should" eleven times in twenty minutes, and I laughed because I hadn't even noticed. She asked me to try replacing "I should" with "I'd like to" and see what changes. I tried it on the drive home, saying it out loud at red lights. "I'd like to call Maren back." It felt less like a sentence I'd failed before I started.

The homework is to send one honest message this week without rewriting it five times. So I did, actually, a short one to Maren at vicky.lindqvist@brightpathmail.com, since she still doesn't have my new work address. I told her I was tired but glad she'd reached out, and I didn't promise anything. I hit send before I could talk myself out of it.

I'm not sure what I expected to feel afterward. Mostly I feel a little lighter and a little exposed, which Dr. Hale says is about right. We'll see what Maren says. Next session is October 17th, and I'll bring this journal with me, or at least the parts I'm willing to read aloud.

input:
Last week I finally got around to writing about our trip north, the one Eitan kept putting off because he said the roads were 'too scary' for someone who doesn't drive. Honestly, the drive from Haifa was the easy part. We left from our flat on 14 Herzl Street in Haifa, Eitan behind the wheel of his silver Hyundai, plate 23-456-78, and by the time we hit the Galilee hills the sun was already sliding behind the olive groves. If you ever need a rental car in Israel, keep your passport handy, because the agency asked for it twice. Mine is number 4471 8829 and Eitan's is written on the back of his receipt, which he insists on keeping.

We stayed two nights in a guesthouse outside Safed, run by a retired teacher who made us the best shakshuka I have had anywhere. Eitan spent most of the first afternoon photographing the old stone alleys, and I posted the best shots on Instagram under @eitan.wanders, so if you want to see the blue doors and the candle shops, go take a look. He also tagged the guesthouse, which the owner found hilarious.

On the last morning we woke before dawn to catch the sunrise from the lookout above the valley. It was freezing, and I regretted every choice that got me out of bed, but the light turning gold over the hills made it worth it. Eitan, of course, said nothing and just held my hand. I'll write again once we're back in the city, when I can finally sort through the eleven hundred photos we took on February 9th.

input:
When I was nine, my grandmother taught me that a good question is worth more than a fast answer. We lived in a small apartment in Belo Horizonte, and every afternoon she would sit with me at the kitchen table while the rain tapped on the window. My name is Kaique Albuquerque Mendes, and I have spent most of my life asking why things work the way they do. Some of those questions led me to a broken radio, some to a neighbor's stalled car, and eventually to the physics textbooks my cousin left behind when he moved to Curitiba.

The question that truly shaped me arrived in my second year of secondary school, when our science teacher, Professora Lúcia, asked the class why the sky is blue. Most of my classmates gave the answer from the textbook. I went home and spent three weeks building a crude spectrometer out of a cardboard box, a CD fragment and a flashlight. It was not elegant, but when I held a prism-shaped sheet of glass to the light and saw the colors spread across the wall, I understood something that no diagram had ever made clear to me. I wrote up my results and sent them to Professora Lúcia, who replied with three pages of notes and a suggestion that I apply to the regional science fair.

That experience taught me that curiosity without patience is only a mood. Patience is what turned my cardboard box into a small but honest investigation. Since then I have volunteered at a community library in Contagem, where I help younger students with mathematics on Saturday mornings. I have learned that explaining an idea clearly is often harder than discovering it, and that the two skills feed each other.

My family has never had much money, and I know that a university education is a privilege my grandmother did not have. When I think about my future, I want to study engineering so that I can design tools that make everyday problems easier to solve for people like the ones I grew up with. My passport and national ID documents are ready for the exchange program I hope to join, and I have already written to the admissions office at kaique.mendes.2009@example-mail.com to ask about the interview schedule.

My dog, Pipoca, has taught me something as well. He waits patiently by the door every evening, certain that I will return, and he never asks for an explanation of why I was late. I hope to bring that same steady loyalty to my studies and to the people I serve. I am ready to keep asking questions, and I am ready to work hard to find the answers.

I'm writing this down so I don't forget what Dr Keane told me at my appointment on Tuesday 12 August at the Riverside Medical Centre in Limerick. My name is Darragh Brennan and I'd been having a dull ache in my lower back for about three weeks, mostly after long shifts at the warehouse. I had also been waking up with tingling in my right foot, which is what finally made me book the appointment instead of just taking ibuprofen and hoping for the best.

Dr Keane asked a lot of questions about when the pain started, whether anything made it worse, and whether I'd had any numbness in my groin or problems with the bathroom. I said no to all of that, which she seemed pleased about. She had me lie on the bed and lift each leg, then pressed along my spine and asked me to bend forward and sideways. The reflexes in my knees and ankle were normal, and she said the foot tingling was most likely a pinched nerve from how I've been sleeping on the sofa.

She was clear that this is a muscular and nerve issue and not anything serious, but she wants me to take it properly seriously. I've been given a referral letter for physiotherapy at the Shannon Physio Clinic, and the receptionist, Sinéad, said they could fit me in from the end of August if I ring on Monday. I need to ring them and ask about a weekend slot because of my shifts. My car is a 2015 Skoda with registration 151-L-4482, which I mention only because the physio clinic asked for it when I rang to confirm my details.

Dr Keane also wants me to do a short exercise routine every morning: a gentle knee-to-chest stretch, a cat-cow movement, and a walk for twenty minutes if I can manage it. She said no heavy lifting for a couple of weeks and to avoid sitting slumped on the sofa for long periods. I wrote the exercises on the back of the appointment card so I can check them each day.

If the tingling spreads, if my leg gets weaker, or if I lose any control of my bladder or bowel, I'm to go straight to the emergency department at University Hospital Limerick and not wait for the physio appointment. I've put that on my phone as a reminder. The next review with Dr Keane is booked for Tuesday 26 August, so I'll see how things are then. For now I'm just going to do the stretches, cut back on the long sitting, and try to remember to ring the clinic on Monday morning.

input:
Friends and family, thank you for being here today to honour Kiran Halloran. Many of you knew her as the woman who could fix anything with a roll of tape and a stubborn look, and some of you knew her as the one who always remembered your birthday. I am Maeve, her eldest, and I have been trying all week to find the right words for a person who never needed many of them.

Kiran was born in Leeds in the winter of 1952, the second of four children, and she never let anyone forget that she was the one who got things done. When she moved to Valencia in 1989, she did it with two suitcases, a secondhand Vespa, and a letter of introduction she had written herself. Within a year she knew every baker on Calle Ruzafa by name and had talked the whole street into planting geraniums along the balconies.

My father, Tomas, always said she was the only person he ever met who could argue with a bus driver and make him laugh at the same time. They were married for forty-one years. She kept a notebook of his bad jokes, which she read aloud at every anniversary, and he pretended to hate it every single time.

In her last years she lived at 14 Carrer de Ruzafa, Apartment 3B, Valencia, where the neighbours checked on her daily and she checked on them back. She sent out a monthly newsletter, handwritten, about the state of the building's roof and the state of the local politics. Several of you received them. Keep them. They are better than any biography.

Kiran, you taught us that kindness is a practical thing, that you show up with soup and a spare key and you do not make a fuss about it. We will miss your voice on the phone, your opinions on everything, and your terrible sense of direction on the Metro. Rest now. We have the roof under control.

I've been going to Kawiarnia Złoty Ul in Kraków's Kazimierz district for almost three years now, and last Thursday was the first time they got my order completely wrong. Grzegorz, the owner, has always been warm, and he remembered that my sister Agnieszka Nowak likes her oat latte with an extra shot. This time the barista served me a flat white and then shrugged when I pointed it out. I didn't make a scene, but I did leave without finishing it.

What keeps me coming back is the atmosphere. The back room has mismatched armchairs, the radiator never quite works, and the banana bread is still the best in the city. On November 12th the place was packed with students and a small book club, and somehow the staff still found time to chat with everyone. Gregor, who runs the morning shift, even brought a free slice of cake to our table when we were waiting for the bill.

If you want to book the larger table for a group, call them on +48 12 431 7790 or send an email to zlotyul.kawiarnia@gmail.com. I'd recommend going on a weekday afternoon if you want quiet. Four stars for the food and the people, minus one for the coffee mix-up. I'll be back, but I'll be checking my cup before I leave.

input:
Okay, so you won't believe what happened to me last Thursday. I was driving back from my shift at Riverside Memorial Hospital, and it was already past eleven. I'm thirty-four now and I still think I can handle anything on four hours of sleep, which, clearly, I can't. Anyway, I stopped at the Shell on Harmon Avenue to grab a coffee and some gum, and when I got back to my car the driver's side window was smashed and my bag was gone. Gone. My laptop, my charger, the textbook I borrowed from Ashworth College for my nursing exam in September, all of it.

I called the police from the parking lot and an officer named Officer Delgado came out in about twenty minutes. He was really kind about it. He asked me to spell my name, Amara Lockhart, and then he asked again, slower, because apparently I was mumbling. He said the store camera might have caught the guy, so I should check back with them in a few days. I told him I'd come in on Monday. I also had to call the bank and freeze my cards, which took forever because the automated system kept asking me to confirm my date of birth, and I kept getting it wrong because I was shaking.

The weirdest part? When I finally got home, my roommate Jules had left a note on the fridge that said, "Don't panic, but your mom called twice." So of course I spent the rest of the night thinking someone had died. Turns out she just wanted to remind me about my cousin's wedding. I cried for about ten minutes straight, mostly from relief. So yeah, that's my week. Call me tomorrow? I need to vent about it properly and I'd love a glass of wine that isn't from a gas station.

Kasia has been writing in this notebook for three weeks now, and tonight I want to be honest about what happened at the clinic on Ulica Mokotowska. Dr. Wojcik asked me again whether I was sleeping, and I lied and said yes, the way I always do. The truth is I wake up at four every morning and lie there replaying the phone call with my mother. She keeps asking why I moved to Krakow when everyone else in the family stayed in Lodz. I don't have a good answer, only that I needed a place where nobody knew my face.

My sister Ewa texted yesterday to say she's worried, and she wanted me to know she'd posted about my recovery on her account, @ewa.k.lodz, so I could check it if I wanted. I didn't check it. I also didn't tell her that I still haven't replaced my passport, the one ending in 8842, which I lost somewhere near the tram stop. The bureaucratic fuss over it has made me feel like an impostor in my own life.

The only steady thing right now is Pysia, my grey cat, who sits on my chest every evening as if she has been assigned to keep me grounded. Afterwards I walked to the Cafe Nowa Fala on Kazimierza and sat with a tea for an hour. Nobody asked me anything there. I think I will go back on Saturday, the 14th of February, and try to write a page about that instead of the four a.m. thoughts.

I want to thank you all for being here today. My name is Claire, and I was lucky enough to be Hélène's younger sister for forty-one years. Some of you knew her as the woman who ran the Tuesday book club out of the back room at Café Lumière on Rue des Tanneurs in Lyon. Others knew her from the early mornings at the bakery on Avenue Foch, or from the way she corrected your French with a smile. She never once let me forget that I still say "gâteau" like a tourist.

After she retired, Hélène threw herself into the community garden behind Rue des Tanneurs. She posted photos of her tomatoes and her grumbling about the slugs under @helene.jardine, and if you ever wondered whether she was happy, one look at those photos would tell you. You can still reach her old landline, 04 78 22 61 09, which she insisted on keeping long after everyone else gave theirs up. Her mail still goes to 14 Rue des Tanneurs, and the postman has asked us not to change it yet, because he likes delivering her letters.

Hélène died on the eleventh of February, a Tuesday, which feels exactly right, since that was always book club day. I will miss her every single week. If you would like to write something down, the family has set up a small notebook at Café Lumière. Please leave your memories there, and then come and have a coffee with us.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ryan Okafor-Blake, Dana's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words before we raise our glasses. Some of you have heard me tell the story of how Dana, at age six, decided she was going to be a veterinarian and then spent the next three years bringing home every injured sparrow on Maple Crescent. Tonight I want to talk about the Dana I've known since the day she was born in Kingston, Ontario, on a snowy morning in January, the kind where the hospital parking lot is a sheet of ice and our dad drove like he was in a rally.

Dana has always been the one who shows up. When I moved back to Ottawa after my divorce, she was the one who drove over with a box of takeout and a stack of old board games and didn't leave until we'd finished three rounds of Scrabble. She's the one who remembers the name of every server at the Bluebird Cafe on Princess Street, and who still, after eleven years, sends a birthday card to her first ever client at the Riverside Animal Clinic. If you've ever needed help, Dana is already on her way with a plan, a snack, and a spare set of car keys.

So, Jordan, I want you to know what you've got. You've got someone who listens to the quiet parts, who will argue with you about the best pizza in town and then secretly order the one you like. Dana, you chose well, and you've always been brave enough to choose what matters. Please join me in raising a glass to the bride and groom. To Dana and Jordan, may your life together be as warm and steady as that January morning our family still talks about.

input:
Dear Babcia,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold hasn't been too hard on your knees this season. I keep thinking about the evenings we spent together at your kitchen table, the radio murmuring in the background while you rolled out dough with that old wooden pin. I have never managed to make pierogi the way you did, though I have tried more than once. Mine always come out a little too thick and a little too lopsided, and I can hear you laughing gently at them from wherever you are in my memory.

Things here have been busy. The new job keeps me on my feet from morning until late afternoon, and I often come home tired enough to fall asleep on the sofa before I have even eaten. Still, there are good moments. A colleague who has been very kind to me invited me to a small gathering last week, and I found myself talking about the stories you used to tell me about the village and the people who lived there long ago. It surprised me how much of it I still remember, word for word, the way you told it.

I have been thinking a lot about the time you taught me to sit quietly and simply listen to the wind moving through the trees. You said that people rush through life because they forget to pay attention to small things. I try to remember that now, especially on the long walks I take after work when the leaves start turning. The colours are beautiful this time of year, and I wish you could see them with me.

I also wanted to tell you that I have been learning more about the traditions you carried with you. I bought a book of old recipes and folk songs, and I have started copying the handwritten notes you once left in the margins of your own cookbook. Reading your careful handwriting makes me feel close to you, even across all this distance. Some of the words are faded now, but I can still picture your hands moving as you wrote them.

Please take care of yourself through the coming months. Keep your scarf close and your tea warm, and do not hesitate to call me if you need anything at all. I will try to visit as soon as I can arrange some time off, and I promise to bring a bag of the good sweets you always liked, even if I have to hide them from you until after dinner.

With all my love and gratitude,

Your grandchild

I'm Jacqueline Thornton, and I have spent the last eleven years working as a data analyst for Harcourt Logistics in Brisbane, where I help freight teams turn messy shipping records into something they can actually act on. Before that I did a graduate certificate in statistics at the University of Queensland, which is where I first realised that numbers are only interesting when someone has a question worth asking of them.

Outside work I am a fairly predictable local. Most mornings you will find me at Bellbird Coffee on Logan Road, usually ordering a flat white and arguing with the barista about whether the new blend is an improvement. On weekends I train at Riverside Strength & Conditioning, and for the past two years I have also volunteered with a community clinic in Woolloongabba, helping coordinate appointment data for patients who struggle to get in.

At home I share a house with my partner and our dog, Biscuit, a three-year-old kelpie cross who has opinions about every squirrel in the suburb. I am proud of the work I do, but I am happiest when it connects to people, and I hope this conference gives me a chance to meet others who feel the same way. You can reach me at jacqueline.thornton@harcourtlogistics.com.au or on 0412 558 219.

Statement of Zachary Lindqvist, drafted for submission to the Halifax Regional Police, Non-Emergency Reporting Unit

I am writing this statement regarding an incident on the evening of April 14 at my residence on Dunmore Crescent, Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. My full name is Zachary James Lindqvist, though most people know me as Zak, and I have lived at the address for six years. I am reporting that a black Honda Civic, which I believe bears Nova Scotia plate KLM 4471, was parked across my driveway for approximately forty minutes before a male individual approached my front door and attempted to force the screen door open.

At approximately 9:15 p.m. I was in the kitchen when my dog, Biscuit, a three-year-old beagle mix, began barking loudly toward the front of the house. I went to the living room window and observed a man in a grey hooded jacket standing on my porch. He was holding what appeared to be a folded piece of paper and was looking through the glass panel of the door. When I turned on the porch light, he stepped back, looked directly at me, and walked quickly to the car. I did not get a clear look at his face, but I estimate he was between 25 and 35 years old, of medium build, and roughly six feet tall.

I called Zak's emergency contact line on my phone at 9:18 p.m. and then dialled the non-emergency number, which is how I was advised to report this. Biscuit remained agitated for some time afterward. I checked the doors and windows and found that the screen door latch had been bent, though the main door was still locked. My neighbour, Mrs. Eleanor Pratt, who lives at number 14, confirmed that she had seen the same vehicle parked on her street earlier that week, though she did not note the plate.

I am asking that officers review any available camera footage from the businesses along Cole Harbour Road between 8:45 p.m. and 9:45 p.m. on April 14. I can be reached at 902-555-0147 or at zak.lindqvist@examplemail.ca, and I am available to meet an officer at the residence at any time convenient to them. I would also like to request a file number for my records.

I declare that the information in this statement is true to the best of my knowledge.

Zachary J. Lindqvist
April 15

input:
I'm a speech and language therapist who has spent most of my career working with children and young adults who find it hard to get their words out, whether that is through stammering, selective mutism or a developmental language disorder. My work sits at the point where clinical practice meets everyday life: the classroom, the family kitchen, the playground. Over time I have come to believe that the most useful thing I can offer is not a list of exercises but a clearer picture of how communication breaks down and how it can be supported in ordinary settings.

Before moving into clinical work I trained in linguistics, and that background still shapes how I approach a case. I am interested in the patterns behind a child's difficulties, in what their speech reveals about their processing and their confidence, and in how those two things feed each other. Much of my recent effort has gone into building simple, shareable tools that teachers and parents can use without needing specialist training, because I have seen how much difference consistent, small adjustments can make over a school term.

I now split my time between direct practice, supervising newer clinicians, and contributing to research on early intervention. I am looking forward to this conference because it brings together people who approach these questions from very different corners, and I hope to leave with a sharper sense of where the field is heading and with a few new collaborations that will help the young people I work with.

I've been going to Shalom Hummus Bar on Ben Yehuda Street for about three years now, and I finally sat down to write something after last Thursday. My name is FadiAlon Ketter, though everyone at Hadassah Ein Kerem, where I work as a respiratory therapist, just calls me Fadi. I came in straight after a double shift, exhausted, and the staff didn't rush me at all. The owner, Miriam, remembered my usual order, a plate of masabacha with extra pine nuts, and brought over a fresh pot of mint tea without me asking.

The food is consistently good. The falafel is crisp outside and green inside, the pita comes out warm, and the portions are generous enough that I usually take half home for lunch the next day. On Thursday the place was packed with a student group from the Hebrew University, so the service was slower than usual, but Yossi, the young guy working the counter, kept everyone updated and apologised twice without being asked. That kind of attention is rare in this neighbourhood.

If you're in the area, go. The prices are fair for Jerusalem, and the kitchen runs until eleven on weekends. Bookings for groups can be made at shalomhummusbar@gmail.com, and Miriam answers quickly. I'll be back on the 14th of June for my sister's birthday, and I already know what I'm ordering.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to provide a reference for Nomvula Dlamini, who worked under my supervision as a senior bookkeeper at Kestrel Freight Solutions from March 2019 until her resignation on 14 December 2023. I have managed our finance department for eleven years, and in that time I have seldom worked with someone as dependable or as thorough as Nomvula.

Nomvula was responsible for accounts payable, monthly reconciliations and the preparation of management accounts for four regional branches. She reduced our average invoice processing time from twelve days to just under four, and she introduced a checklist for month-end close that our auditors have since adopted as a model for other clients. Her figures were always accurate, and when she found an error, she raised it immediately and explained exactly how it had happened and how to prevent it.

Beyond her technical skill, Nomvula has a rare ability to explain complicated financial matters to people who do not work with numbers every day. Our operations managers regularly sought her out for guidance on budgets and cost controls, and she never made anyone feel foolish for asking. She trained two junior clerks during her time with us, and both have since been promoted.

I should also mention that Nomvula was a steady presence during a difficult period for the company, when we were restructuring our Durban depot. She worked long hours without complaint and kept her team calm and focused. Her colleagues trusted her, and I trusted her completely.

Nomvula left us to relocate closer to her family in Pretoria, and we were sorry to see her go. I have no hesitation in recommending her for any role in finance or accounting that values integrity, precision and a genuine commitment to the work. Please feel free to contact me on 011 555 0148 or at jacques.vanderMerwe@kestrelfreight.co.za should you require any further information.

Yours faithfully,

Jacques van der Merwe

input:
I went to see Dr Harrowell at the surgery last week because the pain in my lower back had not eased after a month of rest and stretching. I explained that it was worse in the mornings and that bending to pick things up from the floor had become difficult. She asked me several questions about my work, which involves a lot of lifting and standing, and about whether I had noticed any numbness or tingling in my legs. I said I had not, which she seemed pleased to hear. She examined me on the couch, checking my reflexes and how far I could bend forward, and then explained that the most likely cause was a strained muscle that had been aggravated by poor posture at my desk.

She recommended a short course of anti-inflammatory tablets, to be taken with food, and gave me a leaflet with exercises that focus on core strength and gentle flexibility. She was clear that I should return if the pain spread down either leg, if I developed any loss of bladder control, or if it had not improved within a few weeks. I asked whether I should stop running for a while and she said a gradual return was fine once the pain had settled, but that I should avoid heavy lifting in the meantime.

I left feeling reassured but also a little embarrassed that I had put off booking the appointment for so long. My plan is to do the exercises every morning, set up a proper chair and monitor at home, and take a short walk at lunchtime. I will keep a note of how the pain changes so that I can give a clear account if I need to go back.

I landed in Tel Aviv on a rainy Tuesday in February, jet-lagged and carrying way too much luggage. My name is Zvi Ashkenazi, I'm thirty-four, and I work as a logistics analyst for Meridian Freight Solutions, so this trip was supposed to be a short break before the spring quarter started. Zvi's rule for any new city is simple: find the best coffee in walking distance on day one. Within an hour of checking into my guesthouse in Neve Tzedek, I had found Kafe Ruach on Rothschild Street, a tiny place with mismatched chairs and a barista named Noam who remembered my order by the second visit.

The next few days blurred together in the best way. I walked the Carmel Market in the mornings, bargained for a ceramic bowl I didn't need, and spent one afternoon at a physiotherapy clinic in Florentin after a stupid knee injury from a hostel bunk bed. The clinic staff were patient and surprisingly funny, and they fixed me up in three sessions. If you're traveling and need someone reliable, ask for the clinic on Hashmonaim Street; the front desk can be reached at ortho.florentin@shlomoclinic.co.il.

If you want to reach me about recommendations or just to swap train stories, write to zvi.ashkenazi@meridianfreight.com. Most of my messages get answered within a day, usually from a café table with a flat white and a view of the sea.

My name is Fadi Haddad and I am writing to report a water damage claim for my apartment at 14 Herzl Street, Apartment 6, in Haifa. On the evening of December 9, I came home from work to find water pouring from the ceiling of the bathroom and across the living room floor. My neighbour Yossi Levi, who lives on the floor below, had already called the building manager, and together we shut off the main valve in the stairwell. The water came from a cracked supply line behind the bathroom wall, which had been leaking for an unknown period of time.

I was born in Nazareth and moved to Haifa eleven years ago for my job as a civil engineer. The apartment is my primary residence and I have lived in it since 2016. Fadi, as my colleagues call me, has been working on the rebuild of the Carmel district school, so I was away on site for most of that week, which is why the leak went unnoticed. My friend and colleague Tamar Ronen helped me move my laptop and important documents to her flat on December 10, and she has photos of the condition of the apartment that evening.

The plumber, Eli Avraham, inspected the damage on December 11 and estimated repairs at roughly 14,500 shekels. The bathroom tiles, the subfloor, the living room parquet and a sofa will need to be replaced. I have attached the plumber's report, photographs, and receipts for the emergency drying service. Please contact me at fadi.haddad@netvision.example or on 050-7316482 if you need further information or access to the property for an assessor.

input:
When my family left Lagos for Manchester in the summer of my eleventh year, I assumed the hardest part would be the language. It was not. The hardest part was learning that nobody knew where I came from unless I told them, and that telling them meant performing a version of myself that fit into a single sentence. For a long time I did not know how to do that. I still remember the first week at 14 Hawthorn Lane, our rented flat above a laundrette, where my mother kept a paper list of every bus route she had memorised. Wunmi, my older sister, stopped speaking to us for almost a month. My father, who had been a civil engineer back home, took a warehouse job on the night shift and came home smelling of cardboard and cold air.

The person who changed things was Wale Adeyemi, a colleague of my father's who ran a small kitchen at the back of Sunrise Cafe on Oxford Road. He had come to the city a decade earlier and understood the particular loneliness of being the only one at the table who remembered the old names for things. Every Saturday I washed dishes there for pocket money. Wale taught me to cook egusi properly and to speak about my grandmother's cooking without apology. He also asked questions no teacher had asked: what did I miss, what did I refuse to forget, what did I want to build. I started keeping a notebook of answers. Its first entry, written in careful capitals, was simply: WALE SAYS THE STORY IS MINE TO TELL.

That notebook became the foundation of my application to study social policy, and it is why I want to spend my university years studying how migrant families are counted, housed and heard. I have since learned that my family's registration on our old Nigerian car, a dusty blue Peugeot marked T 4471 KJ in my father's records, was only the first of many small bureaucratic traces that shape a life. I want to learn to read those traces well, and to write policy that starts from the kitchen table rather than the form.
