input:
Dear Nan,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden is behaving itself now that the autumn rains have properly arrived. I've been meaning to write since the Sunday dinner in October, when you told me the story about the Ballyfermot dance hall again, and I realised I'd never once written any of it down. So consider this my attempt to keep it safe.

Mum says you're still driving to the shops on Tuesdays, which I will be bringing up with you in person the next time I'm home, so don't think you're getting away with it. The car is a 2009 silver Corolla, registration 09-D-4471, and I know exactly how much you love that thing. Please just be careful on the hill past Clontarf.

I've been settling into the flat on Cabra Road with Aoife and the two lads from the second floor. The radiator in the front room makes a noise like a ship's horn every morning at six, but the view over the rooftops is lovely when the light comes in low. I've also finally got a proper account set up for the bank, number 4812 9930 17, so Mum can stop asking me whether I've eaten. Tell her yes, I have, and that I'm still living on toast.

You'll laugh, but I've started posting photos of my bike rides and the sea walls on Instagram under @cathalwanders, which Aoife made me do. Nobody has followed me yet except you and my cousin Shane, so the pressure is off. If you want to see the pictures, just ask Mum to show you on her phone.

I keep thinking about how you and Grandad grew up in Drogheda, walking the riverbank with nothing but a tin of biscuits and a football. That's where I was born too, in the old maternity wing on the 14th of October twenty-six years ago, and you swear you cried harder than I did. I'd love to hear more of those stories when I visit at the end of the month.

Until then, give my love to Granny's roses and to the neighbours who still ask after you. Ring me on Sunday if you get a minute.

All my love,

Cian

input:
Tuesday 14 September

I still can't quite believe I'm writing this from a flat in Leeds, not from my old room above the bakery in Porto. Olivia Ferreira Santos, that's me, twenty-nine years old as of this morning, and the first birthday I've ever spent in England. Mum rang at seven, which was already lunchtime for her, and she cried a little before she even said happy birthday. I told her I'd be fine. I'm not sure I believed it.

The move has been harder than the paperwork suggested. The estate agent kept calling the place "cosy" and it is, in the way a shoebox is cosy. Yesterday I finally got my bank sorted out. The account number is 20847361, which I now have to recite to everyone, and the clerk spent ten minutes apologising for a system I'd never heard of called Faster Payments. Afterwards I walked along the canal for an hour, mostly to avoid going home.

The car is another story. I kept the little silver Fiesta, registration KL19 VRX, because selling it in Porto would have cost more than it was worth, so I drove it over on the ferry with half my books in the boot. Every roundabout still makes me nervous, and I keep catching myself on the wrong side of the road. Ollie from work says I'll stop doing it by Christmas. He is an optimist, and also my cousin's husband, which is a complicated arrangement I'm not going to get into here.

My colleague Hannah took me for a drink after my shift at the ward and asked, very gently, whether I wanted to talk about home. I said no, then talked for two hours. She listened without fixing anything, which is rarer than people think. I've decided that counts as a good sign.

Tomorrow I have my appointment at the GP surgery on Chapel Street, 9:40 a.m., to register properly so I can get my prescriptions. I've written it on the fridge in three colours so I can't miss it. Then the rest of the week is mostly boxes.

I'm going to make myself a proper birthday dinner tonight, bacalhau if I can find the right fish, and open the bottle of vinho verde Mum packed in my suitcase. Happy birthday, Olivia. You're a long way from the bakery, but you're doing alright.

input:
Hi all, long-time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone here has dealt with something similar. My rescue greyhound Juniper (everyone at the clinic calls her Junie, which she tolerates) has started refusing to go past our front door on Alder Crescent in Halifax, and it's been about three weeks now. She used to walk happily around the block, but now she plants herself and shakes. I've been taking her to Harbourview Animal Clinic on June 9 and again on June 16, and Dr. Patel thinks it could be a noise thing, maybe a new construction crew two houses down, but the crew finished last week and nothing changed.

What's odd is that she's fine in the car and fine at the dog park on Quinpool. It's only the stretch right outside our house. My friend Tomas, who fosters for the same rescue, suggested it might be a bad association from something that happened on the sidewalk, but I can't think of anything. He also said I should try a short leash and treats, which I've been doing, though honestly it's mostly gotten me stares from the neighbours.

So my question: has anyone had a dog suddenly develop a fear of one specific spot? How long did it take to ease up, and did a behaviourist help more than a vet? I'd rather not force her past it, but I also don't want this to become a permanent thing. Thanks in advance, and any tips for sweet-talking a stubborn greyhound would be welcome too.

input:
We rolled into Whitby on a grey Tuesday morning in August, the kind of coastal light that makes every harbour wall look painted. Charlotte Ashworth, who everyone at Fenwick Grammar still calls Charlie, had been talking about this trip since the spring, mostly because she wanted to walk the 199 steps up to the abbey with a proper sea breeze in her face. She took them two at a time and didn't even pause at the top, which I found slightly unfair given I'd promised my knees a rest at the bench.

The town itself is all crooked lanes, fish and chip queues and gift shops selling jet jewellery. We ate on the quay, watched the gulls circle a dropped chip with the seriousness of stock traders, and then wandered out to the pier. Charlie insisted on buying a postcard for her mum, who works nights at the Royal Infirmary in Leeds and has never once been to the coast in summer. I'm told she'll frame it, which seems like the best outcome a postcard could hope for.

If you go, book a room above the harbour if you can, and go on a weekday. We stayed at a small guesthouse run by a retired lifeboat coxswain who gave us the best tip of the trip: come back down to the beach after dark, when the lights of the fishing boats come on one by one. Charlie said it was the nicest thing she'd seen all year, and she's rarely impressed by anything that doesn't come with a view of a car park.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm the older brother of the groom, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight. My brother and I fought over the back seat of our parents' car for about fifteen years, so standing up here and saying something kind about him feels a little strange. But I'll do my best.

When we were kids, I used to think my brother was the lucky one. Everything came easily to him. Then, a few years ago, I watched him do something I never expected: he slowed down. He started showing up. He learned to listen before he spoke, and he began to build a life around the people he cared about. That's the version of him I got to watch grow up, and it's the one who found his partner. I've never seen him as happy as he is when she walks into a room.

So please raise your glasses. To the couple, to the long road ahead, to the mornings and the arguments and the quiet evenings in between. May you always find your way back to each other. L'chaim, and congratulations to you both.

input:
My name is Dominik Wójcik, and I have spent the last twelve years working as a structural engineer for Kowalczyk Budowa Sp. z o.o. in Kraków, where I lead a small team focused on retrofitting older apartment blocks. I grew up in Tarnów, the son of a railway mechanic and a primary school teacher, and I still think of Tarnów as home even though I have lived in Kraków since 2011. My wife Agnieszka and our two children keep me grounded, and my mother, Halina Wójcik, still insists on calling every Sunday to ask whether I have eaten anything other than cold pizza.

My professional interests have gradually moved from new construction toward heritage work. Last spring I was asked to assess a 1930s tenement near the Planty, and the project taught me more about patience than any textbook could. Dominik is the name my colleagues use, though most of my clients call me Mr. Wójcik. I keep a company vehicle registered as KR 48215 for site visits across Małopolska, and I am still learning to keep my expense reports as tidy as my drawings.

I will be presenting at the conference on the morning of 14 October, where I will talk about moisture control in masonry walls built before the Second World War. I was originally scheduled for 7 October, but the organisers moved the session after I confirmed my attendance. I am grateful for the opportunity, and I look forward to meeting colleagues who share my interest in preserving the buildings that give our cities their character.

input:
I need some help thinking through a situation at home and I'm not sure where to start. My younger brother has been staying with us for about three months now, after he lost his job in Nairobi and couldn't keep up with rent. At first it felt right to help, and I still want to, but the arrangement has slowly turned into something neither of us talks about. The chores aren't shared, money for food keeps coming up in tense ways, and I've started dreading coming home in the evenings. My partner has been patient but has also said, gently, that our small house feels crowded and that we need some space back.

What makes it harder is that my family expects me to keep him here, and bringing up a limit feels like I'd be turning my back on him. He's not a bad person. He's just stuck, applying for work every day without much luck, and I can see how discouraging that is. I don't want him to feel like a burden, but I also don't want to quietly resent him for the next year.

Could you help me figure out how to raise this with him without it turning into a fight? I'd like some practical ways to set expectations, maybe a timeline for him to move out, and a way to talk about it with my family too so they understand why I'm asking. I'm willing to put in the effort, I just need a clearer way forward.

I am making this statement in relation to an incident that occurred on the evening of Thursday 14 May, at approximately 7.40 pm, on Dorset Row in the Smithfield area of Dublin 7. My name is Eimear Brennan and I live at the above address. I am 34 years of age and work as a physiotherapist.

On the afternoon of the incident I had been at Bloomfield Physio and Wellness, the clinic on the corner of Kinsale Street where I have been a member for about two years. I finished my last appointment at around 6.30 pm and walked home the usual way, cutting through the lane behind the Glasshouse Cafe. My dog, Biscuit, a brown and white terrier cross, was with me as he always is in the evenings. Biscuit was on his lead the entire time.

As I came out onto Dorset Row I noticed a silver Skoda Octavia parked half on the footpath outside number 22, with its engine running and the driver's door open. A man in a dark navy hoodie was standing beside it, and when he saw me he said, 'Ellie, you're not going to believe this.' I did not recognise him at first. It was only when he turned under the streetlight that I realised it was Cathal Doherty, whom I had known from the gym years ago and who is known to most people as Cat. He had a cut above his left eyebrow and he was holding his phone in a way that made me uneasy.

I told him I was not interested in talking and carried on walking towards my building. He followed me to the gate and continued to ask me to 'just listen for two minutes'. When I tried to open the gate he put his hand on the top bar. Biscuit began barking and pulling at the lead, and I stepped back onto the path with my keys in my hand. Cat then stepped back himself and got into the car, which drove off towards Stoneybatter.

I am making this statement because this is the second time in three weeks that Cathal has approached me without invitation, and I am concerned about his behaviour. I can be contacted at eimear.brennan@mailbox.ie or on 087 553 2190 to arrange any further information you require. I would also be grateful if the registration of the vehicle could be checked against the camera at the corner of Dorset Row and Kinsale Street.

I have read this statement and I confirm that it is true to the best of my knowledge and belief.

input:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to recommend Victoria Ashworth, who worked under my supervision as Operations Lead at Pennine Freight Solutions Ltd in Leeds from March 2019 until her departure on 14 November 2024. I have managed teams across logistics and supply chain for over fifteen years, and I can say without hesitation that Victoria is among the most capable and dependable people I have had the pleasure to work with.

Victoria joined us at a time when our depot scheduling was causing repeated delays. Within six months she had redesigned the dispatch rota, introduced a daily exceptions review, and cut late deliveries by roughly a third. She has a rare ability to hold a detailed operational picture in her head while still keeping the wider business goals in view. Colleagues in finance and customer service regularly sought her out for advice, and she never once made anyone feel they were asking too much.

What stood out most was her handling of pressure. In late November 2023, during the peak trading period, a major warehouse system failed on the Friday before a bank holiday weekend. Victoria coordinated the response from the start, kept our clients informed, and worked alongside our IT contractor until the system was restored on the Sunday morning. Her calm, methodical approach set the tone for the whole team. I later heard from our client Hartley Retail's operations director, who said he had rarely seen such clear communication during an incident.

Victoria also invested heavily in the people around her. She developed two of our shift supervisors into confident team leaders, and she ran a monthly training session that many staff still speak of fondly. Her work with Priya Desai on the new returns process was a good example of this, as Priya herself has since told me how much Victoria's patience and clarity helped her grow in the role.

If you would like to discuss Victoria's application further, you are welcome to contact me directly at j.ashworth.ops@pennine-freight.co.uk or on the main office line. I would be glad to speak with you and to give Victoria my full support in whatever she chooses to pursue next.

Yours faithfully,

Jonathan Ashworth
Operations Director
Pennine Freight Solutions Ltd

input:
When I first walked into the robotics lab at my secondary school in Lublin, I had no idea what a servo motor was. My name is Bartosz, and for most of my life I believed that engineering was something other people did. That changed in October of my final year, when our team was asked to build a small line-following robot for the regional competition. I volunteered to handle the wiring, mostly because nobody else wanted to crawl under the bench with a soldering iron.

The first version failed spectacularly. The robot veered left every time it crossed a shadow, and I spent three evenings rereading datasheets before I understood that the sensor thresholds were calibrated for the wrong light level. Bartosz, our teacher told me, you are debugging the room, not the robot. That sentence stayed with me. I started logging every test run in a spreadsheet, and by the end of the month our error rate had dropped from nearly half of all runs to under ten percent.

What I value most from that experience is not the trophy we eventually brought home but the habit of patient, evidence-based problem solving it taught me. I want to study mechanical engineering because I want to keep building things that work in the messy conditions of the real world. If you would like to hear more about the project or see my test logs, I can be reached at bartosz.nowak23@mailpl.com.

Dear Parents and Families,

We are delighted to share a few highlights from the autumn term at Kfar Shmaryahu Elementary School. Our Grade 5 classes have been busy with their science fair projects, and this year's standout was a solar oven built by Hadar Levi and her lab partner, Noa Brenner. Their model, which cooked a small tray of shakshuka on a sunny afternoon, drew a crowd of parents and younger students in the courtyard.

Hadar has been one of our most curious students this year. Her teacher, Ms. Tamar Ben-David, says Hadar asks the kind of questions that keep the whole class thinking. Hadar herself would rather talk about the ovens than about the awards, though she did accept a certificate with a big grin.

Please mark your calendars for our winter concert on Thursday, December 14th. Doors open at 17:30 in the main hall, and all Grade 4 and 5 students will perform. Hadar will be playing the recorder in the opening number, so expect a few squeaks and a lot of pride. Tickets are not required, but families are asked to arrive early to find seats.

Hadar's family asked us to share a reminder that her birthday is on December 3rd, and she would love a quiet celebration with close friends after school. Her older brother Yoav, who attends Herzliya Hebrew Gymnasium, has promised to bring his famous homemade lemon cake to the class party on Friday.

Finally, a reminder that the school nurse will be available for flu vaccination appointments on December 9th. Please call the front office at 09-555-0148 or write to office@kfarshmaryahu-school.example to reserve a slot. Thank you for your continued support, and we wish everyone a restful end to the term.

Warm regards,
The Parent Communications Team

input:
Friends, family, thank you all for being here today. My name is Hannah, and I was lucky enough to be Greg's daughter. Dad spent thirty-one years as a senior site engineer at Ironbark Civil Pty Ltd, and if you ever drove across the Gorge Road bridge in Toowoomba, you drove over something he helped build. He would never say that himself. He'd tell you it was the crew who did the hard work, and then he'd make you a cup of tea strong enough to stand a spoon in.

Dad was not a man of many words, but the ones he chose mattered. When I was seven and cried because my bike chain came off on the first day of school holidays, he didn't lecture me. He sat on the kerb with me, greased his fingers, and fixed it while we talked about cricket. Greg Mackenzie believed most problems could be solved if you were patient enough to look at them properly. I think that's the most useful thing anyone has ever taught me.

He loved the Brisbane Lions with a loyalty that frankly didn't always make sense, and he would argue about the umpiring with anyone who sat still long enough. Every Sunday morning, rain or shine, he and Rusty, our old kelpie, walked the creek track behind the house. Rusty was his shadow for fourteen years. Since Dad went into hospital in early March, Rusty has been sleeping by the back door, waiting. We're going to look after him together, Dad, I promise.

In his last few weeks, Dad asked me to read him the letters he'd kept from Mum, and then he asked me to tell him about the grandkids, and then he simply asked for the windows open so he could hear the magpies. He was at peace, and he was surrounded by the people he loved most. That's a good death, as these things go. It's still not enough time.

So today I'm asking you to do what Dad always did for us: show up. Call the friend you haven't spoken to in a while. Fix the thing that's been broken for ages. And if you see a magpie singing on a fence post early in the morning, stop for a moment and think of Greg. He'd like that. Thank you, Dad. We'll miss you every single day.

input: Since moving from Canada to Portugal last year, I have slowly learned that daily life here runs on its own rhythm. Mornings begin early at the padaria, where the bread is still warm and the coffee is strong enough to wake even the sleepiest commuter. Afternoons stretch out lazily, and shops close for a long break that took me a while to get used to. I still fumble my verb conjugations when chatting with neighbours, but they always smile and correct me gently. Little by little, this unfamiliar place has started to feel like home.

input:
Good evening everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Kieran, and I've been Hannah's brother for twenty-nine years, which means I've had a front-row seat to every one of her bad haircuts and questionable life choices. Tonight I get to tell you what I think of the person she's chosen, and I promise to keep the worst of the stories for the after-party.

Hannah and I grew up at 14 Larkfield Crescent in Leeds, a house where the heating was always either on full or broken. She was the one who dragged me to the local bakery on Saturday mornings, and it was at the Crumb & Co counter, of all places, that she first decided she was going to marry someone. She still says it was a coincidence that she went back there every week for a month. I say she's terrible at pretending.

When Hannah moved to Bristol for work, she had two priorities: a flat with decent light, and a dog called Biscuit who would never be allowed on the sofa. She lost the second argument within a week. What she didn't mention was that the dog came with a human who was patient, kind, and surprisingly good at fixing the boiler. I'd like to think that's the moment I started to trust him, though I think it was the day he drove four hours through the rain to bring her a replacement phone charger.

And this is where I have to admit something. Hannah rang me on the 14th of October, a Tuesday, from the car park outside Dr Patel's clinic on Redcliffe Way, crying and laughing at the same time. She'd been given the all-clear and, in the same breath, she told me she was planning the proposal. I was the first person she called, and I'm honoured that she trusted me with the secret for the three weeks it took to organise.

So, to the two of you: may your days be as gentle as the afternoons you spend on the sofa Biscuit was never meant to share with you. May you always find the good bakery, the reliable mechanic, and the friend who will drive through the rain. And may every October remind you of the phone call that started it all.

Please raise your glasses to Hannah and to Sam. Cheers.
output:

input:
Isaiah Whitmore has spent the better part of fifteen years building tools that help small clinics manage their paperwork without losing a single afternoon to it. Trained as a systems engineer at Ohio State, he began his career at a mid-sized logistics firm in Columbus before deciding that the most interesting problems were the ones nobody wanted to solve. In 2014 he moved to Raleigh, where he joined a three-person startup focused on scheduling software for family practices, and he has been working on that same problem, in one form or another, ever since.

The work has taken him further than he expected. Over the past decade he has led deployments across eleven states, sat on a state advisory panel on health data privacy, and spent a memorable winter in Duluth helping a rural clinic recover after a failed server migration. Colleagues describe him as the person who will stay on a call until the last printer is working, and clinic managers tend to remember him for patience more than for technical brilliance.

Isaiah is also an unusually generous mentor. He runs a monthly open session for junior developers who want to move into health technology, and he has helped more than forty people land their first roles in the field. He is quick to point out that most of what he knows came from people who answered his questions when he was too embarrassed to ask them.

Outside work he is a dedicated amateur cartographer and a reliable organiser of local trail clean-ups. Those who follow his online presence know him as @isaiah_maps_nc, where he posts hand-drawn route sketches and occasional, carefully argued opinions about open data standards.

His current project is an effort to make appointment reminders work for patients with limited broadband access, a problem that sounds small until you watch a clinic lose a dozen visits in a single week. He hopes the prototype will be ready for pilot testing by the spring, and he has already reserved a conference room in Raleigh for the first round of feedback sessions.

For his talk at this conference, Isaiah plans to walk through what went wrong in those early deployments and what he would do differently now. He has promised to bring the spreadsheet of failures, which he describes as the most useful thing he has ever built.

Hello Maple Ridge families! My name is Kalvin Brandt and I have been the Grade 7 science teacher here at Maple Ridge Public School for three years now, so I thought it was about time I introduced myself properly in the newsletter. Many of you have met me at pickup or during the fall open house, but for those who haven't, I grew up in Saskatoon, studied biology at the University of Saskatchewan, and still get excited about a good pond dip more than most adults should.

This autumn our class is starting a long-term project on local watersheds. Each student will adopt a small stretch of the creek behind the baseball diamonds and track water temperature, clarity and the insects living there every two weeks. We will be starting our first data collection on September 14, and I'm asking for two parent volunteers to join us on the walk. If you can help, please reply to me at kalvin.brandt@mapleridgeps.ca or call the school office at 306-555-0148 and leave your name with the secretary.

A quick administrative note: for the field trip permission forms that go home next week, I will need a copy of a government-issued ID for any adult accompanying the class, which can be a driver's licence or a passport. Please do not send the number itself by email. Bring the document to the office on September 18 or 19, where the secretary will record the details securely and return the original to you the same day. Kalvin Brandt will be on site for both mornings if you have questions about the paperwork.

We also want to thank the parents who came out to help with the bake sale on September 5. The event raised enough money to replace the classroom microscopes that were damaged last spring, and the new set arrives the week of September 25. Students are already excited to see the magnification on the high-powered lenses, and I suspect the first few weeks will be spent with a lot of onion skin and pond water.

Finally, a reminder that the Friday science club continues this month in Room 12, from 3:15 to 4:15. There are still a few spots open for Grade 6 and 7 students, so if your child has been asking about it, sign-up sheets are at the front office. Thank you for your continued support, and I look forward to seeing many of you along the creek this fall.

I basically wanted to remember what I have to do this week because I keep forgetting things. There's a lot going on with the flat, the landlord said he'd come look at the boiler but he never confirms anything, you know how it is. I keep meaning to ring the bank too because something on the statement looked off, probably nothing, but I'd rather check than just let it sit there.

And the thing with my sister, we had this long argument on the phone last week about who should be doing what for their mum, and honestly I think we were both a bit tired and said things we didn't mean. I want to message her properly, not just a quick text, but I keep putting it off because I don't know how to start. Maybe I'll just say I miss her and go from there. That feels easier than trying to be clever about it.

Work is the usual chaos. There's a deadline coming up that I'm not sure I can hit if I'm honest, and my manager keeps sending these little check-in messages that make my stomach drop a bit. I've started making a list of everything still open so I can see it all in one place, which helps a bit, though the list itself is getting kind of long. input:
Good evening, everyone. For those of you who don't know me, I'm the best man, and I've been given the honour, and the nerves, of saying a few words about my oldest friend. I've known the groom since we were both far too young to be trusted with a shared garden hose, and in all the years since, I have never once seen him back away from a challenge, a bad joke, or a round of drinks he couldn't afford.

What I've come to admire most is how he loves. He isn't loud about it. He shows up. When my car died on the motorway one winter and I rang him at midnight, he was there within the hour with a flask of tea and no complaints, just the quiet patience he brings to everything. That same steadiness is exactly what he has given to the bride, and it's clear to all of us in this room that she feels it every single day.

I want to say something to her now. You have taken a man who once tried to cook a roast by reading the instructions backwards, and you have turned him into someone who plans ahead, remembers anniversaries, and actually answers his phone. Thank you for that. I suspect the rest of us owe you a small debt of gratitude for seeing the good in him long before he managed to see it in himself.

There's a saying that a marriage is two people choosing each other over and over again. I think the pair of you already understand that better than most couples twice your age. You laugh at the same stupid things, you forgive each other quickly, and you still hold hands in the queue for the tea shop, which, for the record, is the single most embarrassing thing about you and I wouldn't change it for the world.

So please, raise your glasses. To the couple, to the years ahead, and to the many evenings still to come when we all get to tease them about how they met. Cheers.

I landed at Ben Gurion on a rainy Tuesday in March, still half-asleep, and the customs officer asked me to confirm my passport number, 512748396, before waving me through. My name is Adrian Whitlock, though everyone in Tel Aviv seems to call me Adi within the first five minutes. My cousin Miriam picked me up in her battered Suzuki and insisted we go straight to Jaffa for falafel before I even dropped my bags at her flat on Rothschild Boulevard.

Over the next week I wandered from the Old City of Jerusalem to the stone terraces of Safed, and I learned that Adrian Whitlock was a name that made shopkeepers in the Machane Yehuda market grin. Miriam kept teasing me that Adi was a better fit for a country where people talk with their hands. She was right. By the third day I was haggling for pomegranates in Hebrew I barely knew, and nobody seemed to mind.

If you go in March, pack a light raincoat and comfortable shoes. The almond trees blossom early, the hills turn green for a few short weeks, and the evenings stay cool enough for a long walk along the Mediterranean. Email me at adrian.whitlock@example.com if you want the full list of cafés I loved, and bring an appetite.

input:
I went to see Dr. Lindqvist again this week, though I am not sure she is a doctor in the way I imagine one. We talked for most of the session about the way I shut down when something feels too big. I told her about the meeting at work where I froze, how my mind went white and I just nodded along to decisions I didn't agree with. She didn't tell me what to do. She asked what I was afraid would happen if I had spoken up, and I realised the answer was mostly that people would think less of me, which is a story I have been telling myself for a long time.

Since then I have been trying small experiments. On Tuesday I asked a question in a meeting, a plain one about timelines, and nothing terrible happened. My hands shook a little under the table, but the room kept going. It is strange how much relief a boring question can bring. I wrote it down afterwards so I would not explain it away later.

The weather has been odd, long grey stretches followed by one bright afternoon that makes everyone rush outside as if they've been told the sun is leaving forever. I walked along the water for an hour on one of those afternoons and let my thoughts run without trying to sort them. Some of them were sad, some were just noise, and a few were hopeful, which surprised me.

I went to see Dr. Lindqvist again this week, though I am not sure she is a doctor in the way I imagine one. We talked for most of the session about the way I shut down when something feels too big. She asked what I was afraid would happen if I had spoken up, and I realised the answer was mostly that people would think less of me, which is a story I have been telling myself for a long time.

Since then I have been trying small experiments. On Tuesday I asked a question in a meeting, a plain one about timelines, and nothing terrible happened. My hands shook a little under the table, but the room kept going. It is strange how much relief a boring question can bring. I wrote it down afterwards so I would not explain it away later.

I'm thirty-four and work as a physiotherapist at a clinic in Ramat Gan. February 9th. Zohar came in today looking tired in a way that was different from last session. He said he had finally sent the paperwork to the municipality in Haifa, the one with the stamp we had talked about, and that the clerk had asked him twice for his national ID number, 318524709, before she would accept the form. He laughed when he told me, but it was not really a funny story to him. He said it made him feel like a file rather than a person. I asked him what it would have felt like to be simply recognised, and he went quiet for a long time before saying he did not remember the last time that had happened.

We spent most of the hour on his brother Zvi, who has been calling him late at night from Eilat. Zohar says he cannot tell whether Zvi is asking for help or just wants to be heard, and he is afraid that if he says no he will become the person who abandoned the family, the way their father did. I noted how often he returned to the word abandoned. He wrote a short message to Zvi while he was here and read it to me before sending it, which I thought was a meaningful step. I want to follow up on whether he actually sent it.

Before he left he asked whether he could bring his passport next time, since the bank in Haifa now wants it for a loan review. I told him we could look at that together. He seemed relieved to have a practical thing to hold onto. Next session, February 16th: check in on the message to Zvi, and on how Zohar is sleeping.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to tell you that my father, John Gallagher, passed away peacefully at Galway University Hospital on Tuesday, 11 February, surrounded by his children. He was seventy-eight. Many of you knew him as the man who ran the hardware shop on Eyre Square for forty years, and some of you knew him only as the fellow who always had a biscuit in his coat pocket for the neighbourhood dogs.

John was born on 3 February 1946 in Clifden, Co. Galway, and he never quite lost the rhythm of that western coast in his speech. He married my mother, Maire, in 1972, and together they raised four of us. Our brother Liam, who lives in Melbourne, asked me to say that Dad taught him to fish off the pier at Salthill and never once let him forget the one that got away. My name is Yusuf Demir and I am making this statement voluntarily at the request of the officer on duty. I was born in Konya, in Turkey, and I lived there until I was nineteen. I trained as a pharmacist at Selçuk University before moving to the United Kingdom in 2011 to work at a hospital in Leeds. I have lived in England since then and I hold a British passport, though I still travel back to Turkey every summer to see my mother.

On the evening of 14 April I was walking home from my shift at Leeds General Infirmary. I usually take the route along Hyde Park Road because the lighting is better there. It was around 22:40 when I noticed a grey Ford Focus, registration partly obscured by mud, parked across the driveway of the house next to mine. Two men were standing beside it, and one of them was holding a black rucksack. I did not think much of it at the time, because my neighbour Mrs Okafor often has visitors late in the evening.

When I got to my front door I realised my keys were not in my coat pocket. I called my flatmate, Yusuf's cousin Emre, who lives with me in Headingley, but he did not pick up. I then walked back toward the street and saw that the car had gone. I checked my phone and noticed that I had received an email from my bank, sent to yusuf.demir82@mailbox.co.uk, asking me to confirm a transfer of 450 pounds that I had not made.

I reported the card issue to my bank by phone on 15 April at about nine in the morning, and they advised me to freeze my cards. I am now 42 years old and I have never previously had any dealings with the police in this country, so I was unsure how to proceed. I would like the officer to know that I am willing to provide my phone records, bank statements, and any footage from my doorbell camera, which I have saved to a USB drive.

I have tried to set out everything I can remember as clearly as possible. I am happy to answer any further questions and to attend an identification procedure if one is needed. I confirm that this statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief.

input:
Ronald was born in Hartlepool on a wet afternoon in the winter of 1948, and he never really left it, not in his heart at least. He told me once that the sea was the first thing he ever loved and the last thing he missed. At seventy-six he still walked the front every morning before breakfast, whatever the weather, and he would come back to the house smelling of salt and complaining about the gulls.

Ron was a man of routines. He drove the same battered blue Vauxhall, registration VK19 HPT, for thirty-one years, and he kept its service book in perfect order because he said a machine that was looked after would look after you. He balanced his household accounts every Sunday evening with a pencil, account number 04-2271-8836 on every statement, and he never once let a bill go unpaid. Ask him anything about money or engines and he had an answer, usually with a story attached.

Ronald, we will miss your stubbornness, your terrible jokes and your way of making a crowded room feel like home. Last Christmas you asked me to tell you when the frost came in, so you could wrap up warm for the walk. Rest now. The tide is coming in, and I think you'd want us to say goodbye with the windows open.

I'm Rachel Donnelly, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a product designer for logistics software, which is a polite way of saying I spend most of my days thinking about why warehouse shelves are laid out the way they are. I was born in Dayton, Ohio, and I still think of it as home even though I have lived in Philadelphia since graduating from Drexel University. My first real job out of school was at a small firm in Fishtown, and I stayed in that neighbourhood for six years, long enough to learn which corner bakery would sell me bread at 7 a.m. and which one would not.

These days I live on Christian Street with my partner Marcus and our dog Biscuit, a three-year-old beagle mix who has opinions about every squirrel in South Philly. Our weekends usually begin at Northwind Coffee on Fifth, where the barista knows my order before I reach the counter, and end at Harbor Strength Gym, where I have been trying, with limited success, to improve my deadlift. I also volunteer two evenings a month at the Mercy Ridge Family Clinic, helping staff the front desk and translating intake forms for patients who prefer Spanish.

I share my design notes, slow-motion dog videos and the occasional rant about pallet racking on Instagram under @rachel.designs.dayton, which is an old joke that has outlived its usefulness. On October 14th I will be speaking about accessibility in industrial interfaces, and I would be glad to hear from anyone who has wrestled with the same problems. Please come find me after the session, and bring your own war stories about the worst warehouse app you have ever used.

input:
Od zawsze wiedziałam, że moje miejsce jest tam, gdzie można zadawać pytania, na które nie ma gotowych odpowiedzi. Nazywam się Olga Wiśniewska i pochodzę z Krakowa, miasta, które nauczyło mnie patrzeć na historię nie jako na zbiór dat, ale jako na ciąg ludzkich decyzji. Dorastałam na Kazimierzu, gdzie w każdej kamienicy kryje się jakaś opowieść, a na lekcjach historii w XV Liceum im. Stanisława Staszica zaczęłam zauważać, że podręczniki rzadko pytają, kto zostawał w tyle.

Przełomem była praca badawcza, którą przygotowałam wiosną ubiegłego roku. Zaczęło się od rodzinnego pudełka z listami, które znalazłam w piwnicy babci, Haliny. Listy pisane były w 1946 roku, a ich autorem był mój pradziadek, Olgierd Wiśniewski, który po wojnie próbował odnaleźć dokumenty swojej rodziny w Lwowie. Przez kolejne tygodnie czytałam je przy kuchennym stole, porównując nazwiska i adresy z archiwami miejskimi. Czasem wystarczyła jedna zmiana w pisowni, by otworzyć zupełnie nowy trop.

Najtrudniejsze było przyznać, że część odpowiedzi nigdy nie zostanie znaleziona. Pani Agnieszka Kowalczyk, nasza nauczycielka historii, powiedziała mi wtedy, że historyk uczy się przede wszystkim rozróżniać to, czego nie wie, od tego, co tylko wydaje się oczywiste. Ta uwaga zmieniła sposób, w jaki czytam źródła, i sposób, w jaki myślę o sobie jako o badaczce.

Z tego doświadczenia wyrosło moje pragnienie studiowania historii na Uniwersytecie Jagiellońskim, a w przyszłości pracy w archiwach. Od zawsze wiedziałam, że moje miejsce jest tam, gdzie można zadawać pytania, na które nie ma gotowych odpowiedzi. Nazywam się Ola Wilczyńska i pochodzę z Gdańska, miasta, które nauczyło mnie patrzeć na historię nie jako na zbiór dat, ale jako na ciąg ludzkich decyzji. Dorastałam na Oliwie, gdzie w każdej kamienicy kryje się jakaś opowieść, a na lekcjach historii w XII Liceum im. Adama Mickiewicza zaczęłam zauważać, że podręczniki rzadko pytają, kto zostawał w tyle.

Przełomem była praca badawcza, którą przygotowałam wiosną ubiegłego roku. Zaczęło się od rodzinnego pudełka z listami, które znalazłam w piwnicy babci, Haliny. input:
I am Esteban Villanueva, a civil engineer based in Mendoza, where I have worked on irrigation and water-management projects for the past twelve years. I was born in San Rafael, a small town in the south of Mendoza province, and I still consider it home. My early years were spent helping my grandfather maintain the canal that ran behind our house, which sparked my interest in how water moves across land. Those mornings shaped the career I have today.

After completing my degree at the National University of Cuyo, I joined a regional consultancy and later led a team that redesigned drainage for several vineyards near Maipu. In my free time I am a regular at Cafe Londres on Avenida Costanera, where I often sketch ideas for new projects over a coffee. I also train at Gimnasio Andes three mornings a week. My dog, Mate, keeps me company on long walks and has become something of a mascot in our office. Outside work I volunteer with a community water-education programme for primary school children.

I am delighted to be speaking at this conference on the topic of resilient water infrastructure in arid regions. My presentation will draw on fieldwork conducted in May, when the first heavy rains of the season tested our newly built channels. Please feel free to reach me at esteban.villanueva@aguasmendoza.com.ar if you would like to discuss collaboration. Thank you for having me, and I look forward to meeting many of you in person.

Asunto: Descripción del siniestro, póliza nº 4471-ES-0923

Estimados señores de Seguros Levante:

Yo, Olalla Requena Benítez, con DNI 52.118.906-K, les escribo para describir con detalle el siniestro ocurrido el pasado 14 de diciembre de 2024 en mi domicilio de la calle Gran Vía de Valencia, número 37, 3.º B. Sobre las 19:40 horas regresé a casa tras una comida familiar y, al abrir la puerta, percibí un fuerte olor a humo en el pasillo. La cocina estaba inundada de agua procedente de la tubería del fregadero, que había reventado en la parte trasera del mueble, y el suelo laminado del salón estaba levantado en tres zonas.

De inmediato llamé a los bomberos y a mi vecino Óscar, que es fontanero de profesión y cerró la llave general del edificio. Los bomberos confirmaron que el agua había llegado a la caja de conexiones eléctricas del pasillo, lo que provocó un cortocircuito y el humo. Adjunto el parte de intervención nº 2024-88213 y las fotografías que tomé esa misma noche, donde se aprecian los daños en el techo del pasillo, la humedad en las paredes de la cocina y el electrodoméstico lavavajillas, que quedó inutilizable.

Mi hermana Olga, que vive en Alicante, me pidió que la informara en cuanto hubiera novedades, y por eso adjunto también la nota de su perito, que visitó la vivienda el 17 de diciembre. Si necesitan contactarme para una inspección adicional, pueden hacerlo en el teléfono 644 317 290 o escribirme a olalla.requena@correo.es. Además, para cualquier comunicación informal y fotos del avance de las obras, mi cuenta de Instagram es @olalla.reqbenit, aunque prefiero que las gestiones formales se realicen por escrito.

Les ruego que revisen los daños en el suelo, el techo y el mobiliario de cocina, y que me indiquen cuándo puede empezar la reparación. El fontanero de la comunidad ya ha sellado la tubería provisionalmente, pero la instalación eléctrica debe revisarla un técnico habilitado antes de volver a usar el pasillo.

Quedo a la espera de su respuesta y agradezco de antemano la rapidez con que tramiten el expediente.

Atentamente,

Olalla Requena Benítez

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm the best man, and I've been given the job of telling you a few things about the groom that he would probably rather I kept quiet. I'll do my best to behave.

I first met him at university, in the middle of a frankly disastrous house party where he was the only person who seemed to know where the kettle was. That's the thing about him: whatever the chaos, he quietly sorts it out and then pretends it was no trouble at all. Over the years I've watched him do this for friends, for family, and for strangers he's only just met, and it has never once stopped being remarkable to me.

When he told me he was going to ask her to marry him, he was nervous in a way I had never seen before. He had planned everything down to the last detail, then lost the ring box twice before breakfast. I'll admit I was worried. But when he finally got down on one knee, the look on his face made it perfectly clear that nothing else in the world mattered to him right then.

And she is more than a match for him. She laughs at his terrible puns, she tolerates his obsession with the weather forecast, and she has a way of making every room feel warmer just by walking into it. The two of them balance each other in a way that is genuinely lovely to watch, and I think anyone in this room who has seen them together would agree.

So please raise your glasses with me. To the couple, to the years ahead, and to the many more kettles they will no doubt boil together. Cheers, everyone, and thank you for being here to celebrate with them tonight.

But when he finally got down on one knee, the look on his face made it perfectly clear that nothing else in the world mattered to him right then.

And she is more than a match for him. She laughs at his terrible puns, she tolerates his obsession with the weather forecast, and she has a way of making every room feel warmer just by walking into it. The two of them balance each other in a way that is genuinely lovely to watch, and I think anyone in this room who has seen them together would agree.

So please raise your glasses with me. To the couple, to the years ahead, and to the many more kettles they will no doubt boil together. Cheers, everyone, and thank you for being here to celebrate with them tonight.

Hey Marta, you asked me to tell you properly what happened in Valencia last week, so here it is. I'm Fernando, but everyone at the language school calls me Nando, and I'd been living in Valencia for about four months when the whole mess started. On the 9th of December I got to the police station on Carrer de Colón with a folder of papers, because my residence renewal needed a fresh copy of my passport, number X18472059, and the clerk insisted the old scan wouldn't do. I had also lost my phone that morning, which meant I couldn't show them my booking confirmation for the appointment, so I spent two hours on a bench just trying to reach someone.

The worst part was realising my Instagram account, the one under the handle @fernando.lopezv, had been hacked the night before. Someone posted a fake "giveaway" from it and tagged half my contacts. My cousin texted me on WhatsApp at 6 am to say so, and I called her back on +34 611 293 847 from a borrowed phone just to calm down. She laughed and said at least the hacker had good taste in photos.

In the end the appointment was rescheduled for the 16th of December, and the officer, a tired but kind woman named Carmen, let me in because my cousin had emailed the station a scanned copy from her own account. I walked out at half past four with a new appointment slip and a lot of sympathy for myself. Honestly, Marta, the whole thing taught me to keep a paper copy of everything. Let me know when you're free for coffee, and bring your patience, because I'll need to vent again.

I am writing to lodge a claim for water damage to my home at 14 Kereru Street, Hamilton, following a burst pipe that I discovered on the morning of Tuesday 9 July. My name is Wiremu Tane Pohatu and I have been the registered owner of this property since 2016. My policy number is listed on the attached schedule. I have lived here with my partner and our two children, and this was the first serious incident we have had in the house.

The leak appears to have started in the laundry, where a copper supply line behind the washing machine split at a joint. We think it had been dripping slowly for some days, because the timber subfloor beneath the laundry was soft when I lifted the access hatch. By the time I noticed the carpet squelching in the hallway, the water had travelled through to the lounge and the bottom two rows of the kitchen cabinets had swollen. I shut the mains off at the meter outside and rang our plumber straight away.

The plumber, Hemi Walker from Waikato Plumbing and Gas Ltd, attended the same morning and isolated the fault. He has provided a written invoice for the repair of the supply line and a short report describing the damage he saw. I am happy to forward a copy of his report. I also contacted a drying company the following afternoon, and they set up dehumidifiers and air movers for about four days. Their moisture readings are attached, along with photographs I took on the first morning showing the wet flooring and the swollen cabinet panels.

I would be grateful if an assessor could contact me to arrange an inspection. The easiest way to reach me during business hours is on 021 555 0148, or you can email me at wiremu.pohatu@example.co.nz. I can make the house available any weekday after 9 July, and I can also arrange for the children's bedroom to be inspected, as the damp reached the wall behind their wardrobe.

I have kept all receipts for temporary accommodation and cleaning costs, which we incurred while the subfloor dried and the kitchen was out of use. I have listed these on the attached claim form. Please let me know if you need any other documents to process the claim. Thank you for your help with this matter, and I look forward to hearing from you.

Kind regards,
Wiremu Tane Pohatu

The plumber, Rawiri Turner from Bay Plumbing and Gas Ltd, attended the same morning and isolated the fault. He has provided a written invoice for the repair of the supply line and a short report describing the damage he saw. I am happy to forward a copy of his report. I also contacted a drying company the following afternoon, and they set up dehumidifiers and air movers for about four days. Their moisture readings are attached, along with photographs I took on the first morning showing the wet flooring and the swollen cabinet panels.

I would be grateful if an assessor could contact me to arrange an inspection. The easiest way to reach me during business hours is on 027 318 4862, or you can email me at waitara.rewi@example.co.nz. I can make the house available any weekday after 9 July, and I can also arrange for the children's bedroom to be inspected, as the damp reached the wall behind their wardrobe.

I have kept all receipts for temporary accommodation and cleaning costs, which we incurred while the subfloor dried and the kitchen was out of use. I have listed these on the attached claim form. Please let me know if you need any other documents to process the claim. Thank you for your help with this matter, and I look forward to hearing from you.

Kind regards,
Waitara Tane Rewi

input:
Right, you asked how the move to Leeds went, so here's the proper version. I'm still Amara from Bradford, as you know, and I still can't get my head round how a city can feel this big and this lonely at the same time. The first few weeks at Leeds Beckett were a blur of induction talks and me getting lost near the library every single morning. Mum keeps ringing me on 07412 558310 at ridiculous hours to check I've eaten, which I love, even when I'm half asleep and grumpy about it.

The real turning point was the 14th of July, which I'll never forget now. I had my hospital check-up at St James's in Leeds, because they wanted to be sure my asthma wasn't going to flare up in the new flat with the damp. Nothing dramatic, thank God, just a new inhaler and a nurse who called me love the whole time. Walking out into the sunshine afterwards, I felt properly settled for the first time since I moved, like I actually belonged somewhere.

So I posted about it on my little account, @amara.writes.north, mostly just a photo of the chippy I found near campus. Three people from my course messaged me within an hour, and two of them are now coming to the Tuesday quiz with me. Honestly, that's the update. I'm getting there, slowly. Come up at the end of summer and I'll show you the proper pubs, and the hill that nearly killed me on my first walk.

input:
I still can't quite believe I'm standing here without Ruth. For forty-one years she was the first person I called with good news and the last person I called when things fell apart. I'm Mark, her son, and I want to thank all of you for coming. Ruth grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and never once let us forget it. She loved telling the story of walking to St. Anne's school every morning past the same red brick house on Maple Hollow Road, the one with the crooked mailbox that she swore she'd fix one day. She never did, but she always waved at whoever was inside.

My aunt Carol says Ruth taught her to drive in the church parking lot on a Sunday afternoon in March, and that she screamed the whole time and still somehow made it to the other side in one piece. That was Ruth. Brave, a little bossy, and deeply, stubbornly loyal. Her best friend Denise, who sat with her every Tuesday for the last eleven years, told me that Ruth once drove across three counties in a snowstorm just to bring her a casserole she had forgotten to deliver. Nobody ever had to wonder where they stood with my mother.

So here is what I want you to take with you today. Call the people you love. Wave at the neighbours. Fix the crooked mailbox if you have one. Ruth would have wanted us to keep showing up for each other, the way she always did for all of us.

Okay, I have to tell you what happened last Thursday, because I'm still kind of shaking about it. So you know I've been staying with my cousin Marcus on Alder Ridge Road since my lease fell through. Anyway, I was supposed to meet Dana at Brewster's Coffee on Fulton Avenue around nine, which is that little place with the mismatched chairs you always complained about. I got there early, grabbed a table by the window, and started answering emails on my phone.

That's when a guy I didn't recognize walked in, looked right at me, and said, "David? David Harlan?" I almost laughed because nobody calls me David anymore, not since high school. Turns out he was a former coworker of my dad's from the paper mill, and he'd seen my photo on the community board at the clinic on Kessler Street, the one where I volunteer on Tuesdays. He was really friendly about it, but I felt a weird chill, like someone had been asking around about me.

I texted Dana right away. She replied, "Stay put, I'm coming," and I could hear in her voice that she was worried too. When she got there she didn't even sit down. She just grabbed my arm and said we should go to her place. Her apartment is at 418 Juniper Court, Apartment 3B, which I'd never been to, and I was grateful just to be somewhere quiet with the door locked.

We sat on her couch for an hour, trying to figure out whether I was overreacting. Honestly, I think I was a little, but I also don't think I'd be okay ignoring it. Dana made me call my mom, who said to email the clinic director, Ms. Okafor, and let her know. I did that, and she emailed back within the hour, saying she'd be more careful about what goes up on the bulletin board.

So that's where things stand. Nothing bad actually happened, but it rattled me enough that I'm going to start being more careful about posting things online. I'll keep you posted, and let's definitely get together this weekend. My treat, since you've been the one looking out for me through all this.

Talk soon,
David

Outside work I run a small community repair cafe on Saturday mornings, and I'm usually the one fixing toasters and arguing about soldering irons. I also write a newsletter on open-source tooling. With all my love,
Nils

Arre, you will not believe the week I've had, so sit down and let me tell you everything. On Monday I finally went to the RTO in Pune to get my license renewed, and of course the form asked for my Aadhaar number, and then for my passport number, which I had to dig out from the bottom of the almirah. Its number is K4471829, and I was so scared I'd write it wrong that I checked it four times before submitting. The clerk barely looked at it. Anyway, that's the boring part.

The real drama started Tuesday. I had parked my Swift outside the office at Sadashiv Peth, and when I came back it was gone for about ten minutes before a security guard found it sitting in the wrong lane. My car number is MH12 AX 3390, and I now know that a lot of people in Pune look for that number on their phones. My colleague Sameer Joshi, who you know from the Bangalore trip, was the one who drove me around searching for it. He was amazing, honestly. He even called the traffic police for me while holding his chai in the other hand.

Wednesday was calmer. Sameer and I went for dinner at a little place near Koregaon Park, and he kept insisting I should stop worrying about every small thing. He's right, I know, but you know how I am. I've always been the one who triple checks everything, from bank transfers to train tickets. Even the bank account number for the rent payment, which ends in 7720, I write on a sticky note on my laptop so I never mistype it.

Thursday I had to go to the bank because my salary account showed a weird charge. It turned out to be nothing, just a duplicate autopay, but the manager made me sit for an hour because I didn't have the right slip. Sameer was on a call the whole time, so I sat there scrolling through old photos from our September trip to Goa, and honestly those made me smile more than anything else that week.

So that's my week, yaar. Lots of paperwork, one missing car, one very patient colleague, and too much chai. Tell me how your week was, and don't skip the juicy parts this time!

I am writing to report a water damage claim for the apartment I rent on the ground floor of a three-storey building. On the morning in question I came home from work to find the bathroom ceiling had collapsed and water was running down the kitchen wall toward the electrical outlets. I shut off the main valve in the stairwell as soon as I could find it and called the building manager, who arrived within the hour. The plumber he sent found that a pipe joint above the shower had cracked, which had been leaking into the ceiling void for what looks like several days.

The damage is extensive. When our mam had her hip done two winters ago, it was Seamus who drove her to Limerick every Tuesday for physio, sat through the dull waiting-room hours, and then brought her home for a fry. Watching the two of you choose each other, quietly and without fuss, has been one of the great pleasures of my life.

I am writing this with a heavy heart to share that my father, Gustavo Almeida Rocha, passed away peacefully at his home in Belo Horizonte on the 14th of July, just four days after his seventy-third birthday. For more than thirty years he served as Chief Engineer at Metalúrgica Vale Verde, and many of the bridges and warehouses across Minas Gerais still stand thanks to his careful hands and even more careful judgement. He was the first in our family to graduate from the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, and he never let us forget how proud that made him.

Gustavo was a man of routine and quiet generosity. Every Saturday he walked to the Mercado Central with his old canvas bag, arguing good-naturedly with the fishmongers about prices. He volunteered for many years with the children's ward at Hospital das Clínicas, teaching the older patients to build small wooden boats. He leaves behind his wife of forty-four years, Marta, and his two children, Lucas and Renata, who will miss his terrible puns and his even worse jokes at Sunday lunch.

In lieu of flowers, we ask that you donate to the Hospital das Clínicas children's ward in his memory. A mass will be held on the 18th of July at the Igreja de São José. Thank you to everyone who sent kind words, meals and memories in these last weeks. Gustavo would have wanted you to eat well and laugh often.
output:

When I think about why I want to study environmental engineering at Michigan State, I keep coming back to the summers I spent in Dayton, Ohio, watching my grandfather test the water in the creek behind our house. Yolanda Brooks, my grandfather's name is Walter, and he has been volunteering with the county watershed group since before I was born. Every March, when the snow melts and the runoff starts, he takes his clipboard and his battered thermometer down to the bank, and I went with him for the first time when I was eleven. I did not understand then that the numbers he wrote down would later become a question I could not stop asking.

That question followed me into high school, where I started a small project mapping which storm drains near our neighborhood emptied directly into the creek. I collected the data myself, built a spreadsheet, and presented my findings to the Dayton City Council on March 18. A councilmember asked me afterward to send my full report to her office, and I still have the reply she wrote, thanking me for the work and promising to forward it to the public works department. I learned that careful measurement can actually change who pays attention to a problem.

I am applying to your program because I want to learn the chemistry, hydrology, and policy that turn observations like my grandfather's into decisions that protect communities. I want to be the kind of engineer who can stand at the creek bank and also sit in the council chamber. You can reach me at yolanda.brooks24@mail.com if you would like to talk further about my application.

I am writing to formally report a collision that occurred on the morning of 14 October 2024 along the Thika Superhighway, just past the Roysambu roundabout in Nairobi. My name is Mercy Wanjiru Kamau, and I am 34 years old. At the time of the accident I was driving my white Toyota Fielder, registration number KCD 417M, which is insured under policy account AC-7730-1182. I was on my way to my shift as a senior claims officer at Pan Africa Assurance Ltd, where I had been travelling in heavy traffic since about 7:20 a.m.

A matatu coming out of a side lane cut across my path without signalling and clipped the rear left panel of my vehicle. I braked as hard as I could, but the impact pushed my car into the barrier. The airbags deployed, and my left shoulder and wrist were bruised. Several bystanders stopped to help, and one of them, Samuel, took photographs of both vehicles and the position of the matatu before it drove off. I have attached those photos along with the police abstract, which I obtained from Roysambu Police Station on 16 October.

For the claim I would like the rear quarter panel, bumper and tail light repaired, and I would also like to be reimbursed for the Kenyatta National Hospital visit on 15 October, where I was examined and given a sick sheet. Mercy is my name in all correspondence, and I can be reached at the phone number on file. Please let me know which documents you still need from me, and I will send them promptly.

Hi, I'm not really sure how to start this, so I'll just write it out. My name is Kevin Ruiz and I'm 34 years old. I live in Córdoba, Argentina, and for the past six years I've worked as a radiology technician at Hospital Italiano de Córdoba. I used to love that job. Lately I dread walking through the front doors in the morning, and I can't figure out why.

Since about early April, things at work have changed. A new supervisor, Marcela Ibarra, started shadowing my shifts and rewriting our procedures without asking anyone. She corrects me in front of patients, and last week she told a resident I was 'careless with the scanner' when the calibration error was clearly hers. I've tried talking to her directly, but every conversation ends with me apologising for things I didn't do. I keep replaying those moments at night and waking up at 3 a.m. with my heart racing.

Outside work, I've been pulling away from people. My friend Kevin's cousin Lucía has invited me to asado twice this month and I keep making excuses. My younger brother Matías called me on April 19 to check in and I let it go to voicemail, which I feel terrible about. I used to play five-a-side football on Thursdays with my old school mates from Colegio Nacional de Monserrat, and I stopped going about three weeks ago because I just didn't have the energy.

I know I'm not sleeping well and I know I'm not eating properly. I've started drinking a bit more red wine than I should, mostly alone on my balcony in the evenings. I'm not in danger of doing anything stupid, I don't think, but I can feel myself getting smaller and quieter, and that scares me.

What I'm asking is this: how do I deal with a boss who undermines me without making things worse? And how do I start feeling like myself again, without it being a huge production? I'd appreciate practical steps, and maybe some honesty about whether I should be talking to someone professionally. Thanks for reading all of this.

input:
I finally made it to Asheville last July, and I have to start with the coffee. My old college roommate Jessica Morales, who is 34 and has lived there since her move west, insisted I visit Lantern Roast on Haywood Road before we did anything else. Her husband Tom and I were both waiting in line when she waved us over, and I swear the cardamom bun alone was worth the drive from Charlotte. Jessica had already mapped out our whole weekend, and she was right about nearly all of it.

We spent Saturday morning hiking the trail behind the Blue Ridge Clinic parking lot, which sounds odd but is actually a gorgeous loop that Jessica's sister Rachel swears by. Rachel, who is 31 and a nurse there, met us at the trailhead with a thermos of lemon tea and a warning about the rocky stretch near the creek. I'm glad I listened. By afternoon my legs were jelly, so we drifted downtown, and Jessica dragged me into every bookshop on the street.

If you go in July, pack light layers and plan to be outside before ten. The mornings are cool and the afternoons are a steam bath, and the locals know it. I'd happily go back, and next time I'll bring Jessica's little nephew Eli, who kept asking when we could see the waterfall again.

input: I still hear Ruth's laugh every time I drive past the corner of Maple Hollow Road and Linden Avenue, where she taught the whole block to play hopscotch the summer she turned seventy-one. Ruth kept her passport, her Social Security card and her Medicare folder in the same faded blue envelope, and she'd hand it to me on every trip we took, just to make sure I knew where things were. Preciso de ajuda para organizar a minha cabeça. Há alguns meses que ando muito ansioso com o trabalho e com as contas da casa, e isso tem começado a afetar o sono e a paciência com as pessoas que eu mais gosto. Quando chega a noite, fico revirando os mesmos pensamentos, imaginando cenários piores do que eles provavelmente são, e de manhã acordo já cansado. Okay so this is me just talking into the phone while I walk back from the shops, so apologies if it comes out in a bit of a mess. I've been meaning to record something for ages because I keep forgetting the little things about the move, and honestly the first few weeks were weirder than I expected. You think you're prepared, you've read all the forums, you know the paperwork is going to be a nightmare, but then you're standing in a queue at some office and nobody understands what you're trying to say and you just think, what on earth have I done. The food is different, the way people queue is different, even the light in the afternoons feels different to me, which sounds daft but it's true.

The thing that surprised me most is how much I miss the small everyday stuff. Not the big things, I mean the way the neighbour would nod at you, or knowing which bus to get without checking. Here I'm still working out the rhythms of everything. I went to a little market last weekend and bought some fruit I couldn't name, and the stall owner laughed at me, but in a friendly way, and I actually felt a bit better after that. So I suppose that's something. Anyway, I'll try to remember to send you the longer version of this when I get home, and maybe we can talk properly then. Right, I think I'm nearly at the door, so I'll stop rambling now.

input:
I was born in Eldoret, in the Rift Valley, and for most of my childhood I believed that the rain was something that happened to other people. My grandmother, Wanjiru Kamau, taught me otherwise. Every January, when the first storms rolled over the tea estates, she would send me out with a bucket to collect water from the eaves of our house, and she would tell me that every drop had a name and a destination. I thought she was joking. She was not. She kept a notebook of rainfall readings for forty years, and it was in her handwriting that I first saw the idea of data as something people could care about.

When I was sixteen, our county's water kiosk closed for three weeks in January because the pump had failed, and I watched neighbours walk two kilometres with jerricans before dawn. I started a small project with two classmates to log outages and share them through a simple WhatsApp group and an Instagram page, @eldoret_water_watch, which now has a few thousand followers. Wanjiru read every post aloud at breakfast, correcting my spelling and asking whether the numbers were right. Her insistence on accuracy taught me more about science than any textbook.

I want to study civil and environmental engineering because I have seen what happens when infrastructure fails the people who depend on it most. I am applying to your programme because of its focus on low-cost water systems and community-led design. I hope to return to the Rift Valley with the skills to build something that lasts, and to keep my grandmother's notebook open on the desk while I work.

I have been going to Piekarnia Zofia on Krakowska Street for about three years now, and I finally felt I had to write a review after last Thursday. My name is Oskar Wiśniewski and I was born in Radom, so I am not a stranger to Polish bakeries, but this one has become my favourite in the city. The rye bread is dense and sour in exactly the right way, and the drożdżówki with plum filling are still warm when you pick them up before work.

Last week I came in to collect a birthday cake for my mother, Halina, whose birthday was on 14 February. I had booked it by phone the Monday before, and the staff remembered the order and had it boxed and waiting. The woman at the counter, Agnieszka, even wrote a small card by hand without me asking. Such small things matter. I also paid by card and the terminal worked first time, which is more than I can say for some places.

Prices are fair, the queue moves quickly even at lunchtime, and parking is easy if you use the side street. I would recommend this place to anyone in the area. If you have questions about a custom order, you can email orders@piekarniazofia.pl or write to me at oskar.wisniewski@gmail.com, and I am happy to share what worked for us. Five stars from me, and I will be back next week for the rye.

input: I finally made it to Galway this September, three days after landing in Dublin on a whim. My old colleague Gráinne Kavanagh, who still works as a senior architect at Corrib Design Partners, insisted on showing me the Latin Quarter before anything else. We ate chowder at a tiny place by the docks, and she laughed at me for ordering a second bowl. Gráinne has lived here for eleven years and talks about the city like a relative she's slightly embarrassed by. I walked the Salthill promenade alone the next morning, grey sea on one side and rain drifting in from the Atlantic. Galway, I decided, is the kind of town that rewards you for being slow.

input:
Dear Grandma,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden is coming along nicely this spring. I have been meaning to write for weeks, but the semester got away from me, and every time I sat down to start, I ended up staring at a blank page. So here I am, finally, with a cup of tea going cold beside me and the window open because the weather has turned so mild.

I wanted to tell you about the thing that has been on my mind lately. My roommate and I finally repainted the kitchen, which sounds small, but it took three weekends and a lot of arguing over shades of yellow. We ended up with something softer than either of us had pictured, and now the room feels like it belongs to us. I keep thinking about how you always said a home is built from little decisions, and I think you were right about that.

Work has been steady, though a bit exhausting. There is a project that is taking more of my time than I expected, and some days I feel like I am pushing a heavy cart uphill. But my supervisor has been patient, and a colleague showed me a shortcut for the reports that saved me an entire evening. Small kindnesses like that make a big difference when the workload piles up.

I also wanted to say how much I appreciated the recipe you sent along last time. I made it for a friend who had been feeling low, and she asked for the name so she could make it herself. We sat on the floor eating it straight from the pot, laughing about nothing in particular. I told her it was your recipe, and she said I should tell you thank you for her too.

I miss our long walks and the way you pointed out birds I would have walked right past. Next time I visit, I want to take you somewhere new and see what we can find together. Maybe we can bring a thermos and sit for a while without needing to be anywhere else.

Please write back when you have a moment, even if it is just a few lines about what the neighbors are up to. Your letters always make the week feel lighter.

With all my love,

Your grandchild

input:
I am a materials scientist whose work sits at the boundary between chemistry and mechanical engineering. For the past decade I have focused on developing lightweight composites for transport and renewable energy applications, with particular interest in how microstructure governs fatigue behaviour under real operating conditions. My research combines laboratory characterisation with computational modelling, and I have found that the most useful insights often come from the mismatch between what a model predicts and what a test specimen actually does.

Beyond the laboratory, I have spent much of my career supervising early-stage researchers and building collaborations across disciplines. I believe strongly that good science depends on clear communication, so I have invested time in teaching workshops on experimental design and data integrity. I enjoy mentoring students who arrive with strong theoretical backgrounds but little hands-on experience, and I take particular satisfaction in watching them gain confidence at the bench.

In my talk I will share some recent findings on crack initiation in layered materials and reflect on what they suggest for future design practice. I am keen to hear from colleagues working on related problems, whether from industry or academia, and I welcome conversations on how we might move promising laboratory results into more durable, scalable solutions.

input:
Tuesday 14 May

I finally got round to sorting the box from under the stairs today, the one Mum keeps insisting is "just paperwork." It was mostly rubbish, but I found my old passport in there, the one with the number ending in 4471, and I sat on the floor for ages turning the pages. Seven years of stamps. Lisbon, Tbilisi, that terrible hostel in Krakow. It made me miss travelling properly, not the weekend-in-Bath kind.

Work has been relentless. I'm still Senior Analyst at Fairhaven Logistics on the Ashgrove Park campus, and this quarter they've moved every deadline forward by a fortnight without asking anyone. Dev says it's because the board wants numbers before the summer review. I say it's because nobody up there has ever had to reconcile a spreadsheet at 11pm. I came home at seven and didn't even take my coat off.

Dinner was at Mum's on Saturday, and Harriet came too, which was lovely. She brought the good sourdough from the place on Brindley Road, the one with the chalkboard by the door. She's been asking whether I've considered moving closer to them in Cheltenham. I told her I'd think about it, which is what I say when I mean no. The truth is I like it here in Hulme, even with the bins that never get emptied on time.
