input:
The first thing you notice about Brazil is the noise, and I mean that in the best possible way. Every morning the streets fill with the sound of vendors calling out their wares, scooters whining past, and somewhere a samba record playing too loudly from an open window. We spent our first few days just wandering without much of a plan, letting the rhythm of the place set our pace. Coffee is strong, bread is warm, and nobody seems to be in a hurry, which took some getting used to after a long winter at home.

One afternoon we took a slow bus up into the hills behind the coast. The road wound through green valleys and past small farms where bananas and mangoes grew right beside the tarmac. The driver played old bossa nova tunes on his radio and hummed along to every one. When we finally stepped off near a little village square, the air was cooler and smelled of wood smoke and fresh cut grass. We sat under a huge shade tree and shared a plate of fried cheese and guava pastries while kids kicked a ball across the dusty ground.

If you go, do not rush the food. The regional dishes vary enormously from one part of the country to another, and each place has its own pride in its recipes. In the markets you can taste fruits you have never heard of, some sweet and floral, others sharp enough to make your eyes water. Ask the people behind the counters what they recommend, because almost everyone will happily tell you their favourite and maybe add a free sample for good measure.

The beaches deserve their reputation, though they are best enjoyed early or late in the day when the sun is gentler. We walked along the shoreline at sunrise, when the fishermen were pulling in their nets and the sand was still cool underfoot. Later, in the evening, the whole coastline seemed to come alive with music, games of footvolley, and families sharing grilled skewers under string lights. It is a place that rewards patience and curiosity.

If you are thinking about visiting, my advice is simple: slow down, talk to strangers, and let yourself get a little lost. The best moments we had were the ones we did not plan. Brazil has a way of pulling you into its everyday life until you forget to check the time at all.

Dear Grandma Vera,

I hope the garden is doing well and that the tomatoes finally ripened this year. I think about you every morning when I make coffee, the way you taught me, with too much sugar and a pinch of cardamom. Here in Toronto the mornings are already cooler, and the leaves on our street in Little Portugal are starting to turn. Mum says you're still refusing to use the new kettle Dad bought you, which doesn't surprise me at all.

I wanted to tell you about the appointment I finally booked. On August 14th I'm going to the immigration office downtown for my citizenship interview, and I'm nervous in a way I didn't expect. Everyone keeps telling me it's just a formality, but after everything you and Grandpa went through to get out of Lisbon, it feels like more than paperwork. Please think of me that morning. My friends call me Vivi, but I know you still say Vivianne when you're cross with me.

I miss the long walks to the bakery on Rua da Madalena, and I miss your stories about the trams. Write to me when you can, even if it's just a few lines about what the neighbours are up to. I'll send you photos from the ceremony if they let me keep my phone in the room. Give my love to Aunt Lucia and tell her I'll call on Sunday.

All my love,
Vivianne Almeida

September 14. Another long day at Brightwater Logistics. I'm still getting used to being a Senior Route Planner here in Tacoma, and today Gregory from the warehouse side finally agreed to let us test the new scheduling software on the Oregon lanes. Zadie, my manager, was thrilled. She said the numbers would be on her desk by the end of the month, so I've been up past midnight building the spreadsheets.

I keep thinking about how different this place feels from Spokane. Tacoma has that gray harbor light in the mornings, and people here talk about the weather like it's a neighbor. I walked down to the water at lunch and just stood there for ten minutes. It helped. Zadie noticed I looked tired and told me to take Friday off if I wanted, but I think I'll come in anyway, since the test starts on the 22nd.

If anyone from the team needs the route files, they can reach me at zadie.morrow@brightwaterlogistics.com. I told Gregory to send his notes there too, so I don't lose track of anything. Tomorrow I'm going to finally sleep before midnight. Probably.

I keep telling myself that writing these things down is supposed to help, so here I am on a rainy Tuesday in Utrecht, trying again. My name is Maartje, and I grew up in Groningen, which I mention only because my mother still reminds me that the wind there built my character. Last week I finally called the clinic at the Radboudumc about the referral my GP gave me in June. I left a message on 07-3152 4486 and nobody picked up, so I stared at my phone for a full hour like it owed me money.

My sister Marit says I should stop waiting for the perfect moment. She is right, which is deeply annoying. Her birthday is on 14 July and she wants everyone at the beach in Zandvoort, but I keep thinking about the last party, when I spent the whole evening in the kitchen avoiding small talk. I told my therapist Dr. van Dijk that I feel like a guest in my own life. She wrote something down and then asked me what I would say to Marit if she felt that way. I did not have an answer ready.

So today I am making a small plan. I will call the hospital again tomorrow morning, I will bring a book to the beach on the 14th, and I will stay for at least two hours. Maybe that is not much. But for someone who has spent months rearranging the furniture in her head instead of moving it, two hours feels like a start.

input:
Hi all, I'm hoping someone here has been through something similar. My partner and I have been together for about six years, and lately we keep ending up in the same argument about money. I handle the bills and the budget, and I feel like I'm the only one who ever checks the account balance or thinks about what's coming up. When I bring it up, it turns into a fight about me being controlling, and then we both shut down for a day or two.

What makes it harder is that I don't think either of us is acting in bad faith. My partner is generous and honestly hates feeling like a burden, so I think when I raise a concern they hear criticism of how they spend. I've tried a shared spreadsheet and a weekly check-in, but the check-ins usually get postponed and the spreadsheet only gets updated by me.

So my question is: how did your couple find a way to talk about money without it turning into a referendum on character? Did you set up separate accounts, a fixed allowance, or something else? I'd especially love to hear from anyone who went from constant tension to something that felt fair. Thanks in advance for any experience you can share.

Friends, family, and everyone who has put up with my cooking over the years, thank you for being here to celebrate Yiannis and Eleni. I have known Yiannis since we were boys running barefoot through the streets of Kalamata, the town where he was born and where his mother still insists on feeding every guest until they can no longer stand. Some people spend their whole lives looking for a home. Yiannis found his the moment he met Eleni, and I have never seen him so calm, so certain, or so willing to let someone else choose the restaurant.

When Yiannis first told me about Eleni, he sent me a photo of her laughing on a ferry deck with her hair completely wild in the wind. He wrote, "This is the one, Nikos." He had already put it on his social media as @yiannis_k_travels, which tells you everything about how fast he moved. I told him to slow down. He did not. Thank goodness.

Eleni, you have given Yiannis something I did not think was possible: patience with his terrible jokes and his even worse habit of reorganising the kitchen without asking. You also took in his dog, Pipiras, who now sleeps across your feet every night and clearly believes this wedding was arranged in his honour. Thank you for making our family bigger and warmer.

I want to mention the day you two officially started planning this celebration. You booked the venue on October 14th, after a long call where Yiannis kept saying he had it all under control while holding a notebook full of question marks. Somehow it all came together, and here we are, surrounded by lemon trees, good wine, and people who love you both.

If anyone needs to reach me about the speech, the photos, or the best place to get grilled octopus, call me at +30 694 512 7830. I will answer, I promise, probably while eating.

So please raise your glasses. To Yiannis and Eleni, to new beginnings, and to a marriage as generous and joyful as the table we are sharing tonight. Yia mas!

input:
Dear Nonna Lucia,

I hope this letter finds you well and that your knees are behaving themselves in this heat. Ilaria here, writing from our little flat off Via dei Tintori in Florence. Mum says you have been asking after me, so I thought I would finally put pen to paper, which I know you will think is very old-fashioned of me.

The first weeks at the Istituto Santa Caterina have been hard work but I am starting to enjoy it. My Italian literature teacher, Signora Benedetti, made us read Calvino aloud in class and I nearly cried during the reading of the bit about the moon. My maths is still a disaster, though Papa says that is hereditary and he should know since he failed it too. Mum says she will drive me to the lessons on the 14th of July if the traffic on the Lungarno is not too bad.

You will be sorry to hear that Zio Marco had a bit of a scare last week. He went to the Ospedale di Careggi with chest pains, and everyone panicked, but it turned out to be a pulled muscle from carrying boxes of tomatoes for the restaurant. He is fine now, and he has been grumbling non-stop about being told to rest. Mum has been ringing you on the landline but you do not pick up, so she asked me to tell you to call her on 055 482 3917 when you get a chance. She also said you should stop worrying about her and about me, which I think is a good idea for both of you.

I have been thinking about the summers we spent at your house in Pistoia, shelling beans on the back step while you told us stories about the war. I miss those afternoons more than I can say. Maybe this year we could all go back together for a few days in late July, if you can bear to have us under your feet again.

Write back soon, even if it is just a postcard with your wobbly handwriting. I will keep the stamps you sent me in the blue tin on my desk.

All my love,
Ilaria

Friends, family, thank you for being here today. My name is Hana Te Aho, and I was lucky enough to be Frank's eldest daughter. Dad was born in Whanganui in 1948, and he never really left the river, even when he moved us up to Tauranga in the seventies. He was seventy-six when he died on the 14th of September, and he still had three ideas for the garden he never got to.

You all knew him as the man at the counter of Riverbend Cafe every Saturday morning, the one who argued with Mrs Pohatu about the price of flat whites and then tipped the lot back into the jar for the kids. He kept his old Holden going on the road with plate number KGT482 long past the point any mechanic thought sensible. If you ever needed a jump start or a lift, you called Frank. The number on the fridge was 027 548 3916, and it rang out to him and to all of us.

Dad loved being online in his own clumsy way. He posted terrible puns and photos of his tomatoes under @frankiethegardener, and he replied to every single comment, even the ones that just said nice one. So if you have a photo of him from the last Christmas, please send it to me. I want to see him grinning the way he did at this very table. Thank you, Dad. We'll miss you every day.

input:
I stand here today for my mother, Veronica Doyle, who would have turned seventy on the 14th of June had she been with us. For forty-one years she lived at 27 Carrigrohane Road in Cork, and that kitchen, with its crooked window and the radio always on the wrong station, was the centre of all our lives. She trained as a nurse at Cork University Hospital in the years when the wards were full of people who needed her, and she never once spoke of herself as brave, though everyone who knew her saw it. Mam was the first to arrive at any crisis and the last to leave it.

She loved Biscuit, the old terrier who followed her from room to room, and she loved the long walks along the Lee with her friend Siobhan Kearney, who could never keep up with her and never once complained about it. Every Sunday they argued about the crossword, and every Sunday Mam won. When Siobhan rang on the morning of the 20th of June to say she was on her way, Mam was already halfway through her tea and telling us all what to do.

I think of her now the way she would have wanted, with the radio on and the kettle going. She taught us that kindness is not a grand gesture but a daily habit, and she practised it without fail. Rest now, Mam. We will keep the kettle on for you.

Dear Westfield Middle School families,

This December, we are proud to celebrate Nolan Varga, a seventh grader who spent the fall term organizing the school's first food drive. Nolan, who is 12, collected more than 400 cans and boxes for the Harbor Street Food Pantry, and he did it while keeping his grades steady. Parents can reach Nolan's family coordinator at nolan.varga@westfieldms.org if they would like to join the next drive on December 14.

Nolan told us that the idea came from a trip to his grandmother's home in Dayton, Ohio, where he saw neighbors lining up at a church pantry. His grandmother, Helena Varga, was born in Dayton and still volunteers there every Saturday. Nolan said he wanted to bring the same spirit to Westfield, and he credits his teachers and classmates for making it happen. Before the drive began, he also had to submit a copy of his passport and a national ID number to the district's volunteer office, which is standard for any student working with outside partners.

Please join us in thanking Nolan at the winter assembly on December 19. We will also be displaying the food drive thermometer in the main hallway through the end of the month. Oi, pessoal! Como professora de Ciências do sexto ano, quero compartilhar com todas as famílias o que aconteceu na nossa feira de ciências deste semestre. Os alunos passaram semanas planejando seus experimentos, desde plantas que cresceram em diferentes tipos de luz até um projeto sobre a água da chuva e como ela pode ser reaproveitada. Confesso que me emocionei ao ver a dedicação de cada um, principalmente dos que estavam mais tímidos no início do ano e agora apresentavam seus trabalhos com segurança e orgulho.

Durante a feira, os visitantes puderam circular pelas bancadas, fazer perguntas e até testar algumas das atividades. Foi bonito ver os pais e os irmãos menores participando, anotando ideias e comentando os resultados. Muitos alunos disseram que gostaram mais de trabalhar em grupo do que imaginavam, e isso me deixou muito feliz, porque a ciência se faz junto.

Agradeço a todos que ajudaram a montar o espaço, trouxeram materiais e incentivaram seus filhos. Em breve vamos publicar as fotos e os relatos completos no mural da escola. Se alguém tiver sugestões para a próxima edição, pode me procurar na secretaria ou escrever no caderno de recados. Obrigada pelo apoio de sempre!

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to provide a reference for Willem de Groot, who worked under my supervision as a senior logistics coordinator at Van Wijk Distribution B.V. in Rotterdam from March 2019 until his departure in January 2025. Willem, whom everyone at the depot knew as Wim, is thirty-four years old and one of the most dependable colleagues I have managed in more than fifteen years in the sector.

Willem joined us after completing his degree in supply chain management at Erasmus University Rotterdam, and he hit the ground running. Within his first year he redesigned the inbound scheduling for our Botlek warehouse, cutting dock waiting times by roughly a fifth. He has a rare ability to stay calm when a shipment goes wrong, and he will always pick up the phone to a driver at six in the morning rather than let a problem sit overnight.

What I valued most was his honesty. When a client's forecast was unrealistic, Willem said so, politely but clearly, and then offered two workable alternatives. He trained three junior planners during his time with us, and all three now hold supervisory roles of their own. He also represented the team on our safety committee, where he pushed for better lighting in the loading area after a near-miss in the winter of 2022.

Outside work, Willem is a keen volunteer. He spends his Saturdays at the community kitchen on the Witte de Withstraat, and he coached a youth football team in the Delfshaven district for four seasons. People trust him, and that trust is well earned.

If you wish to contact me about Willem's application, you may reach me at j.bakker@vanwijkdistribution.nl or on +31 10 555 0142. I can also be reached by post at Havenstraat 18, 3011 MD Rotterdam. I recommend him without reservation.

Yours faithfully,

Jan Bakker
Operations Director, Van Wijk Distribution B.V.

My name is Pavel Levi and I am making this statement at the Tel Aviv Yarkon police station on the morning of 14 October. I am 42 years old and I live in Holon with my wife, Noa, and our two children. I am writing this statement because I want to report that on the evening of 9 October my car, a white Toyota Corolla with licence plate 23-871-45, was broken into while parked on Herzl Street outside the building where my brother Pavel lives. I have not been able to reach my brother since then.

At about 19:30 on 9 October I parked the car on Herzl Street, close to the corner with Ben Gurion Boulevard, because the usual spot near my office was taken. I locked the car and took my bag with me. When I came back down at 07:15 the next morning, the driver's side window was smashed and the glovebox was open. My laptop bag was missing, along with a folder of documents that I keep for my work at the hospital in Holon, where I am a radiology technician. I did not notice anything unusual in the street when I parked.

The folder contained copies of my identity card, my driving licence and a letter from Wolfson Medical Center confirming my employment, as well as a printed schedule for my nieces and nephews at the Gymnasia Herzliya school, where my wife Noa picks them up. I am worried about these papers because they include my home address and phone number, and a list of the school pick-up times. I contacted my bank the same morning and asked them to block my card. I have not yet received a replacement licence.

I also want to tell you about the message my brother sent me on 11 October, which I have kept. He wrote from his phone that he had seen a man near our parents' house on Rothschild Street asking for me by name, and that he would go to the police himself. I replied twice that evening and again the next day, but I have had no answer since 12 October. My parents are very upset and my mother has asked me to press for an urgent response. I am happy to provide the message and my phone records.

I would be grateful if you could confirm the case number, check whether any camera footage from Herzl Street has been recorded, and let me know whether anyone has been questioned about the vehicle or my brother's whereabouts. I can be reached on my mobile at 050-446-3381 or by email at pavel.levi@mailbox.co.il. I am available to come back to the station at any time that suits you.

I confirm that the contents of this statement are true to the best of my knowledge.

input:
When I first walked into the community kitchen where I volunteer on weekends, I did not expect it to change how I think about problems. I had assumed that feeding people was a matter of logistics: enough food, enough hands, enough cooking space. Over time I learned that the harder part was listening. The people who came through the doors each week had needs that no spreadsheet captured, and the most useful thing I could do was ask questions and then actually hear the answers.

That realization pushed me toward the sciences. I began asking why certain neighbourhoods had so little access to fresh produce, and that question led me to read about food deserts, transportation barriers, and the economics of grocery retail. I wanted to understand the mechanisms behind what I was seeing rather than only responding to its symptoms. Reading research papers late into the night became a habit I did not resent.

My interest in chemistry grew from the same curiosity. I was fascinated that a few ordinary compounds could explain why bread rises, why fruit browns, and why some preservation methods work. In my school's lab I designed a small project testing how different storage conditions affected the shelf life of leafy greens. The results were not dramatic, but the process taught me patience, careful record-keeping, and the humility to report findings that did not match my hypothesis.

I have also learned that good ideas rarely survive alone. Working on a student team, I noticed that the most productive discussions happened when quieter members were given space to speak. I began taking on the role of facilitator, making sure every perspective was considered before we settled on a direction. This experience showed me that collaboration is a skill I can deliberately build, not just a personality trait.

I am applying to your university because I want to combine these threads: rigorous scientific training, a commitment to the people my work might affect, and the collaborative habits that make research better. I hope to study environmental chemistry and to pursue research on food systems that is both technically sound and grounded in the realities of the communities it serves.

My name is Yolanda Naidoo and I am 34 years old. I am making this statement at the Rosebank police station in Johannesburg because on the evening of 14 October I was followed from the parking area at Sandton City, and I want the matter recorded properly. I work as a nurse at Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in Parktown and I was coming off a late shift when this happened. My phone number is 082 417 3390 and I am the person to contact about this matter.

At about 21:40 I left the basement parking at Sandton City and walked to my blue Volkswagen Polo, registration CA 884 RZ. I noticed a grey Toyota Hilux with a tinted windscreen reversing slowly behind a pillar. The driver did not switch on his lights. When I pulled out onto Rivonia Road, the Hilux followed me for approximately four kilometres, keeping a distance of about two car lengths, and then flashed its high beams repeatedly.

I drove directly to my sister's flat in Melville and parked inside her gate. I did not stop anywhere else. Her husband, Yusuf, saw the vehicle slow down across the road and then drive off towards Empire Road. He has agreed to give a short statement if required. My sister, Yasmin, also heard me describe the car as I arrived and can confirm that I was visibly shaken.

I have since looked at the security footage from the Sandton City parking, which I obtained from the centre management on 17 October. The footage is not clear enough to read the number plate, but it does show a vehicle matching the description reversing behind the same pillar at 21:31. I have a copy on a USB stick which I will hand over with this statement.

My dog, Pumpkin, a brown Jack Russell, was with me at home that evening and was barking at the front gate when I got back, which is unusual for her. I mention this only because I believe the vehicle may have stopped outside my house in Parktown earlier that week. I cannot be certain, but I would ask that patrols in the area be informed.

I request that an investigating officer contact me on the number above and that the case be opened under the appropriate reference. I am willing to attend any identity parade or further interview. I confirm that this statement is true to the best of my knowledge.

input:
Last month I finally made it to Germany after years of promising myself I would. I started with a slow train ride through the countryside, watching the fields roll past and the little villages with their red-tiled roofs appear and disappear. Nothing about the trip was planned to the minute, which was exactly what I needed. I wandered into bakeries early in the morning, pointed at whatever looked best in the glass case, and ate my breakfast standing on cobblestones while the town slowly woke up around me.

What surprised me most was how easy it was to slip into the rhythm of the place. Shops close on Sundays, so I learned quickly to stock up on Saturday afternoon. Trains run with an almost comforting precision, and the ticket machines, though intimidating at first, turned out to be very forgiving once I figured out the menus. I spent long evenings in beer gardens under chestnut trees, sharing wooden tables with strangers who were happy to recommend hiking trails and hidden cafes.

If you are thinking about visiting, my advice is simple: leave room in your schedule for getting lost. Some of my favourite moments came from wrong turns, like stumbling upon a tiny market square with a fountain and an elderly couple playing chess. Bring comfortable shoes, a bit of patience for the bureaucracy, and an appetite. Germany rewards the curious traveller, and I already feel the pull to go back.

Hello everyone, I'm not sure where else to ask this, so I'm posting here. My name is Rotimi and I'm 27, living in Ibadan with my older brother's family since I finished my NYSC service last year. My sister-in-law, who everyone calls Mama Tobi even though she is only 31, has been very kind to me, but lately things have become difficult between us.

The problem started in early November when I was given a small amount of money by my uncle to help with the rent deposit for a room in Bodija. I did not tell anyone at first because I wanted to handle it quietly. Then Mama Tobi found out from a cousin and she started asking me every day when I would pay her back for the 'loan' she says she made to my account. I never agreed to any loan. My uncle's money was a gift to me, and I have the bank transfer record to show it.

What hurts most is that my brother Rotimi, I mean my own brother, has not said a single word in my defence. Every time I try to talk to him he tells me to respect his wife and to just pay her so there is peace in the house. I respect her, truly, but I do not think I should be forced to pay for something I did not borrow.

I have thought about moving out sooner, but I have no savings after paying the NYSC allowance back to my mother's shop expenses, and jobs in Ibadan have been hard to find since the start of the year. A friend from Lagos, Chidinma, told me to just call a lawyer, but I do not know how much that would cost or whether it is worth doing in a family matter.

So my question is this. Has anyone here dealt with a relative demanding money you never borrowed? How did you handle it without destroying the relationship with your family? I would also appreciate any advice on whether I should involve our father, who is in Abeokuta and rarely gets involved, or my uncle, who gave me the money in the first place.

Thank you for reading. Any honest advice is welcome, even if it is hard to hear.

input:
I've been lurking on this forum for a while, but I finally need some advice from people who have been in a similar spot. My partner and I have been together for about four years, and for most of that time things were fine. Lately though, there's a lot of tension over money. We both work, but whenever we sit down to talk about budgeting, it turns into an argument about who spends more on family obligations and who is doing 'enough.' I feel like I'm always the one being judged, and I'm exhausted from defending every naira I send home.

I've tried bringing it up calmly, and I've also tried writing things down so we can look at the numbers together without emotion. Neither worked very well. Every time I suggest a shared account or a fixed monthly allowance for each of us, the conversation drifts back to old grievances about things that happened years ago. I don't want to walk away from a relationship I still care about, but I also don't want to keep feeling resentful every time a bill comes in.

So my question is this: has anyone found a way to separate personal finances from family duties without it becoming a fight? Are there specific conversation approaches or tools that actually helped? And if you went to a counsellor or a mediator, how did you find the right one and was it worth it? Any honest experiences would mean a lot.

input: I stood at the back of the kitchen for most of my life, watching my mum hum over the stove and pretend she wasn't listening to every word we said. She taught me that a cup of tea can fix almost anything, and that you never leave a neighbour without something warm to take home. She was stubborn, funny in a dry way that sometimes took people a while to catch, and fiercely loyal to the people she loved. I will miss the sound of her laugh drifting down the hall, and I will carry her recipes, her opinions and her impossible standards with me for the rest of my days. input:
Hi all, long time lurker, first time posting. I moved from Manchester to Toronto about eight months ago for a job at a logistics firm, and I'm finding it harder to make friends than I expected. My partner is settled in with her own work, so most of my days are just me and a laptop in a flat I still don't feel at home in.

The one real connection I've made is with a colleague, Priya Desai. She's 34 and grew up in Brampton, so she knows the city inside out. She's the one who told me about the running group that meets on Saturdays at the lakefront, and she's been kind enough to show me around. We get coffee most weeks now, which feels like a small victory. The thing is, she's been pulling back a bit lately, and I can't tell if I've done something wrong or if she's just busy.

I'm also not sure how to handle the social side more generally. Back home I had a pub quiz team, a five-a-side game, and friends I'd known since school. Here everyone seems to already have their circles. I tried one of those meetup apps and went to a board game night in February where I knew nobody and left after forty minutes. I've been posting photos of my runs on Instagram under @hughnorrisruns, mostly to keep a record for myself, but I've gotten a couple of messages from people I don't know, which felt odd.

So my questions are these. How do you turn a work acquaintance into an actual friend without it feeling forced? Is it normal to ask someone out for a drink when you've only known them through the office? And for anyone who has moved countries as an adult, how long did it take before you stopped feeling like a visitor?

I'm also happy to hear what worked for you specifically. I've started going to the Saturday run at 8am from my place on Dundas Street West, so if anyone local is around, come say hi. Thanks in advance for any advice, and sorry this got so long.

input:
Okay so, I'm just going to talk into this because I can't be bothered typing, sorry in advance for the rambling. So the thing with Italy, right, you think you're going to be relaxed about the whole trip and then the train from the airport takes forever and nobody tells you which platform anything is on. Anyway. The place we stayed in had this tiny balcony that looked out over a courtyard, and every morning someone downstairs was hanging out washing and singing, badly, which was honestly the best part. Hannah kept saying we should get up early to see the sunrise but then we never did, we just stayed in bed with the window open listening to the bells.

And the food. I know everyone says this but I genuinely don't think I'll ever be able to eat a sandwich again without being disappointed. We had this little place near the old walls where the owner basically refused to let us order the thing we wanted and just kept bringing out plates. Hannah was trying to explain she was vegetarian and he just nodded and brought her something with ham anyway, and we both got a bit of a laugh about that afterwards. Some of the best meals were the ones we didn't plan at all.

We finally made it to Asheville in the second week of August, and I can already tell this trip is going to be one of my favorites. My name is Sarah Lindqvist, but my friends have always called me Sarah too, nothing fancy there. I flew in after a long week at Brightwater Logistics in Columbus, where my manager promised she would not email me for five whole days. She lasted about two. My sister Megan joined me from Charlotte, and we spent the first morning wandering the River Arts District while she told me, again, about her residency at Mercy Hill Hospital. We laughed the whole time.

The Blue Ridge Parkway was the highlight. We drove it slowly on August 14th, stopping at every overlook, and Megan kept insisting on taking photos for her portfolio. I got a little carsick on the switchbacks, which she still teases me about. Sarah's rule for road trips is simple: always have snacks and a playlist, and never trust the GPS near the mountains. We learned that the hard way near Mount Mitchell.

If you visit, book your cabin early, because Asheville fills up fast in late summer. We stayed near the old Carrier Park area, which felt quiet and close to everything. I would happily go back, maybe with a few more days off so I can actually relax. Write to me at sarah.lindqvist@gmail.com if you want my full list of restaurants and hiking trails.

Ciao a tutti, ho bisogno di un consiglio da chi ci è già passato. Sono Alessia, ho 34 anni e lavoro come grafica freelance da quasi cinque anni a Bologna. Da qualche mese ho un problema con la mia collega e amica Giulia Ferrante, con cui condividevo lo studio fino a dicembre. Lei ha iniziato a prendersi i lavori che avevo proposto io ai clienti, e quando le ho chiesto spiegazioni ha risposto come se fossi io quella che esagera.

Il punto è che non so se sia una questione di malinteso o se stia davvero cercando di farmi fuori. Il 9 gennaio ha presentato a un cliente di Modena un progetto identità visiva che era nato dalla mia bozza di settembre. Quando l'ho scoperto, le ho scritto una mail molto dura, forse troppo, e ci siamo sentite solo tramite avvocati di pari livello... no, scherzo, ma è stata una discussione pesante. Il suo indirizzo di lavoro è giulia.ferrante@studiokappa.it, se qualcuno volesse capire il contesto.

Ancora non ci siamo chiarite. Giulia dice che abbiamo lavorato insieme alla bozza e che quindi la proposta è condivisa, ma io non ricordo nessuna riunione in cui se ne sia parlato. Ho anche pensato di parlarne con Marco, il nostro titolare, ma ho paura che la prenda come una lamentela da bambina e che poi la situazione peggiori. Dall'altra parte non voglio nemmeno lasciar correre, perché i clienti sono il mio sostentamento.

Vi chiedo: avete mai vissuto qualcosa di simile con un collega che consideravate un amico? È meglio affrontarlo in privato, metterlo per iscritto o portarlo subito davanti al titolare? E come si fa a non farsi travolgere dalla rabbia quando si sente di aver perso qualcosa di proprio? Ogni consiglio è benvenuto, anche quelli duri.

Grazie in anticipo, Alessia

July 9th. Dr. Lavi asked me to write these down between sessions, so here goes, even though I keep thinking nobody else will read them. I've been living at 14 Rehov HaYarkon in the Florentin neighbourhood of Tel Aviv for almost three years now, and some mornings the noise from the scooters and the bakery below still catches me off guard. My name is Maya, and I am trying to be kinder to myself than I was last month.

This week was harder than I expected. On Tuesday I cancelled plans with Noa for the third time, and when she texted me "you okay?" I stared at the screen for twenty minutes before I wrote back that I was fine. I'm not fine. I know I'm not fine. Noa has known me since our army days and she deserves better than my half-answers. I told Dr. Lavi I'd reach out to her properly, maybe tomorrow, maybe after the weekend.

On Thursday I finally called the clinic from the balcony, my hands shaking a little, and left a message on the line at 03-555-0182 asking whether the Wednesday group could move to evenings. The receptionist, Ruthi, called back within the hour and was patient about it. I felt a small, stupid flash of pride that I had made the call at all. Later I emailed the group coordinator at maya.kessler.therapy@mailbox.co.il to confirm the change, and the reply came back with a cheerful thumbs-up that somehow made me cry.

I'm trying to notice the good parts too. I walked to the Carmel Market on Friday morning, bought too many apricots, and sat on a low wall eating them while an old man played oud for nobody in particular. Nothing dramatic happened. But I stayed in the moment for a while, which is the thing I keep being asked to practise.

Dr. Lavi suggested I write one thing I am grateful for each day. Today it's the apricots, and Ruthi's voice, and the fact that I am still here writing this. I'll try again tomorrow, and I'll try to call Noa.

input:
When I first landed in Lisbon last March, I had no idea that the little cafe on Rua da Madalena would become my second kitchen. Freddie, the owner, remembers my order before I open my mouth, and on my first real Monday there he taped a handwritten note to my laptop: "Freddie says welcome, Fiona!" It was the kind of small kindness I had forgotten existed after eleven years in Leeds, where I was born in a terraced house and worked as a project coordinator for a logistics firm called Northgate Freight. Moving countries at thirty-four was supposed to be a reset. Instead it turned out to be a long conversation with myself about what I actually want from a life.

The transition has not been all pastries and sunsets. Bureaucracy here runs on paper, patience and the right stamp, and I spent most of October chasing a tax number through three offices in the Baixa. Friends back home keep asking how I cope, and the honest answer is that I lean on people more than I ever did before. My Portuguese teacher, Inês, once told me that the trick is to stop translating everything in your head. She was right. Last week I ordered a bifana at a tiny tasca without rehearsing a single sentence, and the owner laughed and called me "a Lisboeta now."

If you are planning a similar move, my advice is simple: find your corner early. Mine is that cafe, a gym called Ginásio Sete Colinas where I go before work, and a standing Sunday phone call with my sister. Follow my little adventures on Instagram at @fionawanders_lx, and if you ever want a real map of the city, the best one is the one drawn by the people you meet on the same street, day after day.

When I think about why I want to study Chemical Engineering at Imperial, I keep coming back to the summer I spent working at my uncle's garage in Leeds. Nadia was the name everyone there used for me, though my passport says Nadia Farooqi and my school reports say N. Farooqi, which I still find funny. I was the one who sorted the parts bin and kept the diagnostic logbook, and I quickly learned that most problems in an engine are really problems of flow, heat and chemistry, even when they look mechanical.

On 14 May last year I stripped down a 2009 Vauxhall Corsa, registration KX09 FRL, after it had been losing coolant for weeks. The head gasket was fine, but the coolant had degraded and was forming deposits that blocked the radiator. Working out why that happened, and what additive chemistry would prevent it, was the first time a textbook idea felt directly useful to me. My uncle still jokes that I was more interested in the coolant data sheets than in the car.

If you read my application in full, you will also see that I have been volunteering with a local water-testing project run from Leeds, which is how I first met the team at the university. I would welcome any questions at nadia.farooqi@leedsmail.co.uk, and I am hoping the next chapter of my education will take me well beyond the garage.

input:
When I finally left Manchester last spring, I told everyone I was going to 'see how Lisbon felt', and six months later I still haven't got a clear answer. My name is Gareth Whitcombe, though the baristas at Café Lusitano in Alfama have decided I'm just 'Gaz', which I've stopped correcting. That little cafe on Rua de São Miguel has become my unofficial office: strong espresso, a window seat, and a owner who somehow remembers I take my pastéis de nata warm. If you ever need to reach me about the flat or anything else, my Portuguese mobile is +351 912 774 083, though I'll admit I often forget to charge it.

The move itself was far messier than the blog posts make it sound. In February I spent nearly three weeks sorting residence paperwork, chasing a bank that wouldn't accept my old UK address, and sitting in waiting rooms that smelled of toner and damp coats. I ended up registering with a clinic in Graça, a small place run by two doctors who speak better English than I speak Portuguese, which was a relief when I had a nasty chest infection on the 14th of February and couldn't face explaining my symptoms in a second language.

Still, the small wins add up. I joined a local gym near Martim Moniz mostly to justify the membership fee, and I've been going four mornings a week since. The regulars have adopted me, and I now get asked, every single session, whether I've mastered the Portuguese word for 'heavy'. I haven't, but I'm getting closer, and that feels like progress worth writing about.

input:
To the Customer Relations Team,

I am writing to register a formal complaint about the delivery service I received on my most recent order. I placed the order several weeks ago through your website, and the item was promised within a standard window. It did not arrive within that window, and when I contacted your support line I was given conflicting information about where the parcel was and when I could expect it.

I should explain my circumstances, as they make this more than a minor inconvenience. I recently relocated from one country to another, so I rely heavily on online services to receive goods that I cannot easily purchase locally. Your company was one I trusted for exactly that reason. When a delivery fails, I lose not only time but the confidence that made me use your service in the first place.

When the parcel finally arrived, the packaging had been crushed on one side and the contents were damaged. I photographed the box and the item before opening it fully, and I have attached those images to this letter. I then followed the returns procedure described on your website, but the reference code I was given did not match any record in your system. Three separate agents gave me three different instructions, and none of them resolved the matter.

I would like the following addressed. First, a full refund for the item, including the delivery charge, since the service did not meet the terms you advertised. Second, a written explanation of why my order was handled in the way it was, so that I understand what went wrong. Third, a clear and single point of contact for any further correspondence, so that I am not passed between departments again.

I have always found your products to be well made, and I would prefer to continue as a customer. However, a fair resolution to this matter is essential to that. I look forward to your reply within ten working days.

Yours faithfully,

L. Ashworth-Vale

Zara Okonkwo-Lindqvist is a senior data engineer at Brightline Analytics, where she leads the team that builds real-time pipelines for regional hospital networks. Born and raised in Columbus, Ohio, she spent her twenties in Chicago before returning to the Midwest, and today she lives in Madison, Wisconsin with her partner and two rescue greyhounds. At 37, she has spent more than a decade turning messy clinical data into systems that clinicians can actually trust.

Her talk at this year's conference, "Stop Trusting the Dashboard," draws on a project from last June, when Zara and her team discovered that a single timezone bug had been silently misreporting patient wait times for almost two years. She will walk through how they found it, how they fixed it, and what the process changed about their testing habits. Zara is also a volunteer mentor with Girls Who Code Madison and a regular contributor to the local data meetup.

Attendees who want to follow up can reach Zara directly at 608-555-0147 or through the conference app. Zara says she is always happy to hear from people who are early in their careers or who have inherited a data mess they are not sure how to untangle. Her slides will be posted to the event site after her session on Thursday, June 12.

input:
When I was nine, my grandmother taught me that a good story needs a proper ending, and I have been looking for one ever since. Growing up in a small Irish town where everyone knows the name of your dog and the route of your morning bus, I learned early that people are more interesting than the places they live. My reading began with whatever was lying around the kitchen table: old newspapers, a battered copy of a ghost anthology, the back of a seed packet. Each one taught me that words can carry a whole life in a few lines.

As I got older, that curiosity turned toward the question of why some communities stay together while others scatter. During a summer project with a local heritage group, I spent weeks recording the memories of people who had lived on the same stretch of road for seventy years. One woman described the winter of her childhood in such precise detail that I could almost feel the cold coming through the window. I realised then that history is not a distant subject. It is something people carry in their hands, in their recipes, and in the way they greet a stranger.

That project also showed me the limits of what I knew. I had assumed I understood rural life because I came from one, but the people I interviewed corrected me again and again. Their stories were more complicated than my own memories, and listening to them taught me patience. I started to take notes differently, asking questions that left room for silence and for disagreement. I learned that a record is only as honest as the listener who makes it.

I want to continue this work at university, where I hope to study social history with a focus on oral sources. I am drawn to the way archives can be made more open, so that people who were never written into official records can finally speak for themselves. I would like to learn the methods that scholars use to test memory against documents, and to contribute to projects that give ordinary lives the attention they deserve.

Finally, I believe the most valuable thing a student can bring to a university is a willingness to be changed by what they hear. My grandmother was right about endings: they matter less than the care taken in getting there. I hope to spend the next few years learning how to tell stories well, and how to listen even better, so that the voices I have grown up with can keep being heard.

input:
I felt worse this week than I expected to, and I'm trying not to read too much into that. The anxiety came back on Tuesday in the middle of a meeting, that tight feeling in my chest and the sense that everyone in the room could see me falling apart. I left early and sat in the car for a long time before I could drive. Afterwards I noticed I had been holding my breath for most of the afternoon without realising it, which feels like something worth bringing to you.

I did try some of the things we talked about. I went for a walk without my phone, which was harder than it sounds, and I counted the things I could hear on the way round the block. On Thursday I wrote down the thought that kept looping, "I'm going to be found out," and then tried to write down the evidence for and against it. The evidence against was actually quite strong, which surprised me. Some days I can hold onto that; other days it slips away almost immediately.

I think what I want to work on next is the gap between knowing something rationally and feeling it in my body. I can tell myself I'm safe, and I believe it at my desk, but the feeling doesn't always follow. I'd like to talk about whether there's a way to practise staying with the discomfort rather than rushing to make it stop, because the rushing seems to make it louder. I'm not sure how realistic that is yet, but it feels like the right direction.

input:
Last May I finally made the drive west from Dublin, and I can say without exaggeration that the Burren was worth every mile. My name is Aidan Keogh, I'm 34, and I work as a surveyor for Corrigan Geotech in Kilkenny, so landscapes are usually something I measure rather than admire. That afternoon I forgot the clipboard entirely. The limestone pavements stretched out in grey slabs, cracked into clints and grikes, and tiny wildflowers, mountain avens and orchids, were pushing up through the gaps like they had something to prove.

I stayed two nights in Ballyvaughan, in a small guesthouse run by a woman who knew every walking route in the parish. She gave me a printed map, circled three trails, and told me to avoid the coastal path after rain. I followed her advice on the second morning and walked up toward Mullaghmore with a flask of tea and a sandwich I'd bought from the village shop. Nobody else was on the hill until almost noon. If you want to plan something similar, my details are on the booking form, but honestly just email me at aidan.keogh@corrigangeotech.ie with questions. I'll gladly tell you where the best tea is.

Keep your passport handy when you cross over from the north, though: the guesthouse asked for my passport number (P1234567) at check-in, and it's worth having it ready on the ferry from Rosslare too. Otherwise, pack layers, good boots and a little patience. The weather here changes faster than any survey instrument I've ever used.

A flat white and a slice of lemon drizzle is my idea of a good Saturday. On weekday mornings you'll find me at Galway Fit Hub doing a class that's more about surviving than enjoying, but I keep going back. I also run the coastal path in Salthill when the weather allows, which in Galway means roughly three days a month.

I'm looking for someone who can hold a proper conversation, laugh at their own terrible puns, and doesn't mind that I'll happily spend a whole afternoon reading in a pub corner. A bit about the practical side: I'm happy to verify myself before we meet, so if you want to be extra cautious you can ask for my passport number, which is P1184572, or my national ID, IRL-882913-K. I'd rather you were careful than rushed. You can reach me at aoife.kelleher88@gmail.com, though I'm better on a phone call than a text thread, so my number is 087 412 9036 if you prefer to chat first.

My December is usually a blur of Christmas shifts and last-minute gift runs, so I'd love to meet before the festive chaos fully takes over, perhaps on the 6th or the 13th. Coffee at Bean & Bloom would be the easiest start, and I'll bring my best attempt at small talk.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart for my mother, Vera Dunleavy, who died peacefully at home on 14 July, surrounded by family. Vera was born in Ballina, County Mayo, and never really left the west, though she spent forty years on Cathedral Road in Sligo where she raised the four of us. She worked as a bookkeeper for the Cassidy Marine yard for thirty-one years and could tell you the balance of any account from memory.

I'm Niamh, the youngest, and I will miss her ringing me every Sunday at half nine sharp. She loved the garden, the Sunday Mass in St. Joseph's, and a good argument about politics. If you want to share a memory, you can reach me at niamh.dunleavy@sligomail.ie or follow the family page on Instagram at @vera_dunleavy_memories, where my brother Ciaran has been posting old photographs.

Vera's close friend and neighbour, Maureen Gilhooly, has asked that donations be made to the Sligo Hospice in lieu of flowers. Vera would have liked that. Her funeral will take place at St. Joseph's on Thursday 17 July, followed by burial in Drumcliffe. Please join us to celebrate a life well lived.

input:
Dear Oma,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden is coming along nicely. I know how much you love the autumn roses, so I thought of you when I walked past the Hauptstraße florist last week. It has been almost three months since I moved into my new flat in Leipzig, and I still get lost on the tram lines, but the neighbourhood is growing on me.

My friends tease me that I have become a proper Leipziger already. Mostly I spend my evenings reading in the little café on the corner, or walking along the Pleisse with my sister's dog, Biscuit, who has decided that every puddle is a personal challenge. Mama says you are still not sleeping well, so please promise me you will call when you need company. Lukas said he would drive over from Dresden on the 14th of September if the weather holds, and we could have lunch together in the old market square.

My birthday is coming up on the 22nd of September and I will be thirty-four, which feels strangely grown up. I keep thinking about how you used to bake for every one of my birthdays, even when money was tight. I am trying to learn your apple cake recipe from the notebook you gave me, but my version always comes out a little too dense. Perhaps you can show me properly when I visit.

I have also been thinking a lot about the family history you shared last spring, about the letters from Grandpa's time in Hamburg. I would love to see them again, if you are willing to lend them to me. I promise to keep them safe and bring them back in one piece.

Please write back when you can, even if it is only a few lines. You can send a note to my email at marlene.kolb@mailbox-de.net or post it to me at Karl-Liebknecht-Straße 47, 04107 Leipzig. I miss you terribly and I will see you soon.

With all my love,
Marlene

Bedankt voor je bericht van vorige week en sorry dat ik zo lang heb laten liggen. Het is hier de laatste tijd erg druk geweest met de verhuizing en het papierwerk. Zoals je weet ben ik in juni naar Utrecht verhuisd, en sindsdien leer ik nog steeds hoe alles hier werkt. Ik woon nu in een klein appartement aan de Oudegracht, met uitzicht op het water, wat ik eerlijk gezegd heerlijk vind.

Voor het werk ben ik sinds 1 augustus aangesteld als Senior Data Engineer bij Vandermeer Analytics B.V. Het team is klein maar enthousiast, en de projecten die ik mag doen zijn precies wat ik zocht. Mijn eerste weken waren vooral gevuld met inwerken en het regelen van de administratie. Dat laatste was gelukkig minder ingewikkeld dan ik vreesde, al moest ik wel mijn paspoort en een kopie van mijn Nederlandse BSN-document laten zien aan de HR-afdeling. Ik heb ook mijn gegevens gedeeld met de Belastingdienst, zodat mijn salaris goed verwerkt wordt.

Het is misschien niet relevant voor je, maar ik wil je wel iets vertellen over de bankzaken. Mijn rekening staat op naam van Rowan Callister, zoals je weet, en ik heb inmiddels ook een Nederlands mobiel nummer. Voor alles wat met het werk te maken heeft kun je me gewoon bereiken op rowan.callister@vandermeer-analytics.nl. Privé gebruik ik nog steeds mijn oude adres, rowan.callister@mailbox.co.uk, maar dat lees ik minder vaak.

Ik hoor graag wanneer het jou schikt. Laat me ook weten of je nog steeds op 18 augustus in Leeds bent, dan stuur ik je de details van de conferentie die ik daar wil bezoeken.

Nogmaals bedankt voor al je steun in de afgelopen maanden. Zonder jouw advies had ik deze stap waarschijnlijk niet durven zetten. Ik hoop snel van je te horen.

Hartelijke groet,

Rowan Callister
Senior Data Engineer
Vandermeer Analytics B.V.
Utrecht

input:
Hello from the Year 6 corner! Many of you have asked how I'm settling in, so here is a short update from me, Hannah Whitcombe, the new classroom assistant who joined us this term after moving across from Toronto.

The move was a big step for my family. We left Ontario in late July and spent our first weeks in a rented flat near the river in Bristol while we waited for our furniture to arrive by sea. Everything feels unfamiliar at first, from the way people queue at the bus stop to the fact that the shops close so early on a Sunday. I still catch myself saying "washroom" instead of "loo", and the children have been very patient about correcting me.

On 14 August we celebrated my son Owen's ninth birthday with a small picnic in the park, and I was touched by how many of his new classmates turned up with cards. It made the place feel a little more like home. Owen has been reading non-stop and has already joined the school chess club, which he tells me is the only thing he has been able to win since we arrived!

My role here is Teaching Assistant (Literacy) at St Brendan's Primary School, and I have been working alongside Mrs Patel, the Year 6 class teacher, to run small reading groups each morning. Please do drop in if you would like to hear more about how the groups work. I am always happy to share ideas, and I have learned a great deal from the staff and families who have welcomed me so warmly.

If you have any tips for a newcomer, such as the best place to buy wellies or which local walks are worth the effort, I would love to hear them. You can reach me through the school office on 0117 496 2280 or by emailing hannah.whitcombe@stbrendans.example.

Thank you all for making us feel so welcome. I look forward to getting to know many more of you over the coming term.

Meeting notes, team sync. I took these down myself since nobody else was writing anything. We started a bit late because the projector would not connect, and in the end we just used the laptop screen and everyone squinted together. The main item was the backlog. We have far too many open tickets from the last quarter and very few of them have a clear owner. Everyone agreed that the first step is to close out the ones that are already done in practice, even if nobody updated them.

On the release side, the QA group flagged two issues that block the next build. One is a crash on older handsets when the image gallery loads more than a certain number of photos. The other is a layout problem on smaller screens where the submit button sits under the keyboard. Both are reproducible, and both were assigned on the spot. I said I would check whether the crash is also present on the web version before we decide how urgent it is.

We spent a while on the hiring plan. The team is short by two people and the current workload is making people tired. There was a fair amount of back and forth about whether we should bring in a contractor now to cover the gap or wait for a full-time candidate. My own view is that waiting will cost us more, but I could see the point of those who worry about onboarding someone new in the middle of a busy stretch. We did not reach a decision and will revisit it next week.

The last part of the meeting was about communication with the other departments. Several people said they often hear about changes only after they have already been made. We agreed to post a short weekly summary in the shared channel, with a simple list of what shipped, what is blocked and what is coming up. Someone will need to own that summary, and we will rotate it.

Before we closed, I asked everyone to send me their action items by the end of the day so I can consolidate them. Most people agreed. The mood was positive overall, although a couple of people looked exhausted, and I think we all know that needs attention soon.

I stand here today with a heavy heart, and I want to say how grateful I am to every one of you for coming. Many of you knew her as a neighbour, a colleague, a friend at the market or someone who could always be counted on to bring soup when life got hard. She had a way of making every guest feel expected, as though the house had been waiting all week just for them. Her kitchen was never quiet. There was always the clatter of pans, someone laughing at the table, and the smell of garlic and fresh basil drifting out into the courtyard.

She taught me that patience is a form of love. She would sit for hours with a difficult plant, a stubborn sauce or a child who would not stop crying, and she never once rushed any of them. When I was younger I thought her calm was simply who she was. Only later did I understand how much effort it took, and how often she chose kindness when it would have been easier to choose anything else.

So today, let us not only grieve what we have lost. Let us carry forward the small things she gave us: a warm welcome, a seat at the table, and the willingness to slow down for the people who matter. If you find yourself cooking for someone this week, think of her. That is how I will keep her close, and I hope you will too.

input:
When I think about why I want to study environmental science, I remember the summer I spent helping at a community garden on the edge of town. Nobody there had a degree in anything related to soil or water, but every person in that garden knew exactly how the land behaved after a hard rain and how the first frost changed the plants. That knowledge was practical, shared freely, and passed from one neighbour to the next. It taught me that science is not only something that happens in laboratories; it is also something people carry in their hands and their habits.

What I found most striking was how often the questions we asked each other ended in uncertainty. Why were the tomatoes splitting this year? Was the drainage ditch along the fence slowing the runoff, or just moving the problem somewhere else? Our answers were rarely clean. We tested, we argued, we changed one thing at a time and watched carefully. I came to value that patience. I want to learn the methods that turn these everyday observations into evidence that can guide decisions about water quality, farmland and the wider ecosystems that depend on them.

My own path has not been a straight line. I began my schooling expecting to pursue medicine, and I still admire the people who do. Over time, though, I noticed that my attention kept drifting outside, toward rivers, wetlands and the slow processes that shape them. Taking a introductory geology course and then an ecology seminar gave me language for those interests. I started reading research papers for pleasure, which surprised me, and I began to see that the careful, unglamorous work of monitoring a single watershed can matter as much as any dramatic discovery.

I am also aware that environmental problems do not respect boundaries between disciplines. Solving them requires chemists who understand contaminants, engineers who can design filtration, economists who can weigh costs, and community members who know what the land has meant to them over generations. I want to be the kind of scientist who listens across those divides. Working with people who have a different relationship to a place has already changed how I ask questions, and I hope to deepen that habit in a university setting that values collaboration.

Every autumn, the garden I worked in is cleared and the beds are covered for winter. The soil rests, and so, in its way, does the community that tends it. I think often of that rhythm when I imagine my future work: periods of intense effort followed by reflection, and a steady commitment to understanding the places we share. I am ready to bring that commitment to your program, and I look forward to learning from the researchers, classmates and local communities who will help me grow into the scientist I hope to become.

הנזק לרכב שלי היה משמעותי. הפגוש הקדמי נשבר לשניים, פנס הערפל השמאלי התנפץ, וכנף הקדמית הימנית נסדקה לאורכה. לפי הערכת המוסך בקריית ים, שאליו הובלתי את הרכב לאחר התאונה, עלות התיקון מוערכת בכ-18,500 ש"ח. צירפתי לתביעה את דוח השמאי, את צילומי הנזק ואת תצהיר העד שמסר לי השכן, יוסי בן דוד, שראה את הנסיעה של הרכב האחר.

input:
To the Customer Relations Team,

I am writing to formally complain about the faulty dishwasher my partner and I purchased from your Parramatta store on 3 December. The unit was delivered to our home at 14 Carrington Street, Lidcombe, NSW, on 9 December, and within four days it had begun leaking water onto the kitchen floor. I have photographed the damage and retained the receipt, which shows order number AU-448213.

When I called your service line on 12 December, I was told a technician would attend within five business days. No one came. I rang again on 18 December and spoke to a representative named Matthew, who promised a callback that never arrived. I am now writing because I have been passed between three departments and have received no written response to my first email, sent on 10 December from hannah.whitfield@brightkitchen.com.au.

I should explain who I am, since it may affect how you handle this. I work as a Senior Procurement Analyst at Harbourline Logistics in Sydney, so I understand supplier warranties and consumer guarantees better than most. I was born in Ballarat and have lived in Sydney for eleven years, and my friends still call me Hal. None of that should matter here, but I mention it so you know I am not a casual complainant. I expect a considered reply, not a template.

The Australian Consumer Law guarantees that goods must be of acceptable quality and fit for their purpose, and that a major failure entitles the buyer to a refund or replacement. A dishwasher that floods a kitchen within a week of delivery is, in my view, a major failure. I am therefore requesting a full refund of the purchase price, reimbursement of the $87 I spent on a plumber to check the water line, and collection of the unit at your cost.

Please respond in writing within fourteen days of the date of this letter, to the address above or by email. If I do not hear from you by 28 December, I will lodge a complaint with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and seek advice about small claims proceedings. I would prefer to resolve this directly, and I look forward to your prompt reply.

Yours faithfully,

Harold Vandermeer

Bonjour à tous, et merci d'être venus si nombreux ce samedi 14 août pour fêter Pauline et Julien. Je m'appelle Thomas Lefèbvre, je suis le frère de Julien, et je vous avoue que préparer ce discours a été l'épreuve la plus difficile de ma vie, bien plus que le bac ou le permis de conduire.

J'ai connu Julien en 1998, dans la cour de l'école Jules Ferry à Lyon. Il avait une casquette trop grande et il m'a prêté son ballon de foot sans même me connaître. Vingt-cinq ans plus tard, c'est toujours le même garçon généreux. Quand il a rencontré Pauline, à une soirée chez des amis, il m'a appelé le lendemain pour me dire : « Tom, j'ai trouvé quelqu'un. » Je ne l'avais jamais entendu parler comme ça.

Pauline, tu as fait quelque chose d'extraordinaire : tu as réussi à faire rire Julien de ses propres blagues, ce qui n'est pas peu dire. Tu as aussi supporté ses playlists de rock des années quatre-vingt dans la voiture, et ça, c'est de l'amour. Tu as accueilli notre famille avec une chaleur qui nous a tous touchés, maman en particulier, qui ne parle plus que de toi depuis Pâques.

Je voudrais aussi remercier mon ami Hugo Marchand, qui a été le témoin de Julien pendant les préparatifs. Hugo a passé des heures au téléphone avec le traiteur, avec le maire et avec moi, et il n'a jamais perdu son calme. Si vous avez besoin d'un organisateur fiable, son numéro est le 06 45 73 12 98, et il vous dira que je ne suis pas le plus patient des hommes.

Si vous voulez suivre les aventures de ce couple, Pauline a ouvert un compte Instagram pour partager les photos du voyage en Corse, il s'appelle @pauline.and.jules.2024. Je vous encourage à la suivre, elle poste bien mieux que son mari. Et pour les formalités administratives du voyage de noces, il faudra que Julien retrouve sa carte nationale d'identité numéro 12AB34567 : il l'a déjà perdue deux fois.

Alors levez vos verres à Pauline et Julien. À la santé des mariés, au bonheur qui les attend, et à la prochaine fois où Julien me rendra mon ballon de foot, si toutefois il le fait un jour.

input: I stand here today with a heavy heart and a full memory of everything she gave us. For as long as I can remember, she was the one who kept the kitchen warm, who knew exactly how each of us liked our coffee, and who never once let a birthday pass without a handwritten card. Her laughter could fill a crowded room, and her patience with the rest of us was endless. Today we grieve her, but we also celebrate a life lived with generosity, stubborn kindness, and an open door. I will miss her more than words can carry, and I will carry her with me always.

input:
We pulled into Asheville on a humid June afternoon, Tamsin hanging out the passenger window like a golden retriever while I fought for parking near the river. Our Airbnb was at 417 Maple Hollow Road, a converted barn with a wraparound porch and a hammock that Tamsin claimed within four minutes of arrival. She had booked the place herself, using the account number 40218873 that she insisted on reading out to me twice in the car, just in case I wanted to be the one who forgot it. The host, a retired potter named Gilda, left a jar of local honey and a handwritten note about the best trail for sunset.

We spent the next two days wandering the River Arts District, where Tamsin bought a ceramic mug she swore she would use every morning and then never did. On June 14 we had dinner reservations at a tiny Appalachian kitchen downtown, and she wore the green dress she had been saving for months. The waiter brought us cornbread with whipped butter and a story about his grandmother's recipe that made Tamsin cry a little, in the good way. I kept thinking how lucky we were to be the kind of travelers who stop and listen.

On our last morning we drove the Blue Ridge Parkway with the windows down, rental plate ABC-4471 bumping along the switchbacks, and stopped at every overlook. Tamsin took about two hundred photos and deleted most of them before breakfast. If you ever find yourself in western North Carolina in June, go slowly, eat the cornbread, and let someone like Gilda tell you where the sunset is best.

I'm writing these notes up while the impressions are still fresh, mostly so I don't lose the thread of what we agreed. The meeting took place in a small conference room that smelled faintly of espresso, which feels appropriate for a team based in Italy. Most of the discussion centred on the backlog. We have too many half-finished features and not enough people closing them out, so the first decision was to freeze new requests for the rest of the quarter and focus on what is already in progress.

I raised a concern about the review process, which I think has become a bottleneck. Pull requests sit for days waiting for a second pair of eyes, and by the time feedback arrives the author has moved on to something else, so context gets lost. Several people agreed. We discussed a rotating reviewer schedule and a smaller threshold for what counts as a change that needs sign-off. Nobody wanted to add more process for its own sake, so we agreed to try it for two weeks and then revisit.

The second topic was documentation. Right now the knowledge lives mostly in people's heads, and that is fine until someone is away or leaves. There was broad support for a short onboarding guide and a habit of writing a few lines in the ticket before starting work. It was also suggested that we record a short walkthrough of the deployment pipeline, which would save a lot of repeated explanation.

We ran out of time before getting to the hiring question, so that has been pushed to the next session. Before we wrap up, I want to confirm the action items. The backlog freeze takes effect immediately, the review rotation starts after the current sprint, and the documentation owner still needs to be named. I'll follow up on that by message once I've checked who has capacity.

Overall it was a productive hour. There was less disagreement than I expected and more willingness to try something different. I'll circulate a clean version of these notes once the owners have confirmed their items, and I'd welcome corrections if I've misremembered anything from the discussion.

I am writing to describe the water damage that occurred in my basement on the night of the storm. I came home from work to find about two inches of water across the finished floor, which had soaked the carpet, the drywall along the north wall, and several boxes of stored clothing. The sump pump had stopped working, and I believe the power outage that evening was the cause. I shut off the main electrical breaker as a precaution before going down the stairs, and I stayed out of the room until the water was pumped out by a restoration crew the following morning.

The damage includes the carpet and underlay in the rec room, roughly two-thirds of the lower drywall on the north and east walls, the baseboard trim, and a freestanding bookshelf that was warped beyond repair. Some personal items were also lost, including a leather armchair, a box of family photographs that had been stored on the lowest shelf, and a winter coat and boots. I have kept all damaged items where possible and taken photographs before disposal. I have also saved the receipts for the emergency pumping and the dehumidifier rental.

input:
When people ask me where I come from, I usually say Haifa, but the truth is more specific. I grew up on Yefe Nof Street in the Hadar neighbourhood, in a third-floor apartment where the balcony looked down on a falafel stand that my family considered a second kitchen. My grandmother, whom everyone calls Bubbi Rachel, taught me to read Hebrew newspapers at that same balcony table, insisting that headlines were the fastest way to understand a city's moods.

My full name is Maya Levkovich, but on the bus and at the corner shop I have always been just Mimi. The nickname stuck when I was four, after my cousin failed to pronounce my name and I decided the mistake was better. It is the name my teachers at Gordon Secondary School still use, and it is the name I want to carry into the classroom of a journalism program. On October 14, 2023, I wrote my first published piece for the school paper, an account of the neighbourhood's bakery closing after forty years. That article taught me that small local stories can explain larger changes.

I am applying because I want to tell stories like that with more rigour and reach. I have spent two summers interning with a community radio station, and I have learned that listening is the core skill of reporting. Hadar taught me to pay attention to the people who are often overlooked, and I hope your program will help me turn that attention into work that matters beyond my own street.

input:
When I first walked into the Brisbane Youth Mentoring Hub in March, I had no idea that the coordinator, Wendy Okafor, would become the person who shaped my understanding of what leadership really means. Wendy had been running the program for nine years, and she treated every volunteer like a future colleague. I was seventeen, anxious about everything, and convinced I had nothing useful to offer. Wendy simply asked me what I was good at and then gave me a group of eleven students to support. Over the following months I learned that the most valuable thing I could do was listen.

The hardest moment came in July, when one of the students, a quiet boy named Tomas, stopped attending sessions. Wendy and I drove out to his house in Logan together. His grandmother, Lydia, answered the door and explained that Tomas had been caring for his younger brother while their mother worked double shifts. Wendy did not lecture anyone. She sat at the kitchen table and asked questions, and by the end of the afternoon we had arranged for the family to access a free after-school program at the local library. Watching her work reminded me that compassion and competence are not opposites.

That experience pushed me toward studying social work. I want to build the kind of systems that catch students like Tomas before they fall through the cracks. My mum, Wanda, a nurse at Princess Alexandra Hospital, has always told me that caring for people is a practical skill as well as a feeling. I now believe she is right, and I am ready to learn the rest.

input:
I have always believed that the most important lessons are learned in ordinary places. For me, that place is Bluebird Coffee on Alder Street in Tacoma, where I spent three mornings a week during my junior year working the espresso bar. My name is Brianna Okafor, and I have been reflecting for months on what those early shifts taught me about responsibility, patience and listening.

I remember my first real test vividly. It was December 9th, the week before finals, and the line stretched past the bookshelf by seven o'clock. A regular named Mr. Halvorsen was furious because his order had been mixed up twice. Instead of apologizing and remaking his drink in a panic, I asked him to tell me exactly what he wanted. He laughed, told me about his late wife's habit of ordering a cortado after church, and by the end of the conversation he had become my most loyal customer. That morning taught me that a problem is often just a story waiting to be heard.

Before I started at Bluebird, I thought of myself as a quiet student who preferred working alone. Those mornings changed that. I learned to run a team of four during the rush, to keep track of inventory on a clipboard when the register failed, and to call our supplier when the milk delivery was late. Each small task required me to step out of my own head and think about what the people around me needed.

This is why I am applying to your public health program. I want to study how communities make decisions about their own wellbeing, and I want to work on the kinds of questions that a coffee bar teaches you to ask: who is being served, who is being missed, and what would make the next morning better. I have already begun speaking with a community clinic on Pacific Avenue about a volunteer intake project, and I hope to bring the same listening habits I developed at Bluebird into that work.

If you would like to confirm any details of my application or my references, you can reach my former manager, Lucas Pereira, at (253) 555-0148. He has watched me grow from someone who dreaded the morning rush into someone who looks forward to it. I hope to carry that same steadiness into your classrooms and into the communities I will serve after graduation.
