To whom it may concern,

I am writing to provide a reference for Lorraine Whitfield, who worked under my supervision as a senior accounts analyst at Maple Ridge Logistics in Mississauga from March 2018 until her departure in January 2024. I have managed finance and operations teams for over fourteen years, and in that time I have rarely worked with someone as thorough, dependable, and quick to take initiative as Lorraine.

Lorraine led the migration of our accounts payable process to a new ledger system in 2021. The project touched every department and involved reconciling nearly four years of vendor records. She built a testing schedule, trained twelve staff members, and resolved the majority of data discrepancies herself before they reached the auditors. The transition finished two months ahead of the original timeline, and our year-end close that spring was the cleanest the company had recorded in a decade.

What distinguished Lorraine most was how she handled pressure. During a supplier dispute in late 2022, when a major client's invoices were delayed by a billing error on their side, she spent three evenings working directly with their finance department to correct the figures. She did not wait to be asked, and she kept me informed without ever making a problem sound bigger than it was. Her colleague Gordon Pritchard, who sat beside her for most of those years, once told me she was the person he trusted most to catch what everyone else had missed. I came to agree with him.

Lorraine is also a generous mentor. Several of the junior analysts who joined the team had their first real experience of month-end reporting under her guidance, and two have since been promoted. She explained not just the procedure but the reasoning behind it, and she was patient with questions that others might have found tedious. Her sister, Marianne, who once worked in the same building in a different department, often spoke of Lorraine's steadiness at home and at work, a quality that was clearly visible to those of us who saw her every day.

I recommend Lorraine Whitfield without reservation for any position requiring careful financial judgment, leadership, and integrity. Please feel free to contact me at 905-555-0147 or at gwen.tremblay@mapler/ ridgelogistics.ca if you would like to discuss her work further.

Sincerely,

Gwendolyn Tremblay
Director of Finance, Maple Ridge Logistics

input:
The first thing that hits you in Lagos is the noise, and I mean that in the best way. Horns blare, vendors call out their wares over the traffic, and somewhere a generator hums so steadily you stop noticing it after a day. I spent most of my first morning just standing at the edge of a busy market, trying to take it all in while a woman balancing a tray of plantain on her head laughed at me for gawking. Nobody minded. People here are quick to share a joke and even quicker to point you toward the best jollof you will ever eat.

What surprised me most was how much of the country's life happens outdoors. Evenings are for sitting on plastic chairs outside a bukka, sharing grilled fish and cold drinks while the street slowly fills up with music and conversation. Travel between cities can be slow and unpredictable, so I learned to build in extra time, keep a little cash on hand, and accept that the plan will change at least twice. The friendly strangers who helped me find the right bus at every stop made those detours feel like part of the adventure rather than a setback.

If you go, pack light clothing, a good hat, and more patience than you think you need. Bring a sense of humour too. The roads, the heat and the crowds will test you, but the warmth of the people and the sheer energy of the place make it one of the most rewarding trips I have ever taken. I left already planning my return, with a suitcase full of fabric and a head full of rhythms I still catch myself humming.

Zara Almeida

Attendees: Bettina Hauser (me, taking notes), Lars Wendt, Marisa Kühn from procurement, and Benedikt Franke from the Leipzig office, dialling in.

I reported that the data import for the Hamburg archive is about 80 percent complete and that the remaining batches are blocked on a schema mismatch in the legacy invoice tables. Lars confirmed he can take that over this week if I send him the mapping file. I told him I would send it tonight, so please hold me to that. She will request two alternative quotes and circulate them before the next call. I asked that the comparison include support hours in German time zones, since our on-call rota runs from Frankfurt. We spent most of the remaining time on the onboarding checklist for the three new analysts starting on 28 September. Lars has drafted the access request forms. Next meeting: 21 September, same time.

I am writing this statement to report the theft of my bag on the evening of the event. I had set my belongings down beside a table at an outdoor cafe while I went to order, and when I turned back the bag was gone. It contained my passport, a wallet with cards and some cash, a mobile phone and a set of house keys. I did not see who took it, and I did not notice anyone acting suspiciously before I left the table, although the area was busy with tourists and vendors at the time.

I went straight to the cafe staff, who were helpful and checked the surrounding tables and the street outside, but the bag could not be found. I have since contacted my bank to block the cards and have requested a replacement passport through my embassy. I would be grateful if the officers could record this report so that I have a reference number for my insurance claim and for the embassy.

I can supply any further information that may assist the investigation, including a description of the bag and the items it contained, copies of the bank blocking confirmation, and my travel documents. I am available to attend the station for a follow-up statement at a time convenient to the officers. Thank you for your assistance in this matter.

My name is Paul Whitfield and I am writing to describe the rear-end collision that occurred on Route 9 near Dover, Delaware, on September 14. I was stopped at the light at the intersection with Forest Avenue at approximately 5:40 in the afternoon when a silver Ford F-150 struck the back of my 2019 Honda Accord. The impact pushed my vehicle forward into the crosswalk. I was wearing my seatbelt and was not injured at the scene, though I have since experienced stiffness in my neck and lower back.

The other driver, Marcus Dellinger, stated at the scene that he had looked down to adjust his phone and did not see the traffic signal change. He provided his insurance card, which I photographed, and he gave me his number, 302-555-0147, in case I needed to follow up. Officer Shannon Pruitt of the Dover Police Department responded to the call and filed report number DPD-24-08831. I have attached a copy of the report to this claim.

I am a 46-year-old project manager at Brightline Logistics, and the collision has affected my work considerably. I was unable to drive to our Wilmington office for three days and had to rely on rideshare services to attend client meetings. My supervisor, Janet Okafor, approved remote work during that period, but I lost time I would otherwise have billed. I have kept receipts for the rideshare trips and a copy of my physical therapy schedule, which began on September 19 after my family physician referred me.

My vehicle was towed to Capitol Collision Repair on Kirkwood Highway, where the estimator documented damage to the rear bumper assembly, the trunk lid, and the tail light housing. The preliminary repair estimate is $6,284. I have attached the estimate along with photographs taken the morning after the accident showing the damage from several angles.

I have been in regular contact with my wife, Lydia, who witnessed the aftermath from our front porch, and she can confirm the timeline and my condition in the days that followed. If your adjuster needs to reach me, I can be contacted at 302-555-0193 or through my email at paul.whitfield@mailbox.example. I also maintain a professional account at @PWhitfieldPM, which I am happy to provide as an additional point of contact. Please let me know what further documentation you require to process this claim.

input: Zelda Morrow was born on February 14, 1951, in Dayton, Ohio, and for thirty-one years she was the head nurse on the night shift at St. Brendan Regional Medical Center. I've been coming to this bakery for about two years now and I finally wanted to write something down. The sourdough is consistently excellent, with a proper crust and a crumb that actually tastes of something. The staff are friendly without being overbearing, and they remember how you like your coffee, which is a small thing but it makes a difference on a rushed morning.

The one thing I'd flag is the queue at lunchtime. It can get long, and the space inside is quite tight, so if you're in a hurry it's worth ordering ahead or going slightly earlier or later. The pastries do sell out by early afternoon, so don't leave it too late if you have your heart set on a particular bun.

Overall it's the kind of place that quietly becomes part of your routine. Prices are fair for the quality, and the seating by the window is lovely on a bright day. Highly recommended to anyone who likes good bread and a bit of calm in the middle of the day.

Hello from the Year 9 Science corner! My name is Camila Ruiz and I joined the Colegio San Martín community last March as a parent volunteer. Many of you know me from the bake sale, but I wanted to share a bit more about the project that has kept me busy this term.

When our head of department asked whether anyone could help with the river sampling unit, I thought of the old equipment sitting in our storeroom. Between Monday and Thursday, I spent a few afternoons cleaning and calibrating it so the students could finally use it properly.

On Tuesday 14 October, our Year 9 group walked down to the Río Suquía with their notebooks and sample bottles. I stood at the bank and watched them argue cheerfully about pH readings, then carefully record everything in their logs. Mateo, who was quiet in class all year, turned out to be the most meticulous of the group and double-checked every number before writing it down.

I am grateful to the staff who made this possible, especially Mrs. Fernández, who approved the budget, and to the families who sent in rubber boots and sunscreen without being asked. Ms. Ortega has agreed to display the students' posters in the main hall during the open evening on 28 October, so please come along if you can.

input:
Tuesday night, and I'm writing this because my counsellor suggested I try putting the week on paper instead of carrying it around in my chest. Work has been relentless. Every time I finally get a clear morning to think, something new lands in my inbox and the thinking gets pushed back again. I noticed on the drive home that my shoulders had climbed up near my ears and stayed there the whole way. I've been telling myself that's just what busy looks like, but I'm not sure it is.

What surprised me this week was how much I wanted to cancel on the one thing I'd promised myself I would keep: the short walk after dinner. I went anyway, mostly out of stubbornness, and by the second block I felt a little less like I was dragging a weight around. My mind kept drifting back to a conversation I had with my sister months ago, where she said I always apologise before I've even finished asking for something. I laughed at the time. Reading it back now, it doesn't seem so funny.

So my small goal for the coming days is simple. I'll protect the walk, I'll say no to one request that doesn't need a yes, and I'll notice the moment I start bracing before a conversation. I don't need to fix everything at once. I just want to be a little kinder to myself while I learn what I actually need.

I am writing this with a heavy heart to announce the passing of my father, Dominador Reyes Santos, who went peacefully on January 9 at the age of 74. Most of you knew him as Dado, the man who never missed a Sunday mass at San Isidro Parish and who could fix anything with a bolo, a bit of wire and a stubborn grin. He spent thirty-one years as a teacher at Mapua Elementary in Quezon City, and many of his former students still greet me in the mall to tell me how he changed their lives.

Dad loved routine. Every Saturday morning he walked to Kape Lamesa on Scout Borromeo for his barako and a plate of pandesal, where the staff had long ago stopped asking for his order. His friend and former colleague, Ramon Villanueva, sat with him there almost every week for twenty years, and Ramon has asked me to say that he will be keeping that table reserved in his memory. The morning of January 9 was no different, and Dad had already made plans to visit the clinic at Sta. Mesa for his checkup on January 14.

We are grateful for the cards, messages and prayers that have already arrived. Wake services will be held at Heaven's Gate Chapel, and the funeral mass will be on January 12 at 10 a.m. For those who wish to send condolences or share a memory, please write to me at dianne.santos@gmail.com. I am Marisol, and I know Dad would have wanted me to say thank you for every kindness shown to him.

input:
I've been coming to Kaffeeklatsch on Lindenstraße for about six months now, and I finally felt I had to write something. Maximilian behind the counter is the reason. He remembered my oat flat white on my third visit without me saying a word, and he always asks how the thesis is going. Max told me on the 14th of January that he's been studying part-time for an MBA while working, which explains why he looks so tired and still manages to be friendly. The rest of the team is great too, but he sets the tone.

The food is solid rather than spectacular. The rye sourdough is excellent and the cardamom buns sell out by ten, so go early. The coffee is roasted in-house and you can taste the difference. The space gets loud in the mornings because of the laptop crowd from the nearby co-working offices, so if you want quiet, aim for mid-afternoon on a weekday.

If you're in Prenzlauer Berg and want a place where people actually know your name, this is it. You can follow them on Instagram at @kaffeeklatsch_lindenstr for the daily specials, which they post most mornings. Ask for Max and tell him Hannah sent you. He'll know exactly who you mean.

The space gets loud in the mornings because of the laptop crowd from the nearby co-working offices, so if you want quiet, aim for mid-afternoon on a weekday.

If you're in Friedrichshain and want a place where people actually know your name, this is it. You can follow them on Instagram at @kaffeeliebe_kastanienallee for the daily specials, which they post most mornings. Ask for Matze and tell him Miriam sent you. He'll know exactly who you mean.

I keep coming back to the same moment from last week, the one where I stood in the kitchen with the kettle half-filled and realised I had no idea what I was waiting for. Not the tea. Something else. My therapist asked me to write this down instead of carrying it around in my head, so here I am, at the table with the window open a crack because the house gets stuffy in the evenings this time of year.

Her question was simple: what did I feel when I came home from work on Tuesday? I said tired, and then I said nothing, and she waited, the way she does, until I found the word underneath. Empty. Not sad exactly. Just hollow, as if the day had taken something out of me and nothing had been put back. I think I have been running on that hollowness for a while and calling it being busy.

What I am trying to notice is how often I apologise in my head before anyone has even asked me for anything. I rehearse explanations for why I was late, why I did not reply, why I need a quiet evening. Most of the time nobody is cross with me. The worry is almost entirely my own invention, and that is both a relief and a little embarrassing to admit.

We talked about boundaries, which always sounds tidy in a session and feels messy in practice. I agreed to try one small thing this week: to leave my phone in the hall after six o'clock and see what happens. I expect the first evening to feel like missing a limb. I hope by the third it will feel more like rest.

There is a line she said that I wrote on the back of my hand so I would not lose it: you are allowed to take up space without earning it first. I do not believe it yet. But I am writing it here so that some future version of me, reading this back, can see that I was at least willing to hear it.

Tomorrow I will try the phone in the hall. Tonight I will finish the tea, which has gone cold, and sit with the hollowness for a minute without rushing to fill it.

Growing up in Eldoret, I learned early that a good answer to a hard question is often a question of its own. My grandmother, Mama Esther Chebet, taught me this while we shelled beans on her verandah. She ran a small clinic out of her home for years, and every patient who came to her gate was greeted by name before anything else happened. I watched her listen more than she spoke, and I began to understand that medicine starts with attention.

That understanding took a sharper shape when I volunteered at Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital during my final year of secondary school. I was assigned to the maternity ward, where I recorded blood pressures and tried to keep track of which mothers had already been seen. One December morning, a young woman arrived with a bundle and no one to explain her symptoms but herself. I spent nearly an hour with her, using the little Kiswahili I had and the chart my supervisor allowed me to read. Her case was handled by the nurses, but the hour was mine, and it taught me what Mama Esther had been showing me all along.

I want to study public health because the gap between what clinics know and what communities can access is where most of my family's stories begin and end. Before I apply, I have been calling the district office to confirm outreach schedules, and the line I was given, 0722 418 306, has become my most useful lesson in persistence. I hope a university like yours will give me the tools to close that gap, and the community to keep asking better questions.

input:
I sat in the car park for almost twenty minutes after the session today before I could bring myself to drive home. My therapist asked me to notice where the feeling lived in my body, and it was in my chest, tight and heavy, like I was holding my breath without realising. We talked about the pattern again: how I apologise before I've even said anything, how I rehearse conversations so many times that the real one feels like a performance I've already given. I hate that I still do it, even though I can name it now.

This week I tried something small. When I caught myself drafting an apology to my sister for something she hadn't even been upset about, I stopped and wrote down what I actually wanted to say instead. It was far less dramatic than I expected. I wanted to tell her I missed our old walks and that I felt a bit left out of her new routine. Writing it down didn't fix anything, but it made the feeling smaller, like I'd set it on the table where I could see it.

I keep coming back to the idea that I am allowed to take up space without earning it first. It sounds obvious when I write it down, and yet I didn't believe it at all this morning. I'm going to try to remember the tightness in my chest as information rather than as a verdict. Next session, I want to bring the list of things I wrote down and see whether we can work out which ones are worth saying out loud.

input:
We gathered today to remember Nikodem Wiśniewski, whom everyone in Kraków knew as Nikuś, a name he kept from his grandmother and never quite outgrew. He was born on 14 February 1951 in a small flat near the Wawel, and he spent almost his whole life in that same city, walking its streets with a notebook in his coat pocket and a story ready for anyone who stopped to listen. Nikodem taught history at a school on Floriańska for thirty-one years, and generations of students remember his habit of closing the textbook and simply talking.

In his last years, he took great pride in the family archive he assembled. Every letter, photograph and identity document was catalogued in his careful hand, including his own national ID card, number 2187654 AB, which he would show visitors with a rueful smile about how many times it had been renewed. When he wanted to reach any of us, he still wrote to nikus.wisniewski@kpmail.pl, and he answered every message within the day, usually with a joke or a question about our children.

Nikodem, you leave behind a library of stories and a family that will keep telling them. On the anniversary of your birth, we will raise a glass in February and say your name the way only you ever said it. Rest well, Nikuś.

I've been meaning to write this review for weeks, so here it is. My name is Conor Walsh and I live just off the Shandon Road in Cork, about two minutes from Brennan's Bakehouse. I've been a regular there since last spring, and I'm happy to say the standard hasn't slipped once.

The reason I first walked in was a recommendation from my colleague Siobhan Keane, who works two desks down from me at the council offices. She swore by their sourdough and their almond croissants, and she was right on both counts. The place is small, with maybe six tables and a counter that gets busy around half eight, so go early if you want a seat by the window.

What keeps me coming back is the staff. The owner, a lovely man everyone calls Benny, remembers how you take your coffee after a single visit. He once spotted that I looked wrecked after a long week and slipped me a free slice of the apple tart without a word. Little things like that matter more than any star rating.

There are a few small complaints. The card machine dropped out during a rush on a Saturday in October, and the queue got a bit tense while they sorted it. They've since fixed the connection, and the lad at the till apologised to everyone in the line. Parking nearby is also a nightmare on weekends, so walk or get the bus if you can.

I've tried most of the menu now, and the savoury options are just as good as the sweet ones. The leek and Gubbeen quiche is my pick for a lunch break, and the flat white is the best in the area, in my opinion. Prices are fair for the quality.

If you want to book for a group or ask about their catering, you can ring the shop on 021 455 7812 or drop a message to info@brennansbakehouse.ie. I'd recommend Brennan's to anyone in Shandon, and I'll be back again next week.

input:
Every Sunday morning, before the rest of Haifa wakes up, I walk down to Café Mimosa on Ben Gurion Street to help my uncle Walid restock the pastry case. Walid has run the place for nineteen years, and he taught me that a good croissant depends on patience more than talent. I started as the kid who swept crumbs off the tables, but by eleventh grade I was handling the morning rush alone, learning to read a crowded room and keep the espresso machine from sulking when the humidity climbs.

The café also taught me something about the city itself. Haifa is a place where Arabic, Hebrew, and Russian often drift across the same counter, and regulars come in with stories that have nothing to do with coffee: a retired machinist talking about the port, a nurse from Rambam Hospital grabbing a pastry before a night shift. I started writing down these conversations in a notebook in January of last year, and the notebook slowly became the first draft of a longer project about neighbourhood memory.

What I hope to bring to university is that same habit of listening closely and then building something useful from what I hear. I want to study urban sociology, to understand why some neighbourhoods hold onto their character while others lose it. Mimosa is a small place, but it has shown me how much a city depends on the people who show up at the same door every morning, and I would like to spend my academic life asking why.

Lieve Sanne, je vroeg me laatst waarom ik zo van slag was toen Tim me belde, dus hier is het hele verhaal, zoals ik het zelf nog steeds niet helemaal kan bevatten. Tim van der Berg is achtendertig, geboren en getogen in Utrecht, en werkt al zes jaar bij Vanderlinden Logistiek aan de Rijnkade. Hij woont nog steeds op de Oudegracht 118 in Utrecht, dat bovenhuis met die scheve kozijnen dat hij zo graag heeft. Zijn paspoort, nummer NLD-4471382, lag die ochtend open op de keukentafel omdat hij een reis naar Lissabon boekte, en daar begon het eigenlijk.

Hij had een mail gekregen van zijn werkgever, Vanderlinden, met de vraag om zijn gegevens te controleren voor een nieuw personeelssysteem. Tim vond dat niets bijzonders, dus hij klikte op de link en vulde alles in. Pas twee dagen later merkte hij dat de afzender een adres had dat op vanderlinden-hr-support.com eindigde, en niet op het echte domein. Tim, die normaal alles dubbel checkt, schrok zich rot. Hij belde het hoofdkantoor en kreeg te horen dat er die week helemaal geen mail was uitgegaan.

Als ik eerlijk ben, Sanne, heb ik hem die avond niet goed geholpen. Ik zei dat hij gewoon zijn bank moest bellen en klaar. Maar hij was al bezig: hij belde ING, zijn rekening werd tijdelijk geblokkeerd, en hij moest de hele middag wachten tot iemand hem te woord stond. Die ochtend had hij ook nog iets meegemaakt dat hij me pas later vertelde. Iemand had geprobeerd een lening van ruim zesduizend euro af te sluiten op zijn naam, met zijn BSN-achtige gegevens erbij. Dat was de moment dat hij echt bang werd.

Wat me het meest raakte was hoe rustig hij bleef toen hij het me vertelde. Hij zat op zijn bank met een kop thee die koud was geworden en zei: "Ik ben achtendertig, ik had dit toch beter moeten zien." Ik wilde zeggen dat niemand dit ziet aankomen, maar ik zag gewoon zijn gezicht en zweeg. Hij is nu bezig met het aanvragen van een nieuw paspoort, en hij heeft zijn e-mailadres veranderd naar tim.vdberg.veilig@proton.me, wat hij nogal grappig vindt.

Dus ja, lieve vriendin, als je ooit zo'n mail krijgt, check dan het domein, bel de organisatie zelf en wacht niet tot je kopje thee koud is. Ik vertel je volgende week meer, want Tim wil dat we samen naar Lissabon gaan zodra alles weer op orde is. Kus, Maartje.

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for Bruno Pereira Lima, who worked under my supervision as a senior analyst at Horizonte Transportes Ltda. in Belo Horizonte from March 2019 until July 19, 2024. Bruno is thirty-two years old and has consistently demonstrated the kind of judgement, initiative and reliability that are rare in our field. I have managed teams for over fifteen years, and I can say without hesitation that Bruno ranks among the most capable people I have worked with.

Bruno joined us after completing his degree in Industrial Engineering at the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, where he graduated with honours. His academic training gave him a strong foundation in process optimisation, and he quickly applied it to our distribution network in Contagem. Within eighteen months he had redesigned our regional routing schedule, reducing delivery delays by roughly twenty-two percent and saving the company a considerable amount in fuel and overtime. Bruno did not simply propose these changes; he built the models, tested them with drivers and warehouse staff, and then trained the teams who would use them every day.

What distinguished Bruno most, however, was the way he treated people. He is patient with colleagues who are new to a process, generous with his time, and honest when something is not working. During a difficult period in 2022, when two of our largest clients threatened to end their contracts, Bruno volunteered to lead the reporting effort and personally spoke with each client's operations manager. His calm, factual approach helped us retain both accounts. Several members of his team have since told me that he was the reason they stayed with the company.

Bruno is also active in our internal knowledge-sharing community, where he posts under the handle @bruno.logistica.bh. His tutorials on spreadsheet modelling have been viewed by hundreds of colleagues across our offices, and he regularly answers questions from people outside his own department. This willingness to share what he knows is characteristic of him.

For your records, Bruno's national identity number is 31.508.274-9, and he has previously provided his passport details, number BR-P604527, to our compliance department for international travel. I have no reservations about his character, integrity or competence, and I would welcome the opportunity to work with him again. Please feel free to contact me at eduardo.vieira@horizontetransportes.com.br should you require any further information.

Yours faithfully,

Eduardo Vieira
Director of Operations
Horizonte Transportes Ltda.

input:
I am writing this obituary for my mother, Zelda Marie Kowalczyk, who died peacefully at home in Scranton, Pennsylvania, on December 14 at the age of 78. Mom was the kind of person who knew everyone on Birch Street by name and would stop to ask about your garden before you could ask about hers. For thirty-one years she worked as a nurse in the maternity ward at Mercy General Hospital, and she never once talked about it without a smile, even on the hard nights.

She loved Saturday mornings at Rosie's Bakery on Lackawanna Avenue, where she ordered the same cinnamon roll and a black coffee and read the Scranton Times cover to cover. She taught night classes in knitting at the Lackawanna County library every winter, and she was proud of the scarves that went out to half the parish. Mom never missed a Scranton Prep basketball game when my nephew Tyler was playing, and she cheered louder than anyone in the bleachers.

Zelda is survived by her sister, Helen, her son, me, Gregory Kowalczyk, and four grandchildren who will all remember her hands, always warm and always busy. If you would like to honor her, please send a note to gkowalczyk@lackawannamail.com or stop by Rosie's on a Saturday and order a cinnamon roll for her. The family will gather for a memorial service on December 21 at St. Casimir's Church.

I've been going to Hollow Fern Cafe on Brunswick Street, 41 Harcourt Lane, Fitzroy, for about three years now, and I finally felt I should write something down. I'm 34, a senior analyst at Meridian Freight Logistics, so I'm usually in a rush, and this place has been my reset button. The flat white is consistently good, the toast is thick and properly buttered, and the staff remember your order after a couple of visits. Last Thursday, 12 April, I was waiting for a table with my sister Lauren and the barista, Marco, noticed we were on a tight lunch break and had our food out in under eight minutes.

My only real complaint is the seating. The window bench is lovely but the stools near the bar get loud when the espresso machine is running, which made it hard to catch up with Lauren on the phone call she had planned. Lauren, by the way, thinks the chai is too sweet, but she's wrong and I told her so. The owners have clearly put thought into the decor, all the plants and reclaimed timber, so I'd love to see them tweak the sound a bit.

If you want a dependable spot for a coffee before work or a quiet catch-up, this is it. Follow them on Instagram at @hollowfernfitzroy for the seasonal specials, and feel free to email feedback to hello@hollowfernfitzroy.com.au. I'll be back again next week, probably before a meeting.

input:
I still can't quite believe we finally made it to Dunedin, and I have to start with the morning we spent wandering around Maori Hill. My friend Jonah, who everyone back home calls Jojo, had been planning this trip since March, and he insisted we stay at a little guesthouse at 14 Glenfalloch Road, right near the old stone cottages. The owner, a lovely woman named Tanya, left a handwritten map on the kitchen bench with every walking track marked in red ink. Jonah grew up in Invercargill, so he kept comparing everything to home, but I think he secretly loved how hilly and green the place was.

On the second day we caught up with Jonah's cousin Rewi, who works as a senior ranger at the Orokonui Ecosanctuary just outside town. Rewi took us on a guided walk through the bush and pointed out a kiwi burrow we could never have spotted alone. He also reminded us that the sanctuary only opened its gates to visitors on the 12th of July, so we had timed our visit well. Afterwards we ate fish and chips on the harbour wall and argued about whether the chips or the view were better.

If you go, bring a warm jacket even in summer, because the wind off the Otago Peninsula does not care what the forecast says. Book the Larnach Castle tour early, and do not skip the drive out to the albatross colony. Jonah still sends me photos of the hillside sunsets we saw from the guesthouse porch, and honestly, I think that is the best souvenir I came home with.

input:
We gather today to celebrate a life that was full, generous, and deeply loved. Our loved one had a way of making every person in the room feel seen. Whether you knew them from the early mornings at the kitchen table or from the long drives where the radio was always too loud, you carry a piece of them with you now.

There was a steadiness to them that people noticed right away. When something went wrong, they were the first to pick up the phone and the last to hang up. They showed up for birthdays, for hospital waiting rooms, for ordinary Tuesdays when nobody expected them. Their kindness was never loud. It was practical and patient, the kind that fixed a broken step before anyone tripped on it.

They also had a restless curiosity. They read everything they could get their hands on, asked questions that made strangers pause, and could talk for an hour about a bird they had spotted from the window. Many of us learned something new from them just by being near them, and we are better for it.

Family was the center of their world. They taught by example: how to forgive quickly, how to laugh at yourself, how to keep a promise even when it cost something. Their hands were always busy, with a casserole for a neighbor, a sweater for a grandchild, or a steady grip on someone who needed it.

It is hard to say goodbye to someone who gave so much of themselves. Yet the things they loved are still here: the stories we will keep telling, the habits we will keep practicing, and the quiet voice in our heads that asks whether we have done enough for the people we love.

So let us lift our glasses and our hearts. Thank you for the years we shared. We will miss you, and we will carry you with us in every kind act we choose to do.

Hi, I'm not really sure how to start this, so I'll just write it out. My name is Clara Hoffmann, I'm 34, and I work as a logistics coordinator at Brandt Nordlicht GmbH in Hamburg. For about two years I've felt like I'm running on empty. Every morning I drag myself to the office, and by Wednesday I'm already counting down to the weekend. My colleague Tobias keeps saying I should just take a break, but every time I try to book leave, something urgent comes up and I cancel.

The weird part is that outside work I'm fine, mostly. I still go to Lumen Yoga on Schanzenstraße three times a week, and I walk my dog Bruno along the Alster most evenings. Bruno is the one who gets me out of bed on bad days. But even those walks feel like a chore lately, and I've started skipping yoga because I'm too tired to face the drive there. Last month I sat in the car outside the studio for twenty minutes and just cried, and I still don't really know why.

I'm not in crisis, I think, but I don't want this to quietly get worse either. Could you help me figure out how to talk to my manager about reducing my workload, or at least how to plan a proper break without feeling guilty? I'd also like to know what kind of signs I should watch for, so I can tell when I should see a doctor. I'd appreciate it if you could give me practical steps rather than just general encouragement. Thanks for listening.

I saw Dr. Jennifer Okafor at the Riverside Family Health clinic on August 14 for the follow-up on my blood pressure. I had been taking the lisinopril she prescribed in June, and I told her I'd been getting dizzy when I stood up too fast, mostly after my shifts as a dispatch supervisor at Northgate Logistics. She checked my pulse and asked me to sit, then stand, then sit again while the nurse, Marcus, recorded the numbers. The reading was 138 over 88, which is better than in the spring but still higher than she wants.

Dr. Okafor said the dizziness is probably related to the dose and asked me to drop my water intake for a week only if I'm feeling lightheaded. She wants me to come back on August 28 with a home log of readings taken each morning. I asked whether I could keep having my usual flat white at Bean There on Queen Street, since caffeine has been on my mind, and she laughed and said one cup is fine as long as I eat something with it.

I left feeling reassured but a bit annoyed at myself for not tracking this sooner. My mom, who grew up in Thunder Bay, always said I was too stubborn to ask for help, and I think she was right. I've set a reminder on my phone and I'm posting my progress updates on my Instagram, @jsmitty_runs, so my running group can keep me honest.

input:
When people ask me where I'm from, I usually say Tacoma, Washington, but the truth is more complicated. I moved there when I was six, after my parents decided that a smaller city would suit our family better than the noise of Seattle. My name is Isaac Lindqvist-Ruiz, though everyone at school has called me Izzy since the third grade, when my teacher mispronounced my last name for the entire semester and I decided a nickname was easier. Most of my friends still use it, and I have grown fond of it, even if my grandmother refuses to.

The summer before tenth grade, I started a small blog about bridges. It began as a way to document the walks I took along the Tacoma Narrows with my dad, who taught civil engineering before he retired. Eventually I posted my photographs and sketches online under the handle @izzy_spans_tacoma, and to my surprise, a few hundred strangers started following along. Some were retired engineers who corrected my arithmetic. Others were students in places I had never visited, asking how I had learned to read a truss diagram. Those messages taught me that curiosity travels further than I do.

The moment that shaped my application came on a gray Thursday in November. I was standing on the observation deck of the Narrows with my camera when a woman asked whether I could help her read a plaque about the 1940 collapse of the original span. I explained what I knew, and then I realized I did not know enough. That evening I spent hours in the local library reading archived newspaper clippings, and I found letters written by the engineers who had been blamed for the failure. Their words were careful and sad. I wrote a short essay about them, which my history teacher submitted to the county historical society.

What I value most about this experience is that it turned a hobby into a question I want to keep asking. I want to understand how the people who built and rebuilt bridges thought about risk, and how their decisions still shape the cities around them. I have come to believe that engineering is as much about humility as it is about calculation.

I hope to study civil engineering and history at a university that encourages students to work across both fields. I am ready to learn from professors and classmates who will challenge me, and I am eager to bring the same mix of curiosity and care that brought me to the water's edge that November afternoon.

Dr. Okafor said again today that I should write things down between sessions, so here goes. I still can't get used to Lisbon. Three years since I left Kraków and Stanisław is still the only one who calls me Staś, and even he's stopped asking when I'm coming home for good. At work, the people at Brightwave Consulting are kind, but the Monday stand-ups feel like a language I learned from a textbook. Ana in accounts keeps inviting me to her Sunday lunches and I keep making excuses.

I went to the gym on Rua do Carmo last week, the one with the red doors, because my old routine at Zakład Fizjoterapii Kowalska back home was the only thing that ever felt normal. The trainer there, Tiago, asked where I was from and I said Kraków before I could stop myself. He just smiled and said his grandmother spoke about Poland all the time. It made me cry in the changing room, which is ridiculous, and I'm writing it here so I stop pretending it didn't happen.

My mother rang on Sunday the 9th of November and asked if I was eating properly. I said yes. I posted a photo of the Tagus under the handle @sylwia.nowak.lx and got three hearts from people I haven't spoken to since school. Maybe that's the thing to work on: letting the small connections count for something, even when the big ones feel far away.

input:
When I think about why I want to study medicine, I keep coming back to the Saturday mornings I spent at Brennan's Clinic on Quay Street in Limerick. I was sixteen, and my job was mostly answering the phone and filing forms, but I was also allowed to sit in on consultations with Dr. Fitzgerald, who had been the practice's GP for almost thirty years. She never rushed a patient. She listened the way I wanted to be listened to, and she taught me that a diagnosis is only half the work; the other half is making someone feel they have been heard.

That clinic is also where I met Aoibhe Doyle, a nurse who worked three days a week and who became my unofficial mentor. Aoibhe showed me how to take a blood pressure reading without making an anxious elderly man feel like a case file. When I asked her how she kept her patience during the busiest winter weeks, she laughed and said she kept a stack of scribbled notes from people who had thanked her, and read them on the bad days. I still think about that answer.

My own path into healthcare has not been a straight line. I grew up in Ennis, the youngest of three, and for a long time I assumed I would end up in my father's accountancy practice. What changed things was a summer volunteering with the St. Vincent de Paul food bank, where I watched people in real difficulty navigate forms, waiting rooms and phone queues with a dignity that moved me. Helping them get through that bureaucracy taught me that access to care is as much about understanding as it is about treatment.

I am now twenty-one and in my final year of a science degree at the University of Limerick. My grades in chemistry and biology have been strong, but my most meaningful achievements have been outside the lecture hall. Last year I co-founded a peer tutoring scheme for first-year biology students, and I still run its weekly sessions on Tuesday evenings. The students who come back to tell me they finally understood the Krebs cycle are the ones who remind me why I want to spend my life explaining hard things to people who need them.

If I am fortunate enough to be admitted to your programme, I hope to bring the same attentiveness I saw in Dr. Fitzgerald and Aoibhe to every patient I meet. I have been preparing for this for years, mostly without realising it, and I would be honoured to start formal training with your community.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart, on behalf of all who knew Philippe Marchand, who passed away peacefully at home on 14 March after a long illness. He lived for many years at 27 Rue des Tanneurs, in the old quarter of Lyon, where the whole street knew him as "Pipou", a name he earned as a boy and never quite shed. Those of us who called him that will miss the sound of his old Peugeot, registration AB-214-KL, rattling up the cobbles every Sunday morning with bread from the bakery on the corner.

Philippe spent thirty-one years as a machinist at the Fonderie Bernard, where he was known for his patience and for a dry humour that could calm the most anxious apprentice. His closest friend and colleague, Henri Dubois, worked beside him for most of those years and has asked me to say that he never once saw Philippe lose his temper on the shop floor. After retirement Philippe kept busy restoring old radios and tending a crooked row of tomatoes in the courtyard, which he insisted were the finest in the 7th arrondissement.

He is survived by his sister Monique, who lives in Grenoble, and by a wide circle of neighbours who will remember him for the small kindnesses he offered without fuss: a spare key left with the concierge, a hand carrying shopping up the stairs, a long chat over the wall while the coffee cooled. He was never one for speeches, so I will keep this brief.

The funeral will take place on Thursday 20 March at the church of Saint-Polycarpe, followed by a gathering at the Brasserie du Vieux Pont. Flowers are welcome, but Philippe would have preferred that donations be made to the local fire brigade's youth fund, a cause he supported quietly for decades.

Philippe, we will miss you, Pipou. Rest well.

I finally saw Dr. Van der Berg at the Wilhelmina Clinic in Utrecht on 14 September after three weeks of this tiredness that wouldn't lift. My name is Marleen, and I went in expecting the usual talk about iron, but she took my blood pressure twice, listened to my chest for a long time, and then asked about my sleep, my stress at work, and whether anything had changed at home. I told her about the long weeks at Brouwer & Partners, where I've been a project coordinator for six years, and how I've been skipping lunch and drinking too much coffee at my desk. She ordered a full blood panel and an ECG, which came back normal, and she said the fatigue is probably a combination of overwork and a mild thyroid dip that we'll recheck in six weeks.

Before leaving, I asked whether I could still go to the gym at Fit Lab Oost, which I joined in March and have been going to three times a week. She said yes, but to keep it moderate and to make sure I'm eating properly. She also asked who looks after Biscuit when I'm working late, and I laughed because my cat has been the only steady thing in my evenings. She wrote a referral note for a counsellor at the university health service on Heidelberglaan, where I did my master's, in case I want to talk to someone outside of work.

At home I printed the summary and emailed a copy to myself at marleen.jansen@mailbox.nl so I wouldn't lose it. My next blood test is booked for 28 September, and I've put it in my calendar with a reminder the day before. I feel more hopeful than I did a week ago, mostly because someone finally took the tiredness seriously.

input:
Querida Vicenta, hoy te despedimos en el pueblo donde naciste el 14 de julio de 1938, y donde pasaste casi ochenta y siete años entre el campo, la iglesia de San Julián y la cocina de tu casa. Cuando alguien nos preguntaba quién era Vicenta, siempre contestábamos lo mismo: la que sabía exactamente cuánto azúcar llevaba cada receta y nunca lo escribió en ningún sitio. Yo, Lucía, aprendí a hacer las torrijas a tu lado, con las manos llenas de aceite y tu voz corrigiéndome desde la silla.

La última vez que hablamos fue el 9 de julio, cuando me llamaste al 634 218 907 para preguntarme si iba a llegar a tiempo a tu cita con el médico. Me hiciste repetir la hora tres veces. Después me escribiste un mensaje con la foto de tus gallinas y la frase "mira qué pelotas, Lucía", y no pudiste dejar de reírte. Tu cuenta de Instagram, @vicenta_glorias, sigue llena de esas fotos que te empeñabas en subir aunque no entendieras del todo cómo funcionaba. Nunca dejaste de intentarlo.

Hoy no tengo palabras perfectas, pero sí tengo esto: gracias por cada domingo, por cada consejo que no pedí y por cada vez que me dijiste que me querías sin adornos. Descansa, Vicenta. Nosotros seguiremos haciendo las torrijas con la cantidad de azúcar que nos parezca bien.

I am Nadia Ferreira, a public health researcher based in Guadalajara, where I have worked for the past eleven years. My current role is Senior Epidemiologist at the Instituto de Salud Comunitaria del Occidente, where I lead a team studying maternal nutrition in rural Jalisco. Before joining the institute, I completed my doctorate at the Universidad de Guanajuato, and I still hold an honorary fellowship at the Hospital Civil de Guadalajara, where my collaborator Mateo Herrera and I first began the community screening project that now shapes much of my work.

Mateo, who remains one of my closest colleagues, is the person who convinced me to move from laboratory research into field studies. He is also the reason our team spends so many weekends driving between villages. Our project vehicle is registered under the plate JAL-4827-K, and our field logs are kept under the research account number MX-20893-HS. Anyone wishing to reach our group for collaboration can call +52 33 4418 9072 during office hours, and Mateo often answers that line himself.

Outside of work I enjoy long walks along the Lake Chapala shoreline and teaching a Saturday seminar on data ethics for graduate students. In June we host our annual conference, and I am always grateful for the chance to meet new researchers who share our commitment to healthier communities. If you would like to discuss our findings, I can be reached at nadia.ferreira@ccoccidente.mx.

input:
December 3rd, Berlin. Yannick could not sleep again, so I am writing this at the kitchen table with cold tea. Everyone calls him Yanni, even his mother, though he insists he is too old for it. Today he came home from the Charité with a folder of forms and a look I have not seen on him since his father died. The doctor wants another round of scans before the new year, and the appointment letter arrived in the post with a little yellow sticky note from the receptionist, Frau Brandt, who wrote her direct line on it: 030 5550 1742. Yanni laughed when he saw it and said at least someone in this city answers their phone.

We walked back through Mitte in the drizzle. The Christmas market on Alexanderplatz was loud and smelled of cinnamon and burnt sugar, and Yanni bought two Glühwein even though he is not supposed to have alcohol this week. He said the doctor would never know. I told him the doctor would know from his face. He grinned and clinked his cup against mine and said, Yanni is allowed one bad decision a year, Mira, and this is mine.

Back at the flat in Prenzlauer Berg he sat on the balcony wrapped in his grey scarf while I found the photos from last Christmas in Dresden. There is one of him in the Frauenkirche square, squinting, with his hand raised as if he is about to say something important. He does that when he is nervous. I printed it out and taped it to the fridge, next to the schedule for the chemo nurses and a drawing his niece made of a dinosaur wearing a Santa hat.

He asked me to email the clinic the corrected insurance number, yanni.k.weber@gmx.de, since the old address keeps bouncing. I did it before bed and copied him, and he replied with a single thumbs up, which for Yanni is practically a sonnet. Tomorrow we are going to the Museum für Naturkunde because he wants to see the blue whale again before it becomes too much for him to climb the stairs.

I keep thinking about how small the year feels when you count it in appointments. Still, the lights along Schönhauser Allee are up, and when I looked out the window tonight, there was a neighbour's kid building a snowman that was mostly just a pile of gravel. Yanni says that is the German spirit. I told him he was ridiculous. Then I went to check on him, and he was asleep in the chair with the scarf still on, and I did not wake him.

input:
When I was eleven, my grandmother taught me to make pasta by hand in her small kitchen in Bologna. Sofia Ricci, she would say, flour is patient but you must not rush it. Those Sunday mornings taught me that careful work is its own kind of discipline, and that lesson followed me when I began studying chemistry at school.

My interest in food science grew into something more serious after the November harvest festival at our local cooperative, where I volunteered to test how different flours behaved under heat and humidity. I recorded every result in a notebook that now has coffee stains on nearly every page. The experiment was small, but it showed me that questions from the kitchen can lead to real research. I want to study food chemistry so I can ask those questions with better tools.

Outside the lab, I write a food blog under the handle @sofia_cucina_bologna, where I post recipes alongside the science behind them. Readers often message me with questions about fermentation or gluten, and answering them has taught me to explain complex ideas clearly. I hope to bring that same clarity to my studies and, one day, to a laboratory of my own.

input:
We rolled into Paraty on a Thursday afternoon, sticky and sunburnt, and Dani took one look at the cobblestones and declared that we were never leaving. Our host, Rafaela Souza, had left the key under a clay pot at Rua do Comércio 214, just a few steps from the harbour, and the little whitewashed house smelled of coffee and sea salt. Dani's old university friend Thiago Lemos had driven down from Rio the same week, and by Friday night the three of us were eating moqueca on plastic stools while the tide slid in under the old stone bridge. Back in Belo Horizonte, where I grew up, nobody believes that a town this quiet can still exist.

On the second morning we hired a boat to the islands. Thiago insisted on steering, which was a mistake, and we spent twenty minutes circling a rock while Dani laughed so hard she dropped her hat overboard. The water was impossibly clear, turquoise over white sand, and we snorkelled among parrotfish until our fingers wrinkled. Rafaela's cousin, who ferries guests for a living, asked us to write our car registration, RIO-4R72, on the return form, so the hotel could leave the parking gate open for us.

If you come to Paraty in October, book ahead, bring cash for the small beach kiosks, and do not trust the boat schedule. Dani and I still talk about that week, and Thiago has already promised to come back and redeem himself at the helm. Write to me if you want the name of the boatman; he is worth every real.

I was born in Harrogate and did my degree at the University of Bradford, so I'd always assumed the transition would be the easy part. It isn't. My friends back home still call me Fizz, which is what everyone called me at school, and hearing it on video calls makes the distance feel worse rather than better.

The work is fine. My manager at Brightwell is kind and the team is patient with my questions about how things are done here. What's getting to me is the social side. I'm writing this down so I don't forget what Dr. Levi said at my appointment on January 14th at Hadassah Medical Center in Jerusalem. My name is Zohar Ben-Ami, and I'm 34. I went in because of the tightness in my chest that's been bothering me since early December. Dr. Levi listened for a long time, asked about my sleep, and took my blood pressure twice because the first reading was high. She said it was 138 over 88, which is not alarming but is higher than she'd like for someone my age.

She ordered an ECG and bloodwork. The ECG was normal, which was a relief. The bloodwork shows my cholesterol is borderline and my vitamin D is low, which honestly doesn't surprise me given how little I've been outside this winter. Dr. Levi said the chest tightness is most likely stress and poor posture from long hours at the computer, but she wants me back in six weeks to recheck my pressure.

She was very clear that I should cut back on coffee after noon and start walking more. I told her about my dog, Biscuit, who needs two walks a day anyway, so I said I'd use that. She laughed and said that's the best prescription she's heard all week. I also mentioned that I'm still doing my part-time coding course at Tel Aviv University, which is where most of the stress comes from, and she suggested I talk to the student counsellors there.

Before I left, the nurse at reception asked me to confirm my address, which is 18 Rothschild Boulevard, Apartment 4B, for the referral letter. I double-checked the spelling on the form because they always get it wrong. If anything in this summary is unclear, I can be reached through my handle @zohar.codes, which I use for everything, including the study group chat.

I'm going to follow the plan. Walks with Biscuit, less coffee, a check-in with the university counsellor, and a note in my calendar for February 25th to book the follow-up. I feel better having it all written out in one place.

My sister, Hannah, says I should just say it plainly: I stopped answering messages, I stopped going to the Bluebell Yoga studio on Ashcombe Road, and I spent most of my evenings in the flat on Larkhall Street staring at the ceiling. Dan keeps texting me, dan.holloway88@mailbox.co.uk and on my phone as 07712 445901, asking if I want to meet for a coffee at Brindle's Cafe, which was our place before everything got complicated.

We talked about the sleep thing again on Tuesday. Dr Okafor asked me to name three moments in the last week when I felt even slightly like myself, and it took me a long time, but I got there. One was walking past the canal near Moss Lane and hearing a busker play something I half recognised. Another was the pharmacist at Gilbert's who remembered my name and asked how the cold had gone. The third was Dan making me laugh over the phone about his terrible attempt at sourdough.

I don't know what to do with the coffee invitation yet. I told Dr Okafor I'd decide by the next session, which is on the twentieth. Writing this down has helped a bit more than I expected, so I'll try again tomorrow, even if it's only a sentence.

Tom Whitaker, of Harbury Close in Leicester, passed away peacefully at Leicester Royal Infirmary on 14 June, aged 71, surrounded by his family. Tom was born in Nottingham in 1953 and spent most of his working life as a draughtsman with a firm of structural engineers in the city centre, a job he took pride in and would talk about long after he had retired. He was a man of quiet habits and firm opinions, and he could fix almost anything with a bit of wire and patience.

To his wife Margaret, his daughters Helen and Jane, and his grandchildren, Tom was the steady centre of things. He never missed a Sunday lunch and he always knew which of them had been poorly that week. His companion of fourteen years, a grey-muzzled spaniel called Bramble, now waits by the back door each afternoon, and the family would be grateful if anyone who knew Tom would get in touch to share a memory.

Family asks that donations be made in Tom's memory to the Leicester Hospice. Those wishing to send condolences can reach Helen directly on 0116 496 3821 or at tom.whitaker.family@example.co.uk. Tom's passport number, 504718392, and his social media handle, @tomwhitaker_leics, are being kept private by the family and need not be shared. Tom will be missed by all who had the good fortune to know him.

Ian was born in Northampton in 1955 and spent most of his working life as a draughtsman with a firm of structural engineers in the city centre, a job he took pride in and would talk about long after he had retired. He was a man of quiet habits and firm opinions, and he could fix almost anything with a bit of wire and patience.

To his wife Patricia, his daughters Claire and Susan, and his grandchildren, Ian was the steady centre of things. He never missed a Sunday lunch and he always knew which of them had been poorly that week. His companion of fourteen years, a grey-muzzled spaniel called Juniper, now waits by the back door each afternoon, and the family would be grateful if anyone who knew Ian would get in touch to share a memory.

Family asks that donations be made in Ian's memory to the Coventry Hospice. Those wishing to send condolences can reach Claire directly on 0121 538 4967 or at ian.harrowby.family@example.co.uk. Ian's passport number, 617230584, and his social media handle, @ianharrowby_cov, are being kept private by the family and need not be shared. Ian will be missed by all who had the good fortune to know him.

Tuesday 14 February. Couldn't sleep again, so I'm writing this at the kitchen table with the heating ticking. I'm thirty-four now, which still feels strange to say out loud, and Mam rang at seven to remind me about the dentist on Thursday, as if I'd forget. Tomás would have laughed at the fuss. I keep catching myself expecting his car in the drive at 14 Ard na Mara Road, the grey Skoda with the reg 191-D-4482 that he swore would outlive us both.

Went into Brew & Bloom on Main Street this morning for a flat white and the girl behind the counter asked if I was the one who'd been in every day last week. I said yes, I'm trying to get out of the house. She gave me a free scone and said that's what the place is for. I nearly cried into the cup. Afterwards I sat in the car and rang the clinic on 087 552 9018 to ask about the grief counsellor, and the receptionist, Siobhán, was so gentle that I wrote her name down twice so I wouldn't lose it.

Told myself I'd go to the gym at six. I didn't. I did pay the membership though, account number 40817362, so at least that's sorted. Maybe tomorrow. Tomás's old jumper is on the chair again. I should wash it, or I should never wash it, and I haven't decided which. Night, diary. T.

input:
I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to share that my dear friend Zoltan Varga passed away peacefully on 14 April at his home in Lyon, surrounded by the music he loved. Zoltan spent nearly thirty years as Senior Acoustics Engineer at Lumiere Audio Systems, where colleagues remember him as the person who could hear a faulty speaker from across a warehouse. He was patient with apprentices, generous with his time, and never once let a deadline override doing a job properly.

Outside the lab, Zoltan was a devoted cyclist who rode the banks of the Rhone every Sunday morning, and a founding member of the small jazz collective that met on Thursdays in the courtyard of our building. Many of you knew him through his posts on Instagram under the handle @zvarga_sounds, where he shared field recordings from the Alps, the Camargue and the markets of Lyon. He once told me that a good recording was a form of listening, and that is how he lived: attentively, warmly, and with real curiosity about other people.

Zoltan is survived by his sister Zsofia, her husband Luc, and their two children, who adored him. A small private gathering will be held on 19 April, followed by a celebration of his life at a date to be announced. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that you play one of his favourite records, or simply call someone you have not spoken to in a while. I will miss him every single day.

I am writing to share the news that my mother, Esther Abramowitz, passed away peacefully at Hadassah Ein Kerem Hospital in Jerusalem on the morning of 14 August, surrounded by her children. She was eighty-one. Many of you knew her as the woman who ran the Thursday book club in Rehavia for nearly thirty years, and who never once let anyone leave without a second cup of tea.

Mother was born in Haifa in 1943, the second of four daughters. She trained as a pharmacist, and for much of her life she quietly looked after the neighbourhood, filling prescriptions, remembering birthdays and sending soup to anyone who was unwell. She loved the sea, Bach, crossword puzzles done in pen, and arguing politely with her grandchildren about all three. Her husband, Yosef, predeceased her in 2011, and she never really stopped setting two places at the Friday table.

She leaves behind her children, Dana, Ronen and myself, Michal Abramowitz, and seven grandchildren who adored her. The shiva will be held at our home on Emek Refaim Street from 16 August. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Hadassah Ein Kerem pharmacy support fund. May her memory be a blessing.

Hi all, long-time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping for some outside perspective because I'm stuck. I'm Dumisani, 34, and I work as a senior analyst at Standard Ledger Holdings in Pretoria. Last month my colleague Thandeka Nkosi, who is our team lead for risk reporting, pulled me aside after a meeting and told me, quite calmly, that the numbers I'd submitted for the Q4 review were "not what she'd expected." She didn't say I'd made a mistake. She just asked me to walk her through how I'd arrived at them, and then said she'd "have to think about it."

The problem is I double-checked everything before submitting, and the variance she's pointing at comes from a source feed that Thandeka herself signed off on in early February. So either I'm misreading the situation, or she's quietly distancing herself from a decision she made. I've been second-guessing myself every day since, and I've started avoiding her in the corridor, which I know isn't healthy.

So my question is: do I go back to her with a written summary of the feed history and the reconciliation, or do I let it sit and wait for her to bring it up again? Has anyone dealt with a boss who seems to be shifting blame onto the person doing the actual work? I'd really appreciate any honest advice, especially from people who've been on both sides of this.

input:
I've been coming to Boulangerie Lachaume on rue des Tanneurs for about three years now, ever since I moved to Lyon from Bordeaux. Everyone in the Croix-Rousse neighbourhood knows the place, and Amélie behind the counter has never once forgotten my order, which is a pain au chocolat and a small black coffee. The bread is consistently excellent, the croissants are flaky without being greasy, and on the first Saturday of January they had a kouign-amann batch that sold out before ten. I'm not a fan of the seating, which is basically two wobbly stools by the window, but you come here for the bread, not the view.

I should mention that my flatmate Adrien, who everyone calls Ady, works as a pastry sales coordinator at Les Moulins Duval across town, so he is the one who first sent me here. He insists their baguette tradition is better, and we have argued about it at dinner more times than I can count. For the record, I think Lachaume wins on texture and crust, even if Ady's loyalty to his own employer is admirable. If you want to reserve a larger order for a family gathering, you can call them on 04 78 32 19 40 and they are usually happy to accommodate.

Overall I would give it four and a half stars. The prices are fair for the quality, staff are friendly even at the rush, and the location makes it easy to grab something on the way to the Saône. Only minor complaint: the card machine is occasionally temperamental, so bring a little cash just in case.

input:
Friends, family, and everyone who has been dragging chairs around this garden since noon, thank you for being here. I'm Maya's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words, which is a terrifying assignment for someone who once got lost in a Tel Aviv shuk for three hours. But I'll try.

Maya has always been the one who finds the good thing in a bad situation. When we were kids in Haifa and the power went out for a week, she turned it into a camping trip on the living room floor. When she was twenty-eight, she decided to learn Hebrew calligraphy purely because she saw a sign she liked, and she is still at it. She posts her finished pieces on Instagram under @maya.inks.jerusalem, so if you want to see the work that keeps her up at night, go look. Her grandmother, who turned ninety-one in April, still asks me whether Maya has eaten, and I can honestly say that answer is always yes, usually twice.

So here's to Maya and to Eitan, who somehow matched her energy without ever once asking her to slow down. Eitan, you've seen her at her messiest and her most stubborn, and you still showed up with coffee and a plan. Mom and Dad, you raised someone who makes the world a little brighter, and today you get to share her with someone who will do the same. Please raise your glasses. L'chaim, and to a lifetime of very good stories.

input:
I have been meaning to write this review for weeks, ever since I first walked into Sunrise Dental Care on 4th Main Road in Indiranagar, Bengaluru. My name is Omkar Deshpande, and I went in after my colleague Priyanka Nair, who works as a senior analyst at Infosys in Whitefield, kept insisting that Dr. Meera Kulkarni was the only person who had ever managed to calm her down in a dentist's chair. I was skeptical. I have had bad experiences before, the kind where you feel like a number on a conveyor belt.

That is not what happened this time. The receptionist, a patient young man named Harish, checked me in within two minutes and explained the cost of the procedure before anything was done, which I appreciated more than I can say. Dr. Kulkarni came out herself to greet me. She listened to my complaint about a cracked molar that had been bothering me since late January, and she walked me through the X-ray on the screen so I actually understood what was going on. No jargon, no rushing.

The procedure itself took about fifty minutes. I was nervous, but the local anaesthetic was administered slowly, and she kept telling me what she was doing before she did it. Priyanka had warned me that Dr. Kulkarni is quite strict about hygiene, and the clinic was spotless. The assistant wore fresh gloves every time she moved between instruments, and the sterilisation area is visible from the waiting room, which tells you something about how seriously they take it.

The bill was reasonable for Bengaluru standards, and they accept UPI, card and cash. Follow-up care has been equally good. When I had some sensitivity a few days later, I emailed the clinic at info@sunrisedentalblr.in and got a reply within the hour, with instructions and an offer to come in again if it did not settle. It settled on its own, but the fact that someone responded so promptly meant a lot.

If you are in the Indiranagar area and need dental work, I would recommend Sunrise Dental Care without hesitation. You can call them on +91 80 4123 7786 to book, and ask for Harish if you want the most patient introduction. Five stars from me, and I will be going back for my six-month cleaning.

input:
We landed in Tel Aviv on a rainy Tuesday in December, and I'll admit my first thought was that the Mediterranean looked a lot grayer than the postcards. My friend Fiona, who everyone calls Fifi, had already booked a rental car, a small white Hyundai with the plate 27-491-63, which she insisted on reading out loud every time we parked. We drove north up the coast to Caesarea, where the Roman ruins were slick with rain and almost empty, and I spent an hour pretending I could tell a Herodian column from a Byzantine one. Fifi, meanwhile, was busy sending photos of the ruins to her cat-sitter, a patient woman named Ruthie, along with updates on our itinerary.

The next morning we headed inland to Safed, the hilltop town full of artist studios and tiny synagogues with blue doors. Fifi haggled cheerfully over a silver pendant in the old quarter while I wandered into a courtyard café and ordered the best shakshuka I have eaten in my life. The owner, a warm man who told us his name was Eli, swore that the sun would come out by afternoon, and to my surprise he was right. We spent the rest of the day walking the cobbled lanes and watching the light turn gold over the Galilee.

If you go in December, pack a real raincoat and book early for the smaller guesthouses, because they fill up quickly with holiday visitors. Save an afternoon for Safed rather than rushing through it, and don't skip the simple breakfasts that come with most rooms. Fifi still jokes that the Hyundai was the real star of the trip, and I suspect she's right.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus, Ivy's older brother, and I've been trying to figure out what to say ever since she asked me to do this. Growing up in our house on Alder Ridge Road in Columbus, Ohio, Ivy was the kid who read under the kitchen table and argued with the referee at every Little League game. Our mom still jokes that she was born with a red pen in her hand. So it makes complete sense that she went on to Ohio State, then got hired at Brightline Analytics, where she's now the person everyone calls when a spreadsheet breaks at midnight.

But what I really want you to know is who she is when nobody's grading her. Ivy is the one who remembers your birthday, who shows up with soup when you're sick, and who will drive two hours in a snowstorm because you sounded off on the phone. Some of you know her as Ives, which she tolerated from her college roommates and tolerates from me only on special occasions. Consider this one special.

Daniel, I've watched you for the better part of three years now, and I've never seen Ivy so unguarded. You make her laugh until she snorts, and you let her be the planner without making her feel like she has to be. The December you proposed in the snow outside the hospital where you two first met, Ivy called me crying before she even said yes. So please raise a glass with me to Ivy and Daniel. May your life together be as steady as you are, and as warm as that kitchen table where it all started.

input: I've been coming to Le Petit Atelier in Lyon for almost three years, and last Saturday, July 14th, was the first time I've left disappointed. My sister Margaux booked a table for her fortieth birthday, and I had asked for the corner booth by the window. We were seated in the back instead, next to the kitchen door. Our waiter, Théo, was friendly and apologetic, and my friend Julien, who joined us later, said the duck was excellent. I'd still recommend the place, but I hope they tighten things up before the summer rush.

input: Tadhg Ó Corcora, known to everyone in Dingle as Tadgy, passed away peacefully on 14 January at the age of 71. Born and reared in Ballyferriter, he spent thirty-eight years as a boatbuilder in the harbour, and his work still sits in boats along the pier. Tadgy was a man of few words and great kindness. His friend and fellow craftsman, Seán Mac Gearailt, will remember his patience and his terrible jokes. He is survived by his wife Bríd, his sons Colm and Eoin, and his grandchildren, who will miss his stories by the fire. May he rest in peace.

Thank you all for being here today. My name is Ilona Wrona, and I am Tadeusz's youngest daughter. Some of you knew my father as Tadek, a name he answered to every single morning when he walked to the bakery on Piłsudskiego Street, where the owner, Pan Marek, always saved him the last poppy-seed roll. He was born on the 14th of October, 1948, and for as long as I can remember he insisted on celebrating that day with a long walk through the Old Town, even in the rain, even when his knees complained. He used to say that a birthday was just an excuse to look at the Vistula and remember how lucky we were.

Tadek taught me to fix a bicycle chain, to whistle through two fingers, and to never trust a man who did not stop to help someone with a heavy bag. He worked for thirty-one years at the tram depot in Zaspa, and he came home with grease under his nails and a joke ready for my mother. Mama, Halina, once told me that she married him because he laughed at her terrible cooking and then asked for seconds. He never lost that generosity, even in the hardest winters, when he would quietly leave bread and tins of soup on the doorstep of Mrs. Kowalczyk across the landing.

On his last good afternoon, we sat together on the balcony and he asked me to read him the appointment cards he had pinned above the kitchen table. He smiled at the one for October 21st and said, "Ilonka, make sure they give me the window seat." I promise you, Tadek, you will have the window seat. Rest now, my dear father. The rolls at the bakery will taste a little less golden without you, but we will keep walking the Old Town in the rain for you.

We gather today not to say goodbye to a legend, but to celebrate a man who simply lived his life with warmth and loyalty. He was the one who always had the kettle on, who knew the names of every child on the street, and who could fix almost anything with a bit of wire and a lot of patience. Those who knew him best will remember his laugh, which arrived before he did, and his habit of telling the same stories with a fresh twist each time.

He was never one for fuss. Ask him how he was and he would say he was grand, even on the days when it was not true. Yet when a neighbour fell ill, or a friend needed a lift to the hospital, he was the first to arrive, asking nothing in return. Those small, steady acts of kindness were the true measure of him, and they are the reason so many people are here today.

As we say our final goodbyes, let us hold on to the best of him: his generosity, his humour, and his quiet faith in the people around him. He has left us richer than he found us. May he rest in peace, and may the road rise up to meet him.

I live on Rehov Brenner in the Florentin area of Haifa, and I am making this statement because on the evening of 9 November my bag was taken from outside the Cofix branch on Ben Yehuda Street, close to the corner with Ahad Ha'am. I had gone in for a takeaway coffee after my shift at Rambam Hospital, where I work as a nurse on the cardiology ward. My phone, a black Samsung, and my keys were inside a brown leather tote that I had hooked over the back of the chair while I waited at the counter. When I came back out, the chair was empty and the bag was gone.

I did not see anyone leave with it, but a man in a grey hoodie had been standing near the bus stop for several minutes before I went inside, and he was gone when I came out. I also noticed a woman with a green scooter who seemed to be watching the cafe window. I have given the staff at Cofix the CCTV timestamps I remembered, which are roughly 19:35 to 19:50. My banking app shows a transfer attempt at 19:58 from my card, which I have already reported to my bank under reference number 661398, and I have changed my passwords. I have also made a report to the mobile carrier so the phone can be blocked.

I would be grateful if the officer could confirm whether the cafe's camera footage has been requested and let me know the case number, so I can provide it to my insurer. My work email is noa.abergel@rambam-mail.example and my mobile is 052-771-4093. I am happy to attend the station at Herzl Street at any time that suits you.
