Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus, Hannah's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words about the woman I've known for all twenty-nine years of her life. Hannah has always been the one who finishes what she starts. When she was nine she decided she would learn to swim the length of the lake at our cottage, and she spent that whole summer in the water until she did it. That same stubbornness is why she found Jonathan, and why, when she told me she was marrying him, I knew it was going to stick.

Jonathan, I'll be honest, when Hannah first brought you home I was ready to be suspicious. But you showed up to Mum's birthday with a bag of the good coffee and asked her forty questions about her garden, and that was the end of my resistance. You have made my sister laugh harder than anyone I know, and you've shown her what steady looks like. If you ever need a reference, Hannah can be reached at hannah.lindqvist@maplemail.ca, though I'd advise you to just call her, she's usually up for a chat.

So please raise your glasses to Hannah and Jonathan. You've got a life of January mornings, cold feet on the couch and two very stubborn people figuring it out together, and I can't think of two people I'd rather see doing it. Cheers.

When I first walked into the physics lab at my secondary school, I expected the equipment to intimidate me. Instead, I found a space where curiosity was rewarded more than correct answers. Over the years, I have learned that the most interesting questions rarely come with clean solutions, and that patience matters as much as talent. Building a small wind turbine from salvaged motors taught me this lesson more clearly than any textbook. The first three designs failed in ways I did not anticipate, and each failure forced me to re-examine assumptions I had taken for granted.

That experience shaped how I approach my studies. I am drawn to engineering because it combines theory with the messy reality of materials that bend, overheat, or behave unpredictably. I want to understand not only how systems are meant to work, but why they fail when they do. I have started keeping a notebook of these observations, and reading back through it reveals a steady shift from wanting quick answers to asking better questions.

I hope to bring this mindset to your programme. I am eager to work alongside people who see problems as invitations rather than obstacles, and I am prepared to contribute through hard work, collaboration and a willingness to be wrong in productive ways. Studying here would give me the depth of knowledge and the community of peers I need to pursue the questions that currently keep me up at night.

Hey Marta, I finally sat down to write properly, so here's the long version of why I left Lisbon. My name is Joana Ferreira Lopes, and when I moved to Hamburg in January 2019 I was still working as a senior analyst at Banco Atlântico in Porto, which felt like a lifetime ago. Honestly the job was fine. What got to me was the feeling that every year looked exactly like the one before it, and I wanted to see whether I could build something different.

The first few months in Hamburg were rough. Jonas, the man who rented me the flat in Eimsbüttel, kept apologising for the radiator that only worked on Tuesdays, and I spent my evenings trying to decipher the letters from the Ausländerbehörde. I cried more than once in the Rewe near Osterstraße because I couldn't find the right kind of flour. Still, I kept going to the language café on Thursdays, and slowly the German started to stick.

What surprised me most is how much I miss the small things back home, the bica after lunch, the way everyone talks over each other at dinner. Jonas says I'll stop missing them eventually. Maybe he's right. Write back soon and tell me whether Sofia finally got her transfer to the Lisbon office, because I'd love to hear the gossip.

Abraço,
Joana

Kai, the man who rented me the flat in Neustadt, kept apologising for the radiator that only worked on Tuesdays, and I spent my evenings trying to decipher the letters from the Ausländerbehörde. I cried more than once in the Rewe near Hansastraße because I couldn't find the right kind of flour. Still, I kept going to the language café on Thursdays, and slowly the German started to stick.

What surprised me most is how much I miss the small things back home, the bica after lunch, the way everyone talks over each other at dinner. Kai says I'll stop missing them eventually. Maybe he's right. Write back soon and tell me whether Beatriz finally got her transfer to the Coimbra office, because I'd love to hear the gossip.

Abraço,
Ana

After three days in Savannah, I finally found the coffee shop everyone kept talking about: Honeybee Roasters on Bull Street. I walked in on Thursday, November 14th, soaked from a sudden downpour, and the barista, a tall guy named Marcus, handed me a towel before I even ordered. The cardamom latte was worth the detour, and I spent an hour sketching the old oak trees outside the window while the rain drummed on the awning.

Caroline, my travel buddy, had a different itinerary in mind. She wanted to see the squares and the cemeteries, and we ended up at Forsyth Park, where the fountain was glowing in the late afternoon light. Caroline is the planner in our friendship, so she had already booked a table for us at a seafood place down the road. I kept teasing her that she'd reserved more meals than we had days, but she just laughed and reminded me that the Savannah humidity makes everyone hungry.

If you visit, go in November. The crowds thin out, the temperatures are mild, and the city feels like it belongs to the people who actually live there. Just bring an umbrella, because I learned the hard way that Georgia showers come without warning. Caroline's sister, Caroline Jr., who lives nearby, texted me the number of a dry cleaner that rescued my jacket, and I'm sharing it here in case you need it too: 912-555-0148. Happy travels.

input:
I am writing this notice with a heavy heart, and with a great deal of gratitude, for my father, Sébastien Laurent, who died peacefully at home on 14 August, aged 71. For forty years Sébastien was a senior engineer at Vexan Mécanique in Lyon, where he designed the cooling systems that kept our region's trains running through the hottest summers. Those who worked with him remember a man who listened first and spoke second, and who never missed the chance to mentor a nervous apprentice. He was equally at ease on a factory floor and in the kitchen of our flat on Rue Vaubecour, where he cooked on Sunday mornings for anyone who wandered in.

Dad loved his garden, his old Peugeot, and above all his dog, Biscuit, a scruffy terrier who followed him to the bakery every morning and refused to be parted from him. Sébastien is survived by my mother, Odile, by my sister Claire, and by me. Our family is grateful to his colleague and closest friend of thirty years, Yannick Roussel, who sat with him on so many evenings and who made the final weeks lighter than they might otherwise have been.

A service will be held on 22 August at the church of Saint-Polycarpe, followed by a gathering nearby. In place of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Lyon Cardiac Support Fund. Dad, we will miss your laugh, your patience, and your terrible puns. Rest well.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Alejandro Ferrer, and I've been Alex to Marisol's family since the day we met. I want to start by thanking all of you for making the trip to Mexico City, and for the patience it took to find the little chapel in Roma Norte that Marisol insisted on.

I first saw Marisol on a rainy Tuesday in January, at a tiny taquería on Calle Orizaba. She was arguing with the owner about whether the salsa verde had too much cilantro, and she was right, and he knew it. I remember thinking that anyone brave enough to correct a man over his own tortillas was someone I wanted to know better. Her friends still call her Mari, but her grandmother has always called her Chiquita, and I've learned that when Chiquita comes out, it's time to stop talking and start listening.

What I love most about Marisol is that she never does anything halfway. When she decided to learn to surf, she was on the water in Sayulita before she could properly stand up. When we moved into our first apartment on Calle Tonalá, she spent a whole weekend repainting the kitchen a yellow that nobody in her family could believe. It turned out to be exactly right. That's Marisol: bold, warm, and completely certain of what makes a place feel like home.

I also want to say something about her family, because they've welcomed me in ways I never expected. Her mother taught me to make mole over three long afternoons, and her brothers have made it their mission to teach me every swear word in the Spanish language. I'm still working on those, which Marisol says is probably a good thing.

So please raise your glasses with me. To Marisol, my partner, my favorite argument, and the best decision I have ever made. Salud, and thank you all for being here.

Many of you know that our mother, Miriam, has been planning this evening since the day Tomer first mentioned Adi's name. She made me promise to keep this short, so I will try.

When Tomer was nine, he wanted to be a pilot, and he spent a whole summer building a model of a Dassault Mirage out of balsa wood in our parents' garage in Netanya. It never flew, but he never gave up on it. That same stubbornness is what I see in him now, the way he shows up for Adi every single day. Last year, when Adi started her new post as a senior engineer at Rafael Dynamics, Tomer drove up to her office in Herzliya at six in the morning just to bring her coffee before her first meeting. He would never admit that story himself, so I am telling it for him.

Adi, you have become the sister I always hoped for. You make my brother laugh harder than anyone, and you have brought our whole family closer together. Please raise your glasses to Tomer and Adi, and may your life together be as steady as the Mediterranean on a calm June evening. L'chaim!

March 14th. Rain again, the grey kind that gets into your coat and stays there. I have been meaning to write this down for a week because something happened on Tuesday that I still can't fully put into words.

It started at the Fraunhofer office in Leipzig, where I work as a Senior Data Analyst. My manager, Dr. Klaus Brenner, called me into his room at half past nine. I had expected a routine check-in about the Q2 forecasting project, so when he closed the door I felt my stomach drop. He was kind about it, actually. Budget cuts, a restructuring of the team, and a position they are offering me in Munich if I want it. Four years in Leipzig and I am being asked to pack up everything. I told him I needed time, and he said I had until the end of the month.

I walked home along the Karl-Liebknecht-Straße in the rain, phone in my pocket, not answering anyone. When I got in, Mira was waiting by the door, tail going like a windscreen wiper. Mira is our old grey cat, sixteen years old now, and she has decided she is entitled to every warm spot in the flat. She climbed onto my chest on the sofa and purred until my breathing slowed down. Honestly, I think she is the only one who understood what I needed that evening.

I called my sister Anke later. She is thirty-four and has never once let me hide from a hard conversation. She also told me, without any hesitation, that I was going to say yes to Munich. "You always go quiet when you're already decided," she said. Annoyingly, she is usually right. Our mother rang the next morning too, asking if I had eaten. Some things never change, even at my age.

So here is the plan. I will visit Munich next weekend to look at apartments in Schwabing, and I will ask Klaus for a proper written offer. Everyone keeps calling me Hanni, which I secretly love, so I suppose the Munich version of me will be Hanni with a new commute. I am scared, but it is a good kind of scared. Mira is already asleep on my jacket, so I guess that settles where she's coming too.

My name is Mikael Lindqvist, and I am making this statement at the Solna police station on 14 October regarding the theft of my bicycle and the damage to my garden gate. I live at Ekbacksvägen 12, 171 45 Solna, in a two-storey house I have rented for six years. I was born in Gävle, and I still speak with a bit of the Gävle accent when I am tired, which my colleagues at the hospital tease me about.

On the evening of 11 October I came home from my shift at around 19:40. I parked my grey Crescent bicycle in the usual place by the cellar door, locked it with a heavy chain, and went inside. When I went out again the next morning at 06:15 to fetch it for work, the chain was lying cut through on the gravel, and the bicycle was gone. The garden gate was also hanging off its upper hinge, which had not been the case the night before.

I have checked with the neighbours. Mrs. Bergström at number 14 heard a loud scraping sound around 23:00 but thought it was the recycling bins. Mr. Ahlgren at number 10 saw a dark van with no visible registration plate reversing into the lane behind our houses. He did not see anyone get out. I have not been able to find anything on the nearby bicycle sales sites yet.

I would like the police to look into the possibility of CCTV from the petrol station on Solnavägen, which I believe covers that stretch of road. If you need to contact me, my mobile number is 070-438 19 52, and I can also be reached at mikael.lindqvist@posteo.se. I am happy to come back to the station with any documents you require, including the receipt for the bicycle and photographs of the gate.

I should also mention that my dog, Pelle, a small grey terrier, was inside the house during the incident and was not hurt, though he was clearly unsettled afterwards. He barks at anything unfamiliar near the gate, so if anyone was looking around the property, he may have been the one who alerted the neighbours. I have been posting updates on my Instagram account, @mikael.bikes.solna, in case anyone in the area has seen anything similar.

I confirm that the details above are true to the best of my knowledge, and I understand that providing false information to the police is a criminal offence.

Mikael Lindqvist

input: Growing up in Haifa, I learned early that a good idea needs a patient listener. When I was eleven, I spent three weeks volunteering at Rambam Hospital's pediatric ward, and I noticed how often families waited for hours simply because no one had explained the process. That experience pushed me to start a small tutoring project at my school, Hillel Yaffe High, where I now coordinate sessions for forty students. input:
I have been coming to Boulangerie Lambert on rue des Tanneurs in Lyon for almost three years now, and I think it is time I wrote something down about why I keep going back. My name is Sophie Marchand, though everyone at the counter calls me Soph, which I have never minded. I live two streets over and I walk my dog, a scruffy terrier called Biscuit, past the shop every single morning, so it has become something of a ritual. Biscuit has his own opinions about the croissants and he will sit politely at the door until Madame Lambert hands him a tiny crust of something. Nobody asked her to do that. She just does.

The bread itself is consistently excellent. The tradition loaf has a crackling crust and an open, chewy crumb that holds up for three days, which I know because I have tested it. The pain au chocolat is buttery and flaky without being greasy, and on a cold morning in early February, when the windows steam up and the queue spills onto the pavement, it is the best thing I can think of. Sometimes I arrive late, around half past nine, and the best pastries are gone. That is my own fault, not theirs.

What I appreciate most is the service. The staff remember orders. Soph, as they call me, has become the regular who gets the seeded batard without asking. Last Tuesday, 11 February, I came in with a streaming cold and an apologetic face, and the young assistant, Théo, quietly packed a hot tisane in a paper cup with a sachet of honey and would not take any money for it. Small gestures like that are what make a neighbourhood feel like a neighbourhood.

There are a few small complaints, to be fair. The shop is tiny, so at peak hours it is hard to move, and the card reader has been temperamental for as long as I can remember. Parking nearby is nearly impossible, so most people walk or cycle. None of this has ever stopped me from coming back.

If you are visiting Lyon or you live nearby and have not yet tried Boulangerie Lambert, I would urge you to go early, bring a bag for the bread, and say hello to Madame Lambert. Five stars from me, and Biscuit would give six if he could read.

Hi, I'm writing because my internet has been dropping every evening for about a week now. It usually starts around the time everyone in the flat gets home and starts streaming, and then the connection just cuts out for a few minutes before coming back. input:
Theresa Lindqvist was the kind of person who remembered your birthday, your dog's name, and the thing you had been worried about last Tuesday. She grew up on Maple Crescent in the east end of Hamilton, where she learned to ride a bike on a street that sloped just enough to make every trip feel like an adventure. She went on to Dalhousie University to study nursing, and she never stopped talking about the night shifts at St. Joseph's Hospital, where she said she found her real education in people. Those who worked beside her say she could calm a frightened patient faster than anyone on the ward.

Theresa loved her garden more than almost anything. Every April, she was out with her gloves and her old green watering can, planting tulips she swore would come up brighter than the year before. Her beagle, Biscuit, followed her everywhere, and the two of them were a familiar sight along the Crescent, Biscuit tugging at the leash while Theresa stopped to chat with every neighbour she passed. She knew all of their names, and most of their children's names too.

We will miss her laugh, her stubborn opinions about hockey, and the way she always made room at her table. Thank you, Theresa, for showing us what it means to pay attention to the people we love. Rest now. The tulips are coming up, and we will take care of them for you.

I'm Liam Thornbury, though everyone at the lab has called me Tibs since my first week, after a particularly stubborn cat I had as a child. I currently serve as Senior Data Engineering Lead at Maplewood Analytics in Halifax, where I've spent the last six years building pipelines that move healthcare records across provincial boundaries. Before that I worked in Calgary for a shorter stint at a geospatial startup, which is where I first learned that a well-placed map can change the way a city thinks about itself.

My work sits at the intersection of privacy and scale. Most of what I do involves convincing skeptical clinicians that a dataset can be useful without being exposed, and I have come to believe that the technical problem is the easier half. Over the past two years I have led a small team through three audits, each of which taught me something about how fragile trust is when a single misconfigured bucket can undo years of care. I still keep a laminated checklist from our December 14th review on my desk as a reminder.

Outside of work I coach a under-twelve hockey team on Saturday mornings and volunteer with a community literacy program in the north end. If you want to reach me about the talk or about collaboration, my office line is 902-555-0148, and my passport on file for the cross-border project is CA-P7734210, though please use the conference portal rather than sending that number around. I'm looking forward to meeting you in person and hearing what you're building.

input:
Ah Siobhan, you won't believe the week I've had. Where do I even start? You know I've been meaning to tell you about the job interview in Galway, the one I went for at the start of March. Well, it turns out I didn't get it, but the way I found out was so absurd I still can't stop laughing about it.

So I'd been sitting in Bean & Brew on Shop Street since half eight, trying to look calm with my laptop open, when my phone buzzed. It was an email from the HR lady, Orla Keane, sent to my work address by mistake, so she'd meant to write to someone called Sinead Kilbride. I'm not even sure how that happened, but there I was reading a rejection letter that wasn't meant for me while the barista was calling out names for flat whites. I actually said "oh no" out loud and the man at the next table looked up.

I wrote straight back to her, polite as anything, pointing out the mix-up and asking if I could still have the feedback, because honestly I'd rather know what went wrong. She replied within the hour, mortified, and she copied in Sinead too. That's what I like about Galway people, they're quick to fix things even when they've messed up.

Anyway, the reason I'm telling you all this is that it made me realise I've been putting off a lot of things. My check-up at Galway University Hospital is booked for the 18th of March, and I've been dreading the bloods. I told Mam I'd go but I haven't rung to confirm yet. Also my gym membership at Fit Factory runs out at the end of the month and I keep forgetting to renew it, which is ridiculous since I'm there four times a week.

I came home to Biscuit curled up on the radiator, looking at me like I'd abandoned him for a year. He's a daft ginger cat but he's the only one who never judges me for being a mess. I gave him his tea and then sat on the couch with a cup of tea of my own and just decided to sort the admin out.

So that's my week. Give me a shout when you're free, I'd love a proper catch-up. You can reach me at siobhan.mcgrath.galway@gmail.com if the phone's being dodgy again. Love to Conor and the kids.

input:
Good evening everyone, and thank you all for being here to celebrate Matt and Hannah. For those who don't know me, I'm Callum, Matt's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words, which is a bit rich considering I once told him his first girlfriend was "too posh for him" and he still hasn't forgiven me.

Matt has been "Muffin" to our family since he was about three, when he couldn't say Matthew and it came out as something else entirely. Most of you will know him as Matt, but to Mum he will always be Muffin, and I'm sorry to say that tonight she has informed me she's going to use it during the first dance. Brace yourselves.

Matt was born in Stockport, in a hospital that has since been knocked down and turned into flats, which felt about right for a lad who has always been slightly ahead of his time. He grew up two streets from the chippy on Lindley Road, and I'm told the owner still asks after him every time Mum goes in. If you ever want to know where the Brennan family's loyalties lie, look no further than the counter at Cheeky Chips.

When Hannah first came to dinner at our house, on Saturday 14 May six years ago, Matt spent the whole evening pretending he wasn't nervous. He burnt the lasagne, knocked over a full bottle of Rioja and then, while everyone was distracted by the mess, got down on one knee to fix the table leg that had been wobbling since 1998. Hannah laughed so hard she couldn't stand up. I think that was the moment he knew.

Matt, I've watched you grow into a man I'm genuinely proud of. You're patient where I'm impatient, you listen when I talk over people, and you still answer every single message from our old group chat, even the ones about a dog called Biscuit that nobody asked about. Hannah, thank you for putting up with him, and for giving our family the best Christmas card photo we've ever had.

So please raise your glasses to Matt and Hannah. Here's to a long life together, many more Saturday dinners, and Biscuit, who I'm reliably informed is now the one in charge of the house.
output:

Went to see Dr. Patel this morning for the follow-up on my knee. The swelling has mostly gone down since the last visit, though I still get a sharp twinge when I go up stairs. She checked the range of motion, had me walk across the exam room, and pressed on a few spots along the joint. Nothing alarming, she said, and the imaging looked fine. She wants me to keep up the physical therapy exercises three times a week and to stop running for at least another month. I asked about the ibuprofen and she said I can take it with food, but to cut back if my stomach starts bothering me.

The bigger news is that she wants to see me again in six weeks instead of three months, mostly to see how the knee handles the return to the gym. She also reminded me to get my flu shot before the end of the season, which I keep putting off. I told her I would book it this week. Before I left, I asked whether the stiffness in the mornings was normal, and she said it is common after this kind of injury and should ease up as the strength comes back.

Overall I feel more hopeful than I did a month ago. The pain is manageable, I can do most of my daily errands without thinking about it, and I have a clear plan for the next few weeks. I need to be patient with myself and stick to the exercises even when I feel fine, because that is what she said will keep the knee from flaring up again.

input:
Notes from the product sync, Wednesday. I joined late because of a traffic jam on the way in, so I missed the opening roundup, but I caught most of the discussion around the release checklist. The main open item is the onboarding flow for new users. Our designer has a revised mockup that cuts the signup form from seven fields to three, and the team agreed to test it with a small internal group before anything goes live. I raised a concern about how we will handle users who sign up through the mobile app, since the verification step behaves differently there. We did not fully resolve it, so I have it on my list to check with engineering.

On the backend side, the team reported that the nightly data sync has been failing intermittently. Nobody has pinpointed the cause yet. The working theory is a timeout when the batch size grows past a certain threshold. One engineer offered to add logging to narrow it down, and I asked that we set a clear deadline for finding the root cause so it does not drift for weeks. We agreed to revisit it at the next sync.

I also pushed for better documentation of the support escalation path. At the moment, too many questions go through one person, and when that person is out, things stall. The group was supportive of writing a short guide covering who handles which category of issue and what counts as urgent. Someone from the support team will draft it, and I will review it once it exists.

We spent some time on priorities for the coming weeks. Two items are competing for the same people: the reporting dashboard that stakeholders have been asking for, and the cleanup of old feature flags that is slowing down every release. My view is that the flag cleanup pays off sooner, because it removes friction from everything else, but the decision sits with the product lead and was left open for now.

Action items: confirm the mobile verification behaviour with engineering, add logging to the sync job, draft the escalation guide, and bring a recommendation on the dashboard versus flag cleanup to the next meeting. I will send a follow-up summary to the group tomorrow morning so everyone has the same picture before we split up the work.

The unit was installed by your partner firm on 4 March, yet it has shut down three times in the past two weeks, and on the last occasion we were without heating for almost two days. I was told at the time of installation that the warranty covered all parts and labour for two years, so I expected a prompt repair.

Since 4 March I have called your hotline four times, each time being given a new reference number and promised a callback that never arrived. Your technician, who visited on 12 March, could not identify the fault and left without leaving a written report. I have since sent three emails to service@hartmann-elektro.de and received only an automated reply on each occasion. I am now asking for a qualified engineer to attend within five working days, a full written diagnosis, and either a repair at your cost or a replacement unit.

If I do not hear from you by 25 March, I will escalate this matter to the Bundesnetzagentur and to the consumer arbitration board. I would prefer to resolve this directly with your company, and I look forward to your reply. You may contact me at m.keller.freiburg@gmail.com or on the number listed on my account.

Yours faithfully,

Martina Keller

input:
Dear Journal,

It's been three weeks since I started seeing Dr. Helen Marsh on Tuesday afternoons, and today I finally said the thing I've been circling for months: that I feel like I'm performing being okay. Nicola Brennan is the name on the intake form, but at home everyone calls me Nicky, and I've started to hate how light that sounds. Helen didn't flinch. She just asked what it would feel like to stop performing for one afternoon, and I had no answer.

The session on the 3rd of December was hard but useful. We talked about my dad, who never once said he was proud of me, and how I still rehearse conversations with him in the shower. Helen pointed out that I used the word "fine" eleven times in forty minutes. I laughed, then I cried in the car park outside the clinic on Collins Street, which was embarrassing because it was peak lunch hour and there were people everywhere.

My friend Sophie texted me afterwards, asking if I wanted to get dinner at the Thai place in Fitzroy on Saturday. I almost said no out of habit. Instead I wrote back "yes, but can we just talk, not catch up?" and she replied with a heart and "always." I'm trying to remember that people can handle the honest version of me.

Helen suggested I keep a small notebook of moments when the performance slips, not to judge them but just to notice. So tonight, on the 9th, I wrote down three: laughing genuinely at a dumb podcast, telling my landlord the sink was leaking without apologising, and holding Mum's hand at the pharmacy without pretending I didn't need it.

I don't feel transformed. I feel tired and a bit raw. But I also feel, for the first time in a while, like there might be a version of Nicola that doesn't have to hold everything together. I'll see Helen again on the 17th, and I think I'll bring this notebook with me.

Dear Grandma,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the heat in Valencia hasn't been too much for you this June. I'm writing to say that I finally got the job I told you about. Starting on 14 June, I'll be working as a junior analyst at Brightwater Solutions in Madrid, which is a bit of a shock since I thought I'd be stuck in the office in Seville for another year. Mum says I should slow down, but at twenty-six I think it's time to take some risks. Bryony at the clinic on Calle Mayor, where I go for my physio, says I'm mad to move so soon after my shoulder injury, but she's been wonderful and promised to send me exercises I can do at the new flat.

I've been trying to settle in and I've already found a little cafe near the office, Café Alameda, where the owner, Mateo, remembers my order after just two visits. He asked me what I was reading, and when I told him it was your old copy of Jane Eyre, he laughed and said I had good taste. I have also joined the gym at the end of my street, which is much smaller than the one at home, but the trainers are friendly and it keeps me going.

Please write back when you can, or ring me on my mobile. You can also email me at bryony.hollis@brightwatersol.com, though I'm not sure how often I'll check it during the first few weeks. Give my love to Grandad's photo on the mantelpiece, and tell Auntie Carmen I'll bring her the marzipan she likes next time.

Love always,
Bronwen

input:
Tuesday 11 June

I almost didn't write anything tonight. Mam rang at six asking if I'd remembered the form for the bank, and I had to admit I hadn't, not even the copy I printed last week. So I spent the evening at the kitchen table hunting through the folder while the kettle went cold twice. The passport number is on the front of the old one, and I copied the digits onto a sticky note so I'd stop making mistakes: P 4471 9028. My full name is Yvonne Maria Keogh, though nobody in Cork has called me Yvonne since primary school. It's Vonnie to my sister and Keogh to the bank.

The appointment is on Monday 17 June at half nine in the morning, at the branch on Patrick Street. Eoin says he'll drive me, which is kind of him given he hates the Cork traffic more than I do. I've told him the bank will want a utility bill with my address, so I dug out the ESB statement. It says 14 Mill Road, Blackpool, Cork, which still feels strange to write down after two years in the flat above the bakery on Gurranabraher Avenue. Mill Road is quieter, and the back garden gets the sun in the afternoons, which is why I signed the lease.

I called the bank this afternoon to confirm, and the woman on the line made me repeat my number twice. It's 021 555 0192 on the landline and 087 412 6639 on the mobile, the one I actually answer. She said the mobile would be better for the verification text, so I've switched it over in the account settings. Small things like that take ages when you're doing them alone.

Walked down to the river after tea. The light was that long gold June light that makes the whole city look like it's apologising for the rain. Thought about Dad, who would have had opinions about the bank, about the form, about me doing it all myself. He'd have wanted me to get the statement framed. Mam says that's a sign I'm getting sentimental in my old age, and she's probably right.

Tomorrow I'll find the spare photocopy of the passport and put it in the envelope with the bill, so Monday is only the walk and the queue. I'll write again when it's done. Eoin has promised coffee after, and I've promised not to complain about the parking.

I've been going to Kapihan ni Lola on Scout Tuazon Street in Quezon City for almost two years now, and I finally felt I had to write something after last Saturday. My name is Wilfredo Dacanay, but everyone at the counter calls me Willy, and I've been a regular since the place opened. The coffee is still strong, the barako blend is still the best in the area, and the staff remember how I like my kape. Last month they even remembered my birthday, which I'd only mentioned once in passing.

The problem was on October 12, when I came in around 3 PM to pick up a pre-ordered box of pastries for my mother's 70th. I'd paid through their GCash account, reference number 0917-4483-206, and the order was supposed to be ready by two. It wasn't. The barista just shrugged and said the kitchen was short-staffed. Nobody called me, and I had to wait forty minutes while my pancit cooled in my car. My plate number is ABL 4721, parked right out front, and the parking attendant had already flagged me for overstaying.

What bothered me most was how the manager handled it. She apologized, but only after I raised my voice, and she offered a 10 percent discount without asking what happened. I posted about it on Instagram under @willy.eats.qc and tagged the cafe, and within an hour someone from their team replied with a generic apology. I'm not asking for a refund. I just want a call when an order is delayed, and I think that's fair for a place that charges premium prices.

input:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to recommend Gerda Lindqvist, who worked under my supervision as a senior analyst at Brenner Logistik GmbH in Hamburg from March 2019 until she left the company in October 2023. Gerda joined our data team with a degree in statistics from the University of Freiburg, and within her first year she had rebuilt our forecasting models for the northern distribution hub. Her work was precise, well documented and consistently on time, which mattered a great deal during the supply disruptions of 2021.

What distinguished Gerda most was her willingness to explain complex results to people who did not work with numbers. She ran a monthly briefing for the operations managers, and by the end of her tenure they were asking her questions before making decisions rather than after. She also mentored two junior colleagues, one of whom has since been promoted to team lead. Gerda approached every project with curiosity and a steady sense of responsibility, and she rarely needed to be asked twice.

I would recommend Gerda without reservation for any role that requires analytical rigour combined with clear communication. Please feel free to contact me at the address below should you wish to discuss her work further. On 14 October 2023 she had her final review, and I can confirm she met every objective we set for her.

With kind regards,

Markus Feld

markus.feld@brenner-logistik.de

input:
You won't believe what happened on the train home last week. I was half asleep, leaning against the window, when a man across from me started laughing at nothing. Then he got off at the wrong stop and came sprinting back just as the doors were closing, holding a bento box like it was a trophy. Everyone in the car burst out laughing, even the grumpy salaryman who'd been glaring at his phone the whole ride. It made me realize how rarely strangers in a crowded place get to share a moment like that.

I've been thinking about it ever since. Life here can feel so orderly and quiet that small disruptions stand out. I spent the rest of the evening walking through a little shopping arcade near the station, past shelves of mochi and stationery, and I kept catching myself smiling. Nothing dramatic happened, but I felt lighter than I had in weeks.

So I wanted to tell you, because I know you'd have laughed harder than anyone. Next time you visit, let's ride that same line together and see if we get lucky with a little chaos of our own. Maybe we'll even pack ourselves a snack for the trip.

Hi everyone, I'm Oliver from Year 9, and I've been asked to write a little something for this term's newsletter about my first few weeks at Hartwell. Most of you know I came here from Leeds, where I was born and spent my whole childhood, so the move to a smaller town has been a bit of a shock. The biggest change, honestly, is that everything feels closer together. In Leeds it could take forty minutes just to get across the city, and here I can walk to school in under ten.

The person who made the first month easier was my form tutor, Freya Lindqvist. On my first morning she walked me round the building, showed me where the science labs were, and explained the library rota without making me feel like an idiot for forgetting the codes. She also talked me into joining the chess club, which I had been avoiding. We meet on Thursdays in room 12, and I'm told the reigning champion is a Year 11 who never loses on Tuesdays.

If you're new this year, my advice is simple: say yes to things, even the ones that seem awkward. I nearly didn't go to the Harvest Assembly on the 14th of October, and I'm glad I did. My mum still has the photo of me reading a poem in front of the whole school. Thanks for reading, and see you all at the next club meeting.

input:
I have been meaning to write this review for weeks, but after my visit last Saturday I can't keep putting it off. My name is Zawadi Otieno, and I live just off Ngong Road in Kilimani, so I am a regular customer of Sunrise Tailors on Argwings Kodhek Road. I went in on 14 October with a navy suit that needed to be let out for my cousin's wedding, and I was honestly nervous, because the last time I took a jacket to a tailor here it came back with one sleeve shorter than the other.

This time was different. The tailor, a soft-spoken gentleman named Mr. Kamau, measured me twice without any fuss and explained every alteration before touching the fabric. He pointed out that the trousers needed taking in at the waist but that the shoulders were fine as they were, which I appreciated, because some shops would simply charge you for more work. When I asked whether the job could be done in time, he took my number, 0722 418 306, and promised a call once it was ready. The call came on the Wednesday evening, and the suit was perfect.

The prices are fair for Nairobi, and the staff remember returning customers. My sister Zuri, who studied fashion design at Kenyatta University, came with me on the second visit and was impressed by the stitching. She said the seams on the inside were finished more neatly than many boutique pieces she has seen downtown. We also talked to the shop assistant, who was patient with Zuri's many questions about the machines.

The only downside is that the shop is small and parking on Argwings Kodhek can be a nightmare at lunchtime, so plan ahead. Inside, though, it is clean, quiet and well organised, with a rack of finished garments you can browse while you wait.

If you need alterations, I would recommend Sunrise Tailors without hesitation. Ask for Mr. Kamau, bring your measurements, and give yourself a week. I will certainly be back in November for my brother's graduation outfit.

input: My mother, Zahra, never once let a day pass without sending me a message from the kitchen of our little flat in Leeds, where she had lived since she left Lahore in 1979. Paolo Benedetti è nato a Torino nel 1979 e, dopo gli studi in ingegneria, ha iniziato a lavorare nel settore della logistica. Oggi è Responsabile Operativo presso Trasporti Lombardi Srl, dove coordina una squadra di quaranta persone tra il deposito di Settimo e gli uffici di via Cigliano. Chi lo conosce dice che arriva sempre per primo e se ne va per ultimo, ma che trova sempre il tempo per una telefonata a chi ne ha bisogno.

La sua passione per la montagna è nata da ragazzo, durante le estati passate con la famiglia in Valle d'Aosta. Ancora oggi, ogni luglio, riserva due settimane per le escursioni, spesso con gli amici di sempre. Paolo dice che la montagna gli insegna la pazienza, qualità che in ufficio serve più di quanto si pensi.

Nel tempo libero ha anche avviato un piccolo progetto di recupero di biciclette d'epoca nel quartiere di Borgo Vittoria, dove ha il suo laboratorio in un vecchio cortile restaurato. Qui ha formato una decina di ragazzi del quartiere, offrendo loro uno spazio dove imparare un mestiere concreto e sentirsi parte di una comunità.

Chi volesse saperne di più sul progetto, o semplicemente parlare di logistica e di ciclismo, può contattarlo al numero 011 4827165. Risponde volentieri, anche se preferisce che le chiamate avvengano nelle ore d'ufficio.

La mia esperienza con Paolo risale a quando lavoravamo insieme sul primo grande appalto della società. Ricordo che, durante una riunione tesa del 14 luglio 2016, fu lui a trovare la soluzione che tutti stavamo cercando, con una calma che non dimenticherò. Da allora, ogni volta che devo prendere una decisione difficile, mi chiedo cosa farebbe Paolo. Sono Chiara, e questa biografia è per tutti voi che lo ascolterete domani.

input:
Session notes, Tuesday. I told Dr Whitcombe that I've been sleeping badly since my brother Harold moved up to Leeds in June. He rang on the 14th of July to say the new flat has a box room he's already calling mine when I visit, which should have felt kind and somehow didn't. I sat in the car outside the Co-op afterwards for twenty minutes with the engine off. The registration on the Corsa is still KX19 VNR, and I keep thinking about how often I used to drive it up to see him without a second thought.

We talked about the fact that I've been filling the evenings with tasks so I don't have to sit with the quiet. Dr Whitcombe asked what the quiet actually says when I listen to it. I said it says I'm the one who stayed. She asked whether staying has ever felt like a job I was given instead of one I chose. I didn't answer straight away. Our cat Biscuit wandered in during that pause and sat on the notes, which I think made us both laugh.

Homework: write down three things I did this week for myself, not for anyone else. I have one already. I made Harold's favourite lentil soup on Sunday and didn't post a photo of it, which is a start. Next session is the 22nd of July, and I'd like to talk about whether calling him is the same as being with him.

input:
I'm writing this down so I remember what Dr. Lindqvist told me at my appointment on April 14 at the Karolinska clinic in Solna, which is just outside Stockholm where I live. My name is Freja, and I went in because of the tiredness and dizziness I've had since March. Dr. Lindqvist, who is a senior consultant in internal medicine, took my blood pressure twice and ordered a full blood panel. She said my iron levels are low, which probably explains most of what I've been feeling, but she wants to see my thyroid numbers before deciding anything else.

I told her my colleague Anders at the office had the same symptoms last winter and it turned out to be a vitamin D problem. I finally made it to Savannah last month, and I have to admit it lived up to every photo I'd saved on my phone. My name is Nathan Holloway, and I work as a logistics coordinator for Brightwater Freight in Atlanta, so a long weekend away from spreadsheets was overdue. I flew into the airport on September 9th and grabbed a rental car that smelled faintly of pine air freshener. My first stop was the riverfront, where I walked for almost two hours, stopping every few minutes to watch the cargo ships drift past the bluff.

On the second morning I wandered into the Forsyth Park area before the crowds showed up. The fountain was running, the oak trees were draped in Spanish moss, and a retired couple was feeding pigeons on a bench like they had done it for decades. I ate a lunch of shrimp and grits at a small place off Bull Street, and the waiter, a friendly guy named Marcus, told me to come back for the ghost tour. I told him Holloway would probably be expected to stay on schedule, but I might sneak off for it anyway.

If you go, plan at least three days and don't rely on your phone's map once you're inside the historic squares. Getting lost is half the charm. I'm already sketching out a return trip for the cooler weeks of October, and I'll be sure to post an update here when I do. Thanks for reading along, and feel free to send me your own Savannah tips at nathan.holloway@brightwaterfreight.com.

I'm Ben, and I work as a clinical research coordinator at Riverside Medical Center in Columbus, Ohio, where I've spent the last six years helping run trials on cardiac rehabilitation. Most people call me Benji, a nickname my older sister gave me long before I ever wore a lab coat, and I've decided to keep it because it reminds me where I started. I grew up in Dayton, went to Ohio State for my undergraduate degree, and still believe the best ideas come from hallway conversations at the coffee machine.

My path into research was not a straight line. After graduating, I spent two years working nights as a respiratory therapy assistant, which taught me more about patients than any textbook could. That experience is why I push so hard for study designs that ask patients what they actually need. My closest collaborator, Priyanka Rao, joined the team the same September I did, and nearly every project I've been proud of has been one we shaped together over long lunches and too many spreadsheets.

Outside of work I coach a youth soccer team on Saturday mornings and try to keep my weekends free of anything with a screen. If you want to talk about trial recruitment, patient communication, or why cardiac rehab referrals are still so low, you can reach me at 614-555-0187 or stop by my session. I'd love to hear what you are working on.

Session notes for myself, written after my appointment with Dr. Iyer on 14 January. I am thirty-four and still not sure how to say the thing I came to say, so I am writing it down first. Nisha, that is me, has been feeling untethered since my father's health started slipping last autumn. Every evening I come back to 27, Carmichael Road, Flat 4B, Bengaluru, and the silence of the flat presses on me. My cat Biscuit is the only one who greets me, and even he has started sleeping through the afternoons. Dr. Iyer asked me to notice when the heaviness is worst, and it is always between six and eight, when I would have called my mother. I have not called her in weeks.

Some things I did this week that helped, even a little. On Tuesday I walked to the vegetable market near Nisha's old school instead of ordering online, and I stopped to talk with the vendor who remembered my mother's name. On Thursday I made the dal she used to make and burned the first batch, which made me laugh properly for the first time in a month. Dr. Iyer says laughter that surprises me is worth paying attention to. I wrote the date on the fridge calendar, 19 January, as the day I will call my brother Nikhil and ask him to share the caregiving load honestly.

For next time I want to bring the list of evenings I felt okay and see whether there is a pattern. I am tired of treating every bad evening as proof that nothing will change. Dr. Iyer asked me to be gentle with myself, which I found hard to hear, but I am going to try.

Hi all, I've been thinking about the summer trip and I think we need to lock in the plans soon before everyone's schedules fill up. My suggestion is that we go for a full week rather than a long weekend, because the travel time alone makes a short trip feel like it's not worth the effort. Everyone has been saying they want to see the beaches and do some island hopping, so I started looking at options that would let us do both without too much back and forth between places.

For accommodation, I'd lean toward a beachfront place with a kitchen and enough bedrooms that no one has to share a room they don't want to. Breakfast is a big deal for the younger ones, so a place that serves a morning meal would save us a lot of hassle. I've also been reading reviews about the transport between islands, and it seems that booking the ferries a few days in advance is smart because the boats fill up quickly during peak travel periods. I'd rather pay a little extra now than scramble on the day.

On the budget side, I put together a rough breakdown. Flights will be the biggest expense, followed by lodging and then food and activities. I think we should each put in our share into a shared account so that we aren't chasing people for money at the end of the trip. If anyone wants to split the cost of a private boat for a day, let me know early so I can factor it in. I'd also like to set aside a small amount for emergencies, like a missed connection or a sudden rain delay that cancels a planned excursion.

I know some of you have concerns about the heat and the crowds, so I tried to plan around that. I am a British national living in the Setagaya ward of Tokyo, and I am writing to report a theft that took place on the evening of 14 November near Shimokitazawa Station. At about 9:20 p.m. I had set my black leather backpack down beside me while waiting for the train. When I turned to check the departure board, the bag was gone. Inside were my passport, my Japanese residence card, a Sony laptop and about 35,000 yen in cash. I did not see anyone running, but a young man in a grey hoodie had been standing close to me moments earlier.

I reported the loss to the station staff, who called a officer from the Setagaya police box. I was asked to provide my details and a description of the bag, which I have done. Paul is the name on my registration and my card, and my contact number is 090-4471-2038. I can also be reached at paul.whitmore@mailbox.jp. I would be grateful if the officers could check whether any passport or residence card has been handed in to a lost property office, as I need to replace them urgently.

I am happy to attend the police box at any time that suits you, and I will bring copies of my identification and the purchase receipt for the laptop. Please let me know the reference number for this report so I can provide it to my embassy and to the immigration office. Thank you for your help with this matter.

Paul Whitmore

I am writing to submit a claim for damage to my property at 14 Hollins Road, Headingley, Leeds, LS6 3QD, which occurred on the night of Thursday 16 May. I am the sole named policyholder on the buildings and contents cover under policy reference HD-884210-GB, and I have been resident at this address since 2017.

At approximately 22:40 on the evening in question I left the house to collect a parcel from the Wellfield Clinic pharmacy counter on Otley Road, which I expected to close at 23:00. I was gone roughly forty minutes. When I returned up Hollins Road, I found the front window of the living room had been smashed and the glass was scattered across the carpet inside. Nothing appeared to have been taken from the front rooms, but the drawers in the study had been pulled out and the contents strewn across the floor.

I called 999 immediately and an officer attended at about 23:55. He recorded the incident under reference 4417 of 17 May and advised me to secure the property with a temporary board, which I arranged the following morning through Hollis Glazing & Joinery on Kirkstall Lane. Their invoice for the board and the emergency call-out, totalling £186.00, is enclosed along with the police incident log.

Natasha Brennan, a neighbour at number 16, saw a grey hatchback parked outside our house that evening and has kindly provided a short written statement, also enclosed. She described the vehicle as having a roof bar and a partially obscured registration beginning with the letters YK. I have also enclosed photographs of the window frame and the study, taken on the morning of Friday 17 May, and a schedule of the items I believe were disturbed or damaged, including a laptop, a cased watch, and a small cash tin which I had kept in the study desk.

I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this claim and let me know whether you require anything further, such as receipts for the contents or a visit from one of your loss adjusters. I can be reached on 0113 496 2287 or at nathan.holbrook.claims@mail.co.uk. Please note that I am happy to attend an inspection at any time convenient to you.

input:
When I was seventeen, my aunt Adaeze Okonkwo, who works as a senior pharmacist at Lagoon Hospital Ikeja, told me that medicine is mostly about listening. I did not believe her then. I thought it was about memorising drug names and passing the exam. But that June, when I spent three weeks shadowing her on the ward, I started to understand what she meant. An old man came in with a swollen leg and could only speak Yoruba, and it was a nurse named Chinonso Eze who sat with him for twenty minutes until the diagnosis became clear.

I have carried that afternoon with me ever since. It taught me that a clinic is a place where language, trust and money all meet, and that a good doctor has to manage all three. Back home in Ibadan, my younger cousin Tunde and I started a small weekend health talk at our church, and we discovered how many people were afraid to ask questions. Tunde, who is far better with people than I am, reminded me that the best advice is the advice someone actually understands. Our group now meets every second Saturday, and I keep a notebook of the questions people ask most.

I am applying to your programme because I want to learn how to turn that kind of listening into care that reaches more people. I have already written to Dr. Ngozi Balogun, the programme coordinator, about the community placement I hope to join, and I can be reached at mariam.adebayo@example.com or on 08031- 554-219. My student account number for the transcript request is NG-2291-44087.

I saw Dr. Fitzgerald at the surgery in Mullingar on Tuesday 14 November for my six-week check after the knee operation. Jack, my husband, drove me because I'm still not allowed to take the car out. The doctor said the wound has healed well and the swelling has gone down, which was a relief. She asked me to keep doing the physio exercises every morning and to stop taking the ibuprofen unless the pain flares up again. I told her I'd been stubborn about the walking, going out with the dog every afternoon, and she laughed and said Biscuit is no excuse for skipping the rest.

I was born in Athlone, so I told her a bit about how I grew up there and how my mum used to take me to the hospital on the Dublin road when I was small. We talked about my bloodwork too. My cholesterol is slightly high but nothing alarming, and she wants a repeat test in the new year. She also wrote a referral for a dietitian, which my sister Siobhan has been nagging me to get for ages. I'm glad she did, because I honestly didn't know where to start.

My next appointment is on Tuesday 28 November to recheck the bloods and review the physio progress. If anything changes before then, like fever, redness around the scar, or calf pain, I'm to phone the surgery straight away. I've written the number on the fridge and added Jack's mobile as well, just in case.

Jack says he'll drive me again.

I saw Dr. Shapira at Hadassah Ein Kerem last Tuesday, June 11, for the follow-up on my knee. I'm Sarah Lavi, 44, a senior accountant at Meridian Tax Partners in Haifa, and I'd been putting off this visit for weeks because the swelling kept going down and coming back. She asked the usual questions first: where I was born (Netanya, for the record), whether I'd been walking more since the spring, and whether the physio sessions at Gymnest near my flat on Herzl Street were helping. I told her they were, mostly, though I still avoid stairs.

She examined the knee, ordered an MRI for the following week, and said the cartilage on the inner side looked irritated but not torn. We agreed I'd keep up the strengthening exercises and stop the long runs until the scan is back. Sarah, she said, you're doing the right things, you're just doing them too quickly. I laughed, because that's exactly what my husband Yoni says every morning.

The MRI is booked for June 18 at 9:30 in the morning. I'll drop the results into my patient portal, and if anything looks worse I'm to call the clinic on 03-5555214 or email sarah.lavi@meridiantax.co.il. Otherwise, follow-up is set for July 2. I left feeling more reassured than I expected.

Dear Abuela Rosario,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden in Oaxaca is keeping you busy. I keep thinking about the afternoon you told me how Nicolas's grandfather walked out of Tlacolula with one suitcase and a promise to send money home. Nicolas has been telling me the same story lately, and it made me want to write to you properly, the way you taught me.

Nicolas started at Grupo Alvarado Textiles last month, in the logistics office on the north side of Monterrey. He calls it the big leagues, though he admits the coffee machine is worse than yours. He says the people there are kind, and that on his first Friday his supervisor, Ernesto, asked him where he was born. When he said Tlacolula, Ernesto laughed and said his own mother came from a village nearby. Nicolas came home that night glowing about it.

We are planning to visit you on the second weekend of November, if the bus schedule cooperates. Nicolas wants to bring the good mole from the shop on Calle Hidalgo, and I promised I would finally learn to make your tortillas without burning my hand. Please save me a spot at the table. We miss you more than words can carry.

With all my love,
Marisol

input:
I'm Kiri Waititi, and I have spent the last twelve years working as a freshwater ecologist, mostly around the lakes and braided rivers of the Canterbury high country. I grew up in Hamilton, where my grandfather taught me to tell a healthy stream from a sick one by the sound of the water and the things that live under the stones. That early curiosity eventually pulled me south, and I am now a senior scientist at Tui Ridge Environmental, a consultancy based in Christchurch that works with councils, iwi and farming families on water quality and habitat restoration.

My work at Tui Ridge has centred on long-term monitoring programmes. We track macroinvertebrate communities, nutrient loads and sediment movement across catchments that change faster than most people realise. When I started, I assumed the hardest part would be the field science. It turned out the harder skill was listening: sitting at a kitchen table with a farmer who has worked the same valley for forty years and learning what he has already noticed before I arrived with my sampling kit.

In 2021 I led a project on the Rakaia tributaries that combined citizen science with formal sampling. Volunteers from three local schools collected stone samples on a fixed schedule, and we cross-checked their results against our own. The data was useful, but the real outcome was that several students went on to study environmental science at the University of Canterbury. Seeing that pipeline grow has been one of the proudest moments of my career.

Outside work I still spend most weekends in waders. I volunteer with a local trout hatchery and I coach a netball team in Lyttelton, which keeps me honest about teamwork and about the value of a clear, shared goal. My partner Hemi, who runs a small bakery, often reminds me that good science, like good bread, depends on patience and on paying attention to small changes.

Looking ahead, I want to expand our restoration work into the Hurunui catchment, where I think we can prove that modest riparian planting, done with the right community support, delivers measurable gains within five years. I would welcome conversations with anyone at this conference who is interested in collaboration, and I can be reached at kiri.waititi@tuiridge.co.nz. Thank you for the chance to share my work and my story with you.

I'm writing this summary for my own records after my appointment on September 14 at Riverside Family Medicine. My name is Brian Hollis, and I've been seeing Dr. Melissa Okafor for about three years now. I came in because of the tightness in my chest that started about two weeks ago, mostly when I climb the stairs at work or walk the dog around the block.

Dr. Okafor listened to my history first, then asked a lot of questions about my diet, how much I sleep, and whether I've been under more stress lately. I told her about the reorganization at the warehouse, the extra shifts, and the fact that I quit smoking last spring but still have the occasional cigarette when I'm out with my friends. She took my blood pressure twice, once sitting and once standing, and both readings were higher than I'd like. She also listened to my heart and lungs for a while and had me breathe in and out slowly so she could hear everything clearly.

Based on the exam, she wants me to get an EKG done right away, which they did in the office before I left. She also ordered blood work, including a lipid panel and a basic metabolic panel, and asked me to come back in two weeks to review the results. If the EKG or labs show anything unusual, she will refer me to a cardiologist at St. Brendan's Hospital, which is the group she usually works with for cases like this. I asked whether this could be something serious and she was honest that she doesn't know yet, but she didn't think it was an emergency.

She gave me a few instructions to follow in the meantime. I should avoid heavy lifting at work, cut back on salt, and go to the emergency room right away if the chest tightness gets worse, spreads to my arm or jaw, or comes with shortness of breath or sweating. She also asked me to keep a log of when the symptoms happen and how long they last, which I've started doing in my phone notes. She reminded me that my last tetanus shot is due in the spring and that I should keep my flu shot appointment in October.

On the way out I scheduled my follow-up for September 28 at 9:15 in the morning, and the front desk gave me a printout of my visit summary. My wife, Teresa, wants to come with me to that appointment, so I've added it to our shared calendar. I'll update this note once I have the test results. For now, I'm trying not to worry too much while I wait.

input: I grew up in Łódź, in the Bałuty district, on a street lined with old tenement houses where everyone knew each other's business. My grandmother Halina taught me to read the newspaper aloud before I could understand half of it, and my best friend Marta, who lived two floors below us, was the one who first dragged me to the debating club at fifteen. I am now seventeen, and the habit of asking why things are the way they are has shaped everything I want to study. On 14 October last year, after a long argument with Marta about the city's housing policy, I spent a night at the library reading municipal reports, and that night convinced me that I want to become someone who turns questions like these into evidence and, eventually, into change.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ramon Dela Cruz, the groom's older cousin and the person who has been trying to embarrass Paolo since we were kids sharing a bedroom in Quezon City. I've been asked to keep this short, so I'll do my best, though my wife says I have never once kept anything short in my life.

Paolo grew up at 47 Mabini Street, Barangay Sto. Nino, Marikina City, in a house with a leaking roof and a dog named Mochi who ate more of our childhood homework than either of us did. Mochi was the first creature Paolo ever took care of, and honestly, he's been looking after people in the same stubborn, loyal way ever since. When Paolo told me he was getting married, my first question was whether Mochi's great-grandpup would be attending. The answer was no, but the groom did insist on a dog-friendly reception, which tells you everything about his priorities.

Some of you know Paolo as the quiet one. Those of us who grew up with him know better. Paolo is the guy who sat up with his colleague Benjie Santos through an entire week of server outages at the office, and who still brings Benjie a box of pandesal every Monday, no reason given. That is who Paolo is. He shows up. He notices. He does the small things that nobody thanks you for until one day they realise they've been carried for years.

And then there's Patricia. I'll be honest with you, Patricia, when Paolo first brought you to our family's Noche Buena in December, I was ready to interrogate you about your intentions. Then you spent forty minutes in the kitchen with my mother, learning how to make her lumpia, and by the end of the night she was calling you her second daughter. I lost that battle before it started. Thank you for being patient with all of us, and for making him laugh harder than anyone I know.

So please raise your glasses with me. To Paolo and Patricia, may your marriage be as kind as your first conversations, as generous as your family table, and as full of laughter as the nights we spent in that leaky old house. Mabuhay, and congratulations.

input: I have always believed that a summer job can teach more than a classroom sometimes does. Last year I worked at Greggs Bakery on Mill Road in Cambridge, where I was known to everyone as Robbie, a name I picked up at age nine and never quite shook off. My closest colleague, Ashok Verma, trained me on the morning shift and patiently explained that the trick to the lamination was not speed but attention. input:
Dear Parents and Families,

We are delighted to share some news from our Year 7 community this month. Jonathan Adler, who joined us in September from the Ramat Aviv neighbourhood, has been chosen to represent the school at the regional science fair on 14 May. His project, a small water filtration model built from recycled bottles, impressed the judges during our internal round last week. Jonathan spent many lunchtimes in the library researching sand layers and charcoal filters, and we are proud of his persistence.

Jon has been a regular at the Blue Door Cafe on Herzl Street, where he and his cousin Jordan spent a Saturday afternoon sketching diagrams on napkins while waiting for their order. The owner, Mrs. Lior Peretz, has kindly offered to display the finished model in the cafe window for two weeks after the fair, so that neighbours can see what our students are capable of. Several parents have already asked how they can support the project, and we thank everyone who has donated materials.

For families who have not yet met Jonathan's classmates, the Year 7 science group meets every Tuesday in Room 14 of the Rothschild Hebrew Secondary School. Our teacher, Ms. Tamar Golan, asks that students bring a notebook and a willingness to test ideas that might not work the first time. Jonathan's notebook, which he shared with the class, contains more crossed-out attempts than finished pages, and that is exactly the lesson we want every student to take home.

If you would like to help with the fair, please contact the office at office@rothschild-school.example or call 03-555-0142 before 9 May. Volunteers are needed to help transport the models, set up the tables and speak with visiting families. A short schedule will be sent home with students on 8 May.

Jonathan's family has asked us to thank everyone who has encouraged him this year. Congratulations, Jon, and good luck on the day. We look forward to hearing how your filter performs, and we are sure the whole school will be cheering you on.

Warm regards,
The Year 7 Team

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to recommend Sophie Lindqvist, who worked under my supervision as a senior accountant at Halvorsen & Dahl Logistics in Gothenburg from March 2019 until she relocated to Canada in May 2023. Sophie joined our finance team when we were preparing for a major audit, and within her first month she had rebuilt our accounts payable reconciliation process so that month-end closes dropped from nine working days to four. I have rarely worked with someone so precise and so willing to explain her reasoning to colleagues who did not share her training.

When Sophie decided to move to Canada, I was sorry to lose her but not surprised by her ambition. She managed the paperwork for her own relocation with the same care she gave our ledgers, and she handed over every open workstream to her successor in a documented handover that I still use as a template. She is also someone who volunteers without being asked; she ran our quarterly tax clinic for two years and trained three junior staff to take it over.

Since settling in Toronto, Sophie has kept in touch, and she has told me she is looking for a role where she can combine financial controls with analysis. Hanna Berg

I, Sarah Lindqvist, am making this statement to the Halifax Regional Police, Central Division, on October 14. I was born in Sydney, Nova Scotia, and have lived in the Halifax area for the past eleven years. I work as a dental hygienist at a clinic on Spring Garden Road, and I attend a spin class at Pulse Fitness on Gottingen Street most weekday mornings.

On the morning of October 9, I left my apartment on Agricola Street at approximately 6:40 a.m. to walk to Pulse Fitness. My phone was in my jacket pocket. I noticed a grey Honda Civic, plate NSB 4721, parked across from the bakery with its engine running. The driver appeared to be a man in his forties wearing a navy toque. I did not think much of it at the time.

After class, I went to Blue Heron Cafe on Argyle Street with my colleague Megan Porter, who had come along to the 7:30 session. We sat by the front window for about forty minutes. Megan can confirm that I was on my phone for most of that time, and that the same grey Civic drove past the window twice. Megan later told me she recognised the driver from the clinic's parking lot, but she could not remember his name.

When I returned home around 9:15 a.m., I found my back door unlocked, which I am certain I had locked. Nothing appeared to be missing at first, but my laptop bag had been moved from the hall closet to the kitchen counter. I have not been able to confirm whether anything was taken. I photographed the door frame and the scratches near the lock and have attached them to this statement.

I am requesting that the officers review any available footage from the cafe and from the businesses on Agricola Street for October 9 between 6:30 and 9:30 a.m. I can be reached at sarah.lindqvist@example.ca or at 902-555-0148. Please contact me if you need anything further. I have read this statement and confirm that it is true to the best of my knowledge.

input:
I need some help figuring out what to say to my roommate, Oliver, before things get worse. We've shared a two-bedroom apartment in Halifax for almost three years, and it's been fine until this past spring. Everyone calls him Ollie, even his mom, and he's the kind of person who will laugh at almost anything. But lately he's been coming home late almost every night and leaving his dishes in the sink for days. When I brought it up in early July, he just said he'd "sort it out" and then went quiet for the rest of the evening.

The real issue is money. Our rent went up again in July, and I've been covering more of the utilities because Ollie keeps telling me his paycheque is "coming Friday." It's been Friday more times than I can count. I don't want to be the bad guy or start a fight, but I'm starting to feel resentful every time I open the hydro bill. We also have a mutual friend, Marcus, who thinks I should just move out and let it go, but I like this place and I don't want to lose my side of the lease over a guy who won't talk to me.

So what's a fair way to bring this up? I'd like to keep the friendship intact if I can. Should I write him a text first so he has time to think, or is it better to sit down face to face? And if he gets defensive, how do I stop myself from escalating? Any wording suggestions would help a lot.

Hi all, I've finally got the family holiday sorted and I wanted to get it down in writing before Mum starts asking me again. We're going to Doolin in County Clare for the week of 12 August, staying in the cottage Miriam found through her colleague Sinead. Sinead swears the place is right on the water and that the kitchen is big enough for all of us, so Mum, you can stop worrying about that bit. The cottage sleeps eight, which means Dad, Aunt Bríd, the two cousins and the rest of us will fit, just about, if nobody minds sharing a bathroom.

For travel, I've booked the train from Heuston to Ennis on the Saturday morning, and Miriam is going to collect everyone from the station in the people carrier. Miriam says she'll do the driving on the way back too, so the rest of you can relax with a glass of something. I know Dad will want to take the scenic route past the Cliffs of Moher, and honestly I think that's a good idea if the weather behaves. There's a car park at the top, though it fills up fast, so if we go, let's aim to be there before ten.

The plan for the days is pretty loose. Monday we're going to do the Aran Islands ferry, which I've booked for the 9.30 sailing, and on Tuesday there's a walk along the Burren that Sinead recommended, which she says is gentle enough for Bríd. Wednesday is free for anyone who wants a lie-in, a swim at Lahinch, or a pint in one of the pubs in Doolin where the traditional music starts about nine. Thursday evening I've put a tentative booking at a seafood place in Ennistymon, but I'll confirm it once I hear from the others.

A few practical things. Please send me your dietary needs by the 5th, because Aunt Bríd is going to forget again and I'd rather be ready. Bring waterproofs, whatever the forecast says, and sturdy shoes for the walking. I'll set up a shared group for photos and anything last-minute, and my email for bookings is the same one I've always used, so if anything goes wrong, shout at me there. I'm also going to need a deposit from everyone by the end of the month, which I'll explain separately once I've got the numbers from Miriam.

I'm really looking forward to this, and it's been far too long since we were all in the same place for more than a Sunday dinner. Let me know what you think, and if you've got better ideas for the Thursday, I'm all ears. Love to you all, and see you in August.

Maeve

Ladies and gentlemen, I'm Tom, Victoria's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words before we raise our glasses. Vicky and I grew up in Leeds, and I still remember the summer she decided she was going to be a nurse. She'd come home from her work experience at St James's Hospital with a notebook full of questions and a plan. Nobody was surprised when she got her place at Sheffield, and nobody was surprised when she came home every holiday to help out at Bean There Coffee on Otley Road, where she could make a flat white faster than anyone in the city.

What I want to say is this: Vicky has always been the one who shows up. When our dad was ill in January 2019, she drove up from Sheffield on a Tuesday, sat with him through a long afternoon, and then went back to her shift the next morning without a word of complaint. She never asks for credit. She just quietly makes things better, and I think that's why Daniel fell for her, although he'll tell you it was the cinnamon buns at the cafe counter.

Daniel, you have gained something very special. You've married someone who will remember your birthday, pick up the prescription without being asked, and laugh at your terrible jokes even when nobody else will. Vicky, I'm so proud of you. Please, everyone, join me in raising a glass to the bride and groom.

I've been going to Harbor Street Auto Repair for about six years now, and I finally sat down to write this because they earned it. My name is Wesley Donnelly, and I'm a nurse at St. Brendan's Medical Center, so I'm used to people who are stressed and in a hurry. Wes, the owner, gets that. When I brought in my Honda on April 9 with a grinding noise from the front left wheel, he had me on the lift within twenty minutes and called me with a diagnosis before lunch.

What stood out was the honesty. He showed me the worn brake pads and the scored rotor, explained why waiting another month would cost more, and didn't try to upsell me on a transmission flush I clearly didn't need. The quote matched the final bill to the dollar. My dad, who was born in Scranton and still doesn't trust mechanics, came in with me once and walked out impressed.

If you want a shop that treats you like a person and not a ticket number, this is the place. Parking is tight on the side lot, so go in through the front. I'd give them five stars without hesitation.
