input:
Honestly, I still can't believe how the week went. You know how I've been dreading the move back to the coast? Well, it turned out better than I expected. The bus broke down twice on the way down, and we ended up sharing sugarcane and stories with a bunch of farmers while a mechanic tinkered under the engine. It felt like the whole journey was a reminder that nothing here runs on schedule, and that somehow makes it easier to relax.

My younger cousin Peter has been staying with me, and he surprised me by taking over the cooking. He burned the first pot of ugali, laughed about it for an hour, and then made the best sukuma wiki I've tasted in years. We sat on the veranda after dark, listening to the crickets and the distant matatu horns, and he asked me whether I was happy here. I told him I was still figuring that out, but that the evenings like this make it feel possible.

I wanted to tell you all this because you're the one person who always knows what I mean when I say things are hard but good at the same time. Let's plan a proper visit soon. I'll cook, you bring the stories, and we'll see if Peter can finally beat me at cards.

Hi, I'm Ronen Adler, thirty-four, and I've been told I'm either the funniest or the most stubborn person in any room. Probably both. I grew up in Haifa but for the last six years I've lived in Florentin in Tel Aviv, on a quiet street off Yehuda Halevi with a balcony that gets the morning sun and a neighbour who keeps bees. I work as a structural engineer for a firm near the Azrieli towers, which means I spend my weekdays arguing with concrete and my weekends trying to cook things that don't need a load calculation.

My family is loud in the best way. My younger sister Noa is a paediatric nurse who will out-talk you in five minutes flat, and my mother Ruth still sends me recipes with no measurements and expects me to guess. Dinner at their place in Haifa is a standing commitment, and I'll be honest, if you come to one you'll be asked within the first ten minutes what you do and whether you plan to stay in Israel. Apologies in advance.

I love hiking the Ein Gedi trails in winter, long coffees at places that don't have menus, and terrible puns. I play five-a-side on Thursdays and still believe I'm faster than I am. I drive an old white Mazda, plate 23-456-78, which I keep meaning to replace and never do, mostly because it's never let me down on the road to the Galilee.

I'm not very active on social media, but if you want to see the bee photos and the occasional questionable bread attempt, I post as @ronen_builds_things on Instagram. I'm also reachable at ronen.adler@mailbox.co.il, though I'd rather hear from you in person than by a long email.

What I'm looking for is someone curious, a bit sarcastic, and not afraid of a long walk that turns into an accidental dinner. Bonus points if you can tell me something about your own family that makes mine look normal. We can meet for coffee on Sunday, January 14th, somewhere in Florentin, or I can make the bread and you can judge it. Your call.

Jonah Whitcombe has spent the last twelve years building software for rural health clinics across the Waikato and Bay of Plenty. He joined Kōwhai Health Systems in Hamilton in 2013 as a junior developer and now leads its integration team, where he oversees the data pipelines that connect regional GP practices to national reporting. Before moving into management, Jonah spent three summers volunteering with a community clinic in Rotorua, an experience he credits with shaping his belief that good software should disappear into the background of patient care.

Outside work, Jonah is a keen mountain biker and a volunteer firefighter with the Te Awamutu brigade. He is also the author of a small open-source tool for scheduling vaccine cold-chain audits, which is now used by clinics in four regions. Colleagues describe him as patient, direct, and quick to admit when a design is wrong, a habit that has made him a trusted voice in cross-agency planning meetings.

In this session, Jonah will talk about the practical lessons from migrating legacy clinic systems to cloud infrastructure, including the mistakes his team made and the checklist they now use. He is looking forward to meeting attendees over the conference dinner, so please find him after the talk. Contact his office at jonah.whitcombe@kowhaihealth.co.nz or on 07 555 0142 for any follow-up questions.

He said it was 'the market', but the place hasn't been touched since I moved in apart from a new boiler I paid for myself. The thing is, I work part-time at a dental surgery and I'm barely covering rent as it is. If I have to move, I honestly don't know where I'd go in Limerick on what I earn. My sister in Dublin has offered me her spare room, but I'd hate to leave my friends and my job here. So my question is really twofold. Is a rent increase like this legal under Irish tenancy rules, given the rent pressure zone rules? And how do I push back without picking a fight I can't afford? I'd really appreciate a clear, calm breakdown of what my options are, because right now I just feel stuck and a bit useless.

Tuesday, February 11. Dr. Tanaka asked me today to write down what I actually feel when I think about going back to Sendai, which is harder than it sounds. I was born in Sendai and grew up there until I was eighteen, so every street in that city has some memory attached to it. Ryota keeps telling me the rent is cheaper near the station and that my mother would like to see more of me, and both of those things are true. But when I picture the walk from Sendai Station to our old apartment in Aoba-ku, my chest tightens before I even reach the bridge.

I have been at Hoshino Electronics for six years now, in the Osaka office, and my manager, Mr. Kawakami, has been generous about my leave. Still, I keep rehearsing what I would say to colleagues who ask why I left. Rina from the design team sent me a message last week asking if I was still coming to the spring planning meeting on February 24. I haven't answered. Part of me wants to hide behind work because it is predictable, and predictable feels safe right now.

Dr. Tanaka suggested I write one sentence a day about something that went well, even if small. Today it was this: I made miso soup from my grandmother's recipe and it tasted almost right. I want to remember that I can still reach back to her, and that the city I'm afraid of also holds the person who taught me to cook. Next session I'd like to talk about whether fear and longing can sit in the same place.

I want to remember that I can still reach back to her, and that the city I'm afraid of also holds the person who taught me to cook. Next session I'd like to talk about whether fear and longing can sit in the same place.

Hey Marcos, I still can't believe how the whole thing with Fernanda went down last week, so let me tell you properly. You know I'd been putting off the trip to the notary in Belo Horizonte because of the paperwork. Fernanda, my sister-in-law, finally sat me down and said we were going on the 14th of July whether I liked it or not. She had printed everything: my RG number, 12.884.307-2, and the copy of my CPF, which she insisted I carry in a plastic sleeve so it wouldn't get wet in the rain.

The morning of the appointment was chaos. The bus was late, the umbrella broke at the stop, and I arrived soaked and convinced we'd missed the window. Fernanda just laughed at me, the way she does, and pulled a folder out of her bag like a magician. Everything was there. The clerk, a tired but kind man named Anselmo, flipped through the pages, stamped a few things, and told us we were fine. I felt like I'd been holding my breath for months.

Afterwards we went to a little bakery near the praça where they still make pão de queijo the old way. Fernanda ordered two coffees and then, without warning, started talking about our grandmother's house in Ouro Preto and how it would be ours to sell. That was the part that got to me. I wasn't ready to talk about money or memories in the same breath, so I just nodded and ate my cheese bread.

I'm writing this because you asked how I was holding up, and honestly, better than I expected. Fernanda and I have never been close the way cousins on TV are, but this week we shared a lot of small, ridiculous moments that felt important. If you need the notary's number or the office address, just email me at lucas.andrade88@gmail.com and I'll send it over. You can also call me on my cell any time.

Thanks for listening, as always. Next time the drinks are on me, and you can tell me all about the new job. Give Juliana a hug from me, and tell her Fernanda says hello. Let's get together soon, somewhere with better weather than this, if that's even possible in July here.

I would appreciate it if your claims adjuster could coordinate with them so that the process is not delayed further.

Please send all correspondence to my email at jonathan.weiss@mailbox.co.il, or call me on 054-6172839. I would like the claim to be processed as quickly as possible, as I am currently unable to use the living room.

Sincerely,
Jonathan "Jojo" Weiss

input:
Dear Abuela Rosa,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the jacaranda outside your kitchen window is still blooming as beautifully as it was when I visited last spring. I have been meaning to write for weeks, but the semester at the university in Guadalajara has swallowed every free hour. Mom says you have been asking about me, so I wanted you to hear from me directly, not only through the phone calls she keeps translating for us.

I turned twenty-three last month, and I still think about the birthday you insisted on making in the courtyard, with the tamales and the tiny candles stuck into the flan because we could not find a proper cake. Papa laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the lemonade. Your birthday, Abuela, falls on December 14th this year, and I have already marked it on my calendar. I am planning to come down to Oaxaca for a few days so I can cook with you the way you taught me, even if my tortillas still come out lopsided.

School has been intense but good. My thesis advisor, Dr. Lorena Ibarra, says my research on water access in rural villages is finally coming together, and I have been interviewing families in the mountains near Puebla. Many of them remind me of you: they are stubborn, generous, and quick to offer food to a stranger. One grandmother there gave me a jar of honey and refused to take any money for it. I thought of you immediately.

If you want to write back, the old way is always best, but Papa has set up an email for you so we can exchange photos more easily. It is rosa.mendez.home@correo.mx, and he says he will show you how to open it when you visit him at Christmas. Please do not worry if it takes you a few tries. I still remember how long it took me to learn to hold the phone steady when we video called.

I miss your stories, your scolding, and the way you always know when I am lying about eating well. I promise to come home soon and to bring you the good chocolate from the market in Coyoacan. Give my love to the neighbors, to the cat on the wall, and to the saints on your shelf, who I am sure are tired of hearing your requests.

With all my love and gratitude,

Paulina Mendez Ortiz

input:
Je suis là aujourd'hui, en tant que petit-fils de Bertrand, pour dire adieu à celui que tout le monde appelait « Tintin ». Il est né à Lyon en 1941 et il n'a jamais vraiment quitté cette ville dans son cœur, même après les années passées à Bordeaux. Mon grand-père avait quatre-vingt-deux ans. Il est parti le 14 juin, dans son lit, après une semaine où il a encore trouvé la force de râler contre la météo.

Tout le monde ici le connaissait. Au Café des Tilleuls, rue Mercière, il avait sa table près de la fenêtre, et Madame Gilles savait qu'il prendrait un crème à 10 heures pile. À la pharmacie du quartier de la Croix-Rousse, il racontait à chacun ses histoires de pêche. Mon grand-père aimait les gens, et les gens le lui rendaient bien.

Je veux aussi dire merci à mon père, Julien, qui a veillé sur lui chaque matin, et à ma sœur Camille, qui lui lisait le journal à voix haute quand ses yeux l'ont lâché. Grand-père, tu nous laisses beaucoup de souvenirs et une vieille paire de bottes que nous ne jetterons jamais. Repose en paix.

input:
When we finally got to Galway, the rain had stopped and the Latin Quarter was buzzing. Our host, Zara Doherty, had flagged that Shop Street gets packed on Saturdays, so we went early on Tuesday, 14 November, which turned out to be the perfect plan. Zara, who everyone calls Zee back in Galway, had written a list of places to try, and the chowder at the little place near the Spanish Arch was the first thing she made us promise to order. We sat by the window watching the fishing boats bob on the Corrib while a busker in a woolly hat played fiddle outside.

That evening Zara's colleague Niamh Brennan met us at a pub on Dominick Street. Niamh had been the one to suggest the Thursday trad session, so we booked for the 20th and lingered over pints until the music started. If you want to follow along with the trip, Zara posts her photos under @zeedoesgalway, and she is the reason half the photos on our feed are from the same three laneways. Her tip: bring a jacket even in summer, because the wind coming off the bay doesn't ask permission.

By the time we left on the morning of the 22nd, I already had a list of reasons to come back. Next time I want to spend a full day on the Aran ferry and see the cliffs at Dun Aonghasa, and I want Zee to show us her favourite bakery on Quay Street. If you ever find yourself in Galway in November, go out of your way to find the small pubs; the best nights aren't in the guidebooks.

When we finally got to Cork, the rain had stopped and the Latin Quarter was buzzing. Our host, Zoe Hennessy, had flagged that Shop Street gets packed on Saturdays, so we went early on Tuesday, 9 November, which turned out to be the perfect plan. Zoe, who everyone calls Zo back in Cork, had written a list of places to try, and the chowder at the little place near the Spanish Arch was the first thing she made us promise to order. We sat by the window watching the fishing boats bob on the Corrib while a busker in a woolly hat played fiddle outside.

That evening Zoe's colleague Aisling Corcoran met us at a pub on Mary Street. Aisling had been the one to suggest the Thursday trad session, so we booked for the 16th and lingered over pints until the music started. If you want to follow along with the trip, Zoe posts her photos under @zodoescork, and she is the reason half the photos on our feed are from the same three laneways. Her tip: bring a jacket even in summer, because the wind coming off the bay doesn't ask permission.

By the time we left on the morning of the 18th, I already had a list of reasons to come back. Next time I want to spend a full day on the Aran ferry and see the cliffs at Dun Aonghasa, and I want Zo to show us her favourite bakery on Patrick Street. If you ever find yourself in Cork in November, go out of your way to find the small pubs; the best nights aren't in the guidebooks.

input:
I'd been dreading the drizzle all week, but when we rolled into Kinsale on the morning of 14 September, the sky had cleared into that pale, washed blue you only get on the Cork coast. My name is Cathal, though my sister Órla insists on calling me "the Cathal situation" whenever I make a plan, and this trip was entirely her fault. She'd booked a long weekend for us to celebrate her thirtieth, and she had a list longer than my arm of places she wanted to eat, walk, and photograph.

We started at Harbour Crumbs, a small cafe tucked behind the pier that the locals swear by. The owner, a grey-haired woman named Maeve, slid a rhubarb scone across the counter and told us the coffee was "strong enough to wake the dead, so mind yourself." She was right. Cathal, I thought, you're going to be bouncing off the walls by lunch. We sat by the window watching fishing boats nudge against their moorings while Órla read aloud from her guidebook, mispronouncing half the place names on purpose just to annoy me.

Afternoon brought the walk out to Charles Fort, the star-shaped star fortress that looks even more dramatic from the ridge above the town. The wind up there was fierce, and I spent a good ten minutes trying to keep my hat from launching itself into the estuary. Órla, of course, took three hundred photographs and insisted each one was the best. I'm inclined to agree with her, which I'll deny if she ever asks.

On our last morning we made a short detour to Bandon Physio & Sports Clinic, because I'd tweaked my knee on the cliff path and I didn't fancy hobbling onto the ferry with a bad leg. The physiotherapist, a patient young man called Ruairí, had me stretching on a mat within twenty minutes and sent me off with a sheet of exercises and a reminder to take it easy. Honestly, the whole visit was more pleasant than I expected, and I left feeling taken care of.

I'm already planning the next trip, and Órla has already claimed the right to choose the destination. If you find yourself on the Cork coast in September, go slowly, eat the scones, and let yourself get lost for an afternoon. Ireland rewards the people who don't rush it.

input:
When I think back on the summer I spent working at a small bakery near the old market, what stays with me is not the early mornings or the aching hands but the quiet conversations over the ovens. The owner, a woman who had run the place for decades, taught me that bread is a patient art. You cannot rush dough, and you cannot pretend that a loaf has risen when it has not. She would tap the base of each loaf and listen for the hollow sound that meant it was ready, and I began to understand that much of good work lies in learning to wait and to notice.

That lesson followed me into the rest of my year. In school, I had always wanted quick answers, and I often mistook speed for understanding. Working beside the bakery's steady rhythm, I learned to sit with a difficult problem long enough for its shape to become clear. I started keeping a notebook of questions I could not yet answer, returning to them weeks later with a fresh and usually sharper mind. The habit made me a more careful student and a more honest one, willing to admit where my knowledge ended.

I hope to bring that same patience to the study of environmental science. Rivers, soils and cities change slowly and then all at once, and understanding them demands the same attentiveness I first learned kneading dough in the early light. I want to study how communities adapt to a changing landscape, and to contribute research that is careful, unhurried and useful to the people who must live with its results.

I am writing to formally complain about the service I received from your Christchurch branch on 14 October, and to ask for a full review of the charges applied to my account. My name is Rowan Te Huia Walker, and I have been a customer with Kiwi Fleet Solutions for almost six years. In all that time I have never had cause to write to you until now.

On the morning of 14 October I brought my vehicle, registration RKT482, in for a scheduled service. The receptionist, Michelle, told me it would be ready by four o'clock. When I returned, the car was not finished, and I was informed that a part had been ordered that had not arrived. I was not told this when I dropped the car off, and no one called me to explain the delay. I waited for almost two hours before anyone offered me a loan vehicle, and even then it was only after I asked my wife, Tamsin, to come and collect me because I had a school pickup to make.

What concerns me most is the invoice. It came to $612.40, which is well above the quote of $420 I was given by phone the week before. When I rang to query it, I was told the extra cost was for labour on work I had not authorised. I have checked my records and I did not approve any additional work. I asked for an itemised breakdown and have still not received one. Please confirm in writing what was done to the vehicle and why I was charged for it.

I would also like to raise the matter of my account, number 7741-2296-08. Over the past two months I have been billed twice for the same service fee, and the refund I was promised over the phone on 22 October has not appeared. I have now spent more time on hold and on hold again than the actual repair took. For a company that advertises convenience as its core value, this has been deeply frustrating.

I would be grateful if you could refund the difference between the quoted and invoiced amounts, reverse the duplicate fee, and provide a written explanation of the decisions made on 14 October. You may reply to me by email at rowan.walker@kiwifleet.co.nz or by post to my home address, which is on your records. I would appreciate a response within ten working days.

Thank you for considering this complaint. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,

Rowan Te Huia Walker

input:
I finally made it to Whitby this July, and I have to say it was worth the wait. I'd been following the harbour on Instagram for months under the handle @amelia_salt_walks, so arriving at the actual steps of the 199 felt a bit like stepping into my own feed. I'm Amelia, by the way, and by day I'm a senior copy editor at Harrowgate Publishing, which means I spent the whole train journey up mentally correcting the signage. My friend Priya, who works in the same office as a designer, came along for the weekend and insisted we stay near Church Street so we could walk down to the abbey in the evening light.

We spent the first morning on the cliffs, and I dragged Priya up to the bench overlooking the bay where I'd sat years ago. The wind was ferocious, and I was quite glad that our dog, Biscuit, had been left at home with my neighbour in Leeds. He'd have demanded every bit of the chips we bought from the kiosk near the pier. Honestly, the fish and chips here are the best I've had in the country, and I've tested plenty of them on the way up the coast.

On the last afternoon we walked along the pier and watched the boats come in. Priya took about two hundred photos, most of them of me squinting into the sun, and I've posted the best few under the same handle. If you're planning a trip, go in July, book somewhere on Church Street early, and bring a proper waterproof. The sea breeze will find every gap in your jacket.

input:
I still can't quite believe I'm standing up here without Sinéad beside me telling me to keep it short. So I'll try. My sister was the only person I knew who could walk into a room in Phibsboro and leave it with three new friends and a job offer. Everyone called her Sino from the time she was small, and that's the name I'll use today, because it's the one that belongs to the sister I grew up with.

She did her training at Mater Hospital, and I've lost count of the people who have come up to me this week to tell me she was the nurse who sat with them at three in the morning when nobody else could. She never made a fuss about it. She'd just come in, pull up a chair, and ask how your mother was getting on. That was Sino. Attention, always, for whoever was in front of her.

Our mother still keeps the phone number Sino gave her when she moved to Dublin, 087 442 9018, written on the inside of a kitchen cupboard, and she rang it every Sunday for nine years. Sino always answered, even when she was on a shift and should have let it go to voicemail. I used to tease her about that. Now I think I'd give anything to hear her voice on the other end of it one more time.

She loved the sea, and she loved a bad joke even more. If you were ever in the chipper on Sea Road with her in the summer, you'd know she could talk the ear off a seagull. She was loud when she was happy and quiet when she wasn't, and you learned to read the difference, which I suppose is what family is for.

So tonight I'm asking you to do what Sino would have done. Ring someone you haven't spoken to in too long. Sit with someone who's having a hard night. Tell your own people you love them, even if it feels awkward. That's how she lived, and it's the best way I know to keep her with us.

input:
Session notes, Tuesday. I came in saying I was fine, which Ilana noticed before I did. She asked about the week and I ended up talking about my brother Yoni, who called from the hospital in Haifa on the 14th to say the scans were clear but that he was still exhausted. I said I'd visit. I didn't. I told myself it was the drive, the traffic on the Carmel road, but that isn't the real reason. Being in that waiting room again, with the vending machine humming and the smell of antiseptic, brings me straight back to the year Dad was there, and I haven't let myself think about that year in a long time.

Ilana asked what I felt when Yoni said he was tired. I said worried. Then she asked again, and I said guilty, and then something under that which I didn't have a word for until I wrote it down on the bus home: left out. Yoni has always had a way of being the one people orbit. He went to Technion while I was still figuring out which courses at the Hebrew University would count for anything. When he got sick, the family's attention went to him as it should have, and I was relieved, and then I was ashamed of being relieved.

For the next session I agreed to call Yoni before Friday and actually ask how he is, not report on myself. Ilana also suggested I write down three specific things I could do for him this week, small ones, so the guilt has somewhere to go. My list so far: bring soup from the place on Herzl Street, ask him about his physiotherapy, and stop talking about my own schedule for once. I'll bring the list to our next appointment on the 21st of March.

input:
Me llamo Paloma Ríos Herrera, pero desde pequeña todos me dicen Pali. Nací en Oaxaca de Juárez hace diecisiete años, y aunque mi familia se mudó a Puebla cuando yo tenía nueve, mi corazón siempre se quedó en los mercados de Oaxaca, donde mi abuela vendía tejates y chapulines los fines de semana. Fue ahí donde aprendí que una receta puede contar la historia de un pueblo entero, y que cada ingrediente tiene un nombre, una memoria y una razón para estar en la olla.

Esa curiosidad me llevó a tomar la decisión de estudiar gastronomía y ciencia de los alimentos. En mi escuela preparatoria organicé un proyecto con mi compañera Lucía Benítez, que estudiaba química conmigo, para documentar cómo cambia el sabor del mole cuando se usan chiles secos de distintas regiones. Pasamos semanas en la cocina de mi casa, con mi perro Tlaloc sentado junto a la estufa esperando que cayera algún pedazo de pollo, y terminamos presentando nuestros resultados en un congreso estatal el 14 de septiembre de este año.

Quiero entrar a su programa porque busco unir lo que aprendí en la cocina de mi abuela con el rigor de la investigación científica. Sé que la gastronomía mexicana necesita personas que la estudien con método y que la defiendan con datos, y creo que puedo aportar esa mirada desde mi experiencia. Estoy lista para aprender, equivocarme en el laboratorio y volver a intentarlo, como lo hago cada vez que pongo a hervir una olla de mole.

input:
My name is Marites, and I was Mom's eldest, so I've been asked to say a few words this morning. Everyone who knew Mom knows she never sat still. Every morning before the sun was fully up, she was at Kapihan ni Lola in Barangay Poblacion, arguing gently with the barista about the sugar in her kape. Mr. Bautista, who owns it, told me last night that she had been coming in for twenty-two years and never once ordered the same thing twice.

She raised the four of us on a teacher's salary and a lot of stubbornness. When Kuya Mario broke his arm falling off the mango tree, she was the one who carried him to the clinic in Lipa at two in the morning. When I passed the board exam, she cried harder than I did. She was never one for big speeches, but she had a way of making you feel that whatever you were doing was the most important thing in the room.

We will miss her, and we will miss Bantay most of all. That old aspin followed her from the gate to the kitchen every single day, and he has been lying by the front door since Thursday, waiting. Mom, salamat sa lahat. Ingat ka palagi, and we will see you again on the other side. Amen.

Com profunda tristeza, comunico o falecimento de minha mãe, Lúcia Ferreira de Souza, ocorrido na madrugada de 14 de março, aos 82 anos, em sua casa na Rua das Acácias, no bairro Jardim Aurora, em Campinas. Lúcia nasceu em Ribeirão Preto, em 3 de maio de 1942, filha de agricultores que lhe ensinaram desde cedo o valor do trabalho e da palavra dada. Foi professora primária por mais de trinta e cinco anos e nunca deixou de lembrar o nome de cada aluno que passou pela sua sala.

Deixa seus filhos, Ricardo e Helena, e os netos Bruno e Tatiana, que sempre foram o centro de sua vida. Nos últimos anos, quem esteve ao seu lado todos os dias foi a vizinha e amiga de longa data, Odete Pimentel, que cuidou dela com uma dedicação que a família jamais esquecerá. Lúcia também deixa um irmão, Antônio, que mora em Franca, e muitos amigos que a conheceram nas reuniões da igreja do bairro.

O velório acontecerá na capela do Cemitério da Saudade, na quinta-feira, 16 de março, a partir das 9 horas, seguido do sepultamento. Quem desejar prestar uma homenagem pode enviar mensagens para o e-mail familia.ferreira@gmail.com. Que Deus conforte a todos nós e que a memória da Dona Lúcia continue viva em cada um que teve a sorte de conviver com ela.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Brian, Akinyi's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight. Our family's story starts in Kisumu, where Akinyi was born on a rainy August morning. Mum still tells everyone that she refused to come out until the mango tree in our compound had stopped dripping, so you can imagine how patient she has been ever since. Everyone who knows her calls her Akie, a name that stuck when she was about six and has never let go.

When Akie first started dating Kevin, I'll be honest, I was suspicious. He'd turn up at the house with a bag of roasted maize and an apology for being late, and somehow that was enough to win over Dad. Over the years I've watched him show up for her in small, steady ways: the early morning drives to the airport, the long phone calls when her project was falling apart, the quiet way he listens. Kevin, you've earned your place in this family, and I'm proud to call you my brother.

So please raise your glasses to Akie and Kevin. And if you ever need a photo from the old days, Akie, I've got plenty, and I'm still posting them on Instagram at @brian_kisumu_roots. Cheers!

I am writing this statement at the Kallithea police station in Athens on the morning of 14 May, to report the theft of my bag from outside my apartment building at 27 Karaiskaki Street, Kallithea, 176 74, Athens, Greece. My name is Anna Leventi and I am 34 years old. I have lived at this address with my partner for about three years and I have never had any previous difficulty in the area.

At approximately 07:40 on Tuesday 13 May, I came down from the third floor to leave for work. I left my black leather shoulder bag on the low wall beside the entrance while I unlocked my bicycle. When I turned around, the bag was gone. I did not see who took it, although a man on a grey scooter had been waiting at the corner of Karaiskaki and Vasileos Pavlou Streets a few minutes earlier. I can describe him only as wearing a dark helmet and a green jacket.

The bag contained my Greek identity card, a Greek driving licence, two bank cards issued by Piraeus Bank, my work access badge for Stavros Logistics, and approximately 80 euros in cash. My mobile phone was in my jacket pocket and was not taken. I called my bank at once from my phone and blocked both cards, and I reported the loss of the identity card to the municipal office in Kallithea the same afternoon. I am also attaching a copy of the reference number I was given by the bank.

I would be grateful if an officer could record this report and tell me what the next steps are, in particular whether any CCTV from the shops on Vasileos Pavlou Street has been requested. My contact details are anna.leventi@mailbox.gr and my mobile number is +30 694 118 2736. I can be reached there at any time.

I confirm that the information given above is true to the best of my knowledge. I understand that providing false information to the police is a criminal offence in Greece.

Anna Leventi

Mötesanteckningar – projektuppföljning, Nordström Teknik AB
Datum: 14 november
Närvarande: Karin Lindqvist, Mattias Berg, Elin Sjöberg

Vi började mötet med en genomgång av den senaste leveransen till kunden i Göteborg. Karin rapporterade att den tekniska testningen är klar men att dokumentationen fortfarande saknas för två av modulerna. Mattias, som kallas Matte av alla på kontoret, påpekade att han kan ta över den delen om Elin hinner granska kodändringarna före den 21 november.

Elin berättade att hon har fått ett nytt uppdrag från ledningen och att hennes kapacitet därför blir begränsad under de närmaste tre veckorna. Vi enades om att Karin tar över kontakten med kunden så länge, medan Elin fortsätter att vara tillgänglig för frågor via chatten. Karin tyckte att det var en rimlig lösning men bad om att få en tydlig avstämning varje måndag.

Diskussionen gick sedan över till budgeten för nästa kvartal. Det konstaterades att kostnaderna för molntjänster har ökat något, och att vi behöver se över abonnemangen innan årsskiftet. Mattias föreslog att vi tittar på alternativa leverantörer, och Karin ska kontakta inköpsavdelningen för att få fram offerter.

Vi gick även igenom den interna utbildningen som planeras till början av december. Eftersom flera i teamet redan är bokade den 3 december flyttade vi fram sessionen till den 5 december. Elin påpekade att lokalen i tredje våningen är upptagen den dagen, så vi får boka om till konferensrummet på bottenplan.

Till sist stämde vi av nästa steg. Karin skickar ut en uppdaterad tidsplan till alla senast fredag, och Mattias bokar en tid med kunden för att gå igenom dokumentationen. Vi avslutade mötet strax före elva. Nästa möte är planerat till den 28 november, och kontaktuppgifterna till kunden finns i den delade mappen under projektet.

input:
I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to tell you that my father, Akira Tanabe, passed away peacefully at Seirei Hospital in Hamamatsu on the evening of November 9th, surrounded by family. He was 74. Many of you knew him as Aki-san, a name he carried proudly through the bakery he ran for thirty-one years on the corner of Motomachi Street, and it is the name I will always hear when I think of him.

Dad grew up in Shizuoka and studied agriculture at Shizuoka University, where he met my mother, Yoko, at a student dance in 1971. He often told us that he had only gone because a friend owed him a favour, and he would laugh every time, because that favour turned into fifty-three years of marriage. He believed in hard work, early mornings and telling the truth even when it was inconvenient. He taught me to knead dough by feel rather than by the clock, a lesson I still try to follow.

For the last decade Dad was a regular at Kissa Maruyama, the small coffee house near the station, where he read the newspaper aloud to anyone who would listen. He also attended the morning sessions at Fitness Kamo three days a week, insisting that a man in his seventies needed to keep his legs strong for the hills of his beloved Enshu region. The staff at both places have asked us to say how much they will miss his stories and his terrible puns.

Our family dog, Kuma, a patient old shiba mix, will be lost without his evening walks, and I know Dad would want me to mention him. Dad's last errand before he fell ill was to drive his silver Toyota Corolla, registration 33-41 Shi 8216, to the vet for Kuma's checkup. He cared for every living thing around him with the same quiet devotion.

A private family ceremony will be held on November 14th at Hamamatsu Shinto Shrine. In lieu of flowers, we kindly ask that donations be made to the Shizuoka Prefectural Cancer Research Fund, a cause Dad supported quietly for many years. Thank you to everyone who visited him in hospital and sent messages of comfort.

Dad, you will be missed every single day. Rest well, Aki-san.

Tuesday 14 March. Madrid is grey and drizzly today, which suits my mood after the morning I've had. I'm Katherine Doyle, and I'm writing this on the metro because I can't face going straight home. Mum rang at lunchtime. Grandad's hip op at St. Vincent's Hospital in Dublin has been moved to the 21st, and she sounded exhausted, so I promised I'd fly over for the weekend before it. I haven't even told my supervisor at the Complutense yet that I'll be missing the seminar.

The worst part is that Ciara, my sister, has already booked everything without asking me. She says I always wait until the last minute, which is probably fair, but she could have at least checked whether my flat-share lease lets me leave for a few days. I found it in the drawer last night, under the old electricity bills. I keep meaning to organise that drawer.

He's a good listener, even if he steals the last of the olive oil. Tomorrow I'll call Mum back, email Professor Ruiz, and try to get a cheap flight that doesn't leave before dawn. Goodnight, diary.

I'm Dylan Harrowfield, and I was born in Whanganui in 1984, the middle of three children in a household that ran on early mornings and very strong tea. My grandmother Rangi taught me to fish off the breakwater when I was six, and I still think about her every time I tie a knot. After finishing my degree in Dunedin I spent a decade working in hydrology, mostly on river monitoring projects across the South Island, which is how I came to care so much about water quality and the people who depend on it.

These days I run a small consultancy from a converted garage in Nelson with my partner Maren and our dog Biscuit, who has opinions about every conference presenter I have ever met. I drive a battered Subaru with the registration KBR417 and it has taken me to more field sites than I can count. Most of my clients now are iwi groups and councils trying to make sense of long-term data, and I find that work more rewarding than anything I did before.

If you want to talk about catchment modelling, or just compare notes on the best places to fish in the Top of the South, I am always happy to chat. input:
Growing up in a small apartment above a bakery, I learned early that the smallest routines can carry the most weight. Every morning the smell of bread drifted up through the floorboards, and every morning I would sit by the window with a notebook, trying to make sense of the city waking beneath me. Those quiet hours became the foundation of how I think: patiently, and with an eye for the details others pass over.

My interest in engineering began not in a classroom but on a crowded bus. The vehicle stalled at the same intersection almost every day, and I started timing the lights, counting the passengers, and sketching how the traffic flow could be improved. What began as idle curiosity turned into a sustained habit of asking why systems fail and how they might be redesigned. I eventually wrote a short proposal to the local transit office, which was politely acknowledged but never implemented. The disappointment taught me that good ideas need persistence, clear communication, and people willing to listen.

That lesson shaped my work in the robotics club at school. Our team struggled for months with a sensor that gave inconsistent readings whenever the room got warm. Rather than simply replacing the part, I proposed calibrating the system against temperature changes and documenting every trial. The process was tedious, and several teammates doubted it would work. When the robot finally navigated the course without error, I felt a satisfaction that no grade had ever given me. It also reinforced my belief that careful measurement matters as much as inspiration.

Beyond engineering, I have found meaning in tutoring younger students who feel discouraged by mathematics. Many of them arrive convinced they are simply bad at numbers. I try to show them that confusion is a normal step toward understanding, and that a problem can be broken into smaller pieces. Watching a student's expression change from frustration to confidence is one of the most rewarding experiences I have had, and it has made me want to teach as well as build.

I hope to pursue a degree that combines technical rigour with a commitment to the people my work affects. I bring a habit of observation, a tolerance for setbacks, and a genuine desire to make everyday systems work better for everyone who depends on them. I am ready to keep learning, and I believe this program would give me the tools and community to do so.

I'll admit I almost skipped Byron Bay altogether, but my friend Vivienne insisted we stop for a week on our way up the coast, and I'm so glad she did. We rented a little weatherboard place at 14 Marlin Court, just a short walk from the beach, and the first thing I did was wander into Salty Fig Cafe on Jonson Street for a flat white and the best smashed avocado I've had in years. The owner, a cheerful woman named Renata Holm, told me the morning crowd thins out after nine, which turned out to be perfect for reading on the verandah.

We spent the next few days doing the usual things: sunrise walks along the headland, a swim at the Wategos end of the beach where the water was clear enough to see fish, and an afternoon at the lighthouse watching for whales. On the third morning Vivienne dragged me to Ridge Strength Gym for a class she'd found online, and I'll confess I was sore for two days afterwards. Still, the instructors were friendly and the views from the outdoor deck were worth every groan.

If you're planning your own trip, I'd recommend booking anything popular ahead of time, especially around the Easter long weekend, which we unluckily hit on April 18th. The town was packed, parking was a nightmare, and we queued forty minutes for pancakes. Next time I'd come mid-week in late April, when the weather is still warm and the crowds have moved on.

Before we left, Vivienne and I got a little sentimental and made a list of all the places we wanted to revisit. I've been posting photos from the trip under the handle @wanderwithjo_travels, so if you want more tips or pictures, feel free to follow along there. You can also reach me directly at jo.hartley.travels@gmail.com, and I answer every message I get.

All in all, Byron Bay surprised me. It's busy and a little pricey, but there's a warmth to the place that's hard to describe. I left with sand in my shoes, a sunburnt nose, and a plan to come back before the year is out. Vivienne has already started looking at flights.

We spent the next few days doing the usual things: sunrise walks along the headland, a swim at the Angourie end of the beach where the water was clear enough to see fish, and an afternoon at the lighthouse watching for whales. On the third morning Priscilla dragged me to Summit Strength Gym for a class she'd found online, and I'll confess I was sore for two days afterwards. Still, the instructors were friendly and the views from the outdoor deck were worth every groan.

If you're planning your own trip, I'd recommend booking anything popular ahead of time, especially around the Easter long weekend, which we unluckily hit on April 11th. The town was packed, parking was a nightmare, and we queued forty minutes for pancakes. Next time I'd come mid-week in late April, when the weather is still warm and the crowds have moved on.

Before we left, Priscilla and I got a little sentimental and made a list of all the places we wanted to revisit. I've been posting photos from the trip under the handle @roamwithpip_travels, so if you want more tips or pictures, feel free to follow along there. You can also reach me directly at pip.moss.travels@gmail.com, and I answer every message I get.

All in all, Yamba surprised me. It's busy and a little pricey, but there's a warmth to the place that's hard to describe. I left with sand in my shoes, a sunburnt nose, and a plan to come back before the year is out. Priscilla has already started looking at flights.

When I joined Banco Aurora in 2019, I had no idea how much I would grow in those four years. Je tiens à laisser cet avis pour la Boulangerie Lenoir, rue des Tanneurs, à Dijon. Je m'appelle Théophile Marchetti et je suis un habitué du quartier depuis presque six ans. Ce n'est pas la première fois que je viens ici, mais c'est la première fois que j'éprouve le besoin d'écrire quelque chose, parce que la qualité du pain a vraiment changé ces derniers mois, et dans le bon sens.

La baguette tradition est croustillante à la sortie du four, avec une mie alvéolée qui tient bien le beurre sans s'effondrer. Le pain de campagne au levain est, selon moi, le meilleur de la ville. Je l'achète chaque samedi depuis le mois de juin dernier, et je n'ai jamais été déçu. La boulangère, Marguerite, m'a même conseillé une variante aux noix quand je lui ai dit que je cherchais quelque chose pour accompagner le fromage de mes beaux-parents.

L'accueil mérite aussi une mention. Théo, le jeune qui tient la caisse le matin, est toujours souriant, même quand la file atteint la porte. Il se souvient des prénoms, ce qui n'est pas si courant aujourd'hui. Un matin de juin, alors que je pressais le pas pour attraper le train, il m'a glissé un croissant « pour la route » sans que je demande rien. Ce genre de geste fait toute la différence.

Je dois reconnaître deux petits points négatifs. Les viennoiseries du dimanche partent très vite, et il vaut mieux arriver avant dix heures si on veut un pain au chocolat. Par ailleurs, le parking est quasi inexistant, ce qui oblige souvent à se garer dans la rue voisine. Ce ne sont que des inconvénients mineurs au regard de la qualité générale.

En résumé, je recommande vivement la Boulangerie Lenoir à tous ceux qui apprécient un pain travaillé avec soin. Pour toute question ou réservation de gâteau pour un événement, vous pouvez écrire à theophile.marchetti@lamail.fr, je serai ravi de partager mes adresses préférées du quartier. Mon chien Bastien, qui m'accompagne presque chaque samedi, a aussi approuvé en recevant un petit biscuit du comptoir.
output:

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment last Tuesday so I don't forget the details. I'm Emma Lindqvist, and I live in Hamburg, so I went to the outpatient clinic at Universitätsklinikum Eppendorf, which is about twenty minutes from my flat in Winterhude. Dr. Brandt, the internist, took my blood pressure twice because the first reading was high, and she wanted to rule out anything serious before we talked about medication. She asked a lot of questions about my sleep and how much coffee I've been drinking since starting the new job.

The bloodwork results came back on 14 November, and Dr. Brandt's office called me the next morning to say my thyroid levels are slightly elevated but nothing urgent. She wants me to repeat the test in six weeks, on or around 26 December, and to keep a log of my blood pressure at home. The nurse, Herr Vogt, gave me a printed sheet explaining what the numbers mean and reminded me to bring it to the next visit.

I left feeling reassured but a bit overwhelmed. If anyone reading this has been through something similar, I'd love to hear how you managed the follow-up appointments. You can reach me at emma.lindqvist@gmx.de if it's easier than leaving a comment here. For now, I'm going to try cutting back on coffee after noon and see what happens.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to recommend Nina Hartmann, who worked as a barista and shift lead at Café Lindenhof on Schwedter Straße in Prenzlauer Berg from March 2019 until August 2023. I managed the café during that period, and I can say without hesitation that Nina was one of the most reliable members of my team. She opened the shop most mornings, trained four new staff members, and kept the espresso machine running even on the busiest Saturdays when the queue reached the door.

What stood out most about Nina was her judgement under pressure. Harold "Hal" Whitcomb, 81, of the Elmwood Park neighborhood on Lindell Street, passed away peacefully on February 9 surrounded by his children. Born in Dayton, Ohio, Hal spent four decades as a machinist at the Brenner Tool & Die Company, where colleagues knew him for his steady hands and his bad jokes at the Friday lunch table. He coached Little League for twenty-two summers and never once missed a Saturday game at Kessler Field.

Hal is survived by his wife of fifty-three years, Doris; his son Mark Whitcomb and daughter-in-law Lynn of Columbus; and his daughter Janet Whitcomb-Ellis of Toledo. Friends will remember him as "Hal the Hammer" on the bocce court, a title he defended with more stubbornness than skill. Those who knew him as Hal, the neighbor who shoveled the whole block after every storm, will miss him most.

A memorial service will be held Thursday, February 18, at St. Brendan Lutheran Church, 410 Orchard Avenue, at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Elmwood Park Youth Baseball fund. Questions may be directed to Janet at jwhitcombellis@gmail.com.

Today is my first day as Senior Product Manager at Fennel & Hart in Limerick, and I wanted to share a bit about the journey that got me here. I'm 41 now, and for most of my twenties I told myself I'd switch careers "once things settled down." Things never settled. What finally pushed me was a quiet January evening, sitting at the kitchen table in Kilkenny, when I realised I'd spent eight years building products I didn't believe in.

The last few months were a scramble. I rewrote my CV three times, took a pay cut I'd been dreading, and spent more evenings than I'd like to admit on video calls with recruiters. My partner Ciarán was patient through all of it, and my rescue greyhound Biscuit gave me a reason to get out for a walk whenever my head was spinning. Biscuit has no interest in career advice, but she is an excellent listener.

To anyone sitting on the fence right now: the leap feels enormous from the inside, but it usually looks smaller once you're standing on the other side. If you're thinking about it, reach out. I'm happy to share what I learned about interviews, negotiating and making the case for yourself. Thank you to everyone who cheered me on, and especially to the friends who told me to stop talking about it and just apply.

I am writing to describe the water damage at my home at 2214 Alder Ridge Court, in the Westbrook neighbourhood of Columbus, Ohio, which I discovered on the morning of January 9. My name is Nolan Brickley, though my coworkers at Halvorsen Logistics Group, where I work as a regional operations manager, usually call me Nolly. I am 41 years old and have lived at this address for six years. When I came down to make coffee, the hallway ceiling had collapsed and water was pouring from the light fixture into the kitchen. I shut off the main valve and called my neighbour, Tomas Riedel, who came over with a flashlight and helped me move furniture out of the way while I phoned the claims line.

The damage covers roughly sixty square feet of hardwood flooring in the hall and kitchen, the drywall and insulation above the hallway ceiling, and a kitchen island that swelled and cracked. Tomas took the photographs you will find attached, and he has offered to provide a written statement about the conditions when I found the water. Because the leak appeared to come from a supply line running through the upstairs bathroom, I also had a plumber, Gary Lindqvist of Lindqvist & Sons Plumbing, inspect the line on January 11. His invoice is enclosed. I have kept a log of every expense since then, including the hotel I stayed at for three nights while the kitchen was unusable.

I have posted updates about the repairs on my social media account, @nolly_brickley_home, mostly so that friends could follow the progress, and I am happy to share those posts if they help document the timeline. I am asking the company to cover the structural repairs, the flooring replacement, the damaged island, and the temporary lodging costs, totalling the amounts listed on the attached estimate. Please contact me at nolan.brickley@brickmail.example or by phone at (614) 555-0182 with any questions. I can make the house available for an adjuster to inspect at any time that suits you.

The short version is that my roommate has been leaving dishes in the sink for days at a time, and when I bring it up he just laughs it off and says he'll get to it. So my question is: has anyone dealt with something similar? Did you sit down for a direct conversation, set up a chore chart, or just accept it and move on? I'd especially like to hear from people who've been on the messy side of this, since I'd like to understand what would actually make it easier for them to change. Thanks in advance for any advice.

I have been coming to Hartley's Bakery on Fenwick Row for almost three years now, ever since I moved over from Toronto and needed somewhere that didn't feel like a chain. Jonah, the owner, remembers that I take my sourdough sliced thin and that I'm allergic to sesame, which sounds like a small thing until you're a stranger in a new city. My colleague Priyanka Raman brought me here on my first week at the firm, and she was right that the cardamom buns alone are worth the detour. The place is small, so on Saturday mornings expect a queue out the door, but the staff move quickly and never make you feel rushed.

A few things to know before you go. They take cards and cash, but the card reader was down the last time I visited, so keep a few notes in your wallet. Parking is tricky on the street, and the lot behind the laundrette fills up by nine. I also had a small mix-up on April 12 when my order for a birthday cake was logged under the wrong pickup slot. Jonah apologised, rang me back within the hour, and had the cake ready by four with no extra charge. That is the kind of service that keeps me coming back.

If you are looking for a neighbourhood bakery that treats regulars like family, this is it. I left my passport number on the pre-order form by mistake once, and they quietly shredded the slip and asked me to rewrite the order, which I appreciated more than I can say. Four stars, and I will be back next Tuesday for the rye.

input:
Diario, 14 de febrero

Hoy me he despertado pensando en lo rápido que pasa el tiempo. Mi hermana Marta me llamó a las siete y media para recordarme que el domingo 23 de febrero es el cumpleaños de mamá, y que quiere que vayamos todos a comer a casa. Le dije que sí, por supuesto, aunque sé que va a querer que le ayude con la cocina otra vez. Desde que vivo en Valladolid, cada vez que vuelvo a Burgos me siento como si tuviera que pedir perdón por no estar más cerca.

Esta mañana fui a la clínica de la calle Santiago para la revisión de la rodilla. El traumatólogo, el doctor Rubén Ortega, me dijo que la recuperación va bien pero que tengo que seguir con los ejercicios al menos tres veces por semana. Me dio hora de control para el 27 de febrero a las doce menos cuarto. Apunté todo en la agenda, aunque sé que se me olvidará si no lo pongo también en el móvil. El teléfono de la clínica es el 983 214 567, por si alguna vez tengo que cambiar la cita.

Después de la clínica me encontré con Lucía en la plaza Mayor. Hacía años que no la veía. Me dijo que todos la llaman Lucy en su trabajo nuevo, y que a ella no le importa, pero que prefiere que yo la siga llamando Luci, como cuando éramos niñas. Nos tomamos un café y se rió mucho cuando le conté lo del curso de cerámica que hice el año pasado y que dejé a medias. Quedamos en que me mandaría su correo, lucia.navarro.8@gmail.com, para organizar una excursión a la sierra la próxima primavera.

Por la tarde me puse a ordenar los papeles del salón. Encontré una carta de mi tío Ernesto fechada en 2009, en la que me contaba cómo era la vida en el pueblo cuando él era joven. Me emocionó leer su letra torcida y pensar que ya no está. Mi madre dice que siempre hablaba de mí como su sobrina preferida, aunque yo sospecho que lo decía a todas. Guardé la carta en la caja de madera donde guardo las fotos.

Antes de dormir he repasado la lista de cosas pendientes para la semana. Tengo que llamar al banco, comprar un regalo para mamá y escribir a mi antigua compañera de piso, que me debe el último recibo de la luz. También quiero volver a empezar los ejercicios de la rodilla, aunque sea solo diez minutos al día. Mañana será otro día y, si me organizo bien, quizá por fin me sienta una persona ordenada. Buenas noches, diario.

input:
Bonjour, je ne sais pas trop par où commencer, mais j'ai besoin de mettre des mots sur ce qui se passe depuis quelques mois. Je travaille dans une petite entreprise de services depuis plus de cinq ans, et depuis le printemps l'ambiance a radicalement changé. Mon responsable direct me fait des remarques devant les collègues, souvent sur des détails sans importance, et je sens que chaque réunion devient une épreuve. Je commence à douter de mes compétences alors que jusqu'ici on me les reconnaissait.

Le pire, c'est que je n'arrive plus à dormir correctement. Je me réveille vers trois heures du matin en repassant mentalement les échanges de la journée, en imaginant ce que j'aurais dû répondre. Le matin, c'est difficile de me motiver pour prendre le métro. Je mange moins, je suis irritable à la maison et je me sens coupable de rapporter cette fatigue à mon entourage, qui fait déjà beaucoup pour moi.

J'ai essayé d'en parler à un collègue de confiance, qui m'a conseillé de ne pas réagir sur le moment et de tout noter. C'est ce que je fais depuis trois semaines : je consigne les dates, les propos, les témoins éventuels. Mais tenir ce journal me demande une énergie que je n'ai plus, et je me demande si je ne suis pas en train de m'enfermer dans une spirale d'obsession.

Je voudrais savoir comment on distingue une vraie situation de harcèlement d'une période de tension qu'on exagère parce qu'on est épuisé. Et surtout, quelles sont les étapes raisonnables à envisager sans tout faire exploser d'un coup : parler aux ressources humaines, consulter la médecine du travail, ou voir d'abord un médecin généraliste pour le sommeil et le moral ?

Je ne cherche pas une solution miracle. J'aimerais simplement être accompagné dans la réflexion, avec des questions qui m'aident à clarifier ce que je ressens et ce que je veux. Si vous pouvez m'indiquer les informations juridiques de base en France sur ce type de situation, ce serait utile, mais je préfère d'abord comprendre ce que je vis.

Merci de prendre le temps de lire ce message. Cela me soulage déjà un peu de l'écrire.

input:
I've been coming to this bakery for almost a year now, ever since I moved over from abroad and needed somewhere that felt like home. The sourdough is excellent, with a proper crust and an open crumb, and the staff remember how you like your coffee after just a few visits. The pastries are a little pricey, but you can taste the butter and the care that goes into them, so I don't mind paying for quality.

The one real complaint I have is the seating. The room is lovely in the morning, but by lunchtime there is barely a free table, and the wooden stools near the window are uncomfortable for anyone staying longer than twenty minutes. I've started going early or taking my orders to go, which works fine, though it does rather defeat the purpose of a cafe. Still, the team is friendly and patient with the queue, even on busy weekends.

What keeps me coming back is how the place has become a small anchor in my new routine. Settling into a different country is lonelier than people admit, and a warm loaf and a familiar face on a grey afternoon have helped more than I expected. Four stars from me, with the hope that they add a few more tables before winter.

Wale Adeniyi

input:
Growing up in Ōtāhuhu, I learned early that a community is built out of small, repeated acts. Every Saturday my grandmother and I walked down to Hillcrest Road to pick up bread from Mana Bakehouse, and the owner, Tane, always asked me how school was going before he handed over the change. That habit of being seen by people who know your name shaped how I think about belonging. When I started volunteering at the Mangere Community Clinic at sixteen, I found myself doing the same thing: greeting families in Samoan and Tongan, remembering their children's names, and helping them fill out forms in English without making them feel rushed.

The clinic is where I first understood that health is not only about medicine. On 14 January last year, a woman named Losana came in with a toddler who had a fever and no way to get to her appointment the next day. Our coordinator, Mere, and I spent the afternoon arranging transport and writing a reminder card. Losana later posted a thank-you on the clinic's page, tagged as @oliviamakes_nz, and it was the first time I saw how a single afternoon could ripple outward. I want to study public health so that I can make those afternoons routine rather than exceptional.

Beyond the clinic, I have spent three summers working at a cafe on Great South Road, where I have learned how much logistics and empathy overlap. Running a busy counter taught me to anticipate needs before people voice them, a skill I will carry into any role where I work with patients, communities and colleagues. I am ready to bring that same attentiveness to the university's programme, and I hope to contribute to a community of students who believe that caring for others is the most practical thing we can do.

input:
C'est avec une immense tristesse que je vous annonce le décès de notre père, Jean-Baptiste Lefèvre, survenu le 14 novembre à l'âge de 78 ans, entouré des siens à son domicile de Quimper. Il laisse dans le deuil son épouse, Marie-Claire, ses enfants Julien et Anne-Sophie, ainsi que ses petits-enfants qui n'ont jamais cessé de le faire sourire.

Jean-Baptiste est né à Brest en 1946, dans une famille de pêcheurs. Très jeune, il apprit à lire la mer comme d'autres lisent un livre. Après des années passées sur les chalutiers de la baie d'Audierne, il reprit en 1978 le petit atelier de réparation de filets de son oncle Yves, qu'il transforma en une entreprise respectée de toute la région. Jean, comme nous l'appelions tous, aimait répéter que la patience était le premier outil d'un bon artisan.

Il était aussi un homme de famille, profondément attaché à ses racines. Chaque dimanche, il recevait ses proches autour d'une grande table et racontait, avec sa voix grave et ses mains toujours tachées de goudron, les tempêtes qu'il avait affrontées. Il savait aussi écouter, et beaucoup d'entre vous se souviendront de ses conseils donnés sans jamais rien imposer.

Ses derniers mois furent difficiles, mais il les traversa avec une dignité qui nous a tous bouleversés. Il tenait à remercier l'équipe de soins de l'hôpital de Quimper pour leur présence et leur douceur. Ceux qui souhaitent lui rendre hommage peuvent prendre contact avec la famille au 06 48 27 19 53 ou par courriel à jean.lefevre.famille@mailbox.fr.

La cérémonie d'adieu aura lieu le mardi 19 novembre à 14 heures en l'église Saint-Corentin de Quimper. Pour les personnes qui le désirent, des dons peuvent être adressés à la Société nationale de sauvetage en mer. Pour l'administration du dossier, nous rappelons le numéro de pièce d'identité du défunt, 09AB27561, afin de faciliter les démarches auprès des services compétents.

Je vous remercie, au nom de toute la famille, pour votre présence, vos messages et votre affection. Jean-Baptiste repose désormais en paix, face à la mer qu'il a tant aimée.

Growing up in Haifa, I used to watch the ships slide into the port from my grandmother's balcony, and I believed that everything worth understanding could be seen from up high. That belief changed the summer I spent volunteering at Rambam Health Care Campus. I was assigned to the paediatric wing, where I learned to fold blankets, carry charts, and listen. Mira, a nine-year-old with a stubborn grin, taught me more about patience than any textbook. On May 14th, she asked me to read her the same chapter of a science book three times, and I did, because I finally understood that attention is itself a form of care.

Since then I have tried to bring that same attention to my studies. At the Technion, where I completed my first year of engineering, I found myself drawn to biomedical design, particularly to devices that help children recover mobility after surgery. My lab partner, Omer, and I spent long evenings sketching a lightweight brace prototype, and when it failed our first test, we treated the failure as data rather than defeat. Our professor later said that the difference between a good engineer and a great one is how quickly they can turn a mistake into a question.

I want to continue asking those questions at a university that values collaboration between clinicians and engineers. I believe my experience in Haifa, from the quiet hospital corridors to the crowded lab benches, has prepared me to contribute as both a thinker and a listener. I hope to be part of a community where curiosity is rewarded and where every problem begins with the people it affects.

Hi all, I've finally started sketching out our trip for next summer, and I wanted to get everyone's thoughts before I book anything. Mum's turning sixty-two in late September, so my plan is to make the whole thing about her. My sister Sabine has already said she can take two weeks off, which is a miracle, so I'm building the itinerary around her availability. Brother Tomas, you're in charge of the car rental, since you're the only one who actually enjoys driving on the wrong side of the road.

Here's what I'm thinking so far. We start in Florence for four nights, mostly because Mum has been talking about the Uffizi since she was a teenager and I'd like to let her finally see it without us rushing her through in a single morning. From there we drive south to a farmhouse outside Montepulciano that I found through a friend of Sabine's husband. It has a pool, a big kitchen and a terrace that looks over the vineyards, which is exactly what we need after a city stretch. I've pencilled in six nights there, but I'll confirm once the owner gets back to me on the exact dates.

The last leg is the coast. I know some of you want Amalfi, but honestly the traffic on that road is brutal in the afternoons, so I'm leaning towards Sorrento instead, with a couple of day trips by ferry. Everyone's dietary stuff is noted, so I'll make sure the restaurants I shortlist can handle the gluten-free and nut allergy requests. Tomas, I know you'll want to nap in the shade after lunch, so I've picked a place with a proper garden.

Budget is the thing I'm least sure about. My rough estimate is around four thousand euros for the whole group, excluding flights, but that number moves a lot depending on whether we go for the farmhouse or split into two hotels. I'd rather we decide this together, so if you can reply by the end of the month with a yes or no on the overall plan, I'll start putting down deposits. Let me know if anything is a hard no for you, and I'll see what can be worked around.

Love you all, and I'm genuinely excited about this. Mum still has no idea, so please keep the group chat quiet around her. I'll send a proper calendar invite once we've locked in the final dates.

Sophie

So here's the situation. My coworker Marcus Delgado and I have worked together for about four years at a logistics firm in Columbus, Ohio. We were close at first. We'd grab lunch, cover for each other, the usual. About six months ago that started to change. Marcus got promoted to team lead over me, which I honestly didn't mind at first because he's good at it. But since then he's been different. He reassigns my projects without telling me, and last week he took credit for a route optimization report I wrote in front of our director.

I tried talking to him privately on October 3rd. He said I was being sensitive and that he was just trying to streamline things. Maybe he believes that, maybe he doesn't. Either way it didn't fix anything. Another coworker, Jenna, told me she'd noticed the same thing with her own work, so it's not just me, which is both reassuring and kind of worrying.

Here's my dilemma. I don't want to blow this up. Marcus has a new baby at home and he seems stressed out most days. Part of me wants to give him grace. Another part of me is tired of watching my name get erased from my own work. I've been documenting everything in a private notes file with dates and emails, just in case.

So, my questions: Should I go to HR now or wait and see whether it settles? If I do go to HR, how do I keep it factual without sounding like I'm attacking him? And is there a way to rebuild the working relationship, or is it time to start looking at other teams?

Any advice from people who've dealt with a friend turned boss would mean a lot. Thanks for reading all this, and sorry for the length. I'm Tamara, by the way, but you can call me T.

input:
Friends and family, thank you for being here tonight as we celebrate Tove and Johan. Many of you knew Tove long before she ever met Johan, back when she was simply Tovan to her cousins on Drottninggatan, the girl who could never sit still and always had a plan for the next adventure. Her grandmother Ingrid used to say Tove would argue with the weather and win. I think that stubbornness is exactly why Johan was lucky enough to catch her attention.

Johan, you have spent the last six years proving that patience and kindness can be just as powerful as ambition. You learned to bake Ingrid's cardamom buns, you took the dog Pelle on walks even in January sleet, and you never once complained when Tove redecorated the whole flat at midnight. The day you two moved into the house on Skolgatan 14, Tove phoned me in tears of happiness and said, "Johan carried the sofa up three flights and didn't even ask for help." That is the man she married, and I am so glad.

So please raise your glasses to Tove and Johan. May your life together be full of long dinners, wild plans, and quiet mornings with coffee and a little Pelle barking at the door. Skål!

October 14. I can't sleep, so I'm writing this at the kitchen table with the radio on low. Today Isaac finally got the call back from Mercy Regional Hospital about his mom's scans. Ivy had been sitting by the phone since morning, pretending she wasn't. The nurse, a woman named Denise, said the results were mostly clear, which made Isaac cry in the parking lot like a little kid. I told him it was okay to cry. He said he wasn't crying, it was just cold, even though it was seventy degrees.

After that we drove over to Lincoln Elementary to pick up Maya from her after-school art club. She had painted a huge sunflower on a piece of cardboard and wouldn't let anyone else carry it. On the way home she asked if Grandma would be okay, and Isaac said yes before I could answer, which I think was the first honest thing he'd said all day. Later he texted his sister, Ivy's twin Imogen, from his phone: "Call me back at 555-0148 when you can." She did within ten minutes.

I keep thinking about how small the good news felt and how big it still is. Next Thursday is the follow-up appointment, October 22, and I already marked it on the fridge calendar in red marker. I'm going to try to sleep now. Tomorrow I'll bake something, because that's what I do when I don't know what else to do.

But my cousin Tamar drove up from Be'er Sheva the weekend before and basically moved me in herself, which I did not expect. She refused to let me carry a single box, and she labelled everything in that tiny handwriting of hers, so now I know exactly where the kettle is.

The first real test was registering at the clinic on Herzl Street, the one run by Dr. Shapiro's team. I was so nervous I forgot half my documents, but the receptionist, a woman named Ruthie, was so patient that I almost cried. She even printed out my appointment card and wrote Tamar's number on the back in case I got lost again. Honestly, Vered, that small kindness made the whole week feel survivable.

Then there's Café Lilach, which has basically become my office. The owner, Nadav, remembers that I take my coffee with oat milk and no sugar, and on Tuesday he slipped me a free slice of lemon cake because I looked exhausted. I've been working on my translation project there every morning, and the Wi-Fi is fast enough that I can finally send files without the usual panic. If you ever visit, you have to go.

I've also started going to a small gym called Iron Olive near the port, mostly because the trainer is strict and I need someone to shout at me about my form. It's been good for my head, even if my legs hate me. I joined on June 4th, which feels like a lifetime ago now, and I'm already noticing the difference.

If you need anything from me, the best way to reach me is still vmarkovitz@gmail.com, though I'm checking my phone less these days. I miss you and your terrible jokes. Tell Yoni I said hi, and that he owes me a rematch at backgammon. Write back soon, okay? I want to hear everything about your new job.

Love,
Vivi

input:
We spent our last morning in Jerusalem wandering the lanes of the Old City, and I finally found the little bakery I'd been hunting for since we landed. The owner, a cheerful man named Chaim, handed me a warm sesame bagel and told me the place has been at 14 Beit Hadfus Street since 1961. My wife, Clara, insisted we come back before our flight on May 19, so we ended up there twice in one day. If you want to try it, call ahead at +972 2 555 0148, because the shop sells out of its morning batch before most tourists even wake up.

Later that afternoon we took the bus down to Tel Aviv, which felt like stepping into a different country within an hour. The city was loud, sunny and full of people on bikes, and Clara spent a long time photographing the Bauhaus buildings near Rothschild Boulevard. I kept thinking about how two places so close together can have such different rhythms. Jerusalem moves at the pace of centuries, while Tel Aviv seems to live entirely in the present.

If you're planning a trip in May, I'd recommend building in time for both cities. Bring comfortable shoes, carry some water, and don't be shy about asking locals for their favourite spots, because they will always have an opinion. Clara has already started a list of places we need to revisit, and I suspect the bakery will be at the top of it. Feel free to email me at clara.hensley@example.com with questions, and I'll gladly share the rest of our itinerary.

Dear Customer Services Team,

I am writing to make a formal complaint about the handling of my broadband installation at my home in Leeds, which was booked for 14 October and never completed. I was told by your agent on the phone that an engineer would attend between 8am and 1pm on the day, and I took the whole day off work to wait in. No engineer arrived, and no one from your company contacted me at any point to explain why.

When I rang the helpline the following morning, I was given a reference number and told the matter would be escalated. I was then transferred three times and eventually spoken to by an advisor who could find no record of the escalation. I was promised a callback within 48 hours. That callback never came. I am Eleanor Whitfield, the account holder, and I have been a loyal customer for six years, so I did not expect to be treated so carelessly.

The disruption has been considerable. I work from home for a company based in Manchester, and without a stable connection I lost two client calls and had to submit a report late. I also have a child who studies at Leeds Grammar School and relies on the internet for homework, so the lack of service has affected the whole household. Eleanor's schedule, and that of my son, has been thrown into chaos, and I have had to pay for mobile data out of my own pocket to get by.

I would therefore ask that you investigate the missed appointment and the failed escalation, and confirm in writing what went wrong. I expect the installation to be rebooked at a time that suits me, and I would like a full refund of the monthly charges for the period without service, along with compensation for the costs I incurred on mobile data. Please also provide the name of a senior manager who will take personal responsibility for resolving this.

I would appreciate a written response within 14 days. You can reach me at eleanor.whitfield@example.co.uk or on 0113 496 2187. I have kept copies of all correspondence, including the reference number issued on 15 October, and I am prepared to take this matter to the Office of Communications if it is not resolved satisfactorily.

Yours faithfully,

Eleanor Whitfield

I keep coming back to the Tuesday session, when you asked me what I actually wanted from my week and I said nothing at all. It was true, and it scared me a bit to say it out loud. I'm Pádraig, and I've been at Glasnevin Logistics for six years now, the last two as Senior Operations Coordinator. On paper that sounds like I have it together. Most mornings I'm up at half five, I drive in past the depot on the N7, and I spend the first hour clearing emails before anyone else arrives. By the afternoon my shoulders are up around my ears and I can't remember eating lunch.

I tried something new this week. On Thursday I went to Brigid's Kettle Cafe on Parnell Street before work instead of grabbing a sandwich at my desk, and I sat by the window for twenty minutes with a flat white and did nothing. Nobody needed a signature. The girl behind the counter, Niamh, remembered my order from the first time and said good morning as if I were a regular, which, I suppose I am now. It sounds small but I felt something loosen. I also booked back into the gym at Liberty Fitness on Saturday, the one I'd let lapse since March, and I'm going to try the 9am class even though it's early.

You said the aim for the next few weeks is to notice when I'm tipping over into the old pattern rather than trying to fix it all at once. I wrote that on the back of my hand so I'd see it. Things to check in before the next session: whether I've moved the gym sessions around again, whether I answered work messages after nine, and whether I can say no to the extra rota cover that Mairéad keeps asking for. I'll bring my notes next time, and I'll try to be less apologetic about being a mess.

I'm a data engineer based in Portland, Oregon, where I have spent the last eleven years building pipelines for logistics companies and, more recently, a small healthcare analytics startup. My path into the field was not a straight line. I started out studying marine biology, spent two summers counting seabirds on the Oregon coast, and eventually realised that the most interesting part of my work was never the fieldwork itself but the spreadsheets afterward.
