Dear journal, I want to get down what happened on Thursday, because I keep replaying it. Kieran sat across from me in the kitchen of the flat in Phibsboro and asked whether I'd actually filed the paperwork for my passport renewal, number IE4471920, before the deadline on the 14th of October. I hadn't. I said I had, and then I felt my stomach drop because I knew he'd check. He did check, later, on the laptop, and found my reminder email to the consulate still sitting unsent in drafts. I felt small and stupid and then angry at myself for feeling small.

My therapist, Dr. Niamh Gallagher, says the lying is less interesting than what it protects. When I mentioned it at Tuesday's session she asked what I was afraid would happen if I'd simply said I'd forgotten. I didn't have a good answer. I think I'm afraid of being the friend who lets things slide, the one Ciaran jokes about at the pub in Smithfield. I told her the emotional thing and the admin thing had gotten tangled, and she said that's exactly the kind of tangle worth sitting with.

So this week I'm trying something small. I emailed Kieran at kieran.doyle.87@mailsprint.ie and said plainly: I dropped the passport ball, I'm sorry I said otherwise, and I'm booking the appointment tomorrow morning. He replied within the hour with a thumbs up and a line about how he'd rather hear the truth than a neat story. I'm holding onto that. Tomorrow I'll do the form, and I'll write down how that feels too.

Ciao Marco, ti scrivo perché non riesco a togliermi dalla testa quello che è successo domenica scorsa. Sono sceso con Sara fino al Quartiere Pigneto, dove abbiamo mangiato in quella trattoria in via del Pigneto che ti avevo consigliato, quella con i tavoli fuori. Sara ha ordinato le orecchiette con le cime di rapa e io i carciofi alla giudia, e mentre aspettavamo il dolce mi ha confessato che aveva ricevuto un'offerta dalla Bellucci Logistica, la ditta di spedizioni di Ostia. Ha detto che non ci avrebbe pensato più di tanto, ma gli occhi le brillavano in un modo che non le vedevo da anni.

Io, come al solito, ho reagito male. Le ho detto che Bellucci Logistica non aveva una buona reputazione, e lei si è irrigidita. Sara mi conosce abbastanza bene da capire quando parlo per paura e non per ragione, e alla fine me l'ha detto chiaramente: non ha bisogno che io decida per lei. Abbiamo passeggiato fino a piazza Vittorio in silenzio, e lì ho capito che avevo sbagliato.

Le ho chiesto scusa il giorno dopo, il 9 agosto, al telefono. Mi ha risposto che l'avrebbe accettata comunque, e che voleva solo sentirsi appoggiata. Ci ho pensato tutta la notte. Credo che la prossima volta dovrò ascoltare prima di parlare. Fammi sapere cosa ne pensi, e salutami Chiara.

input:
Joseph Alvarez Tran, 71, of Lakeview, Ohio, passed away peacefully on March 9 surrounded by his family. For thirty-four years Joe served as senior facilities manager at Halvorsen Mechanical Supply, where colleagues knew him as the one who could fix anything with a wrench and a joke. He never missed a Monday morning safety briefing and kept a spare coffee mug in every break room he ever visited.

Born on March 22, 1953, in Toledo, Joe grew up fixing bicycles for the neighborhood kids and later restoring a 1967 Ford Falcon that he drove until the day he retired. He is survived by his wife of forty-six years, Marisol, their daughters Anna and Lena, and five grandchildren who called him Grandpa Joe and never once let him forget his promise to take them fishing at Lake Erie.

Joe, we will miss your slow Sunday pancakes, your terrible puns, and the way you always waved from the porch until our car turned the corner. Rest easy. The lights in the garage will stay on for you. - Your son-in-law, Marcus

input:
Hi all, long-time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone who has been through something similar can give me some honest advice. I moved to Rosario about eight months ago for a job at a logistics firm, and I've been struggling more than I expected. I'm 29, I came over alone, and my Spanish is still shaky enough that I feel like I can't really make friends beyond the people I work with.

What's making it harder is my health. Back in March I had a persistent cough and chest tightness that wouldn't go away, so I went to the Hospital Italiano de Rosario on Santa Fe street. The doctors there were great, honestly, and the staff spoke enough English to walk me through everything. They ran a bunch of tests and told me it was probably a bronchial infection, but I still haven't felt right. Hernan, the nurse who helped me with the discharge paperwork, told me to come back in April if things didn't improve, and I think I'm going to have to do that.

I've tried to build a routine to feel more settled. I joined a small gym near my apartment, Gimnasio Fuerza Sur, and I go most mornings. The people there are friendly and the owner, Marcelo, has been patient with my Spanish. I also started going to the cafe across the road, Cafe Lorenzo, to read and write in the afternoons. It helps, but it still feels like I'm going through the motions. I haven't really made a close friend yet, and the loneliness is starting to wear on me.

My main question is this: has anyone else found that the adjustment period was much longer than they expected? Did you find a good way to meet people outside of work, especially if you aren't fluent yet? I've looked at language exchanges and a couple of community groups at the local university, the Universidad Nacional de Rosario, but I'm not sure which would suit someone like me.

I'd also welcome any tips on managing the health side. I know I should go back to the hospital in April if the cough returns, but I'd love to hear from anyone who had a similar experience and how they handled the emotional stress that came with it.

Thanks in advance for reading. Any advice, big or small, would mean a lot.

input:
Eitan Shalom passed away peacefully on March 9 at the age of 71, surrounded by his children in Rehavia, Jerusalem, the neighbourhood where he had lived for nearly forty years. He was a man who measured a day by its small pleasures: a strong coffee at Café Hillel on Emek Refaim, a long walk along the Valley of the Cross, and the newspaper read cover to cover before noon.

Eitan was born in Haifa in 1953 and spent most of his working life as a structural engineer at Mekorot Ashdod Engineering Ltd., where colleagues remember him as patient, exacting and quietly generous with his time. He could explain a load-bearing wall to a twelve-year-old and make it sound like a bedtime story. Those who worked beside him say he never raised his voice, only his eyebrows.

To his family he was simply Abba, Saba and Eitan, and each name carried its own weight. He taught his daughter to ride a bicycle on the quiet paths of Gan Sacher, sang off-key at every Shabbat table, and never once missed a grandchild's recital. Every Thursday he went to the Maccabi clinic on Ben Yehuda for his blood pressure check, and he always brought the nurse a box of sweets from the Mahane Yehuda market.

Eitan's family asks that, in lieu of flowers, donations be made to the Hadassah children's ward in his memory. Friends are welcome to share their own memories of him online; his grandson has created the page @eitan.remembers, where stories and photographs are being gathered.

The shiva will be held at the family home on Rabbi Akiva Street from March 10 to March 16, and visitors are welcome at any hour. Eitan leaves behind his wife of forty-six years, Miriam, two children, and five grandchildren, who will carry his stubborn kindness forward in all that they do.

May his memory be a blessing.
output:

I am writing this with a heavy heart to say goodbye to my mother, Cathryn Ashworth, who died peacefully at home on 14 October, aged 79. Mum lived at 27 Larkhall Crescent in Harrogate for almost forty years, and the front room there was the heart of our family. It was where the Sunday roasts happened, where the grandchildren did their homework, and where she would sit with a pot of tea and a crossword, correcting everyone's spelling but never her own.

Before she retired, Cathryn spent twenty-two years as Head of Patient Liaison at Harrogate District Hospital NHS Trust. Colleagues often told me that she could calm a frightened family faster than anyone they had ever worked with. She had a gift for listening, and she never once let a long shift stop her from remembering a patient's name. Many former colleagues have written to us since her death, and each letter mentioned her kindness in some small, specific way.

Mum leaves behind her husband Robert, her daughter Helen and me, her son Simon, and four grandchildren who adored her. We will hold a service at St Mary's Church on Saturday 25 October at 11am, followed by tea in the village hall. Mum would have wanted us to eat plenty of cake, so please come and do exactly that. Thank you, Mum, for everything.

input:
Last winter I finally made it out to Churchill, Manitoba, mostly because my colleague Ellery Sutton kept insisting the polar bears were worth the bone-chilling flight. Ellery works as a senior analyst at Northwind Logistics in Calgary, and she has been planning this trip since we first met at the office holiday party. We landed on January 14 under a sky so pale it looked like frosted glass, and the wind off Hudson Bay cut straight through my parka. Ellery just laughed, handed me a pair of mitts, and said I'd get used to it by lunch. She was right, mostly.

Our guide, a quiet man named Gordon Ashby who has run tours out of town for nearly two decades, drove us in a heated tundra buggy along the frozen shoreline. We spotted a mother bear and her two cubs resting near the old fort ruins, and Ellery kept whispering that she could hardly believe we were so close. Between sightings we warmed up in a little café on Kelsey Boulevard, where the cinnamon buns were the best I've had anywhere in the country. Ellery swears the baker makes them fresh before dawn every morning, and I believe her.

If you go, pack more layers than you think you need and book early, because the tours fill up fast in January. I'm already texting Ellery about returning next winter, this time for the northern lights. Let me know in the comments if you have a favourite cold-weather destination in Canada, because I'm hungry for new ideas.

I am writing this statement to report an incident that took place on the street outside my apartment building on the evening of the event. At around nine o'clock I was walking home from the bus stop when a man approached me from behind and demanded my bag. I did not see his face clearly because it was dark and the streetlight on that corner has been out for some weeks. He was of medium height, wearing a dark jacket and a cap, and he spoke in Spanish with a rough, hurried tone. When I refused to hand the bag over, he pushed me against the wall and took it before running off toward the main avenue.

The bag contained my wallet, a phone, a set of keys, and some documents related to my work. I was not physically injured, although I was shaken and my shoulder is sore. I went straight to the building entrance and asked the doorman to call for help, and he phoned the emergency line while I sat down in the lobby. Two officers arrived some time later and took a short account from me at that point. I have since cancelled my cards, reported the lost keys to the building management, and blocked the phone.

I would like to request that the matter be investigated and, if possible, that any available camera footage from nearby shops or the avenue be reviewed. I am willing to provide any further information that may assist, and I can attend the station at a convenient time to sign a formal version of this statement. I confirm that the information in this account is true to the best of my knowledge.

input:
I've been dealing with a problem at work for about three months now and I can't seem to get out of my own head about it. My manager keeps giving me feedback that feels vague, things like "be more strategic" or "think bigger," without any examples I can actually act on. I've tried asking for specifics in our one-on-ones, but the conversations end up going in circles and I leave feeling more confused than when I walked in. I'm starting to doubt whether I'm good at my job at all, and that doubt is leaking into everything, including how I talk to my team.

What makes it harder is that I used to really enjoy this work. I took on a bigger project in the spring that I was proud of, and now I catch myself rehearsing arguments in the shower about why I'm being unfairly judged. I know that isn't productive. I also know I'm probably not seeing the whole picture, because I'm too close to it and my perspective keeps narrowing.

So my question is practical. How would you suggest I approach a conversation where I ask my manager for concrete examples without it sounding defensive? And separately, is there a way to tell the difference between feedback that's truly vague and feedback that's just hard for me to hear? I'd like to walk into the next review with a plan rather than another round of second-guessing.

input:
Friends, family, thank you for being here today. I stand before you with a heavy heart and a full memory of the person we are gathered to honour. My father was never one for big speeches, so I will try to keep to the things he actually cared about, which were honest work, a good cup of rooibos in the morning, and making sure everyone at the table had enough to eat before he sat down himself.

He was a man who believed in showing up. When the rains came and the roof leaked, he was the first to climb the ladder. When a neighbour's car broke down on the side of the highway, he was the one who stopped, even when it meant being late for his own appointments. He never kept a tally of the favours he did, and I suspect he would be embarrassed to hear me list them now. But I want the people who knew him to know how many lives were quietly steadier because of his kindness.

He had a laugh that could fill a room, usually at his own expense. He loved telling the same stories over and over, and somehow they never got old, because he told them with such delight. input:
Good afternoon, everyone. For those who don't know me, my name is Ramon Dela Cruz, and I was lucky enough to grow up three houses down from Victoria on Mabini Street in Barangay San Roque. She was the one who taught me to ride a bicycle on that narrow road, always shouting encouragement from her doorway whenever I wobbled too close to the gutter. Vicky, as the whole street called her, never met a stranger. If you walked past her gate, you were getting a plate of pancit or at least a long conversation about the weather.

Victoria passed away peacefully on the 14th of March, surrounded by the family she loved more than anything. Many of you know how fiercely she guarded her Sunday mornings at the parish of San Roque, where she sang in the choir for over forty years. She never once missed a fiesta, and she never let anyone leave her house hungry. Even in her last weeks, she asked whether the neighbours had eaten, and whether the kids on Mabini had finished their homework.

So today, let us remember her the way she would have wanted: loudly, generously, and with a little too much food on the table. Vicky, thank you for every lesson, every meal, and every time you waved me back from the edge of that road. Rest now. We will keep the gate open for you.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Martin, Harriet's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words about the woman who has been driving me up the wall since 1994. I've known Harriet for every single one of her thirty-one years, and I can honestly say I have never once seen her back down from a challenge, a bad sandwich, or a dodgy DIY project.

Harriet grew up at 14 Larkspur Close, a crooked little house in Hollins Green where the back garden flooded every February without fail. Our dad spent most of one winter trying to build a rockery that would keep the water out, and Harriet spent the same winter telling him it was never going to work. She was right, of course. She usually is, which is one of the more irritating things about her.

When Harriet moved away to study, she took with her a rucksack, a stubborn streak, and a truly alarming collection of houseplants. She also took with her a talent for making friends everywhere she went. Mum says it's because Harriet listens properly, and I suppose that's true, though I think it's mostly because she can talk anyone into anything. I have it on good authority she once talked a bus driver into waiting while she finished a conversation about his grandson's football.

Then, a few years ago, Harriet met Thomas, and for the first time in my life I saw my sister go quiet. Not sulky quiet, the good kind, the kind where she's just content to be in the room. Thomas is patient, funny in a dry way that takes a while to land, and entirely unfazed by Harriet's opinions on everything from parking to pastry. I think that's exactly why it works.

So please raise your glasses to Harriet and Thomas. May your home always be warm, your plants always thriving, and your arguments always short. Thank you all for coming, and Harriet, I love you. Now sit down before you embarrass yourself further.

I finally made it to the Dordogne this winter, a trip I'd been promising myself since my first year at university. I'm Amelia, and I work as a senior conservation archivist at the Lowther Heritage Trust in Bristol, so when the Trust agreed to let me take a week of leave in January, I packed my notebooks and set off by train from London. The weather was grey and damp, but the villages around Sarlat were almost empty, and I had the lanes to myself. I spent one afternoon wandering through a stone market town where the bakery still sells walnut bread in the same paper wrappers my grandmother used to buy.

On the third morning I rented a small Peugeot from the depot near the station. The paperwork listed the registration as KX-318-LM, and I kept repeating it under my breath so I would not lose track of the car in the car park. The roads wind endlessly between limestone cliffs and châteaux with their shutters closed for the season, and I stopped whenever the view demanded it. Before leaving I had called the hire desk on +44 117 496 2083 to confirm the drop-off time, which turned out to be sensible, because the agent had changed my slot to the 14th of January without telling me.

If you are planning a winter visit, my advice is simple: bring a warm coat, book your tables in advance, and keep your phone charged. Email me at amelia.lowther@heritagetrust.org.uk if you want my list of quiet cafés. I will happily send it along, though I warn you it is mostly bakeries.

When I was nine, my grandmother Galit taught me to bake challah in her small kitchen in Haifa, and I have been trying to get it right ever since. She never measured anything. She would press the dough with the heel of her hand, close her eyes, and tell me when it was ready. Those Sunday mornings taught me that patience is a kind of attention, and that the things worth doing rarely follow a recipe.

That lesson followed me into my work at the community food bank in Haifa, where I volunteered every Thursday during my last two years of high school. I started by sorting donated tins, but soon I was helping coordinate deliveries to families in the Hadar neighbourhood. I learned to keep a ledger, to call suppliers when a truck was late, and to listen when someone told me what they actually needed rather than what the form asked for. On March 14 last year, we served a record two hundred and twelve households in a single afternoon, and I remember how quiet the volunteers became when the last box was handed over.

I want to study public policy because I have seen how small logistical failures become hunger, and how careful planning can prevent it. If admitted, I hope to continue this work. You can follow our food bank's updates through my account, @galit_bakes_hope, and I have included my passport number, 2847 6193, on the enrolment form so the office can verify my records.

input:
I've been putting off writing this for weeks, mostly because Dr Byrne said I should try to get things down on paper when they feel too heavy to say out loud. So here goes. Sinéad is the name I answer to, though my sister still calls me Neasa when she's annoyed with me, which is most of the time these days. I work as a senior analyst at Lakeshore Data Solutions in Athlone, and since the restructuring in early November I have been sitting in meetings where nobody quite meets my eye.

The mornings are the worst. I've started going to Brew & Bloom on Church Street before work, mainly because the barista, a young lad called Ciarán, remembers my order and doesn't ask how I am. That small kindness has become the best part of my day, which tells me something about where I've ended up. Afterwards I walk along the canal with our old spaniel, Biscuit, who is fourteen and moves like she's apologising for every step. She doesn't need me to be anything other than present, and I find that very restful.

My mam rang on Sunday, as she does, and wanted to know whether I'd be coming home for her birthday on the 22nd. I said I would, which was a lie I told out of habit. I haven't told her about the job, or about the nights I lie awake running through spreadsheets in my head. My brother Eoin thinks I should just be more positive, which is easy for him to say from his desk in Galway.

I posted something on Instagram last week, a photo of the canal at dusk with a line about starting again, and tagged it @sinead.walks. A few people I hadn't spoken to in years commented with hearts and encouragement. It was nice, but it also made me feel like a fraud, performing a recovery I haven't actually got.

Dr Byrne asked me on Tuesday what I need right now, and I didn't have an answer. I think I need permission to not be fine. I need to stop measuring each day against some version of myself from last spring. I'm going to try to book the next session for the 14th, if the clinic has a slot, and bring the list I've started writing in my phone under the heading "things I'm allowed to feel."

input:
Woke up before the alarm again today, which I am choosing to believe is progress. The sky over the hills was that pale washed-out colour it only gets right before the sun clears the ridge, and I stood on the balcony with my coffee for a while without thinking about anything at all. Mostly I just listened to the neighbours arguing cheerfully about parking and a dog barking somewhere down the street.

Work was long. There was a meeting that could have been an email, then a bit of real progress on the thing I've been stuck on for a week. I'm trying to be less hard on myself about the days that feel slow. Some of them are just the groundwork for the ones that aren't.

In the evening the air finally cooled off and I walked to the market for bread and a few tomatoes that actually smelled like tomatoes. I ate standing up over the sink, which is not how grown adults are supposed to eat, and I felt fine about it. Tomorrow I want to call an old friend I've been meaning to phone for months. Writing it down so I actually do it.

input:
After almost six years at Lumière Analytics, I am excited to share that I have joined Vectra Logistics as Senior Data Lead, starting this May in Lyon.

When I joined Lumière in 2019, I was a junior analyst who mostly cleaned spreadsheets and hoped someone would let me build a dashboard. Looking back, the most important thing I learned there was how to explain numbers to people who don't live in them every day. Those lessons came from long Thursday lunches at the little bistro on Rue Saint-Dominique, where my colleague Mathilde Durand would sketch charts on napkins while we argued about whether our churn model deserved to be trusted.

Mathilde taught me that a good analysis is only as good as the question behind it. She also taught me to stop apologising for asking "dumb" questions in meetings, which may be the most useful career advice I have ever received. When I mentioned I was thinking about moving on, she was the first person to tell me to go for it, and the first to remind me to keep in touch.

The new role gives me the chance to lead a team of six and to build the data infrastructure for a company that moves goods across three countries every day. I am particularly looking forward to working on forecasting problems that affect real people: drivers, warehouse staff and customers who just want their parcels on time.

If you are in the Lyon area, or if you have experience in logistics analytics and would like to talk, my inbox is open at rmoreau.data@gmail.com. I am always happy to swap notes with people who are thinking about their own next step.

Thank you to everyone at Lumière for six good years. I will carry what I learned with me, along with a few napkin sketches I may or may not have kept.

So my questions are: can a landlord in Nairobi raise rent this sharply without notice in writing? Does the Rent Restriction Act or the Landlord and Tenant provisions help someone in my position? Hi all, long time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone who has been through a similar thing can give me some honest advice. I'm Jared, 34, and I work as a kitchen manager at a small cafe in Ponsonby called Bellbird & Co. I've been there nearly four years and I genuinely love the job, but things have got messy lately.

A couple of months ago my landlord decided to sell the building, and the new owners want to do a full renovation. They've told us the lease will end on 28 June, which gives me about three weeks to sort out somewhere new. Honestly, I'm not panicking yet, but I'm stressed. The rental market in Auckland is brutal and every flat I look at gets forty applications within a day.

The really annoying part is that the application forms want everything upfront. Proof of ID, my IRD number, my passport number for the reference check, and a letter from my employer. I sent my passport copy to one agency and then realised I'd emailed it to the wrong address, a Gmail account I don't even use anymore. I've messaged them to ask them to delete it and I'm waiting to hear back. Should I be worried? Is there anything I should do besides ask nicely? I'm not sure whether to report it to the Privacy Commissioner or just let it go.

input:
I have been asked to write something for the Hartley family's notice in the Yorkshire Post, and I find I cannot do it in the usual way. My name is Ian Crowther, and I was Iris Mallory's neighbour for almost thirty-one years, first on Brackenfield Road in Harrogate and then, after the move, in the cottage at the end of Cold Harbour Lane. Iris died on 14 July at the Harrogate District Hospital, with her daughter Joanne holding one hand and the crossword folded under the other. She was eighty-three.

Iris taught Latin and history at the girls' grammar school for nearly four decades, and I am told she once made a Year Nine boy cry over a misplaced ablative and then spent the rest of the lesson helping him fix it. She did not suffer fools, but she never once refused a favour. When my wife Margaret was ill in 2009, Iris arrived each Tuesday with a casserole, a library book and an opinion about whatever I had been reading. She was right more often than I liked.

Her rules were simple. Post the letters before noon. Never buy a car you have not driven in the rain. Her Vauxhall, registration K 214 HWR, was the most reliable thing she owned and she drove it until the week before she went into hospital, usually to the Saturday market for lemons and gossip. Joanne has asked me to say that the account for the church flowers is still in her name and she would like someone else to take it over. Those with a question about that, or about the memorial bench, can write to joanne.mallory@harrogatemail.co.uk.

Roughly a hundred people came to the crematorium on 19 July, and Jenny Ashworth from the crossword circle read a poem Iris had copied out by hand years ago and kept in her handbag. Several of us stayed on afterwards and told stories until the staff politely began stacking the chairs. I was asked to speak at the funeral and could not get through the first line without stopping, so I am grateful to have a page on which to say it properly.

Iris, you were a terrible driver in the wet and an excellent friend in every other weather. I will miss the lemons, the arguments and the crossword clues you were certain I could not solve. Rest well.

I write this with a heavy heart, as my wife Sheila passed away peacefully at home on 14 August, surrounded by those who loved her. She was born in Kendal in 1947, the eldest of four children, and she never quite lost the Westmorland vowels that made everyone in our kitchen smile. Sheila spent thirty-one years as a district nurse in Lancaster, and I don't think a single patient on her round ever forgot her steady hands or her habit of bringing a flask of tea on the cold winter visits.

She was a keen gardener, a terrible card player and the most generous host you could imagine. Her Sunday lunches were legendary, and the rhubarb crumble she made every summer will be missed by everyone who ever sat at our table. Sheila loved the fells above Kendal, and in her last months she would ask me to drive her up the valley just to look at the hills one more time.

She leaves me, our daughters Sarah and Helen, and six grandchildren who adored her. Those who wish to pay their respects are welcome at the service at St Thomas's Church on Thursday 21 August at 11am, followed by refreshments at the Golden Lion. Donations in Sheila's memory may be made to Marie Curie. Sheila, you were loved more than you knew, and you will be missed every single day.

input:
I finally made it to Kyoto this September, and I want to share a few notes before the details fade. I stayed in a small guesthouse in Gion, on a narrow lane off Hanamikoji Street, run by a woman named Keiko who insisted on serving miso soup at 7 a.m. no matter how many times I said I could grab a convenience store breakfast. She also reminded me, very kindly, to keep my passport number handy for the hotel registry, which is apparently still a paper-and-pen affair in many places. My passport number is ending in 4471, if you're wondering how paranoid I got about carrying it.

The real highlight was a day trip to Nara, where the deer are far more aggressive than any guidebook warned. I'd been told by a colleague at Hartwell Logistics, the freight company I work for back in Chicago, that the deer bow for crackers. That is technically true, but only if you have a cracker in hand and are prepared to be mobbed. Dan, my travel partner, learned this the hard way when a young buck nudged his camera bag right off his shoulder. We laughed about it for the rest of the afternoon over matcha and mochi near Todai-ji.

If you go, book your ryokan early, especially on weekends, and don't underestimate how much walking the temples require. Ten kilometres a day is normal here, and your feet will tell you so by evening. Dan and I both agreed the trip was worth every yen, even the moment I realised I'd left my phone charger at the guesthouse and had to ask Keiko to ship it to me in Osaka.

Most weekdays you'll find me arguing with spreadsheets about load tolerances, but I promise I leave the calculator at the office. On weekends I'm usually at Brewbean Roasters on 9th Avenue, because I believe a good flat white is the closest thing to a reliable foundation. I'm the one with the chipped mug who never finishes the crossword.

I run, I cook too much pasta, and I've recently committed to Tuesday night climbing at Ascent Bouldering, where I am humbled weekly by people half my age. I'm looking for someone curious, a bit sarcastic, and not afraid of a long conversation about nothing in particular.

Hey Marcus, you won't believe the mess I got myself into last week. Remember my cousin Hannah? Everyone back home calls her Bunny, and she's the one who dragged me to the consulate on August 14th because my passport was expiring and she swore they'd never let me travel to the wedding without a fresh one. I had my folder of papers, my passport number is C48219037 (I still know it by heart), and I was nervous as a cat in a bathtub. The clerk at the Denver office, a patient woman who introduced herself as a senior records officer, took one look at my date of birth and asked if I was really only twenty-nine. I laughed and said I felt about ninety after the drive.

Anyway, Bunny met me afterwards at a diner off Colfax and we split a massive plate of pancakes. She kept insisting that the whole thing was a sign, that I'd finally stop putting off the big moves in my life. Honestly, she's right more often than she admits. I was going to mention the job offer too, the one from Halvorsen Logistics where Harriet Doyle, the hiring manager, wants me to start as a regional operations coordinator. It's a step up and the pay is decent.

So that's my news. The passport is done, the job is maybe happening, and I'm stuffed on pancakes. Call me when you get a minute, and tell me honestly whether I should say yes.

I keep telling myself that the anxiety is just the job talking, but on the night of June 14th I sat in my car outside Brightwave Analytics in Pune for almost forty minutes before I could make myself go up. I'm Nisha, senior data lead, and on paper everything is fine. The quarterly review went well, my manager Ravi says I'm the steadiest person on the team, and yet I feel like I'm pretending every single day. My sister Meera keeps asking if I'm sleeping. The honest answer is not really.

Dr. Anand asked me last week to write down three things that went right each day. I've been doing it, mostly to humour him, but a pattern is showing up. Almost every entry includes Kiran. She stayed back with me during the migration crisis in May, and she covered my standup when I was too tired to speak. I've started calling her Kittu again, the way we did in college, and it made her laugh when I said it out loud. I think I've been treating her kindness as something I have to repay instead of something I can simply accept.

The session I'm dreading is the one on June 21st, when Dr. Anand wants me to talk about the promotion panel. I want to tell him that I'm not sure I want it. Writing that sentence down for the first time, I feel lighter and more frightened at once. Maybe that's what progress feels like. Nisha, you are allowed to take a breath before the next thing.

The first thing you notice about Cape Town in May is how the light changes. By mid-morning the mist has burned off Table Mountain and the Atlantic wind carries the smell of kelp into Sea Point, where we rented a tiny flat on Regent Road. Yolanda had planned the whole trip on a spreadsheet, colour-coded by day, but the spreadsheet fell apart the moment we reached the promenade and saw the penguins at Boulders Beach waddling across the path as if they owned it.

My cousin Thandeka met us on the second morning. She is a senior programme coordinator at the Bokamoso Youth Trust in Woodstock, and she insisted on driving us through Bo-Kaap before the tour buses arrived. The pastel houses were freshly painted for the season, and an elderly man sat on his step selling koeksisters from a steel tin. Thandeka grew up two streets over from there, and she pointed out the school she attended with the kind of fondness reserved for places that taught you something hard.

For the Winelands day, Yolanda insisted we book with a small operator run by a couple near Stellenbosch. The owner, Pieter van Wyk, walked us through the cellar with a glass of chenin blanc in each hand and talked about the drought years with real emotion. We lunched on a veranda overlooking vines just beginning to bud, the mountains purple in the distance.

On our last evening we walked down to the harbour at V&A Waterfront, where the sea was rough and the sunset turned the water copper. Yolanda kept her phone out, sending photos to her sister and typing little notes. If you ever plan this trip, message her at yolanda.m@capemail.co.za or call +27 21 555 0148 and she will happily send you the spreadsheet. Go in May, bring a warm jacket, and do not skip the koeksisters.

I wanted to write this review because Kevin Brandt at Sunrise Auto Care in Tulsa went well beyond what I expected last Tuesday. My car, a silver 2016 Honda Accord with plate KXT-4471, had been making a grinding noise when I braked, and I was ready for a long, expensive afternoon. Kevin, who is the service manager there, listened carefully, took the car up on the lift himself, and called me back before lunch with a clear explanation.

The pads and rotors on the front were worn down to almost nothing, which was the source of the grinding. What I appreciated most was that he didn't push me toward extras. He showed me the worn pads with the old ones next to the new, explained what could wait six months, and told me straight out what I didn't need. My friend Marcus Hale, who works in the parts department at the same shop, had recommended the place to me, and he was right about the honesty.

The front desk team was friendly too. Lena, who handles scheduling, remembered my name when I walked in and had the paperwork ready before I reached the counter. The waiting area is clean, with decent coffee and a television that actually has something on besides the news.

The bill came to a little under four hundred dollars, which included parts, labour and a fresh brake fluid flush. That is fair for the work and the time. I've already scheduled the next oil change for February 18th.

If you're in the Tulsa area and need brakes, a tune-up, or just an honest second opinion, I'd recommend Sunrise Auto Care. Ask for Kevin and tell him Kay sent you. You can also follow their updates at @sunrise_autocare_tulsa on Instagram, where they post tips for winter driving.

Hej, jag behöver lite hjälp att tänka igenom en situation på jobbet. Jag heter Karin Lindqvist och jobbar på Nordvik Logistik i Kista sedan två år. Sedan förra månaden har min kollega Mikael Dahlberg tagit åt sig äran för ett projekt som i praktiken var mitt. På mötet den 14 januari presenterade han allt som sitt, och när jag försökte förklara vem som gjort vad blev han irriterad och sa att jag tar saker för personligt. Chefen, Anders, verkar inte vilja ta i det alls. Jag har börjat tvivla på mig själv och vet inte om jag överreagerar.

Förra veckan satt jag och fikade på Kafé Solrosen på Hornsgatan med min vän Sara, och hon sa att jag borde dokumentera allt. Jag har börjat skriva ner datum och mejl, och jag har även sparat skärmdumpar från Slack. Men jag känner mig lite paranoid, som om jag håller på att bli en person jag inte vill vara. Dessutom låg jag och vred mig i sängen i förrgår och tänkte på att jag kanske borde lägga ut något på Instagram under @karin.l.writes, bara för att få ut det ur systemet, men jag vet att det vore ett dumt drag.

Så min fråga är: hur tar jag upp detta med Anders utan att låta gnällig, och hur hanterar jag Mikael framöver? Jag vill inte bli den som skapar stök, men jag vill inte heller att min insats försvinner. Tack på förhand för dina råd.

Så min fråga är: hur tar jag upp detta med Johan utan att låta gnällig, och hur hanterar jag Oskar framöver? Jag vill inte bli den som skapar stök, men jag vill inte heller att min insats försvinner. Tack på förhand för dina råd.

input:
I still can't quite believe Dale is gone. I met him twenty-six years ago at the Ohio Valley Tool & Die plant in Dayton, where he was the first person to show me how a torque wrench was supposed to feel in your hand. He grew up in Marietta, Ohio, the son of a riverboat pilot, and he never let anyone forget where he came from. He loved the Ohio River, bad coffee at six in the morning, and telling the same three jokes at every holiday party.

For the last decade, Dale's closest friend and fishing partner was Marcus Hollis, who drove him to every chemo appointment without once complaining about the traffic on I-71. Marcus told me Dale insisted on bringing his old beagle, Biscuit, along on the drives, and that the dog would sit in the back seat like a tiny chaperone. Biscuit outlived several of Dale's plans, but she never outlived his love for her, and she followed him from room to room until the very end.

Dale passed away peacefully at home on April 14th, surrounded by family and the sound of the television tuned to the Reds game. He is survived by his wife of thirty-one years, Carol, his two daughters, and four grandchildren who called him Papa Dale. We will gather at St. Mark's Lutheran in Marietta on April 22nd to celebrate a life that was loud, generous, and entirely unforgettable. In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to the Washington County Humane Society in his honor.

Dear diary, today was one of those grey, drizzly days that make you want to stay under the duvet until spring. I spent most of the morning sorting out the spare room, which has become a dumping ground for boxes I never unpacked after the move. Found a stack of old letters, a tangled bag of charging cables, and a jar of buttons I'd completely forgotten about. Took a while, but the room finally looks like somewhere a person could sit.

In the afternoon I walked down to the harbour with a flask of tea. The wind was sharp off the water and the gulls were making a fuss over something on the rocks. I sat on a bench for ages watching the boats bob about and just let my mind go quiet. It's funny how a cold walk can clear your head better than anything else.

Tonight I cooked a proper dinner for once, a big pot of soup with lentils and whatever vegetables were left in the crisper drawer. It turned out better than I expected. I ate it by the window with the lamp on and felt, for the first time in weeks, a little bit settled. Tomorrow I'll call my sister, I think. We've been meaning to catch up for far too long.

input:
I'm writing this down because my memory of appointments tends to go soft after a few days, and I want a clear record for myself. My name is Elena, and on Tuesday 14 November I went to the health centre on Calle de Atocha in the Lavapies neighbourhood of Madrid. I had been feeling a dull ache under my right shoulder blade for about ten days, plus a tiredness that didn't match how much I'd been sleeping.

The doctor, Dr. Ortega, was patient and thorough. She listened to my chest, checked my blood pressure (a little high, 138 over 88, which she said was not alarming but worth watching), and asked a lot of questions about my diet, my work at the bookshop, and whether I'd been under stress. I said yes to the stress. She also asked about my family history, and I mentioned my father's heart trouble at sixty-one.

She ordered a full blood panel and an ECG, which I had done the same morning in a small room that smelled of antiseptic. The nurse, Marisol, was kind and explained each step before doing it. Dr. Ortega said the ECG looked normal, which was a relief, and that the bloods would take about five working days to come back.

Afterwards I texted my friend Lucía, who is a nurse at the Gregorio Marañón hospital, to ask whether the shoulder pain could just be muscle strain from carrying stock boxes. She said it probably was, but to call the surgery on 912 345 678 if the pain spread to my arm or jaw, or if I felt short of breath. I've saved that number in my phone under "Dr. Ortega clinic."

Results are due around 20 November, so I've booked a follow-up for 21 November at 10:30. I'll bring my blood pressure notes from the pharmacy machine, which I have been checking each morning. For now I am cutting back on coffee, walking to work instead of taking the metro, and trying to get to bed before midnight. I'll update this note once I have the results.

I am writing this with a heavy heart to say goodbye to Bruno Marchetti, who died peacefully on 14 December at the age of 81. Bruno was born in Brescia in 1943, and he never quite lost the accent of those early years, nor the habit of arguing with waiters about the proper way to make a risotto. For forty years he ran the small hardware shop at Via Garibaldi 27 in Lucca, where generations of families came to him for a screw, a bucket or a sensible opinion. He always found time to ask about your mother's knee or your son's exams before he got to the matter at hand.

Bruno is survived by his wife of 56 years, Lucia, and by me, his daughter Giulia, who learned from him that patience and stubbornness are often the same thing wearing different coats. He leaves behind his grandsons, Matteo and Tommaso, who were convinced he could fix anything with a piece of wire and a sigh. We will miss his terrible puns, his Sunday drives in the old blue Fiat, registration FR 482 KT, which he refused to sell even when it no longer started without a push, and the way he hummed opera while watering the geraniums.

The family thanks Dottor Paolo Ferrante and the nurses of the Lucca hospital for their kindness in the final weeks. Friends may gather at the church of San Frediano on 18 December. In lieu of flowers, Bruno would have wanted a donation to the local fire brigade, to account IT60 X054 2811 1010 0000 0123 456. Ciao, Babbo. We will keep the shop lights on for you.

input:
When the admissions committee asks what has shaped me, I could point to any number of achievements, but the one that matters most happened in a hospital corridor in Heidelberg. Oskar Lindemann was my grandmother's name for me when I was small, and it is still the name my family uses, so I have grown used to hearing it in the mouths of nurses who were trying to find me in the waiting room at Universitätsklinikum Heidelberg. I was there for my grandfather's surgery in the first week of May, sitting with a clipboard and a phone that kept buzzing with messages from home.

What I noticed that week was how much of the work happened in the gaps between official procedures. A ward clerk who knew that Mr. Berger preferred the window seat. A cleaner who explained the rules of the staff football league to a bored teenager. Lindemann, the name on my grandfather's file, was the thread that connected all of it, because every form I signed had to be matched to the correct patient record before anything could move forward.

I came to see that those forms were not bureaucracy for its own sake. The tiny reference codes, including the insurance number ending in 4471 and the account number 2026-7713, were how a hospital of thousands of people kept track of one man's knee. I wanted to understand the systems that make care possible, and that curiosity is why I have applied to study health informatics.

At my school in Mannheim I had already started building small tools for the science club, a timetable app and a spreadsheet that tracked lab supplies. Those projects taught me that the most useful software is often the least glamorous. In the hospital I saw the same lesson at a larger scale, where a slightly confusing screen can cost a nurse several minutes she does not have.

My grandfather is home now, grumbling about the physiotherapy exercises and asking me, in the mock-serious tone he uses for things he loves, whether I have finally decided what to study. I have. I want to work where patients meet the systems behind their care, and to make those systems clearer, faster and kinder. I hope this university will give me the training to do that.

input:
I was born in Ennis, County Clare, in a house on Drumcondra Road that my grandmother still says leaked every winter. My name is Brendan, though my family has always called me Bren, and I grew up believing the rain was simply part of who we were. It was not until I moved to Galway at seventeen to study that I realised how much of my thinking had been shaped by the small, damp streets of home. Galway is a louder city, full of students, buskers and sudden weather, and I found myself listening to people differently because of it.

My application to read Environmental Science grows out of those early years. On Saturday mornings in October, my father and I would walk the Fergus estuary with a notebook, counting birds and noting the water level. He never called it research. He called it keeping an eye on things. I now understand that those walks were my first lessons in measurement, patience and the uncomfortable fact that the places we love are changing faster than we notice.

What I hope to study at your university is how those changes can be tracked and, where possible, reversed. I have spent the past year volunteering with a community group in Salthill, helping to log storm damage along the promenade, and I have learned that data gathered by ordinary people can be just as valuable as data from a laboratory. I want the training to match that ambition, combining rigorous science with the local knowledge I have been lucky enough to gather. I believe I can bring that mix of curiosity and practical care to your programme.

I have spent the past year volunteering with a community group in Ballybrit, helping to log storm damage along the promenade, and I have learned that data gathered by ordinary people can be just as valuable as data from a laboratory. I want the training to match that ambition, combining rigorous science with the local knowledge I have been lucky enough to gather. I believe I can bring that mix of curiosity and practical care to your programme.

Waseem Ahmed Qureshi

input: My name is Tomasz, and I was lucky enough to call Franciszek my brother-in-law for thirty years. Everyone at the Kowalski Logistics depot knew him as Franek, and nobody could say his name in the morning without a grin. He started there on 14 January 1994 and never once missed a shift he had promised to cover. I am writing to provide a reference for a former colleague who worked under my supervision for several years in a mid-sized engineering consultancy. Throughout that time, they demonstrated a rare combination of technical rigour and practical good sense. They took responsibility for complex project scoping, often identifying risks that others had overlooked, and they consistently delivered work on time and to a high standard. Their written reports were clear enough that clients frequently forwarded them internally without any need for explanation.

Beyond their technical contribution, they were an exceptionally reliable team member. They mentored junior staff with patience, took the time to explain their reasoning rather than simply issuing instructions, and were quick to share credit with colleagues. When a project encountered difficulties, they remained calm, communicated openly with the client and the team, and worked steadily toward a workable solution. Their judgement under pressure was among the qualities I valued most.

I recommend them without reservation for any role requiring analytical ability, dependable execution and a genuine commitment to collaborative work. They would be a valuable addition to any organisation fortunate enough to employ them. Please do not hesitate to contact me should you require any further information.

Dear Eltern und Schüler of the Gymnasium am Lindenweg, we are delighted to share a small but heartening story from this term. Olivia Brandt, our Year 9 science representative, spent three weeks organising the recycling drive that collected over 600 kilos of paper and batteries from families across the district. Olivia worked closely with her friend Lena Hoffmann from the parents' council, and together they made sure every collection point had clear labels and volunteers on hand. Olivia credits much of the success to Lena, who handled the logistics with remarkable patience.

Anyone wishing to join next term's planning meeting, or to suggest a new collection site, can write to Olivia directly at olivia.brandt@lindenweg-gym.de or reach the student council through their account @LindenwegSchoolCouncil. Paper and battery drop-offs continue every Thursday at the school's main gate, 14 Lindenweg, 40219 Düsseldorf, until the end of July. Olivia asked us to thank everyone who brought along a bag, even the ones that were only half full.

We are grateful to Olivia and Lena for showing what a small group of committed students can achieve. If you have ideas of your own, Olivia would love to hear from you before the summer holidays begin.

Elle aime les longues balades au bord du Rhône le dimanche matin, les marchés de la Croix-Rousse et les soirées où l'on refait le monde autour d'un bon vin. Ce qui la fait sourire le plus ? Sa sœur aînée, Camille, qui la traîne chaque année au même petit restaurant de Vienne le 14 octobre pour fêter leur anniversaire commun, et qui lui répète depuis des mois qu'il est temps de trouver quelqu'un de bien.

Lucie cherche une personne curieuse, qui sait rire de ses propres maladresses et qui n'a pas peur de dire ce qu'elle pense. Elle n'est pas pressée, mais elle n'a plus envie de jouer à des jeux compliqués. Si vous aimez la cuisine improvisée, les films d'Agnès Varda ou les week-ends sans programme, vous avez déjà un point commun.

I had been putting off writing this review for weeks, but Yvonne Harrowgate at Fairweather Tailoring deserves every star I can give. I came in on 14 October with a wedding suit that had been bought second-hand in Leeds and fitted nothing, and she spent close to an hour with me pinning, measuring and talking through the cloth. She didn't rush me once, even when I kept changing my mind about the lapels. Yvonne grew up in Huddersfield, which she mentioned while we were chatting about wool, and she has the careful eye of someone who learned the trade from her gran.

The result is superb. The jacket sits across the shoulders the way it should, and the trousers no longer bunch at the ankle. She also took in the waist on my partner's coat without making a fuss about it. The shop itself is small and calm, with a radiator that always seems to be on and a cat called Biscuit asleep on the fabric samples. Biscuit has been there longer than most of the staff, I suspect.

Prices are fair for bespoke-level care, and they have a turnaround of about ten days for alterations. I'm 34 and have never had clothes fit this well. If you live in Sheffield, where I'm based, it's worth the short train ride. Ask for Yvonne by name and tell her Mark sent you.
output:

Mate, I still can't believe what happened last Tuesday, so let me tell you properly. I'm writing from my flat in Newtown, Sydney, the one above the bakery on King Street that you always said smelt like a Sunday morning. Anyway, Yasmin rang me around seven in the morning, which is never good news, and said she'd been admitted to St Vincent's Hospital overnight with a really bad asthma flare. I was out the door before I'd even found my keys.

When I got there she was sitting up in bed looking grey and furious at the nurses for making her wear the oxygen mask. Yasmin Hadid is the stubbornest person I know, and I say that with love. She'd tried to ride it out at home for two days because she didn't want to make a fuss, which is classic her. The registrar was lovely, though, a tall guy named Patrick who explained everything without making me feel stupid for asking the same questions twice.

Here's the bit that really got me. While she was being monitored, Yasmin asked me to email her uni supervisor at the University of Sydney, because she had a submission due in May and she was panicking about an extension. I typed it out on my phone in the corridor, sent it from yasmin.hadid@sydneyuni.edu.au, and the supervisor replied within the hour saying no problem at all. Honestly, a small mercy.

She was discharged the next afternoon, and I drove her home to Marrickville, where her mum has been fussing over her ever since. We got pho on the way back, the good place near the station, and she ate two bowls, which the doctors would have approved of. She's sounding much better now, though she's still banned from doing the stairs at her place without someone around.

Anyway, I just wanted to get that off my chest, because I felt pretty helpless sitting in that waiting room. Call me when you're free this weekend and I'll tell you the rest, including the ridiculous thing the orderly said about my hair. Love you, Sarah.

input:
I'm Tane Whakaari, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a civil engineer specialising in stormwater and flood resilience. I grew up in Te Atatū South, Auckland, where my grandfather ran a small hardware store on Te Atatu Road, and I still think of that shop whenever I open a set of drawings. Those early Saturdays taught me to read a problem by walking around it before touching anything, a habit that has shaped every project since.

My first major role was with a regional council team in Hamilton, where I helped redesign culverts along the Waikato River floodplain after a run of heavy rain in December 2013. We had three weeks to model the worst case, and the lesson I took away was that data is only useful if the people living with the outcome understand it. Since then I have made a point of running community sessions before any construction begins, usually in a school hall with bad coffee and a lot of questions.

For the last four years I have been a principal engineer at a Wellington consultancy, Harbourline Infrastructure Ltd, leading a team of nine on coastal defences in the Hutt Valley. Our work now centres on sea-level projections and on designing barriers that can be raised over time rather than replaced. It is slower and less glamorous than building a new bridge, but I find it more honest about what we can and cannot promise.

Outside work I am a keen cyclist and a fairly average runner. I ride most mornings along the Hutt River trail, and in winter I can usually be found at the Petone rowing club, which has taught me more about patience than any textbook. I also write a small blog about infrastructure for non-specialists, and I am most active online as @tane_builds_rivers, where I share photos from site visits and the occasional frustrated rant about drainage codes.

If you are reading this before my session, thank you for coming. I hope to leave you with two things: a clearer sense of how flood risk is actually decided, and an invitation to ask me the questions I should have answered better in my own reports. My office details are in the programme, and I am always glad to hear from you, especially if you think I have got something wrong.

input:
I still can't quite believe how the Drakensberg caught me off guard. I'm Hannah Verwey, twenty-nine, a Pietermaritzburg girl who thought she'd seen mountains before. We set off from the Sani Pass road on the 9th of January, and by the time we reached the top my lungs were burning and my hands were shaking from the cold wind. Before leaving I had to show my passport, number A47812093, at the border post, and I still have the stamped pages tucked into my day pack like treasure.

The hike itself was rougher than the brochure promised. Our guide, Thabo, laughed when I asked whether the path ever got easier, and he was right to. I kept a small notebook of the trip and wrote my contact at the back in case anyone found it: hannah.verwey@mailbox.co.za. My rental, a silver Toyota with plate CA 455-921 GP, was waiting in the lot below, its windscreen dusted with pale grit. Honestly, I was so tired that I almost forgot where I'd parked it.

If you're planning a similar trip, book early, bring more layers than you think you need, and let someone know your route. I learned that the hard way when my phone died near the second waterfall and I had to rely on the kindness of a couple from Durban. They shared their flask, their jokes and a spare headlamp. I'll go back in January next year, when the rains have eased, and I'll be sure to thank them properly this time.

input:
Growing up in a small town outside Enugu, I learned early that electricity was a privilege rather than a given. Some evenings the generator would sputter and die, and my grandmother would light a kerosene lamp so we could finish our homework. Those evenings taught me to read by candlelight and to notice how much of daily life depends on systems most people never think about. I began asking why the power failed, who decided where the lines ran, and what it would take to change things.

That curiosity led me to volunteer with a community water project, where I helped record which households had access to clean supply and which relied on untreated stream water. The work was tedious. We walked from compound to compound with clipboards, and many people were suspicious of anyone asking questions. Slowly, though, I learned that good data only matters when it reaches the people who can act on it. I started translating our findings into simple charts for community meetings, and I saw residents begin to argue for their own needs with confidence.

I want to study engineering because I believe the problems I have seen up close are solvable with careful design and honest collaboration. I am drawn to programmes that combine technical rigour with fieldwork, because I know that a solar microgrid or a water filtration unit only succeeds when it fits the community that depends on it. I hope to return home with skills that let me build infrastructure that lasts, and to keep listening to the people it is meant to serve.

input:
Hey Sanne, you won't believe what happened to me on Tuesday. I'm still shaking a little, so forgive the rambling. My name is Cornelis van der Berg, but you know everyone just calls me Cees, and I'm thirty-four now, which somehow makes me feel older than my dad was at that age.

So I was driving home from the depot in Utrecht, the usual route along the Amsterdamsestraatweg, and I stopped at the light by the canal near Lombok. My car is a grey Volkswagen Golf, plate XB-471-K, which I know by heart because I've been fighting the parking fines on it for months. Anyway, the light turned green and this cyclist came out of nowhere, no lights, no helmet, just a blur in a dark hoodie. I braked hard and she (it was a she, Marleen, I found out later) went over the handlebars onto the cobbles.

I got out, my heart pounding, and she was sitting there holding her wrist and swearing in Dutch that would make a sailor blush. Turned out she was fine, mostly scraped up. Her name is Marleen Dekker and she works at the same logistics firm as my colleague Joost, which is how the whole thing got sorted out. Joost rang me the next morning, May 14th, to check I was alright, and apparently Marleen had already sent him a message complaining about me. Typical.

What got me is that she didn't press charges, and she even asked if I'd like to grab a coffee to make sure she hadn't cracked anything. I said yes, obviously, because I'm a bit of a fool when it comes to people who've just fallen off their bikes in front of me. We met at a little place on the Oudegracht last Friday and she laughed at me the whole time for worrying.

So that's my week. Tell me I didn't make a complete mess of things, and tell me you're coming to the drinks on the 22nd, because I need someone to witness the awkward way I'm going to explain this to my mother.

input:
I am writing this statement at the request of the officer who took my initial report, and I want to set down everything I can recall while it is still fresh. On the evening in question I had finished work later than usual and was walking home along a narrow street lined with vending machines and small restaurants. The area was quiet but not deserted. Shopkeepers were pulling down their shutters, and a few people were waiting at the bus stop across the road.

As I passed a parked van with its hazard lights blinking, I heard a sharp noise behind me, like a bag being dropped onto concrete. When I turned, I saw a man in a dark jacket moving quickly away from the entrance of a convenience store. He had a cap pulled low and was carrying something under his arm. I did not see his face clearly, and I cannot say whether he was on foot or had come from the direction of the station.

I went into the store myself to ask the cashier whether anything had happened. She seemed shaken and told me that the rear door had been forced open, though nothing appeared to have been taken from the front counter. She had already called for assistance before I arrived, so I did not make a second call. I waited with her until a patrol car came, and I gave my account to the officer on duty there.

I have tried to be careful not to add details that I did not actually observe. I am not certain about the colour of the van, the exact time I left the office, or whether the man spoke at all. Where I was unsure, I have said so, and I would rather the statement reflect honest gaps than guesses presented as facts.

I am willing to attend the station again if further questions arise, and I can provide my contact information to the investigating team. Please let me know if there is anything else I should clarify or any documents you would like me to review.

input:
Dear Abuela Josefina,

I hope this letter finds you well and that your knees are behaving themselves in this heat. It has been raining almost every afternoon here in Oaxaca since the start of July, which means the streets smell of wet stone and fresh tortillas by evening. I think of you every time the rain comes down hard on the tin roof of our little courtyard.

Work at Grupo Verdalia has been busy. My manager, Ricardo, asked me to lead the new hire training, and I am trying to be as patient with the trainees as you were with me when I was learning to make mole. Most days I finish at seven and then walk over to Café Lupita on Calle Macedonio Alcalá, where Doña Lupe has kept a corner table for me. She asks about you every time, and I tell her you are still the best cook in our family.

Pancho is doing well, although he has discovered that the neighbor's cat sleeps under our Nissan and he refuses to come out when it is there. Last week he tore a hole in the screen door chasing it, so Mamá has been furious. I told her he is simply protecting the car, which is registered under plate number JKN-4827 and which I am still paying off, so that argument did not go over well.

I also wanted to tell you that I finally went to the clinic on Avenida Juárez for my check-up, the one you kept nagging me about. Everything is fine. The doctor, Dra. Ortega, said my blood pressure is much better than last year, and she gave me the same speech about walking more that you always gave me. You would have been proud of me for listening.

I am enclosing a photo from the Guelaguetza preparations in the zócalo. The dancers in the blue and white costumes made me think of the summer you took me to the festival when I was eight. Please call me at 951-447-8820 on Sunday, after your program, so we can talk for longer than the last time. I miss your stories and your terrible jokes.

With all my love,
Javier Morales Reyes

I am writing this statement in relation to the theft of my bicycle, which I reported at the Hillcrest Road station on the morning of 14 September. My name is Sophie Anderton and I have lived at 27 Carrow Lane, Bristol, BS5 8QT, since I moved back to England from Lyon last spring. I worked for most of the past three years as a translator in France, so this is the first time I have had to give a formal account of anything to the police here, and I apologise if the details below are not in the order you would prefer.

On Friday 11 September I cycled to the offices of Northfield Legal Services on Dock Street, where I met my colleague Marcus Hale to review a set of contracts before a deadline. I locked my bicycle, a dark green Pashley with a black rear rack and a brass bell, to the railings outside the main entrance at about 8.40 in the morning. Marcus was with me and saw me lock it. I was inside until shortly after five in the afternoon, and when I came back down the bicycle was gone. The cable lock had been cut cleanly, and the cut pieces were still attached to the railing.

I have since been asked by a member of the building staff whether I had left anything else in the bicycle basket. I had not. My helmet was hanging from the handlebars, and it was still there when I returned, which I mention only because it seems odd to me that a thief would take the bicycle and leave the helmet. My house keys and phone were in my bag, which I carried inside with me.

I have spoken with Marcus about the afternoon and he has confirmed the timings above. He also remembers a man in a grey hooded top walking slowly along that stretch of pavement twice while we were working, though he did not pay particular attention to him. I have not been able to recall a face. I am happy to provide a copy of the purchase receipt, which I have located in my email, along with the serial number recorded at the time I bought it.

I would like to know whether any cameras cover the entrance to Northfield Legal Services or the adjoining car park, and whether footage can be requested before it is overwritten. My contact number is 07700 900412 and my email address is sophie.anderton@mailbox.co.uk. Please do let me know if you need anything further from me.

Sophie Anderton

Hello everyone, and welcome back to a new school year at St. Brigid's National School in Ballyfermot! I'm Dara Keane, and I've been asked to share a few words for this month's newsletter as the parent representative on the Board of Management. It's been a busy start already, and I want to thank all the families who came out for the Welcome Coffee Morning on Monday, 9 September. The turnout was wonderful, and the hall was buzzing with chat about new teachers, new uniforms and the usual scramble for the right school bag.

This year we have some exciting changes. Ms. Orla Gilligan, who many of you will know from her time on the Ballyfermot Youth Project, has joined our staff as Learning Support Coordinator. She is already working with the junior infants to get them settled, and the early feedback from children and parents has been very positive. Please do pop in to say hello if you see her at the gate.

My own family has been part of this school community for a long time, and this autumn is a bit of a milestone for us. My daughter Niamh starts fifth class, and my husband Colm is taking on a new role as a volunteer reading buddy every Tuesday morning. Our house on Cherryfield Avenue is a short walk from the school, so you may well spot the two of us heading up the road with the dog in tow. Writing this down because Dr. Lefèvre suggested I keep a journal between sessions, and honestly I'm not sure what else to do with the evenings. Today I walked past Café Mirabelle on rue des Tanneurs in Nantes, the place where I used to meet my sister Charlotte on Sunday mornings. I didn't go in. I stood by the window for a minute, saw the old waiter who always remembered Charlotte's order, and kept walking. Wren, you did well not going in, I told myself. Still, my chest was tight all the way home.

I was born in Nantes too, in the clinic near the river, so I suppose I carry the city around in a way that's hard to shake. On April 9th I finally emailed Charlotte at wren.marchand@orangemail.fr to ask whether she'd meet me for a coffee somewhere neutral, maybe the gym she likes near Bellevue, not the cafe. She hasn't replied yet. I keep checking my phone and then feeling silly for checking.

Dr. Lefèvre asked me what I was hoping would happen. I didn't have a good answer then, and I don't have one now. Maybe I just want Charlotte to know I'm trying. Maybe I want to stop hearing her silence as a verdict. Next session, I'll bring this up before I lose my nerve.

I'm Elena Duarte, and I was born in Rosario, a river city in Santa Fe province where the Paraná runs wide and brown past the old port. I grew up above my grandmother's bakery on a noisy corner, and I still measure most things by the smell of bread at six in the morning. At 34, I work as a civil engineer on water infrastructure projects across the Litoral region, which means I spend more time in mud boots than in conference rooms, though I'm happy to trade one for the other today.

My path into engineering was not straight. I studied at the Universidad Nacional de Rosario, then spent two years in Mendoza on a drainage study that taught me more about flash floods than any textbook. Between site visits I kept sane at Cafe Lunares, a tiny place on Calle Córdoba where the owner, Marcelo, remembers everyone's order. Much of my best thinking about sewer capacity happened over his terrible-but-lovable cortado. Last spring I also started going to the Club Atlético Ferro gym after my shifts, which has been the only reliable way I've found to stop worrying about pipe gradients.

What I care about most is making sure that when it rains in Argentina, the water goes somewhere useful and not into people's living rooms. I'll be presenting our team's findings on stormwater retention in peri-urban neighbourhoods, and I would be delighted to talk with anyone who has tried to solve the same problem. You can reach me through the conference app or at elena.duarte@ingenieria-litoral.com.ar. Thank you for having me, and I look forward to hearing what everyone is building.

When I first walked into the chemistry lab at Hartwell Grammar School in Leeds, I had no idea that a single afternoon would change how I think about medicine. Zara Okonkwo-Reid, the lab technician, had set up a titration for our Year 12 group, and I was the one who misread the burette and nearly spilled the whole flask. Instead of scolding me, she walked me through the calculation step by step, and by the end of the lesson I understood not only the chemistry but why accuracy matters to people who depend on it.

That moment stayed with me. Over the following months I volunteered on Saturday mornings at the Leeds General Infirmary, where I helped sort prescriptions and shadow the pharmacy team. I learned that a dosage error is never just a number on a page. It is a patient, a family, and a decision someone has to live with. Watching the pharmacists double-check every label, I began to see clinical work as a discipline of care as much as of science.

I am applying to study Pharmacy because I want to be the kind of practitioner who explains, not just dispenses. input:
I have been asked to write something about my mother, and I keep starting and stopping, because she would have found all of this fuss a little embarrassing. She was the kind of woman who fed everyone who walked through the door, who remembered the names of the neighbours' dogs, and who could fix a broken hem faster than most people could find the thread. She taught me to cook by feel rather than by recipe, and she never once measured anything, which still drives me a little mad whenever I try to recreate her beans.

She loved music, especially the old samba records she played on Sunday mornings while she swept the front steps. She sang along badly and without shame, and she would wave the broom at anyone who tried to correct her. Her laughter carried through the whole house. Those mornings are the ones I think about most, the sound of the radio, the smell of coffee, the scrape of the broom on the tiles.

To those of you who knew her, thank you for your kindness over the years and for the many visits, the phone calls, and the casseroles. She was proud of her friendships and of the family she built with patience and humour. We will miss her terribly. We are grateful that we had her for as long as we did, and we will carry her stubbornness, her generosity, and her wonderfully terrible singing with us for the rest of our lives.

input:
Okay, so you know I've been dreading telling you this, but I finally want to get it off my chest. Last Thursday I got let go from Brightwater Logistics. Yeah, after almost six years. They called it a restructuring, which is corporate for "we don't need you anymore but we're too polite to say it." Marcus from HR sat on the video call with his camera slightly off-center the whole time, like he couldn't bear to look at me. I think he was more upset than I was, honestly.

The weird part is that I saw it coming, and I still wasn't ready. Back in February my manager, Dana Whitfield, started cancelling our one-on-ones and stopped answering messages in the team channel. I kept telling myself it was just busy season. Then in early March they moved all my accounts to someone in Ohio without telling me first. I found out because a client emailed me asking why I'd stopped replying. Embarrassing. I should have pushed harder for answers.

So here I am, a week later, sitting in my kitchen in Columbus, which is not where I expected to be on a Tuesday. I've been trying to keep things light online so my family doesn't panic. I posted a little something on my Instagram, @mikaela.drives.coffee, just a photo of a latte and a line about taking some time to figure out the next move. Got a bunch of sweet comments, a couple of old coworkers reached out, and one recruiter slid into my DMs before I'd even finished my first cup of coffee that morning. Not sure how I feel about that yet.

Here's what I'm trying to do now. I'm updating my résumé tonight, which I keep avoiding because it means admitting this is real. I'm also going to call my cousin Renata on Saturday, since she's worked in operations for years and always knows who's hiring. And I'm giving myself until the end of the month to be sad, angry, relieved, whatever shows up, without judging it.

Anyway, that's the update. Thanks for not making it weird when I went quiet on you. Can you come over this weekend? I'll make the good pour-over and you can help me figure out whether I should apply to the jobs that keep emailing me or just take a few weeks off. I really need someone to tell me I'm not crazy.
