Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Data Analyst position at Vantra Logistics in Utrecht, which I found through your careers page on 12 March. I recently completed my BSc in Applied Statistics at the University of Groningen, where I graduated with honours and spent two years as a student assistant in the faculty's research office. That role taught me to clean messy datasets, build dashboards for non-technical colleagues, and explain results without hiding behind jargon.

Since finishing my degree, I have worked part-time at Brouwerij Koffie & Co, a small cafe in Haarlem, where I manage the weekly stock forecasts and the point-of-sale reports. Reducing waste by roughly eleven percent over the last six months was a result I am proud of, and it convinced me that good analysis can change everyday decisions. I also volunteer two evenings a month at the Sint-Anna Medical Centre in Leiden, helping the admin team track appointment no-show rates. It has shown me how much clarity matters when people are waiting on the answer.

My technical skills include Python, SQL, R and Power BI, and I have completed a certificate in cloud data warehousing. My final thesis modelled regional delivery delays in the Netherlands using three years of anonymised transport records, and I would welcome the chance to discuss how similar methods could help your network planning team.

Outside work I keep a fairly disciplined routine. I run along the canals before breakfast, and in the evenings I look after Pim, my rescue greyhound, who has strong opinions about my keyboard habits. I also write a short monthly newsletter on public data sets for a small community group, which is where I first developed the habit of writing for a general audience.

Thank you for considering my application. I would be glad to talk in person or by phone; you can reach me at +31 6 1234 5678 or at sanne.vermeer@mail.nl. I have also attached my portfolio, and you can see my work on GitHub under the handle @sannev_data.

Kind regards,

Sanne Vermeer

Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Junior Data Analyst position at Vetor Analytics in São Paulo. I graduated from the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro in 2022 with a degree in Statistics, and since then I have worked on reporting and forecasting projects for a regional logistics company. Standing here today, it is hard to find the right words for someone who gave so much of herself to everyone around her. She had a way of making a room feel warmer the moment she walked into it. Whether it was a neighbour who needed a hand with the garden, a friend who needed a listening ear over a cup of tea, or a grandchild who needed someone to believe in them, she was always there, quietly and without fuss.

She loved the bush, the beach on a summer morning, and a good long conversation that ran past dinner time. She had opinions about most things and was never shy about sharing them, usually with a laugh that let you know she was half teasing. Those who knew her well will remember her stubbornness, her generosity, and the way she could tell when you were pretending to be fine.

As we say goodbye, let us carry forward the kindness she showed us. Let us check in on the people we love, make the time for the small things, and keep the kettle on for whoever happens to drop by. That is how she would want to be remembered: not for the grand gestures, but for the everyday ones that made all of us feel at home.

input:
Quand je suis arrivée à Lyon en avril, je pensais simplement passer deux jours dans les bouchons et les bouchons de saucisson. Mais dès le premier matin, mon amie Zoé, que tout le monde appelle Zozo depuis le lycée, m'a traînée dans le Vieux Lyon avant même que j'aie fini mon café. On a marché le long des traboules, ces passages secrets entre les immeubles, et elle m'a montré des murs couverts de fresques que je n'aurais jamais remarquées seule. Zozo tient aussi un petit compte Instagram, @zozo.dans.les.traboules, où elle poste ses photos de la ville chaque matin, et je vous conseille vivement de la suivre si vous venez.

Le soir, on a dîné dans un bouchon près de la place des Terreaux. Le serveur connaissait Zozo et nous a apporté une quenelle de brochet qui était à tomber par terre. Je ne sais pas si c'était le vin ou la compagnie, mais j'ai passé la soirée à rire aux éclats. Avant de partir, Zozo m'a aussi présenté Biscotte, son vieux chat roux qui règne sur l'appartement de la rue Léon-Blum comme un petit empereur. Il a immédiatement décidé que mon sac était son nouveau trône.

Le dernier jour, nous avons pris le funiculaire jusqu'à Fourvière, et la vue sur les toits et la Saône, le 14 avril au matin, valait toutes les heures de montée. Si vous passez par Lyon, n'hésitez pas à demander à Zozo de vous faire visiter. Elle connaît chaque escalier et chaque cachette de la ville, et je suis repartie avec la promesse de revenir.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Tomasz, Dominik's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight. Growing up in Wadowice, Dom was the kid who could never sit still. He'd spend whole afternoons at Kawiarnia Sztuka on Rynek, nursing a single espresso while sketching in the margins of his school notebooks, and our grandmother Halina used to say he'd either become an architect or a professional daydreamer. Turns out he became both.

What I want you all to know about Dom is that he's loyal in the quietest way. When our father was in hospital in September three years ago, Dom drove up from Kraków every single morning before his shift at the clinic on Zielona Street, brought Mum a fresh bun from the bakery, and sat with Dad until the nurses shooed him out. He never once mentioned it to anyone. I only found out because Mum told me.

Anna, you've taken a man who is stubborn, sentimental and terrible at remembering birthdays, and you've made him better at all three. Dom, I'm proud of you, and I'm lucky to call you my brother. Please raise your glasses to the bride and groom.

input:
I have been going to Brennan's Hardware on Kilmore Road in Drogheda for about six years now, and I keep coming back for one reason: Fiona behind the counter actually knows what she's talking about. I came in last Saturday, the 14th of May, with a leaking tap that I was sure needed a whole new unit. She had me look at the washer first, showed me the old one, and sent me home with a 40 cent part and a tiny bit of advice that saved me a plumber's call-out fee. That kind of honesty is rare.

The shop itself is a bit cramped and the aisles can be hard to navigate when there's a delivery in, but everything is labelled and the staff are happy to walk you to the right shelf. Prices are fair, and they will order in anything they don't stock, usually within three or four working days. I've had a garden hose fitting and a set of replacement hinges arrive exactly when promised.

Fiona also remembered my dad's name when he came in with me last week, which I found genuinely touching. There's something to be said for a shop where the staff know the regulars and treat them like neighbours rather than transactions. Several of the other customers were chatting with her about the local GAA results while they waited, which tells you a lot about the place.

If you're in Drogheda and need something fixed around the house, go to Brennan's. Ask for Fiona, tell her what's going on, and let her point you in the right direction. You can also reach the shop at info@brennanshardware.ie for special orders, though I'd recommend calling in person if you can. I wrote this review on the bus home, having just tested my new washer successfully, so I'm happy to report the tap is no longer dripping.

Five stars from a loyal customer, and I'll be back the next time something breaks, which in an old house in Drogheda is always soon.

Rosalind Okafor-Brandt has spent the better part of fifteen years moving between two worlds, and she still describes herself as a translator first and a researcher second. Born in Enugu, she trained as a nurse at the University of Nigeria before taking a post at Royal Infirmary Ashdale in 2012, where she met her closest collaborator, Heather Lindqvist, over a shared frustration with discharge paperwork. Their partnership led to the paper that first brought Rosalind's name to the wider community of clinical educators.

She now lives in Millbrook with her partner Tomas and their dog Juniper, a rescue greyhound who has opinions about every walking route in the valley. Rosalind arrived in the city on 9 April 2016, carrying two suitcases and a box of notebooks that she still refers to as her real luggage. Her friends say the move changed her teaching more than her research, and that she is at her most animated when explaining how a hospital ward looks different depending on which side of the ocean you stand on.

Rosalind is looking forward to the spring session, when she will present on bilingual patient handover. Those who know her say to expect a talk that begins with a story about a patient in Enugu and ends with a question for the audience. If you see her in the coffee queue, ask her about Juniper; she will happily tell you more than you asked for.

I'm writing this down so I remember what Dr. Ferrer told me at my appointment on 14 February at the centro de salud in Valencia. My name is Olivia Brennan and I came in because of the tightness in my chest that started after my sister Marisol's wedding last month. I was worried it was my heart, the same thing that runs in our family, so I wanted to be sure before I went home.

Dr. Ferrer listened to my chest, took my blood pressure, which was a bit high but not alarming, and ordered an ECG and bloods. She said the ECG looked normal and that the tightness is most likely muscle strain and stress from the last few weeks, especially with all the wedding planning. She asked me to cut back on coffee and to walk for twenty minutes each morning, and she wants to see my blood results when they come back.

I told my husband Tomas everything when I got home, and he laughed at me for going in without him. Marisol called too and asked me to make sure I am not hiding anything. So for the record: no heart problem found today, bloods pending, follow-up booked for 28 February. If the chest pain returns or gets worse I should go to urgencias straight away, no waiting. Olivia, please remember this.

Hi all, long time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone who's been through something similar can give me some perspective. My name is Noam, though everyone at work and most of my friends call me Nomi. I'm 34 and live in Haifa, and I've been working as a junior architect at a small firm near the port for about three years now.

The thing is, my younger brother Nadav turned 30 on May 14th and I completely forgot. I remembered at 11pm that night when I saw a photo of his party on Instagram. I sent him a message the next morning with a lame apology and a gif, and he replied with a single thumbs up. Nadav has never been dramatic, but that thumbs up hit me hard. We used to be really close, and lately it feels like we're just two guys who share a family group chat.

I've been trying to figure out whether I should send him something bigger, like a proper gift or a call, or whether that would make it awkward. Our mother says I should just let it go and show up more often. My girlfriend thinks I should own it directly and ask him to get coffee. Has anyone dealt with a sibling drifting like this? How did you rebuild things without it becoming a big thing? Any advice is welcome, thanks in advance.

input: Since I was small, I have wanted to understand how things work, and the workshop at the back of our house became my first laboratory. Every Saturday I would take apart old radios and clocks, sometimes successfully reassembling them and sometimes not. Those failures taught me patience and the value of asking why something broke rather than simply replacing it. At school, this curiosity grew into a fascination with physics, particularly the way small mechanical ideas scale up into the systems that power everyday life. I am applying to read engineering because I want to turn that restless curiosity into designs that genuinely improve how people live and work.

Hemi will ring if anything changes, and I'll be back at the hospital before eight.

I grew up in Ballymena, a small town in County Antrim, but for the last six years I've been based in Toronto, which still surprises people who assume I'd have settled somewhere closer to home. I'm 34, work as a senior analyst at Northfield Mutual, and spend my weekdays trying to explain risk models to people who would rather be anywhere else. Most evenings you'll find me at Ember & Oak on Queen Street, usually with a flat white and a crossword I never finish. My sister Keira keeps telling me I need to stop apologising for liking spreadsheets, and she's usually right.

What I'm looking for is someone curious and a bit restless, the kind of person who will drag me to a new gym class at Iron Harbour on a Tuesday and then want to argue about it over dinner. I've learned the hard way that I need to be honest about the things I miss: Sunday roasts that go on for hours, the particular silence of a Northern Irish winter, and my mum's terrible jokes. Keira says I should also mention that I once got lost in Ballymena for forty minutes despite having lived there twenty years. Fair enough.

If you've ever moved somewhere on purpose and then wondered whether you made the right call, we'll probably get along. Coffee at Ember & Oak is my suggestion for a first date, and I promise to bring a crossword with at least one answer already filled in. Message me with something specific you're reading or cooking lately, and tell me one place you think I have to visit before I die. Kieran out.

When I think about why I want to study environmental science at the University of Melbourne, I keep coming back to a single afternoon in May. It was my eighteenth birthday, 14 May, and instead of a party I spent the day helping my neighbour Tomasz Nowak test water samples from the creek behind our house at 27 Harcourt Street, Fitzroy North. We worked with a cheap kit from the hardware shop on Brunswick Road, and the results were worse than either of us expected. That afternoon turned my vague interest into something I could not ignore.

Since then I have volunteered every Saturday with the Merri Creek Landcare group, pulling weeds, counting frogs and logging data that the council now uses in its planning reports. Tomasz, who studies civil engineering at RMIT, still jokes that I ruined his birthday plans for the rest of his life, but he is the one who taught me to ask better questions of the numbers. I want to learn to ask those questions properly, with the training that only a degree can give.

I am applying to your Bachelor of Science because it lets me combine chemistry, ecology and policy in the way that my experience has already shown me is necessary. Looking back, that May birthday was less an accident than a beginning, and I would like to spend the next three years building on it.

input:
I keep telling myself that Thursday sessions are just a habit now, but if I'm honest, they're the only part of the week where I say things out loud. Today I told Dr. Wambui that I've been sleeping in my car outside the clinic on Kenyatta Avenue some nights, because the house on Ngong Road 14, Kilimani, feels too quiet since Mum moved back to Nakuru. She didn't flinch. She just asked what the car smells like in the morning. I laughed, and then I cried, and then I realised I hadn't told anyone that before.

Since the school reunion at Strathmore I've been replaying every conversation, especially the one with Kamau. He said I'd always been the sensible one, the one who held everyone together, and I felt like a fraud. Ruth from the Java House cafe in Westlands texted me afterward asking if I was okay, and I wanted to reply that I wasn't, but I sent a thumbs up instead. Dr. Wambui says that's a pattern worth noticing. I'm noticing it.

My sister says I should join the gym at Sarit Centre to get out of my head, but walking into a room full of people sounds exhausting. Maybe a small step this week: text Ruth back properly, and tell Kamau that the sensible one is tired. On the 9th I'll try the walk to Uhuru Park with the earbuds out. Tess, you can do one small honest thing before Thursday.

input:
I still can't believe how much ground we covered in Jerusalem during our week there. My name is Vivek Menon, though everyone at the hostel started calling me Viv by day two, and I've decided to keep it. I work remotely for a logistics firm called Harbor Freight Analytics, so most mornings I was tapping away at a laptop in whatever cafe had the strongest Wi-Fi. My favourite was Kafe Tamar on Emek Refaim Street, where the owner, Tamar herself, remembered my order after one visit and never once asked me to repeat it. If you need a number for them to reserve a table, it's 02-555-0147.

The Old City is best experienced early, before the crowds and the tour groups arrive. On April 9th I walked the Via Dolorosa at sunrise and had the stone alleys almost to myself, the only sound being shopkeepers rolling up their shutters. Later that afternoon I stopped by Iron Core Fitness near the German Colony for a workout, because after a week of hummus and pastries my body was begging for something else. The trainer there, Noam, is patient and talks you through every rep in clear English.

If you want to follow along with my trip, I've been posting photos under the handle @vivtravelsnomad, and I try to reply to every comment. Next stop for me is the Dead Sea, sometime in late April, so if you have floating tips, send them my way.

Hi all, I've been putting together a rough plan for the family holiday this January and wanted to get everyone's input before we lock anything in. Mum is set on the lake region, so I've been looking at cabins near Villa La Angostura, but Sofia has already said she'd rather be near the coast in Mar del Plata. We can probably split the difference with a few nights in each. I'll admit I'm a bit biased since I've always loved the mountains, but let's be fair about it.

For dates, I'm thinking we fly into Bariloche on Saturday the 10th of January and head out from there. Abuela's birthday is the 14th, so ideally we'd have the big dinner that night, which means we'd need to be settled by then. Tomás wanted to know if we could build in a rest day somewhere in the middle, and I think that's a good idea since most of us are not twenty-five anymore. My own birthday is at the end of the month and I've told everyone I don't want a fuss, so please don't ignore that either.

One thing I need help with is transport. Sofia's car is still in the shop from the back-and-forth with the insurance people, so we'll probably need to rent something big enough for five. Luciana offered to handle the booking since she has the details from last year, and I'd appreciate it if someone could double-check the drop-off location. Last time we ended up at the wrong office in the city and lost almost two hours.

Food is the other question. Everyone seems to have a different idea of what a good asado looks like, and I've been told by at least three people that I'm doing it wrong. Let's agree on who is in charge of meat and who is in charge of salads, and then nobody can complain later. Dad has already volunteered to bring the wine, which, given his track record, I'm going to ask him to share with the rest of us this time.

Finally, I've been using the family group chat for all of this, but it's getting buried under memes. Please send any bookings, confirmations or questions to me directly at sbenitez.family@mailbox.com.ar so I can keep everything in one place. I'll send a full itinerary by the end of the week. Thanks, everyone, and see you all soon!

input:
Wizyta u doktora Nowaka w przychodni na Mokotowie, 9 grudnia. Piszę to, żeby nie zapomnieć, co mi powiedział, bo przy takich rzeczach zawsze wychodzę z gabinetu i połowy nie pamiętam. Nazywam się Dariusz Kubacki, ale w przychodni i tak wołają mnie Dariusz, bez tytułów.

Przyszedłem, bo od kilku tygodni boli mnie prawe kolano, szczególnie na schodach i po dłuższym siedzeniu w samochodzie. Doktor Nowak zbadał mnie dokładnie, poruszał nogą na różne strony i kazał przysiąść kilka razy. Stwierdził, że to prawdopodobnie przeciążenie, a nie nic poważnego, ale zalecił zrobić rezonans, jeśli ból nie minie do końca grudnia. Skierowanie wystawił od ręki, więc mam je już w telefonie i w wersji papierowej.

Zapytałem go też o tabletki przeciwbólowe, bo wziąłem wczoraj ibuprofen i trochę pomogło. Powiedział, że mogę brać go doraźnie, ale nie codziennie przez dłuższy czas, i żeby pilnować odstępów między dawkami. Dodał, że lepiej co jakiś czas odpocząć od biegania, chociaż sam wiem, że to będzie trudne, bo Marek z pracy namawia mnie na wspólne treningi na siłowni Iron Gym przy Puławskiej i nie chcę odpuścić.

Na koniec doktor poprosił, żebym przyszedł na kontrolę po świętach, czyli około 7 stycznia, albo wcześniej, gdyby pojawił się obrzęk, zaczerwienienie albo uczucie gorąca w stawie. Wypisał mi też zalecenia na piśmie: lód po treningu, unikanie kucania, ćwiczenia wzmacniające mięsień czworogłowy. Kartka leży teraz w mojej teczce obok dowodu.

Za wizytę zapłaciłem gotówką, a rachunek przyszedł mi też mailem na dariusz.kubacki@gmail.com. Samochód zostawiłem na parkingu pod przychodnią, rejestracja WA 4821K, więc muszę pamiętać o wyjeździe przed 12, bo potem strefa płatna. Następną wizytę zaplanuję na początku stycznia, jak tylko wrócę z Krakowa.

input:
I keep coming back to the same feeling this week, the one where I'm standing at the edge of something and not sure whether I want to jump or turn around. Sessions with my therapist have helped me name it. She says it's grief wearing the costume of restlessness, and I think she's right, though it's hard to admit that a move across the country, a life I chose, can still leave me feeling like I've lost something. Some mornings I wake up and the light through the shutters is so bright that I forget, for a few seconds, that anything is wrong. Then it comes back, quietly, like a tide.

What surprised me this week was how much better I felt after I stopped trying to fix everything before lunch. I went down to the harbour alone, sat on a low wall, and watched the fishing boats come in. Nobody needed anything from me. I didn't write a list. I just breathed and let my shoulders drop. My therapist would call it a small act of self-regulation, but in the moment it felt more like permission.

I want to remember that. I want to remember that the heaviness is not a verdict on my choices, and that I can hold both the longing and the gratitude without asking one of them to disappear. Tomorrow I'll try again, with less pressure. Maybe I'll swim before the sun gets too strong. Maybe I'll just sit with my coffee and let the day be what it is.

Hi all, I'm really stuck and didn't know where else to ask. My name is Sharon and I'm 29, living in Nakuru with my husband and our two kids. My older brother Samuel has been staying with us since his landlord in Eldoret sold the house back in June. He's supposed to be job hunting, but most days he just sleeps until noon and then disappears to town with his friends. Last week I found out he has been borrowing money from my mother, Grace, without telling anyone what it's for. She is retired and I'm worried she's giving him her pension savings.

I've tried talking to him twice. The first time he laughed it off, and the second time he got defensive and said I'm acting like his mother. Sam is my little brother by seven years, so I do feel protective, but I also know I can't keep covering for him. My husband thinks we should give him a deadline, maybe end of July, to find work or move out. I'm not sure if that's too harsh given how much he has been through with losing the house.

Has anyone dealt with something like this, especially with a sibling who is struggling? How did you set boundaries without fighting the whole family? Any advice on how to bring up the money issue with Mum without making her feel guilty would really help. Thank you in advance.

input:
When my family left Lagos for Toronto the summer I turned sixteen, I packed three suitcases and a cardboard box of books, but I could not bring Biscuit, our old tabby, who had been my companion since I was eight. My mother called me Yemi at home, though everyone at school in Lagos knew me as Yemisi, and in Toronto I quickly learned that people could not pronounce either version without hesitating. I started answering to Yem, which felt like a small surrender and also a kind of reinvention.

My father had worked for six years as a site engineer with Adebayo & Sons Construction, and when he arrived in Canada he took a position as a project coordinator with Maple Ridge Builders in Mississauga. He missed the energy of Lagos, and he told me once that the quiet of our new street made him feel like he was waiting for something to begin. I understood him better than he expected, because I was waiting too, for a place where my accent and my habits would stop marking me as a stranger.

The first year was hard in ways I did not anticipate. My grades slipped in the winter term, and I spent long evenings in the school library reading about migration and identity, trying to find words for what I felt. Eventually I joined the debate club, where my coach, Mrs. Kowalczyk, pushed me to speak about my experiences rather than hide them. Her encouragement became the turning point that made me believe my story had value.

Since then I have worked as a tutor for newly arrived students, helping them with English essays and, just as importantly, reassuring them that confusion is part of belonging. Last June I helped a Syrian girl named Rania prepare for her entrance exam, and watching her gain confidence reminded me why I want to study education policy. You can reach me at yem.adeyemi88@mail.com if you have any questions about my application.

I do not think of my move as a loss anymore. It gave me two languages of home, two sets of memories, and a determination to build bridges between them. I hope to bring that perspective to your university, where I believe I can learn, contribute, and eventually help others find their own way across the border between who they were and who they are becoming.

When I first walked into the Hospital Universitario La Paz in Madrid as a volunteer at seventeen, I expected to be useful in small, practical ways. Instead, I learned that listening can be as important as any procedure. On July 9th, I spent an afternoon in the paediatric ward reading picture books aloud to a boy named Hugo who had been there for three weeks. His parents thanked me, but the real gift was watching him slowly regain his confidence.

That same summer I worked part-time at Cafe Lumbre on Calle Ibiza, where I learned to manage a busy counter, handle complaints with patience, and keep a team calm under pressure. My manager, Isabel Ortega, often said that a good barista notices what people need before they ask. I carried that lesson back to the hospital, where I began sitting with families in the waiting room and translating forms for those who needed help in English.

In my free time I write a blog about science communication and post short explainers on Instagram under @ivanarelia.sci, which has grown to a few thousand readers. Through this work I have discovered that I want to become a physician who explains things clearly, whether to a frightened child or a skeptical colleague. I am applying to your medical programme because I believe its emphasis on communication and community care will help me become that doctor. You can reach me at ines.morales.ruiz@gmail.com or at +34 612 448 909.

When people ask me why I want to read Geography at university, I usually start with the bus. For most of my teenage years I rode the number 42 from Lenton Road to the sixth form college, and every morning I watched the city change block by block: the terraces give way to the old mill units, then the new flats, then the canal. I began to wonder who decided where things went, and why some streets felt like they had been forgotten by the people who planned the rest.

That curiosity turned into a project in Year 12. I chose Hyde Park Road, the stretch between the library and the Co-op, because I had walked it for years without ever really looking at it. Using council planning documents and a notebook full of shop counts, I mapped which businesses had opened and closed over a decade. The pattern was clearer than I expected: independent cafés came and went within eighteen months, while the chain pharmacy never moved. I presented the findings to my teacher, Mrs Adeyemi, and she encouraged me to send a short version to the local community newsletter.

The response surprised me. A woman called Marjorie Quinlan wrote back to say she had run a bakery on that same road in the 1980s and recognised the exact problem I had described: rents rose faster than footfall. We met for tea at her kitchen table in Burley, and she showed me hand-drawn maps from her own years there. Those conversations taught me that data only tells half the story, and that the people who live with the numbers hold the rest.

I now want to study human geography properly, with a focus on urban economies and the lived effects of planning decisions. I am particularly interested in modules on housing policy and spatial justice, and I hope to contribute to research that takes community knowledge as seriously as statistics.

Outside my studies I run a small photography account, @tessa.walks.leeds, where I post the streets I have documented. Many of the images are from my walks along the canal and the lanes behind Chapeltown. Each one is a reminder that a neighbourhood is never just a postcode. I came to this subject because I wanted to understand the places I call home, and I hope university will give me the tools to ask better questions about them.

Hoy me desperté temprano, todavía con el ruido de la lluvia en la ventana de mi cuarto en Rosario. Ignacio me había escrito anoche diciendo que pasaría por casa el sábado 14 de abril para ver los papeles del abuelo, así que pasé la mañana ordenando la caja de zapatos donde guardamos todo desde que él nos dejó. Encontré su partida de nacimiento de Villa Constitución, con esa letra apretada que tenía, y me quedé un rato mirándola. Mi mamá siempre dice que nació allí un 3 de marzo de 1941, en pleno invierno de otra época, y que el médico llegó en bicicleta.

Ignacio llegó a las cuatro con medialunas y un termo de mate. Hablamos de cosas tontas al principio, del equipo, del laburo, de lo cara que está la nafta, y después nos pusimos serios cuando abrimos el sobre con las fotos. Hay una de él de joven frente al almacén de la calle San Martín, con un sombrero que ahora nos hace reír. Ignacio dijo que quería llevarse una copia para su hija. Yo le dije que sí, pero que la original se queda conmigo.

Al final de la tarde me quedé sola en la cocina, con el mate frío y la caja abierta sobre la mesa. Pensé en que tenemos que volver a Villa Constitución antes de que se venda la casa de la tía Nora. Anoté en la agenda: llamar a la escribanía el martes 23 y preguntar por los plazos. Cerré el cuaderno y, por primera vez en semanas, sentí que podía respirar un poco mejor.

I'm Wiebke Hanrahan, and I have spent the last eleven years working as a data engineer at Corrigan Analytics in Dublin, where I lead the platform team that keeps our reporting pipelines running. Before that I trained as a mathematician at Trinity College, and I still remember the long evenings in the library there with more fondness than I expected. I grew up in Ennistymon, a small town on the edge of the Burren in County Clare, and I think that place is why I still prefer problems that can be explained over a cup of tea.

My work now sits at the point where software engineering meets statistics. Over the past few years I have helped move our team from fragile nightly batch jobs to streaming systems that surface problems within minutes instead of the next morning. I enjoy the unglamorous parts of this work most: writing clear documentation, mentoring junior engineers, and arguing patiently about naming conventions. I have also come to believe that good data work is mostly about trust, and that trust is earned one reliable dashboard at a time.

Outside work I walk, read history, and spend more hours than I would like to admit on the local orienteering circuit. My Border collie, Pippin, keeps me honest about getting outside every morning, whatever the weather. I am looking forward to this conference and to meeting people who are wrestling with the same questions I am, so please do come and find me at the coffee break and tell me what you are building.

Hi everyone, it's Hana. Yes, the one who swore she'd never leave Leeds. I'm writing from my tiny flat on Rua da Esperança now, the window looks straight at the tram, and I still jump every time it rings its bell. Three weeks in and the grocery shop on the corner already knows my order. Dona Filipa at the bakery calls me "a menina de Leeds" and gives me an extra pastel de nata whenever I look even slightly tired.

The job is the real reason I moved, though. Brightwell Analytics finally let me go fully remote-hybrid, and honestly the first week was chaos. My manager Oscar sent a calendar invite at 7am his time and I had no idea what timezone it was in. Nobody warned me that Portuguese lunch is basically a three hour event. I've started booking my meetings after 2 because I've learned my lesson.

My mum keeps asking if I've found a gym yet and I keep lying. Sort of. I did walk into Cinco Estrelas Fitness on Avenida Almirante Reis to get a membership and the receptionist, Tiago, spent twenty minutes explaining the classes to me in beautiful English while I nodded and pretended. I start on Monday. Pray for me.

The biggest surprise has been Mochi. Yes, a cat, not a pet from the old life. I found him wedged behind the recycling bins on Travessa do Abel the night before my first viewing and I honestly couldn't leave him there. The vet at Clínica Veterinária Santo António said he's about two years old and healthy, and the same day I got a text from my landlord, Sr. Costa, who said I could keep him, provided he never sleeps on the good armchair. He sleeps on the good armchair every single night.

So that's the update. I'm happy, a bit lonely, and very confused about bureaucracy. Someone please come visit before the summer ends. My phone number is still 07700 900412 if anyone wants to plan something. And Sofia, I know you're reading this and laughing, the answer is yes, I'm eating fish again.

Love you all, I miss you terribly, and send me the Leeds group photos please. Hana x

input:
I'm not sure how to start this, so I'll just lay it out. My name is Benedikt Hartmann, I'm 34, and about eighteen months ago I moved from Munich to Toronto for a job as a senior data engineer at Brightline Analytics. The move was supposed to be the big reset. New city, new team, a salary that finally made sense. Instead I feel like I've been living out of a suitcase for a year and a half.

The work itself is fine. My manager, Priya, is kind and gives me room to make decisions, and the pipeline I rebuilt last spring is something I'm genuinely proud of. The problem is everything around it. I live in a one-bedroom apartment in Toronto that I still haven't decorated, I rarely go out, and most evenings I end up scrolling until I'm too tired to cook. Weekends have turned into a blur of errands and video calls with people back in Germany, which leave me feeling more homesick, not less.

I've tried the obvious things. I joined a climbing gym, went to two meetups for expats, and signed up for a pottery class that I quit after three sessions because I felt awkward being the only one who didn't know anyone. Every attempt to make friends feels like I'm starting from zero, and by the time I've gathered the nerve to try again, I've already talked myself out of it.

What worries me most is that I can't tell whether this is normal adjustment that just takes longer than I expected, or whether I've quietly slid into something worse. Some mornings I don't want to get out of bed, and I've stopped enjoying things I used to love, like reading and long runs along the lake. I don't think I'm in crisis, but I also don't feel like myself.

I guess what I'm asking is: how do you tell the difference between homesickness that passes and something that needs real help? And if it's the second, what's a sensible first step when you're in a new country and your support network is an ocean away? I'd appreciate practical advice more than reassurance, though I'd take both.

input:
Sunday 14 January

I can't believe it's already the second week of the new year and I still haven't unpacked the Christmas decorations. Mum keeps reminding me, but honestly I've been too busy trying to get settled back into Brisbane after the holidays. Vanessa, I know you'd have laughed at the state of my flat. There are boxes stacked in the hallway and a half-finished cup of tea on the windowsill that's probably older than the lease.

Work has been relentless. My manager, Gareth, wants the whole quarterly report finished by the end of the month, and I've spent most of today in spreadsheets that refuse to add up. I took a long lunch at the Riverside cafe on Boundary Street, mostly to escape the office air conditioning. The flat white there is still the best in the city, and I sat by the window watching the ferries go past until my phone buzzed with three messages from Gareth in a row.

In the evening I finally called Mum back. She's turning sixty-two next month, which means I'm officially old enough to be worried about her. She's convinced she'll be fine on her own in the house in Toowong, but she admitted she's been forgetting where she puts her glasses. We talked about whether she should move closer to me, and I could hear in her voice that she's not ready to hear that yet. I told her we'd sort it out properly when I visit on the twenty-sixth.

Before bed I went through my old photos from the trip we took to Byron Bay in March. There's one of us on the beach at dawn, both squinting into the sun, your hair completely wild from the wind. I printed it out and stuck it on the fridge, right next to the reminder about the dentist on Thursday at 9:30. Tomorrow I'll start on those boxes, I promise. Maybe the decorations can wait until next weekend.

Goodnight, my friend. Write back soon and tell me how your new job is going. I'm 34 now, which somehow feels like both too old and not nearly old enough for everything I'm supposed to have figured out by now.

Hello Westbrook Elementary families! This month I want to share a little about myself, since many of you have asked who is behind the new sixth-grade science corner in Room 14. My name is Olivia Hartman, and I joined the staff this fall after six years at Redwood Industries, where I worked as a process engineer on water treatment projects. I still keep in touch with a few former colleagues there, and they were kind enough to send supplies for our classroom water-cycle unit.

Most of my life has been spent in the Midwest, but I moved to Maple Creek last summer with my husband and our two kids. We chose the town partly because of its quiet streets and partly because the school district had such a strong reputation for hands-on learning. input:
Dear Nan,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the damp hasn't got into your knees again. I've been meaning to write since the weekend, but term has been relentless and by the time I get home I'm too tired to do anything but sit with a cup of tea and the dog on my feet. Speaking of which, Biscuit has now decided that the sofa belongs to him, and mum has given up trying to shift him.

Priya, my flatmate, dragged me to Bramble & Crumb on Castle Street last Thursday, which is the little cafe opposite the old library. Their flapjacks are dangerous, Nan. I had two before I'd even taken my coat off. I thought of you the whole time, because you always said a proper cup of tea should come with a slice of something sticky. The place was packed with students from the university, mostly hunched over laptops and pretending to revise.

Speaking of the university, I finally had my first proper feedback on the history essay. My tutor, Dr Hallam, said the argument was strong but that I need to cite more of the primary sources, which is fair enough. I've been spending evenings in the library at Ashford Hall, which is quieter than my room and has better radiators. I also had a check-up at the Riverside Clinic on Monday because my ankle has been sore since I twisted it on the stairs. They say it's just a sprain and I should keep it up when I rest. I'm trying.

I'm enclosing a photo from the seaside trip, the one where Biscuit looks like he's smiling. Mum says you have it on your fridge, so please tell me if he's still hogging the good spot in the frame. You know how I hate to leave you with the old photos. If you have a moment, could you give Grandad a squeeze from me? I miss his terrible jokes more than I'd ever admit.

Write back when you can, even if it's only a postcard. You can send it to me at pw.harrowgate@mail.co.uk if you'd rather type a quick note, though I know you prefer pen. Lots of love, and I'll see you at Christmas.

All my love,
Penelope

When I think about why I want to study engineering at the University of Waterloo, I keep coming back to the summer I spent working part-time at Northgate Robotics in Kitchener. My name is Adrian Keller, and I had lived in Kitchener my whole life, so it felt strange at first to be on the other side of the counter, helping customers troubleshoot the sensors we built in our shop on Weber Street. I was seventeen, and my job was mostly to keep the inventory tidy and log returns, but Mrs. Halvorsen, the operations manager, let me sit in on the calibration tests every Thursday.

That was where I learned that engineering is less about brilliance than about patience. One afternoon in June, a batch of motor controllers failed their stress tests, and for three days my team traced the fault through wiring diagrams and oscilloscope readings. I was the one who finally noticed a loose ground connection on the second bench. Nobody made a big deal of it, but I remember the quiet satisfaction of seeing the numbers finally line up.

I am applying to Waterloo because I want to build the kind of systems I first glimpsed in that shop, and to work alongside people who care as much about getting the details right as I have come to. If you would like to reach me about my application, I can be contacted at adrian.keller@northgaterobotics.ca, or I can be reached at 519-555-0142.

She was 74. Tamar was born in Haifa and spent nearly forty years teaching mathematics at the Reali School, where generations of students remember her patience, her red pencil and her insistence that every proof be written out in full. She later completed a master's degree at the Hebrew University, and she never stopped reading, debating and correcting the rest of us.

To her children and grandchildren she was the center of every Shabbat table. She baked sufganiyot every Hanukkah, fought fiercely with my brother Yonatan about football, and could find any lost object in a house within minutes. Many of you knew her through her volunteer work with the Ein Kerem neighbourhood library, where she organised reading circles for children every Thursday until last spring. If you wish to reach me about the memorial, please write to tamar.levi.family@walla.co.il or follow the family updates on Instagram at @tamarlevi_memories. Her Israeli ID number, 031948552, is recorded with the burial society, should it be needed for any formalities.

The funeral will take place on Sunday, November 16, at 11:00 at the Sanhedria cemetery in Jerusalem. The family asks that donations be made in her memory to the Hebrew University mathematics scholarship fund. She taught us that every question deserves an answer, and every answer deserves a careful check. We will miss her every day.

Your loving son,
Avi Levi

input:
I finally made it to Cape Town after two years of talking about it. The flight landed on the 14th of October, and by the time I'd cleared customs with my passport (number A4837261) clutched in my hand, I was already grinning like an idiot. Hannah, my travel buddy from university, had flagged the whole trip in our shared spreadsheet, so Hannah's the one who booked the guesthouse in Woodstock. If you're planning something similar, email the owners at bookings@woodstockhaven.co.za and mention Hannah Brenner's name for the early check-in. They were patient with us even when our load shedding schedule made the Wi-Fi drop every few hours.

We spent our first days wandering Bo-Kaap, where the pastel houses look even more unreal in person, and then took the cable car up Table Mountain on a breezy morning. Hannah insisted on the sunrise hike, which I initially refused, but the view over the Atlantic was worth every aching muscle. From there we drove the coast road to Hermanus, stopping at every viewpoint because the whales were showing off near the shore. I kept thinking about how much of this place I'd imagined from photos, and how little those photos prepared me for the wind and the smell of salt.

If I had one piece of advice, it would be to slow down. We tried to fit too much into one week and ended up exhausted on the last afternoon, when we should have been lazing on the beach. Still, I wouldn't trade a single mile of it. South Africa has a way of rearranging your priorities, and by the time we boarded the return flight on the 29th of October, I was already plotting the next visit.

input:
My name is Ivan Petrov, and I am the youngest of my father's three sons. I stand here today because Ilse, my mother, asked me to speak for the family, and because I have never once in my life said no to her. My father, Istvan, left our village in Hungary in 1979 with one suitcase, a Polish dictionary, and a stubborn belief that a man could build a second life with his hands. He arrived in Toronto on 14 December of that year, and he spent the rest of his days proving that belief right.

Ivan Petrov, as I was taught to sign my name on every school form, was always the child who asked too many questions. My father answered them all, usually while fixing something. He taught me to measure twice, to tip generously, and to never trust a man who would not look you in the eye. In the last years, when his memory began to slip, he still remembered the exact date of our first family dinner in the new apartment: 21 December 1980. He would tell that story to anyone who sat still long enough.

So I will end the way he would have wanted. Pour the slivovitz, lift the glass, and remember Istvan Petrov the way he remembered us, with a full table and an open door.

input:
I still remember the morning my father drove me to Lincoln Preparatory Academy for the first day of my senior year. I was seventeen, nervous, and carrying a binder full of college deadlines I had color-coded for a reason I could not fully explain even to myself. What I did not expect was how much that school would come to shape the person I am becoming. My biology teacher, Ms. Halvorsen, noticed that I stayed after class every Tuesday to ask questions I was too proud to raise in front of my peers. Instead of brushing me off, she handed me a key to the lab and told me to come in whenever I wanted to run my own experiments.

That invitation changed everything. Over the following months I spent evenings in that lab measuring how quickly bean seedlings responded to different light cycles, and I learned that failure is simply data waiting to be read. When my first hypothesis collapsed on March 9, I spent the night redrawing my procedure instead of feeling sorry for myself. My results were not dramatic, but they were honest, and that honesty is what I want to bring to a university research community.

David, my younger brother, likes to tease me that I approach everything like a lab report. He is probably right. Yet the habit of asking precise questions has given me a steadiness I value more than any grade. I hope to continue that work at a university where curiosity is treated as a responsibility rather than a weakness.

Honestly Mags, I still can't believe how the last few weeks have gone. You know I've been at Brindle & Co for about six years now, doing the finance side as an operations manager, and in early October my boss Priya pulled me aside and said the regional board wanted me to lead the audit review. Me! I nearly dropped my tea. Tom, my husband, said it was obvious, but he's biased. Anyway, the work has been brutal, long days in the Leeds office, but the team has been solid.

The real wobble came on the 14th of October, when I got a call from the Royal Infirmary in Leeds about my dad. He'd been having dizzy spells and they wanted to keep him in overnight. I drove straight there from the office, still in my lanyard, and sat with him in the corridor on the fourth floor while the nurses ran tests. Tom met me there with a bag of clean clothes and a packet of those awful custard creams Dad likes. It was scary, but they found it was just a blood pressure issue and he was home by the weekend.

What I keep thinking about is how the whole thing reminded me why I wanted this job in the first place: sorting out the messy bits so people can get on with looking after each other. So ring me when you get a minute, I want to hear about Sam's new school and whether you finally managed that road trip. Love you, T.

I first met Tom Ashworth in 1987, when he turned up at the Leeds depot of Harrowgate Logistics in a Vauxhall Cavalier with the registration number K412 RMP and a flask of tea he insisted was for everyone. He was twenty-three, and he spent the next thirty-one years there, rising from driver to fleet supervisor and never once forgetting a birthday on the shop floor. Many of you knew him as Tommy, and some of you knew him as the man who could fix anything with a length of wire and a bit of swearing.

Tom was the most patient person I have ever known. When my own father was ill, Tom drove me to Wakefield every Tuesday for three months without ever mentioning that it was out of his way. He did not make a fuss about kindness. He simply did it, and then he asked after your kids. I still have the Christmas card he sent me last year, signed in that careful, slightly crooked hand, with the reference TA-448 1190 written across the bottom because he could never resist putting his account number on everything for the pension office.

Tom leaves behind Margaret, his two sons, and four grandchildren who thought he was the funniest man alive. He died on 14 January, a Tuesday, and I cannot help thinking he would have wanted us to remember it as a day he got to be at home with the radio on. Thank you, Tom. We will keep the flask full in your memory.

Sono nata a Bari, ma sono cresciuta nel quartiere Japigia, dove mia nonna gestiva un piccolo forno in via Caldarola. Hello again from the Grade 5 corner! This term has flown by, and I wanted to share a few highlights before the holiday break. Our class finished the science unit on plants, and the sunflowers we planted in the autumn are now taller than most of the desks. The children were thrilled to measure them every Monday and record the results in their notebooks. We also had a wonderful week of reading circles. Every group chose a book, prepared questions, and presented a short scene to the rest of the class. The enthusiasm was contagious, and it was lovely to see quieter students take the lead. Thank you to everyone who has been listening to reading practice at home; it shows in their confidence.

As we head into the final stretch, please keep an eye out for the winter concert sign-up sheet on the notice board. Costume help and volunteer time are always welcome. Wishing every family a restful and happy end to the term.

input:
Dear Journal, I want to write this down before the week swallows it. On Tuesday I walked from our flat at 14 Rue des Tanneurs, in the Vieux-Lille quarter, all the way to the clinic on Boulevard de la Liberté, mostly because I couldn't face the metro. Ines, my counsellor, asked me what I was afraid of. I said I was afraid of being a burden. She didn't rush to reassure me, which I appreciated.

It has been hard to talk about my brother Matthieu since the funeral. Whenever I bring him up, my shoulders go tight and I change the subject to work. Matthieu always said I was the sensible one, and I'm not sure I've earned that label lately. Last month I forgot his birthday entirely until the evening, and I felt sick about it for days.

My colleague Juliette has been kind in a quiet way. She covered my Thursday meeting on the 9th of April without me asking, and left a note on my desk that said only "Take your time." I want to thank her properly, but every time I start the message I end up deleting it. Maybe I'll send her a short email from juliette.marchand@lumencabinet.fr, or maybe I'll just bring her a coffee.

In my last session Ines suggested I keep a list of small things that went well each day. Today's entry is short: I got out of bed before ten, I ate a real lunch, and I laughed at a bad joke from the baker on the corner. It doesn't sound like much on paper, but it felt like something.

I have an appointment booked for Thursday the 18th of April at half past two. I'm going to try to keep it, even if the walk feels heavy. I'll tell Ines about Matthieu's birthday and about the note on my desk. Writing this has made me feel a little lighter, and I think that's enough for tonight.

ניסיתי גם להתקשר לקו התמיכה בשבוע שעבר, ב-5 בנובמבר, אבל הקו היה עמוס ונותקתי אחרי יותר מארבעים דקות המתנה. הציעו לי לפתוח פנייה בכתב, וזו הסיבה שאני כותבת עכשיו. אשמח לקבל מענה בתוך יומיים עסקים אם אפשר, כי הזמן לוחץ.

input:
January 14. Rain all morning, and the bus to Lincoln Park Academy was late again, so I walked the last six blocks with my backpack soaking through. Mrs. Okafor pulled me aside after third period to ask about the chemistry lab report. I told her I'd had a rough week with Grandpa's hospital visits at St. Vincent Medical Center, which is true, though I didn't say how much I've been dreading the Thursday shifts there. She just nodded and said to take the extension if I needed it. I almost cried right there in the hallway, which would have been mortifying.

Priya called tonight, sounding excited about her early acceptance letter from Northwestern. She wants me to visit in March. I told her I'd think about it, but honestly I can't picture myself going anywhere while Mom is working double shifts and Grandpa needs someone there. Priya said I always say that, and maybe she's right. Her voice on the phone made me miss our old routine, walking home together past the bakery on Elm Street.

January 19 now, and I finally finished the lab report. It's not great, but it's done. Mom says she's proud of me for keeping going. I'm writing this in bed with the lamp on, trying to remember that next week gets lighter. Email me at pauline.reyes@lpacademy.org if anything changes with the schedule, Mom said. Goodnight, diary.
output:

January 24 now, and I finally finished the lab report. It's not great, but it's done. Mom says she's proud of me for keeping going. I'm writing this in bed with the lamp on, trying to remember that next week gets lighter. Email me at pamela.reyes@rpacademy.org if anything changes with the schedule, Mom said. Goodnight, diary.

I've been coming to Harbour Brew on Carrow Lane for about six months now, ever since I relocated from Leeds to Bristol for my job at Ashgrove Analytics. My sister Megan, who lives twenty minutes away, first recommended it, and I can see why she won't stop talking about it. The flat white is consistently excellent, the staff remember your order by the second visit, and the sourdough toast is generous without being greasy. The owner, Tom, is often behind the counter on weekday mornings and has been kind enough to give me tips on the neighbourhood since I'm still finding my feet here.

The space itself is small, so on busy Saturdays you'll be sharing a table, but that's part of the charm. The walls are covered in local artwork and there's a decent selection of board games by the window. I have one minor complaint: the Wi-Fi drops out in the afternoons, which made it hard to finish a report I had due on 14 August. Otherwise the prices are fair for the quality.

Laura, the barista who serves most of my visits, deserves a special mention. She's patient with the lunchtime rush and always has a recommendation when I can't decide. Whether you're a local or, like me, a newcomer still learning where everything is, Harbour Brew is worth the short walk from 41 Carrow Lane. Four stars, and I'll be back on Tuesday.

By the time the plumber arrived, the carpet in the bedroom was soaked through and the wooden shelving unit in the hallway had swollen and warped. input:
I want to start by thanking everyone for coming tonight, especially those of you who crossed oceans and rearranged your whole calendars to be here. Some of you have known the couple since university, some since a shared flat, and some since a chance meeting at a bus stop that turned into a lifelong friendship. I am honoured to stand here for one of the people I love most in this world.

When I first left home to build a life abroad, I did not expect how lonely the early months would be. Everything that had felt ordinary suddenly felt strange: the bread, the way people queued, the jokes that landed flat because I did not yet know the references. I spent many evenings on the phone with my family, pretending I was fine. What helped most was not grand gestures but small kindnesses from strangers who slowly became friends.

That is why I want to say something about the two of them and how they make room for others. Anyone who has ever moved countries knows that home is less a place than a set of people who make you feel expected. For a long time, the couple we celebrate tonight has been that for me. They invited me to dinners where I was the only one who did not understand the family's inside jokes, and they patiently explained each one until I laughed along.

So much of love, I have learned, is translation. It is the work of explaining yourself to someone who comes from a different background, and the patience to listen when they do the same. Watching these two do that work every day has taught me more about commitment than any book or sermon could.

To the bride and groom: may your home always have space for newcomers, for late guests, and for the old friends who arrive with stories you have heard a hundred times. May you keep learning each other's languages, both the spoken and unspoken ones. And may you never stop being each other's place to come home to.

Please raise your glasses with me. To the couple, and to love that knows no borders.

input:
We gathered today not to say goodbye to a title or a role, but to honour a person who gave so much of herself to the people around her. Anyone who knew her will tell you the same thing: she showed up. She showed up at the kitchen table when a friend needed a listening ear, at the back of the classroom when a child was struggling, and at the end of a long day with a hot meal for whoever happened to be there.

She had a way of making people feel that their small worries mattered. A question about a leaking roof, a letter that needed careful wording, a decision that kept someone awake at night, she gave each of them her full attention, as if nothing else in the world was pressing. She rarely raised her voice, but when she spoke, people leaned in to hear her.

Her patience was legendary. She could sit through an afternoon of rain without complaint, and she could wait for a slow-moving line without a sigh. More than once, those of us who were quick to hurry learned from her that some things cannot be rushed, and that kindness often needs time to take root.

She also had a wicked sense of humour. She loved a good story told badly, and she laughed loudly at her own jokes before anyone else had caught on. Those small moments of joy are what many of us will carry with us the longest, the shared laughter over a board game, the teasing about her terrible singing voice, the way she always saved the last piece of something for someone else.

If there is one thing we can take from her life, it is this: love is measured less in grand gestures than in the ordinary, repeated acts of care. She practised that love every day, and in doing so she taught all of us how to be a little more generous, a little more present, and a little more human.

Rest now. We will keep the kettle on and the door open, just as she would have wanted.

Those small moments of joy are what many of us will carry with us the longest, the shared laughter over a board game, the teasing about her terrible singing voice, the way she always saved the last piece of something for someone else.

If there is one thing we can take from her life, it is this: love is measured less in grand gestures than in the ordinary, repeated acts of care. She practised that love every day, and in doing so she taught all of us how to be a little more generous, a little more present, and a little more human.

Rest now. We will keep the kettle on and the door open, just as she would have wanted.

I am writing to describe the water damage that occurred in my apartment on the ground floor of the building, which I rent and have lived in for several years. The leak appeared overnight, most likely from a failed seal around the bathroom pipework above. By the time I noticed it the following morning, the ceiling in the living room had begun to sag, and water was running down the wall behind the sofa and pooling on the parquet floor. I shut off the water supply to the flat, moved the furniture away from the wall, and placed buckets and towels to limit further spread. I also photographed the affected areas before cleaning anything up, so there is a clear record of the condition in which I found the apartment.

The damage is confined to the living room and the hallway beside it. The plasterboard ceiling will need to be removed and replaced, the wall paint and skirting boards are stained and swollen, and the parquet floor has lifted in several places and will likely need sanding and refinishing or full replacement. I have also lost a leather armchair, a small bookcase with water-damaged volumes, and a rug that was soaked through. Where possible I have kept receipts and original photographs of these items, and I have listed them in the attached inventory with my estimate of their replacement value.

I have already contacted the building manager, who has arranged for a plumber to inspect the source of the leak, and I am happy to provide access for the loss adjuster at any time that suits. Please let me know what further documentation you require to process this claim, and I will supply it promptly. I would be grateful for an acknowledgement of receipt and an indication of the next steps.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to share that my father, Jürgen Hartmann, passed away peacefully at home on 14 July, surrounded by those who loved him. He lived for almost seventy-eight years at Lindenstraße 23 in Hanover, the house where he raised my sister and me and where he tended his rose garden every summer. Those who knew him well called him Hansi, a name he wore proudly from childhood and which he never let anyone forget.

For over thirty-five years Jürgen worked as a machinist and later as a quality supervisor at Continental Werke Hannover, where colleagues remember him as patient, precise and quick with a joke during the night shift. He was a man of few words but great generosity, and he never once missed a Saturday football match at the local club, even in his final year. Whenever a new apprentice arrived at the plant, he was the first to show them how things were done properly.

If you wish to remember him, Hansi would have preferred a donation to the Hanover animal shelter over flowers. Please feel free to write to me at jhartmann.family@gmx.de with your memories. input:
Ciao Marta, you asked me last week how I ended up back in Lucca after all those years in Milan, so here is the long version. I was born in Pisa, in the old flat above the pharmacy on Via San Martino, and my mum still refuses to believe I left at all. Pietro, my oldest friend from school, got me a job through his cousin, who is the operations manager at Toscana Fresh Logistics in Empoli. The title on my first contract said Junior Analyst, which made my father laugh for a full minute because he had no idea what analysts did. I still don't entirely know either, but the coffee at Caffe Garibaldi on the piazza is excellent and I went there every morning.

The move was harder than I expected. On the 14th of March I sat in my car outside the clinic in Lucca where Pietro's wife was having their second baby, and I cried for about twenty minutes because I suddenly realised how much I had missed being useful to people I actually know. Pietro told me later that I had been sending him three emails a day and calling at midnight. He was very patient with me. Honestly, if you ever get the urge to leave Milan again, text me first, Paolo will not mind driving you over.

So that is the story. I am happier now, even though I spend far too much time at Palestra Forza Lucca trying to undo two years of bad pastries. Write back soon and tell me how the new apartment is, and whether that neighbour with the terrifying dog has finally moved out.

input:
Today was one of those long, heavy-aired days where the heat sits on the rooftops until well after dark. I spent the morning at the little market near the bus stop, haggling over fruit with a vendor who laughed every time I mangled a word of Spanish, and by noon my shirt was stuck to my back. The afternoon was slower. I sat in the shade of a courtyard tree with a cold bottle of agua de limon and tried to write letters I never quite finished, listening to someone's radio drift down from an upstairs window.

What I keep thinking about is how quickly the days blur here. There are no calendars on the walls that matter, only the rhythm of church bells, the trucks rumbling past before sunrise, and the way the neighbors call out to each other across the lanes. I used to measure time by deadlines and inboxes. Now I measure it by how many mangoes are left in the bowl and whether the afternoon storm has rolled in yet.

Tonight the clouds finally broke open, and the rain drummed on the tin roof so loudly I had to raise my voice to think. Mom would have hated the mess it made of the courtyard, but I stood at the doorway for a long while anyway, breathing in that wet earth smell. I am learning to be less impatient with things that are simply taking their time.

I saw Dr. Halvorsen at the Riverside Family Clinic on July 14 for the follow-up on my blood pressure. I'm Wendell Garrity, 58, and I was born in Scranton, Pennsylvania, so the drive out was familiar. My readings from the home cuff had been running high, around 150 over 94, mostly in the mornings. Dr. Halvorsen wanted a full look at the numbers, so she reviewed the log I'd been keeping and checked my weight, which is down about six pounds since spring. I told her I'd been walking my dog, Biscuit, every evening and cutting back on the salt in my cooking.

Her recommendation was to keep the walks going and add a few days a week at the gym on Maple Street, which I'd been avoiding. She also wants me to cut out the afternoon coffee I usually get at Millbrook Cafe, though she was kind enough to say a single cup is fine. We set a new blood pressure medication to start on July 21 at a low dose. I'll bring the cuff back in for a recheck on August 4, and she asked me to call the office at 555-0187 if I get dizzy or have chest pain.

Walking out, I felt more hopeful than I expected. Wendell, she said, you're doing the work, and the medication is there to help the rest. I plan to hold her to that and to keep Biscuit happy with a longer loop around the park.

I still remember the morning we rolled into Naxos harbour, the ferry horn echoing off the whitewashed houses while I tried to keep Ptolemy, our scruffy terrier, from leaping onto a fishmonger's crate. My name is Yiannis Halvorsen, though most people in Greece call me Yanni within a day, and I had promised my sister Ilse that I would finally take the holiday she'd been nagging me about since we both finished at Ashworth Medical College. Nobody warned me that a July crossing from Piraeus would feel like sailing into an oven. Still, the Aegean looked impossibly blue, and I felt twenty years younger the moment my sandals hit the stone quay.

We spent the first three days wandering the lanes of Chora, where bougainvillea spills over every balcony and old women sit on doorsteps shelling beans and watching the tourists go by. On the twelfth of July, Ilse and I took the bus up to the Temple of Demeter, and Ptolemy, who had behaved beautifully on the ferry, decided the ancient columns were his personal racetrack. I chased him around the marble for a good ten minutes while a patient guard pretended not to notice. I still laugh thinking about it. That was also the day I got a call from Dr. Asmara Quintero at Ashworth, confirming my follow-up appointment for the twenty-sixth. I had nearly forgotten about it, and I cursed myself for letting my phone's roaming charges stop me from checking my email more often.

The real magic came with the village of Apeiranthos, perched high in the mountains, where I met a silversmith named Stelios who told me, with a wink, that his grandmother was born in the same mountain town where I was born, Ravensworth Hollow in Kent. He laughed at how small the world was. Ilse snapped a photo of us over a tiny cup of Greek coffee, and I promised to send it to him via yianni.halvorsen@mailbox-greece.net once we got back to England. He gave me a silver pendant for Ptolemy's collar, which the dog immediately tried to bury under a cushion.

We ended the trip in Plaka, watching the sun sink behind the Cycladic hills while sipping cold retsina. Ilse said it had been the best holiday of her life, and I had to agree. The island had a way of slowing down my heartbeat and reminding me that rest is not a luxury. As we boarded the ferry back to Piraeus on the twenty-second, Ptolemy stuck his head out of the window like a proud captain, and I made a silent promise to return. Greece, I have decided, is not a place you visit once; it is a place that keeps calling you back.

input: Today I sat with the heaviness instead of trying to push it away, which felt strange but also a little like progress. I noticed how often I rehearse conversations in my head before they happen, usually bracing for the worst and then feeling exhausted before anything has even started. My therapist asked me what I might be protecting myself from, and I didn't have a clean answer, only a sense of wanting to stay small so nothing could hurt me. We talked about how that instinct once made sense and how it may not be serving me now. I left feeling tender but clearer, and I want to practice noticing the moment I start bracing, and simply breathing through it before I decide what it means.

I'm Frances Lowell, and I spend most of my working hours on distributed storage systems, though I still get a small thrill when a bug turns out to be a simple off-by-one. I grew up in Dayton, Ohio, where my mother taught middle school science and my younger brother Gideon spent every summer trying to take apart our kitchen appliances. He is now a civil engineer in Phoenix and still sends me photos of bridges he has inspected, usually with a single line of commentary that I find more useful than most design reviews.

After a decade in consulting, I joined a small infrastructure team in Columbus and have been there ever since. We recently moved our offices to a converted warehouse at 1184 Harmon Ridge Road, Suite 320, and I now have a view of the river from my desk. The move was tiring, but the new space has made our Monday planning meetings far more pleasant. My dog Biscuit, a rescued beagle with strong opinions about elevators, has become something of an unofficial mascot. He insists on greeting every visitor, which has led to some memorable introductions.

Outside of work I volunteer with a literacy program that pairs adult learners with tutors, and I've been helping organize its annual fundraiser, which falls on October 18 this year. When people ask about my background, I tell them that the most important thing I bring is patience, a trait I credit to my mother and to years of debugging code at two in the morning. My passport, issued under number 548213907, has taken me to conferences in Lisbon and Seoul, and I hope to add a few more stamps before I retire. I look forward to meeting many of you at the sessions ahead.

I am writing this statement at the request of the attending officer following the incident on Saturday 12 April at approximately 9.40pm outside my flat on Ashgrove Road, Leeds. My name is Nadia Okafor, I am 34 years old, and I work as a pharmacist at the Hollins Street branch. On the evening in question I had walked back from my sister Ruth's house with my neighbour, Callum Pryce, who lives two doors down from me and who was carrying my bag because I had hurt my wrist.

As we reached the gate, a silver hatchback with a dented rear door pulled up across the pavement. The driver, a man in a dark grey hooded top, got out and asked Callum whether he "knew where Marcus was." Callum told him he had no idea who Marcus was. The man then took hold of Callum's arm and pushed him against the railings. I shouted and my neighbour's dog, Biscuit, began barking from behind their front window, which I believe is what caused the man to get back into his car and drive off towards the Headingley end of the road.

I did not see the registration plate clearly, though I believe the last three characters were KLM. Callum has a graze on his left elbow and says he is willing to give his own account. I would be grateful if someone could follow up on the CCTV from the newsagent on the corner, which may show the vehicle. I can be contacted on 07700 900412 or at nadia.okafor@mailbox.co.uk.

Hiroshima is a city that rewards slow wandering, and on our last morning I finally took the tram out to Hijiyama Park, where a small crowd had gathered under the cherry trees. I'm Tomoko's guest here, and she had warned me that the blossoms in late March come and go within a week, so we rushed out before breakfast. Tomoko works as a senior nurse at Hiroshima Municipal Hospital, and she knew the paths better than any guidebook. Her son Takeshi, who attends Jonan Elementary School, ran ahead of us the whole time, shouting at every pigeon he could find.

We ate onigiri on a bench by the pond, and Tomoko told me how her shifts had been stretched since winter. She laughed about the nurses' station kettle, which has outlived three directors. Later, when I asked whether she planned to take leave for the spring holidays, she simply said she would go wherever the trains were quietest. I wrote her email address, tomoko.hayashi@hmh-kango.jp, on a napkin so I could send her the photos.

If you visit, go in the morning, bring more food than you think you need, and do not expect the crowds to be polite. The park is calm once the tour buses leave, and the river walk beside it is the best place to finish the day, especially when the lanterns start to flicker along the water.

My name is Dieter Hallmann, and I was born in Leipzig on 14 February 2006. For most of my life I have been the kid who fixed the family's broken radio before anyone else noticed it was broken. That habit led me, at sixteen, to volunteer at a repair café in the Südvorstadt district, where I learned that a machine taken apart carefully is almost always a machine that can be put back together. Dieter is the name my grandmother gave me, and she still insists I bring my soldering iron to every visit.

When the Hallmann family moved into our flat at Karl-Heine-Strasse 47, 04229 Leipzig, I decided to build a small weather station on the balcony. The sensors cost less than a week of my part-time wages at the bakery, so I designed the enclosure myself and printed it at the school makerspace. The first readings were wrong by almost four degrees, and that error taught me more about calibration than any textbook. Dieter, my younger brother, still reminds me that the station once recorded snow in July.

I am applying to your engineering programme because I want to work on problems where precision matters to people's daily lives. My passport number, D4K7R2901, is listed on my registration form, and my email is dieter.hallmann@mailbox.de should you need anything further. I hope to bring the same patience to your laboratories that I brought to a broken radio and an uncooperative balcony sensor.

input:
When I started volunteering at the Kauri Bay community garden in Whangarei, I did not expect it to change how I think about my own future. My first real friend there was Wiremu Parata, a retired surveyor who had given up his Saturdays to teach teenagers how to compost and read soil. Wiremu had a habit of asking questions I couldn't answer, and over the months I found myself chasing those answers in library books and late-night reading. By June of my second year, I had helped plant the winter brassicas and had started keeping a notebook of rainfall and frost dates, which Wiremu said was the first useful data the garden had collected in a decade.

The garden is also where I learned that community work is rarely glamorous. Some mornings it was just me and Wiremu hauling mulch from the depot on Maunu Road, arguing about whether the kale needed more lime. Other days we would stop for flat whites at Harbourside Roasters before heading back to sort seedlings. Those small rituals taught me patience, and they showed me that a place can be held together by ordinary people who keep showing up.

When I think about what I want to study at university, I think about that notebook. I want to understand the systems behind everyday things, like why one paddock drains and the next one floods, and to use that understanding to help communities make better decisions about the land they depend on. Wiremu once told me that a good surveyor leaves a trail anyone can follow. I hope my own work can do the same.

My work sits at the intersection of warehouse operations and streaming analytics, and I enjoy translating messy operational data into dashboards that dispatch teams actually use. Most weekday evenings you will find me at Chai Adda on FC Road, which doubles as my unofficial office. My dog, Biscuit, a rescued Indie mix, accompanies me on most of my morning walks and has become something of a fixture in our neighbourhood.
