input:
My name is Thomas, and I am Ada's older brother. Ada was 74 when she died on January 9th, in the house on Maple Street where we grew up. For most of her life she was the person everyone called when something needed fixing, whether it was a leaky faucet, a sick neighbor, or a kid who needed a ride home from practice. She never asked for thanks, and she rarely got it in the way she deserved.

When our mother got sick, Ada moved back to Ohio to take care of her, and she didn't complain once. She learned how to change the IV line, how to read the pharmacy labels, and how to sit with a frightened woman at three in the morning and make her laugh. Ada's daughter Megan, who was just nineteen then, watched her mother do all of it and told me later that she learned more about courage from that year than from anything else.

Ada loved crossword puzzles, bad detective shows, and the Cincinnati Reds, even in the seasons when there was nothing to cheer about. If you ever visited her kitchen, you left with a plate of something warm. I will miss her voice on the phone every Sunday, and I know many of you will too. Thank you all for being here to say goodbye to my sister.

input:
STATEMENT OF WITNESS

I, Vanessa Ruatapu, make this statement about the incident I witnessed on Saturday 14 May at approximately 9:40 pm outside 42 Tennyson Street, Island Bay, Wellington. I am 34 years old and I currently work as a radiographer at Wellington Hospital, where I have been employed for six years. I live with my partner two doors down from the address mentioned.

On the evening in question I had walked my dog along the footpath towards Shelly Bay Road. As I reached the corner, I noticed a silver Toyota Corolla, registration plate KLT 482, parked with its hazard lights on. A young man in a dark grey Canterbury hoodie was standing beside the driver's door, speaking loudly into his phone. I did not recognise him at that point, though I have since been told by a neighbour that his name is Tane Whakaari.

As I passed, the man turned and asked whether I had seen anyone run past. I said no. He then said, "Just tell Tane's mum I'm fine, I'll sort it out tomorrow." I thought this was an odd thing to say to a stranger, so I looked back and saw him get into the passenger seat of the car while another man, shorter and wearing a navy cap, got into the driver's seat. The car then pulled away quickly towards the Island Bay shops.

I went home and told my partner, Ross, what I had seen. He suggested I contact the police. I did not have a phone number for the local station so I checked the website and found the non-emergency line. I was advised to come in and give a formal statement, which is why I am here today, Friday 20 May.

I can add that I have no connection to either man and no dispute with anyone on the street. I am willing to provide any further information, including my phone number, 021 555 0148, and my email address, vanessa.ruatapu@xtra.co.nz, if the officer needs to follow up. I understand this statement may be used in court and I confirm that everything written here is true to the best of my knowledge.

Signed: Vanessa Ruatapu

input:
I'm thrilled to share that after nine wonderful years, I've stepped away from my role at Harbourline Logistics in Wellington and taken up a new position as Operations Lead with Kōwhai Freight in Christchurch. It's a big move, both professionally and personally, and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on it.

When I joined Harbourline, I was fresh out of university and not entirely sure what I wanted. Frank, my old flatmate, used to say I'd never sit still long enough to find out. He was half right. I did sit still for a while, but I learned more in those nine years than I ever expected: how to keep a warehouse running through a storm, how to talk a driver down from a bad day, and how to build a team that actually trusts each other. The people there, from the dock crew to the finance team, made every hard week worth it.

The decision to leave wasn't easy. Wellington has been home for most of my adult life. I have my favourite coffee spot on Cuba Street, a Saturday routine at Mojo Coffee in Newtown, and a gym at Fitzroy Street Strength that has kept me sane through more stressful quarters than I care to count. Leaving those rituals behind felt strange. But when Kōwhai came calling with a role that combined ownership of a regional network with the chance to grow a new team from scratch, I couldn't say no.

Christchurch is already teaching me new things. The rebuild has created a city full of energy, and the business community here is generous with its time. I've been meeting people for coffee at Cafe Gamma and Hargreaves Street, and I'm slowly learning the local shortcuts that make the commute work.

To anyone reading this who is weighing a similar move: take the leap if the work excites you and the people feel right. You'll miss what you leave behind, but you'll also find out how much you're capable of. I'm grateful to everyone at Harbourline who helped me get here.

If you're in Christchurch and fancy a catch-up, send me a message. I'd love to hear what you're working on.

input:
Dear Zaidy,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the new hearing aids are working out. Mom says you have been beating everyone at cards at the community centre, so I am not worried about you at all. I have been thinking about you a lot since the holidays, especially about the story you told us about growing up in Safed before the family moved south. Frankie, that is what you still call me when you are teasing, and I miss hearing it in your voice.

Life in Haifa is busy. The university keeps me running between lectures and the lab, and the sea wind here is stronger than anything I remember from Tel Aviv. On March 14th I finally finished the project I told you about on the phone, and my advisor said it was clean enough to submit. I wanted you to hear that from me first. I stayed up far too late that night, eating cold falafel on the balcony and watching the lights along the Carmel.

Please write back when you can, even if it is just a few lines in that shaky handwriting. Tell me what you are reading and whether Grandma's garden is still producing those ridiculous tomatoes. I will call on Shabbat, and you are not allowed to hang up on me this time. With all my love,

Francesca

input:
I want to tell you about my mother, Irene Callahan, who passed away peacefully on December 9th at the age of 81, surrounded by the people she loved most. Irene was born in Dayton, Ohio, and never once let us forget it. She raised three children in a yellow farmhouse at 1148 Whitcomb Road in Marietta, where the kitchen was always warm and the coffee was always on. For thirty-four years she worked as a claims supervisor at Great Lakes Mutual Insurance, and she took more pride in that job than she ever let on. Her coworkers used to say she could spot a fraudulent invoice from across the room.

My mother had a gift for patience that I still struggle to match. She taught Sunday school for decades, spent Saturdays volunteering at the food pantry, and never missed a birthday, anniversary, or sympathy card. Her garden was the envy of the street, and her tomatoes were the only ones my father would eat without complaint.

She is survived by her children, Ruth, Ben, and me, along with five grandchildren and her faithful companion, a gray tabby named Pickles, who has been sitting by the front window every afternoon since the funeral. Irene, we will miss you more than words can hold. Rest now. Your garden is in good hands.

Hi all, long-time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone who has dealt with this in Israel can give me some direction. I'm Keren, I'm 34, and I live on Herzl Street 18, apartment 5, in Haifa. Last month my car, a white Hyundai i20 with registration 62-814-37, was towed from the street outside my building. I had parked there for years without any issue, so I didn't think to check the signs. The tow company told me the car was impounded and that I owed 1,240 shekels before they would release it. I paid it, but the receipt doesn't list any violation, which is what's bothering me.

When I called the municipality, the person on the phone was polite but vague. She said the complaint came from a private party and that I should file an objection in writing. I asked her to email me the details, and she said she would, but nothing has arrived yet. I've also been trying to get through to the tow company's customer service line, and I keep getting put on hold for forty minutes before the call drops.

So far I've been drafting an objection letter, but my Hebrew is good only for everyday conversation, so I'm writing it in English and having a friend translate. Has anyone here objected to a towing charge in Haifa? Did you go in person to the municipal office, or is it better to do it by email? I know some people mention a deadline, and I'm worried I've already missed it.

I'd also like to know whether it's worth going to the cafe on the corner of my street, Kafe Lev, where I was sitting that afternoon, to see if the owner noticed anything. I'd rather get a witness than rely on my word alone. My sister thinks I'm overreacting, but this is a lot of money for me right now.

Any advice on the process, the deadline, or how to word the objection would be hugely appreciated. Thanks in advance, and sorry for the long post.

Hi, I'm Tanvi Deshmukh, 29, and I've lived in Pune for most of my life, though I was born in Nashik, which my mother still reminds me is the better city for grapes and worse for traffic. I work as a pharmacist at a hospital in Kothrud, which means I spend my days counting tablets, reading handwriting that would confuse a cryptographer, and occasionally explaining to elderly uncles why they shouldn't mix two painkillers. I like to think I'm calm under pressure, which is useful when the queue at the counter starts to look like a cricket crowd.

On weekends you'll find me at the Sinhagad road cafe with a notebook, or on a hill trek with a group of friends who have strong opinions about which path is shortest and none about which is least painful. I'm learning Kathak after years of telling everyone I would never be able to do it, and so far my teacher has been kind enough to say my footwork is "improving at a dignified pace." I read more crime novels than is probably healthy, and I cook dal the way my grandmother did, which is to say without measurements and with a lot of confidence.

I'm looking for someone who can hold a proper conversation, who doesn't treat a long silence as a problem, and who laughs at things that are only slightly funny. I'd like a partner who is curious about the world but also content to sit on a balcony in the evening and watch the sky change colour. Bonus points if you can tell the difference between filter coffee and instant without flinching.

A few things I'm not interested in: games where you ask a stranger to guess your mood, long messages that say nothing, and anyone who thinks a single photo at a waterfall counts as a personality. If you've read this far, you already have more patience than most people, which I appreciate.

I was born on 14 April 1995 and I'm a Taurus, so yes, I'm stubborn, but I'm also very good at making plans and keeping them. If you want to get to know me, send a message about something specific you've enjoyed this month. Tell me about a book, a meal, or a place you keep going back to. I'll reply, and I promise it won't be a single word.

Contact for the app: tanvi.deshmukh@mailnest.in

input:
Antoine Lefebvre passed away peacefully at home on the 14th of January, at the age of 78, surrounded by the people who loved him most. For forty years he ran the small bookbinding workshop off Rue des Tanneurs in Lyon, where generations of local readers brought him their worn volumes and left with something almost new. He had a dry wit, an unshakeable opinion on every French cheese, and a habit of humming Piaf while he worked. Those of us who knew him will remember his patience with apprentices and his gift for making everyone feel they had been expected.

He is survived by his wife, Marguerite, and their son, Julien, who will miss his father's steady hand at the bench and his Sunday lunches more than he can say. Antoine's old friend and business partner, Bernard Dubois, spent every Thursday evening with him over chess and a bottle of Côtes du Rhône, and has asked that we keep the second chair at the table empty for a while. Their yellow Labrador, Biscuit, has been pacing the hallway since the morning and will need a little extra love in the weeks ahead.

Antoine, we will keep the workshop light on for you. Thank you for every book you saved and every friend you gathered along the way. Rest well, old friend. Your absence fills the room, but your craftsmanship will sit on shelves across the neighbourhood for many years to come.

Louise Moreau

I am writing to describe the water damage that occurred in our apartment on the evening of 14 August, and to request that the claim be processed under our contents and building policy. My name is Fenna de Vries, and I live on the third floor of a building on the Lange Houtstraat in Utrecht, which my partner Pieter and I have rented since 2019. On that Thursday, I returned from work shortly after six and noticed that the hallway floor was wet and that the ceiling in the living room had begun to bulge near the corner by the window.

At first I assumed a neighbour had left a tap running, so I knocked on the doors of the apartments above and below. Nobody answered on the fourth floor, and the resident on the second floor confirmed that they had heard nothing unusual. By the time I called my mother, Marieke, for advice, water was dripping steadily from the light fixture. She told me to turn off the main valve under the kitchen sink and to photograph everything before touching anything else, which I did. I also called the building manager, Mr. Jansen, whose office number is on the notice board in the entrance hall.

The plumber, Dirk Bakker of Bakker Loodgieters, attended the following morning, on 15 August, and traced the leak to a failed compression fitting on a supply pipe that runs behind the bathroom wall. He replaced the fitting and dried the cavity, but he said the plasterboard in the living room ceiling and the laminate in the hallway would need to be replaced. Our total estimate for the repairs and for a dehumidifier rental is EUR 2,840, and the itemised invoice is attached to this letter.

I have also lost a number of personal items, including a wool rug that belonged to my grandmother, a set of books that were stored on the lower shelves, and my son's electric piano. I have listed each item in the attached inventory with approximate purchase dates and values, and I have included photographs where I still have them. Please let me know if you require receipts for any of the larger items, and I will try to locate them.

You may contact me by email at fenna.devries@example-mail.nl, or by telephone on 06 1234 5678 during the evenings. I would be grateful for confirmation that my claim has been registered and an indication of when an assessor might visit the property. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Hey, I still can't stop thinking about what happened at the bakery last week. You know the one near the tram stop, the place with the cramped little tables? I went in just to grab a coffee before work, and the woman behind the counter, who I've seen every morning for ages, looked up and actually remembered my order. It sounds small, but after the rough winter I've had, it genuinely made my whole day. I sat by the window with my pretzel and watched people hurry past in their heavy coats, and for once I didn't feel like I was rushing through my own life.

That got me thinking about how much we underestimate those little routines. Some mornings I'd dread getting out of bed, but the walk through the park and that familiar bell over the door gave me something to look forward to. I'm not saying everything's fixed, because it isn't, but there's a steadiness in those ordinary moments that I'd forgotten about. Honestly, I think I needed the reminder more than I realised.

So that's my update. Wendy would tell you I've been overthinking things again, and she's probably right. Anyway, next time you're in town, let's go there together. I'll buy you the pretzel and we can talk properly over a long, lazy breakfast. I really miss our conversations, and I'd love to catch up on everything you've been up to.

I'll buy you the pretzel and we can talk properly over a long, lazy breakfast. I really miss our conversations, and I'd love to catch up on everything you've been up to.

input:
I am Aditya Raman, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a data engineer at Vantage Lattice Solutions in Pune. Most mornings I take the metro from my flat in Kothrud to our office in Hinjewadi, though on rainy days I give in and book a cab. People often assume that a career in software means a life lived entirely behind a screen, and while there is some truth to that, I have always tried to keep one foot in the physical world. Pune has been generous that way. The hills, the old lanes near Deccan, and the steady hum of its tech corridors have all shaped how I think about my work and my community.

My journey into data began almost by accident. As an undergraduate in Nagpur I was fascinated by how small patterns in messy information could reveal something meaningful about people. That curiosity led me to a internship at a logistics firm, where I spent a summer building pipelines that tracked delivery routes across Maharashtra. I remember the first time a dashboard I had built helped a dispatcher avoid a costly delay. It was a modest win, but it convinced me that technical work could have a very human impact.

Outside the office, I am fortunate to have a close circle of friends who keep me grounded. My closest colleague and friend, Sanjana Iyer, has been my partner in more late-night debugging sessions than I can count. We share a love of long walks around Kothrud Lake and an unreasonable enthusiasm for filter coffee. Together we have mentored a small group of junior engineers, and watching them grow has been one of the most rewarding parts of my career.

Home life is quieter but no less important. My golden retriever, Mango, greets me at the door every evening with more enthusiasm than my day usually deserves. He has become something of a neighbourhood celebrity on our lane in Kothrud, and he has taught me more about patience than any management course ever did. Whenever a project feels overwhelming, I remind myself to slow down, take him out, and let the evening air reset my perspective.

If you would like to discuss data quality, team mentoring, or the realities of building analytics in fast-growing Indian cities, I am always happy to talk. You can reach me at +91 98221 47630 or through my professional email, aditya.raman@vantagelattice.in. I look forward to meeting fellow practitioners at the conference and hearing about the work that inspires you.

input:
I landed at Ben Gurion on a Tuesday evening in March and by the time I had collected my hire car I was already running late for the drive north. The rental agreement had my name on it, Jonah, and a booking reference that was really just a string of letters and numbers I kept re-reading on my phone, but the car itself was the part I had to remember: a small white Hyundai with the plate 74-512-39 stuck on a little paper sticker in the glovebox so I could tell the attendant which one was mine. The roads out of the airport were quieter than I expected, and the lights of Tel Aviv spread out to my left like someone had spilled a box of sequins across the coast.

The next morning I met my friend Jordan at a bakery in Jaffa, the old port town where the streets bend back on themselves and every doorway seems to have a cat asleep in it. Jordan had been living in Haifa for two years and insisted I try the sabich there, so we took the coastal road up in his battered Peugeot, windows down, the sea glinting on our right the whole way. We talked about everything and nothing, and by the time we reached the Carmel ridge the afternoon had gone soft and gold. If you ever find yourself in the north in March, go slowly. The wildflowers come out in patches along the hillsides and the light makes everything look like a painting that hasn't quite dried.

By the end of the week I had a small notebook full of scribbled addresses, phone numbers I would probably never use, and a long list of places I had promised myself I would return to. Jordan drove me back to the airport on the Sunday, and I remember thinking how strange it is that a country can feel both enormous and intimate at once. I will be back, and next time I will leave the car keys somewhere I can actually find them.

input:
When I was eleven, my grandmother taught me to bake bread in the old oven in our apartment in Haifa, the one that ran hot on the left side and never quite on the right. She would tell me to watch the crust instead of the clock, and I think that lesson stuck with me more than any math problem I have solved since. Zohar was the name my parents gave me, after a book my father loved, and I have spent most of my life trying to live up to the quiet, careful person it describes.

My days now are split between the school bus, a part-time shift at the library on Herzl Street, and the robotics club that meets in the basement of the community centre. Robotics is where I learned that failure is not the opposite of progress but usually its first draft. Last year our team built a line-following robot that worked perfectly on the practice mat and then drove straight off the table during the regional competition. I remember standing there, feeling my face burn, and thinking that everyone would remember the fall more than the design. We rebuilt the sensor array that night, and the following October we placed third in the national round.

The library has taught me something different. Most afternoons I help elderly patrons learn to use the catalogue terminals and access digital newspapers. One man, a retired engineer who comes in every Tuesday, once asked me why anyone would bother reading a physical book when everything was online. I did not have a good answer then. I have one now: a book asks you to slow down in a way a screen rarely does, and that slowness is where I do my best thinking.

I am applying to your programme in environmental engineering because I want to work on water. Growing up in a city where every drop is measured, I became interested in how communities plan for scarcity and how technology can make that planning fairer. I have started a small project with two classmates to map rainwater collection on the rooftops of our neighbourhood, and we have reached out through our account @zohar.hydro_haifa to share our findings with local residents. The response has been modest but encouraging, and it has shown me that engineering is at its best when it listens.

I know that my path is not a straight line, and I do not expect one. What I bring is a habit of returning to problems after they have humbled me, and a willingness to ask the people affected what they actually need. I hope to bring that habit to your university, to learn alongside people whose experiences differ from mine, and to contribute to a future in which the water we depend on is shared more wisely.

input:
Hoy llegué a la sesión con las manos temblando otra vez. Tomás, mi terapeuta, me preguntó qué había pasado en la semana y no supe por dónde empezar. Le conté lo de mi madre, que me llamó el 12 de septiembre para decirme que mi hermana Lucía no le contesta los mensajes desde hace tres días. Le dije que sentí lo mismo que cuando era niña en Oaxaca, en el pueblo de San Pablo Etla, cuando mi papá se iba al campo y no volvía hasta la noche. Tomás me escuchó sin interrumpir, y eso ya es un avance.

Después de la sesión pasé por el Café Los Nogales, en la colonia Roma, a escribir un rato. Pedí un americano y me quedé mirando la ventana, pensando en Teo, mi perro, que se quedó en casa con la vecina. Teo es un mestizo café con una oreja caída y sé que extraña el patio cuando me voy tanto tiempo. Me di cuenta de que cargo con la culpa de estar lejos de todos, incluso de él. Tomás dice que la culpa no es un hecho, es una historia que me cuento. Quiero creerle.

He decidido llamar a Lucía mañana, aunque me dé miedo. Si no contesta, le dejaré un mensaje corto y no uno de reproches. Anotaré también en mi libreta que, aunque tengo ganas de huir, hoy me quedé. Esa es una pequeña victoria, y la quiero recordar. Escribo esto para mí, Tatiana, para no olvidar que puedo sostenerme cuando tiemblo.

Okay so, this is me just talking into my phone while I walk back from the market, so bear with me if it's all over the place. So I got here last week and honestly the heat is something else, like you step outside and it just hits you. But the food, oh my god, I've been eating these tamales from a lady on the corner every morning and I think I might be a little addicted now. Don't tell anyone, it's embarrassing.

Anyway, the thing I wanted to actually tell you about is the bus situation. I thought I'd figured it out, I had like a little map and everything, and then the bus just didn't come, or it came and was already packed so full people were hanging off the door. Which, fine, that's just how it works here I guess. I've kind of stopped being annoyed about it and started just walking more, which is honestly nicer when it's not the middle of the day.

So the people here have been really nice to me, which I did not expect at all. Like the guy who runs the little shop downstairs from where I'm staying, he always asks how I'm doing and then tries to teach me a new word every time I buy water. My Spanish is still terrible, like I can order food and say thank you and that's about it, but everybody is so patient with me. I'm trying to practice more, I've got an app going and I talk to myself a lot, which I'm sure the neighbours think is weird.

I also went to this little plaza yesterday evening where there were kids playing soccer and old men playing chess and some musicians just sort of wandering around. I just sat on a bench for like two hours and watched everything. It was the most relaxed I've felt in months, which is kind of wild to say given that I'm literally in a new country where I don't really know anyone yet.

Okay, I think I'm almost back, I can see the building. Ugh, the stairs are going to kill me. Anyway, I'll send you more soon, maybe a proper message when I'm sitting down and not sweating through my shirt. Miss you, tell everyone I said hi. Bye bye.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Tom, Charlotte's older brother, and I've been given the job of telling you a few things about my sister that she would rather I didn't. Charlie has been my partner in crime since the day she was born, which is a polite way of saying she has been finding ways to get me into trouble for thirty-one years.

I still remember the first time Charlie decided she was going to be a lawyer. She was nine, she had a school tie borrowed from our dad, and she spent the whole of Sunday lunch cross-examining Nan about why she couldn't have a second slice of pavlova. Nan lost that argument. Nan loses most arguments to Charlie, and she has never once minded.

When Charlie met Daniel, I'll be honest, I was suspicious. Anyone who wants to spend their weekends hiking up Mount Wellington in the rain and calling it fun is either brave or slightly unwell. Dan turned out to be both, and somewhere along the way he became the brother I didn't have to be jealous of. He knows how to make Charlie laugh until she snorts, and he knows when to just hand her a cup of tea and sit beside her.

The two of them bought their first place together on Cormorant Avenue in Newtown, a little terrace with a wonky back fence and a fig tree that has never once produced fruit. They have spent every weekend since trying to fix one or the other. Charlie insists the fig tree is just shy. Dan says it's been hiding from her renovation plans. I think it's the most Charlie thing in the world that she would argue with a tree.

So please raise your glasses. Charlie, Dan, you have always been good for each other, and we are so lucky to be standing here celebrating you. Mum is already crying, so I'm going to sit down before I join her. Cheers to the happy couple.

My name is Mfon Akpan and I am writing to report the loss of my laptop bag and its contents during a break-in at my apartment in Ikeja, Lagos, on the night of Saturday 14 October. I returned from a late shift at around 11:30 pm and found the front door forced open and the living room in disarray. My younger brother, Emeka Akpan, who lives with me, was asleep in the back room and was not harmed. Our dog, Biscuit, a brown mongrel, barked for most of the night and was found locked in the bathroom, which I believe the intruders did to keep him quiet.

The items taken include a silver Dell Latitude laptop, a Western Digital external hard drive, a Tecno smartphone, a gold wristwatch that belonged to my late father, and cash of approximately NGN 180,000 kept in a drawer. I have attached receipts for the laptop and phone where I could locate them. I've been coming to Harbourside Bakehouse in Newcastle for almost three years now, and I'm writing this review because my daughter Lachlan insisted I share how much we both love it. Lachlan is seven and has a serious opinion on sourdough, so when she tells me the cinnamon scroll is the best thing in the city, I believe her. The staff remember her name and always ask after her soccer game, which says a lot about the place.

Last Saturday, 14 May, we were in around eight and the line was out the door, but the team kept things moving. Lachlan's brother Lucas ordered a pie that he couldn't finish, and the barista boxed it up without a fuss. Lucas is nine and still insists it was the best pie he's ever had, so I'd say that's a solid endorsement.

The coffee is good, the prices are fair for what you get, and the seating by the window is lovely on a cool morning. My only complaint is that parking on Hunter Street is tight after nine, so get there early. Lachlan says five stars, and honestly, I can't argue with her.

I still find myself reaching for the phone to tell Cassie something funny, and then remembering that I can't. Cassandra Louise Pretorius, known to everyone in Grahamstown as "Cass Bug" since her school days, passed away peacefully on 14 September at the age of 71. I was her younger sister, Marianne Hattingh, and I am writing this with a heavy heart and a lot of gratitude for a life that filled so many rooms.

Cass was born in Grahamstown in 1953, the eldest of four, and she never really left it in her heart even after decades in Durban. She taught Grade 3 at the same primary school for thirty-one years, and generations of children learned to read at her kitchen table on Saturday mornings. She had a laugh you could hear across a braai and a habit of phoning people on their birthdays before the sun was up, just to be first.

She is survived by her husband Pieter, her daughters Lize and Anel, five grandchildren, and me. A memorial service will be held at St Andrew's Church on 21 September at 10:00. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that you read a story to a child in her memory. I know she would have liked that very much.

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for the candidate who worked under my supervision as a senior software engineer at our Israeli development office over the past several years. In that time, they consistently demonstrated technical excellence, a calm approach under pressure, and a genuine commitment to the quality of the work their team produced. They led the redesign of our internal deployment pipeline, which substantially reduced release failures and gave engineers far more confidence when shipping changes. Colleagues frequently sought their advice on architecture decisions, and they had a rare ability to explain complex trade-offs clearly to non-specialists.

Beyond their technical skills, they were a generous and patient mentor. They invested real time in onboarding newer team members, reviewing their code with care and encouraging them to ask questions without hesitation. When a project faced unexpected setbacks, they were the person who kept the group focused and communicating openly, rather than assigning blame. Their reliability was never in doubt; deadlines were met, and when they were not, the issue was raised early and handled transparently.

I am confident they would bring the same dedication, judgement and collaborative spirit to any role they pursue next. I recommend them without reservation and would welcome the chance to discuss their qualifications further.

Good morning, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ciarán, Mam's eldest, and I want to thank you all for coming to Clonmel to say goodbye to Catherine. She taught for thirty-one years at St. Brigid's National School in Sligo before she ever set foot in a hospital ward, and she used to say the children there were the only people who could out-talk her. Many of you were her pupils, or your kids were, and I've lost count of the times someone has stopped me in a supermarket to tell me she once gave them a second chance when nobody else would.

Mam had a rule that nobody left her kitchen hungry, and she applied it to strays as well as family. Our old collie, Brisa, was the best example. She turned up on the back step in 2009 and Mam decided, with no discussion, that she was staying. Brisa followed her around the garden every morning, and I think she was the only one who never once heard Mam complain about the weather. If you ever visited the house in Sligo, you'll remember the dog sleeping across the doorway like a guard.

If you'd like to write to us, or share a memory, you can reach my sister Niamh at niamh.doyle@tuatha-mail.ie, and she'll gather everything for the family. Mam left us her stubbornness, her kindness and a fierce loyalty to the people she loved. We'll try to live up to all three. Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to provide a reference for Emily Carrington, who worked under my supervision as a staff nurse on the medical ward at St Aldric's Royal Infirmary in Leeds from March 2019 until April 2024. In that time Emily consistently demonstrated clinical judgement well beyond what is expected at her grade. She led the handover for her shift with clarity, managed a heavy caseload of post-operative patients, and was the first person the junior doctors turned to when a patient's condition began to slip overnight.

Emily is also exceptionally good with families. During a difficult period on the ward in April 2023, she spent long hours supporting the relatives of a patient who was receiving end-of-life care, and she did so with a patience and compassion that the family later described to me in writing. She also took the initiative to set up a peer teaching session on early warning scores, which has since become a fixture of our training calendar. Her willingness to share knowledge is one of her defining qualities.

I should add that Emily has been active in our trust's communications work, and she maintains a professional nursing account on social media under the handle @emcarrington_rn, where she shares evidence-based tips for patients and students. I have no hesitation in recommending her for any role in nursing practice, and I would be glad to discuss her application further if you wish to contact me.

Yours faithfully,

Dr Helen Asquith
Clinical Lead, Medical Division
St Aldric's Royal Infirmary, Leeds

Nov 4. I still can't believe it's been three weeks since the flight from Manila landed in Toronto. Mom keeps asking if I've settled in, and honestly I'm not sure what settled even means yet. Today I went to the registration desk at Ridgeway Collegiate to sort out my transcripts, and the woman there just stared at my Philippine report card like it was written in code. I had to explain the grading scale twice. Marisol, my cousin who lives two streets over, laughed when I told her, but she also offered to come with me next time.

Nov 11. Had my first appointment at St. Clement's Hospital today because my asthma inhaler ran out and the pharmacy here wanted a new prescription from a local doctor. The waiting room was packed, and I kept thinking about how Lolo used to take me to the clinic in Cebu with a bag of mangoes just to make the wait go faster. I called him from the parking lot. He said, "Ma, you're not gone, you're just somewhere else now." I wrote his line down so I wouldn't forget it.

Nov 19. Emailed my old teacher, Mrs. Dela Cruz, from my new address, mariafernandez.writes@gmail.com, which I set up for school applications. She replied within an hour saying she's proud of me. Also got my first Canadian paycheck, which is small but feels like proof that I can do this. Tomorrow I start at the library, and I'm going to tell Mom everything over video call before I lose my nerve.

When I was nine, my family moved from Limerick to a small house outside Ennis, and the first thing I learned was that rural life runs on favours. My father Gerard drove a delivery van for a feed merchant, and on Saturdays I rode along to keep him company. That is where I first met Mr. Cahill, the depot manager at Clare Agri Supplies Ltd, who taught me to read a manifest and to respect a schedule. Our old van, registration 181-CE-2274, was always breaking down, and Mr. Cahill would drop everything to help fix it.

My own work began in the summer I turned sixteen, when I took a job as a junior stock assistant at Clare Agri. By July I was counting pallets, checking invoices and handling the phone line while Mr. Cahill was out on deliveries. I noticed that customers trusted the depot more when the paperwork was right the first time, and I started building a simple spreadsheet to track orders. The owner, Ms. Ryan, asked me to present it to the staff, and that was the first time I felt I could contribute something useful.

I want to study agricultural economics because I have seen how small decisions in a rural business ripple outward. Growing up, I also cared for our family dog, a lurcher named Biscuit, who waited by the gate every evening for Gerard's van. Biscuit taught me patience and loyalty, and the depot taught me that good systems keep people working together. I hope to bring both lessons to university, where I can learn the economics behind the farms and businesses I have always known.

I am writing this with a heavy heart to share that my dear father, Krishnan Iyer, passed away peacefully on the 14th of June at the age of 72. For forty-one years he served as a senior accountant with the Tamil Nadu State Transport office, and those who worked beside him will remember his patience, his neat handwriting in every ledger, and the way he never let a colleague leave for home without a cup of filter coffee.

Dad grew up in Thanjavur and later studied commerce at Pachaiyappa's College in Chennai, a place he always spoke of with enormous pride. He was a man of routine. Every Sunday he drove his old white Maruti, registration TN 09 AK 4471, to the Kapaleeshwarar temple, and he insisted on taking the long way round so that he could pass the bookshop on Ring Road. Even in his last months he would ask me to check whether the rain had reached Mylapore yet.

He is survived by my mother, Lakshmi, my sister Kavitha, and me, along with four grandchildren who adored him. The funeral will be held on the 18th of June at the Besant Nagar crematorium at 4 p.m. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made to the Government Royapettah Hospital, where Dad received such kind care in his final weeks. We thank you for your prayers and for every kindness shown to him.

Krishnan Iyer, may your soul rest in peace.

input:
Dear diary, the generator went quiet again this afternoon, right when I was ironing my work blouse for tomorrow. Everyone on the street came out with their buckets and jerrycans, grumbling and laughing at the same time, the way we always do when the light goes. Mama sent me to the corner shop for matches and I came back with three bottles of cold Fanta instead, because the lady at the counter said the fridge would only last until the power went off completely.

After dinner we sat on the veranda and listened to the neighbours' radio playing old highlife tunes, and somebody's pikin kept running up and down the compound shouting for no reason at all. The mosquitoes found us anyway, even with the coil burning. I keep thinking about the interview I have on Monday. I have practised my answers in front of the mirror until I sound like a stranger to myself, but I still feel my hands shake when I imagine sitting across from those people.

If I get this job, I will finally be able to help pay for the roof repairs and maybe buy a proper fan for the bedroom. For now I will just sleep with the window open, listen to the rain on the zinc, and hope the light comes back before morning. Good night, diary.

Hey Emily, you asked me to tell you properly what happened with the flat, so here it is. I'd been living at 14 Elmwood Terrace in Leeds for nearly six years, and the landlord, a man called Graham Pritchard, decided in January he wanted to sell. He gave us notice and I spent weeks trawling Rightmove at night. In the end I found a place near Headingley, and the agent asked me for everything: proof of ID, my passport number, the usual. I had to scan my passport twice because the first one came out blurry, which was a nightmare at eleven o'clock on a Tuesday.

The signing was booked for 14 February, Valentine's Day, which Mum thought was hilarious. I rang the agent, Sophie Lyle, on the Monday to confirm, and she said to email any last documents to sophie.lyle@haywardandbrooke.co.uk before ten. I nearly missed it because my phone kept dropping signal in the lift at work. Still, I got it sent, and on the day I walked in with a coffee and a folder and signed everything in about twenty minutes.

So I've got the keys now, and the new address is 27 Ashworth Gardens, LS6 3PQ, which I've already had to write on about nine forms. Honestly it's a bit of a relief. The kitchen is tiny but the window looks over a park, and there's a bakery across the road that smells incredible at seven in the morning. Come round when you're back from Glasgow and I'll make you a proper cup of tea in my actual mugs, not the ones from the old place that I had to fight with the removal men over.

input: I saw my GP this morning because the lower back pain I've had for about three weeks hasn't eased with rest or paracetamol. Vaughn examined me, asked about my sleep and work, and checked my reflexes and leg strength, which were all normal. He thinks it's a muscle strain aggravated by long hours at the desk and has suggested gentle stretching, a heat pack in the evenings, and a review in two weeks if it isn't improving. He also said to come back sooner if I get numbness, tingling, or any loss of bladder or bowel control. I left feeling reassured but a bit frustrated that there's no quick fix, and I've booked a standing desk assessment with the physio.

I'm Henrik, though most of my colleagues in Uppsala know me as "Hank," a nickname that started during a summer internship in 2009 and never quite went away. I work as a data engineer, mostly on pipelines that move sensor readings from northern wind farms into forecasting models. Before settling into this field, I spent six years in software consulting, which taught me more about deadlines than about algorithms.

My current work focuses on making real-time systems more resilient when connectivity is poor, which in Sweden means a lot of the time. I have presented at several regional meetings on edge caching and on the trade-offs between batch and streaming architectures. I enjoy the practical side of these talks: showing what broke, what we changed, and why the fix looked obvious only in hindsight.

Outside of work I run a small open-source project for parsing meteorological data formats, and I am always happy to hear from people who use it or want to contribute. The best way to reach me is by email at henrik.lindqvist@example-mail.se. Hank, Henrik, or any other version of my name is fine with me.

Ichiro Kaneda

I am writing this with a heavy heart to share that Karen Levitan passed away peacefully on May 14, after a long illness borne with the same quiet courage she brought to everything. Karen was born in Netanya in 1951, and she never fully stopped being a girl from the coast. She loved the sea, strong coffee, and arguing politely about politics with anyone who would sit down with her.

For more than twenty years, Karen was a fixture at Café Ginat on Herzl Street, where she ran the Tuesday morning crossword table and knew the names of everyone's children. Many of us first met her there, and we will miss her steady presence in that corner booth. Her weekly visits to Shalom Physio Clinic also gave her the chance to tease the staff mercilessly, something they still speak of fondly.

Karen is survived by her sons, Oren and Yoni, her granddaughters Noa and Tamar, and her loyal old cat Biscuit, who has been sitting by the window every day since she left. Karen, we will keep your seat warm and your crossword half-finished. May her memory be a blessing. The funeral will take place on Thursday, May 22, at 11 a.m. at the Netanya cemetery.

input:
Tuesday 14 October. Rain all day in Uppsala and I still haven't got used to how early it goes dark here. Caspar had his first proper walk in the forest this morning and came back looking like a mud puddle with a tail. Mum would have had a fit. I stood in the hallway with the towel for ten minutes while he shook himself over everything. Still, he's settling in, which is more than I can say for me.

Work was long. Ingrid from HR at Nordbyggen AB called to confirm my start date as Senior Project Coordinator, and I nearly cried, honestly, because I've been sending applications since March. She said I'd need to bring my ID and the bank details to the office on the 21st. I wrote that on my hand so I wouldn't forget. After that I went to Kaffe & Kanel on Svartbäcksgatan to warm up, and the girl behind the counter remembered my order from last week, which felt oddly like being known.

I turned 34 on Sunday and nobody had told me that Swedes treat birthdays with a kind of quiet seriousness. My colleague Erik left a cinnamon bun on my desk with a little note. Tonight I finally registered the Volvo, plate ABC 412, and realised I still need to switch my insurance over before the 28th. Note to self: call Länsförsäkringar tomorrow. Caspar is snoring on my feet as I write this, so that's the end of today.

I'm not really sure how to start this, so I'll just lay it out. My name is Ben Whitlock, I'm 34, and I live in Leeds, just off Harrogate Road at 18 Chapeltown Gardens, LS7 3QP. I've been at Brightwater Logistics for six years, mostly on the night shift, and for the last few months I've been struggling to sleep at all. I lie awake until four or five in the morning, then drag myself in and can barely string a sentence together by lunch.

The worst part is that it's affecting my relationship. My partner, Ellie, has started sleeping in the spare room because I toss and turn so much, and last week she said she's worried I'm not telling her what's really going on. She's right. I've been posting late-night rants on my account, @benwhit_nights, and I've started to feel like I'm more honest with strangers online than with the people who love me. I know that's a bad sign.

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for Gwen Holloway, who worked under my direction as shift supervisor at Brightwater Dental Group in Columbus, Ohio, from March 2019 until December 14, 2023. My name is Thomas Reinholt Ashby, and I served as the practice operations manager for the full length of her tenure. I have supervised a great many staff over the years, and very few have combined reliability with genuine warmth the way Gwen does.

Gwen joined us as a front-desk coordinator and within a year had taken on responsibility for scheduling across three chairs. Patients often asked for her by name. She has a rare ability to calm an anxious caller within the first thirty seconds, and she handled insurance verification with a precision that saved our billing team countless hours. When our software migration in the fall of 2022 threatened to disrupt appointments for two full weeks, Gwen built a manual backup process, trained four colleagues on it in a single afternoon, and kept our patient wait times nearly unchanged.

Beyond her professional skills, Gwen is the kind of colleague people trust. Several of our hygienists still refer to her as Gwennie, a name she tolerates with good humour, and that same easygoing nature makes her a natural mentor. She regularly covered for others during illness and never once made a shift feel like a favour she expected back. When a new hire struggled in her first month, it was Gwen who sat with her during lunch, reviewed her questions, and quietly made sure she felt welcome.

For verification of her employment, our records list her as employee number 4471 and her identification on file was a U.S. passport, number 548207193, which she provided during onboarding. Please feel free to contact me directly at thomas.ashby@brightwaterdental.com or through the practice at (614) 555-0182.

I recommend Gwen Holloway without reservation. She will bring the same care, competence and steadiness to any team fortunate enough to hire her, and I would be pleased to work with her again.

Sincerely,

Thomas Reinholt Ashby
Practice Operations Manager
Brightwater Dental Group

My name is Shira Levi, and I was lucky enough to be Sagi's older sister for thirty-four years. Most of you knew him as the man who ran the early Saturday group at Kafe Hadar on Dizengoff, who could talk a stranger into a second espresso and a long conversation about football. Some of you knew him from Maccabi Tel Aviv's fan chats, where he went by SagiTheSpur on Instagram, and where he once argued with me for three days straight about whether a bagel counts as bread. He was loud, he was generous, and he never once forgot a birthday.

Sagi worked for nearly a decade at Tahal Software in Herzliya, first as a junior tester and later leading the team that rebuilt their scheduling platform. He used to say the job taught him patience, but I think the truth is he simply loved solving problems that other people had given up on. He would come home from the office, eat standing up in the kitchen, and then spend another two hours helping a neighbour's kid with physics. That was Sagi. He never kept a good thing to himself.

On the morning of December 14th, he went for his usual run along the Yarkon, and he waved at the old man who sells newspapers by the bridge, the same way he did every day. I want that to be the last thing we remember about him: a wave, a smile, and someone who always made room for everyone else. We will miss you more than words can hold, Sagi. Yehi zichro baruch.

My mother, Rivka Ben-Ami, lives in Ramat Gan, and I had already told her that I would bring the documents for her birthday on March 16th, so I checked the folder where those papers are normally kept and found it missing.

When I looked around the flat further, I could not find Pippin, my grey tabby, who is almost seven years old and usually greets people at the door. Zo, as we call him at home, has been missing since that evening and I am very worried, as he has never stayed out overnight before. I'll admit I nearly didn't book the guesthouse in Dingle after the email came through with the wrong postcode, but Victoria Keane, who runs the place with her brother, was patient with me on the phone and sorted it out in minutes. My name is Vanessa Doyle, and I'm writing this from the back room at 14 Strand Road, Dingle, Co. Kerry, which has the best view of the harbour I've had on any trip so far. If you want to ring ahead, the number is 066 915 2287, though Victoria mostly answers messages on Instagram under @vickeane_dingle, where she posts photos of the morning fishing boats coming in.

I'm originally from Ennis, so the drive down the Wild Atlantic Way felt like coming home in a strange, rewritten way. Victoria recommended I leave early on the 14th of September, before the coaches arrived, and she was right: I had the cliffs at Slea Head almost to myself, with only a few sheep and a very confident robin for company. Lunch was a bowl of chowder at a pub on the pier, and the woman serving it asked where I'd come from before I'd even sat down, which is the kind of welcome you only get in small towns.

If you go in September, pack a proper waterproof, because the weather changes three times before lunch, and bring a notebook for the little things Victoria tells you over breakfast. Dingle is quiet by then, the hikes are clear, and the pints taste better when the evenings start to cool. I already have the next trip planned for the end of the month.

Okay, so you asked how I ended up in that mess with the landlord in Valencia, and I think I finally have the energy to tell it. My name is Pablo Ferrer, I'm thirty-four, and back in April I was supposed to be moving out of the flat on Calle de Sueca by the 12th. Instead, I spent the whole week chasing a deposit that Mr. Navarro swore he'd already sent. I kept emailing him from pablo.ferrer88@gmail.com, copying in the agency, and getting nothing but silence and a single "we'll see".

What really got me was the morning of April 9th, when I sat in the little café near Ruzafa with my laptop and a cortado, rereading every message like a detective. Pablo, my brother-in-law, kept telling me to just let it go, but I'm stubborn, you know that. I'd already booked the removal van for the 14th, so there was no room to be patient. I actually cried a bit into my coffee, which was embarrassing, and the waiter pretended not to notice.

In the end the money turned up on the 13th, a day early, thanks to a single phone call from the agency's office manager, Lucía, who was far more helpful than anyone else in the whole saga. I still think about how close it came to going badly. Anyway, I'm buying the drinks next time, and you're not allowed to laugh at the cortado incident.

input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Paloma, and I've had the honour of being Marisol's older sister for thirty-one years now, which means I have also been her unpaid editor, her driver, and occasionally her alarm clock. Tonight I get to be the one who talks, and I have been practising this speech in the car for a week, mostly in the traffic around Colonia Roma, so if I sound a little rushed, blame the Insurgentes at rush hour.

Marisol has always been the person who notices things. When we were kids in Coyoacán, she was the one who saw the stray dog waiting outside the bakery every morning and quietly started leaving bread for it, long before anyone else thought to. That is Marisol. She sees the small thing that needs doing and she does it, without a speech and without wanting any credit. So when she told me that Gabriel had spent three months quietly learning the names of every street vendor on his block, I was not surprised at all. I was just relieved she had finally found someone who pays that kind of attention too.

Gabriel, I want to say something to you directly. You came into our family at a moment when my mother was still getting used to the idea that her youngest daughter would be living in another neighbourhood. You never tried to take anyone's place. Instead you asked my mother for her tamale recipe, got it wrong twice, and asked again. Your brother Mateo told me you once drove four hours to help a friend move a sofa, and then complained the whole way back that the sofa was ugly. That, I think, is a good sign.

To Marisol and Gabriel, may your life together be full of ordinary Tuesdays that turn out to be better than you planned. And if either of you ever needs me, you know my number is 55 4821 9073, though I would ask that you call during daylight hours. Please raise your glasses. Salud to the two of you.

input:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for Victoria Lindqvist, who worked under my supervision as a senior nurse coordinator at Mercy Lakeside Hospital from March 2019 until she accepted a position elsewhere in late January of this year. My name is Gregory Whitfield, and I served as the Director of Nursing for the medical-surgical division for nearly nine years. In that time I came to know Victoria as one of the most capable and steady clinicians on our floor.

Victoria joined us after completing her Bachelor of Science in Nursing at the University of Minnesota Duluth, and she quickly distinguished herself. During her first year she volunteered to lead our discharge planning initiative, which had been struggling with long delays and missed follow-up appointments. Within six months, Victoria had redesigned the workflow, trained eleven staff members on the new process, and reduced average discharge delays by more than a third. She approached the work with patience and a clear sense of accountability that I rarely see in people with less experience.

What I valued most about Victoria, however, was her character under pressure. During the winter surge in January of last year, when our census ran well above capacity and several colleagues were out sick, she never once lost her composure. She stayed late to cover gaps, mentored newer nurses through difficult admissions, and made sure that patients and families felt heard even when conditions were chaotic. Several families wrote to our administration specifically to praise her compassion, and I have kept those letters in my personal file.

Victoria is also a dependable collaborator. She worked closely with physicians, pharmacists, social workers, and our respiratory therapy team, and she was known for communicating clearly and directly. When disagreements arose, she addressed them professionally and focused on what was best for the patient. Her reputation across the hospital reflected this, and she was frequently asked to represent our unit on interdisciplinary committees.

I recommend Victoria without reservation for any clinical leadership role in which she would be responsible for a team and for patient outcomes. Should you require further information, you may reach me at gwhitfield@mercylakesidehealth.org, or contact our human resources office, referencing her employee file. Thank you for considering her application.

Sincerely,

Gregory Whitfield
Director of Nursing, Medical-Surgical Division
Mercy Lakeside Hospital
National ID on file: 482913067
